Christened the “Temu Range Rover” online, a nod to the cheap goods available on the Chinese online marketplace and the luxury 4X4 made by Jaguar Land Rover that it resembles, its success showed British drivers’ new-found taste for cut-price Chinese cars.
Overall, 23 per cent of new cars bought in Britain last month were Chinese models, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, with several electric and hybrid models ranking highly.

Ukraine will stop hitting refineries if Russia halts energy attacks, Zelenskiy says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ukraine will stop hitting refineries if Russia halts energy attacks, Zelenskiy says
KYIV, Oct 11 - Ukraine is ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceases its own strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Sunday, after US President Donald Trump demanded that Kyiv unilaterally stop its strikes.
On Saturday, Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for raising US diesel prices and said Zelenskiy had "better damn well stop", adding that Ukraine should replace him as leader because he had missed several opportunities to strike a deal with Moscow.
The steep rise in global diesel prices, which followed the outbreak of the Iran war in February, has become a political liability for Trump's Republican Party ahead of next month's midterm elections, when opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress.
Zelenskiy on Sunday repeated Ukraine's long-standing position that it was willing to halt attacks on Russian refineries only as part of a mutual de-escalation of the conflict, which would require Moscow to cease its own strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure.
Any such deal would need to come with "real guarantees", Zelenskiy said.
"The real cause of the war in Europe is Russia and Russia alone," Zelenskiy said, without alluding specifically to Trump's remarks. "It's possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so."
On Saturday, Zelenskiy responded angrily to Trump's announcement of a diesel supply deal with Russia, which he said would embolden Moscow's attacks on Ukraine.
Analysts said Trump's agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices, with the volumes still much lower than what Russia usually exports when its refineries are not under attack.
The diesel deal was also criticized by US lawmakers, including one of Trump's fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions, not lift them.
On the streets of Kyiv, several residents expressed anger at Trump's suggestion that Ukraine should find a new leader willing to make a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"No one has the right to tell us what to do, especially since elections cannot be held during wartime," said Sabina, a 40-year-old primary school teacher, referring to Ukraine's prohibition on elections under martial law` for security reasons.
"In my view, it is a betrayal by our partners," she said, describing Trump's remarks.
Zelenskiy said he would continue discussions with European leaders on Sunday, and there were daily conversations around additional air defence packages, including ammunition for combat aircraft that are used to down Russia's jet-powered drones.
On Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha is due to participate in a European Union Foreign Affairs Council meeting that is expected to discuss increasing sanctions pressure on Russia and advancing negotiations on Ukraine’s EU accession. REUTERS

In a statement, the army’s Taiz Military Axis said airstrikes targeted Houthi positions, gatherings and vehicles at al-Maqrami, al-Jaasha and al-Sallal hills east of Taiz city, as well as Hisn al-Mukhaf and the Bala’an area on the Aqrouz front in the south of the province.

Polish police detain 76 following school stabbings
Polish police said on Saturday they had checked nearly 50,000 educational facilities nationwide, detaining 76 people, after two school stabbings, including one fatal, sent shockwaves across the country.
"Police operations are ongoing throughout Poland, aimed at ensuring the safety of children, youth, and all staff at educational institutions," police wrote on X.
By 6am local time, officers had logged 231 incidents involving suspected crimes or offences, the force added, noting that work was still underway to clarify them.
The checks came on the heels of two school stabbings and one foiled attack in Poland's central Mazowieckie province this week, forcing law enforcement to monitor schools and kindergartens across the region.
On Thursday, a 37-year-old caretaker died after being stabbed by a 15-year-old former pupil at a school in Leszczydol-Nowiny. The teenager also attacked two other people at the facility.
A 19-year-old injured nine people in a knife attack at a school in Ostroleka on Wednesday, authorities reported.
In Sierpc, a 17-year-old who made threats online to "do something bad at school" was detained on Wednesday. Officers recovered two knives from his belongings and found search history related to mass attacks on his mobile phone. He was charged on Thursday with making criminal threats and placed in pre-trial detention.
On Friday, 24,000 police officers monitored educational facilities and surrounding areas nationwide, while internal security agents and the Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime (CBZC) in cooperation with the Internal Security Agency (ABW) monitored online security, police added.
Police patrols will return to schools on Monday, with officers remaining in direct contact with school staff, Iwona Kijowska of the National Police Headquarters told PAP later on Saturday, adding that the law enforcement would remain on site for as long as necessary. (PAP)

Could Tutankhamun's tomb hold clues to a mysterious Egyptian queen?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:56:05 UTC
19:56:05 KST

A growing body of research is generating renewed interest in potential hidden spaces beyond the decorated walls of Tutankhamun’s burial chamber in Egypt.
Some researchers have raised the possibility that these concealed chambers—if they exist—could contain the burial place of Nefertiti, Tutankhamun’s stepmother and mother-in-law. Nefertiti was made famous by a remarkable painted bust of her head found in Tell-el Amarna, Egypt, in 1912.
The hypothesis about hidden rooms was first proposed more than a decade ago. A key advocate of the idea, archaeologist Nicholas Reeves, mentions clues that he believes may point to Nefertiti’s burial being nearby. These include “hidden” hieroglyphics that were painted over on the north wall of Tutankhamun’s tomb.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
A team has now published a review of archaeological and geophysical investigations at Tutankhamun’s burial chamber (also known as KV62), including results from a survey carried out between 2023 and 2024.
Lead researcher Mamdouh Eldamaty told Nature that the results were suggestive of concealed structures beyond KV62. A decision on whether to carefully drill through the north wall and deploy miniature cameras could be made in coming months. However, other experts are cautious about the findings.
There is a delicate balance between speculation, hypothesis testing, and discovery. Some of the greatest scientific and archaeological breakthroughs have come from researchers willing to challenge paradigms and pursue ideas drawn from vague and improbable historical clues.
However, limited evidence combined with great expectations can encourage conclusions that run ahead of the data. The possibility of hidden chambers beyond the tomb of Tutankhamun sits precisely at this intersection.
Yet the distinction between evidence for unexplored spaces and evidence for the burial of Nefertiti remains substantial. The challenge is not to decide what we hope to find, but to evaluate objectively what the available evidence does, and does not, support.
The media readily gravitates toward the most spectacular conclusions. The search for Cleopatra’s tomb at Taposiris Magna provides a cautionary example.
Previously looted tombs, artifacts, and even the renewed investigation of a subterranean hydraulic tunnel were frequently presented as indications that the discovery of Cleopatra’s tomb was imminent. Yet the existence of an aqueduct consistent with Hellenistic (Greek-influenced) urban infrastructure does not constitute evidence for a royal burial.
A more measured approach can be seen in the work of Greek archaeologist Calliope Papakosta in Alexandria, Egypt. During a visit to her excavations, she showed me evidence suggesting that Alexander the Great’s tomb might lie nearby. The most compelling object was a marble statue of a young warrior that she argued, and I agree, may depict Alexander.
The style was consistent with the school of Lysippus, Alexander’s court sculptor. Unfortunately, the sculpture had been discarded within a Roman fill layer and thus removed from its original context.
Papakosta recognized both the promise and limitations of the evidence. While hopeful that her work might illuminate the fate of Alexander’s tomb, she consistently framed her discoveries within the bounds of what the data demonstrated.
The debate surrounding Tutankhamun’s tomb raises similar issues. The burial site is unusually small for one hosting a pharaoh, and Nicholas Reeves has argued that it represents only the outer portion of a larger Amarna-period (roughly 1350–1325 BC) royal burial complex.
The abnormality of the tomb is widely accepted and it has been presumed to be a small private tomb that was hastily adapted for the king because of his death at a young age.
A suggestion of door seams in the decorated north wall of the burial chamber stimulated the extended tomb complex theory, but damaging the wall to probe it would be out of the question. Progress would therefore depend upon geophysics providing a means to peer through the wall without damaging it.
The first investigations employed relatively low-frequency Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR), principally in the 400-900 megahertz (MHz) range. Such frequencies provide greater penetration into the surrounding limestone than higher-frequency radar. But this comes at the expense of spatial resolution. Later investigations expanded this range and included frequencies as high as 3 gigahertz (GHz).
My own inclination would have been to place particular emphasis on the highest-frequency radar antennae (the parts of the GPR system that transmit and receive electromagnetic pulses) because resolving whether the north wall contains evidence of a door seam is an important first step to answering other key questions.
High-frequency systems offer less penetration but are generally better suited to detecting subtle structural discontinuities immediately behind the wall surface.
More recent investigations added microgravity surveys made from above the theorized complex. These measure minute variations in the Earth’s gravitational field caused by differences in density below ground. Higher-frequency GPR has also now been added to the team’s toolkit.
This was a sensible evolution of the research strategy. The problem was, to protect the wall paintings, the GPR antennae could not be placed directly against the decorated surfaces.
The resulting air gap weakened coupling between the antenna and the wall, reducing signal quality and complicating interpretation. For GPR, the farther the antenna is from the surface, the more difficult it becomes to resolve subtle architectural features.
Microgravity surveys do not suffer from this limitation. They are capable of identifying anomalies within the limestone below the sensor. The challenge facing both types of investigation is that they have not produced unambiguous evidence for a large open chamber immediately beyond the wall.
To account for this, proponents of the hidden chamber hypothesis have suggested that any passageways may have been deliberately backfilled with rubble, obscuring the void signatures that investigators originally expected to detect. This is plausible and merits further testing, but it remains an interpretation, not fact.
Some investigators have argued that the currently available geophysical evidence does not demonstrate the presence of hidden chambers.
This has led to the next logical step in the scientific process: direct testing. The current proposal to drill a small borehole and deploy miniature cameras into one of the identified anomalies has the potential to move the discussion from inference to observation.
Whatever the outcome, the investigations undertaken by Eldamaty and colleagues represent the most comprehensive scientific assessment of the question to date.
Currently, the hidden chamber theory remains exactly what a good scientific hypothesis should be: intriguing, testable, and worthy of investigation. What it is not, at least yet, is a discovery.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

Poland on alert amid possible attack on PM, defense minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:48:00 UTC
19:48:00 KST

Poland on alert amid possible attack on PM, defense minister
October 11, 2026
Authorities in Poland were meeting on Sunday to discuss a potential assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, Interior Ministry spokesperson Karolina Galecka said.
The emergency meeting at the Internal Security Agency's (ABW) Counter-Terrorism Center was convened after police received information about a possible attack, Galecka said in a post on X.
While the nature of the apparent threat was not immediately clear, the meeting comes as Polish authorities are on high alert after a wave of violent attacks at schools in the country this week.
Poland, which borders Ukraine, has also been facing growing security threats from hybrid attacks by Russia in recent months.
What do we know about the school attacks in Poland?
Poland is reeling from three knife attacks at schools in just four days this week, which have left at least one person dead and injured many others, including children.
The first incident was on Wednesday, when a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in the central Mazovian province injured nine people when he attacked his fellow students and teachers with a sharp object.
A day later, a 15-year-old killed a school caretaker and injured two others at his former school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, also in the same province. Tusk said the suspect had worn a camera mounted to his helmet to film the attack.
On Saturday, a 21-year-old woman attacked an adult education school in Warsaw, wounding three other women.
Polish police have detained 117 people across the country for carrying knives or dangerous weapons, as well as for threatening to attack schools or students. Police checked 64,000 schools, most of them in central Mazovian province.
Police said Friday that cybercrime investigators have found no evidence that a social media challenge is fueling the wave of youth violence, or that the attacks were coordinated.
What did Tusk say about the attacks?
On Sunday morning, Donald Tusk said the attacks were "spontaneous actions" that were fueled by rising "glorification of violence" online.
"We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said during the government crisis meeting.
"In the past years and months, we have noted — globally and in Poland — a rise in the fascination with violence," Tusk continued.
The prime minister blamed "nihilistic violence" for the wave of attacks, rather than a specific political ideology. However, he did acknowledge that "some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment."
Tusk added that authorities have observed an increase in online searches for Nazi or far-right content and for "mass killers who have become idols online."
The prime minister pointed to a "civilizational phenomenon" of children becoming more exposed to violence online through video games or crime stories.
Tusk added that police checks would continue at schools across the country next week to make sure children who have been exposed to these stories of knife attacks do not "get stupid and unsafe thoughts" of perpetrating copycat attacks.

US police criticise Anthropic after Claude AI submits false information about an unsolved murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:45:42 UTC
19:45:42 KST

The US police called the delay in detecting and reporting the incident “unacceptable”, but said there was no indication of unauthorised access to their systems or compromised data.
Anthropic’s artificial intelligence (AI) model Claude submitted a false tip about an unsolved homicide to a police website during testing, the company and US authorities said.
The incident adds to concerns about AI systems taking unintended actions as they gain the ability to interact with websites and carry out tasks.
The false tip was submitted on 18 July through a website collecting information about unsolved killings, according to a statement from police in the US city of Philadelphia.
Anthropic said Claude Haiku 4.5, an older model in its Claude range, was carrying out example tasks on randomly selected webpages when it encountered the site. It submitted fabricated information suggesting it had seen someone near the scene, leaving the name and contact fields blank.
Philadelphia Police said Anthropic discovered the incident on 28 September but did not notify the department until 7 October. Following a briefing the next day, officers located the submission and confirmed it had been marked as spam and never forwarded to investigators.
“Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the department said in the statement.
“Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement.”
The US police called the delay in detecting and reporting the incident “unacceptable”, but said there was no indication of unauthorised access to their systems or compromised data.
In a report published on Friday, Anthropic outlined other cases of AI models submitting real government forms instead of practice copies, or submitting forms they had been told not to submit.
Claude also exploited a flaw in a university server to run a calculation and accessed government data without paying the required fee, according to the same report.
Anthropic described most of the behaviour as “persistence”, with models working around restrictions instead of stopping. It said it was modifying training and suspending live internet access for all internal evaluations until safeguards proved reliable.
The company said it had briefed the White House and notified the US government agencies involved.
Growing concern over AI agents
The incidents come amid wider concern about AI agents, systems that can take a sequence of actions to complete tasks, and whether developers can reliably control them.
In July, OpenAI disclosed that its AI models had escaped a controlled testing environment and hacked into the systems of Hugging Face, a platform for sharing AI models and datasets.
Meanwhile, Australian authorities revealed in September that an OpenAI model had also accessed restricted files on a government health statistics website during testing in June.
Such incidents fuelled calls in September from leaders of major AI companies for stronger regulation and international oversight, amid warnings that increasingly powerful systems could escape human control.

Yemen fighting expands as Houthis attack Saudi airport: What to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:45:15 UTC
19:45:15 KST

Yemen fighting expands as Houthis attack Saudi airport: What to know
Saudi coalition blames Houthi group for the missile strike that struck King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia has vowed to “firmly” retaliate against an attack on Riyadh’s international airport, which left at least 12 people dead, with US President Donald Trump calling the attack “terrible”.
The Saudi-led military coalition on Sunday blamed Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi group for Saturday’s attack on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a “full-fledged war crime”. The Houthis have not claimed responsibility for the latest strike.
However, on Sunday, the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, renewed their warning to airlines, airport workers, and travellers against using Saudi airports, saying the warning should be taken seriously and that the kingdom “bore responsibility for failed interceptions”.
The attack comes amid escalating fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces following the collapse of a UN-brokered ceasefire largely in place since 2022.
The fighting has raised fears of a wider regional confrontation, with the US President suggesting Washington could join Saudi military operations against the Houthis.
Dania Thafer, executive director at the Gulf International Forum, said Saudi Arabia will likely hit back at the Houthis “pretty hard”.
“I still think that the Saudis probably want de-escalation. They don’t want long-term escalation but the Houthis are making it very difficult by not only being a threat to Saudi national security but also a threat to international maritime security,” Thafer said. “So this battle is much bigger than just a tit-for-tat.”
Here is what you need to know:
What happened at Riyadh’s international airport?
According to Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority, the attack struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday. It wounded at least 309 others, some of them critically.
The dead included four Saudi nationals, two Bangladeshis and one citizen each from the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. It was the deadliest attack on the Kingdom in more than a decade.
“The cowardly terrorist attack by the Terrorist Houthi Militia … which resulted in deaths and injuries among civilian passengers and airport staff, constitutes a full-fledged war crime,” coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Malki said in a statement on X.
The Houthis, who have yet to take responsibility for the attack, said on Sunday that they “renew their warning to all aviation companies, experts, employees, workers, and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, because they are exposed to targeting and are a theatre of operations by our forces”.
“They urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions,” military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post on X.
Airport operations were suspended, with flights cancelled or diverted. Schools across Riyadh were also ordered to switch to remote learning for a week following the attack.
The attacks have disrupted international flights, with several airlines suspending services to Saudi destinations. Later on Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition said a projectile had fallen near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam in the country’s east.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, said the Iran-backed group was retaliating by attacking what it called Saudi Arabia’s “most precious assets”, which are Aramco oil facilities and the airport in Riyadh.
“Although Saudi Arabia has said it will retaliate, let’s not forget that it’s carried out many air strikes across Yemen, and the Yemeni group is still able to launch ballistic missiles and drones towards Saudi Arabia,” he added.
What other areas have the Houthis targeted?
The Iran-aligned Houthis have launched a series of missile and drone attacks targeting airports, military installations and oil facilities across Saudi Arabia, including areas near the border with Yemen.
On Monday, attacks on King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Airport in the southwestern city of Jazan and Najran international airport wounded three people and caused material damage, according to Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority.
On Tuesday, attacks on Abha airport and Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport killed three people and wounded 36 others, according to Saudi authorities.
The Houthis also claimed to have targeted an Aramco oil refinery in Rabigh, on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast, with missiles and drones, saying the attack caused a fire. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the claim.
The Houthis imposed a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia in July following the outbreak of the latest round of fighting.
Yasmeen Al Eryani, the executive director for knowledge production at Sanaa Center, said that the Houthis are trying to put “maximum pressure” on Saudi Arabia.
“But they’re also mobilising the internal front lines in a really major way, moving even away from the west coast battle into Taiz and more densely populated areas,” Eryani, from the think tank based in government-controlled Aden, told Al Jazeera.
“We could see further mobilisation, they have very high momentum. They will probably continue to capitalise on that momentum, internally,” she said, adding that “the [Houthi] cross-border attacks” will put pressure across the region.
Eryani added that the Houthis were “provoking” Saudi Arabia, the US and regional states, which could potentially join in the conflict.
What is the latest in the fighting?
Houthi-affiliated media on Sunday reported an air strike targeting Naqil al-Zarbi in the Hayfan district of Yemen’s Taiz governorate in southwestern Yemen, as well as a missile attack on the Sahar district in the northern province of Saada.
Forces belonging to Yemen’s internationally-recognised government also released footage purportedly showing the downing of a Houthi drone over Mount Sabr in Taiz.
Meanwhile, Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said early on Sunday that forces intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards al-Kharj province, as well as a drone in the kingdom’s Eastern Province.
On Saturday, Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, the spokesman for Yemeni government forces, said at least 1,150 Houthis were killed in almost 2,000 targeted operations across the country since the internationally-recognised government’s counteroffensive began.
He said the army had destroyed Houthi ammunition dumps and at least 180 combat, transport and supply vehicles operated by the Houthis, adding that ground forces “continued to advance their assault”.
Al Jazeera was not able to independently verify the competing claims.
Fighting has intensified across several fronts in Yemen, with Saudi-backed government forces launching the Dawn of Yemen offensive on October 4 to recapture Houthi-held territory, including the port city of Mocha and the island of Mayun.
While the internationally-recognised government’s forces said they had retaken Mocha and the Dhubab district near the strait, the Houthis have disputed the claims.
The Houthis have also tightened their siege of Taiz after capturing territory south of the city earlier this month, including al-Turbah. Taiz has been one of the most heavily contested cities in the war.
Fighting has also spread to Marib and al-Jawf, two governorates east of Sanaa, where government forces have reported advances against Houthi positions.
What has been the international response to the Houthi attack on the airport?
The attack has drawn condemnation from the US and the United Nations, while several foreign governments have warned their citizens to avoid the airport.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed that an American was among those killed and condemned the attacks.
“These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now,” Rubio said.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also condemned Saturday’s strike, stressing that attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure violate international law.
The US, Canada, Germany and several other countries issued travel warnings, while some diplomatic missions restricted staff movements through the airport.
Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif described the attack as “heinous” and reaffirmed Islamabad’s commitment to Saudi security.
On October 5, Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under a mutual defence pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by Yemen’s Houthis. This came weeks after the three countries signed the Mecca Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement.
Will the US join Saudi strikes against Yemen’s Houthis?
Trump has left open the possibility of US military involvement but has not announced a decision.
“We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump told reporters on Saturday.
The US President also said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, describing the attack as “not acceptable”.
According to US media reports, Washington has already provided intelligence sharing, target identification and planning assistance for the latest Saudi-backed offensive.
When the Saudi-led coalition intervened in the civil war in March 2015, Washington provided intelligence, logistical assistance and weapons to support its campaign against the Houthis, but did not directly participate in the coalition’s air strikes.
But in 2021, the Biden administration ended support for the Saudi-led offensive in Yemen, citing the humanitarian crisis. More than 100,000 Yemenis were killed and millions were displaced at the time.

Pope Leo says will undergo surgery for small growth on lung
VATICAN CITY, Oct 11 - Pope Leo said on Sunday that doctors had detected a small growth on his lung during a recent health check and he would be undergoing surgery this week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff's tenure.
Leo told pilgrims in St. Peter's Square for his weekly Sunday prayer that the growth was "well-contained" and had been spotted early.
"Recently, during some medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung," said the pontiff. "It was detected at a very early stage and is well contained."
"The doctors believe it is advisable to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it," he said. "The operation is already scheduled for the next few days."
A nodule on the lung is a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors.
Leo, elected pope by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to previously have had health issues.
The late Pope Francis, Leo's predecessor, died at age 88 and was increasingly frail in his later years.
The Vatican press office said Leo's recovery from surgery was expected to take about a week. It did not immediately provide further details about the pope's health.
Leo keeps a busy schedule and is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6-17.
Before mentioning his health issue in his address on Sunday, the pope referred to the trip, thanking Catholics for their prayers "for the pastoral visit I will undertake." REUTERS

The European Commission is finalizing proposals to tighten visa regulations for Russian citizens visiting the EU as tourists, aiming to reinforce the bloc’s defenses against state-sponsored sabotage and hybrid threats, Politico reported.
Citing EU officials, the report stated that the EU executive plans to present the legislative package in January, following pressure from a coalition of member states including Sweden, Poland, and Estonia.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The proposed measures seek to restrict the issuance of Schengen visas to Russian nationals and establish targeted entry bans against former combatants who served in the Russian armed forces during the war against Ukraine.
Approximately 478,000 Schengen tourist visas were issued to Russian citizens last year, a substantial portion of which were multiple-entry permits that allow unrestricted travel across the 29-nation border-free zone.
European security officials argue that maintaining open travel channels provides hostile intelligence services with operational conduits to execute surveillance, arson, and infrastructure sabotage across the continent. Swedish Justice Minister Gunnar Strömmer warned that current border protocols leave member states exposed to foreign infiltration.
“It’s obvious I think for everyone that we have vulnerabilities in our system that can be used by our enemies,” Strömmer told Politico.
US Lawmakers Draft Bill to Block Russian Oil Purchases
“As far as I understand things, the Commission is preparing a proposal that, according to what I have heard, should be launched in January next year. From a Swedish point of view, we would love to see it even earlier.”
Strömmer welcomed growing support among EU capitals for a stricter visa framework, noting that cross-border travel rules must align with contemporary security realities.
Security risks and ex-combatant entry ban
Frontline European governments plan to elevate the visa debate during a meeting of the EU Foreign Affairs Council on Monday, Oct. 12, where ministers will also consider prospective travel restrictions on accredited Russian diplomats moving between member states.
Estonia has advocated for a comprehensive, EU-wide entry ban specifically targeting former Russian military personnel. Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna estimated that approximately 650,000 former combatants could eventually seek entry into Europe, warning that without unified screening protocols, individual national bans would prove insufficient to safeguard the Schengen area.
“I believe that a significant number of these former combatants, supported by Russian intelligence services, will come to Europe,” Tsahkna told Politico.
“They will take control of our organized crime, be well-armed, and be supported by Russia to carry out terrorist attacks or assaults on our society. So this is very serious.”
European Commissioner for Migration Magnus Brunner noted that while Russian visa issuances initially fell following the February 2022 full-scale invasion, travel volumes have plateaued rather than continuing to decline.
“The numbers are no longer decreasing,” Brunner stated, urging national immigration authorities to exercise greater discretion. “We call on member states to do a better job and issue fewer visas to Russian citizens. You never know who these tourists really are.”
Sanctions friction
The initiative to restrict Russian traveler access arrives amid broader debates within the EU regarding economic pressure and diplomatic countermeasures directed at Moscow.
In late September, EU member states agreed to extend sanctions against more than 3,000 Russian individuals and entities for a multi-year term of three years, moving away from standard six-month or one-year rollover intervals.
However, that agreement followed contentious negotiations during which ambassadors approved the removal of Russian tycoons Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov from the sanctions registry following legal challenges and diplomatic requests from several member states.
The delistings drew criticism from Kyiv.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned that easing individual restrictions sends counterproductive signals to the Kremlin during an expanding campaign of Russian hybrid actions against European transport networks, industrial plants, and communications infrastructure.
European security services have linked Russian military and intelligence agencies to multiple kinetic sabotage incidents across EU territory over recent months, including arson attacks on logistics hubs in Poland and the United Kingdom, GPS jamming affecting civil aviation over the Baltic Sea, and drone surveillance of critical defense installations.

Fear and uncertainty for civilians as Yemen’s capital comes under attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:42:35 UTC
19:42:35 KST

Fear and uncertainty for civilians as Yemen’s capital comes under attack
Sanaa has come under intense bombing since the Yemeni government announced a campaign to take the capital from the Houthis.
Sanaa, Yemen – At midnight on Tuesday, air strikes rattled the Yemeni capital Sanaa, a city that has been mostly spared bombing since a truce was announced between the internationally recognised government and the Houthis in 2023.
The head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, Rashid al-Alimi, had recently announced a new military offensive was being launched, named Operation Dawn of Yemen, to take Sanaa from the Houthis, who have held the city since September 2014.
Government ground forces remain hundreds of miles away from the capital and embroiled in fighting with the Houthis on Yemen’s west coast and around Taiz.
This means attacks on Houthi positions in Sanaa must come from the air, but the air campaign has caused civilian casualties.
An air strike on Monday hit a location in the Sa’wan area of Sanaa governorate, killing a child and wounding seven other civilians.
The Yemeni government has pledged to continue its attacks until it achieves its objectives, notably the recapture of Sanaa. Regardless of the political opinions of Yemenis in the capital, most fear their city, far from the front lines, will become a war zone once again.
Decisive Storm
Strong memories remain of the Saudi-led coalition’s Operation Decisive Storm, launched against the Houthis in March 2015, which saw hundreds of civilians in Sanaa killed in air strikes.
Since the start of the new Yemeni government offensive, dozens of strikes have hit the capital, including an attack on Sanaa’s international airport, which killed two workers. Both operations were aimed at Houthi sites.
Ghamadan Abood, a 30-year-old courier and Sanaa resident, said the new wave of attacks on the city has heightened fear among residents.
“When I learned about the new operation on Sunday, my feeling of security shrank,” he told Al Jazeera. “At any time and anywhere, air strikes may hit, and civilians could become the next casualties.”
On Monday, Abood was travelling on his bike when air strikes hit Sa’wan, just two kilometres from where he was. With Houthi military facilities believed to be positioned in the city, and the government sometimes hitting residential areas, the bombing highlights the vulnerability of civilians in Sanaa.
“The strikes could be aimed at missile launch pads, military equipment or facilities, but some of these facilities could be near neighbourhoods, farms or roads. So, innocent people could be killed, injured or left terrified,” Abood said.
Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government, has also come under repeated missile attacks by the Houthis, including two strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the latest on Saturday killing 12 people.
On Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said Sanaa, Saada, and Amran were among the primary sources of Houthi missile threats. The coalition has noted that ongoing military operations are aimed at curbing the group’s ability to launch missiles on the kingdom.
Fear of displacement
More than 200,000 people have been displaced since fighting in Yemen escalated in recent weeks, according to the International Organization for Migration.
Most of those forced to leave their homes have come from Taiz governorate in southwestern Yemen, where the most intense ground fighting between government and Houthi forces has taken place.
Saleh Ayidh, a 50-year-old resident of Sanaa and father of five, fears the new air strikes will also force people from their homes in the north.
“Today, we see Sanaa as a safe place and distant from the front lines. For me, no place is safe in Yemen, particularly in the north, and war can spread anywhere,” he told Al Jazeera.
At the start of the Saudi-led coalition’s operation against the Houthis in March 2015, Ayidh’s family left the city for a home in the countryside. They lived there for six months, far from the assault on the Yemeni capital.
“Now we do not know what will happen to us. We will decide whether we need to leave the city if the air strikes keep intensifying,” Ayidh said. “Without safety, life is hard.”
Stocking up
The recent air strikes are widely viewed in Sanaa as a sign that war has returned to the capital, prompting residents to stock up on food and fuel.
When Operation Decisive Storm began in 2015, the cost of goods and fuel rose due to disruption to logistics and panic buying. The same trend is being seen again in Sanaa after the recent resumption of hostilities.
Grocery owner Nashwan, 24, has boosted his inventory of essentials such as rice, cheese, milk, biscuits, cooking oil and sugar, before they become too difficult to find.
He also stocked up on petrol, buying 100 litres to use for his minibus if a fuel crisis hits the capital.
“These commodities may become expensive in the coming days. If the war keeps escalating, buying them would cost me more,” Nashwan said. “I do not want to feel the impact of the war immediately.”
Any road closures or a decline in imports caused by the war and a Saudi naval siege on Houthi areas will present major challenges for civilians.
“Rising prices of food and fuel are a real worry for the entire population amid the war and will worsen the humanitarian situation in Yemen,” Wafiq Saleh, executive director of the Taiz Centre for Yemeni-Gulf Studies, told Al Jazeera.
Last week, the UN World Food Programme warned that three-quarters of families in parts of Yemen were going hungry.
There are fears an escalation of the fighting will lead to a more intense food crisis across Yemen, which the WFP has already described as “absolutely devastating”.
Yemen fighting
Despite the optimism of the internationally recognised government when announcing Operation Dawn of Yemen, few in Sanaa believe it has the ability to recapture the capital from the Houthis any time soon.
Raiman al-Hamdani, a London-based Yemen analyst, said government forces are big on paper, but remain scattered across multiple fronts, while soldiers are using outdated gear.
“They can hold their lines but can’t push the Houthis out of their mountain strongholds,” Raiman told Al Jazeera last week.
Fuad Ali, 40, a university graduate in Sanaa, said the Saudi-backed government has lost the public’s trust, particularly its claim that it could capture the capital after it suffered a series of embarrassing military defeats in recent weeks on the coast.
“The government has failed to seize the coastal Hodeidah province or Al-Jawf desert province. The fight there could be easier given the topography. How can it recapture the mountainous Sanaa?” Ali told Al Jazeera.
Operation Dawn of Yemen will bring more “destruction to the country’s facilities and increase civilian casualties”, he added.
Ali doubts the operation will return the government to Sanaa. But he also believes the government and Saudi-led coalition have learned their lessons from 2015, when huge civilian casualties from air raids drew international condemnation.
“I am still optimistic that Operation Dawn of Yemen will not damage Sanaa as Operation Decisive Storm did,” Ali said.

Archaeologists reveal huge stretch of ancient Lower Aqueduct into Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:39:47 UTC
19:39:47 KST

A 300-meter stretch of the Lower Aqueduct into Jerusalem has been revealed exactly where archaeologists thought it would be – about 5 kilometers south of Temple Mount, near Kibbutz Ramat Rachel. It was unearthed during works to build a new neighborhood, the Israel Antiquities Authority announced on Sunday.
Knowledge of the aqueduct was actually never lost since the structure remained in use for over 2,000 years, apparently since the Hasmonean period in the late second century to first century B.C.E. In fact it only fell out of favor about a century ago, when newfangled inventions such as electricity enabled better alternatives. But it was covered over by the debris and detritus of time; and archaeologists assessed where it was based on surveys starting in the 1970s, explains Benyamin Storchan, co-director of the IAA excavation together with Gil Freid and Rotem Cohen.
In addition, there aren't many options to route a constantly declining water conduit from the Gush Etzion settlement bloc about 12 km southwest, where this structure begins, to the Old City of Jerusalem. Hence even though this section of the aqueduct hadn't been located before – the archaeologists had an idea where it had to be, and it was.
Note that pieces of this aqueduct can be seen here and there along its route, all but hidden in the modern development. This time the plans for the new neighborhood take this ancient element into consideration and will work around and showcase it, Storchan says.
The winding road deterrent
We cannot be sure the aqueduct was used without cease from the Hasmonean, Herodian and/or Roman periods until the British Mandate. It is possible that usage stopped here and there, but there is clear historic evidence of use in the Byzantine and later periods. One example is an inscription in Arabic from the Mamluk period associated with its reconstruction. Moreover, come their time, the Ottomans would line the aqueduct with ceramic pipes.
The British, says Storchan, even thought of reinvigorating the conduit in their time using long metal pipelines but gave up, because in order to maintain its decline from the point of origin, the aqueduct winds around hills, which short ceramic tiles can do but long straight pipelines can't.
In the day, actually, there were two ancient aqueducts into Jerusalem, the Upper and Lower, and neither has been securely dated. It appears however that this Lower one was built first, Storchan says, based on the assessment that the upper one seems more structurally sophisticated. It also seems to follow a straighter path, he adds.
That said, the "unsophisticated" Lower Aqueduct seems to have lasted longer than the fancier Upper one, he adds.
The starting point for Jerusalem's water system was natural springs in Gush Etzion. Each feeds into a small water channel that in turn feeds into the so-called Solomon's Pools in Bethlehem, which is just a large manmade reservoir. Thus the two aqueducts begin at Solomon's Pools.
The pools are traditionally linked to King Solomon some 3,000 years ago based on the verse: "I made myself pools from which to water the forest of growing trees" – Ecclesiastes 2:6 – but it's a misnomer, Storchan says. This reservoir had nothing to do with the fabled king, but is instead apparently from the Hasmonean era, which lasted from 142 to 37 B.C.E.
So, from somebody's pools, the Lower Aqueduct runs through Bethlehem, looping around the Jerusalem hills and to the Armon Hanatziv neighborhood, passing beneath what is today the Abu Tor promenade where the ancients carved a tunnel through the mountain. A fine one, with shafts for ventilation and to remove quarrying debris. The path then proceeds looping around Hutzot Hayotzer, traverses the Guy Ben Hinnom valley, goes around Mount Zion and into the Old City, somewhere around the Dung Gate, to the Temple Mount.
One understands why the British decided to give up rebuilding this path using modern pipes.
This newly unveiled 300-meter stretch is the biggest found to date of this monumental structure, which runs 26 kilometers as it winds around the hills, the archaeologists say.
All in all, from its start, the aqueduct declines all of 40 to 30 meters in height, which was a tremendous feat of ancient planning, Storchan marvels. No later and more technically advanced civilizations changed a meter of the route, not the Byzantines nor the later Umayyads – it was good enough. "It wasn't as fancy as some of the aqueducts in Italy," he adds, but its engineering prowess was phenomenal.
Meanwhile, there is an academic debate about its dating. "The problem is that it was used for 2,000 years and each repair or subsequent phase of usage built on the old structure," he explains. To date it more precisely than pottery or coins can do – they can remain in circulation for decades or even longer – the archaeologists have to do a sort of reverse engineering, peeling off plaster layers. In short, this is in progress.
Sometime in the 20th century, archaeologists learned to date sites by changes in pottery styles; no reputable Israeli researcher would mistake a Roman cooking pot for a Byzantine vessel or an Umayyad creation. Plaster too changed over time, to a degree – it always needed lime, but in some eras it could be more pink, or more gray, Storchan explains. One Umayyad layer has small pebbles impressed into their plaster. That said, plaster isn't a date book. Another challenge with securely dating the aqueduct is that while its entire course had once been covered with stone slabs, those slabs are gone.
Things that never change
But two things were unchanging throughout its lifetime: the force of gravity, and theft.
Along the aqueduct in general, archaeologists have identified spots where the local farmers poked holes into the pipeline to steal the water, and we know this because they found the repaired holes, a lot of them.
"This was an official governmental structure, whether Hasmonean or Byzantine or whatever," Storchan points out.It wasn't a private project, it was a national one and that involved not only clever engineers but armed guards on patrol for villagers ruining the branch into which they were poking holes.
So we knew of the aqueduct and its route; now a large stretch has been found and what have we learned from it?
"Mainly that looking at it today, in many sections it looks like a terrace. The rear wall is covered with dirt while the front wall is exposed, like a step," Storchan says. "Excavating the back portion, we see that the sedimentology soil buildup was more gradual than thought – it hadn't been backfilled. The original Hasmonean construction of may have stood as a freestanding element. Through natural processes over 2,000 years it was covered by soil flow. It didn't seem to have bothered anyone that the backwall was becoming covered up," he added.
Augmenting the Gihon Spring and unreliable rain as a water source for Jerusalem, the Lower and Upper Aqueducts enabled the city to expand in the Hasmonean period, and would continue to provide water for the next 2,000 years.
"What's really cool about this is that we literally see a cross section of time in one element," Storchan sums up. Jerusalem archaeology can be a terrific mess, with layers upon layers and some of them mixed up, Roman ruins lying over Byzantine mosaics, for instance – horrible. It's partly due to destructions and partly due to repurposing. But in the aqueduct, you can see all the time periods in a single installation, one that brought water to the Temple Mount for ritual cleansing – plausibly at the very set of monumental mikvehs archaeologists revealed just last month.

The campaigns of the central government, be it Make in India or Vocal for Local, are benefiting Tamil Nadu as well."He said manufacturing growth had created direct and indirect employment for lakhs of young people across the country, with Tamil Nadu playing an important role."Due to the growth in manufacturing, lakhs of direct and indirect jobs have been created for youth in the country and Tamil Nadu has played an appreciable role in this growth..."PM Modi also stressed the importance of public transport in urban development. He said metro services had expanded to 25 cities over the past 12 years, with the network growing from 250 km in 2014 to 1,100 km in 2026."Urban development is a major priority for us in Tamil Nadu... and public transport plays a major role in it, as it enhances ease of living..."He added that the newly launched projects would make travel easier and support economic activity across the state.
Vijay seeks approval for metro projects, release of funds
Vijay thanked PM for inaugurating Phase II of the Chennai Metro Rail project. He said his government was working towards providing a corruption-free and inclusive administration.The chief minister said Tamil Nadu had set a target of becoming a $1.5 trillion economy by 2036. He urged the Centre to approve Phase III of the Chennai Metro and reconsider metro rail projects proposed for Coimbatore and Madurai.
Vijay also sought the Centre's support for an interstate metro rail project connecting Bommasamudra and Hosur.Among his other demands were the Godavari-Cauvery river-linking project, recognition of Tamil as an official language of the Madras High Court, and high-speed corridors between Chennai and Coimbatore, and Chennai and Kanyakumari.He also pressed for the release of pending funds under the Samagra Shiksha scheme.The projects launched by PM Modi cover highways, ports, railways and other infrastructure sectors. The Prime Minister said the investments would help improve transport, strengthen trade and generate employment in Tamil Nadu.

Ukrainian Drones Strike $50 Million Radar Used by Russia’s S-400 Air Defense Systems

Ukrainian Drones Strike $50 Million Radar Used by Russia’s S-400 Air Defense Systems
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian 96L6 radar station used by S-300 and S-400 air defense systems, targeting a key component responsible for detecting aircraft, missiles, and drones at distances of up to 300 kilometers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s 15th Separate Artillery Reconnaissance Brigade, known as “Black Forest,” on October 10, the radar was located, tracked, and attacked by Ukrainian drones. The brigade released footage of the operation, identifying the equipment as a 96L6 radar valued at approximately $50 million.
The footage shows a Ukrainian reconnaissance drone following the radar station as it moved toward a deployment position near a wooded area. Once the equipment stopped and deployed, Ukrainian strike drones carried out two attacks, hitting the area around its antenna.
The 96L6 is an early-warning radar operating in the C-band frequency range. It forms part of Russia’s integrated air defense network and provides targeting information to command centers and missile launchers.
The system is designed to detect and track various aerial threats, including fighter jets, cruise and ballistic missiles, and unmanned aircraft. According to its stated specifications, it can detect targets at distances of up to 300 kilometers and simultaneously track as many as 100 objects.
The radar can also operate alongside other detection systems, allowing Russian air defense units to coordinate surveillance and missile engagements across a wider area.
Disabling such equipment can reduce the detection capabilities of Russian air defense formations, particularly those operating S-300 and S-400 missile systems, which depend on radar data to identify and engage incoming threats.
Earlier, a Ukrainian missile strike on Russian command centers in temporarily occupied Donetsk on August 26 killed 20 Russian officers, including seven colonels and six lieutenant colonels. The attack marked the highest confirmed number of Russian officer deaths in a single strike since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Tensions flare in Syria's Hasaka as Arab protesters target Kurdish symbols
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:32:04 UTC
19:32:04 KST

Concerns are mounting over protests and clashes in Syria's Hasaka, where Arab demonstrators have confronted Kurdish residents. The US has expressed concern over the escalating unrest, Kurdish media outlet Rudaw reported.
The US is urging all sides to refrain from violence and resolve their differences through dialogue. The State Department made the comments in response to questions from Rudaw.
"The United States is closely monitoring and concerned by reports of unrest in Hasakah and urges all parties to exercise restraint, reject violence and incitement, and resolve differences through peaceful dialogue," a US State Department spokesperson told Rudaw’s Diyar Kurda.
Wladimir van Wilgenburg, an author, journalist, and expert on Kurdish affairs, also highlighted the tensions, noting that the Kurdish National Council in Syria (KNC) had issued a statement addressing the unrest.
The KNC “affirmed that the future of the Syrian Jazira region cannot be built through exclusion or the fueling of divisions, but rather through partnership and the safeguarding of the dignity and rights of all its people. It emphasized that this approach strengthens the prospects of building a democratic, pluralistic Syria founded on freedom and justice." The statement was distributed to Welat TV.
“The Council stressed that preserving relations among the region's inhabitants requires respect for ethnic and cultural distinctiveness, the rejection of accusations of treason, arrogance, and exclusion, and the prioritization of dialogue and national responsibility."
Arab-Kurdish tensions threaten Syria's integration efforts
The unrest in Hasaka has involved Arab demonstrators protesting against the Kurdish population. The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) previously controlled the city until an agreement was reached with the central government in January 2026.
That agreement followed clashes between the SDF and Damascus. The SDF had received US backing since 2015 and played a central role in the campaign against ISIS, defeating the terrorist organization and liberating areas such as Hasaka from its control.
Hasaka has a mixed Arab and Kurdish population, making it a potential flashpoint for ethnic tensions. Some Arab residents have long resented Kurdish rule.
According to reports, Arab protesters are demanding control of the city's governing institutions. A compromise arrangement currently allows Kurdish officials to retain influence and authority in Hasaka and other areas previously administered by the SDF.
“Tensions escalated after protesters targeted Kurdish symbols, including flags and an image of a woman's braid, which has recently emerged as a symbol of Kurdish resistance in northeast Syria (Rojava),” Rudaw noted.
“Kurdish residents subsequently staged counter-protests, leading to confrontations with state-affiliated security forces. Footage circulated by the UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR) showed security forces firing into the air to disperse demonstrators.”
Several issues are contributing to the tensions, including Kurdish-language instruction in schools and the use of Kurdish on government signs. Relations between Arab tribes and former SDF members have also remained strained.
In September, a Kurdish soldier was murdered, while other Kurds died in a prison riot in Kobane.
Damascus and local authorities have generally sought to reduce tensions. However, efforts to preserve stability have often meant that perpetrators on either side have not faced charges.
The Syrian government has also sought to integrate the SDF into the new Syrian army, with some Kurdish commanders retaining senior positions. Sipan Hamo, a prominent SDF commander, became a deputy defense minister.
Hasaka Governor Nour al-Din Ahmed, who is Kurdish, said on Friday that individuals and groups opposed to the integration agreement between the Kurdish administration in northeastern Syria and the central government were responsible for fueling unrest.
“His remarks came amid rising tensions in Hasaka city, where pro-government protesters have attacked Kurdish symbols, prompting counter-protests by Kurdish residents,” Rudaw noted.
Meanwhile, the US said it “supports a unified, sovereign Syria in which Kurds and all other communities enjoy equal citizenship, security, and meaningful participation in governance.”
The US State Department went on to say, "We urge the Syrian government, which includes Kurdish leaders, and local authorities to uphold their commitments, address legitimate concerns, and take practical steps to rebuild trust,” Rudaw added.
Ahmed also addressed opposition to the integration process.
"Some figures and parties oppose the agreement [between the SDF and Damascus] and do not want it to be implemented. So they have sought to play with the emotions of the community by finding pretexts to mobilize the public.”
Ahmed was appointed governor by the SDF and approved by Damascus. He is a key figure in efforts to reconcile the former SDF-held areas with the central government and integrate their institutions.
Former SDF commander Mazloum Abdi also spoke in Hasaka province on Friday, reiterating his commitment to integration.
It remains unclear when the tensions will subside.
Saddam Hussein imagery highlights deeper ethnic divisions
Some protesters carried an image of former Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein during a demonstration on Friday.
Several Arab tribes in the Middle Euphrates River Valley near Hasaka have longstanding ties to Iraqi tribes and historically tended to support Saddam Hussein.
Many Kurds are aware of the genocide Saddam committed against the Kurdish population in Iraq. Displaying his image therefore sends a message of hostility toward Kurds.
The use of Saddam's image also highlights the continuing sentiments of some Arab tribes, whose historical connections to Iraq may be stronger than their ties to Syria.
Syrian state media appears to be ignoring the clashes in Hasaka. North Press, a media outlet based in eastern Syria, has also largely avoided covering the unrest.
This may reflect a belief that avoiding publicity will help tensions dissipate.
Meanwhile, the Syrian government announced on Sunday that it was seeking to develop a national approach to combating hate speech.
The initiative brought “together relevant national institutions and experts from the Office of the United Nations Special Envoy for Syria to discuss priorities, coordination and preparations for a national policy.”
Syrian state news agency SANA reported that the meeting was “organized by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates at the Golden Mazzeh Hotel; the workshop examines public discourse in Syria, international principles and standards, approaches adopted in other countries, and the existing national framework and challenges in addressing hate speech.”
The tensions in Hasaka illustrate that combating hate speech requires more than holding meetings.

Iran’s future will be decided by its people, not separatist factions - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:31:49 UTC
19:31:49 KST

My recent article in The Jerusalem Post issued a critical warning to Israeli and Western strategists: Do not jeopardize the historic, civilizational bond with the Iranian people by flirting with marginal, transnational separatist factions. Predictably, the piece provoked a flurry of angry, highly personalized reactions from anonymous quarters and regionalist echo chambers.
Rather than addressing the hard geopolitical, demographic, and historical facts I raised, these counter-arguments resorted to emotional deflection and historical revisionism. This visceral anger and the complete evasion of historical evidence, however, only serve to validate the core arguments of my thesis. To misread the reality of Iran at this critical historical juncture is a luxury neither Israel nor the free world can afford. The narrative presented by these critics is fundamentally detached from reality, completely falling apart when confronted with seven undeniable truths.
Seven undeniable truths from Iranian history
FIRST, MY critics deliberately misinterpret antiquity and my invocation of Bistun and Taq-e Bostan. I referenced these monumental landmarks in the Kermanshah province to highlight an undeniable civilizational continuity. These ancient monuments prove that for over 2,500 years, this region has been a foundational pillar and a vital core of Iranian national sovereignty and territory, not a peripheral borderland waiting to be fractured.
Second, they attempt to obscure the clear line I drew between ordinary citizens and transnational separatists, calling it a “false dichotomy.” This is a classic distortion. My article explicitly separated the patriotic majority of the population from “transnational separatist movements.” It is these transnational cults and factions that actively pursue separation, whereas the actual population remains deeply integrated into the fabric of the nation.
Third, they entirely erase the strongholds of Iranian nationalism: Kermanshah and Ilam. My critics imply that the identity of the people in the western provinces is entirely defined by the political ambitions of armed rebel groups. They conveniently ignore the demographic and ideological reality of major urban centers including Kermanshah, the most populous Kurdish city in the region, and Ilam that have historically stood as fortresses of Iranian patriotism. In Kurdish regions, the local cultural identity is recognized not as an opposition to Iran, but as the most authentic and ancient narrative of being Iranian.
Fourth, they politically exploit shared suffering, attempting to weaponize selective regional cases to paint a picture of an isolated, uniquely targeted territory. This is not a valid analytical response; it is a distortion of tragedy. The Islamic Republic’s brutal execution apparatus does not target an isolated area; it commits atrocities across the entirety of Iran. Just on Monday, October 5, 2026, the regime executed Alireza Sepahi and Alireza Raeisi, two young protesters arrested during the uprisings in Isfahan. When young citizens from the heart of Isfahan face the exact same gallows, it proves that state terror is a structural affliction holding the entire nation hostage. Weaponizing this universal Iranian tragedy to legitimize the political ambitions of armed, factional groups is a grotesque deflection from a shared national struggle against a common oppressor.
Fifth, there is a telling and total silence from my critics regarding the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), its leader, and their anti-Israel legacy. This glaring omission is proof of intellectual bankruptcy. They completely evade the fact that many transnational separatist movements look up to Abdullah Ocalan as a foundational figure, despite Ocalan’s continuous anti-Israel legacy. Furthermore, they have no defense against the historical fact that the PKK operated as a proxy for the Assad regime, trained alongside armed anti-Israel Palestinian factions in Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley front, and fought directly against Israel. Because certain armed groups operating in Iran are direct branches of this terrorist PKK network, my critics completely censor this history, knowing it destroys their attempt to appeal to an international audience.
Sixth, my critics deliberately rewrite the history of the 1979 catastrophe to hide their own role in Iran’s destabilization. Armed regional factions were an active part of the disastrous 1979 coalition – alongside Islamists, Marxists, and Mossadeghists – that brought down the nation. Leaders like Abdul Rahman Ghassemlou openly pledged allegiance to Ayatollah Khomeini, only to later clash over the spoils of the revolution when the Islamists turned around and purged them.
If these timed factions, disguised as political parties, truly sought a democratic, unified Iran rather than secession, why did they immediately exploit the country’s chaotic vulnerability just days after February 11, 1979, the exact day the previous regime fell and the Islamists seized power? Specifically, on February 20, 1979, a mere nine days after the revolution, they aggressively raided and looted the national army garrison in Mahabad, assassinating its commander and stealing heavy weaponry, including tanks, heavy artillery pieces, and thousands of rifles. They then marched on Sanandaj, and had it not been for the fierce resistance of the Iranian National Army’s 28th Division garrison, they would have completely captured the city.
Let us ask an honest question to an international audience: Would the Israeli government or public ever tolerate a so-called political faction that raids and captures an IDF base? Calling these militant groups “freedom fighters” is an insult to sovereign nations.
Finally, they seek to erase the historical reality of local resistance, such as the Paveh events of August 1979. They imply that armed groups have always naturally represented the collective will of the local population. History records otherwise. During that critical juncture, it was the local, indigenous patriotic population of Paveh in Kermanshah province who actively took up arms and resisted the violent, armed incursion of separatist factions. This historical event proves that the people themselves have historically been the first line of defense for Iran’s territorial integrity against armed groups.
ULTIMATELY, THE angry reactions to my piece fail to counter its core warning. By flirting with marginal, transnational separatist elements, outside powers risk alienating the patriotic majority of the Iranian public.
The true, lasting strategic asset for Israel and the West is the 2,500-year-old civilizational bond with a unified Iranian nation, not short-sighted investments in armed factions like the PKK and its branches that carry a historical legacy of hostility toward the West. We must look toward a future democratic Iran based on historical territorial integrity, national unity, individual liberty, and equality before the law.
The writer is the communications director to Prince Reza Pahlavi and an Iranian journalist who previously served as editor-in-chief of news at Manoto TV, a UK-based Persian-language television network.

Modi is in trouble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:31:45 UTC
19:31:45 KST

Modi is in trouble
The CJP protests sweeping through the country have exposed India’s hollowed-out democracy.
It is said that if you pluck a chicken one feather at a time, nobody notices. That is how some people deceive themselves into believing that small wrongs will never catch up with them.
The trouble with this method is that, one fine day, the truth stands bare, impossible to ignore. This October, Indian democracy resembles a plucked chicken, stripped of its plumage, as protesters who ironically call themselves “cockroaches” swarm our streets.
A lot of feather-plucking went on for 12 years before Prime Minister Narendra Modi found himself cornered, retreating behind barricades, facing the wrath of students for whom the slow erosion of democracy has left little to lose and even less to fear.
Confronted with a major protest on October 10 demanding the reversal of a purge of the voter rolls, he went on a self-incrimination spree. His government imposed measures reminiscent of the emergency era: no trains to New Delhi, paramilitary forces deployed at protest sites, the internet disrupted.
Ahead of the demonstration, leading figures linked to the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest movement – Ratna Singh, Abhijeet Dipke, Dhruv Rathee – were detained. Many other known activists, including Mahatma Gandhi’s great-grandson Tushar Gandhi, were also detained.
Regardless, demonstrators poured into the streets of New Delhi, trying to reach designated protest sites, in a scene that repeated in city after city across India. Through the day, the police played an endless game of whack-a-mole with the protesters, who kept resurfacing across the capital city, reassembling in one corner after another, driven from the designated protest sites but unwilling to disappear.
By the evening, at least 2,500 protesters and 15 journalists were detained across the city and taken to detention centres set up in various locations. Many have since been released.
These acts further erode the tenuous position Modi is in, prompting more rebuke from critics who now question his fitness to occupy the office of the prime minister. On Friday, the opposition parties, led by Rahul Gandhi, met President Draupadi Murmu and submitted to her that the government had subverted India’s democratic framework.
Under Modi’s watch, problems have accumulated like barnacles on the side of the ship. Every time he has been challenged, he has gone farther away from the democratic principles on which this nation was founded.
The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls – the last feather he plucked – was an exercise in bureaucratic fascism. There is simply no other way to frame an event that strips 130 million Indians of their right to vote.
The fact that this process helped sway elections is no longer up for debate. That the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw SIR, is not resigning – out of shame – is astonishing. Even more so now that a corruption case from 2006 against him has resurfaced.
The chaotic, angry, defiant tableaux in the streets of New Delhi and beyond represent a reckoning that has been long in the making. The young, diverse protesters are a stark contrast to Modi and his cabinet – old, humourless men, who have bet on a strategy of demonisation and exclusion to succeed. His cabinet is filled with men full of self-importance, who had, mistakenly, wagered that crimes of elected officials should be tolerated and that a country can be governed indefinitely by creating fissures and manufacturing enemies.
We have now seen what happens when breakers of the law become makers of law. Criminal behaviour has been the organising principle of the party, and together, the values of these people have defined the years that Modi has ruled India. In the process, he has presided over the shredding of the Constitution of India.
Now that all this has come back to haunt him – in the form of “cockroaches” he is unable to exterminate – Modi has turned New Delhi into a fortress and unleashed all the power he has at his disposal on unarmed protesters. This is consistent with his policy of pretending to aspire to peace but unerringly generating conflict throughout his tenure: with neighbouring nations as well as among neighbours within cities.
October 10 is just an opening salvo. Over the next few weeks, Modi’s troubles will likely deepen. The CJP has announced protests will continue. Opposition parties have said they will protest on Monday.
The “cockroaches” seem to have resolved any remaining questions regarding Modi’s utter ineptitude as prime minister. They have laid bare the hollowed-out democracy that India holds up to the world as exemplary.
As his rule draws to a close — for now, the writing is on the wall — it can be safely said that history books will cast Modi in his proper role as the man who caused an entire generation of Indians to lose all respect for the government, the army, the Delhi Police, as well as the whole structure of governance.
New Delhi is temporarily suspended in a transition between a suffocating present and a promising future. This particular scrap of time, no matter how hard, will pass.
When that dust settles, what will become of all the institutions destroyed by regulatory capture and right-wing ideology – only those on the streets today will answer. This understanding is implicit in everything the “cockroaches” do. Because the whole point of it is power to the people.

One year after Trump's Gaza ceasefire, questions remain about possible next steps - analysis
