19:31:37 KST

The Gaza ceasefire took shape a year ago. In September 2025, US President Donald Trump met with key Arab leaders, which eventually led to a ceasefire in Gaza. Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law who has played a key role in the 20-point peace plan, posted about the significance of the one-year anniversary of the ceasefire.
“One year ago today, on October 9, 2025, we reached an agreement on President Trump’s 20-point peace plan for Gaza many believed impossible,” he wrote.
He noted the importance of ending the devastating war. He wanted an agreement that created “a path to reunite hostage families with their loved ones, bring security to Israel, relieve the suffering of the Palestinian people in Gaza, and build a different future for the region.”
Kushner praised the progress since October 9, 2025, when Hamas accepted Trump’s 20-point peace plan, noting some of the milestones since that day.
On October 13, “all 20 living Israeli hostages return home. Something many believed would never happen.” He also noted how the UN backed the US plan.
He didn’t mention all the important pieces that came together in the following weeks. For instance, the US-backed CMCC in Kiryat Gat was set up. This was set up largely by US Central Command and brought together a number of countries. The concept was to coordinate aid deliveries and monitor the ceasefire. By January 2026, Kushner notes that the UN said that “100% of basic food needs being met in Gaza for the first time since 2023.”
In January 2026, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza was established. This is supposed to be the Palestinian technocratic government for Gaza. So far Israel has not permitted it to operate in Gaza. Two million civilians are still stuck under Hamas rule in around 40 percent of Gaza.
The Board of Peace, established as part of the Trump plan, has tried to do some work on the sidelines to see what might happen after Israel’s elections. In general, the theory is that Israel won’t do anything on Gaza until after the elections.
For instance, the peace plan was supposed to see the creation of an international security force. This ISF only seems to have a few dozen personnel so far. Albania and Kosovo were some of the first to come forward. In June, reports indicated that Morocco and Greece might help support it. Reports also indicated that Kazakhstan would be helpful. Israel, meanwhile, has expelled some countries from the CMCC over diplomatic disputes.
On the border of Gaza, a new logistics facility called LSA Endurance has taken shape. However, a lot remains to be seen.
Kushner noted that the remains of all the deceased hostages had been returned by late January 2026. He also noted that on July 31, “Hamas signs an actionable, step-by-step framework for decommissioning its weapons, developed with the support of Nikolay Mladenov and mediators from Egypt, Turkey, Qatar, and the United States. Implementation remains a critical next step.”
The last thing on the Kushner list was a meeting on September 23 where the “Board of Peace hosts an open meeting on the sidelines of UNGA releasing the next steps in the Gaza recovery plan.”
Board of Peace efforts overshadowed by Iran war
Some of the work of the Board of Peace has been overshadowed by the war with Iran. The US administration has been sidetracked to some extent. It also has to deal with other fronts that Israel is involved with.
For instance, the administration has had to help Israel in Lebanon with the Lebanese government, where the US also backs a ceasefire. The US also tried to smooth relations between Israel and Damascus and to prevent Israel-Turkey relations from becoming a crisis. At the same time, recent reports indicate Iran is rebuilding its missile and drone program, and Hamas continues to recruit in Gaza.
Kushner notes that “There is still hard work ahead. Disarmament must be implemented, security established, essential services restored, and communities rebuilt. None of this will be easy. But we have a thoughtful plan, committed partners, and a path forward that did not exist a year ago.”
The challenge in Gaza is that it’s not clear what comes next.
Arab News noted that “Reconstruction of the devastated Palestinian territory called for under the ceasefire plan has still not materialized.” The report says Israel controls around seventy percent of Gaza. “Nothing has changed for the better; everything has gotten worse, they lie to us, it is all lies,” Fatima Awkal, a displaced woman in Gaza City, told AFP. The AFP article is the basis for the Arab News report.
It says, “On the streets of Gaza City, rows of white tents line passageways that have been cleared of rubble from destroyed homes, while in the distance blown-out windows gape from the facades of buildings that remain standing.” This report also says around “82 percent of all standing structures in Gaza either damaged or destroyed as of mid-2026 per the UN.”
It notes that the concept of the plan was for there to be a political transition in Gaza away from Hamas rule. This has not happened. In the past, Israel has accepted Hamas rule in Gaza, and prior to October 7, 2023, there was cash entering Hamas-run Gaza from Doha. The Hamas leadership continues to live in Qatar. As such, it’s unclear whether the promised change under the Trump plan will happen.
The Arab News report and others paint a concerning picture of Gaza. People there say little has changed. While Kushner has praised the peace deal, the question is what happens next. This has always been the challenge in the past as well. Getting a ceasefire is one thing. Changing the status quo is another.
Israeli voices call to resettle Gaza Strip
Some voices in Israel’s politics have vowed to resettle Gaza and have encouraged people to emigrate from the enclave. There do not appear to be many voices discussing how to remove Hamas or whether policymakers in Jerusalem want Hamas removed. The war largely resulted in moving people in Gaza from place to place, with Hamas hiding among them.
The most recent IDF data says that the Israeli military carried out 100,000 strikes in Gaza in three years of war. Many of these were carried out in the first months of the fighting. The IDF also says that it eliminated four heads of Hamas military branches along with 17 brigade commanders, approximately 60 battalion commanders, and approximately 300 company commanders. Hamas only had 24 battalions and five regional brigades. As such, it would appear that in many cases the brigade commanders and battalion commanders were eliminated twice.
he same goes for the company commanders. What this means is that Hamas replaced the ones who were killed, and then the replacements were killed. Israel also estimates it has eliminated 4,000 of the 6,000 people who attacked Israel on October 7, some of them Hamas and some of them members of other groups or civilian looters.

Palestinians have been left angry and heartbroken by Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas’s decision to again postpone the long-delayed Palestinian Legislative Council elections, with candidates who had planned to run telling The Jerusalem Post and posting publicly that the two-decade absence of legislative elections shows the PA is putting the “status quo ahead of the public interest.”
Abbas announced on Saturday that the elections, originally scheduled for November 28, would be postponed until September 11, 2027, citing Israeli-imposed obstacles and arguing that Palestinian factions had agreed there was no choice but to delay the vote. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar denied the PA’s accusations, calling them "yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability."
Though Dr. Nabil Kukali, founder and president of the Palestinian Center for Public Opinion, told the Post last week that the Palestinian majority would likely understand a postponement if elections could not take place in east Jerusalem and Gaza, provided the public saw a genuine desire to hold them, New Path leader Samer Sinijlawi said the decision to postpone had been made as part of a campaign by Palestinian Vice-President Hussein al-Sheikh and Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine Deputy Secretary-General Jamil Mezher.
Reports that Sheikh sought to cancel the elections have circulated for months, with Yoni Ben-Menachem, a senior researcher at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs, saying he had been told that the vice-president had explicitly cited east Jerusalem as a pretext to cancel the vote, as Abbas did in 2021.
“These efforts disregarded the hopes of millions of Palestinians who had waited two decades and welcomed this democratic opportunity,” Sinijlawi said. “It would have allowed them to participate in the political system by exercising their most basic right: electing their representatives to the Legislative Council and making their voices heard after years of being silenced.
Abbas's decision harmful to Gaza candidates
Sinijlawi said he found it “difficult” to view the postponement as “anything other than putting the interests of those who benefit from the status quo ahead of the public interest” and added that “the right to vote is not a favor granted by anyone. It must not remain hostage to the calculations of those who fear the people’s choice.”
Explaining to the Post how Abbas’s decision was particularly harmful to candidates in Gaza, he shared that “many stepped forward” while living in tents and that they had put all their efforts into running “because they believed they could help shape a different future.”
“Their candidacy was an act of hope: a chance to move from surviving devastation to representing their communities and rebuilding their lives,” he continued. “They now face another year of uncertainty, with no guarantee that the new date will be honored. The damage goes beyond disrupted campaigns. It undermines trust in peaceful democratic change and tells a generation that has never voted that its voice can wait again. Gaza’s emerging leaders deserve the opportunity to lead, and its people deserve the right to choose them.”
Ahmad Shadid, leader of the Phoenix list, also expressed distrust in the PA’s explanation for the postponement, writing: “If I were one of those behind the idea of postponing [the elections], I would have some self-respect and be honest, and tell people: ‘The Authority is in our hands. We decided to hold elections, and then we changed our minds. You can go to hell.’ But I shouldn’t act like an idiot and talk about circumstances, national dialogue, and … legitimacy.”
Postponing elections reflects 'depth of current crisis'
Majda Al-Masri, deputy secretary-general of the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP) and head of the Unity and Democratic Change list, wrote that “postponing elections reflects the depth of the current crisis and the inability of existing institutions to address the challenges” and called for a national dialogue to “unify efforts to confront the occupation and its plans.”
Mustafa Barghouti, head of the Palestinian National Initiative list and a former information minister in the Palestinian unity government formed in 2007, made clear he opposed the postponement and demanded on X that the Palestinian Authority guarantee that the election will not be delayed again next September.
Despite opposing the postponement, Barghouti said he welcomed the fact that legislative and presidential elections would be held in unison and said it was necessary to review restrictions ahead of September that would “undermine the democratic right to stand for election and to vote.”
“This comprehensive national dialogue must also be devoted to developing a unified national strategy to confront the ongoing genocidal war in the Gaza Strip, as well as the war of settler terror and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and Jerusalem,” he added.

'The Prime Ministers': New book covers Begin, the ‘Altalena,’  and the October 27 election - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:31:16 UTC
19:31:16 KST

Baroness Thatcher poured the tea, pushed a brass tray of peppermints across the table, and asked Israeli diplomat and author Yehuda Avner to tell her about “Mr. Begin.”
It was a bright April morning in 1992, in a borrowed mansion on Eaton Square, barely a month after Menachem Begin’s funeral. Thatcher had made no bones about opposing his settlement policies, she said, but she had greatly admired his convictions.
Avner told her he thought Begin had been worthy of a second Nobel Prize.
“For what, pray?”
For securing Israel’s parliamentary democracy, he said.
Thatcher’s voice sharpened. Surely he exaggerated. Israel was universally famous for its democracy, one of the most robust in the world.
Not at the outset, Avner said.
Twice, just before independence and just after, Begin had saved the country from civil war.
In 1944, the Hagana seized Irgun men and handed them over to the British; Begin ordered his fighters not to retaliate. Not one of them did. He explained himself afterward in a ramshackle Galilee cinema, speaking over the sound of rain hammering a corrugated roof.
The Second Temple fell because Jews hated each other into civil war. There are fateful times, he told them, when the choice is between blood and tears. Against the British, blood had taken the place of tears. Jew-against-Jew, tears had to take the place of blood. God forbid that a decision of a democratically elected government should ever be defied by force.
He was talking about the Altalena – found intact on the seafloor recently.
Avner says plainly that he was not there and is familiar with the scene through eyewitness accounts years later.
Begin on the burning deck, black with smoke, flinging up his arms and shouting at his own men not to fire.
On the beach, one of the officers ordered to shell her was Yitzhak Rabin, who believed Ben-Gurion’s warning that Begin was mounting a coup and told Avner decades later that his gun crew fired the shell that set her alight. Two of this book’s four prime ministers were at opposite ends of that gun.
Thatcher had no idea, and she said so.
Avner once asked Begin what the most important thing he had done in his life was. “Twice I prevented civil war,” came his answer. That is recorded near the end of The Prime Ministers, and it is the boldest claim in 700 pages. Published in 2010, Avner’s tome is more relevant than ever.
ISRAELIS VOTE on October 27, at the end of only the second Knesset since 1988 to serve a full term – the other 13 having dissolved early.
Avner’s claim is that there is anything to vote in at all because a man twice refused to fight for power he believed was his, and then brought in the voters nobody else wanted, most of them from Arab and Asian countries with no parliamentary tradition and hardly a voice in the new state. They put him in office after eight consecutive electoral defeats.
Thatcher’s own Foreign Office had briefed her that Israel had elected a warmonger and a demagogue.
‘A Jew should never hate another Jew’
Avner never argues any of this on the page. He puts down what he saw and lets you do the rest.
In May 1967, with Egyptian divisions in Sinai, the leader of the opposition walked into Levi Eshkol’s study and asked the prime minister to stand down in favor of David Ben-Gurion.
How could Begin, of all people, ask him to make way for the man who had abused him at every turn and compared him to Hitler? “The enmity is his, not mine,” Begin said. “I live by the maxim that a Jew should never hate another Jew.”
Eshkol went to the window, looked out at picketers holding signs telling him to go, then yawned and refused in Yiddish. “These two horses cannot pull the same wagon together,” he said famously, referring to himself and Ben-Gurion.
Born Haffner in Manchester
Avner was born Haffner in Manchester in 1928, reached Palestine at 18 in November 1947, and dug trenches during the siege.
From 1963, he wrote the English-language speeches of Eshkol, Golda Meir, and Rabin, holding no party card in a country where public jobs ran through Mapai. He was in the room for much of it and scrupulous about when he was not, sourcing Golda’s confrontation with the Socialist International to her own memoir and a colleague she told of it on her return.
In June 1977, the country changed hands for the first time, and the incoming prime minister told his predecessor’s speechwriter he was keeping him.
There had to be continuity, Begin said, and the world had to see it. “This government has come to serve, not to reap.”
Avner stayed six more years. The peaceful transfer of power is not an abstraction in this book. It is the author’s employment record.
The book is also funny, and the joke is rarely where you expect.
Eshkol gets into his car one morning and asks Yankele the doorman, in Yiddish, how he is doing as prime minister. Yankele closes one eye and says the taxes are far too high. Eshkol, one leg in the car, cups a hand to his ear and spends several minutes explaining the defense budget and immigrant housing to his doorman, while his speechwriter wonders how many prime ministers ask a doorman his opinion, listen, and then try to explain themselves.
The word Carter had to ask about
Underneath it is one thing, and Thatcher walks into it. Avner tells her you cannot understand Begin without the Holocaust, that almost his whole family was murdered. In 1979, she admits that she had not really known what Auschwitz was. In the White House Cabinet Room in 1977, under a portrait of Truman, Begin told then-US president Jimmy Carter that, in the past, Jewish men had to deliver their women and children to their executioners. “We were tertiated, Mr. President.”
Carter lifted his head and asked what the word had been. Tertiated, not decimated, Begin said. Decimation is one-in-10. For the Jews it was one-in-three. He rose to his full height, banged his fist on the table, and swore an oath before the president, in the name of the Jewish people, that it would never, ever happen again.
Then Begin broke, knuckles white against the tabletop, blinking back tears, while the clock on the mantelpiece became audible and all the president’s men looked at the floor.
None of it is neutral, and Avner says so, explaining in an author’s note that he reconstructed conversations, edited speech, and thought Begin the most exceptional of the four. It shows in the Sabra and Shatila chapter, which spends more energy on the unfairness of the coverage than on the decision that put Phalangist militiamen inside those camps.
He ends where the man did.
The funeral Begin had specified: no lying in state, no guard of honor, no delegations, not even eulogies. A shroud, a prayer shawl, Irgun veterans carrying him, four kilometers of mourners on the road to the Mount of Olives.
Then, in that London drawing room a month later, Thatcher asked whether Begin had left a memoir.
No, Avner told her, and he could not explain the silence to himself, let alone to her.
What he had was the end of an old Time magazine interview, where, when the reporter rose to leave, he had turned back and asked how Begin wanted to be remembered in history. Avner repeats the answer and adds nothing: “As a decent human being, and a proud Jew.” ■
THE PRIME MINISTERS: AN INTIMATE NARRATIVE OF ISRAELI LEADERSHIP
By Yehuda Avner 
The Toby Press 
715 pages; $38

From peaceful protests to free movement: 9 directions SC issued amid CJP stir in Delhi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:30:36 UTC
19:30:36 KST

The SC directed authorities to prevent illegal detentions, restore normal Metro services and protect peaceful protests and free movement amid the CJP stir.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Sunday stepped into the row over restrictions imposed during the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) protest in Delhi, directing authorities to prevent illegal detentions, ensure normal Metro and railway operations and protect the ability of lawyers and journalists to perform their duties. The court also ordered the removal of a notice board announcing prohibitory restrictions near its premises, saying citizens and lawyers must have access to justice.A bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued notice to the Centre on a contempt plea alleging that authorities had violated the court's October 9 directions on public transport restrictions. The hearing came a day after more than 7,000 people were detained during a security crackdown on the planned mobilisation at Jantar Mantar against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.During the special sitting, lawyers alleged that detentions and movement restrictions had extended beyond the areas covered by prohibitory orders. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, however, told the court that restrictions on October 10 covered 45 of Delhi Metro's 303 stations and that most detainees had already been released.Here are the key actions and directions from the Supreme Court hearing.
Authorities told to prevent illegal detentions
The court made clear that people assembling peacefully cannot be detained outside the bounds of the law, particularly in areas not covered by prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).
"There shall not be illegal detention, save and except by procedure established by law, particularly with regard to assemblage of people beyond the area within which it's imposed," the bench said.The issue was raised by senior advocate Kapil Sibal, appearing for RJD MP Manoj Jha. Sibal alleged that police were detaining people travelling by train and individuals outside the four-kilometre radius of Jantar Mantar, where prohibitory orders were in force.
Normal Metro and railway operations to be ensured
The Supreme Court directed that Delhi Metro services should operate according to their normal schedule and asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, to ensure that the authorities concerned complied with the direction. It also called for railway services to function without a blanket prohibition, subject to lawful and necessary restrictions.The direction followed the court's October 9 order, passed after a separate petition challenged the closure of 57 Metro stations and cancellation of trains in view of the planned protest.On Sunday, Mehta said entry and exit had been restricted at 45 of the network's 303 stations on October 10, accounting for around 15 per cent of the total. Lawyers appearing before the court had alleged that the restrictions continued despite the earlier order, with some stations completely inaccessible to passengers.
Internet access must not be disrupted unlawfully
The bench directed the authorities to ensure that internet services remained undisturbed, subject to law and order requirements. It also clarified that the direction did not curtail powers available under the Information Technology Act."Internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, as per law....When we are saying internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, we are not taking away the powers under the Information Technology Act," the bench said.The court's observation sought to ensure that restrictions imposed amid the security operation did not extend to internet connectivity without lawful justification.
Free movement
The court called for free movement of people, subject to traffic regulations, and for authorities to review the need for barricades that could impede movement across Delhi.Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan urged the bench to direct the removal of barricades and restoration of services at Metro stations. Lawyers had argued that restrictions were affecting not only protesters but also other residents and commuters.The court's broader directions sought to ensure that security measures did not impose unnecessary hardship on people moving around the capital.
Lawyers, journalists must be allowed to work
The bench directed authorities to ensure that lawyers, journalists and others were not obstructed from discharging their professional duties.The direction came amid allegations that several lawyers had been detained during Saturday's protests. Senior advocate Shadan Farasat, who said he was detained by Delhi Police, told the court that he and other lawyers had faced violence."It's about citizens' right to protest. The sense I got yesterday was that we were one step away from a police state. Kindly restore citizens' right to protest peacefully in the capital. Yesterday, that right was destroyed," Farasat said.Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan also informed the bench that senior advocates Dinesh Dwivedi, Uttara Babbar and Farasat had been detained.
Section 163 notice board near SC ordered to be removed
The court directed the concerned authority to take down a notice board announcing the imposition of Section 163 of the BNSS in and around the Supreme Court premises, if it had not already been removed."We have been informed that a notice board stating imposition of Section 163 BNSS in and around the vicinity of the Supreme Court has been put up," the bench said."We direct the authority concerned to take down this board, if not already done, so that citizens as well as lawyers can have access to justice," it ordered.The direction was specifically linked to ensuring access to the court for citizens and members of the legal profession.
Peaceful protests permitted, but must remain within the law
The bench observed that peaceful assemblies must be allowed in accordance with law, particularly outside areas where prohibitory orders apply. It also reminded protesters that demonstrations must remain peaceful and should not instigate others.The hearing centred on the distinction between lawful regulation to maintain public order and restrictions that effectively prevent people from exercising their rights.In its October 9 order, the Supreme Court had said authorities could regulate Metro and railway operations but should not impose an outright prohibition on their movement. It had also asked the government to publicise transport arrangements and issue traffic advisories to minimise inconvenience.
Habeas corpus and related pleas listed for October 13
The court said petitions concerning alleged mass detentions and other connected matters would be heard alongside the main cases on October 13.One of these was a habeas corpus petition filed by senior advocate Menaka Guruswamy concerning the detention of political leaders. The bench was also hearing Jha's plea alleging disproportionate use of force, illegal detention, house arrests and harassment of protesters by Delhi Police.The allegations in Jha's petition included claims of sexual harassment of women protesters. These were allegations before the court and had not been established by the directions issued on Sunday.
Centre issued notice in contempt plea
The bench issued notice to the Centre on a contempt petition filed by advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi, which named Union home secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi Metro Rail Corporation chairperson D Thara as respondents.The petition alleged that authorities had breached the Supreme Court's October 9 order by restricting public transport and detaining protesters on October 10.The earlier order had followed a plea challenging the closure of Metro stations and cancellation of trains ahead of the CJP mobilisation. The court had observed that notifications appeared to go beyond regulation and impose a complete ban on essential public transport.
The bench had said: "Upon our indication that a distinction exists between total 'prohibition' and the 'regulation' of metro and other train movements, the solicitor general of India has fairly agreed to impress upon the authorities to reassess such prohibitions."The court's latest intervention came as it considered allegations that the earlier directions had not been followed. It also reiterated its responsibility under Article 32 of the Constitution to protect and enforce fundamental rights.

Inside the Muslim Manosphere Policing Women Online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Mariam recently disabled Facebook Messenger. As the administrator of a Facebook group for women in the United Arab Emirates with close to 400,000 members, she’d become accustomed to receiving messages from strangers. But then came a shift in the volume—and nature—of those messages until they were impossible to ignore.
“Being the admin of this group has subjected me to all kinds of harassment,” says Miriam, who asked to be identified only by her first name because she fears online retaliation. They “either want to advise you to be holy and cover up, or they want to sexually harass you—or both.”
Mariam has run the group for more than a year. And even though intended for women, the group’s size and visibility has meant that Miriam also gets a lot of messages from men. She has received a deluge of unsolicited messages telling her how to dress, not to raise her voice or wear makeup, and to cover her hands with gloves so that no skin is visible.
“I couldn’t take it any longer. It was starting to affect my mental well-being,” Miriam says.
Many women who are conspicuous on the internet have been harassed online. That comes in countless forms, even if the same misogyny underlies it. The particular variety Miriam was subjected to stems from a section of the “manosphere” dressed in the clothes of religion—the Muslim manosphere.
At its core, the manosphere is built around male grievance and antifeminist ideology—though whether that’s entirely organic or engineered to sell supplements and other products is up for debate. Regardless, it has no shortage of subcultures to chose from: Incels, pick-up artists, men’s rights activists, and followers of the Red Pill.
Some nuances may make these groups distinct, but they largely share a common worldview: Feminism has destabilized society, women have acquired too much power, and men must reassert control. And the Muslim manosphere is no different. It’s adopted those ideas circulating through the wider manosphere and rebranded them in the language of faith.
Sarah Kaddoura, a feminist researcher and creator of the YouTube channel Haki Nasawi, examined the Arabic-speaking manosphere in a 2025 report. In her study, she describes some of the most prominent influencers, such as Jordanian relationship coach Kareem Atta’i, who posts online as Coach Kareem or Red Pill Arabic.
Atta’i packages his ideas as relationship advice, but his videos frequently frame interactions between men and women as contests for power. Atta’i’s videos, which WIRED Middle East has watched, describe violence as a means of “disciplining” women or retaliating against sexual rejection.
The Arabic manosphere does more than translate Western Red Pill content. Its creators have adapted the ideology to local anxieties around religion, masculinity, marriage, money, and social change.
Kaddoura says influencers use financial insecurity, political instability, religious identity, and fears about declining morality or social cohesion to build their audiences. Misogyny becomes an explanation for a much wider sense of frustration—and women become its most visible target.
The problem is not religious expression online but the use of religious authority—real or claimed—to legitimize misogyny, harassment, and the public surveillance of women. The Muslim manosphere is also not confined to the Arab world. Like the broader manosphere, it crosses borders, languages, and platforms.
Take prominent UK-based creator Ali Dawah, whose channel features street debates and commentary about relationships, gender roles, religion, and Western culture. In one clip, Dawah says he hates Muslim feminists “the most.” In another video, he approaches women in public and challenges them over clothing he describes as immodest.
“Dawah” is not just this YouTuber’s name. In Arabic, it means to make an invitation to someone to learn about Islam. Ali is just one of many influencers often called “Dawah Bros,” and they’re generally known for being more aggressive than offering an invitation when it comes to promoting their manosphere-esque content.
Kaddoura sees the Dawah Bros as a platform-native successor to an older variety of media figure. During the 1990s, Islamic television programs in Egypt and Saudi Arabia regularly featured sheikhs answering callers’ questions about relationships, clothing, and acceptable behavior. However, unlike television preachers, today’s influencers are not limited to scheduled broadcasts, and they aren’t only interacting with people who’ve chosen to call in.
For many Muslim women—especially those who are in prominent places on the internet—these ideas do not remain confined to podcasts or debate videos. They spill into comment sections and private messages, where strangers appoint themselves enforcers of morality.
A 2026 report by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue analyzed nearly 14,000 comments directed at 40 prominent public figures and influencers on Instagram in Jordan over a 12-month period. Among comments classified as hate speech, harassment, or abusive language, 72 percent targeted women, 11 percent were classified as religious or moral harassment, and the vast majority of those comments—85 percent—targeted female influencers.
Additionally, all of the comments classified as sexual harassment were directed at women, underlining the pervasive contradictions in how women are policed on the internet—the same online environment that instructing women to make themselves invisible also subjecting them to unwanted sexual attention. That contradiction is visible in the messages Mariam has received.
The manosphere’s reach is shaped in part by the recommendation systems that determine what users encounter in their feeds. “As soon as you create an account on TikTok, YouTube, X, Instagram, and others as a male, it doesn’t take long for the algorithm to start recommending misogynistic content,” Kaddoura says.
Engagement-based systems can amplify emotionally charged and polarizing content, including manosphere videos. Content blaming women for men’s loneliness or financial insecurity can generate reactions from supporters, critics, and the women being targeted. Those interactions may increase its visibility.
That becomes even thornier when religion enters the picture. The relationship coaches and other men preaching religion online often present personal opinions as religious instruction, Kaddoura says. This can make disagreement appear immoral, and criticism can then be presented as evidence that the creator is defending the faith against hostile forces.
But how exactly a user’s behavior tips over from passively encountering the content to actively engaging with it remains an open question. Researchers can examine publicly available videos and identify influential accounts, but they have limited access to the internal data needed to trace how users move between creators and communities. This leave key questions unanswered, such as whether prolonged exposure changes their behavior.
For women such as Mariam, the technical route behind the harassment may be invisible, but its effects are not. A creator publishes a video. Recommendation systems carry it into other users’ feeds. And then, eventually, users repeat its message in women’s comment sections and inboxes. Repeat ad infinitum.
WIRED Middle East contacted Ali Dawah and Kareem Atta’i for comment. Neither responded by the time of publication.
This story originally appeared in WIRED Middle East.

Indonesia evacuated eight orangutans after fires on Borneo
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:28:05 EEST
19:28:05 KST

Indonesia evacuated eight orangutans after fires on Borneo
Kyiv • UNN
In Indonesia, eight orangutans were moved to a protected forest after fires on Borneo. Since August, 46 animals have been rescued.
On Sunday, Indonesian authorities and conservationists reported the successful relocation of eight orangutans to a safe place after forest fires on the island of Borneo destroyed the habitat of these endangered primates, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The publication notes that Indonesia is battling the strongest forest fires in 11 years, which have mainly affected the islands of Sumatra and Borneo; the government warned that the fires could continue until November, intensifying due to the El Niño weather phenomenon.
The animals rescued between August and September included three pairs of mothers with their offspring and two adolescent males; they were removed from several different locations, according to a joint statement by the Indonesian government and the conservation foundation Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI).
"The relocation to the Batu-Nyambu protected forest is expected to give these eight orangutans a chance to return to life in the wild," the statement said.
According to the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), orangutans are great apes on the verge of extinction; in the wild, they are found only on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra (Southeast Asia), with Indonesia being home to all three recognized species of these animals. Their populations have declined due to deforestation, fires, and poaching.
The relocation operation took six hours by car, one hour by boat, and another two hours on foot; the orangutans were transported in cages secured to bamboo poles. Before the transport, YIARI specialists checked the animals' health.
According to Murlan Dameria Pane, head of the West Kalimantan Natural Resources Conservation Agency, since August the agency, together with YIARI, has rescued 46 orangutans affected by the fires.
From January to July of this year, fires in Indonesia destroyed approximately 202,000 hectares (500,000 acres) of land. Official data for the following months have not yet been released; however, according to estimates by nongovernmental organizations, the fires have since destroyed at least another 600,000 hectares of forest. Smoke from the fires caused 175,000 cases of respiratory illness in Indonesia; the haze also spread to neighboring Singapore and Malaysia, where many schools were closed on Friday due to deteriorating air quality.
Recall
As UNN reported, forest fires in Indonesia are affecting an important research area where orangutans on the island of Borneo are studied, and now threaten a renowned scientific camp—the site of one of the world's longest-running studies of wild great apes.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to "get a new leader" following Volodymyr Zelenskyy's criticism of Washington’s decision to ease Russian diesel sanctions, as Trump faces surging fuel prices ahead of midterm elections.
Trump, whose Republicans face dim prospects in next month's vote partly because of soaring energy costs, defended a deal allowing more Russian diesel onto global markets after saying Vladimir Putin strongly wanted to reach a settlement in Ukraine.
Trump accused Zelenskyy of blocking a deal with Moscow and ignoring instructions not to strike Russian refineries, while Kyiv and its European allies warned that easing pressure on Moscow would help fund the Kremlin's war.
Meanwhile, the latest Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least 21 people, including children.
Trump announced Friday that he had spoken to Putin and agreed Russia would release large amounts of diesel into global markets.
Ukraine and its European allies expressed dismay, with Zelenskyy telling reporters Friday it was a "weak decision."
Asked about the criticism, Trump said Zelenskyy had disobeyed his orders not to strike Russian refineries and that the attacks risked worsening fuel shortages linked to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
"He better damn well stop," Trump said.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals that, for some reason, he never does," Trump said.
Trump later said Putin was interested in ending the war.
"Russia would like to make a deal ... but for whatever reason, Zelenskyy does not want to make a deal," he told reporters.
"President Putin would like to see a settlement, strongly."
The U.S. president also criticized Zelenskyy for not holding an election since Russia's 2022 invasion.
"I think he should have an election and he could have settled this thing many times," Trump said.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said lifting sanctions on Russian diesel would only help sustain Russia's war effort.
"This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't," she wrote online.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated his "complete solidarity" with Zelenskyy in a call.
Downing Street said Burnham also pledged that Britain would "strengthen its sanctions on Russia."
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga also backed his president. "He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide," he said in a post on X.
On Saturday, a Russian glide bomb attack on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia killed 20 people, including three children, according to Ukraine's state rescue service.
"Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
A Russian drone attack in the central Dnipropetrovsk region killed an 11-year-old boy, regional officials said.
Russian strikes also caused widespread power cuts in Kyiv.
Russia's Defense Ministry said it had hit a "data center" used by Ukraine's military.
The diesel deal was announced as U.S., Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami in a renewed bid to end the conflict.
Ukraine's delegation was headed home on Saturday, an aide to Zelenskyy said.
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said on X the talks involved "the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO."
He described the discussions as "constructive" and focused on ways to "de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace."
The Kremlin said Saturday that Trump had conveyed his ideas about how to de-escalate the war to Putin during a phone call Friday.
Putin received the proposals "with understanding," the Kremlin said, without elaborating.
Russia, which launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, now occupies roughly one-fifth of Ukrainian territory.

Gurdwara body files complaint against Kejriwal, AAP workers for 'disrupting' Bangla Sahib's sanctity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:26:23 UTC
19:26:23 KST

DSGMC chief accuses Keriwal's AAP of “dirty politics” over protest attempt inside Gurudwara Bangla Sahib, says "not arena for your politics”
NEW DELHI: The Delhi Sikh Gurdwara Management Committee (DSGMC) on Sunday approached the Delhi Police with a complaint against Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) leaders, including party chief Arvind Kejriwal, accusing them of disrupting the sanctity of Gurudwara Bangla Sahib and spreading "misleading" videos of the incident during Saturday's anti-CEC protests.The controversy erupted after a group of protesters gathered inside the gurdwara premises while attempting to reach Jantar Mantar to demonstrate against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. Police stopped them from proceeding and detained them.In its complaint, the DSGMC alleged that AAP workers and supporters entered the gurdwara and staged protests, creating a disturbance and using the sacred premises for political purposes."The protesters also raised political slogans inside the sacred premises, disturbing the religious atmosphere and violating the sanctity and maryada of Guru Ghar. Such deliberate political activity inside a revered place of worship has deeply hurt the religious sentiments of the Sikh Sangat," the complaint read as per news agency PTI.
DSGMC seeks action against protesters
A delegation of DSGMC office-bearers, led by president Harmeet Singh Kalka, submitted the complaint at the office of the Deputy Commissioner of Police for New Delhi district.
The delegation also provided videos purportedly showing protesters inside Gurudwara Bangla Sahib.The committee urged the police to identify those seen in the footage and investigate who had organised and directed them to enter the premises."We request Delhi Police to identify each of these persons from the videos, ascertain who mobilised, organised and directed them to enter the Gurdwara premises, and take appropriate legal action against all those involved," the DSGMC said.The complaint further accused AAP leaders and MLAs of sharing videos on social media that allegedly presented a "distorted version" of the incident and blamed the gurdwara management."Arvind Kejriwal also publicly supported and amplified this narrative, despite the conduct of his party workers and the circumstances leading to the disturbance being visible from the available material," it alleged.The DSGMC said the incident and the subsequent circulation of "selective and misleading" videos raised concerns about a possible coordinated attempt to trigger controversy at a place of worship, hurt religious sentiments, damage the committee's reputation and gain political mileage.
Row over police entry into gurdwara
Kalka also raised concerns over the conduct of police personnel who entered the gurdwara premises to detain the protesters. He alleged that policemen accompanying Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann had worn shoes when he visited Bangla Sahib.However, Kalka clarified that the Delhi Police personnel had used a passage inside the premises to reach the protesters and had not entered the Darbar Hall, the gurdwara's main sanctum. He added that the policemen should not have entered the premises in uniform.The police, meanwhile, offered a different account of the incident.Deputy Commissioner of Police (New Delhi) Sachin Sharma said in a post on X on Saturday that the personnel had walked through a common passage used by devotees to reach the designated area where they remove their shoes before entering the gurdwara.Sharma also alleged that the video circulating on social media had been shared with "malicious intent" and assured that legal action would be initiated against those responsible.
Bhagwant Mann backs protesters
AAP leaders had alleged that the police entered the gurdwara to detain protesters who had taken shelter there.Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann also defended the protesters' presence inside Bangla Sahib in a post on X, condemning the police action.
"I strongly condemn in the harshest terms the BJP's police forcibly entering Gurdwara Sri Bangla Sahib in Delhi yesterday..." he said.Mann argued that gurdwaras had traditionally opened their doors to people in need and said protesters should have been offered shelter."If the youth of this country protesting yesterday had entered there, the principle of the Guru's house is that the sevadars would grant them shelter...," he said.The competing allegations have turned the incident into a dispute over both the conduct of the protesters and the police response, with the DSGMC seeking an investigation into the events inside the gurdwara and the videos subsequently circulated online.

Yemen's Houthis renew warning over Saudi airports after deadly Riyadh attack
DUBAI/RIYADH, Oct 11 - Yemen's Houthis warned airlines, travellers and airport workers on Sunday to stay away from Saudi airports, a day after an attack on Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 others.
It was the deadliest such attack in the kingdom in more than a decade and comes amid an escalation of fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.
"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina," the Houthis said in a post on X.
"We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions."
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war on Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.
The Saudi-led coalition said on Saturday that a projectile had also fallen near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, in the kingdom's Eastern Province. The coalition also reported intercepting a drone in the region on Sunday.
INTERNATIONAL ENERGY CONFERENCE STILL GOING AHEAD IN RIYADH
Saturday's attack has forced the temporary closure of King Khalid International Airport but the Saudi energy ministry said a long-planned international energy conference was still going ahead in Riyadh on Sunday.
The five-day WPC Energy Congress is taking place at a convention centre some 10 km (6 miles) from the airport. State TV said more than 70 ministers, 300 company executives and representatives of over 25 international energy organisations have confirmed their attendance.
It was not immediately clear whether the participants would attend in person or virtually.
A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum is also set to go ahead on Sunday, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors, according to a media advisory. No further details were immediately available.
Separately, Saudi authorities notified parents that in-person classes would be suspended and shifted to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday for all students, teachers and administrative staff.
In Saturday's attack, the third on Riyadh's airport in a week, the 12 dead included 4 Saudis, 2 Bangladeshis and nationals of the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, Saudi authorities said.
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said airport operations were temporarily suspended pending damage and safety assessments, without specifying when flights would resume.
Two previous attacks on Riyadh's international airport earlier in the week had killed four people and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac. REUTERS

According to a preliminary assessment shared by IPPAN, an association of private-sector power developers in Nepal, four hydropower projects along the Budhi Gandaki River and its streams have been affected.
The Budhi Gandaki Hydropower Project suffered damage to its main camp, which was swept away by the floodwaters, IPPAN said. Some construction equipment was also washed away.
Similarly, the Dobhan Khola Hydropower Project sustained damage to some houses in its camp area, while a Bailey bridge used for construction work at the project site was swept away, the association said.
A Bailey bridge supporting construction work at the Yaru Khola Hydropower Project was also damaged, while construction materials and equipment were washed away.
The Machha Khola Hydropower Project sustained damage to its access road and the bridge connecting the project site, according to the assessment.
Nepal has witnessed multiple floods caused by landslides over the past month following the devastating floods of Aug. 26. The disaster has claimed 1,455 lives, while 5,285 people remain missing, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. ■

Update: 109 dead, over 116 missing after boat capsizes off Djibouti coast: IOM
China
Unknown Publisher

19:21:17 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- At least 109 migrants, including 15 children, have died and more than 116 others remain missing after a boat carrying 350 capsized off the coast of Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Sunday.
The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized during the night between Thursday and Friday. IOM teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance, according to the United Nations organization.
"This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives," said Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti. "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities."
Among the 109 bodies recovered are 52 men, 42 women and 15 children. More than 80 people survived the shipwreck, all Ethiopian nationals, the United Nations migration agency said in its statement released on Sunday, adding that Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations as fears grow for those still missing.
Local authorities are also providing medical care to survivors and arranging dignified burials for those who died, according to the statement.
The latest boat accident is one of many similar deadly calamities that have occurred in Djibouti's Red Sea coast area. In most of these incidents, desperate East African migrants attempted to cross the dangerous route, hoping to reach the Middle East via war-torn Yemen, with the main destination being Yemen's northern neighbor, Saudi Arabia. ■

DUBAI/RIYADH – Yemen’s Houthis warned airlines, travellers and airport workers on Oct 11 to stay away from Saudi airports, a day after an attack on Riyadh’s international airport killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 others.
It was the deadliest such attack in the kingdom in more than a decade and comes amid an escalation of fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi militants and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.
“We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina,” the Houthis said in a post on X.
“We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions.”

Interview: Georgian Conductor Nikoloz Rachveli on Music, Ukraine and Solidarity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:17:00 UTC
19:17:00 KST

For Nikoloz Rachveli, music has long transcended the concert stage. The Georgian conductor, pianist and composer, who has worked with musicians and orchestras across the world, made supporting Ukrainians part of his artistic and civic commitment after Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
On Feb. 24, 2022, the rehearsal hall of the Georgian Philharmonic Orchestra in Tbilisi spontaneously became a gathering place for a massive show of solidarity with Ukraine. In late May 2022, Rachveli traveled to Kyiv with singer Nino Katamadze and performed in the metro, on a stage between the tracks, for Ukrainians living through the war.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Since then, he has repeatedly returned to Ukraine, performing in Kyiv, Lviv, Odesa, Kharkiv, Poltava, Dnipro, Ivano-Frankivsk, Uzhhorod, Chernivtsi, Zhytomyr, Lutsk and Rivne. He has worked with Ukrainian musicians while introducing audiences back home in Georgia to Ukrainian classical music.
Today, Rachveli speaks about Ukraine as a country to which he feels connected not only through music but also through a profound sense of personal responsibility.
Kyiv Post: Feb. 24, 2022, marked the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. In Georgia, musicians rallied around you and Nino Katamadze. How did that response begin?
Nikoloz Rachveli: On Feb. 23, we had a rehearsal with the Georgian Philharmonic Orchestra. There was a sense of tension; everyone was expecting something terrible to happen. One of the orchestra musicians suggested adding a piece by a Ukrainian composer to the program. On Feb. 24, I was planning to listen to Ukrainian works and choose one.
There Will be no Breakthrough in Peace Talks, - Stefan Korshak
But early that morning, we woke up to the horrifying news. Everyone in the orchestra’s group chat was writing that something terrible was happening. We decided to gather in the rehearsal hall, if only to be together. I posted on Facebook that the doors were open to everyone.
By 10 a.m., musicians from different Georgian orchestras were already on stage. Around 800 to 900 people arrived, carrying flags and banners and bringing yellow-and-blue flowers.
We went live. Nino Katamadze came, along with other singers, soloists, opposition politicians and television crews. The rehearsal hall became the epicenter of support for Ukraine in Georgia.
We reached out to musical communities around the world and began performing the national anthems of Ukraine and Georgia. Nino sang “Chornobryvtsi” (“Black-Eyed Susans”), and we concluded with music by Giya Kancheli.
It later became clear that our gathering was the first initiative of this scale organized by an artistic community anywhere in the world. It became one of the symbols of support for Ukraine.
When did you decide that you wanted to come to Ukraine in person?
I felt that urge immediately. On the evening of Feb. 24, I was calling friends and asking what we could do. I had this impulse: “Give me a weapon. I want to fight.” The same instinct had awakened in me in 2008.
When Russia attacked Ukraine, all the unhealed wounds in Georgians opened up again. I wanted to take up arms, but my friends in the military talked me out of it.
                                                                                                                                                                         Nikoloz Rachveli, Nino Katamadze, Lviv National Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra “INSO-Lviv”. (Image courtesy of Nikoloz Rachveli’s personal archive)                             
Because music can be a weapon, too.
Exactly. I focused on charity and artistic work. In early April 2022, we organized a major televised fundraising marathon and invited artists and musicians from Ukraine, including the Lviv-based INSO-Lviv orchestra and Jamala. All Georgian television channels broadcast the event.
People could donate to the account of the Embassy of Ukraine in Georgia. Across several such initiatives, we raised around $500,000.
In late May, Sofiko Chkonia, founder of Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Tbilisi, suggested organizing a trip to Ukraine. She brought Nino and me together, and we decided to go.
We discovered that Ukrainians and Georgians share a powerful, deeply rooted – almost genetic – longing for freedom. That is what makes our peoples spiritually related.
You and Nino Katamadze performed in the Kyiv metro at the time. It was a very special concert for all of us.
Looking back on my life, that concert was the most special, the most important and the most emotionally intense performance I had ever given, before or since.
Because of the security situation, we were offered the opportunity to perform in the metro. I remember Kyiv with almost no cars on the streets and restaurants and cafés closed. The management of the Fairmont hotel took us in, even though nobody was working there apart from one person who opened the doors for us. They brought us bread, and we made our own sandwiches.
Bono had performed at Maidan Nezalezhnosti metro station shortly before us. Later, our musical program took place there, too. I asked some dear Ukrainian friends who play string instruments to join us. That is how the Ukrainian-Georgian performance came together.
Our stage was between the tracks. The trains did not stop, but the drivers were asked to slow down. We could see people inside the carriages.
They recognized Nino, waved to us and made heart signs with their hands. We also performed for military personnel returning from the front and for field medical staff.
It was incredible. Nothing like that happens in ordinary life.
Later, we performed together in Lviv in support of Ukraine. We returned to Georgia and realized that we wanted to come back to Ukraine again. Since then, I have personally crossed the Ukrainian border 29 times and served as musical director for approximately 50 events.
                                                                                                                                                                         Nikoloz Rachveli, Sviatoslav Vakarchuk, Jamala and Nino Katamadze. (Image courtesy of Nikoloz Rachveli’s personal archive)                             
How has the war changed your understanding of music?
My understanding has changed profoundly. But it is not just my attitude toward music that has changed. My attitude toward life itself and toward the people who perform music has changed, too.
Previously, the most important things for me were the concept of a concert, the composition and the performance. Now, the person comes first – the person with whom I create music or for whom I create it.
When you are in Ukraine, especially in Kyiv, rehearsing with colleagues who risk their lives every day, you come to rehearsal after a terrifying night and look around, wondering: Is everyone here today?
I remember a concert last year. There had been a massive attack before the dress rehearsal. That morning, on stage, I began quietly counting the children – we were rehearsing with the Shchedryk choir – to make sure that everyone who had been there the day before had returned.
Later, I heard the story of a little girl who refused to go to a shelter with her father because she could not leave her mother, who has a disability, alone. The entire family stayed at home.
There are so many stories like these. Today, I understand the word “life” differently.
Here, life means constant risk. You never know what might happen in an hour, or even in a minute. That is why I have learned to value every moment in an entirely different way.
What power does music have under such circumstances?
Just look at our concert – the closing event of Kyiv Music Fest 2026, titled “Let There Be Light,” on Oct. 3. In this bleak psychological state, music gave both the audience and those of us on stage an extraordinary, boundlessly positive energy.
                                                                                                                                                                         Closing concert of Kyiv Music Fest 2026, “Let There Be Light,” Oct. 3. The Academic Symphony Orchestra of the National Philharmonic of Ukraine, conducted by Nikoloz Rachveli of Georgia, with the Dumka National Choir and soloist Bohdana Pivnenko. (Image via Dmytro and Viktoriia Holovchenko)                             
It helps us survive, stand firm, keep hope alive for the future and stay sane. That is why I value the power of music so deeply.
Composer Giya Kancheli played a special role in your life. During a recent performance of Styx in Kyiv, you found it difficult to remain at the conductor’s podium during one of the rehearsals. What happened?
After a terrible night of shelling, I heard the Dumka choir for the first time at rehearsal. Those wonderful singers had come and were singing in my native Georgian. As I conducted, I was so overwhelmed by emotion that I lost my composure and began to cry.
The story of Styx is unique for me. When Giya Kancheli wrote the piece in 1999, he specifically added a piano part to the orchestration for me. I was 19 and in my first year at the Vienna Academy of Music. Even then, Kancheli supported me enormously and had great hopes for my future as a composer and conductor.
He insisted that orchestras invite me to perform the piano part at every premiere of Styx. So, 27 years ago, I became one of the musicians who first brought the work to life, performing it in many countries around the world.
Later, I conducted Styx myself in concert halls internationally. When you perform a piece very often, it becomes almost your own. But this time in Kyiv, I experienced every measure and every note differently. Everything felt deeper, warmer and, at the same time, more emotionally intense.
My feelings were transmitted to the orchestra musicians and the choir, and then to the audience. The performance prompted unusually prolonged applause, cries of emotion and genuine tears – on stage and in the hall alike.
You knew Giya Kancheli for many years. What was your creative friendship like?
In 2002, an idea emerged in Georgia to create a stage production based on Kancheli’s music for film and theater. I proposed new arrangements and orchestration, along with vocal, theatrical and choreographic elements.
The premiere took place at the Tbilisi Opera Theatre in 2003 and played to full houses for several consecutive days. The project introduced a new generation to Kancheli’s music. Giya often thanked me for bringing this part of his work back to life on stage and giving it a new existence.
For my career, Giya was the key person who helped me move from Georgia onto the international stage. When orchestras in other countries commissioned works from him, he recommended me to them. That is how I began conducting premieres of Kancheli’s compositions with European orchestras.
Toward the end of his life, he told me something incredibly important: When he composed music, he could already imagine it being performed under my baton, in my interpretation.
For a performer, that is the highest recognition an author of his stature can offer.
                                                                                                                                                                         Nikoloz Rachveli and Giya Kancheli. (Image courtesy of Nikoloz Rachveli’s personal archive)                             
One of your main areas of work today is Ukrainian music. What are your plans in this field?
One of my main goals is to perform Ukrainian composers’ works more frequently in Georgia. At the end of November, I will conduct a concert in Tbilisi with our orchestra featuring works by Hanna Havrylets, Bohdana Frolyak, Liubava Sydorenko and other Ukrainian composers.
The Soviet Union did a great deal to ensure that almost nothing was known in Georgia about Ukrainian symphonic and chamber music. The past four and a half years have been a period of constantly discovering new Ukrainian names and compositions for me.
In Lviv, I worked with INSO-Lviv on the Genocode project, which tells the story of Ukrainian classical music through excerpts from symphonic, chamber and operatic works.
That is why I see my mission as more than allowing the war to unite us in resisting Russian imperial policy. Creativity must unite us, too.
Ukrainian audiences know and love Georgian dances and music. I want people in Georgia to know and love Ukrainian composers just as much, and to look forward to hearing their music performed. I have already organized a Ukrainian music festival in Tbilisi twice. Now I am planning a third edition.
                                                                                                                                                                         Nikoloz Rachveli. (Image via Dmytro and Viktoriia Holovchenko)                             
You spend much of your time abroad. How has the political situation in Georgia affected your life and work?
Yes. The political situation in Georgia has become extremely tense. Friends of mine – artists, directors, writers and journalists – are in prison because of their active participation in protests. Among them is Paata Burchuladze, a legend of the international opera world. Unfortunately, our country is beginning to resemble Belarus under Lukashenko.
At the same time, our orchestra and concert hall remain oases of freedom, places from which free speech can still be heard, along with a handful of media outlets. But more and more musicians, including members of our orchestra, are receiving heavy fines for taking part in protests.
Democracy and Georgia’s movement toward the West have weakened considerably. Nevertheless, I still do not want to believe that members of the Georgian government are pro-Russian at heart. I think some are driven by fear of war, while others are motivated by financial interests. This part of society accounts for no more than 15 percent of our population, but unfortunately, it is the group holding the levers of power.
Still, I would like to end our conversation in a major key. We need to imagine positive scenarios. What future do you dream of for Ukraine and Georgia?
Since you mentioned the word “dream,” yes, I have one: I want Ukraine and Georgia to share a common border. (Smiles.)
It is a playful dream, but if you look deeper into history, the territories between us were once connected to both Ukraine and Georgia. Perhaps, if that happened, historical justice would be restored.
We are already neighbors and brothers in spirit. I want us to become geographical neighbors, too. (Smiles.)
Seriously, though, I dream that future generations of Ukrainians and Georgians will live peacefully and without fear, will not be afraid of their neighbors and will not have to pass this struggle on to their children.
I very much want Russia to break apart as an empire and for a democratic society to emerge there afterward. Geographically, we are neighbors, and there is no escaping that reality. That is why it is important for Russia to change not only its politics but also its mindset – to acknowledge its crimes and undergo a process of moral cleansing.
After World War II, German society underwent serious work in this regard. A country that committed the Holocaust has become a model state in protecting European values and now supports Ukraine so strongly.
Of course, it is difficult for me to imagine Russia accomplishing this. But first and foremost, it must suffer a crushing defeat. Only then will its society have a chance at moral salvation.
Ukraine had already won when the enemy failed to capture Kyiv – of course, at the cost of countless lives and thanks to its extraordinary heroes. Knowing the character of the Ukrainian people, I believe in victory to the very end, a victory that will bring Ukraine a bright future. And a bright future for Ukraine also means a bright future for my homeland.
                                                                                                                                                                         Bohdana Pivnenko, Nikoloz Rachveli, Mariana Holovko and the Kyiv Camerata National Ensemble of Soloists. (Image via Bouquet Kyiv Stage)                             
Ukraine’s victory is essential to the history of humanity and the history of religions. It must show future generations that evil can be defeated by good. Otherwise, everything on which our civilization rests will lose its meaning.
Glory to Ukraine!
Glory to Georgia!
Glory to the heroes of our two countries!

Labour has got the message – developing nations suffer most from bond market turmoil | Heather Stewart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:11:19 UTC
19:11:19 KST

From Washington to Paris, London to Tokyo, policymakers in every large economy have been counting the costs of bond market turmoil in recent weeks. But the brunt of the pain is being borne by heavily indebted developing countries that have little hope of influencing the whims of global investors, but pay the price regardless.
Markets have responded to the war in the Middle East, and a spendthrift White House, by dumping government bonds – driving up borrowing costs just about everywhere.
Finance ministers and central bankers gathering in Bangkok this week for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank may be loth to point the finger at Donald Trump’s regime, but all are at least in part hostage to the US president’s war plans.
That has made what was already a perilous situation even worse – just as the world is battling an energy crisis, and as developing countries urgently need to invest in adapting to the climate emergency.
Even before the latest market gyrations, experts calculated that debt servicing costs absorbed 45% of government revenues in the global south, and 70% in low-income countries. That crowds out desperately needed spending on public services and investing for the future.
There have been growing demands for reform of the framework for international debt in recent years, including from African Union heads of state, and under the G20 chairs of Brazil and South Africa.
The G20 – the forum in which Gordon Brown coordinated a global fiscal stimulus package in the depths of the financial crisis in spring 2009 – is meant to be an important body for discussing international economic issues. With a much wider membership than the G7, it has coordinated previous efforts on debt, including establishing the IMF-administered Common Framework, to which struggling countries can apply, and suspending repayments for hard-hit borrowers during the Covid crisis.
However, this year’s chair has been Trump’s US, which has placed much more emphasis on other aspects of the G20’s remit, including promoting global economic growth – somewhat ironically, given the main obstacle to achieving it is the war on Iran.
Next year, the presidency falls to the UK, and Labour has made clear it will have different priorities. These will include seeking a global agreement on AI regulation, which seems a faint hope but is clearly worth pursuing.
The UK also intends to put unsustainable debt on the agenda. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, who will be in Bangkok, told Labour conference delegates last month: “Friends, I promise this. We will use our G20 presidency next year to meet our responsibilities and mobilise the world, building on the great achievements on debt and development of the last Labour government.”
He was referring to 2005, when Brown and Tony Blair rode the vociferous Make Poverty History movement to the Gleneagles G8 summit and beyond, securing significant debt relief for more than 30 countries.
As the development minister, Kirsty McNeill, herself a veteran of that campaign, said recently, the circumstances now are very different, for two reasons. First, she said, “we’re now dealing with private creditors – the debt isn’t held by us. So that is quite a big shift.” And second, she suggested it was harder now to delineate a group of countries clearly deserving of support.
“There isn’t this really clear demarcation between the very poor world and the very rich world that was true when I was starting out, and it was just a much starker and therefore more readily told story because the antagonists and the protagonists were just much clearer,” she told an event at the Labour conference.
Yet she and other ministers have made clear they are open to proposals – and ready to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind making progress on this formidable challenge.
One ambitious plan drawn up by the thinktank Development Finance International (DFI) and shared with the government would involve 27 of the most heavily burdened countries being given a 10-year “holiday” during which their debt service costs would be slashed to below 10% of their revenues.
Implemented by cutting interest rates and extending loan terms rather than writing off debt altogether, the $13bn-a-year cost would fall primarily on private creditors – which might have to be coaxed, cajoled, perhaps even legislated into taking part, as in previous debt relief initiatives.
The “hope initiative” also envisages potential relief for another six small island developing states that do not meet the threshold on the basis of their debt burden but are regularly battered by natural disasters. These could be offered a five-year “holiday” from the moment of the next extreme weather event they face, at the cost of a further $700m a year.
An even more expansive version would embrace another five countries, including Pakistan and Angola.
Crucially, because the international financial institutions – including the IMF and the World Bank – tend to be preferred creditors, only chipping in when other help is exhausted, the costs to them would be relatively low.
Echoing Andy Burnham’s slogan – so far confined to the domestic sphere – Matthew Martin, DFI’s executive director and the author of the plan, says: “Let’s bring hope back to the poorest countries in the world, through an ambitious but financially and politically feasible initiative, which will free up $13bn for them to spend on their climate and development goals.”
It remains to be seen how bold the government is prepared to be in setting its G20 agenda, but the groundwork is being done.
Labour trashed its reputation as a champion for international development when Keir Starmer took the axe to aid spending to pay for defence. Perhaps 2027 could be the year Burnham starts to rebuild it.
