Excavations resume at ancient Tyana Roman Baths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:30:06 UTC
17:30:06 KST

AA Photo
Excavations have resumed at the Roman Baths in the ancient city of Tyana, located in the town of Kemerhisar in Türkiye’s central province of Niğde’s Bor district, following a 20-year hiatus.
The work, conducted under the Turkish Culture and Tourism Ministry’s Heritage for the Future Project, aims to identify earlier phases of the baths and uncover associated structures, such as a palaestra (an exercise area or courtyard) or a gymnasium (a center for physical and intellectual education).
Archaeologists also hope to uncover evidence of cultural activity dating to well before Roman rule.
Osman Doğanay, head of the Tyana Excavation Team and a professor in the Department of Archaeology at Aksaray University’s Faculty of Arts and Sciences, told state-run Anadolu Agency that excavations at the Roman Baths had resumed after a two-decade hiatus.
Doganay noted that at least two other baths are believed to exist in the ancient city beyond the complex currently being excavated, adding that efforts to locate them would begin.
Tyana was a major metropolitan center in Cappadocia during the Roman period, and the baths under excavation were built by Emperor Caracalla in AD 213, he said.
“Changes were also made to the structure of these baths during the reigns of emperors who succeeded Caracalla. We can confirm this with certainty,” Doğanay said.
Excavations at the baths began in 2002 and continued for four years, uncovering numerous remains and artifacts. Researchers have since established the structure’s layout and confirmed that it was a public bathhouse, he said.
Located on the southern slopes of Tyana Mound, the baths were positioned to receive the greatest amount of heat, Doğanay said.
He added that archaeologists believe the complex received a significant portion of the water carried by aqueducts from the Roman Pool, citing water pipes discovered during excavations between the pool and the baths.
HH Bronze Age layer discovered beneath baths
Doğanay said the primary objective of the current excavation season was to identify earlier phases of the bath complex. Much of the work this year has focused on clearing layers of rubble and debris from the site.
Test excavations extending nearly 2 meters below the surface revealed that the baths had been built over a Bronze Age layer, he said.
“In our upcoming work, we will uncover all the sections of the baths and determine whether structures associated with sporting activities, such as a palaestra and a gymnasium, are present.
“At the same time, we expect to find important evidence of the city’s cultural heritage dating to periods long before the Roman era,” Doğanay said.
He added that measures were being taken during the excavations to protect the structure.
The team also hopes to make the historic Roman Baths a new regional tourist attraction.
“There is no comparable bath complex of this kind in the Cappadocia region. As part of our efforts to promote Tyana as a destination for tourism and contribute to the regional economy, we are working to include the Roman Baths in visitor routes through the ancient city and establish the complex as a destination in its own right,” Doğanay said.

The Saudi-led coalition vowed a decisive response Sunday after a strike at Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people, wounded hundreds, marking the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in over a decade.
The coalition blamed the Iran-backed group for the strike on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a "full-fledged war crime" that a diplomatic source attributed to a missile.
The attack came during an unprecedented wave of Houthi strikes on the kingdom since a truce in the group's long-running war with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government unraveled in July.
The spiraling violence has raised the possibility of a wider escalation, with U.S. President Donald Trump signalling Washington could join military action against the fighters.
One passenger said they witnessed a strike in the airport's domestic terminal.
"I was on gate 403," the witness said. "I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."
Four Saudi citizens were among those killed in the attack, as well as two Bangladeshis, one U.S. citizen, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said in a statement.
It said some of the 309 wounded were in serious condition.
Operations at the airport were suspended following the attack and authorities said damage assessments were ongoing.
The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the "serious emergency situation," a medical source said.
Two doctors told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that several pilgrims headed to Mecca were among the wounded.
Schools in Riyadh switched to remote learning for the second time in a month.
Parents in the capital received emails Sunday, citing an order from the education ministry, saying "all schools in Riyadh will switch to distance learning for the entire week".
"The cowardly terrorist attack by the Terrorist Houthi Militia ... which resulted in deaths and injuries among civilian passengers and airport staff, constitutes a full-fledged war crime," coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said in a statement on X.
Earlier, the coalition said it had intercepted missiles targeting Saudi Arabia and destroyed launch platforms.
The Houthis claimed a series of attacks targeting the airport Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not immediately take responsibility for any new strikes Saturday.
Saturday's attack was the deadliest in the kingdom since May 2015, when a suicide bombing by the Daesh terrorist group killed 21 worshippers in a Shiite mosque in the eastern Qatif governorate.
The civil war in Yemen flared back to life in July after a four-year, U.N.-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015 and is now being drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbor's conflict.
Asked Saturday whether he had changed his mind about joining Saudi strikes on the group, Trump said: "We may."
He said he would be speaking with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, calling what happened in the kingdom "not acceptable."
U.S. media outlets have reported that previous Saudi requests for U.S. military assistance in dealing with the Houthis have been rebuffed.
The U.S., Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia warned their citizens to avoid the airport.
A senior Western diplomat told AFP that several embassies were banning their staff from using the airport "over the next week."

The latest attack came on the eve of Saudi Arabia's high-profile convention and entertainment season, which begins this month.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas the group captured last month around the Bab el-Mandeb strait, military sources told AFP.
The Yemeni government last week announced a counteroffensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis.
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab el-Mandeb area – a key choke point for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping – but claimed to have repelled them.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

Two Renoir paintings stolen in France recovered: mayor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:29:52 UTC
17:29:52 KST

Two paintings by French master Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been recovered a month after they were stolen from a museum in southern France, the town’s mayor has said.
In September, thieves broke into the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer and managed to escape with two works by the French impressionist painter, abandoning two others as they fled.
“These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city’s history,” said Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer.
“Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief.”
There has not yet been any statement from the police and Masson did not give any details regarding where the works were found or their condition.
The suspects cut through a fence to enter the museum’s tree-lined grounds, smashed a window to get inside, and used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings, Masson said at the time of the robbery in early September.
The theft took place in just a matter of minutes, shortly before 6 a.m. 
A source close to the probe told AFP earlier this week that police had arrested five people as part of the investigation.
According to Masson the museum alarm and police sirens forced the burglars, which he described as “well equipped and well informed” about the museum, to hurry.
They made off with a portrait titled “Madame Colonna Romano” and the depiction of a woman at a well called “Jeune femme au puits,” his office said.
The paintings dropped during their escape include “Madame Pichon” and “Coco lisant,” a portrait of Renoir’s young son Claude reading.
The police said at the time of the robbery that it was clear that they were not first-time offenders, and that they had scoped out the premises before the crime.
The Renoir Museum lies a half-hour drive from the southern city of Nice, in Renoir’s last home before he died aged 78 in 1919. Its collection comprises nine paintings by Renoir, according to the museum.
It also includes several sculptures by him, as well as objects and furniture that belonged to the painter, such as his easel and wheelchair.

Angus Taylor became the first sitting Opposition leader to address the Australian Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in Brisbane on Saturday as the Coalition and One Nation vied for the fractured right-wing vote.

Dimitar Paskov: The Bulgarian scientist who pioneered a treatment for polio

BG contribution
Dimitar Paskov: The Bulgarian scientist who pioneered a treatment for polio
His development of Nivalin earned him international recognition and helped pave the way for a medicine still used today
Sunday 11 October 2026 10:35
Sunday, 11 October 2026, 10:35
PHOTO Facebook / BNT
Font size
At the height of the polio epidemics that swept through the world in the 1950s, a Bulgarian doctor received what seemed like guidance from above – an insight that would offer hope to children facing lifelong paralysis.
According to a widely told story, he noticed a sudden improvement in the condition of a young girl who had drunk water from a glass of snowdrops standing on her bedside table in hospital. From this apparent coincidence came an idea that would help bring about an important advance in the treatment of polio-related paralysis, thanks to a medicine called Nivalin.
PHOTO Pixabay
The story of the remarkable Bulgarian doctor Dimitar Paskov begins on 18 October 1914 in the village of Gorno Brodi, near what is now the Greek city of Serres. After the First World War, Aegean Macedonia remained outside Bulgaria's borders, and his family, along with hundreds of thousands of refugees, decided to settle in Sofia.
In 1940, Dimitar Paskov graduated from the Faculty of Medicine at Sofia University and became a doctor in the village of Byaga, in southern Bulgaria. Four years later, he found himself at the front, tending to wounded Bulgarian soldiers. There he earned a reputation as “a universal favourite among soldiers and officers, helping everyone and always having a kind word for all”.
After the Second World War, he chose a career in science and travelled to Leningrad, determined to lay the modern foundations of Bulgaria's school of experimental pharmacology. There he met traditional healers and worked alongside medical specialists conducting research into animals and plants.
Paskov’s book on Nivalin and its applications.
PHOTO Knizhen Pazar
On returning to Bulgaria, Paskov became head of the Department of Pharmacology at the Higher Medical Institute in Sofia. His knowledge of the country's wealth of medicinal plants – a wealth which, he believed, was surpassed only by that of the Himalayas – helped him make his great breakthrough in 1956. His research into plants containing galantamine, including the common snowdrop (Galanthus nivalis) and the summer snowflake (Leucojum aestivum), led to the development of Nivalin, a medicine based on this naturally occurring alkaloid.
“After consuming cooking oil adulterated with machine oil, I fell ill and went blind. I travelled to Vienna, Brussels and London in search of a cure, but without success. I heard that in Bulgaria there was a professor who treated blindness like mine with a medicine derived from snowdrops. I arrived in Bulgaria blind and returned home able to see with both eyes. Three words I shall never forget: snowdrop, Nivalin, Paskov,” the Frenchwoman Marcella Goetz wrote in her diary.
PHOTO mu-sofia.bg
While the medicine was gaining recognition around the world, a bitter campaign was unfolding against Dimitar Paskov in his own country. He was accused of plagiarising the achievements of “great Soviet science” – possibly, according to accounts of the controversy, under Soviet pressure to ensure that the discovery remained Soviet intellectual property. Although Academician Sergei Anichkov, under whom the Bulgarian scientist had defended his doctorate, acknowledged Paskov's contribution to the development of the medicine*, a series of reprisals followed. Paskov was dismissed from his leadership position at the Institute of Experimental Medicine and resigned from the Higher Medical Institute.
Meanwhile, the man who had become the target of envy and intrigue in his own country was winning international recognition for his pioneering contribution to Nivalin, a Bulgarian medicine developed using locally sourced plant material. In 1961, French television broadcast a film about the scientist and his medicine. He was also invited to lecture at the Sorbonne.
A year later, the University of Bologna published Paskov's first work, Pharmacology and Clinical Application of Nivalin. Shortly afterwards, he published a monograph, translated into Italian and Russian, in which he described his research in detail. The work also became a model textbook of experimental pharmacology.
Undoubtedly, his greatest honour was the international Ennio Award for scientific achievement, presented to him in Naples and described as the equivalent of a medical “Oscar”.
PHOTO Pixabay
Dimitar Paskov died in 1986, leaving humanity a medicine whose active ingredient remains in use today. Galantamine is now used particularly in the symptomatic treatment of Alzheimer's disease, while Nivalin has also been employed in treating various neurological and neuromuscular conditions.
His legacy also includes some 120 scientific papers in pharmacology, a textbook for doctors and medical students, 20 inventions and a number of medicinal preparations based on Nivalin. Those who believed they owed their recovery to him expressed their gratitude in many ways. There were even press reports of a newborn girl being given the name Nivalina.
Voted “Person of the Century” by the people of the town of Peshtera, the scientist was laid to rest amid a sea of snowdrops. Thousands came to bid him farewell, lining his final path with the delicate, fragrant flowers whose medicinal properties had helped him bring hope to people suffering from paralysis far beyond Bulgaria's borders.
PHOTO Pixabay
* Although galantamine had previously been isolated and studied by Soviet researchers. Paskov's pioneering pharmacological work, alongside that of his Bulgarian colleagues, helped turn the substance into Nivalin, a medicine used in treating neurological and neuromuscular disorders, including paralysis associated with polio. - Editor's note.

English editor: E. Radkova

Musk promises affordable Starlink in India — whom he wants to outdo

This intensified his criticism of the billionaire rival just days before Jio's parent company plans to conduct the largest initial public offering (IPO) in India's history, UNN reports, citing Reuters.

The strategy of providing cheap mobile internet helped Jio succeed in India; Musk used the same approach in markets such as Kenya to undermine the position of local telecommunications operators. Now SpaceX plans to enter the mobile operator market itself, starting in the United States.
Elon Musk’s SpaceX is negotiating a $40 billion loan for Nvidia chips08.10.26, 03:18 • 6262 views

"In fact, competition will benefit ordinary Indian citizens by giving them more choice, as it always does. Ambani's profits will decrease, but his business will not cease to exist," Musk added.
In addition

What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:22:02 UTC
17:22:02 KST

What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts
Fossil fuels produce 81 percent of global energy. We look at the Middle East’s role and what happens when supplies are cut.
A major energy conference is going ahead in Riyadh from Sunday despite a Houthi attack on the city’s King Khalid International Airport that killed 12 people and injured 309, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said on Sunday that the 25th World Petroleum Council Energy Congress has begun in Riyadh. The 17th International Energy Forum (IEF) Ministerial will be held on the sidelines of the conference, called Riyadh Energy Week, which is to run until Thursday.
But Italy, the cohost of the IEF, will join the meeting via videolink. Nigeria, the other cohost, is sending a representative to the event.
The IEF brings together 68 countries that account for more than 90 percent of global oil and gas supplies and demand. Its members include Saudi Arabia, the United States and Russia. The meeting comes as the US-Israel war on Iran has disrupted energy flows and pushed governments to reassess their energy security.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at where the world’s energy comes from, how much is produced in the Middle East and which countries have strategic reserves to fall back on.
Where does the world’s energy come from?
Energy heats our homes, fuels our cars, keeps the lights on and runs the factories that make what we buy. It comes from fossil fuels such as oil, coal and gas as well as nuclear power and renewables.
Despite rapid growth in renewables, fossil fuels still account for nearly 81 percent of global energy consumption. Oil is the largest source at 31.4 percent, followed by coal at 25.9 percent and natural gas at 23.5 percent. Traditional biomass, nuclear power and other sources make up the rest.
Production is concentrated in a handful of regions, so disruptions in any of them ripple through global markets.
The Middle East is the largest oil-producing region, and North America is the largest natural gas producer. Russia and Central Asia are also major producers of both.
How Middle East energy reaches the world
The Middle East’s importance to energy markets is also about geography. Three narrow waterways connect its producers with consumers around the world.
Before the Iran war, about 27 percent of global seaborne oil trade and almost 20 percent of liquefied natural gas trade transited through the Strait of Hormuz on the eastern side of the Arabian Peninsula.
On the peninsula’s western side, the Bab al-Mandeb strait links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, and the Suez Canal connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean. As the Iran war has spilled over into other areas of the Middle East and Yemen’s civil war has ramped up, traffic has been reduced through both the strait and canal, forcing some energy shipments on longer routes around Africa.
“That’s probably the first time we’ve really seen a major constriction of a chokepoint,” said Richard Matthews, director of consultancy and research at Gibson Shipbrokers, a London-based shipbroking and maritime advisory service.
He told Al Jazeera that what makes the Strait of Hormuz different from other chokepoints is “there is no alternative maritime route. There are some pipelines, but there’s no alternative, which is why it’s been so significant in terms of cargo volume.”
Gulf ports are where much of the region’s energy begins its journey to the rest of the world.
Which countries rely most on Middle East oil?
Further down the supply chain, people and businesses are feeling the disruption through the rising cost of essentials.
Countries that rely on oil, gas and fertiliser from the Gulf face higher prices, longer waits for shipments and the need to find other suppliers. Even where deals have kept goods moving, the extra costs are being passed down the chain.
Eritrea and Madagascar are the most dependent on Middle Eastern oil, each sourcing about 90 percent of their supply from the region. They are followed by Pakistan (78 percent), Japan (77 percent) and Kenya (77 percent).
Which countries rely most on Middle East gas?
Gas has been even harder to replace than oil because most of it travels as liquefied natural gas from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates through the Strait of Hormuz.
Countries that depend on these shipments are paying more for fuel and electricity and competing for a smaller pool of cargoes. Poorer importers with little storage have struggled the most to find alternatives.
The countries that rely most heavily on Middle Eastern gas are mostly in Asia. South Korea sources 31 percent of the gas it uses from the region, followed by India (29 percent), Pakistan (27 percent) and Taiwan (26 percent).
Who has the largest emergency oil reserves?
Countries keep emergency oil stocks for when supplies are cut off or reduced, and these have been the world’s main cushion during the war. That cushion is now wearing thin.
Western countries have little left to release, energy industry leaders warned, and the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest level since 1982.
“Estimates suggest less than 6 billion barrels of commercial inventories remain today with the vast majority not practically available,” Amin Nasser, head of Saudi Aramco, told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday.
The International Energy Agency, which coordinates emergency stocks for its members, released a record 400 million barrels of oil in March. It is now preparing to release another 100 million barrels of crude and diesel to ease soaring diesel prices although some of this may be oil from the March release that has yet to reach the market.
A storm in the Gulf of Mexico and attacks in Saudi Arabia are now threatening supplies again, keeping oil prices above $100 a barrel.
Before this year’s releases, China held by far the largest reserves, an estimated 1.4 billion barrels, more than the rest of the list combined. The US was second with 413 million barrels, followed by Japan with 263 million.

Slovakia and Russia Resume Military Contacts at Attaché Level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:20:00 UTC
17:20:00 KST

Slovakia and Russia have resumed military contacts through their military attachés for the first time since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The Slovak news outlet Aktuality reported the development.
During his visit to Moscow in May, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico promised Russian President Vladimir Putin that Slovakia would restore military-diplomatic ties with Russia.
“We have taken specific steps to resume the work of military attachés at our respective embassies. We purchase significant amounts of energy resources from you, but apparently that is not enough to limit our cooperation to this area alone,” Fico told Putin during his visit to Russia in May 2026.
The opposition had already warned that the government’s efforts to strengthen ties with Russia could be dangerous. The last Russian military attaché stationed in Slovakia was Sergei Solomasov, who was later expelled from the country.
Slovakia has already appointed its military representatives in Moscow. Brigadier General Slavomír Staviarsky will serve as military attaché, with Colonel Ivo Gachir as his deputy.
The new Russian military attaché in Bratislava is likely to be 46-year-old Maksim Verezhan. The naval officer previously served at the Russian Embassy in Rome and has spent the past few years in Moscow.
Following the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Slovakia and Russia expelled each other’s military attachés. Before his expulsion, the Russian attaché was suspected of involvement in a spy case. He allegedly bribed Bohuš Garbar, an employee of the Hlavné správy news website, who spread disinformation at his direction.
Slovak opposition politicians have called the decision a serious mistake and warned about the arrival of a Russian spy. Tomáš Valášek, an MP from the Progressive Slovakia party, says the exchange of military attachés primarily benefits Russia, as Slovakia’s representative is unlikely to have access to sensitive information in Moscow.
Meanwhile, Valášek warns that the Russian military attaché could be given an opportunity to take part in disinformation and influence operations in Slovakia, fuel social tensions, and shape public opinion about Russia.
In September, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico expressed skepticism about invoking Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. He stressed that despite Slovakia’s membership in NATO, he wanted to avoid direct involvement in combat under any circumstances.
“Can you imagine, ladies and gentlemen, invoking Article 5 of the NATO Treaty? Can anyone imagine being told to prepare 5,000 or 10,000 soldiers to go and fight somewhere, without even knowing where they are going, who they are fighting, or what they are fighting for?” Robert Fico said at the time.

Australia gets second batch of HIMARS two years early
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:17:59 UTC
17:17:59 KST

- The Australian Army received a second batch of HIMARS launchers two years ahead of schedule for the 10th Fires Brigade’s regiment in Adelaide.
- Australia plans to field up to 90 HIMARS across two long-range fires regiments, firing GMLRS rockets and Precision Strike Missiles.
The Australian Army has received a second batch of HIMARS rocket launchers from the United States, two years earlier than planned and about a year after the first batch arrived, Australia’s Department of Defence said.
The new launchers are going to the long-range fires regiment of the Army’s 10th Fires Brigade, based in Adelaide. Defence did not say how many launchers were in the second batch or when the next delivery is due. Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said the program is now on track to be fully operational four years ahead of schedule.
HIMARS, short for High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, is a Lockheed Martin-built launcher mounted on a six-wheeled truck. It fires a pod of six GMLRS guided rockets with a range of about 70 km (43 miles), or a Precision Strike Missile, known as PrSM, which Australia says can hit targets up to 500 km (310 miles) away. Defence expects future versions of PrSM to reach beyond 1,000 km (620 miles).
Australia plans to field up to 90 launchers, bought through the U.S. Foreign Military Sales program, across two long-range fires regiments within the 10th Fires Brigade. The first two HIMARS reached Australia in March 2025, and Australian troops fired a PrSM for the first time during Exercise Talisman Sabre in July 2025, two years earlier than originally planned.
In April, the government picked HIMARS and PrSM over a rival bid for a second long-range fires regiment under its LAND 8113 Phase 2 project, committing A$2.3 billion (about $1.6 billion) over the next decade. The new regiment will be based at the Edinburgh Defence Precinct in South Australia. The government says it is spending up to A$37 billion over the decade on targeting and long-range strike capabilities overall.
Australia is also building its own ammunition for the launchers. A GMLRS factory opened at Port Wakefield, South Australia, in December 2025, and in April the Army test-fired the first Australian-made GMLRS rocket from a HIMARS at the Woomera Test Range. Australia is the only country outside the United States producing GMLRS. Canberra and Washington set up a cooperative PrSM program last year, and the government says it plans to expand local production to include PrSM.

17:10:10 KST

- A U.S. fighter jet disabled the Panama-flagged cargo ship Ocean Molica in the Gulf of Oman after it tried to run the blockade of Iran, CENTCOM said.
- CENTCOM says it has disabled four commercial ships and turned back 135 since resuming the blockade on July 14.
A U.S. fighter jet struck and disabled a Panama-flagged cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman on Oct. 10 after its crew ignored repeated warnings and tried to break the American naval blockade of Iran, U.S. Central Command said.
The jet hit the stern of the M/V Ocean Molica, also known as the Arika Sun, with a precision-guided munition, knocking out the ship’s propulsion without injuring the crew, CENTCOM said in a statement posted on X. The command said the vessel had left an Iranian port and was trying to sail on through regional waters. CENTCOM did not say what type of aircraft or weapon was used, what the ship was carrying, how many people were aboard, or what will happen to the vessel now that it cannot move under its own power.
U.S. forces resumed enforcement of the blockade on July 14, targeting all vessels entering or leaving Iranian ports. Since then, CENTCOM says, American forces have disabled four commercial ships, including the Ocean Molica, and turned back 135 others. The command also says it has destroyed 10 tankers it links to a shadow shipping network run by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Disabling strikes have been the main tool for ships that refuse to stop. The first came within a day of the blockade’s resumption, when U.S. aircraft fired Hellfire missiles into the smokestack of the Curacao-flagged tanker Belma as it headed toward Iran’s Kharg Island oil terminal in the Persian Gulf. Aiming at the engine room or stern lets U.S. forces stop a ship without sinking it or targeting the crew.
The Gulf of Oman sits at the southern approach to the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passage between Iran and Oman that before the war carried about a fifth of the world’s oil. Traffic through the strait has fallen sharply during the conflict, with Iran and the United States each claiming control over who can pass.
CENTCOM urged ship crews to follow blockade instructions from U.S. naval forces, monitor Notice to Mariners broadcasts and stay in contact with U.S. warships on bridge-to-bridge radio channel 16 when sailing in the Gulf of Oman and near the Strait of Hormuz.

Istanbul generates more than $800 million from congress tourism since 2022

Congress tourism has generated more than $800 million in foreign currency revenue for Istanbul since 2022, according to Şekib Avdagiç, president of the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce (ITO) and the Istanbul Convention and Visitors Bureau (ICVB).
A total of 67 congresses were held in Istanbul during the first eight months of this year, attracting around 30,000 participants and generating approximately $120 million in revenue from accommodation, transportation, sightseeing, food and beverage services, he noted. He said the number of congress visitors is expected to increase further by the end of the year as activity typically intensifies in the autumn months.
According to Avdagiç, Istanbul has hosted nearly 500 congresses since 2022 with the support of the ICVB.
Around 200,000 congress tourists visited the city during that period, spending up to $4,000 per person and generating more than $800 million in foreign currency income for the local economy.
He noted that the benefits of congress tourism extend beyond hotels, supporting a wide range of businesses including restaurants, retailers, tourist guides and transportation companies. The figure of more than $800 million reflects only direct spending, while the overall economic impact is significantly larger as visitors often extend their stays, return with family members and recommend the city to others, according to Avdagiç.
Avdagiç noted that Istanbul’s infrastructure supports continued growth in the sector, with seven congress centers and three exhibition centers capable of hosting events ranging from meetings of 100 participants to gatherings with more than 30,000 attendees.
He added that the ICVB is continuing its efforts to attract future international congresses to Istanbul across fields including health sciences, engineering, energy and transportation. 
The number of international congresses held in Istanbul increased to 95 in 2025 from 58 in 2022, while the city ranked 18th globally last year, its strongest performance in a decade, Avdagiç said. The long-term goal is to place Istanbul among the world’s top 10 congress destinations, he added.

In Pennsylvania, a man killed eight relatives — children and a pregnant woman among the victims
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

In Pennsylvania, a man killed eight relatives — children and a pregnant woman among the victims
Kyiv • UNN
In the city of Erie, a man shot eight people, including children and a pregnant woman, and then took his own life. Police are investigating the motive.
In the city of Erie, Pennsylvania, a man killed eight people—including a pregnant woman, children, and other relatives—in their home, then committed suicide, UNN reports, citing the AP.
Erie Police Chief Rick Lora said the 45-year-old man was related to seven of the eight victims of the shooting that took place the previous day; the eighth victim was a friend of the pregnant woman.
According to the police chief, video and audio recordings obtained by investigators captured muffled sounds of gunshots from inside the house just before two distressed women approached it and began banging on the door (this happened shortly before 5:00 p.m. on Friday). The shooter came outside and shot them as they ran toward him, then returned to the house.
When police arrived at the scene, they found the bodies of two women outside. Using a drone and a robot, law enforcement entered the house and found the bodies of a 5-year-old boy and a 1-year-old girl (on the first floor), two more women and two young men (on the staircase), as well as the shooter himself (on the second floor).
"Out of respect for the victims and their families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers saw inside the house," the police chief said at a news conference. "But I want our community to understand the seriousness of what happened and the profound impact of this tragedy both on those directly involved in the incident and on our community as a whole."
Lora declined to discuss the motive for the crime but said investigators would speak with other relatives and examine the mobile phones of the women killed outside the house.
"They knew something was happening in this house," he said. "We need to find out exactly what."
Lora said police arrived within minutes of receiving an alert from ShotSpotter—a controversial gunshot-detection system that uses artificial intelligence and a network of microphones to identify the sounds of gunfire. No more shots were heard afterward.
"The sounds that could have been mistaken for gunshots actually came from flash-bang grenades—chemical special-purpose devices—used by SWAT officers," he explained. Governor Josh Shapiro said he had offered the "full support" of his administration to Erie Mayor Daria Devlin, who personally addressed the victims' families during the news conference.
"I am deeply sorry. What happened to you is horrific, and none of us can say anything today that would ease your pain," she said. "But you must know this: our entire community is with you; we grieve with you. And we are here to support you."
District Attorney Elizabeth Hirz urged the public to refrain from speculation while the investigation is ongoing.
"Please do not allow rumors, conjecture, or unverified information to compound the pain these families are already enduring," she said.
The city of Erie is located approximately 120 miles (190 kilometers) north of Pittsburgh.
Speaking at a campaign rally near Philadelphia, Shapiro mentioned both the killings in Erie and the shooting in which two Philadelphia police officers were injured early Saturday morning.
"Today has been a dark day for our entire state," he said.

Third prototype of Russia’s armed Yak-130 jet takes flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:04:28 UTC
17:04:28 KST

- The third Yak-130M prototype made its first flight at the Irkutsk Aviation Plant, according to United Aircraft Corporation.
- UAC said the added test aircraft will help complete trials on time and begin deliveries in 2028.
The third prototype of Russia’s Yak-130M, an upgraded version of the Yak-130 jet trainer reworked to carry radar and guided weapons, has made its first flight, Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation said.
The aircraft, carrying side number 137, took off from the Irkutsk Aviation Plant in Siberia with Yakovlev test pilots Oleg Mutovin and Alexander Guskov at the controls. UAC said all systems worked normally and the crew completed the full flight plan. The company did not give the date of the flight, saying only that it took place in recent days.
UAC said adding a third test aircraft will let the program finish trials on schedule and begin deliveries in 2028. It did not say who the first customer will be or how many aircraft are planned.
The original Yak-130 is a two-seat subsonic jet that Russia uses to train pilots for fourth- and fifth-generation fighters. The Yak-130M keeps the same airframe and engines but adds equipment meant to turn it into a light combat aircraft. According to UAC, the new version carries the BRLS-130R radar, which Russian sources describe as an active electronically scanned array, the KSS-130 communications suite, a SOLT-130K pod combining a camera, thermal imager and laser designator, and the President-S130 self-protection system in a pod. The company says the jet can use a wider range of guided and unguided weapons by day and night and in any weather.
Russian officials have pitched the Yak-130M partly as a drone hunter. When UAC unveiled the first prototype in 2025, Rostec said the aircraft would be able to intercept unmanned aerial vehicles and carry air-to-air missiles as well as satellite- and laser-guided bombs.
Yakovlev first showed the Yak-130M as a mock-up at the Army-2024 forum near Moscow, saying the goal of the upgrade was to make the aircraft more competitive on the export market and that three test aircraft would be built. The first prototype made its maiden flight on June 25, 2026, a sortie of about 50 minutes flown by Guskov and test pilot Andrey Voropaev. A second prototype was rolled out in October 2025.
The only export customer named so far is Vietnam. In July, Irkutsk Aviation Plant head Andrei Soynov said during a visit by Vladimir Putin that a contract was being signed for 18 Yak-130Ms.

Missing Israeli tourist's body found on Mount Olympus after weeks of searching by Israeli team
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:01:39 UTC
17:01:39 KST

After nearly three weeks of searching on Mount Olympus in Greece, a team from the rescue organization Haverim Mechaltzim located the body of missing Israeli Ami Yogev on Friday, following a search effort initiated after Sivan Zamir, from the Greece and the Islands website, called for help.
Yogev had been missing since September 20. The four Israeli rescuers searched mountain streambeds, navigating cliffs, waterfalls, and dense vegetation in terrain that required climbing equipment and ropes.
The breakthrough came when one of the rescuers spotted an Israeli passport during the search. Yogev's personal belongings were discovered nearby, and his body was subsequently found concealed by vegetation.
Greek rescue teams had previously searched the same area but had been unable to locate the body because of the difficult terrain.
Following the discovery, the Israeli rescuers joined Greek rescue personnel in a complex recovery operation that lasted several hours.
Behind the rescue team was an extensive support network operated by Haverim Mechaltzim, part of the Gvanim nonprofit organization. The network included command centers in Israel and Greece, technology experts, assistance with analyzing cellular communications data, coordination with local authorities, and logistical support for the team in the field.
According to the organization, 12 search and support groups were involved in the efforts to locate Yogev and provide assistance.
The operation was conducted through four main groups: the family, volunteers, the rescue delegation, and the team coordinating the search.
At the heart of the operation were approximately 35 people actively involved in the effort, alongside external teams and additional support personnel.
The organization's core personnel contributed an estimated 740 person-hours to the operation. Each of the four rescuers who traveled to Mount Olympus spent approximately 50 hours searching before Yogev's body was located.
Head of rescue group expresses shared grief with Yogev family
"Unfortunately, the mission ended with devastating and painful news for the Yogev family, and we share in their grief. Our four rescuers acted with extraordinary determination and professionalism under extremely difficult terrain conditions, alongside the Greek rescue teams, who demonstrated impressive cooperation,” Yiftach Shavit, head of rescue operations at Haverim Mechaltzim, said.
"Behind every rescuer in the field stands an entire network of people who step forward, each contributing their own expertise, toward a single goal. That is the strength of Haverim Mechaltzim: the ability to bring together people and professional capabilities from around the world to help Israelis at the moments when they need assistance most."
The organization emphasized its close cooperation with Greek rescue teams and their contribution to the operation. It also thanked all the volunteers and other parties who assisted in the search and recovery efforts.

US DOJ launches investigation into news networks for possible antitrust violations in TV pool
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:01:13 UTC
17:01:13 KST

The US Justice Department has launched an investigation into five of the country's largest television news networks for possible antitrust violations, examining how they operate a shared television pool covering the White House.
The investigation concerns the television pool, a longstanding arrangement under which ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC share responsibility for filming presidential events and distributing footage to other news organizations. The arrangement allows a single television crew to cover events where access is restricted, such as meetings in the Oval Office or presidential trips.
The issue arose after US President Donald Trump barred CNN from entering White House grounds last month. After the network's exclusion, the then-chairman of the television pool announced that because CNN could not fulfill its scheduled coverage duties, no replacement crew would be assigned.
As a result, shared television coverage of Trump's events was suspended for several days, until a federal judge issued a temporary order blocking the exclusion of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico.
The legal proceedings are ongoing, with the Justice Department defending the Trump administration's decision.
Justice Department investigating television network pool
The department has now launched a separate investigation into the networks' conduct within the television pool. According to two sources familiar with the matter, lawyers representing the networks received requests to provide documents concerning the establishment of the arrangement and how it has operated recently.
A Justice Department spokesperson confirmed the investigation, saying that "members of the television pool boycotted coverage of White House events" and that "group boycotts among commercial competitors may violate the Sherman Act."
The spokesperson said the department's Antitrust Division was examining whether the news organizations had violated the law.
The five networks, which have made up the television pool for decades, have not issued any significant public response.
The arrangement itself is considered essential to White House coverage, partly because it eliminates the need to station multiple television crews at events where space is limited. The networks take turns filming events and share live broadcasts and recorded footage with other news organizations.
Networks release joint statement criticizing CNN White House ban
After CNN's exclusion, the five networks issued a rare joint statement saying "the public has a vital interest in receiving accurate and independent information about the government" and that "no administration should restrict a news organization because it is unhappy with its coverage."
Press freedom organizations criticized the investigation, arguing that news organizations' efforts to defend their First Amendment rights have nothing to do with antitrust law.
The investigation could also become part of the ongoing legal proceedings CNN, MS NOW, and Politico brought against the administration. In that case, the news organizations would argue that the White House excluded them in retaliation for the nature of their coverage.

‘Under tremendous strain’: CIA analyst turned spy novelist on a fraying US-UK alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:00:20 UTC
17:00:20 KST

The “special relationship”, the time-honored emotional bond between the US and Britain that has sustained through war and peace, is in trouble.
The ties of history, culture and language that have bridged an ocean and bound the two countries politically for generations are fraying as perhaps never before – strained relentlessly by Donald Trump, who has gleefully sacrificed traditional alliances and diplomatic niceties on the altar of his “America first” agenda.
Against that troubled backdrop, David McCloskey, a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) analyst turned spy writer and podcast host, has sketched out how things could get darker still. His case – laid out in a new novel – has been reinforced by the serendipity of real events.
The past month alone has seen the US president openly consider abandoning Washington’s de facto support for Britain in its dispute with Argentina over the Falklands Islands, and vocally welcome the idea of a united Ireland.
Last weekend, the Trump administration hurriedly withdrew 12 B-1 bombers from a British airbase, RAF Fairford, following intelligence reports that they could be targeted in an Iranian drone attack. The move, presaged by jeering attacks on Britain from some of Trump’s most ardent supporters, reinforced a growing sense of the US pulling back from a strategic partnership that, at times, has been intimate.
Nothing denotes the special in the relationship between the US and Britain as the sharing of intelligence. In London Station, his new novel, McCloskey somewhat ghoulishly explores where it could all go wrong, depicting a calamitous collapse in cooperation as the CIA comes under the guidance of a new Trump-like director who scorns MI6, the British intelligence agency, as “freeloaders” and “pickpockets”.
McCloskey’s imagined scenario seemed plausible even before recent developments, as two allies that faced the cold war and other conflicts in lockstep drifted apart on a number of fronts, including Russia’s war with Ukraine and Trump’s decision to attack Iran, signaling a geopolitical trend that he calls “fairly alarming”.
“I do think we’re at a period in the special relationship where there’s a lot more divergence between [Britain and the US],” said McCloskey, speaking by phone from a London cab. “A lot of the cultural affinity that the two nations have have felt for each other, going back to the second world war, is thinning out a little bit – and it created a lot of opportunities to think about how this relationship, as shown in the novel, could get even worse.”
The “ton of research” McCloskey carried out while writing uncovered serious fears for the special relationship’s future on both sides, but especially in Britain. “We’re seeing a lot of concern here in London about what do we do with this really hard-elbowed US foreign policy under Trump that seems to minimize the contribution of of allies and sort of pull traditional enemies closer,” he said. “So I think I think the relationship is under a tremendous amount of strain.”
One source of British concern is Trump’s affinity for Vladimir Putin, which has left British spies leery of sharing information for fear that the US president could pass it on, or betray the source.
“If I was deep inside Vauxhall Cross [the London headquarters of MI6] working on Russia, and I had a very sensitive piece of intelligence from a sensitive source, would I have more qualms about sharing that with the Americans right now? Probably,” suggested McCloskey, recalling the occasion when Trump reportedly passed on Israeli intelligence to the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, during his first presidency.
Worried British intelligence officers McCloskey has consulted had posited such a scenario “as a reasonable hypothetical”, he said, quickly adding that he could not confirm if any intelligence had actually been withheld.
What he could verify was tension, resentment on the British side at being the junior partner, and – curiously – mutual feelings of intimidation, with US agents being deferential to the UK side’s native abilities.
“One of the very common themes of my conversations with UK intelligence officers was this feeling of real tension with the US and fear because there wasn’t anything the UK, as the junior partner, could really do about it,” said McCloskey, who regularly unpicks murky realities of the British-US intelligence partnership with the former BBC security correspondent Gordon Corera on The Rest Is Classified podcast.
“For example, if you’re in a third country and you have an [MI6] officer and a CIA officer pursuing the same target, and both services sort of deconflict that, it was almost always the case that the US would win out because it just has more heft and more resources,” he said. “Many of the MI6 [insiders] I interviewed, I think, frankly, resented the [CIA] and didn’t care for it. Yet there was this sense of like, ‘What can I do? We’re very reliant on this partner.’”
CIA officers had their own problems. “I found any number of CIA officers who could recount instances where they had personality conflicts with their British counterparts,” said McCloskey. “The CIA officers felt here was a intimidation [from] the Brits, stemming from education, how articulate they were, their sense of refinement.”
Yet none of this means the relationship is doomed.
US agents, virtually without exception, saw merit in the alliance. “Almost every CIA officer I spoke to really felt like the Brits brought a great deal to the table,” recounted McCloskey.
The “five-eyes” cooperation agreement – providing signals intelligence-sharing between the US, Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand – remains intact, and is likely to survive for the foreseeable future.
The US-UK relationship still has “depth and flexibility”, in McCloskey’s view, giving it the potential to evolve and survive, regardless of future leadership in either country.
Nevertheless, he conceded, things have permanently changed. Tensions between the intelligence services will likely escalate – albeit not necessarily to the extent depicted in London Station – as foreign policy interests of the US and UK go their separate ways.
“A lot of the structural changes we’re seeing in the special relationship are not specific to Trump, and will outlast him,” McCloskey said. “Unlike the cold war, we don’t have an overarching geopolitical enemy to unify us, and so we’re seeing more divergence.
“There’s are a lot of areas where I could imagine the two intelligence services slightly downshifting their level of exchange.”
The end result is a relationship that may remain friendly, at times close – but perhaps less than special.
“Framing it as a special relationship makes it seem like the two countries should agree on almost everything at all times, everywhere – and that is too much pressure to put on a bilateral relationship between two independent nations,” concluded McCloskey. “It’s a cliche, but true, that nations don’t have permanent relationships – just interests.”

‘Afife’ ballet returns to the stage after 28 years

17:00:00 KST

Twenty-eight years after its premiere, a modern ballet depicting the turbulent life of Turkish theater pioneer Afife Jale has returned to the stage at Istanbul’s Atatürk Cultural Center (AKM) Türk Telekom Opera Hall.
The production was staged by the Istanbul State Opera and Ballet (IDOB) and brings to the stage the life of Jale, who became the first Muslim Turkish woman to perform on stage despite the restrictions of the period.
First staged by the Ankara State Opera and Ballet at the same venue in 1998, the work has been revived in a new production by IDOB.
With music by Turgay Erdener and a libretto and choreography by Beyhan Murphy, the ballet uses a dramatic narrative to recount Jale’s final days at Bakırköy Mental Hospital before her death. Under the supervision of caregivers, she recalls four distinct periods of her past before dying in the arms of her first love, Ziya.
Four dancers, each represented by a different color, portray separate stages of the artist’s life. İlke Kodal plays Afife, while Berin Günay performs as “Golden Afife,” Gizem Atik Tuncay as “Red Afife,” Deniz Kılınç Tunçeli as “Purple Afife” and Berfu Elmas as “Silver Afife.”
Jale’s inner circle comes to life through Berkay Günay as her cousin and first love, Ziya; Batur Büklü as her husband, Selahattin Pınar; Zuhal Karaca as actress Elisa Binemeciyen; and Emre Karaca, Ahmet Şahin, and Taner Güngör as the caregiver figures known as the “Three Shadows.”
Under the baton of conductor İbrahim Yazıcı, the Istanbul State Opera and Ballet Orchestra brings the performance to life, complemented by Efter Tunç’s set design, Bahar Korçan’s costumes, Cem Yılmazer’s lighting and video design by Aisha Hajiyeva.
The ballet will continue its run at the AKM Türk Telekom Opera Hall on Oct. 14, 15, 17 and 29 as part of the season program.

Three Swiss cantons accused of historical complicity in slavery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Three Swiss cantons accused of historical complicity in slavery
Can past injustices be brought before the courts? The Swiss Office of the Attorney General must now investigate whether the historical predecessors of the cantons of Zurich, Bern and Solothurn were guilty of aiding and abetting slavery.
A criminal complaint filed against cantons Zurich, Bern and Solothurn has brought the question of Switzerland’s role in the slave trade before the courts. At its heart is the allegation that the historical predecessors of the three cantons helped to finance a system founded on the slave trade in the 18th century.
The complaint was filed in early September by Swiss lawyer Catherine Reiter on behalf of activist Shelley Moorhead. It draws on an expert report by historian, writer and political activist Hans Fässler. Both Reiter and Fässler are based in St Gallen, in northeastern Switzerland.
Fässler has been delving into Switzerland’s links to colonialism and slavery for years. In his study, he examines the role played by members of the Old Swiss Confederacy – a loose alliance of independent small states that served as the precursor to modern-day Switzerland – within the colonial economic system.
A main argument of the study is that the three city-states were not merely observers of a distant system. Rather, they benefited economically from colonial structures linked to the transatlantic slave trade and plantation economies.
Bern, Zurich and Solothurn made a mint
Fässler cites several examples relating to Zurich. In the 18th century, the city invested in the British South Sea Company, which was involved in the transatlantic slave trade.
Later, the state-owned Bank Leu conducted business with the Danish Crown and granted loans to companies and banks with ties to plantation agriculture and the slave trade. According to Fässler, Zurich thus participated economically in colonial structures and reaped profits from them.
Bern also features prominently in the historian’s report. As early as 1719, the city-state invested substantial sums in the South Sea Company, and it held Danish government bonds for decades. These investments, Fässler argues, helped to fund a state whose Caribbean colonies relied on slave labour. At the same time, the investments proved profitable, generating considerable returns for the Bernese state.
As for Solothurn, the report refers primarily to holdings in the French Mississippi Company, which drove France’s colonial expansion in North America and relied on slave labour.
Another chapter in the study is devoted to the Karrer Marine Infantry Regiment, which was later known as the Hallwyl Regiment. This Swiss regiment in French service was stationed across various French naval depots and colonial garrisons in North America and the Caribbean. Its units, Fässler writes, were deployed against indigenous populations and took part in suppressing slave rebellions. The Swiss cantons condoned these deployments, although they were not actually provided for under the mercenary contracts of the time.
A major question for Fässler is what the political and economic elites of Switzerland at the time knew about slavery. Drawing on travel accounts, newspapers, scholarly works, correspondence and biographies, he concludes that educated circles were certainly aware of the slave trade, plantation agriculture and the living conditions of slaves.
Consequences across generations
However, the criminal complaint focuses less on the historical question than on the legal one. Reiter argues that enslaving people was already prohibited at that time under the prevailing principles of international law.
The complaint traces the evolution of anti-slavery sentiment from the 16th to the 19th century and concludes that a ban on slavery was established under customary international law at latest during the 18th century.
Leading on from this, the lawyer makes a far-reaching claim: that crimes against humanity are not subject to statutes of limitations, meaning that there is no time limit to filing charges, no matter how many years have passed. The Office of the Attorney General must now examine whether the financial transactions of the three city-states at the time constitute complicity in slavery. And today’s cantons should bear legal responsibility for the actions of their historical predecessors, the lawyer argues.
The complaint has been filed on behalf of Moorhead, an activist from the US Virgin Islands who describes himself as a descendant of slaves in what were then the Danish West Indies. Through the African-Caribbean Reparations and Resettlement Alliance (ACRRA), Moorhead has been campaigning for years for recognition of the long-term consequences of slavery and colonialism. These consequences, the complaint argues, persist to this day. They include economic disadvantages and possible transgenerational trauma.
The complaint is “by no means symbolic in nature”, Reiter said in response to an inquiry. The aim is to prompt the investigation of specific criminal offences committed to the detriment of her client. This entails determining any damage caused, identifying further victims and establishing whether any other parties were involved.
Major legal hurdle
Researchers have by now widely established that Swiss merchants, banks, investors and political figures played a role in colonial economic structures. What is still disputed, however, is the political or legal consequences that should follow on from this. The current claim against cantons Zurich, Bern and Solothurn constitutes a virtually unprecedented attempt in Switzerland to bring historical slavery before the courts as a crime against humanity that remains prosecutable today.
A key hurdle lies in criminal law itself. As a rule, it is individuals who are prosecuted, not historical communities. Those presumed to be guilty have long since died. The complaint seeks to get around this problem by holding today’s cantons accountable as the legal successors to their historical predecessors. Through their investments, the cantons of the time acted as economic players and can therefore be held liable in a similar way to companies, the lawyer argues.
Reiter does not comment on the prospects of success for the proceedings. Assessing the criminal complaint is, she says, up to “the competent authorities and courts”.
The Office of the Attorney General must now decide whether there is sufficient initial suspicion to warrant further investigation. The filing of a criminal complaint should not be equated with the opening of criminal proceedings, said spokesperson Claudia Balzli. The complaint is currently being examined “in accordance with standard procedure”, she added. This involves determining whether the matter falls within federal jurisdiction and whether there is sufficient suspicion of an offence.
Edited by Balz Rigendinger. Adapted from German by Julia Bassam/gw.

Economic issues will dominate the Turkish Parliament’s agenda throughout October, with lawmakers set to begin deliberations this week on a bill concerning repayments to investors in liquidated funds and preparations for the 2027 central government budget.
A nine-article legislative proposal submitted by the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) on repayments to investors affected by funds under liquidation will be taken up by Parliament’s Planning and Budget Commission on Oct. 14.
Deputy finance minister, officials from the Capital Markets Board (SPK) and the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BDDK), as well as representatives from Borsa Istanbul, the Central Securities Depository and Takasbank, are scheduled to attend the commission meeting.
After the proposal’s sponsors provide an overview of the legislation, lawmakers from both the government and opposition parties will be given the floor.

Bureaucrats will then respond to lawmakers’ questions.
Parliamentary sources expect discussions on the bill to last two days, with the proposal likely to be submitted to the General Assembly the following week.
The bill sets out the principles under which claims owed to approximately 455,000 investors will be repaid and establishes the rules governing the order of priority for payments.
If the proposal is enacted as planned, the interim payment of up to 1 million Turkish Liras to investors will be completed within this month.
Under the proposal, the principal amounts invested in the funds will be adjusted for inflation up to the date of liquidation. The inflation adjustment will be calculated using the average of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and the Domestic Producer Price Index.
The resignation or departure of fund founders and managers from their positions will not relieve them of liability for transactions carried out during their tenure.
The 2027 central government budget will also be a major focus in October. The budget bill, signed by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, is scheduled to be submitted to Parliament on Oct. 16.
Following a week-long review period, budget deliberations are expected to begin in the Planning and Budget Commission with a presentation by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, followed by debates on the overall framework of the budget proposal and reports prepared by the Court of Accounts.
This week is also set to be busy for Türkiye in terms of economic data releases.
The economic calendar will be highlighted by the release of August balance of payments figures and September budget data. Retail sales, along with output indicators for the services and construction sectors, will offer fresh insights into economic activity.

Trump’s diesel deal with Putin draws calls for EU resolve
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:57:33 UTC
16:57:33 KST

- Urgewald urged European leaders not to weaken Russian energy sanctions after Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Putin on Oct. 9.
- The U.S. Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel through April 2027, days before the Graham Act’s Oct. 18 implementation deadline.
A German environmental and human rights group has urged European leaders not to weaken sanctions on Russian energy after President Donald Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply diesel fuel to the United States and global markets, a week before a new U.S. sanctions law on Russia reaches its first implementation deadline.
Urgewald said Europe should keep its restrictions on Russian liquefied natural gas, or LNG, and on the shipping, insurance and professional services that support Russia’s energy exports, regardless of the shift in Washington.
“Trump’s deal with Putin is an affront to the civilised world. While Russia continues its assault on Ukraine, he is handing Moscow a fresh energy lifeline. With just over a week until the Lindsey Graham Act’s implementation deadline, this deal undermines the pressure Congress intended to impose,” said Alexander Kirk, sanctions campaigner at Urgewald.
“This is Europe’s Churchill moment. European leaders must stand firm against aggression. Washington’s retreat must not become an excuse to weaken European sanctions or reopen the door to Russian energy. There must be no watering down of restrictions on Russian LNG or the shipping, insurance and professional services that keep this trade moving,” said Kirk.
Trump announced the deal on Oct. 9 after a phone call with Putin. In a post on Truth Social, he said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons after that. He later said Russia could deliver about 3 million more tons depending on the condition of its refineries. The Kremlin said the call, which lasted about an hour and a half, covered large-scale economic initiatives including fuel supplies.
The same day, the U.S. Treasury Department issued a general license that temporarily waives sanctions on Russian diesel through April 2027. The White House has presented the move as a way to bring down fuel prices, which have surged worldwide since the start of the war with Iran and as Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries forced Moscow to restrict diesel exports. Trump publicly thanked Putin for the agreement. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned it, and some energy analysts said the deal helps Russia sell off summer-grade diesel it no longer needs before winter.
The timing has drawn attention because of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Trump signed on Sept. 18 after it passed the Senate 86-11 and the House 262-159. The law requires the president to impose many of its measures by Oct. 18, including sanctions on Russian state-linked companies and banks, action against “shadow fleet” tankers carrying Russian oil, and tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the largest buyers of Russian crude and gas. It also allows the president to waive measures by certifying to Congress that a waiver is in the national interest.
The White House has not said whether the diesel deal will affect how it implements the Graham Act, and neither Washington nor Moscow has released the terms of the fuel agreement, including pricing or which buyers will receive the diesel. European Union officials have not publicly said whether the U.S. move will change their own sanctions timeline on Russian energy.

Members of the US Congress are preparing bipartisan legislation to prohibit purchases of Russian petroleum, moving to challenge US President Donald Trump’s commercial agreement permitting Russian diesel imports onto American and global markets.
The legislative initiative, titled the “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act,” is being drafted by Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, with Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska confirming he will join as one of its initial co-sponsors.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The bill aims to establish a statutory ban on purchasing Russian oil and petroleum products, seeking to reverse the administration’s regulatory exemptions and curtail revenues funding the Russian military.
We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil. It will be called the “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act.” It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly. #PeaceThroughStrength
— Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick 🇺🇸 (@RepBrianFitz) October 10, 2026
In comments to Ukrainska Pravda, Bacon criticized the administration’s diesel agreement, characterizing the decision as a grave policy misstep that projects weakness toward the Kremlin while providing financial lifelines to Moscow’s defense sector.
“Allowing the purchase of Russian diesel fuel gives money to the Russian economy and its war machine,” Bacon said.
“A year ago, the president criticized Europeans for purchasing Russian gas. I completely disagree with this decision, and I consider the president’s policy regarding Russia and Ukraine a failure. I and ‘old school’ Republicans, supporters of Ronald Reagan, are deeply disappointed.”
Ukraine Should Keep Striking Russian Refineries, Kellogg Says
Bacon attributed the administration’s decision to domestic political calculations ahead of the upcoming midterm elections, noting that retail diesel prices approaching $6 per gallon have created pressure on voters. However, the lawmaker argued that the transactional approach undermines the nation’s strategic and moral standing.
Writing on X, Fitzpatrick also reaffirmed congressional backing for Kyiv, stating that President Volodymyr Zelensky maintains the overwhelming support of lawmakers and the American public.
“Russia illegally invaded Ukraine, a sovereign and freedom-loving nation, and Russia is squarely to blame for all damage and destruction, to both lives and treasure, that has resulted from Putin’s unprovoked attack,” Fitzpatrick stated.
“We have your back, and we will stand with you until Ukrainian victory is achieved.”
Congressional resistance to the Trump-Putin diesel arrangement
The push for legislative intervention follows Trump’s announcement on Friday, Oct. 9, of a bilateral arrangement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to American and international buyers.
Under the terms announced by Trump following a telephone conversation with Putin, Moscow agreed to deliver 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter, with prospective deliveries scaling up to 3 million tons depending on the operational status of Russian refineries.
To enable the transactions, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The waiver was enacted only three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Sept. 18, a statute intended to expand secondary sanctions and tariff mechanisms across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.
The announcement drew condemnation from Ukrainian officials, who noted that the deal coincided with multilateral peace consultations in Miami involving US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. President Zelensky characterized the timing of the Miami talks as a “smokescreen” for bilateral energy concessions.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned that offering economic accommodations to the Kremlin signals Western weakness, arguing that the Russian leadership interprets concessions as appeasement rather than an incentive to negotiate.
Sybiha maintained that only an energy ceasefire – under which Russia halts attacks on Ukraine’s electrical and heating infrastructure in exchange for a pause in Ukrainian refinery strikes – can sustainably reduce fuel costs.
Lawmakers backing the new bill argue that allowing Russian refined hydrocarbons back into Western supply chains directly contradicts allied efforts to starve Moscow’s wartime budget.
The draft statute must be formally introduced in the House of Representatives and pass both chambers of Congress before it can be submitted to the president, setting up a potential legislative confrontation over executive sanctions waivers and energy trade with Russia.

Japan Turns to Ukraine’s Battle-Tested Drone Killers, Signs Deal With SkyFall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:50:27 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Japan Turns to Ukraine’s Battle-Tested Drone Killers, Signs Deal With SkyFall
Japan has signed a contract to purchase Ukrainian-made interceptor drones from defense manufacturer SkyFall, marking a new step in defense cooperation between Tokyo and Kyiv as Japan seeks to strengthen its counter-drone capabilities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, speaking at a press conference on October 9, the Japanese Ministry of Defense has already finalized the procurement agreement and is working to arrange deliveries as quickly as possible.
Neither the number of drones ordered nor the contract’s value has been made public. Japanese officials have also not specified which SkyFall interceptor models or configurations will be delivered.
SkyFall develops several types of military unmanned aerial vehicles, including the Vampire heavy bomber drone, Shrike FPV attack drones, and the P1-SUN family of aerial interceptors.
The P1-SUN series includes multiple configurations, some equipped with artificial intelligence modules. The company has also developed the P1-SUN JetKiller, a faster variant designed to intercept high-speed aerial targets, including Russian jet-powered drones.
In late September, SkyFall released footage showing a P1-SUN JetKiller intercepting a Russian Geran-5 jet-powered drone, demonstrating the system’s ability to engage targets moving at higher speeds than conventional propeller-driven attack drones.
During the press conference, Koizumi also highlighted Ukraine’s experience in developing and continuously upgrading military technology under battlefield conditions.
The Japanese defense minister pointed to Ukraine’s rapid feedback process, which allows manufacturers to introduce improved drone configurations approximately every two to three weeks based on operational experience.
Koizumi said Japan could learn from Ukraine’s approach to defense innovation, particularly its ability to translate battlefield feedback into technological improvements while expanding domestic defense production.
He also emphasized the importance of strengthening Japan’s deterrence and response capabilities, indicating that Tokyo would continue examining measures to reinforce its defense industrial base.
Earlier, on June 12, SkyFall signed a strategic partnership agreement with Airbus Defence and Space to develop next-generation air defense solutions. The cooperation focuses on integrating SkyFall’s P1-SUN interceptor drones with Airbus’s Air C2 airspace management system to strengthen protection against aerial threats across Ukraine and Europe.

The Commercial Court of Zaporizhzhia Oblast has ordered the Russian Federation to pay Agro Alliance LLC UAH 101.74 million (US$2.2 million) in damages and lost profits for property lost in temporarily occupied territory.
Source: the court's ruling
Details: Agro Alliance is registered in the village of Kopani, Zaporizhzhia Oblast. The company grew cereals, legumes and oilseeds and engaged in wholesale grain trading, among other activities.
According to the case documents, in early March 2022, Russian troops entered the company's premises while armed, illegally took up residence there and seized its property.
The company lost access to its property complex, movable assets and inventory, as well as the ability to conduct business.
The court found the claims justified and ordered the full amount to be recovered from the Russian Federation, represented by the Prosecutor General's Office of the Russian Federation.
Agro Alliance LLC was established in 2000. Its founders include Volodymyr Dudka, who also heads the company, Oleh Romanenko and Nina Arshukova.

Spanish PM Sanchez kicks off election campaign amid housing crisis protests
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez launched his campaign for a snap November election on Saturday. The vote comes as a deepening housing crisis is driving protests and putting pressure on his left-wing coalition.

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez aimed to pull off another unlikely comeback as he began campaigning on Saturday for a snap vote dominated by housing protests that have shaken the country.
When 87-year-old Madrid pensioner Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home two weeks ago, no one could have expected Spain was headed for upheaval that would bring forward a general election scheduled for 2027.
The eviction of Abascal, who became the face of the country's chronic housing crisis, catalysed nationwide protests that piled pressure on Sanchez's left-wing coalition to present urgent decrees.

But after the minority government failed to pass its measures in parliament, Sanchez rolled the dice and called an election for November 29.
Read moreSpanish PM Sanchez calls snap election as pressure mounts over housing crisis
Sanchez, in power since 2018, has acquired international prominence in recent years as his clashes with US President Donald Trump and Israel endeared him to disillusioned global progressives.
He is a divisive figure at home and trails in most polls to the main conservative Popular Party (PP).
At his rally Saturday, Sanchez vowed to strengthen legislation protecting tenants against "real estate speculation" if his party wins an absolute majority.
"Maricarmen and all those who campaign for her, as well as all those who take action for the just cause of housing, have opened the way," he said, voicing his "affection" for Abascal, who died on Wednesday in hospital.
