Wages, housing, pensions
Sanchez chose the symbolic location of Dos Hermanas, a commuter town outside the southern city of Seville and a historic Socialist stronghold, to kick off his electioneering.
He launched his 2023 election campaign from Dos Hermanas and went on to thwart the predictions by retaining office, even though the PP won more seats.
Dos Hermanas was also the scene of Sanchez's political resurrection after he resigned as Socialist party leader in 2016, following two bruising general election defeats.
As Sanchez began his rally, Isabel Morales, a 67-year-old pensioner in the crowd, told AFP she viewed his term in office as "very positive".
"He's done a lot of things for the working class. He raised wages, raised pensions, enacted a housing law, a lot of things that are extremely positive. Let's hope he continues," she said.
'A total change'
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo was also rallying his followers on Saturday, in Madrid. He has his sights set on becoming prime minister after failing to form a government in 2023.
"Spain needs a future and he (Sanchez) needs to be in the past," Feijoo told a rally in Madrid on Sunday. "We are proposing a total change."
The PP leader, who tops most polls, has focused his criticism on the government's handling of a migration crisis in Ceuta, where he held an event on Wednesday promising to restore normality.
More than 70,000 migrants streamed into the Spanish north African enclave from neighbouring Morocco in late July. Thousands have remained for months in largely chaotic conditions, sparking anger among locals.

"We want to pull our country out of the ruin, the corruption, the shady practices that we've been seeing recently," he said.
Housing, long a top public concern, was a topic hanging large over both of Saturday's rallies as hundreds of protesters camped in Madrid's emblematic Puerta del Sol square and in other cities demanding more protection for tenants and affordable prices.
The main unions have called a general strike for November 11 – the first such stoppage in Spain since 2012 – to crank up the pressure over housing and wages before the vote.

US races Russia and China to build a nuclear reactor on the moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:45:46 UTC
16:45:46 KST

In 2019, Russia tested a nuclear-powered cruise missile. The test failed, and the missile plunged to the bottom of the White Sea in northern Russia. Shortly afterward, a large explosion occurred near the crash site, causing radiation levels in the area to spike. U.S. intelligence officials assessed that the explosion took place during a Russian operation to recover the missile from the seabed. At least five nuclear scientists and employees of Russia's state-owned nuclear energy company, Rosatom, were killed. Russia quickly denied that the missile was nuclear-powered, but Rosatom subsequently all but acknowledged what had happened.
Now imagine a rocket carrying an actual nuclear reactor to the moon crashing into the ocean. It sounds like particularly dangerous science fiction, but until just a few years ago, the possibility of artificial intelligence taking over the world also seemed like nothing more than science fiction. With the world's major powers locked in a frantic race to install a nuclear reactor in space, such a scenario may be just around the corner.
A dangerous undertaking
About two months ago, NASA asked private contractors to prepare to build a nuclear reactor capable of surviving a journey through space and operating without maintenance near the moon's south pole. The target launch date: December 2030. The goal: to beat Russia, which aims to have a reactor operating on the moon by 2036 as part of a not-so-secret partnership with China. In 1961, President John F. Kennedy challenged America's leading scientists to land a man on the moon before the end of the decade. Now the goal is to have a functioning nuclear reactor on the moon within four years.
Even before sending nuclear reactors to the moon, the United States plans to put humans back on its surface as part of the Artemis program. The third test flight is scheduled for summer 2027, while the crewed Artemis 4 mission is planned for early 2028.
The somewhat dystopian race to install a reactor on the moon is probably inevitable, and it has implications for the entire future of space exploration. For example, a lunar day lasts about 14 Earth days, followed by 14 consecutive Earth days of complete darkness. During that time, solar panels cannot generate electricity, and temperatures plunge to minus 130 degrees. A nuclear reactor provides continuous electricity and heat around the clock, regardless of sunlight. Any ambition to reach Mars, let alone establish habitable conditions there, also requires nuclear energy.
Establishing a base on the moon is critical to the search for resources and the launch of missions into the depths of the solar system. All of this makes control over access to lunar resources essential, and the major powers believe a nuclear reactor is the foundation for achieving these ambitions. But it is a dangerous undertaking.
As in the case of the Russian missile in 2019, debris from a reactor falling back to Earth could scatter radioactive materials, as happened in Canada in the 1970s. An explosion or reactor core meltdown on the lunar surface could also render entire areas of the moon off-limits. All three countries promise that their reactors will remain inactive until they reach the moon, but these days it is difficult to take their leaders at their word, especially when the race is also, of course, a display of nationalist power.
Leading scientists warn that governments are moving too quickly at a time when space exploration has experienced a string of failures over the past six years. Chinese, American and Russian rockets have exploded, and space debris regularly falls back to Earth.
"There will always be a space race going on, and if you enter nuclear power into that mix, then it could take a potentially more dangerous turn,” said Edwin Lyman, the director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists.
A deadline pushed back
When it comes to nuclear power in space, Russia has no rivals. It has launched more than 30 reactors into Earth orbit, primarily aboard Cold War-era satellites in the 1970s and 1980s, and holds the largest stockpile of what is considered the safest nuclear fuel for space missions.
The last space reactor NASA tested, in 2018, used highly enriched uranium, which is lighter and cheaper to launch than other fuels. But its use is dangerous because the material can be turned into a nuclear weapon. That leaves the option of using low-enriched uranium fuel, except that the Americans do not have enough of it and cannot import it from Russia because of a ban imposed in 2024 in response to the war in Ukraine.
To date, the United States has invested more than $20 billion in space nuclear programs. Last month, the Pentagon selected a company called Antares to develop and demonstrate a space microreactor, while NASA is accelerating its timetable out of concern that a Russian-Chinese reactor could effectively establish an exclusion zone on the moon.
Such a move could, in practice, prevent American astronauts and rovers from accessing large areas of the lunar surface. That would itself violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, but international agreements are being violated on a daily basis these days.
Despite the sense of urgency, all the major powers have repeatedly pushed back their target dates, and few experts believe they will meet their deadlines. None of them even has a proven lunar lander capable of delivering heavy, potentially radioactive materials to the moon's unforgiving surface.
There is, of course, the option of international cooperation, as has happened time and again in space exploration. But the current global climate leaves little room for optimism.
"Governments have always achieved more by working together than by competing," Katy Huff, head of the Department of Nuclear Engineering at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, told The New York Times. "Collaborative, team-based science in space has always managed to rise above our fraught international politics."

Couples looking to have children often turn to surrogacy agencies in Georgia without understanding the hidden costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:45:00 UTC
16:45:00 KST

Surrogacy in Georgia is booming, but at what cost?
October 11, 2026
Three years ago, Olga, 40, and Daniel (both names changed to protect the their identities) from Hamburg decided to employ the services of a surrogate mother. But surrogacy is illegal in Germany, and people whose children are born through surrogacy must pursue the legal recognition of their parenthood in German courts.
Olga is a German citizen, but was born and raised in Russia. That's why the couple wanted to learn more about the surrogacy market in Russia. But foreign customers have been banned from signing Russian surrogacy contracts since 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, many international agencies that liaise between surrogates and intended parents moved to Georgia. So, Olga and Daniel traveled there.
Georgia the new destination for surrogate mothers
In the past years, Georgia, a mountainous country in the Caucasus region, has become a sort of surrogacy hub, with women traveling from all over the world to work as surrogates. According to Georgia's Public Service Development Agency, over 3,000 surrogate mothers were registered in 2023 across the country. Since 2012, they've given birth to over 5,000 children. And since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine, the number of children born to surrogate mothers has skyrocketed. While an estimated 300 surrogate mothers gave birth in 2021, that number leapt to over 1,100 by 2023.
Anastasia, 39, is a surrogate mother from Russia working in Georgia. She has a grown daughter and has already seen through three surrogate pregnancies. Her first was in 2021, which she used to finance a property down payment.
Anastasia says she completed her first two surrogacies in Russia, and her third — for a Japanese couple, brokered through the branch office of a Moscow clinic — in Georgia. Like many surrogate mothers, she went home to Russia after the embryo was implanted, and returned to Georgia when she was 22 weeks pregnant.
"I live in an apartment with another surrogate mother who carried twins to term. This program was the easiest and most practical one for me, but maybe I just got lucky with the right clinic," Anastasia told DW. "Other women who gave birth in Georgia told me they had difficulties. For example, after giving birth, they had to wait a long time before they were paid." She says she's ready to become a surrogate mother again.
Estimates vary, but there are about 19 clinics that offer such services across Georgia. And at around €45,000 ($50,400) to €55,000, the average service costs for agencies in Tbilisi or Batumi are only about a third of what agencies in other countries charge.
Several surrogate mothers who gave birth in Georgian clinics told DW that their average salary was between €18,000 and €28,000, with premiums added for birthing twins, for example.
Surrogate mothers from Ukraine in demand
Daniel and Olga told DW that they spent months looking for surrogacy agency in Georgia. "Pretty soon, we had access to a list of women from Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and Georgia, and were given a detailed description of the process, along with the contact information of lawyers who could help take care of the formalities," they recount. "We were a little concerned that not every agency could give clear answers about the health of some of the surrogate mothers."
Both work in the medical field, and Olga says perhaps some of their questions about the physical health and possible genetic disorders might have been too probing. "We picked a 30-year-old woman from Ukraine who had already been a surrogate mother once for a European couple," she says. The Russian-Georgian agency set up half-hour long Zoom call, "but that hardly seemed enough to make a final decision," Olga adds.
In the spring of 2024, the married couple traveled to Georgia's capital to meet Elena (her name has been changed to protect her identity). Following a long discussion, the agency had seemed reluctant when they agreed to bring her to Tbilisi for the meeting. Elena made a good first impression on the couple from Hamburg, showing them pictures of her children and telling them she wanted to use the money she earned to renovate her apartment.
"They had initially told us that the surrogate would spent the entire pregnancy living in a rented apartment in Tbilisi," Olga and Daniel tell DW. "But then we found out that Elena was going back home for a few months after the embryo was implanted, back to Ukraine, where there's war."
Human rights experts criticize legislation
Georgian laws have a weak spot, the human rights lawyer Nino Bogveradze tells DW: They only regulate the relationship between the surrogate mothers, the intended parents, and the clinics, but they do not consider the roles that agencies play.
In Georgia, surrogate mothers have limited rights. Most concerns related to their pregnancy, medical care or payment are not regulated by national law but in contracts between the involved parties. And the state does not set minimum standards for social guarantees or contractual terms.
After an embryo has been implanted, surrogate mothers are not allowed to keep the child, leave the program, or end the pregnancy. Several human rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the International Women's Health Coalition say the established practice in Georgia violates women's rights to reproductive self-determination.
Agencies guided by material interests
"Agencies often speak of their special mission to help people have the child they've been dreaming of," Olga Doletskaya from the University of Leeds tell DW. "But in reality, they're primarily driven by financial interests. And that's why they exploit the precarious situation of surrogate mothers, and pressure intended parents."
Olga and Daniel from Hamburg agree. "We were constantly being made to understand that we should decide as quickly as possible. We had to hurry because apparently several other couples were also interested in our surrogate," Olga says.
And the agency kept stressing that it had paid out of pocket for bringing the potential surrogate mother to Georgia, despite that not being contractually agreed. "At some point, a representative noticed my emotional state and asked me how long I wanted to remain childless," Olga recounts. "I felt like I was being manipulated."
The couple returned to Germany with mixed feelings and decided to shelve the idea of employing a surrogate mother — at least, for now.
Mark Sheider and Asja Lokina contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Russian.

Saudi-led coalition vows firm response after deadly attack on Riyadh airport
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
15:42:22 CST
16:42:22 KST

RIYADH, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has vowed to respond firmly to a Houthi attack on a passenger terminal at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 12 people and injured 309 others.
Coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Malki said early Sunday on social media platform X that the coalition's Joint Forces Command would respond firmly to what he described as a "terrorist attack" in accordance with international humanitarian law.
In separate posts on Sunday, Al-Malki said the Saudi-led coalition had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile and a drone launched by the Houthi group toward Saudi Arabia.
The fatalities in the airport attack included four Saudi citizens and eight foreign residents -- two Bangladeshis and one each from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan, according to the Saudi aviation authority.
The authority said the injured were receiving treatment at several hospitals, with some in serious condition, and that airport operations had been temporarily suspended.
The attack came as the Houthi group and Saudi Arabia continued exchanging strikes on major airports and other facilities.
Three people were killed and 36 others injured in two separate attacks targeting Abha International Airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia and King Khalid International Airport on Tuesday and Wednesday, respectively. On Thursday, three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed and several others of other nationalities were injured in two Houthi attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported earlier on Saturday that Saudi Arabia launched a new wave of air and missile strikes across Houthi-held areas in Yemen, targeting Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held capital, areas near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait and several northern provinces.
Also on Saturday, Yemen's government forces said that more than 1,150 Houthi fighters had been "neutralized" and over 180 military and logistical vehicles destroyed or damaged in over 1,900 strikes across multiple fronts in Yemen over the preceding 24 hours.
The figures could not be independently verified.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, now based in the southern port city of Aden. The renewed fighting marks a major escalation after a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday that the United States "may" join Saudi Arabia in striking the Houthi group.
"We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he told reporters on the South Lawn of the White House.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Sunday strongly condemned Saturday's Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
"Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately," he wrote on X. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Mainland Taiwan affairs experts said the speech delivered on Saturday by Taiwan leader Lai Ching-te in Taipei is filled with deception, noting that his refined rhetoric cannot conceal his push for separatism.

"The remarks fully expose Lai's stubborn separatist mindset and his intention to incite confrontation across the Strait," Chen added.
Chen pointed out that facts have repeatedly shown Lai and the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities as the source of undermining cross-strait stability and social harmony in Taiwan.
"Lai's speech skirted the economic and social challenges facing Taiwan," Chen said. "The remarks were apparently designed to serve the DPP's interests in the upcoming local elections."
The Taiwan question originated from a civil war fought between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Kuomintang (KMT) about eight decades ago. In 1949, the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, while the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC.
The unresolved civil war and foreign interference have left both sides of the Taiwan Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. However, the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed.
Both history and reality make clear that Taiwan's future should be jointly decided by all Chinese people, including Taiwan compatriots. Differences in political systems are neither an obstacle to China's reunification nor an excuse for splitting the country.
Liu Xiangping, an expert on Taiwan studies at Nanjing University, said Lai's hyping of "whole-of-society defense resilience" is essentially a pretext for increasing the island's defense budget and a way to rationalize dragging Taiwan residents onto his separatist chariot.
"Lavishing the people's hard-earned money on military expansion at the expense of their livelihoods will ultimately backfire," Liu said.
Liu criticized Lai's attempt to curry favor with the United States and the West. "By parroting Western ideological rhetoric, Lai has fully exposed his eagerness to act as a pawn for external forces," the expert said.
Lai said he would "never allow the distortion of World War II history." Yet his own words have repeatedly distorted history, said Wang Yingjin, director of the cross-Strait relations research center of the Renmin University of China.

by Xinhua writers Wang Yanan, Ma Ruxuan
GENEVA, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- The China-proposed Global Development Initiative (GDI) is notable for its emphasis on practical measures to support and advance development, rather than merely serving as a declaration, according to Carlos Correa, executive director of the South Centre.
The GDI "is not just a declaration, it is a program of work," Correa said in a recent interview with Xinhua on the fifth anniversary of the GDI. "One important element of this initiative is that it has promoted practical measures. The focus on development is very important as well."
Correa said the GDI has made an important contribution to global development cooperation and the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
In his view, the GDI is inclusive, as it promotes development in all countries without any discrimination or distinction, and is based on the important principles of cooperation, innovation and harmony with nature. "These principles are fundamental to have a better world for all our people to live in."
At a time when many of the Sustainable Development Goals are facing obstacles, the GDI is "very important to keep the focus on the goals to be achieved by the international community and to implement practical measures to achieve them," said Correa.
More than 130 countries and international organizations support the GDI and have participated in cooperation under the initiative, said Correa, noting that the high-level meeting on the GDI held in Beijing in July this year reaffirmed the strong support this initiative enjoys as well as its development direction.
"The GDI and the Chinese government are taking the lead in showing the world that there is an alternative to the approach that seeks to stop others from developing and to adopt unilateral measures to the benefit of just one country. This initiative shows that a different spirit can guide the international community," said Correa.
"Regarding the South Centre, we are very much interested in promoting and being part of these efforts," said Correa.
In his view, this initiative promotes, through programs and financing, South-South cooperation, during which China has shared its experience in areas such as poverty reduction, food security and digital transformation.
Asked what he would like to see for the GDI over the next five years, Correa said, "Just to continue with what is being done and emphasizing the need for international cooperation and solidarity."
Correa also called on all parties to "contribute to the success of this initiative, to expand it and to bring in new actors to enhance South-South cooperation."
Headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland, the South Centre serves as the intergovernmental think tank of the Global South, committed to advancing shared interests among Southern nations. ■

Meteoric Surge: Food prices rose by nearly 20% under Netanyahu’s current government term - new study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:36:52 UTC
16:36:52 KST

Meteoric Surge: Food prices rose by nearly 20% under Netanyahu’s current government term - new study
A new study from Tel Aviv University found that in the past four years, a basket of 80 products has increased in price by about 19.6% in neighborhood stores and by 19% online
Almost a fifth more for the same shopping basket: Food prices in Israel have risen sharply over the past four years, according to a new study from the Faculty of Management at Tel Aviv University. The study tracked the prices of a basket of 80 popular products between September 2022 and August 2026, and compared them to the four years prior, from September 2018 to August 2022.
According to the findings, the price of the basket increased by 19.6% in neighborhood stores, by 19% in online channels, and by 14.5% in discount branches. In the previous period, however, the price increase amounted to 4.3% in neighborhood stores, 4.1% online, and 2.8% in discount chains.
According to the study, the rate of price increase over the past four years is nearly five times higher than in the preceding period.
Suggested articles
The price increase is also noticeable in specific products: a 100-gram Elite "Para" chocolate bar has become about 78% more expensive in neighborhood stores, a package of 800-gram Maadanot cheese borekas has risen by about 31%, and a kilogram of Sugat classic jasmine rice has increased by 17.7% in discount chains.
Significant gaps were also found in the comparison between supermarket chains across the two periods. At Shufersal Deal, prices rose by about 22.7% over the past four years, compared to about 0.6% in the previous four years. At Victory, there was an increase of about 16%, compared to 1.2% in the previous period, and at Rami Levy, prices rose by 10.3%, compared to 6.1%.
At my Shufersal, prices have increased by 19.6% in the recent period, compared to 2.3% in the previous period. At Freshmarket, there was an increase of 19.6%, compared to about 6.3% in the four preceding years.
A similar trend emerges from online purchase data. At Rami Levy Online, prices rose by 14.1%, at Shufersal Online by 24%, and at Victory Online by 18.6%. In the earlier period, price increases at these chains amounted to 9.3%, 0.1%, and 3.8%, respectively.
The research also illustrates the gap in shekels: at Shufersal Deal, the basket became more expensive by 231 shekels in the past four years, compared to just six shekels in the previous period. At Shufersal Sheli, the price increase totaled 222 shekels, compared to 26 shekels previously. At Victory, the basket rose by 160 shekels, compared to 12 shekels in the earlier period.
Prof. Itai Ater from the Faculty of Management at Tel Aviv University notes that among the factors that may explain the price increases are the rise in VAT rates and the increase in property tax, water, fuel, and electricity tariffs, alongside the rise in the prices of regulated products. On the other hand, the strengthening of the shekel and the decrease in the global food price index, which peaked in 2022, reduced import prices and could have moderated the price hikes.
According to Ater, the changes in production and import costs alone cannot explain an increase of about 20% over four years. He also points to the lack of ongoing governmental action regarding the issue of the cost of living, and the fact that public and media attention is directed towards other topics.
In such a situation, After says, companies in the food market may take advantage of the opportunity to raise prices.
The professor also emphasizes that the gap between the moderate price increases in the early period and the recent surges in prices indicates that the high cost of living is not an inevitable fate. According to him, an effective fight against the phenomenon requires government mobilization, the promotion of structural reforms, addressing centers of power, improving regulation and removing barriers, alongside broad public and media discourse.

Likud assembles special team to lure defectors from Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party after election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:27:55 UTC
16:27:55 KST

Just two and a half weeks before Israel's October 27 election, Likud has established a special team tasked with persuading several lawmakers from former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! party to defect. Yedioth Ahronoth and ynet have learned that the team consists of Likud lawmakers and several strategic advisers whose sole purpose is to facilitate the movement of lawmakers between political blocs immediately after the election.
The tactic has been used in the previous two election cycles, with considerable success. Likud figures managed to draw Amichai Chikli, then a newly elected lawmaker, away from former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's party, followed later in the government's term by Idit Silman, who served as coalition chairwoman. This time, however, Likud has expanded the number of people involved and developed more systematic methods for pressuring potential defectors.
In the past, candidates reported being subjected to various forms of pressure, including demonstrators appearing at synagogues attended by their family members, maintaining a regular presence in their neighborhoods and gathering near their children's schools. Those efforts were carefully orchestrated, and Likud now appears to have refined its methods, determined to take the strategy a step further.
The newly established Likud team is conducting extensive background checks on every candidate on Eisenkot's list, with particular attention to newcomers who have right-wing political backgrounds or close ties to right-leaning circles. The examination includes past public statements, personal and broader social networks, whether candidates consult rabbis and which other influential figures might sway their decisions. Likud intends to use that information to launch an intensive pressure campaign immediately after the election, focusing primarily on diplomatic and security policy differences and offering a package of promises to those willing to switch political blocs.
That was also the approach used with Chikli and Silman, both of whom received guaranteed places on Likud's candidate list for subsequent elections and ministerial positions after switching sides. Chikli managed to retain his place in Likud and even strengthen his standing within the party. Silman, however, who served as environmental protection minister, failed to survive the party primaries, ending her latest political chapter bitterly amid claims that Netanyahu's inner circle had "used her and thrown her away."
Eisenkot's Yashar! party appears well aware that similar efforts could begin immediately after the election and has reportedly placed particular emphasis on screening candidates. In recent weeks, reports suggested that candidates were required to sign commitments pledging not to defect from the party, although senior party officials denied those claims. Even if such loyalty declarations had been signed, however, they would carry no legal force and would have no significance beyond a symbolic commitment.
Bennett learns from past defections
Naftali Bennett was among the politicians most severely affected by the tactic. Beyond Chikli and Silman, former lawmaker Nir Orbach, a member of the religious Zionist community, informed Bennett that he no longer intended to vote with the coalition. It later emerged that Orbach had also faced intense pressure from Likud and other right-wing figures, until he eventually broke ranks. During one Knesset vote, he left the chamber and was quoted as saying of the coalition government formed with Mansour Abbas and his Arab Ra'am party: "The experiment has failed."
As a result, Bennett has adopted a far more rigorous screening process for candidates running on his Together party list in the current election, including extensive background checks into each candidate's political history and previous positions. During preparatory meetings, prospective candidates were asked dozens of questions about various hypothetical political scenarios designed to test their loyalty to Bennett.
Yashar's No. 7: ‘There are no Silmans here, and there never will be’
Shaul Meridor, a senior figure in Eisenkot's party, said last week in an interview with "120 and One," ynet's political podcast: "There are no Silmans here, and there never will be. Everyone on our list has undergone thorough scrutiny of their positions and fully agrees with Eisenkot's approach."
Likud officials, however, believe the political balance after the election could be extremely close and argue that Eisenkot lacks experience in selecting and retaining political candidates, leaving some members of his list potentially vulnerable to defection. A Ukrainian drone strike targeted a major Yandex data center in the Russian city of Vladimir early Sunday morning, Oct. 11, forcing the facility to suspend operations and causing widespread disruption across more than 80 digital services and cloud infrastructure components.
According to ASTRA and Crimean Wind Telegram channels, the attack on the 40-to-50-megawatt facility in Vladimir’s Energetik district marks the third precision strike on Yandex server infrastructure in four days.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The facility, designed to house up to 2,880 server racks, represents one of the Russian tech company’s foundational processing hubs.
Following the explosions, Yandex confirmed that operations at the Vladimir data center were halted. The disruption cascaded through Russian digital infrastructure, affecting consumer applications including the Alice voice assistant, Yandex Music, the Telemost videoconferencing tool, and Yandex Smart Home.
Enterprise systems hosted on Yandex Cloud suffered extensive outages across computing, storage, database management, and development pipelines.
Disrupted services included Compute Cloud, Object Storage, Managed Kubernetes, PostgreSQL, and ClickHouse databases, alongside developer tools and artificial intelligence interfaces such as the YandexGPT API, SpeechKit, and Vision OCR.
The outages extended beyond core Yandex applications, affecting third-party commercial platforms across Russia and neighboring countries. Users reported connectivity failures in banking applications, ride-hailing platforms, and major retail chains including Magnit and Fix Price.
Russia, With Uganda’s Help, Backs UN Resolution Calling Unilateral Sanctions Unlawful
Vladimir Region Governor Aleksandr Avdeev reported that drone strikes damaged local electrical substations, knocking out municipal power grids. Avdeev said utility crews restored heat and water supplies alongside roughly 80 percent of electrical service in affected areas of Vladimir by Sunday morning.
The Russian Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses intercepted 479 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight across 16 Russian regions – including Vladimir, Belgorod, Bryansk, Kursk, and Rostov regions – alongside occupied Crimea and the Black Sea.
Consecutive strikes on Russian cloud architecture
The strike in Vladimir follows consecutive attacks against Yandex facilities earlier in the week, reflecting an expanding campaign targeting Russian digital networks and data-processing logistics.
On Thursday, Oct. 8, Ukrainian strike drones struck a Yandex data center in Sasovo, located in the Ryazan region, igniting a fire and forcing a full operational shutdown. That strike disabled server infrastructure used by Russian Railways (RZhD), mobile network operator MegaFon, and several national media outlets.
The following day, on Friday, Oct. 9, drones hit another Yandex facility in the regional capital of Kaluga, located southwest of Moscow. Yandex confirmed that multiple hardware modules were disabled in that attack.
Following the initial strikes, Yandex removed the locations of its data centers across four Russian regions from its digital mapping platform. The repeated disruptions contributed to a decline in Yandex shares of approximately 4 percent on the Moscow Exchange earlier in the week.
Ukrainian military analysts have noted that systematic interdiction of enterprise data centers and communications networks complicates Russian state logistics, disrupts corporate administration, and impairs digital command-and-control capabilities supporting the Russian war effort.

Aggressors must answer for ecocide: Araghchi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:24:54 UTC
16:24:54 KST

Speaking Sunday at the international conference "Ecocide: the Silent War Crime" in Tehran, Araghchi said the environment is humanity's shared heritage, not an arena for rivalries or a victim of short-term economic and military calculations.
 
He said the term ecocide is structurally similar to genocide and represents a concept beyond a war crime against the environment, suggesting "nature-killing" as a Persian equivalent.
 
Araghchi said war damages water, soil, air, forests, farmland, energy resources, natural habitats and biodiversity, with effects that can last for years or decades after fighting ends.
 
He cited environmental devastation in Gaza, where UNEP has reported unprecedented damage including destruction of olive groves and contamination of water and soil; in Lebanon, where fires destroyed forests and tens of thousands of olive trees; and in Iran, where UNEP confirmed in March 2026 that attacks on oil facilities released hazardous compounds, recalling the "black rain" over Tehran.
 
Araghchi called for three axes of international cooperation: strengthening legal frameworks and clear criteria for identifying and addressing severe environmental destruction; creating scientific and impartial mechanisms to document damage from armed conflict; and developing regional and international cooperation to prevent destruction, rebuild ecosystems and support affected countries.
 
He said Iran supports recognising ecocide as an independent international crime, is ready to use its scientific, legal and diplomatic capacities, and called COP31 a suitable opportunity to draw global attention to the environmental effects of military attacks.
 
"We must not allow aggressors to escape responsibility for their criminal actions," he said.

Demographic change: Germany's population is declining, but not everywhere
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:21:00 UTC
16:21:00 KST

Germany's population is shrinking, but not everywhere
October 11, 2026
Germany's population is expected to decline from 83.5 million in 2025 to around 81.8 million by 2045, according to a new study from the Berlin Institute for Population and Development (Berlin-Institut für Bevölkerung und Entwicklung), in collaboration with the Wüstenrot Foundation, a non-profit that supports research on housing, urban development, and social change.
The decline in population alone is not the central challenge. More significant is the continuing rise in the number of retirees alongside a steadily shrinking workforce. Across Germany, the working-age population is projected to decrease by 4.7% by 2045.
"The baby boomer generation is retiring, while significantly smaller cohorts are following. Birth rates are falling, and immigration is not sufficient to offset the growing surplus of deaths over births," said Institute President Catherina Hinz when presenting the study in Berlin.
The term "baby boomers" refers to those born in the 1960s, when annual births exceeded one million. Thereafter, the birth rate fell sharply, effectively halving.
The economy matters
Germany's population may be shrinking, but according to the study, this trend is far from uniform across the country. In the years ahead, a region's economic attractiveness, and the financial strength that comes with it, will become even more important than it is today.
"Some regions will lose substantial numbers of residents and workers in the years ahead, while others continue to grow. Even within eastern Germany, southern Germany, and rural areas, the demographic and economic divide is widening," said Hinz.
"Demographic change is unfolding before our very eyes, and its effects are being felt across the country," Hinz added. "Its consequences can still be mitigated, but they can no longer be avoided. And the longer we wait, the narrower our scope for action will become."
Hinz's warning is echoed by Frederick Sixtus of the Berlin Institute. Almost every region now records more deaths than births, he notes, a consequence of decades of low birth rates. The implication is clear: Migration, both inward and outward, now shapes a region's demographic trajectory. Over recent decades, immigration from abroad has repeatedly helped stabilize population trends. Yet migration alone is no longer enough to halt the aging of society.
According to the study, several factors are critical if a region is to remain attractive to people relocating from abroad or from other parts of Germany: High-quality jobs offering good pay and working conditions, a sufficient supply of skilled workers for local businesses, financially robust municipalities, reliable childcare, and efficient transport and mobility infrastructure.
Berlin leads the way
Many major cities are expected to continue to grow in the years ahead, according to Manuel Slupina of the Wüstenrot Foundation. The study projects that Berlin will lead the way, with the capital's population increasing by almost 10% by 2045. Other cities expected to attract people include Hamburg, Frankfurt am Main, Munich, and Düsseldorf in western Germany, as well as Leipzig, Dresden, and Potsdam in the east.
The study's authors argue that the familiar distinction between urban and rural areas does not hold true everywhere. The hinterlands of many major cities are also expected to grow. While young people are increasingly drawn to metropolitan centers, families with children tend to settle in the surrounding areas. Among the places likely to lose population are several large cities in western Germany, including Bremen, Duisburg, Dortmund, and Kaiserslautern, whose economic appeal has gradually diminished. At the bottom of the ranking are many sparsely populated regions, a large number of them in eastern Germany.
Competition for talent
Twelve of the 20 districts and independent cities with the weakest overall ratings are now located in eastern Germany, up from five in the previous assessment in 2019. According to the study, these regions are also expected to see the steepest declines in their working-age populations, with losses of up to 18% by 2045. The authors conclude that competition for workers is therefore set to become one of the key demographic challenges of the decades ahead.
In this competition, the southern German states of Bavariaand Baden-Württemberg are regarded as having the strongest prospects. Bavaria ranks particularly highly thanks to its robust economy, which is thriving across much of the state, and its strong labor market. Women, older people, and people without German citizenship are also more likely to be employed in Bavaria than elsewhere. The ranking shows that economically successful regions are more effective at integrating different population groups into the labor market than weaker ones.
Policymakers must find local solutions
Under Germany's constitution, the country is committed to ensuring that people enjoy comparable opportunities, and with them the prospect of a good life, regardless of where they live.
The researchers offer clear recommendations to policymakers. They argue that the focus must be on addressing structural challenges and regional disparities. "What may be the right response for a growing major city is not necessarily the right one for a shrinking rural district," says Slupina. Tailor-made solutions are needed, but they require the right framework conditions. "There needs to be less rigid regulation, more scope for local initiative, and greater financial resources, especially for municipalities and those actively engaged at the local level." Slupina's message is clear: Regions should be trusted to shape their own futures.
Local authorities would no doubt welcome that. For years, mayors and district administrators have been calling for greater financial autonomy. They are currently seeking a larger share of overall tax revenues for municipalities. The federal government and the states, however, argue that they face budgetary constraints of their own. Yet both sides recognize that, sooner or later, Germany will have little choice but to reform its system of fiscal federalism.
This article was originally written in German.

Pentagon raises official US death toll in Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:20:35 UTC
16:20:35 KST

Pentagon raises official US death toll in Iran war
The Pentagon has revised its previously underreported tally of US military deaths linked to the war with Iran, raising the official count to 21.
The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) initially listed 18 US military deaths from hostile and non-hostile causes since the conflict began on February 28. The Washington Post reported last month, citing six US officials, that the database understated the number of deaths. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth called the findings “a complete lie.”
On Friday, the database was updated to include Army National Guard Maj. Sorffly Davius, 46, who died in Kuwait on March 6, and an unidentified Navy member who died by suicide in September.
It also recorded the death of Sgt. Devin A. Seibel, 26, who died in a training accident in Iraq in May. The military, however, did not link the incident to the war with Iran and classified it under Operation Inherent Resolve, the decade-long campaign against Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS). His inclusion brings the broader number of US military fatalities in the Middle East since February 28 to 22, in line with the figure previously reported by the newspaper.
The updated records also show 865 wounded service members.
Democratic Representatives Adam Smith and Chrissy Houlahan criticized the incorrect count, calling it “an embarrassment” for the military.
“There is no excuse for a mistake of this magnitude,” they said in a joint statement.
Approached by the Washington Post, the Pentagon did not address the changes but said it “continues to maintain a steadfast commitment to the transparent, accurate accounting of all service member casualties.”
Last month, the US Navy acknowledged that eight sailors assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during a ten-month deployment that included the Iran war. The disclosure followed reports of burnout, declining morale, and shortages of food and basic supplies.
Despite US President Donald Trump’s insistence that the campaign has been a success, a Reuters/Ipsos poll in September found that 62% of Americans disapprove of military strikes against Iran.
The conflict has also deepened political divisions ahead of November’s midterm election, with the financial cost and economic fallout drawing scrutiny. US Central Command estimated the bill at $43.6 billion through September 3, according to figures provided to lawmakers and seen by AP.
Trump previously said the war would end immediately after the election, subsequently telling Axios that he faces a “big decision” over whether to resume major attacks to bring it to a close.
In a phone call on Friday, Trump discussed Iran with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who stressed that a diplomatic settlement remains possible and reiterated Moscow’s offer to accept Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium to help resolve the dispute over its nuclear program. Trump welcomed Russia’s diplomatic involvement, according to presidential aide Yury Ushakov.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Sunday directed authorities to ensure that people gathering peacefully are not illegally detained and that metro and railway services function normally. The court's directive came a day after Centre's crackdown on CJP's proposed protest at Delhi's Jantar Mantar.The court issued notice to the Centre on a plea seeking contempt proceedings against authorities for allegedly violating its earlier directions on transport restrictions during the protest.“In view of the urgent applications alleging violation of our earlier order dt. October 9, 2026, and also alleging illegal detention of large number of individuals at Delhi on October 10, 2026 this court had assembled for an urgent hearing,” a bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said during a special sitting.“Senior counsels submitted there was a flagrant violation of the directions -- metro railway was not functioning, New Delhi and Nizamuddin railway stations remained closed, no traffic advisories were issued and a large number of persons were subjected to undue harassment and illegal detention even beyond the area which was covered by the prohibitory order under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023,” the bench said.
The Supreme Court asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta to ensure that the Delhi Metro operated according to its normal schedule and that internet services were not disrupted, subject to law and order conditions. It also directed that lawyers, journalists and others should not be impeded from discharging their professional duties.Mehta, appearing for the Centre, defended the authorities’ action and submitted that entry and exit had been restricted at only 45 of the 303 stations across the Delhi Metro network on October 10.The court was also hearing a habeas corpus petition filed by senior advocate Menaka Guruswamy concerning the detention of political leaders. It said it would grant a hearing to all lawyers involved in the matter.
What the Supreme Court said
No illegal detention: Authorities must ensure that people gathering peacefully are not illegally detained.
Normal metro operations: The Centre was asked to ensure that Delhi Metro services function according to their normal schedule.
Internet services: There should be no disruption to internet services, subject to law and order conditions.
Professional duties: Lawyers, journalists and others must not be impeded from discharging their professional duties.
Contempt proceedings: The court issued notice to the Centre on a plea alleging violation of its earlier directions.
What is contempt plea about
The contempt petition, filed by advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi, names Union home secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi Metro Rail Corporation chairperson D Thara as respondents.The plea refers to the Supreme Court’s October 9 order, passed while hearing a separate petition challenging the closure of 57 metro stations and the cancellation of trains to Delhi in view of the proposed protest. The latest applications alleged that the restrictions and detentions on October 10 violated the court’s directions.
The court’s intervention followed the CJP’s call for a mass mobilisation at Jantar Mantar, alongside student organisations, demanding action against CEC Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the functioning of the Election Commission.The government thwarted the planned demonstration through an extensive security crackdown across the national capital. More than 7,000 protesters were detained, including CJP leader Abhijit Dipke, several opposition leaders and YouTuber Dhruv Rathee.

Leaders are scheduled to meet to dicsuss the bloc’s budget.
Ireland, which holds the EU's rotating presidency, suggested on Oct. 10 slashing the bloc's next proposed budget by 140 billion euros ($155 billion), in a quest to bridge deep divisions and reach a deal by the end of the year.
Leaders from the 27-nation bloc will meet in Brussels this week to discuss the plan as they seek to reach an agreement on the 2028-2034 budget by Christmas.

The new budget would still far outstrip the EU's last one, which was worth around 1.2 trillion euros.
"Nobody's going to get everything that they wanted in any proposal, but we think that there is something there for all of the member states,” Ireland’s Europe minister Thomas Byrne said.
"We are still far from an agreement. The size of the new proposal is not a basis for agreement," German chancellor Friedrich Merz said in a statement.
Meanwhile lawmakers at the European parliament said the cuts went too far and the new draft "cannot be the starting point for an agreement."

Malaysia, Egypt agree to deepen trade, investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:08:02 UTC
16:08:02 KST

AFP Photo
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi held bilateral talks on Oct. 10, focusing on expanding trade, investment, and strategic cooperation during the Egyptian leader’s first state visit to Malaysia since taking office in 2014.
The leaders met privately at the Seri Perdana Complex in Putrajaya before broader discussions covering bilateral relations and regional and international developments, the state-owned Bernama news agency reported.
The two countries are seeking closer cooperation in semiconductors, automotive manufacturing, renewable energy, infrastructure, agriculture, digital technology, and the halal industry.
They also discussed the Palestinian issue and regional security, including maritime navigation in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
The visit included the exchange of four memoranda of understanding aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation.
Bilateral trade volume reached $870 million in January-August 2026, up 74.7 percent from the corresponding period last year, exceeding the $720 million recorded throughout 2025.
Egypt was Malaysia’s seventh-largest African trading partner last year, the report said.
Sisi’s visit marks the first by an Egyptian president in nearly three decades, following Hosni Mubarak’s visit in 1997.

Members of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement condemned the recent Houthi attack on Riyadh's international airport, which left at least 12 people dead and over 300 wounded, with Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif calling the Houthis’ actions a “flagrant violation of international law” that must be stopped immediately.
“Attacks targeting civilians and critical infrastructure are completely unacceptable and constitute a serious threat to regional peace and stability,” Sharif stated, extending condolences to those wounded and the bereaved families.
“Pakistan stands in unwavering solidarity with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its leadership and brotherly people.”
“In accordance with the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement and the enduring bonds of brotherhood between our two countries, we reaffirm our steadfast commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.”
Turkey’s Foreign Ministry released a statement condemning the strikes and wishing a quick recovery to the wounded.
Calling for an immediate end to the strikes, “which target civilians and civilian infrastructure,” Turkey reaffirmed its “full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reiterated our call for the resolution of ongoing conflicts through dialogue and diplomacy.”
'Attack on Saudi Arabia is an attack on Yemen'
The Saudi-backed head of Yemen's Presidential Council, Rashad al-Alimi, denounced the attack on Riyadh’s airport in his own post, extending his condolences to those wounded and the families of those killed.
“This criminal attack reflects the Houthis’ terrorist nature and their disregard for civilian lives and the interests of the Yemeni people,” wrote Alimi. “This comes as Saudi Arabia continues its fraternal support for Yemen’s economy, public budget, and citizens’ welfare, including recent facilities for Yemeni residents.”
“The security of Saudi Arabia and Yemen, and the interests of their peoples, are intertwined. Any attack on Saudi Arabia is an attack on our security, interests, and the future of our generations.”
“We reaffirm our shared resolve to continue the ‘Dawn of Yemen' Operation to end the terrorist threat and restore state institutions, whatever the sacrifices,” he said.
The Qatari Foreign Ministry condemned the strikes as well, “considering them a grave violation of Saudi Arabia's sovereignty and a direct threat to regional security, the safety of civilians, civilian infrastructure, and air navigation.”
It reiterated Qatar’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia, emphasizing “that the security of Saudi Arabia is an integral part of Qatar's security and the collective security system of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) States.”
Jordan's King Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also condemned the attack in their own X posts.
Trump weighing joining Saudi retaliation against Houthis
US President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House, was asked whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks, saying they "demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life."
“I am deeply shocked by & strongly condemn Saturday’s lethal attack by the Houthis on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, which reportedly killed 12 people & injured hundreds of civilians,” stated UN Secretary-General António Guterres in an X post.
“Attacks on civilians & civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately.”
Reuters contributed to this report.
