No whining and women: This Witches? Festival returns with a salute to female musicianship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:05:51 UTC
16:05:51 KST

Orit Messer-Yaakobi is not one to moan and groan. Her sunny outlook was patently clear from the first cheery “hello” of our telephone chat ahead of this year’s Witches? Festival, which celebrates female movers and shakers in the classical music world. One can, of course, home in on egregious discrimination, inequality of pay and professional opportunities, and, more tragically, the continuing acts of violence perpetrated against women, but the cellist-conductor was more focused on the positive aspect of the female side of the musical domain across the ages.
The official blurb describes the fifth edition of the festival, which takes place at the YMCA and Hansen House October 16-17, thus: “A musical journey following women who made a difference in the world of music and culture, from medieval times, through ancient eras to 20th-century jazz.” The two-day agenda duly provides plenty of collateral for that gender-oriented claim.
The event was initiated by Jerusalem Baroque Orchestra (JBO) founder-conductor-artistic director David Shemer, with the JBO performing predominantly baroque scores. But the programming purview stretches into more contemporary and other cultural and philosophical spheres too.
Broader road to music appreciation
Messer-Yaakobi features in the curtain-raiser at Hansen House, on cello. The October 16 (11 a.m.) date goes by the evocative and eclectically-leaning name of “Daphnis and the Winds of Love: A Balkan Myth.” An instrumental trio, which also includes recorder player Doret Florentin and guitarist Gideon Bretler, complemented by the Hakdoshot vocal threesome, follows a broad stylistic arc from the realms of Greek mythology through to contemporary material, dipping into French Baroque music and folk melodies en route.
The JBO principal cellist is heavily invested both in the ensemble, of which she is a longtime member, and in the Witches? format. “I am very happy with the festival because it allows us to take an immersive approach to a particular subject,” she notes. “When you have a festival, which lasts just a few days, and you invite other ensembles to take part, that allows us to research and deeply explore a specific topic. We can address it from all sorts of perspectives, and that makes it very interesting and very daring.”
The latter attribute is not a feature one regularly associates with classical music in its wider sense. Artistic and musical directors tend to shy away from more challenging works from contemporary times which incorporate, say, atonal or electronic music. It is very much, particularly in these financially strapped cultural times, about putting bums on seats. That generally leads to programming that treads tried and tested areas, with crowd-pleasers by the likes of Beethoven, Tchaikovsky, Brahms, and Bach.
Messer-Yaakobi says that Witches? has always looked to flex strictly defined genre and stylistic delineations. “The repertoire we perform is not run-of-the-mill stuff. We don’t do the bestsellers – the Magnificat [by Bach] and such like. And we perform in beautiful locations and with very good ensembles.” Seems like a recipe for success, both on the stage and at the box office.
Celebrating female players in classical music domain
The core themes of the whole venture revolve around female composers and performers of classical music across the ages, with each annual agenda based on a more focused feature of that field of endeavor. “We had various themes,” the cellist recalls, “like fate, warrior women, and healing women. Then we had the [post-Oct. 7] war and, you know, things always resonate.”
That brought us neatly around to this year’s thematic linchpin, Echo. Messer-Yaakobi says the programming mindset, for this edition, followed a far more positive planning ethos. “In past years, the festival was generally about women whose voices were suppressed or were pushed aside. Specifically, this year it is about women whose presence and deeds changed the face of music.”
That sounds like a refreshing proactive line to follow. “Each concert takes a different approach – either about women with initiative, women who wrote and performed their music, or patrons or muses, or heroines. It is very fascinating and, I think, very liberating, relieving.”
The accent is very much on upbeat vibes. “This year we are not looking at women who were not heard, so then we’ll have the festival,” the cellist proclaims in a faux weepy voice. Determined philosophy notwithstanding, this is not an under-the-carpet sweeping exercise. “Things are tough enough for women now, [in the classical music arena], and it was much tougher back in the 17th century,” Messer-Yaakobi continues.
Barbara Strozzi is a striking case in point. Not only did she have the “temerity” as a woman to write music, and that despite being the illegitimate child of a servant, her works were duly lauded in 17th-century Venice, with Strozzi performing her own charts as vocalist. Her stellar contributions are noted in the “Virtuosissima cantatrice” concert at the YMCA on October 17 (1:30 p.m.). The Italian show title translates as “the most virtuoso female singer,” which, by all reports, is a fair description of Strozzi’s musical performance abilities. The vocalist spot for the Witches? recital will be taken by soprano Daniela Skorka, supported by violinist Kati Debretzeni, with Shemer on harpsichord.
Strozzi was, it seems, a fearless character who let no social mores or political tenets of the day stand between her and getting the fruits of her artistic labors out there to the public. “She is one of the few female composers who had their scores printed. She operated out of Venice, from a very male-dominated society, and she was very highly regarded,” Messer-Yaakobi advises. “She also ran a very important music salon. But she was exceptional.”
That fits this year’s line of programming thought. “We have presented numerous works by female composers and musicians who were marginalized, but this year that’s not the case. This year the festival is very powerful.”
It is, the cellist simply states, about the music. “There is no intent on righting the situation [vis-à-vis sexual discrimination]. We want to give women their place without the [politically-oriented] crutches. If you look at the concerts, you see that each ensemble, with its program, offers something very interesting. And the gender is of no importance. It is just by chance that the composer is a woman [with regard to the quality of the work in question].”
Messer-Yaakobi proceeds to proffer the evidence for that level playing field strategy in the two-day agenda. “There is the “A Woman’s Song” recital that addresses love, motherhood, and war and peace. That is a triangle that can convey a universal historic passage.” The program comprises texts presented by female characters, at times a mythological or religious figure, or a mother, and other times a basic, clear human call. The voices resonating from the texts are woven into a single storyline that is personal yet universal, historical yet, as we painfully know, more relevant than ever today.
As per Messer-Yaakobi’s claim of eclecticism, the titillatingly titled “High Heels” show, at the YMCA on October 16 (10 p.m.), should have the audience members appreciating the onstage action in a more animated manner. “That is something cute with a very different color,” she chuckles. “They will play swing music from the 1940s and 1950s.” That shuffles the sonic festival pack. “It will bring a different color, and celebrate the music. You don’t always have to play intricate heavy material. You can just enjoy life,” she laughs.
It is also highly likely that the folks who make it over to the YMCA for the outdoor gig, in the YMCA Arcade, should by then be in a suitable frame of mind to make the most of the energized entertainment. “It is scheduled for the end of the first day, when anything goes.” The lineup for the fun run out includes three female vocalists and a piano-led jazz trio.
The women behind the celebrities
The second day opens with a reminder – or eye-opener – of how much poorer the classical music world would be without female contributors, in all walks of musical life.
The 11 a.m. “Vienna-Weimar-Siberia: A Journey with Musical Women” slot, at the YMCA, asks the simple and, no doubt, for some of more conservative, narrow minds, provocative question: What would classical music look like without the women who worked behind the scenes as students, patrons, musicians, and salon hosts? The Israeli Romantic Ensemble foursome, led by Gili Rinot on clarinet, will perform works by the likes of Mozart, Mendelssohn, and Bach. One of the former’s star students was a certain Franziska von Jacquin, one of quite a few female disciples of the feted Austrian composer. It seems he was particularly taken with von Jacquin, both for her talent and her diligence, and composed his Piano Sonata No. 14 and Fantasia in C minor with her in mind.
His early student register included one Thérèse von Trattner who, in fact, kept the then young composer, recently arrived in Vienna from his native Salzburg, financially afloat. She also provided him with accommodation, spread the word about him, and organized subscription concerts of his music in the imperial capital in 1784. The program for those groundbreaking events included Mozart’s Piano Concertos Nos. 14, 15, and 16, and provided him with a firm foothold in the Viennese artistic and hierarchical social domains.
Other women who get a well-deserved salute at the morning concert include German Jewish philanthropist Sara Levy, who was also the great-aunt of Mendelssohn and duly supported his writing efforts, and pioneering female French cellist Lise Cristiani, whose musicianship prompted Mendelssohn to dedicate a slot in his Songs Without Words series to her. “This is a fascinating story of women who changed the history of music,” the festival textual backdrop declares.
There is a nod to biblical climes with “The Golden Apple” concert, with the Nari Ensemble quartet of soprano Liron Givoni accompanied by recorder player Naomi Hasson, cellist Yotam Haran, and harpsichord player Guy Pardo. The Garden of Edenesque storyline subtext features an angel and a man who sets out in search of the woman worthy of receiving a golden apple and bringing the mother of Jesus into the world. En route, they encounter biblical heroines, from Eve to Esther, each of whom is portrayed musically in Baroque works from Bohemia, Italy, England, and Germany. That multilayered sequence creates a compelling musical-theatrical performance in which story and music shed new light on the iconic characters.
Straddling the gender divide
The whole Witches? shebang comes to a climactic end with the closer at the YMCA, at 8:30 p.m. on October 17. The JBO will take the stage with all guns firing for the Cleopatra and Giulio show. Mezzo-soprano Shaked Bar performs the titular royal role, which, considering the fabled Egyptian ruler inspired numerous composers of the Baroque era, is a neat thematic fit. The chap in the concert moniker is better known around the English-speaking world as Julius Caesar, and Bar and the orchestra will perform works by Handel, 18th-century German composer and singer Johann Adolph Hasse, 17th-century Venetian composer Antonio Sartorio, and 18th-century German composer and singer Carl Heinrich Graun. The virtuosic and intimate arias will unpack the romantic relationship between the two fabled protagonists, with Bar navigating her way across demanding bifurcated female-male bridges as she moves between the two characters.
“The grand finale has the whole [JBO] ensemble, as opposed to the other, chamber orchestra-based, concerts,” Messer-Yaakobi notes. The latter approach, she says, adds charm and a welcoming ambiance to the whole program. “When the orchestra organizes a festival, it makes sure to invite outside artists and ensembles. Some of the artists appear with us in the long run but, in fact, these are ensembles that propose programs and the JBO hosts them. That, for me, is wonderful.”
It also offers the paying public a greater breadth of performance styles while keeping the whole Witches? venture fresh and intriguing. “There are all sorts of festivals whereby the host orchestra performs the majority of the concerts,” the principal cellist adds. “With us it is very varied. That is why the festival is so colorful and rich.” That philosophy, she feels, offers across-the-board benefits. “That puts the baroque orchestra in a special place in the [music] scene.”
With its purely sunny affirming take on women’s part in the musical timeline, it is to be hoped that the current Witches? roll out helps to right the male-skewed view of classical music per se, and may even lead to the discovery, by professionals and the public alike, of more hidden, talented and, no doubt, determined female artists.
For tickets and more information: 
jbo.co.il/en/festivals/witches-
festival-2026-echo/

====================================================================================================

Jerusalem Women's Film Festival explores trauma, healing, and hope - preview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:05:51 UTC
16:05:51 KST

A couple of eons ago, an Australian pop singer called Helen Reddy had a hit with a song called “I Am Woman.”
The 1971 number was a clarion call to the predominantly male-dominated world to sit up and take note of the distaff side of the populace.
The opening stanza sets the uncompromising tone: “I am woman, hear me roar, in numbers too big to ignore.”
That makes perfect sense, considering close to half the residents of Mother Earth are female.
Further down the lyrics, Reddy sings: “But I’m still an embryo, with a long, long way to go, until I make my brother understand.”
Sadly, the gender imbalance, in terms of pay, career openings, and plenty of other areas of daily life, including those of a fundamentally existential nature, continues to leave women trailing in their male counterparts’ wake.
However, strides are being made across certain fields, particularly in the arts.
There is clearly plenty to roar about at this year’s Jerusalem International Women’s Film Festival – the seventh edition to date – with screenings and other events and activities set for all kinds of locations and venues around the city October 12-16, spreading out from its traditional hub of the Jerusalem Cinematheque.
The five-day agenda, curated by Lihi Sabag and Shira Meishar, takes in thematically appropriate feature films, from here and around the world, documentaries, and shorts.
Many local filmmakers and the odd offshore visitor will attend the screenings, and there will be Q&As and discussions about the movies.
As per the norm these days in this troubled part of the world, the emotional ricochets of the barbarous Hamas attack down South, and the ensuing hostage situation and violence in Gaza, there is no getting away from those horrific, heartbreaking events.
“More and more things come out, each year on October 7,” Sabag says. “There is emotional baggage we carry with us. It’s hard.”
There’s been no getting away from that, certainly in the past three years, which followed ever so neatly on the heels of the COVID-19 business, lockdowns and all. But, somehow, Sabag and Meishar have kept the Women’s Film Festival on the road.
“Roni [Mahadav-Levin], the CEO of the Cinematheque, told me he has never known such challenging years for a festival to navigate.”
Indeed, Sabag and Meishar have endured seven years of scrapping for budgets and dealing with daunting logistics.
But Sabag remains steadfast and optimistic, dipping into scriptural climes for encouragement. “I told Roni we’ve had our seven challenging years, like the seven thin cows [in Pharaoh’s dream, interpreted by Joseph] in the Bible. Now we’re going to have seven good years, like the seven fat cows.”
If the output of our filmmakers is anything to go by, Sabag’s vision of prosperity and good times in the coming years seems perfectly reasonable, paucity of funding sources notwithstanding.
The artistic director is well and truly in the game herself. “I am also a documentarist and am currently working on two films. The competition here [for financial backing] is very fierce. You submit lots of films to a corporation, to Yes and Hot, and ultimately only a few receive funding. That makes things very complicated.”
Why the festival?
I asked Sabag a simple, naive question to get the informed professional lowdown on the project backdrop. Why is there a need for a women’s film festival in this country?
“Shira [Meishar] and I have this sort of ‘sports’ activity,” she fires back. “Every time they hold Israeli Film Day – that happens about twice a year – we check the list of movies being filmed. Out of 35 films, there are three or maybe four directed by women.”
That, says Sabag, may not be the result of an anti-female stance per se, but the scarcity of works created by and featuring women, she feels, besides other salient points that could be raised in the context, simply doesn’t make artistic sense.
“I don’t know if that is a matter of discrimination, but we want to say we have amazing female artists, and it is important to give them a stage. The stage doesn’t always have room for everyone; there are lots of festivals, and the focus is not always on them [women creators].”
That is one, definitively polite, way of putting it.
“We want to celebrate the artistry of women. It is important for us to have our narrative, our perspective, with the same amount of screen time [as male filmmakers].”
Then again, it is not just about achieving quantitative parity at movie theaters and other venues where films are shown.
“Even if we do get that, we will still have the Women’s Film Festival,” Sabag points out. “We want to tell the story from our [female] standpoint.
“It is also because it is more difficult for women to direct films. I don’t know why. But we see fewer films by women, so their stories are less front and center. We have to do something about that.”
Next week’s festival is certainly one way.
The female touch
The female touch is definitively in the creative mix in Frank & Louis. All the main protagonists are male, as you might expect from a drama-thriller set in a prison populated by inmates who have committed serious crimes. But Swiss director Petra Biondina Volpe has imbued the characters with a certain tenderness and humaneness.
Those are not attributes one would normally associate with tough-looking lifers, people who have been shut away from society for terrible acts of violence.
“There is such a sense of compassion in the movie,” Sabag observes.
Having a woman at the helm, she says, makes all the difference.
“I see all these prison-based series, and they are always so hard-hitting. With Frank & Louis, I feel something completely different. That is a statement. You always have violence and knives and all that in prison series.”
Shades of October 7 and its very human emotional and societal aftermath. “You feel the healing in the film,” Sabag posits.
That is integral to the plot. The storyline feeds off the real-life Gold Coats program at the California Men’s Colony in San Luis Obispo, whereby long-term prisoners are trained to act as carers for elder inmates suffering from dementia.
There is no gratuitous violence in the movie, and Volpe skillfully steers clear of melodrama. That can only come from a sensitive hand on the directorial wheel, which, in this case, happens to belong to a woman.
French drama La Maison des Femmes is another female-crafted drama that should tug at festivalgoers’ heartstrings and even bring the occasional smile to their faces.
Directed by Melisa Godet, it tells the story of a healthcare and support center for women in all sorts of predicaments, including being subjected to abuse and violence by partners, and rape.
Again, Godet could easily have gone overboard with the pathos and tear-jerking. The stark existential subject matter is tailor-made for expressions of extreme emotion.
However, all the actors put in convincing performances, and Godet manages to keep her viewers on board to the end, the optimistic yet non-formulaic close.
Looking for identity
There is more emotive filmic quality on offer in My Underground Mother by American journalist-filmmaker Marisa Fox.
This is as gripping a documentary as you could hope to see, as Fox slowly and tenaciously unravels the real story behind her late mother’s – Tamar’s – life.
It was only years after Tamar’s death that Fox managed to get her show on the road, somehow scraping the grants and other financial assistance together in adequate amounts, and setting off to meet Tamar’s former friends, fellow inmates in a forced labor camp in Poland.
The documentary is the ultimate voyage of discovery as Fox chases down every alleyway of cold hard tangible facts and/or clearly, and sometimes tearfully, retrieved recollections by women who shared Tamar’s fate during the Holocaust, and some during her relatively brief, yet very significant, time in pre-state Palestine and the young Israeli state.
Again, a deft, empathetic hand was required on the directorial tiller.
“It was an urgent desire. It was like, how can I know myself if I don’t know where I come from? It was as if I might have been living a lie. Am I living a life? Who am I?”
If she’d been looking for actors who could have done the business in a feature film, Fox could not have hoped for a better or more compelling bunch than the cast of characters that people the documentary.
The film is also superbly designed, as Fox sews animation segments betwixt the real-life encounters and the photogenic locations, crafting a seamless flow as the storyline unfolds.
There are so many emotions, sensibilities, and attributes across the 88-minute work, as Tamar’s former friends and co-survivors spin out the stirring nuts and bolts behind her incredible timeline, meandering through the trauma, resilience, pain, and ultimate victory.
There are even snippets of humor – generally of the darker ilk – that grab you and bring a smile to the face, and even laughter.
“Humor is a balm for atrocity and for trauma,” Fox declares.
It is, she feels, part and parcel of our history and our ability to work our way through anything and everything that is thrown at us.
“I think that’s why Jews are such great comics. We know hardship, and we know that one of the best defense mechanisms is to laugh about it and move on.”
There is popular evidence for that claim. “Just look at how effective [now 100-year-old Jewish American director, producer, writer and actor] Mel Brooks was with [1967 dark satirical movie] The Producers and so many of his movies. He knew that humor goes a long way in shining a light on injustice and trauma. It also helps us look at it in a right way.”
There are other, broader messages in My Underground Mother, relating to all-female Nazi camps and the way this then-incipient country mistreated Holocaust survivors. Neither of these two topics seem to attract the attention of documentarists or historians. Perhaps Fox’s work, which was around 15 years in the making, will help to eventually address that.
Local industry progress
And in case you haven’t taken note of developments in the local film industry over the past couple of decades or so, you should know that Israeli cinema has come on in leaps and bounds, particularly in the documentary arena.
However, the festival opens with a feature film by Klil Kovesh called Wild Things. After a bunch of shorts she made over the past decade or so, Kovesh’s first full-length effort looks at questions of identity, relationships, and societal values.
Celebrated actress, screenwriter, playwright, film director, and social activist Hanna Azoulay Hasfari gets a well-deserved lifetime achievement tribute, and several of her works, including Sh’Chur and Orange People, are on the festival roster.
Alice. Last Conversations is one of the more eye-catching items on the documentary side of the five-day program.
The film tells the life story and lifework of German-born, British-bred Prof. Alice Shalvi, who made aliyah soon after the creation of the state.
She was an educator and tireless mover and shaker behind the fledgling feminism field here, lobbying politicians, pounding the protest march beat, and doing her damnedest to ensure as many young women as possible, across all religions and ethnicities, gained a solid education.
The film, made by Nurit Jakobs Yinon, offers an intimate portrait of Shalvi in the last year of her long, fruitful life as she runs the rule over her 96 years on terra firma, recalling her triumphs and failures, her achievements and regrets. Jakobs Yinon will attend the screening.
Several competitions dot the festival lineup, including Independent Shorts, Student Films, and Young Directors for budding high school student filmmakers.
The former includes Tal Kushner’s intriguing Mikveh, which offers a behind-the-scenes glimpse at issues faced by religious women relating to intimacy, relationships, motherhood, and hopes.
With all our trials and tribulations here in the security-political and individual spheres, there is, sadly, no shortage of thematic raw material to fuel exploratory projects. The documentaries in the festival lineup duly offer immersive, often highly personal looks at challenging life predicaments.
The Jerusalem Cinematheque is the festival’s traditional hub, but there are screenings and events scheduled at locations all over the city, including at women’s shelters, the Mazkeka, the Van Leer Institute, and, surprisingly, in haredi neighborhoods.
There are workshops, video therapy sessions, as well as a slew of free slots across the five days.
Notwithstanding the heavy subject matter of many of the films, Sabag expects Jerusalem Women’s Film Festival attendees to come away from the festival in a buoyant, hopeful frame of mind.
“In recent years, we have endeavored to bring movies that are not overly challenging. Our approach is that we need to present the public with more encouraging material. We have enough horrors around us in real life.”
Ain’t that the truth.
For more information: www.jwff.co.il

How will Saudi Arabia retaliate against Houthi attacks on civilian infrastructure? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:05:47 UTC
16:05:47 KST

Saudi Arabia has vowed a firm response to a deadly attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that killed 12 people and wounded 309 others on October 10.
The attack is part of a growing campaign by the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen targeting Saudi Arabia’s airports and civilian infrastructure. It comes as fighting intensifies in Yemen and maritime security concerns spread across the Gulf.
This deadly attack will require a response. The attack was designed to spread terror and strike at strategic infrastructure. Similar to how Iran targeted US bases in the region, Iran’s allies in Yemen are seeking to disrupt civilian life in Saudi Arabia by getting airports closed and flights canceled.
This is a challenge for Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has expensive air defenses. However, the Iranians and Houthis have proven in the past that they can penetrate these defenses, not only in Saudi Arabia but also in the Gulf and sometimes even when attacking Israel.
“The attack on King Khalid International Airport is a terrorist act and will be met with a firm response,” Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, said in a statement carried by the Saudi Press Agency, according to Arab News. Al-Maliki described the attack as a “full-fledged war crime” and said the coalition would respond in accordance with international humanitarian law.
“The Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will respond to this terrorist attack firmly and in accordance with international humanitarian law and its customary rules,” he said, according to the Arab News report.
Riyadh is building a case now to respond, and the question is how. It has already been using its air force to strike at the Houthis. The Houthis have less to lose than Saudi Arabia. They don’t have a lot of strategic infrastructure. Riyadh has already been fighting them since 2015.
Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said on October 11 that the attack killed four Saudi citizens and eight foreign nationals, including citizens of Bangladesh, Palestine, the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, and Sudan. “The attack also left [many] others injured, including individuals in critical condition,” the authority said, according to Arab News.
The attack forced authorities to suspend operations at the airport while damage was assessed. Arab News reported, citing FlightAware, that at least 291 flights were canceled over a 24-hour period. International airlines have also suspended services to Saudi airports.
The attack followed several days of Houthi strikes on Saudi aviation infrastructure. On October 6, two women, one Moroccan and one Algerian, were killed in an attack on Abha International Airport. A Sudanese man was killed in an attack on Riyadh’s airport the following day.
On October 8, there were other attacks on Riyadh airport that killed three people, including Saudi pilot Capt. Hamoud Ali AlKalthami, whose aircraft was struck while on the ground. “This attack comes amidst ongoing blatant assaults targeting civil aviation facilities in the Kingdom,” the Saudi aviation authority said.
The Houthis have also targeted other Saudi cities and infrastructure, including Khamis Mushayt, Jazan, and Najran. According to Arab News, a projectile fell near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Saturday. Saudi forces also reported intercepting a drone targeting the eastern region and a ballistic missile over Al-Kharj. The US has condemned the attacks on Saudi Arabia. It is not yet clear if the US will also help the Saudis carry out airstrikes. The US has been supporting the Saudis in other ways. Pakistan and Turkey are also backing Riyadh.
Rubio condemns Houthi attack on Saudi airport
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks, noting that an American citizen was among those killed. “These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now,” Rubio wrote on X/Twitter. He also noted that “the United States strongly condemns the recent attacks on the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by the terrorist Houthis, including today’s strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that took numerous innocent lives, including an American citizen.”
He went on to note that “we stand with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people and extend our condolences to the victims and their families.”
The latest escalation by the Houthis has focused partly on Yemen’s western coast and the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. Last week, the Yemeni government forces launched a counter-offensive to try to push the Houthis back on some fronts. According to Al-Ain News, the Southern Giants forces said on October 10 that they had destroyed five Houthi armored vehicles during an attempted advance toward Dhubab Airport, west of Taiz.
The forces said they “destroyed 5 Houthi armored vehicles and killed those on them, during the militias' desperate attempt to advance towards Dhubab Airport on the west coast.”
Military sources told Al-Ain that the Houthis were mobilizing fighters in the Al-Shamaitain district, south of Taiz, and may be preparing to attack Al-Mudharabah Al-Ulya and outflank the Giants forces.
Region faces maritime insecurity amid attacks on oil tankers
The renewed fighting threatens shipping routes at a time when the wider region is already experiencing increased maritime insecurity. This means that Iran is not only involved in backing the Houthis but also continuing threats along a frontline that stretched from Bab el-Mandeb to the Strait of Hormuz to Iraq.
In a separate incident over the weekend, the United Arab Emirates National Guard announced on October 10 that its Coast Guard had rescued 22 crew members from an oil tanker that caught fire in the Arabian Gulf. According to Arab News, the National Guard said emergency teams responded to a distress call, located the tanker, and evacuated all 22 crew members. They received first aid and were reported to be in stable condition.
The announcement followed an incident involving the Panama-flagged tanker Gem No. 2, which was struck by an unidentified projectile off the UAE coast on October 9, sparking a fire. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said the vessel was hit approximately 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazirah Al Hamra. No group claimed responsibility, and the available reports did not establish whether the rescue involved the same tanker.
The combination of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, renewed fighting around Bab el-Mandeb and threats to shipping in the Gulf illustrates how the Yemen conflict is increasingly intertwined with the broader regional confrontation. This has always been the Iranian modus operandi. It sees the region as a 3,000-mile frontline.
When Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, Iran also mobilized its proxies in Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, and Yemen. Although Iran lost Syria when the Assad regime fell, it still has powerful partners in Hezbollah and the Houthis. There are also Iraqi militias that support Iran.
Saudi Arabia has said it will not allow Yemeni territory to be used as a launchpad for attacks on the Kingdom or threats to international navigation. With Riyadh promising further action and the Houthis continuing their attacks, the escalation poses growing risks to civilian aviation, regional infrastructure and commercial shipping.

The colors she lives by: How one mother is keeping her son's memory alive after October 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:05:33 UTC
16:05:33 KST

‘My son Ilai was born on March 4, 1996, on Purim eve,” Adital Zu Aretz says. “On the day he was born, 13 people were killed in a suicide bombing at Dizengoff Center. That was how Ilai’s life began, and how it ended – with evil. The kindest child in the world was born into that evil.”
On Oct. 7, 2023, Ilai Baram and two of his friends were killed by Hamas terrorists near Kibbutz Gevim, as they were driving back from the Supernova music festival.
“Ilai had ADHD,” his mother notes. “He was very, very intelligent, sensitive, full of love and warmth, and very deep. He wanted to get to the bottom of everything, to understand things from the inside out. He loved friends and people. He was very intelligent and thoughtful.”
Despite having asthma, Baram joined a combat unit and became a squad commander in the Nahal Brigade.
“Once, during an exercise near Rosh Pina,” Adital recalls, “he called me and said, ‘Mom, I can’t breathe. Get me an inhaler.’ I drove two and a half hours to bring him one. That was how much he wanted to be a combat soldier.”
After completing his military service, Ilai learned about Wim Hof, a Dutch motivational speaker and extreme athlete known for his ability to withstand extreme cold. Hof developed the Wim Hof Method, a practice that combines breathing exercises, ice baths, and mental focus. The cold triggers the body’s stress response, increasing alertness, heart rate, and breathing.
Ilai took courses in the Wim Hof Method and began leading workshops in Israel. “Once he began taking it seriously and doing it exclusively, he became extremely successful,” Zu Aretz says. “He worked with many hi-tech companies, such as Microsoft, Google, and others, running sessions for CEOs and everyone else.”
Zu Aretz learned of his death on Oct. 7 before receiving official notification, when a photo of his damaged car with the bodies of Ilai and his friends appeared on Telegram.
“Thousands of people came to his funeral,” she says. “He was like the Pied Piper. I think that all of Tel Aviv knew him. He helped so many people. After he was murdered, so many came to tell me how he had helped them, whether by carrying shopping bags, persuading someone not to smoke, or encouraging someone to do meaningful army service. He touched everyone.”
Comfort in color
After her son’s death, Zu Aretz found comfort in painting and colors. Her Tel Aviv apartment walls are adorned with her colorful artwork.
“I’m a strong person by nature, so at first I didn’t really know how to express the pain. I cried, but I have a very strong inner resilience, and I didn’t want to fall apart. I suffered such a devastating blow that I didn’t know how to express my feelings. So I immediately turned to colors and painting, and I felt how much it helped. It still helps me today. On a day when I paint, I feel okay. When I don’t paint, I cry. Three years have passed, and I can still cry every day. It isn’t something that goes away. But at least when I paint, I have a good day.”
‘Green and Pink’
Zu Aretz says that colors can heal and open one’s heart. In this spirit, she wrote Green and Pink, a book that uses a self-healing, emotional expression method using colors and shapes to tap into the subconscious. She explains that green brings confidence and a sense of grounding, while pink brings a sense of embrace. “Green and pink are the colors of the heart,” she says. “There are many studies about colors and how they affect us physiologically, mentally, and emotionally.”
Green and Pink was first published in Hebrew in December 2025 and outlines over 100 exercises. It has also been published in English and Italian. Zu Aretz explains that the activities can help people move forward. They explore themes including self-confidence, self-love, emotional expression, creativity, and coping with fear and pain.
To spread her teachings, she has established color “embassies” in Rome, Amsterdam, and Barcelona, where she teaches her method in workshops for women. “I want people all over the world to know how to help themselves heal and express themselves through color,” she says.
Zu Aretz also conducts large seminars at major companies, as well as for small groups in her home. Trained as a marriage and couples therapist, she says that her use of color has changed her therapeutic approach. “I always could help, but today I incorporate color, which I didn’t do before Ilai was murdered. For example, when I work with a young woman and explain how to love and respect herself so she can be in a relationship, I combine that with color.”
If someone in a relationship has trouble communicating, she will show them light blue and other blues, along with oranges and reds. “Something that gets him moving, talking, and expressing himself instead of staying silent, eating himself up inside, and damaging his relationship.”
Since Oct. 7 and Ilai’s death, Zu Aretz has not returned to her work fully. “I only do workshops, and I don’t count that as work,” she says. I hold a workshop at home once a week and occasionally see people for treatment. I can’t really say I’ve returned to myself. I don’t think I’ve returned to myself at all.”
A children’s book
Her second book, Ilai and Henry in the Kingdom of Pacifiers, is intended for children. The book was published in October 2025, marking two years since Ilai’s murder.
“The story is exactly about Ilai. He had a hard time giving up his pacifier. The story follows what happened to him. Henry was Ilai’s dog. Gradually, I talked to him about needing to feel his own strength. That’s the story itself.”
What does she expect will happen when parents read the story to their children? “I want the child to gain strength and understand that they have power within them and can stop using the pacifier. They don’t have to have it. The pacifier gives them security, so they don’t want to let go of it. It gives them strength. They need to understand: ‘I have that strength without the pacifier. The pacifier is temporary, for a particular age, and then I let it go.’
“It’s for the parent, too. The parent also understands that we’re all the same in this respect. Giving up a pacifier, giving up cigarettes, giving up drinking, or giving up other things – it’s all the same idea as in the book about Ilai. It’s about believing that you can do it at all.”
The two-world future
Zu Aretz is honest and open and aware that she will feel the grief of the loss of her son for the rest of her life. But she adds, she has two other children and an eight-month-old granddaughter. “I need to be there for them. I need to be happy for them. I live in two worlds: the world of pain and the world of joy.
“You have to understand that you can’t exist only in grief. You also have family and people around you. You can’t fall entirely into it. There’s nothing more down there. In that pit, the darkness is only more darkness and more darkness. The deeper you go, you won’t find anything new – only more darkness. My work, and the work of people who have lost loved ones, is to enjoy the blooming of the flowers, the sun shining, good music, a joke, and delicious food. All of that still exists.”
By reading her books, Zu Aretz hopes people will remember her son Ilai: “that he was a great light and that he still shines today. He is gone, but he is present. At family meals, he was always the one making us laugh the most, singing songs, bringing joy, and dancing. His light is here all the time. We must also find joy for his sake because he couldn’t bear to see people down. He wouldn’t allow it. Although he sometimes had low moods himself, he always tried to lift people, be happy, and keep being happy. In Green and Pink, they can find the colors, and in Ilai and Henry in the Kingdom of Pacifiers, they can find strength.
“I won’t go back to feeling the way I did before Oct. 7,” Zu Aretz concludes. “But I try to live with as much joy and love as possible; to look for laughter and happiness rather than sink into mourning and sorrow because those are with me all the time. I want us all to be friends, this whole country. I want us to be well, with no blackness, only color, and for people to see the good even in the bad. We’re living through difficult times, with everyone against everyone else.
“I want us to find the good in each person, rather than look for the bad – only the good.”■

The 200-year-old &quot;Grandmother&quot; cottonwood was destroyed for Trump&apos;s border wall — dozens of protesters arrested
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:04:29 EEST
16:04:29 KST

The 200-year-old "Grandmother" cottonwood was destroyed for Trump's border wall — dozens of protesters arrested
Kyiv • UNN
In Arizona, contractors felled a 200-year-old cottonwood during construction of the border wall. Protesters had been trying to save the tree for more than 70 days.
The 200-year-old cottonwood near the US-Mexico border, known as “Grandma,” was destroyed to make way for Donald Trump’s border wall — despite the sustained efforts of protesters who tried to save it, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
At the end of July, land defenders began a protest by taking up residence in a tree in the abandoned town of Lochiel, Arizona; they took turns staying on a platform installed high in the canopy. The group remained there for more than 70 days.
Then, at dawn on Monday, more than 80 federal agents surrounded the protesters’ camp, located on private property; they made arrests and prevented people from approaching the cottonwood. Videos and photos on social media, as well as eyewitness accounts, show that agents, who had risen in a steel basket on a telescopic lift, forcibly removed a person from the platform in the tree. Other participants in the protest were shoved and knocked to the ground as they tried to reach the tree to prevent its destruction.
After that, contractors from Fisher Sand & Gravel, the company building this section of the wall, brought down the tree with an excavator: it split and fell to the ground. The land defenders shouted, cried and hurled accusations at the federal agents.
“Seeing this is heartbreaking,” said Eric Meza, coordinator of the Borderlands project at the Sierra Club, who had fought for months to save the trees, beginning with a series of letters to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).
“This tree brought many people together,” he said. Now, Meza added, “the community is responding with outrage. People are furious.”
The process of felling the cottonwood was filmed by a team from the far-right political organization Turning Point USA; they appeared to be accompanying the Border Patrol and had unrestricted access to the closed public road.
One of the land defenders climbed another ancient cottonwood that was growing directly on the border with Mexico. On Thursday, US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers and Mexican police — the latter had already been at the site for several days and were openly cooperating with US authorities — dismantled the activist’s platform while they were in the tree and also confiscated food and water supplies. Alex Chubbott, an environmental activist who had periodically stayed at the camp for more than a month, reported this.
Late Friday evening, the activist climbed down from the tree on his own after going several days without receiving new supplies.
The forces involved in the operation included Border Patrol officers (a CBP unit) and the BORTAC special operations tactical team, whose officially stated mission is “responding to terrorist threats.”
The tree-sit protest began shortly after contractors felled and destroyed three other old cottonwoods nearby on July 27.
Two 30-foot-high walls (about 9 meters) are being built in this area — the San Rafael Valley, a remote and once-idyllic highland prairie where the film “Oklahoma!” was shot. This valley, along with the Patagonia and Huachuca Mountains rising on either side of it, forms one of the most important regional wildlife corridors between the US and Mexico. It provides migration routes for animals such as jaguars, ocelots and bears, and in recent years even beavers and porcupines.
Government contractors have already completed construction of 88 miles (140 km) of secondary wall — an additional 30-foot-high barrier installed some distance from the main wall of the same height. According to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), construction is continuing on another 444 miles of secondary wall (a significant portion of it in Arizona), using billions of dollars allocated under Trump’s initiative, which he called “one big beautiful bill.”
Protesters say construction in this area is moving at a rapid pace and continuing around the clock. In recent days, Fisher Sand & Gravel completed construction of a secondary wall along the private-property section where the camp is located (including the site where a tree stood); the work involved installing 30-foot steel panels into a trench filled with rebar and concrete. These trees, which depend on a regular supply of groundwater, are a distinctive feature of riparian forests, an endangered ecotype found throughout Arizona and the Southwest, said Russ McSpadden, an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. The ecological significance of these trees is one of the driving factors behind the land defenders’ efforts.
Water use for wall construction has depleted wells in the Southwest, threatening natural features such as the Quitobaquito Springs. U.S. Customs and Border Protection does not disclose how much water is being used for the current construction, but in 2008 it estimated that a smaller wall nearby could use up to 710,00 gallons per mile to build; the current project is likely consuming more because it is larger.
To add
Since Monday, dozens of land defenders have been arrested; many of them for entering the road between private property and the border, which federal authorities ordered closed in late September because of wall construction. Every morning, protesters pray on this road, near the tree.
According to Chabbott, some of those detained were beaten, resulting in bruises and facial injuries.
Several other people tried to stop or slow construction using nonviolent resistance methods; in particular, on August 7, one woman chained herself to a concrete mixer, as shown in videos posted on social media.
According to witnesses and videos on social media, agents used tear gas against the protester, knocked her to the ground, and forcibly twisted her limbs, causing her pain.
The truck was later driven away while the land defender was still chained to it; later that evening, she was freed by being detached from the vehicle. According to information provided by authorities to the activists’ lawyers, she is currently in custody.
Julia Butterfly Hill, who lived for two years in the late 1990s in a redwood tree in Humboldt County, California, said she was shocked by the border agents’ mistreatment of the woman, which she saw in a livestream.
The land defender’s courage and her commitment to nonviolent resistance in the face of brutality "moved me to tears," Butterfly Hill said. "She is a true hero."
U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) did not respond to a request for comment about this and other incidents, but the agency has previously said that walls in such areas would help combat illegal immigration. Santa Cruz County Sheriff David Hathaway, who also did not respond to a request for comment for this article, previously said that constructing a wall in this area was pointless because no significant instances of illegal activity had been recorded in the remote valley. Fisher Sand & Gravel did not respond to a request for comment. During a news conference on October 8, Congresswoman Adelita Grijalva, who represents the district, said she was deeply saddened by the loss of the “matriarch” trees and announced her intention to introduce a bill that would strip the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) of the authority to disregard any laws during the construction of border infrastructure.
The tree-sit began shortly after contractors cut down and destroyed two other ancient cottonwood trees nearby on July 27.
By cutting down the trees, contractors and federal agents "are trying to break us, but we have not been broken," said Kate Scott, one of the action’s leaders. "We are starting a movement, and we are not going anywhere. We have put down roots here, just like these matriarch trees."

‘Going bankrupt’: Iran shopkeepers struggle as war dims demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:01:11 UTC
16:01:11 KST

This photo taken on October 7, 2026 shows shoppers walking along an alley of Tajrish Bazaar, a traditional market in Tehran.
At a Tehran bazaar where fragrant herbs and spices whet the appetite, shopkeeper Nasir says locals once bought his nuts by the kilo but soaring prices caused by the U.S.-Iran war have eaten into sales, leaving businesses fighting for survival.
The marketplace in the Iranian capital's north would usually be abuzz with customers, but shops now sit mostly empty with only small numbers of people walking its old narrow paths, a jarring shift for the sellers shouting to promote their goods.
"There used to be customers who bought two to five kilograms. Now, they're down to buying one kilogram or half a kilogram," said the 61-year-old.
"Prices are truly high. We all know it, and it would be a lie to say otherwise."
Nasir called on authorities to stabilise the currency so businesses could plan ahead.
"We're left in limbo, everyone is," said the fruit and nut seller.
"They need to stabilise the dollar exchange rate."
Iran's economy has been battered by years of sanctions, but the conflict that began in February with US-Israeli attacks and an American blockade of the country's ports has put extra strain on daily life.
Rising inflation, nearly 90 percent year-on-year in September according to official figures, and erratic currency exchange fluctuations have driven up the cost of everyday items. Food prices have more than doubled since last year
At the bazaar, a historic covered market in Tehran's Tajrish square, locals surrounded by Iranian flags and Persian signage try to escape the economic gloom, scanning sweets, jewellery, traditional garments and cuts of meat before their weekend begins. 
In an alley, a street artist plays a guitar while another drums his hands on a box to draw tips from passersby.
But across the commercial district, many struggle to see a future for their businesses.
"It is a desperate, last-ditch struggle. Manufacturers are going bankrupt, laying off staff and closing shops, and the impact inevitably reaches us," said Ali Nowruzi, 36, who runs a sportswear shop in the bazaar.
The businessman now orders only a few items for display on his shop's shelves to stop them from looking bare like his warehouse, which he says lies empty due to lack of demand.
"We have absolutely no plan for the future. When people don't come to buy... it effectively spells bankruptcy for the business," he said, citing rising rent and utility bills.
"We just need some stability."
Many shoppers, whose purchasing power has weakened since the outbreak of war, are seen leaving the bazaar without buying anything.
Azadeh, a 45-year-old woman currently out of work, says she just goes there to "watch the shops."
Mounting pressure over the war saw Iran's GDP contract 10.1 percent year-on-year between late March and late June, according to official figures.
The rial traded at around 2.7 million to the dollar on the unofficial market in the past week, compared with about 1.7 million before the war.
The minimum monthly wage that stood at around $120 a year ago has fallen to $65.
The country's economy minister has rejected predictions of an imminent economic collapse, accusing Iran's foes of trying to fuel public anxiety and drive up exchange rates.
Azadeh offers a price comparison of a kitchen cloth bought several months ago for 22 cents. She says that item now costs $1.10, five times more.
"It shows that prices haven't just gone up — they've truly skyrocketed," she said.
She has stopped buying some fruits and says she can no longer afford holidays.
"We aren't meant to just exist, we're meant to actually live, right?" she asked.
Car mechanic Mojtaba Rezaei says his customers have "dropped to a tenth of what it was" because "goods now cost two or three times as much".
"I actually feel embarrassed telling prices to customers. People just come in, ask the price, and leave," the 57-year-old told AFP at the bazaar.
"So many things — buying clothes, going out for leisure, dining at restaurants — have all been cut out of our lives."

Migrants in Lithuania: Where do they come from and where do they work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Lithuania’s foreign population is increasingly diverse, though people from the neighbouring non-EU countries – Ukraine, Belarus – remain by far the biggest groups of foreign residents.
The number of workers from the Philippines, India, Uzbekistan, Pakistan and Tajikistan have risen sharply in recent years, while the country’s economy has become more dependent on non-EU labour, official data show.
Ukrainian and Belarusian citizens remain the largest groups of foreign residents, according to the Migration Department. As of September 1, about 80,300 Ukrainians and 47,900 Belarusians held residence permits in Lithuania, followed by 13,300 Russians, 12,600 Uzbeks and 9,400 Indians.
Other sizeable communities include citizens of India, Tajikistan, the Philippines, Kyrgyzstan, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Pakistan, Turkey, Georgia, Latvia, Bangladesh, Zimbabwe, Moldova, Germany and Morocco. More than 2,000 foreign residents were stateless.
The fastest growth since January 1, 2024, has been among Filipinos, whose numbers increased by 5,100, or tenfold. The Indian population grew by 4,800, doubling in size, while the number of Uzbeks rose by 4,400, or 50%. The number of Pakistanis increased by 2,500, more than tripling, and the number of Tajiks grew by 1,800, or 30%.
A widening range of countries of origin
Data from the State Data Agency on immigrants’ previous countries of residence show that the United Kingdom was the largest source of arrivals last year, a category that may include Lithuanians returning home.
However, “other countries” was the largest category in both 2023 and 2024, indicating that Lithuania is attracting people from an increasingly broad range of countries. Belarus was the leading source in 2023, Ukraine in 2022 and the United Kingdom in 2021.
Foreign workers become essential to key industries
The changing migration picture reflects a significant shift in Lithuania’s labour market over the past decade, according to research published in late September by the Bank of Lithuania.
Linas Tarasonis, a senior research economist at the central bank’s Research Centre, and Dominykas Vaičiūnas, a student in Vilnius University’s quantitative economics program, found that the number of non-EU citizens in Lithuania increased more than twelvefold between 2010 and 2024, rising from 11,500 to 143,100.
Their share of all employed people grew from 1% to 10% over the same period. By contrast, the number of employed EU citizens increased much less, from 1,900 to 4,500.
Foreign workers are concentrated in a relatively small number of industries, particularly transportation and warehousing, construction and manufacturing.
The transportation and warehousing sector illustrates the extent of this reliance. Non-EU citizens accounted for just a small share of its workforce in 2010, but by 2024 they made up 46%, or nearly half, the researchers said.
Their share reached about 16% in construction and 11% in accommodation and food services. They also accounted for about 8% of workers in real estate and administrative services, while manufacturing employed a significant number of foreign workers.
“This means that over more than a decade, parts of the Lithuanian economy have become significantly dependent on foreign labour,” Tarasonis and Vaičiūnas wrote.
They said the transportation sector would probably struggle to operate at its current scale without workers from outside the EU. Dependence on foreign labour has also become important in construction, parts of manufacturing and some service industries.
Drivers, construction workers and welders in demand
Migration Department figures show that many foreign workers fill jobs in transport and construction, as well as skilled trades.
In August, the most common occupation among immigrants was international freight truck driver, with 6,700 workers. Other leading occupations included concrete workers, with 644; welders, with 590; cooks, with 237; and plasterers, with 227.
The list also included electricians, butchers, pipeline installers, bricklayers and scaffolders.

‘It was a terrible thing’: Panama declares state of emergency as quake aftershocks rattle communities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
06:56:08 UTC
15:56:08 KST

Panama’s government has declared a state of emergency on Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours.
Officials did not attribute any deaths to Friday’s 7.7- and 6.6-magnitude earthquakes, but reported damages in all 10 of Panama’s provinces and two Indigenous territories.
The earthquakes toppled buildings near the epicentre and prompted evacuations across the Central American country. Seismologists recorded more than 100 aftershocks, including ones measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2.
The earlier quake, also felt in neighbouring Colombia, was centred about 10km (6 miles) south-west of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, according to the US Geological Survey. It struck at a depth of 10km (6 miles).
The presidential minister, Juan Carlos Orillac, announced the emergency during a news conference in the capital, Panama City. He said homes, schools, healthcare facilities, roads and hotels were among the damaged facilities.
Malitzie Rivera, the deputy director of the National Civil Protection System, said 27 people had been reported with injuries, ranging from minor to moderate.
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos.
About 420 homes and the same number of public schools had been damaged, according to the Civil Protection agency. It also reported that seven hotels, at least 13 churches and nine bridges were affected by the earthquakes.
In La Villa de Los Santos, a colonial-era community about 64km (40 miles) north-east of the epicentre, homes and a historical Catholic church collapsed. People who spent the night on the streets were waiting for the government’s guidance on what to do next.
“We’ve been here since 1 pm yesterday; we haven’t moved,” Tony Jiménez, whose home partially collapsed, said, while sitting with relatives under a tent. “It was a terrible thing. I can tell you with absolute certainty that in my 90 years, I had never experienced anything like it. It was intense – truly intense.”
Officials did not report any missing people on Saturday but said some communities remained cut off due to landslides and road damage.
That the country appeared to have avoided widespread deaths could be due to its strict building codes, especially governing the construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdés, the head of the seismology department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico.
Messages of support and offers of assistance were sent from across the region shortly after the earthquakes. Mulino on Friday thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others.
The US Department of State on Saturday said it mobilised a disaster response team to help local authorities with search and rescue expertise as well as aerial and on-the-ground assessments. The US government also pledged $5m for humanitarian assistance.
The US military’s southern command said two helicopters, supported by the state department’s drug-control bureau, had delivered 2,000 pounds (907kg) of food to people affected by the earthquakes.

Scientists reveal mechanism behind evolution of brain folds regulated by ancient gene
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:47:03 CST
15:47:03 KST

KUNMING, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- A group of Chinese scientists has uncovered the mystery behind how an ancient gene regulates the development of brain folds, shedding new light on the evolution of the human brain. The findings were recently published in Nature Genetics.
The human brain is covered with intricate wrinkles and grooves, which constitute one of the important biological foundations for the emergence of advanced human cognitive functions. The traditional view holds that the expansion of the primate cerebral cortex was primarily driven by newly evolved genes.
However, a research team led by Shi Lei, a researcher from the Kunming Institute of Zoology under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, proposed an alternative possibility: certain ancient and highly conserved genes could also play a key role in human brain evolution by reshaping their expression levels through changes in regulatory elements.
The team compared transcriptomic data from different layers of the embryonic cerebral cortex of mice, tree shrews, marmosets, macaques and humans. They found that an ancient gene called "CCNB1IP1" was already expressed in the brain of the tree shrew, a close relative of primates, long before primates emerged but at relatively low expression levels.
The team further discovered that during the following course of evolution, the expression level of this ancient gene showed a clear stepwise increase among tree shrews, marmosets, macaques and humans, reaching its highest level in the human brain.
"The expression level of this ancient gene is closely correlated with the degree of cortical folding," said Shi, who noted that in marmosets, which have smooth brains, the expression level of this gene is similar to that in tree shrews. In macaques, whose brains have folds, the expression level is markedly elevated. In the human brain, this gene is expressed at the highest level.
Moreover, the team identified a key regulatory sequence, CRE1, that drives the elevated expression of CCNB1IP1.
To verify the gene's function, the team constructed a mouse model carrying the gene. The experiment showed that mice, which normally have a smooth cerebral cortex, developed cortical folding structures after the gene knock-in. Meanwhile, the modified mice exhibited enhanced learning and memory abilities in behavioral tests.
The team noted that this study not only provides a new perspective for understanding the evolution of the human brain, but also offers new clues for exploring the causes of neural development disorders. ■

"Operations at the data centre have been completely suspended," it added, advising users to activate disaster-recovery plans as the platform operated in emergency mode.
"The remaining resource configuration is considered unstable," the company said, warning that technical support communications could also be disrupted as teams assessed the damage.
On Friday, Yandex said a drone attack had damaged a data centre in the Kaluga region, putting several modules out of service and causing disruptions to some services.
A night before, an attack sparked a fire at a Yandex facility in the Ryazan region, causing major outages that affected transport and e-commerce platforms.

Ukrainian prisoners of war and defectors have been gathered into a Russian battalion to face Ukrainian forces — why? And how?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
06:38:00 UTC
15:38:00 KST

Who are the Ukrainian 'volunteers' under Russian command?
October 11, 2026
Pavlo Oliynyk, 25, says he joined enemy forces to escape Russian captivity. Before his capture in the Donbas region in 2024, he was a senior lieutenant for Ukraine's armed forces.
As a prisoner of war (POW), he says he was electrocuted, beaten, and psychologically tortured. So when he received the offer to join the Maksym Kryvonis battalion — named after a famous 17th-century Cossack commander — he accepted.
Oliynyk says he wanted to use this opportunity to reach the front lines, so he could escape to Ukrainian-controlled territory. DW was able to contact Oliynyk through his lawyer.
'Ukrainian volunteers' consist mostly of POWs
Reports of Russian combat units consisting of Ukrainian prisoners of war and former servicemembers of Ukraine's armed forces began emerging in late 2022. Several detachments were initially formed and in August 2026, they were merged into the so-called "Ukrainian Volunteer Special Forces Brigade."
Of the individual units, the Maksym Kryvonis battalion has perhaps drawn the most public attention for having evidently taken part in combat. Its true size is unknown — Russian media reports claim about 200 fighters while available footage only suggests several dozen.
An investigative team of the Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne has identified over 30 members and confirmed they are all former Ukrainian servicemen, captured by Russian forces between 2023 and 2024.
An 'imitation' of Russian legions fighting for Ukraine
Pavel Luzin, an expert for Russian foreign policy and defense at the Center for European Policy Analysis, believes these units are an "imitation" of the Russian Volunteer Corps and the Freedom of Russia Legion — units in the Ukrainian armed forces, consisting of Russian citizens — and an attempt by Moscow to distract from the fact that these units exist in the first place. Ukrainian intelligence services tend to agree.
"It bothers them that Russians would fight on Ukraine's side, but Ukrainians won't fight on Russia's side," Yevhen Shybalov, author and veteran of the war in Ukraine, tells DW. He adds that Russian troops have never tried to hide the fact that Russian volunteer units in Ukrainian ranks were the main reason Russian forces wanted to create Ukrainian units for their owns ranks.
Just how voluntary are these combat units?
In 2025, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) reported that 95% of the released Ukrainian POWs interviewed reported torture or ill-treatment during Russian captivity.
Bill Wiley, executive director of the NGO Commission for International Justice and Accountability (CIJA), says that the physical and psychological state of the returned combatants raises serious doubts that their recruitment was voluntary. Mykhailo Savva of the Center for Civil Liberties, a Kyiv-based human rights organization, points to the criminal procedures running against several of the battalion members, which he says indicates that these suggest the combatants had switched sides voluntarily.
But where to draw the line between voluntary and involuntary recruitment? The war veteran and human rights activist Maksym Butkevych, who spent 28 months as a prisoner of war, says the conditions in Russian captivity make that line hard to distinguish. On the one hand, he says, there is a constant atmosphere of pressure, and on the other hand, it's not implausible that some prisoners defected out of ideological proximity.
How were Ukrainian prisoners made to join Russian forces?
Butkevych tells DW that between 2022 and 2023, all Ukrainian prisoners of war had received offers, "more or less persistently," to join the Russian army. In his case, he recounts, it was after he had been severely mistreated. "They showed us they could do anything they wanted to us," the veteran explains, "which was why we should agree to everything."
The veteran Shybalov reports similar experiences. He speaks of attempts to force confessions of war crimes, or to recruit members for Russia's intelligence services, and tells DW all prisoners were first interrogated and then made certain propositions under duress.
"You can torture people to get them to confess, but there comes the difficult moment when you need to give them a weapon," he says. "That's why it's more about psychological pressure, and forcing voluntary compliance."
Butkevych confirms these accounts with his own tales. But neither veteran has ever met someone willing to join Russian units, they say.
What happens after conscription?
Oliynyk, from the Maksym Kryvonis battalion, says he initially turned down multiple bids to join Russian forces. He says he only accepted the fourth offer so he could flee.
He claims he didn't sign official Defense Ministry paperwork, but a private contract with an individual offering military services. Afterwards, he says, he was brought to a room where he heard lectures and saw videos and photos he was later asked to retell.
Control and mistreatment
He says fellow servicemembers in the Maksym Kryvonis battalion consisted both of those who had switched sides of their own volition, and those who had been forced.
In a video circulating online that appears to be of a trial in Ukraine, he also says that former Ukrainian POWs in the unit were followed and guarded by mercenaries of the private military company Redut. In the same video, he also speaks of beatings and torture, and receiving monthly wages in envelopes handed out by a member of Russia's military intelligence.
He tells DW he had been given a phone, but that he was too scared to call anyone in Ukraine because it was under constant surveillance. He denies having fought against Ukrainians, as he fled in March 2025 before his first deployment in the Donetsk province. After running across a field, he says he spent two days hiding from drones in basements and houses before making contact with Ukrainian fighters.
Now, Oliynyk has been in detention in Ukraine for nearly two years while authorities investigate possible treason. He has yet to be formally charged.
Sergey Nikitin contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Ukrainian.

The World Bank is negotiating with 30–40 countries on crisis assistance
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:33:16 EEST
15:33:16 KST

The World Bank is negotiating with 30–40 countries on crisis assistance
Kyiv • UNN
The World Bank is discussing crisis financing with 30–40 countries amid energy shocks and rising prices. The bank is ready to mobilize up to $100 billion.
World Bank President Ajay Banga told Reuters that the institution is negotiating with 30–40 countries on providing potential crisis assistance to help overcome the effects of energy shocks and rising prices caused by the war in the Middle East, reports UNN.
Details
According to Banga, the global economy has proved fairly resilient — partly thanks to significant investment in artificial intelligence and adjustments in oil supply and demand. As a result, few countries have sought the initial $25 billion crisis financing package that the World Bank allocated at the start of the war (in February).
However, a sharp increase in diesel and fertilizer prices, as well as other factors — including the possibility of a strong El Niño weather phenomenon — are exacerbating the challenges faced by developing countries. Banga said this ahead of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, which will take place this week.
"There is pressure, so I assume that in the coming months more countries will seek some of that initial $50–60 billion," Banga said, referring to the initial $25 billion plus another $35 billion that countries can access by reallocating resources from already approved World Bank projects.
"We will see, but we are ready. We are actively working on this and negotiating with a number of countries — as I have already said, 30 to 40 countries are in dialogue with us," he added.
Many developing countries have been hit hard by the surge in energy prices and high interest rates, which have increased borrowing costs. This is happening while their budgets are already strained by spending on measures to combat the COVID-19 pandemic and the effects of high inflation caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
According to World Bank estimates, developing countries will have to repay around $400 billion to external creditors in 2026, with interest payments alone accounting for one-third of that amount.
Banga noted that more countries are showing interest in restructuring existing projects than in using the emergency crisis assistance mechanism to address liquidity problems. According to him, if the situation worsens, the Bank could provide up to $100 billion in financing, exceeding the $70 billion allocated during the pandemic.
Last month, the World Bank announced that it had mobilized a record $112 billion in private capital during the year ending in June (compared with $69 billion the previous year). This figure is more than three times the total amount mobilized in 2022 — the period before Banga, the former CEO of Mastercard, became the bank's president.
This amount supplemented the $123 billion invested from the bank's own resources during the same year, bringing the total to $235 billion. Banga stressed the importance of using all available resources, especially at a time when Western countries have sharply reduced official bilateral assistance for development purposes.
"There is no one-size-fits-all solution to problems of the scale the world is facing. We need to act based on the opportunities available," Banga said.
He expressed hope that private capital flows would continue to grow in the coming years thanks to expanded political risk guarantees provided by the World Bank's Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), increased local-currency financing, and continued work on regulatory reforms that make it easier for foreign investors to operate.
The greatest increase in private capital mobilization was observed in projects in upper-middle-income countries (such as Argentina and India)—they accounted for $50 billion—as well as in lower-middle-income countries (including Bangladesh and Angola)—$37 billion. At the same time, additional efforts are needed to increase the volume of private capital directed to low-income countries (currently, this figure stands at about $3 billion).
"In smaller countries, this figure has not increased sufficiently; there are certain challenges," he noted, adding that this week the bank would announce new initiatives aimed at ensuring access to private capital for micro-, small and medium-sized enterprises as well. Banga said that growth in private capital volumes had been observed across various regions: the largest increase was recorded in Latin America and the Caribbean ($36.3 billion of last year's total), followed by Europe and Central Asia ($21.3 billion), South Asia ($19.2 billion), and Africa ($22 billion).
According to the Bank, the top 10 recipient countries included Brazil, India, Türkiye, Romania, Nigeria, Argentina, South Africa, Bangladesh, Mexico and Chile.
Banga noted that the World Bank and the IMF were working together to address the problem of high debt levels affecting many developing countries. This work is being carried out as part of a range of initiatives, including those aimed at increasing domestic revenue mobilization in these countries.
The Bank has already implemented debt-for-development financing swaps for Angola and Côte d'Ivoire, and has also provided a portfolio guarantee for Argentina; more than a dozen similar projects are currently in the pipeline.
"We have 14 or 15 projects under development that are helping countries replace old debt with high servicing costs with new debt on more favorable terms, supported by our guarantees," he said, adding that the funds freed up are directed toward financing programs in education, health care, water supply or environmental protection.
