Flooding in Nepal destroyed homes and bridges; authorities announced an evacuation
Kyiv • UNN
A landslide blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, causing flooding in five districts of Nepal. Homes and bridges were destroyed; no casualties have been reported.
On Sunday, Nepalese authorities urged local residents to move to safer locations after a powerful flood on a river in the central part of the country destroyed several homes and infrastructure facilities; no casualties have been reported so far, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
According to the authorities, a landslide (not involving water) in the village of Chumnubri (Gorkha District, approximately 100 km west of Kathmandu) blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, causing flooding downstream.
The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli River. It flows downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse in August caused a catastrophic flood that claimed the lives of 1,457 people, while thousands are still considered missing.
Nepal plans to drain four glacial lakes after a deadly flood02.10.26, 13:56 • 8942 views
"We have asked residents living along the riverbanks downstream to evacuate and ensure their own safety," said Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, head of the Gorkha District administration.
Mishra said the flood swept away several homes and two suspension bridges, and also damaged a hydropower facility.
National disaster response services warned residents living along the river in Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan, East Nawalparasi and West Nawalparasi districts about the flooding.
"Please help ensure the timely relocation of people from dangerous areas to safe places and facilitate search-and-rescue operations as needed," the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said in a social media post.
Officials said rescuers from the army and police had already arrived at the scene and were monitoring the situation from a helicopter.

Around 80 Japanese companies considering Ukraine as potential partner – expert
As reported by Ukrinform, this was stated in Lviv by Eiji Tanaka, Deputy Director General of the Export and International Affairs Bureau of Japan’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, who headed the Japanese delegation, according to the Lviv Regional Military Administration’s Department of Agricultural and Industrial Development.
The meeting was attended by officials from the Lviv Regional Military Administration and representatives of its departments, Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Embassies of Japan in Ukraine and Poland, as well as representatives of Japanese businesses.
During the meeting, the Japanese delegation was presented with the agricultural potential of the Lviv region, the main areas of development of its agricultural sector, and opportunities for expanding international cooperation.
“First of all, I want to say that we remain unwavering in our support for Ukraine. Before the full-scale war, 30 Japanese companies operated in Ukraine, and they did not leave the market after the hostilities began. Now nearly 80 companies are considering Ukraine as a potential partner and want to develop their technologies here. We know that Lviv region is a rear-area region, and the development of agriculture is important not only at the regional level but also at the national level,” Tanaka said.
In turn, representatives of Japanese companies presented their Business Development Plan for Ukraine. The ideas include exporting Japanese food products such as rice, tea, snacks and sweets; developing businesses in composting; and supporting the development of Ukrainian agriculture through land reclamation technologies. They also proposed using satellite data, artificial intelligence and machine learning to obtain practical information about agricultural land.
The meeting provided a platform for exchanging information about opportunities available in the region and to Japanese businesses, as well as identifying promising areas for further cooperation in agricultural development, the regional administration said.
As reported, the agricultural sector accounts for approximately 20% of the Lviv region’s GDP, while the region’s share of Ukraine’s gross agricultural output exceeds 4.3%. The region is home to 1,443 agricultural enterprises, including 1,038 farms, while the total area of agricultural land stands at 1.24 million hectares. In 2025, gross agricultural production reached UAH 52.4 billion.

Farming and solar power are competing for land. Can agrivoltaics solve the problem?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:02:20 UTC
14:02:20 KST

Agrivoltaics could help to prevent farmland abandonment by protecting crops and boosting income. But some say the solution ignores the real problems.
As the sun moves westward across the sky in Murcia, Spain, solar panels capture its rays while sheltering diverse crops, from bell peppers to wine grapes and dragon fruit.
Known for its agriculture and abundant sunshine, this southeastern region is exploring whether, rather than competing for land, farming and solar energy can coexist peacefully.
“Agrivoltaics is the integration of food production with renewable energy production,” explains Silvia Tomasi, Senior Researcher at Eurac Research. This entails installing photovoltaic panels above, in between or at the margins of agricultural production, she adds.
A 2023 study estimated that Europe has the potential to generate 25 times its current electricity demand via agrivoltaics, also known as agri-PV.
Yet solar power is fraught with its own environmental and social costs. Requiring more land than other energy sources to generate the same amount of electricity, it has sparked conflicts over land use, especially in rural areas.
“Agrivoltaics has great potential: both economic benefits and environmental ones,” Tomasi says. “But then it’s always a matter of how the technology is implemented and who really benefits.”
Governments and Big Tech turn to agrivoltaics
The idea of turning southern Europe into a solar powerhouse received a high-profile endorsement in January, when Elon Musk said sparsely populated areas of Spain and Sicily could theoretically generate enough solar power for all of Europe.
Big Tech has already caught on. In southern Italy, Amazon and Apple have signed contracts to purchase power from large-scale agrivoltaic projects with a combined capacity of over 150 megawatts – enough to meet the yearly needs of roughly 100,000 Italian households.
Europe is also funding the shift. The EU-funded AGRISOL project intends to invest €1.9 million in agrivoltaics projects, including in Italy and Spain, while Italy alone has secured €1.7 billion in state aid for the initiative.
“For now, [agrivoltaics] is just a minimal contribution,” says Angelo Gentili, national secretary of Legambiente, Italy’s largest environmental organisation. “But if it expands, it will represent a big impulse for decarbonisation goals.”
Managing the impact on crops and land
EU and national rules increasingly require agriculture to remain a meaningful part of land where solar panels are installed. In France, projects must maintain at least 90 per cent of crop production compared to locally determined reference yields. In Italy, at least 70 per cent of the area must remain dedicated to agriculture.
Experts say not just any combination of solar and agriculture should qualify. “More than a definition, what we really need is a classification,” says Pilar Flores, who coordinates an EU-funded agrivoltaics project at the Murcian Institute for Agricultural and Environmental Research and Development (IMIDA). She says protecting agriculture should drive all classifications: “The key is to ensure there’s minimal loss [of arable land].”
Why use farmland rather than empty or abandoned land in the first place? Flores says the requirements are similar: relatively flat and near the grid. Unused land may also hold ecological value. “It’s not just a simple calculation of how much free land is left,” she says.
How agrivoltaics can benefit farmers
In some cases, agrivoltaics have been found to improve water-use efficiency, protect crops from extreme weather and increase the productivity of land. Solar installations can also help farmers face climate change. “Excessive rainfall and heat have heavily damaged agricultural fields, pushing farmers to abandon farmland,” says Gentili. “Agrivoltaics represent a great instrument to avoid land abandonment and profit gaps for farmers.”
Panels cast shade that can reduce evaporation, help soil retain moisture and offer relief to farmworkers and grazing animals. They can also protect crops from hail. Farmers can use the energy to power their own operations and sell any excess to the grid, or rent the space above their fields to energy producers.
But the benefits are not guaranteed, Flores warns. “All these opportunities are sometimes discussed as if they always happened, but it depends on the agrivoltaic system used and the specific characteristics of the site.” In Murcia, her team found that water-stressed peppers grew better under solar panels than well-watered ones. “You have to analyse each case and each location,” she says.
But who really benefits from agrivoltaics?
Not all farmers are convinced. To Fabrizio Garbarino, president of the Italian farmers’ union Associazione Rurale Italiana, agrivoltaics fail to address the root problems farmers face. “Agrivoltaics are taking advantage of the farming sector crisis in Italy while we should actually focus on real solutions for preventing farmland abandonment,” he says. “To me, this just sounds like a shortcut.”
Startups representing larger companies, including data centre developers, are hounding farmers for their land, he says. “Even if the energy produced is good, we’re taking away [farmers’] land to support businesses that require a lot of energy.”
Big Tech firms say agrivoltaic power-purchase agreements help them reach net-zero targets. But a PPA does not necessarily mean that the electricity from a particular solar farm physically supplies a particular company facility, and the exact carbon footprints of AI data centres remain opaque.
A 2025 study co-authored by Tomasi, based on expert interviews across four European regions, found that the benefits of agrivoltaics can favour large-scale farmers, landowners and investors over smaller farmers and local communities. It also found that excluding residents and ecosystems from decision-making can deepen existing power imbalances.
High upfront costs and grid connection queues mean large projects backed by multinationals tend to dominate the sector. A 2025 review by the Italian newspaper Today.it found that about 86 per cent of the roughly €775 million in government funds for agrivoltaic projects went to large-scale projects, including ones owned by foreign multinationals.
In September, a new agrivoltaics project financed by an Israeli company in Tuscany sparked widespread outrage and raised concerns over who gets to profit.
Tomasi says local communities must have a voice to ensure a just transition. “Big investors going into places they really don’t know anything about, with a top-down approach… and getting the economic benefits from the renewable energy generation side of agrivoltaics… shouldn’t be labelled as agrivoltaics, from my point of view.”
‘Agriculture should not be a secondary concern’
Flores says administrations can help by offering farmers funding and giving agrivoltaic systems priority access to the grid.
There is also the question of what kind of agriculture the income supports. To live up to the environmental promise, one study has noted, “the type of agriculture funded by the rental income from agrivoltaics should not be a secondary concern”. Instead, the author argues, this rent could subsidise agroecological practices or help farmers transition away from industrial farming.
Agrivoltaics has the potential to be mutually beneficial to farmers and the renewable energy sector. It can help protect farmland, support farmers facing climate change and contribute to Europe’s decarbonisation goals. But it also risks becoming a greenwashing opportunity, a crutch for unsustainable farming practices, or a way of meeting growing corporate energy demand on arable land. On its own, it is not a silver bullet. Much depends on how the systems are designed, who owns them and, ultimately, who benefits.
“The goal of agrivoltaics is to protect farmland and the entire ecosystem; that’s the philosophy,” says Flores. “We have to be able to distinguish that from other interests.”
Reporting for this story was made possible by the Magma Environmental Reporting Fellowship.

Indian Cafe Racer, Birmingham B5: ‘A good news tale for the local food scene’ – restaurant review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:02:16 UTC
14:02:16 KST

Indian Cafe Racer on Bristol Street, Birmingham, spent its fledgling years tucked behind a curtain at the back of the Wellington pub just a few doors up from its fancy new home. There was a Royal Enfield motorcycle, chequerboard floors and a psychedelic Indian soundtrack, but this small, homespun spot from Azad Kayes quickly became culty, then oversubscribed, then in need of a bigger home. It’s a good news tale for the Brum food scene.
For those who remember it, south Birmingham’s Balti triangle once ran to 30 bustling restaurants along Ladypool Road and Stratford Road. Only two now remain. Something has gone amiss with supply and demand. Indian Cafe Racer, meanwhile, has enough fans for a new, 65-cover, grown-up restaurant, serving an ever-changing menu that, when we visited, featured shaktiman and salad (named after an Indian comic-book superhero), gol gappa (crisp shells filled with chickpeas and potato), chicken pepper fry and grilled aubergine and portobello mushrooms, known as farzi steak.
Kayes dips into Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai and Kolkata, with a scattering of Indo-Chinese small plates: gobi manchurian (fried cauliflower in sweet-and-sour sauce) and chilli chicken, say. The cocktail bar serves cold, potent liveners with names such as Angry Young Man, Red Carpet and Tiger Rides Bike, alongside endless karak chai, a heavily spiced, very sweet, milky tea brewed strong with cardamom and condensed milk. Jump on our Cafe Racer, the menu says, and let us give you a mast taste of India. No visa required.
In fact, the new Indian Cafe Racer has about it a sprinkling of Dishoom: paper menus with faux-olde font, wipeable tables and functional rather than fancy-pants hospitality. The room is elegant with small dashes of eccentricity, and there’s a sense that, in its expansion, some of its silliness has been tidied away. The large glass windows face on to the realities of a dual carriageway, and the room errs on the dark side. Still, the welcome is warm and we kick off with a round of dahi puri: crisp, plump, puffed flour shells filled with potato, sweet yoghurt, tamarind and mint chutney. We know the drill: eat them in one, though these ones are so large and so liquidy that there’s a fine line between extreme pleasure and being legally waterboarded.
Recovering, we move on to chicken 65, named, depending on who you ask, after its position on a Chennai hotel menu in 1965 (other origin stories are available) – fried with curry leaves, green chillies and arguably a little too much mustard seed. A round of spiced lamb chops – two cutlets a portion, marinated overnight and finished in the tandoor – are genuinely succulent.
The tandoori king prawns in house masala are lovable, zinging with crushed ginger and sticky with honey, while the Rajastani lamb is a standout: slow-cooked and finished with smoked charcoal and butter. The increasingly ubiquitous dal makani arrives deeply and sweetly rich in its creamy tomato sauce, but the naans are a bit thin and functional. Indian Cafe Racer’s cooking is sometimes bang on, sometimes a little slapdash, but then the likes of gobi manchurian pique your interest all over again. If cocktails feel too much by this point, there’s always a cold Bombay Bicycle IPA.
Cafe racers were the lads who raced motorbikes such as that Royal Enfield, which was once made in nearby Redditch, between roadside cafes in the 60s. Today, Royal Enfield is made in Chennai. The bike went from the edge of Birmingham to India, and this restaurant closes the circle. Arguably, with Indian Cafe Racer’s mature new home, some of the spirit of foot-to-the-pedal mayhem has been lost. Still, it opens every day (including Monday), if you have a horde to feed it will make a huge fuss of your group, and there’s enough choice to excite the desi food disciple who wants Rajastani lamb and mango machli, without spooking the horses if you’re with Sheila who “doesn’t do” spice – she can have the paneer makani. Indian Cafe Racer is well worth a ride, and maybe even a return ticket.
- Indian Cafe Racer 88-90 Bristol Street, Birmingham B5, 0121-238-7972 Open lunch Wed-Sun, noon-4.30pm, dinner all week, 5-11pm. From about £30 a head à la carte, plus drinks & service

Tehran showcases urban market management, food security expertise to foreign delegations
TEHRAN- Tehran Municipality’s first program in the series of specialized visits “Introducing Tehran’s Urban Management Capabilities,” focusing on urban markets, logistics, and food security, was held on Saturday, October 10, in cooperation with the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) and the Asian Mayors Forum (AMF).
In this program, representatives of foreign countries and international organizations visited the Jalal Al-e Ahmad Fruit and Vegetable Market and the Beihaghi Shahrvand Store and became acquainted with Tehran’s urban management capacities in supplying and distributing essential goods. After these visits, a specialized meeting was held aimed at examining areas for joint cooperation.
This program, held under the title “Specialized Visit to Tehran’s Urban Markets, Logistics and Food Security” by the International Deputy of the Communication Center of Tehran Municipality, was welcomed by those present.
The purpose of this measure was also to develop urban diplomacy and introduce Tehran’s management capacities to representatives of international organizations.
During the visit to the Shahrvand Store, a press conference was held in the administrative section of the store. Davood Qorbanian, CEO of Shahrvand Store; Mehdi Bakhtiari-Zadeh, CEO of the Organization of Markets; Hamid Reza Gholamzadeh, Head of the Communication and International Affairs Center of Tehran Municipality, as well as the Secretary-General of the Asian Mayors Forum; and Mohammad Ali Shafiei, International Deputy of the Communication and International Affairs Center of Tehran Municipality, were present, and specialized topics concerning urban market management, supply of goods, and food security were discussed.
Fruit and vegetable markets ready to transfer experience and develop export of Iranian products
The CEO of the Organization for Management of Fruit and Vegetable Markets of Tehran Municipality, referring to the capacity of the capital’s market network, announced the organization’s readiness to develop international cooperation in the fields of transferring technical knowledge, supplying and distributing food products, and expanding exports of Iranian products.
Emphasizing the municipality’s responsibility to ensure citizens’ food security, he said: Access to high-quality, healthy, and reasonably priced food products is one of the main axes of the municipality’s activity. In this regard, an extensive network of fruit and vegetable markets and Shahrvand stores has been formed across the city.
Bakhtiari-Zadeh added: Currently, about 320 fruit and vegetable markets are active in Tehran, and citizens can, on average, access one of the municipality’s food product distribution centers by traveling less than 900 meters.
Referring to quality control mechanisms, he said: To ensure the health of products, a direct supply chain and continuous testing are on the agenda, and goods that do not meet the required quality and health standards will not be allowed to enter the markets covered by the organization.
The CEO of the Organization for Management of Fruit and Vegetable Markets of Tehran Municipality, referring to the capacity for cooperation with the countries present at the meeting, stated: This complex can cooperate in transferring technical knowledge, exchanging experience, and presenting models of management and distribution of food products.
Referring to Iran’s agricultural capacity and the production of diverse products in different seasons of the year, he added: Cooperation with traders and economic actors can provide the basis for developing the export of fruit and vegetable products and protein products.
Bakhtiari-Zadeh noted: Currently, trade in agricultural products between Iran and some of the countries present at this meeting exists, and cooperation with Tehran Municipality’s extensive network can help strengthen these relations and develop export routes.
In the end, he expressed hope that this visit would pave the way for expanding commercial and technical cooperation with friendly countries and forming more sustainable relations in the field of supply, distribution, and export of food products.
Shahrvand ready to develop commercial cooperation and exchange experience with foreign companies
Davood Qorbanian, CEO of Shahrvand Company, also emphasizing the necessity of expanding international cooperation, said: Familiarizing representatives of countries and embassies with Tehran Municipality’s services can pave the way for strengthening relations among countries and developing commercial and trade communications.
Referring to the company’s capacities for cooperation with trade and retail actors in various countries, he stated: Shahrvand is ready to provide the ground for the exchange of knowledge, experience, and technology and the development of commercial exchanges. In this regard, we invite the representatives of the countries present to introduce capable companies from their countries to begin joint cooperation.
Qorbanian, who is also the vice chairman of the country’s Chain Stores Union, added: The possibility of developing communications and exchanging experience exists not only for Shahrvand Company but also for other chain stores in Iran.
Stating that Iran enjoys significant capacities in the production of agricultural products and foodstuffs, as well as a broad consumer market, he said: Foreign companies can identify new opportunities for developing their commercial activities by understanding the needs of the Iranian market.
The CEO of Shahrvand Company continued: The areas of cooperation are not limited only to the supply of food, agricultural products, and meat; they also include the field of retail technologies, including enterprise resource planning (ERP) software, store management, and marketing systems. Shahrvand Company is ready to benefit from the specialized knowledge and experience of foreign companies in these areas.
Qorbanian at this meeting, referring to the role of Shahrvand stores and fruit markets, added: Iranian producers and industries can use the capacity of Shahrvand stores to offer products, introduce brands, and access the consumer market. In return, this company can be a platform for introducing and offering products of various countries in the Iranian market; a cooperation that includes areas such as raw materials, agricultural and food products, packaged goods, and retail-related technologies.
He asked the representatives of the countries present to provide the ground for communication with capable companies and economic actors through their commercial counselors and the economic sections of their embassies.
In the end, Qorbanian expressed hope that these visits would lead to practical and sustainable cooperation among Shahrvand Company, Iranian traders, and foreign companies and provide the ground for market development, exchange of knowledge and technology, and mutual supply of the parties’ commercial needs.
Tehran municipality seeks to turn sister-city relations into practical economic cooperation
The Secretary-General of the Asian Mayors Forum at this meeting emphasized using the capacity of relations among cities to develop commercial cooperation, transfer experiences, and engage economic companies.
Referring to Tehran’s experience in large-scale distribution of goods and maintaining citizens’ access to essential products, he spoke of the capacity for cooperation with regional cities in the fields of export and import of products, transfer of technical knowledge, and provision of urban services.
Gholamzadeh also introduced the “Zero Inflation” initiative, aimed at stabilizing the prices of 12 essential goods for six months, as one of Tehran Municipality’s measures to support citizens.
Foreign diplomats emphasize Tehran’s capacity in supplying and distributing essential goods
At the end of the program, representatives of foreign countries and the Deputy Secretary-General of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO), in conversations with reporters, considered Tehran’s capacities in supplying and distributing food to be significant.
ECO emphasizes Tehran urban management’s role in strengthening regional food security
The Deputy Secretary-General of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) also considered the city’s experience in supplying and distributing food valuable and emphasized the role of municipalities in strengthening food security and citizens’ affordable access to essential goods even in crisis conditions.
Emre Hengut also called for the continuation of specialized visits and the exchange of experiences to develop cooperation among cities and regional institutions.
The list of guests present in the half-day tour organized by Tehran Municipality, included Kim Junpyo, Ambassador of South Korea, and his wife; Ahmad Soueidan, Ambassador of Lebanon; Khalid Ibrahim Elsheikh, Deputy Head of Mission in the Sudanese Embassy; Bahador Nazir, Counsellor of the Tajik Embassy; Mostafa Diabate, Counselor of the Burkina Faso Embassy; Vladislav Perpelkin, Counselor of the Russian Embassy; Hubert Przybyszewski, First Secretary of the Polish Embassy; Deputy Ambassador of Oman; Faizan Taimoor Saqib, Third Secretary in Embassy of Pakistan, Counselor of the Pakistani Embassy; Jadidzadeh, Economic Officer of the United Nations Coordinator’s Office; Chentaei Emre Angut, Deputy Secretary-General of ECO; and Lola Gheybollahzadeh, Head of ECO Coordination and Follow-up Department.
Overall, the specialized visit served as a practical step in strengthening Tehran’s urban diplomacy and presenting its integrated network of fruit and vegetable markets and Shahrvand stores as a working model for food supply, price regulation, and access to essential goods.
By bringing together foreign ambassadors, international organizations such as ECO and the Asian Mayors Forum, and Tehran Municipality officials, the program created a platform for exchanging technical knowledge, expanding trade in agricultural and food products, and encouraging joint investment and retail cooperation.
If followed by concrete agreements and sustained follow-up, such initiatives could help transform sister-city and international relations into tangible economic partnerships, enhance regional food security, and open new export and knowledge-exchange opportunities for both Iran and participating countries.

China urges focus on climate change, cooperation at Arctic Circle Assembly
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:00:59 CST
14:00:59 KST

Former Chinese Vice Foreign Minister Fu Ying holds a dialogue with former Icelandic President and Arctic Circle Chairman Olafur Ragnar Grimsson during the 2026 Arctic Circle Assembly in Reykjavik, Iceland, Oct. 9, 2026. Fu Ying called for greater international cooperation on scientific research and environmental protection in the Arctic, saying climate change, rather than imagined security threats, is the real challenge facing the region. Fu made the remarks while leading a Chinese delegation to the 2026 Arctic Circle Assembly, held from Thursday to Saturday in Reykjavik, the capital of Iceland. More than 2,500 representatives from over 70 countries and regions attended the event to discuss issues related to understanding, protecting, developing and governing the Arctic. (Xinhua/Zhang Yuliang)
REYKJAVIK, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Former Chinese Vice Foreign Minister Fu Ying called for greater international cooperation on scientific research and environmental protection in the Arctic, saying climate change, rather than imagined security threats, is the real challenge facing the region.
Fu made the remarks while leading a Chinese delegation to the 2026 Arctic Circle Assembly, held from Thursday to Saturday in Reykjavik, the capital of Iceland. More than 2,500 representatives from over 70 countries and regions attended the event to discuss issues related to understanding, protecting, developing and governing the Arctic.
During a plenary session themed "How to Understand China," Fu held a dialogue with former Icelandic President and Arctic Circle Chairman Olafur Ragnar Grimsson.
Fu said the real challenge currently facing the Arctic is climate change, and countries should devote more attention and resources to scientific research and environmental protection, rather than engaging in geopolitical competition over imagined security threats.
Too much of the current geopolitical discussion is based on imagined threats, which wastes valuable time and resources, she said.
Changes including melting Arctic sea ice, shrinking ice sheets and rising temperatures are already taking place, Fu said, adding that climate change is the real issue that countries need to confront together.
She called on countries to pool their strengths and resources, enhance scientific research cooperation, jointly assess the challenges posed by climate change, and make early preparations.
Fu noted that a joint statement issued by the leaders of China and Iceland last year stressed stronger cooperation on climate change and green energy. Such practical cooperation can better demonstrate China's policy and intentions regarding its participation in Arctic affairs, she said.
Speaking about China's development and its international role, Fu said China remains committed to peaceful development, has no intention of seeking global hegemony, and does not believe the world needs a new hegemon.
China is willing to strengthen cooperation with other countries and promote a more just and equitable global governance system, she said.
Founded in 2013, the Arctic Circle holds its annual assembly in Iceland every October and serves as an important global platform for dialogue on Arctic affairs. ■

Europe is world-famous for its Christmas markets, and more than 1,500 take place every year. Choosing which to visit can be as tricky as putting together your present wish list. Here are the top picks, as voted for by travellers.
As we get deeper into autumn, it feels as if we’ll blink and Christmas will be upon us.
With the festive season comes new opportunities to book a winter trip away, and a favourite must-do for many travellers is to visit a Christmas market.
There are more than 1,500 in Europe alone, and this year more than 800,000 travellers have voted for their favourites via the European Best Destinations platform.
A total of 20 were included in the final ranking, and we’re taking a closer look at the top five to give you some inspiration on where to go to shop, drink gleuwein and get into the festive spirit in 2026.
European Christmas markets: The top picks by travellers
Craiova, Romania
You might never have heard of Craiova, but the Romanian city has pipped far more famous Christmas markets to the top spot.
It’s an absolutely huge space, with more than 280,000 square meters transformed into a festive wonderland each year.
The theme in 2026 is The Nutcracker, and visitors will be able to see giant ornaments and toy-shaped sculptures along with countless sparkling lights.
The market, which runs from mid-November to early January, will also boast Eastern Europe’s highest-flying Santa sleigh, as well as an ice rink, a Ferris wheel, and traditional hand-painted chalets.
Visitors to the Craiova market also sing the praises of the food on offer here, which celebrates the flavours of Eastern Europe and beyond, serving dishes from the likes of Armenia, Georgia, Greece, Bulgaria and Serbia.
Zurich, Switzerland
Zurich may be better known for its chocolate and banking than Christmas markets, but the Swiss city has made a name for itself as one of Europe’s top festive destinations.
The main attraction is Wienachtsdorf at Sechseläutenplatz, between the Opera House and Lake Zurich. The market is filled with wooden chalets, twinkling lights and a huge Christmas tree, combining traditional Alpine touches with the city’s more polished feel.
There’s plenty more to discover beyond the main market, which was also voted as the most beautiful Christmas market in Europe. Weihnachtsallee near the main station is now in its third year, with around 80 rotating stalls selling international food, design-led crafts and, of course, plenty of fondue.
There’s even a dome dedicated to mulled wine, making it a popular spot for locals and visitors looking to warm up.
Zurich also puts its own artistic spin on the festive season with the Illuminarium at the Swiss National Museum. The courtyard is transformed with lights, music and immersive displays, adding something a little different to the city’s Christmas celebrations.
Riga, Latvia
Riga may not have the same name recognition as some of Europe’s bigger Christmas destinations, but Latvia’s capital puts on a seriously atmospheric festive display each winter.
The main market takes over Doma Square in the heart of the UNESCO-listed Old Town, with wooden chalets selling Latvian crafts, cosy knitwear and local treats.
From late November to early January, the square fills with the smells of mulled wine, roasted almonds and cinnamon, while choirs and folk performers add a distinctly Baltic feel.
But Riga’s Christmas appeal goes well beyond the market itself. The city is known for its spectacular lights, with parks, squares and canals transformed into a glowing winter wonderland.
Head to places including Opera Square, Bastejkalns and Kronvalda Park to see installations inspired by Latvian fairy tales, with light, music and storytelling bringing the festive season to life.
Lisbon, Portugal
Lisbon offers a slightly different take on the Christmas market, swapping snowy streets for mild temperatures and winter sunshine.
Wonderland Lisboa takes over Parque Eduardo VII from late November to early January, with the Portuguese capital’s biggest Christmas market returning for its 11th edition in 2026.
This year’s theme, “The Roots of Christmas”, brings together nature, art, food and entertainment, with local artisans, live performances and plenty of family-friendly attractions.
There’s also a Ferris wheel offering views across the city, alongside a traditional carousel and plenty of opportunities for Christmas shopping.
Food is a big part of the experience too, with the Wonderland Lisboa Food Court serving Portuguese festive favourites, regional specialities and seasonal sweets.
More than 1.2 million people visited in 2025, making it a popular choice for anyone who wants their Christmas market with a side of sunshine.
Debrecen, Hungary
Hungary’s second-largest city may be less famous than the capital Budapest, but it certainly knows how to do Christmas properly.
In the winter, Debrecen’s main squares and pedestrian streets are transformed with glowing installations and wooden stalls selling handmade crafts, toys, decorations and Christmas ornaments.
There’s plenty of food to enjoy too, with classic festive treats including mulled wine, roasted chestnuts and kürtőskalács, the sweet Hungarian chimney cake.
More than 100 cultural events are held throughout the season, featuring more than 200 performers, while families can make the most of an ice rink and the Fairytale Town attraction.
There are also plenty of special events, including traditional advent candle-lighting ceremonies and a St Nicholas weekend complete with a carriage arrival, concerts and a mini train.

ESA director general reveals €10bn plan to get to space without NASA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:00:33 UTC
14:00:33 KST

The space industry, currently valued at €600 billion, is expected to grow by 10% a year, according to European Space Agency (ESA) director general Josef Aschbacher. He spoke to the Big Question about how Europe can benefit from this booming industry.
The European Space Agency received record budget commitments of more than €22 billion from member states at its ministerial council meeting in 2025, a 32% increase on 2022.
Member states also gave ESA a historic mandate to use space technology for non-aggressive security and defence, including technologies to monitor external borders.
With that backing, ESA director general Josef Aschbacher wants Europe to take its next big step: developing the ability to launch its own astronauts into space.
In the latest episode of The Big Question, Josef sat down with Hannah Brown to discuss Europe’s independent future in space.
‘Why don’t we do it ourselves?’
Since its founding in 1975 (and its first astronaut mission in 1983), the European Space Agency has relied on international partners, including NASA and Russia, for astronaut launches.
And while this arrangement has worked for all this time, geopolitical tensions are pushing Europe to seek an alternative.
Only the US, China and Russia have the capability to launch astronauts into space. But political tensions with China and Russia leave ESA reliant on the US.
And in recent years, NASA has partnered with SpaceX to launch astronauts into space. One way or another, today, ESA astronauts travel to space aboard a US spacecraft.
“SpaceX has already announced that they want to decommission Falcon 9 and Crew Dragon (the crew vehicles that bring the astronauts to space) probably around 2029,” Josef explained.
“That means in a few years, we will not have at least this capability available anymore. There may be others coming up, which we do not know today.”
This leaves Europe facing uncertainty over how to get its astronauts into space in the future.
To ensure reliable access and support investment in European industry, Josef is developing a plan for Europe to strengthen its position as a global space power by gaining the ability to launch its own astronauts.
Is space autonomy good for the European economy?
Of course, this won’t happen overnight and it needs political approval from ESA’s member states to secure funding.
Here’s how it might work.
Europe isn’t starting completely from scratch. It already has strong technological capabilities and world-leading programmes like Copernicus (Earth observation) and Galileo (satellite navigation constellation), as well as a talented workforce.
But Europe lacks its own crew vehicle and recovery system, in other words the means to get astronauts up there and bring them safely back to Earth.
Josef estimated that with a budget of around €10 billion, ESA could develop these independent capabilities in the next 10 years.
And yes, €10 billion is an enormous amount of money, but what’s the alternative?
ESA is facing the prospect of spending billions of euros in the coming years either way. The question is how to turn that spending into an investment in Europe’s space industry rather than simply a cost.
The International Space Station is essentially a floating laboratory where ESA does much of its vital science. After its decommission in 2032, this is likely to be replaced by a commercial space station.
Without its independent access to space, Europe will have to continue to rely on buying seats aboard US spacecraft with uncertain availability and then rent facilities aboard commercial space stations for research. Josef estimated that this would come at a cost of around €5 billion over the next 10 years.
“But the money is lost, or lost in the sense it's being spent not in Europe. So I'd rather invest this funding in Europe, strengthen our industry, increase the autonomy of Europe in this domain,” Josef explained.
But he stressed this would not mean an end to international collaboration for Europe.
“[We could] even offer a seat maybe to our friends and colleagues from Japan or Australia or some other countries, and I think this is also something that Europe could consider to build up its own strength, its autonomy, not to isolate, not at all - the opposite, but to be a strong partner internationally to other countries and other agencies.”
The Big Question is a series from Euronews Business where we sit down with industry leaders and experts to discuss some of the most important topics on today’s agenda.
Watch the video above to see the full discussion with the European Space Agency.

‘Restore the authority’: the challenge for the BBC’s new director of news
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:00:18 UTC
14:00:18 KST

With looming job cuts and an ongoing pay dispute, there has not been much to smile about for BBC journalists working in “the pit” – their pet name for the newsroom deep in the belly of New Broadcasting House.
On Monday afternoon, however, they were greeted by a grinning figure conducting a tour of the news floor. She was Rachel Jupp, the BBC’s newly appointed director of news and current affairs. Jupp engaged in a series of polite if brief conversations with her new troops.
It was a small but welcome gesture for a newsroom that had been desperate for a sense of direction from a new, permanent leader. The shock resignation of Deborah Turness, Jupp’s predecessor, was almost a year ago. Frustration has grown among journalists awaiting a grand plan.
“We just need a set direction of travel,” said one. “A north star, as startups call it. Lay out a timeline and tell everyone what cuts are coming and what needs to be done.”
Beyond the small talk, figures at all levels of the corporation acknowledge that Jupp faces a huge task. Running the world’s most scrutinised newsroom is a tall order at the best of times, even without the turmoil over pay and job losses.
Jupp takes the helm at BBC News as it is gripped by an angst-ridden debate about the place of its journalism in an increasingly digital world. It is one she has been tasked with resolving.
It is a world in which the BBC’s hallmarks of impartiality and authority – and focus on television and radio news – are pitted against content creators and a myriad of other established media brands converging to reach audiences via a handful of smartphone apps.
Inside BBC News, a series of announcements about show closures and strategy shifts have fuelled a “clicks v public service” debate. There are competing views over how the BBC should adapt its content for commercially driven digital platforms favoured by younger audiences – while sticking to the corporation’s founding principles of informing the public.
“I’ve heard the DG [director general, Matt Brittin] and [the deputy director general, Rhodri Talfan Davies] have been saying to people that they want the new director of news to restore the authority of BBC News,” said Roger Mosey, the former head of BBC TV News.
“I think that’s what a lot of us have been arguing for. BBC News does all sorts of good things and it’s generally an impartial and fair service. But it hasn’t been able to translate the authority of the really big brands of TV and radio into an online world.”
Those concerned that the corporation is at risk of losing its bearings point to a BBC website piece about penis fillers or recent social videos of reporters holding cheap mics, content creator-style. Meanwhile, they fear flagship shows such as the Today programme or the 10 O’Clock News, which continue to attract large audiences, have not been nourished or championed online.
Those pushing for a faster embrace of new platforms say it is clearly where audiences are heading and the broadcaster’s requirement to cater for everyone is at the heart of its public service remit. As one BBC figure put it: “Rachel’s task and challenge is to show how we can do what every news organisation is having to do – go digital, without becoming a value-free click factory.”
Above all else, Jupp’s willingness to take on this precarious task is why she was handed such a big promotion.
While the BBC’s relatively new director general, Matt Brittin, inherited many of the cuts being announced across the BBC, Jupp’s appointment was in his hands. At an all-staff call this week, he said he wanted the organisation to be “a bit more Elvis – a little less conversation, a little more action”. In Jupp, Brittin believes he has found one of his best Elvis impersonators, willing to make changes for the digital age.
Jupp triumphed from a shortlist of four candidates. There was a recognition that one of her competitors, Jonathan Munro, had managed to avoid any major crises as the interim head of BBC News – an achievement not to be underestimated, given recent criticisms.
However, the job came down to Jupp and Esme Wren, the editor of Channel 4 News. Wren was recognised as a formidable champion of journalists and journalism, but the conclusion was that the BBC’s news machine produces plenty of high-quality, award-winning material.
While Jupp had not run a big organisation before – something Brittin had been looking for – the director general believed Jupp had two important qualities. The first was solid editorial judgment – a requirement after bruising criticisms over a Gaza documentary that had to be pulled and a spliced-together Trump speech that led to a multibillion-dollar lawsuit.
Jupp had been tasked with overseeing the BBC’s documentary and long-form journalism content after the Gaza row, so was seen as someone who would safeguard the BBC’s authority as it pushed deeper into digital content.
Her second quality was an appetite for transformation, the buzzword for the mammoth task of translating the BBC’s journalism on to new digital platforms without losing its authority – seen, at best, as a work in progress. Jupp has also been at the heart of the BBC’s use of generative AI, and Brittin – a former Google executive – believes this can have a bigger role if used in the right way.
It also helped that Jupp could start almost immediately, given the pace at which a cash crisis is forcing the BBC into big, strategic choices.
Jupp also begins her tenure with another underrated advantage: she is genuinely liked by close colleagues and respected by journalists who have worked with her in previous roles at Channel 4 News, Newsnight and Panorama.
As her tour of the pit illustrated, starting with the support of her staff is seen as essential as she embarks on a transformation of BBC News that will include some difficult and unpopular decisions.

‘Stab to the heart’: arrest of German ex-spymaster sparks calls for reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:00:18 UTC
14:00:18 KST

The ex-spymaster August Hanning once criticised Germany’s own intelligence services as “vegetarians” among prowling carnivores, demanding broader powers to keep the country safe in a treacherous world.
Often described as a “godfather” of Germany’s 21st-century security architecture, Hanning is now charged with treasonous espionage and handing state secrets to a foreign power in one of the most spectacular alleged intelligence breaches of the postwar period.
If true, Hanning may have irreparably damaged Germany’s global security cooperation while exposing grievous internal vulnerabilities, in a tale ripped from a far-fetched political thriller.
“This is an incident that has the potential to escalate into a genuine national scandal,” said Konstantin von Notz, a Bundestag member who sits on the parliamentary intelligence supervisory committee.
Von Notz warned of a “devastating” loss of trust among partner countries “whose support we cannot do without in the current extremely tense security situation”.
Tuesday’s scenes from a small town in Germany staggered even seasoned spy watchers: masked commandos led Hanning from his estate in his birthplace, Nordwalde, to a black police van, his familiar bespectacled face framed by neatly combed white hair. His expression was calm and focused, his wrists without handcuffs.
The detention of the 80-year-old, who ran the federal foreign intelligence service (BND) from 1998 to 2005, marked a first in a western democracy given his previous rank, according to experts.
Federal prosecutors believe Hanning ran his former chief of staff, identified only as Manfred D, as a mole at the BND, paying him to spirit out nearly 2,000 documents, at least some of them classified, over 12 years.
He then allegedly exploited the intelligence for clients of the private consulting firm he launched after retiring – a legal business model that drew fierce criticism over the course of a tumultuous week.
Hanning is in pretrial detention and has, through his lawyers, denied passing on confidential documents to foreign powers. If convicted, he could face 10 years in prison.
Many of the compromised files are believed to have been briefing papers prepared for top officials including the chancellor.
The former BND vice-president Arndt Freytag von Loringhoven described the material as the “crown jewels of the BND”, telling Der Spiegel magazine they were “the most important assessments that a BND president provides”.
The explosive case sent allied secret services scrambling to assess the possible damage. A western official told Reuters that US foreign intelligence was included in documents stolen from the BND. The CIA has not commented on the case.
Luca Manns, managing director of the Intelligence Services Research Unit at the University of Cologne, called the case a “stab to the heart” of the BND, causing incalculable damage to allied cooperation.
“It won’t be an abrupt break,” Manns said, predicting a “creeping erosion of partnerships”.
The suspected betrayal could be corrosive within the agencies as well as in public perception, said Dieter Bacher, a historian at the University of Graz in Austria specialising in secret services.
“When the former head of a service does something like this, the implications are, of course, enormous,” he said. “A loss of trust is certainly inevitable. As information from partner services was apparently also involved, the impact on agency ‘business’ is all the greater.”
The news broke in a week in which Germany’s intelligence service directors had testified to parliament about the heightened threat posed by powers including Russia and China.
The BND chief, Martin Jäger, a former ambassador to Ukraine, warned of a possible violent conflict with Moscow, accusing the Kremlin of mounting a “shadow war” of hybrid and drone attacks.
“We sincerely want to be Germany’s first line of defence,” he said.
Jäger was reportedly already aware of Henning’s impending arrest at the time of his testimony, which came weeks after a foiled drone bomb attack that Berlin has blamed on Moscow.
Russia does not appear to be the recipient of Hanning’s alleged activities, according to reports, at least not directly.
Der Spiegel named Azerbaijan and China among the possible clients, claims not confirmed by authorities. Baku has denied involvement, although Hanning served on the board of the German-Azerbaijani Forum “fostering ties” with the authoritarian-run key energy transit country.
Hanning’s primary motive may have been financial.
He sat on the board of failed Latvian bank PNB Banka, which was declared insolvent in 2019. Bild newspaper said Hanning and another member of the supervisory board – reported to be the former Nato secretary general Anders Fogh Rasmussen – were held liable for up to €4m.
Bild reported that Hanning’s pension had been confiscated to service the debt.
The secret services are facing a reform drive long held back by sensitivities over abuses under the Nazi and communist dictatorships. A law due to pass parliament this year would lift many of the restraints imposed during the postwar period.
Manns warned against any call to stop the measures in light of the Hanning case, saying it would “play into the hands of our opponents, who want a weak German foreign service”.
Hanning was the face of German intelligence during a turbulent period of the post-cold war period, overseeing anti-terror strategy after the 9/11 attacks which were planned in part by a cell in Hamburg.
Investigators only learned of his alleged criminal activities while gathering evidence in a separate child kidnapping case involving a steakhouse restaurant dynasty, which he is accused of abetting using his Israeli intelligence contacts.
The treason charges have sparked a range of troubling questions. Were there other moles? How could his espionage have gone undetected so long? Was the classified information passed to third parties? And who will still trust Germany’s intelligence agencies?
The charges against Hanning are hardly the first scandal to rock the country’s secret services in recent years, with high-profile cases involving spying for Russian intelligence and the CIA.
More broadly, the former head of the domestic intelligence service, Hans-Georg Maaßen, has allied himself with hard-right groups and causes, raising doubts about the neutrality of the agency on his watch.
And the former chancellor Gerhard Schröder, once a Social Democratic stalwart and respected economic reformer, has shocked Germans by taking on a string of lucrative Russian corporate jobs since leaving office in 2005 while becoming a close friend of Vladimir Putin, even attending the Kremlin strongman’s 74th birthday celebrations in Moscow this week.
And with the far-right, pro-Russian party Alternative für Deutschland on the brink of power in a German state for the first time since the second world war, authorities are racing to restrict its access to sensitive intelligence.
With criticism mounting of the legions of former senior German officials who cash in on work relating to their previous activities, Von Notz and Manns joined a chorus calling for a lifelong lobbying ban for high-ranking intelligence officers.

France’s other schools problem – the teens violently smashing up their old primaries: ‘They think it’s not worthy of respect – so they trash it’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:00:17 UTC
14:00:17 KST

Like most French primaries on Wednesdays, Marcel Pagnol school, in the eastern suburbs of Lyon, was shut on 19 June 2024. But at 6.30pm that evening, two boys turned up late for school – by two years. Former pupils there, the 13-year-olds struggled to break through the crispy lattice of the front-door window with a garden fork and a broom. Using a window-breaker, they finally created an opening large enough to force their way in without hurting themselves.
What happened next is captured in a video the pair subsequently posted on Snapchat. Once inside they prowl the classrooms, corridors and canteen, slinging around scooters and smashing up computer equipment, setting off fire extinguishers and upending furniture. They help themselves to pouches of Capri‑Sun from the fridge: “I don’t give a fuck – I’m taking the lot.” The boy not filming sets small fires as they move through the building, squirting each one with a little jet of lighter fuel. “I love what’s happening here!” says his accomplice. “I love fire.”
But the exhilaration soon turns to panic. With a thick black canopy of smoke creeping along the ceiling of the main corridor, they realise it’s time to go: “Come on, come on, there’s smoke everywhere. Fuck, I can’t see a thing!” They’re soon scarpering into the surrounding streets in broad daylight, the cameraman sipping his Capri-Sun as a column of smoke rises from the school, and police cars converge on the site.
The Marcel Pagnol arson was perhaps the most serious incident of a phenomenon that has swept the whole of France in recent years: comprehensive trashings of school premises that go well beyond isolated acts of vandalism. There were at least 15 cases in 2025; a similar number in 2024. The damage inflicted on at least 24 high schools across the country during this month’s student protests seem to some extent to fit this pattern – though these actions are fuelled by particular shared grievances, including dilapidated facilities and endemic staff shortages. Perhaps attacks on schools like Marcel Pagnol should have served as canaries in the coalmine for rising tension, resentment and nihilistic feeling among students towards the institutions supposedly there to guarantee their future. Such events crop up in other countries, but here they seem to fit a pattern of carnivalesque destruction – like the mass burning of cars during urban riots – that seems distinctively French. In a sense, trashings are the country’s equivalent of school shootings in America – though obviously far less deadly and generally perpetrated by groups, not loners.
To highlight a few: smashed computers and broken windows at Rabelais secondary school in Vitry-sur-Seine in March 2024, the fourth break-in in six months; graffiti of a swastika, an anarchist symbol and anti‑Rassemblement National (RN) slogans left behind by ideologically confused hooligans at André Malraux secondary school in Baignes-Sainte-Radegonde, near Bordeaux; “Foke les profs” (Fuck the teachers) scrawled amid the devastation at Jean Moulin primary school in Montgeron, on Paris’s southern edge; one primary school and two nursery schools laid waste to in 2025 in working-class neighbourhoods of the Provençal city of Arles.
In a strikingly large number of cases, it is primary schools that are attacked. When the perpetrators are caught, they are often children of early secondary-school age returning to wreak havoc. In many cases, they’re trashing the same schools in which their younger siblings are still taught. “My sister’s got school here tomorrow,” crows one of the intruders in the video from École Marcel Pagnol. On the one hand, there’s a festive misrule in such acts: the paint-lashed walls, the upturned shelves, the rainbow debris of playbricks strewn across play areas. On the other, there’s an aspect of psychological self-harm in play, akin to destroying the family home, that’s also visible in this month’s lycée attacks. It’s hard to square this beguiling clash of motives.
What’s clear is the impact on the surrounding community. Two years after the attack, on a humid June Monday morning, the final one before the summer holidays, pupils and parents are ambling up to Marcel Pagnol to start the school day. It’s situated in the suburb of Meyzieu, a relatively well-off and unremarkable commuter dormitory of Lyon set in the arable land that sprawls towards the city airport. The school’s cream, two-storey blocks have been restored to pristine condition – at a cost of €1.9m to the Meyzieu municipality (partly covered by insurance).
But the attack caused a real sense of violation. “I’m sad,” six-year-old Lino told reporters from TV station BFM right after the arson. “All my drawings burned.” And the feeling still lingers. “They set the school alight with a toxic product,” says Evan, a boy of eight or nine with thumbs inside his backpack strap. “There were flames.” Audrey Granger, a member of the parents’ association, points out the children had to process seeing their charred drawings on the walls, the burnt exercise books. She didn’t tell her daughter, who attended the nursery school next door, what had happened. “We wanted to leave her in her own little bubble,” she says.
“It was as if you left your office and someone said to you: you have no right to come back,” Juliane Fauriat, the headteacher, says. “You didn’t anticipate it, you have to leave everything behind, which is very difficult.” Her staff removed salvageable equipment in crates provided by the town hall; two traumatised teachers walked out with empty boxes from their entirely burnt-out classrooms.
The following academic year, Marcel Pagnol’s 240 pupils were housed in prefab annexes on an empty field opposite – a novelty for some of them. But with the canteen severely damaged, lunchtime had to be split between two other school sites: one a bus ride away for the younger children; another 15 minutes’ walk away for the older ones. “They had to do it in the heat of summer and in winter,” says Sabrina, a mum in a flowery dress lingering at the end of the school run. “Can you imagine? My daughter was crying sometimes – she was always running late.”
The two 13-year-old perpetrators – one of whom shows his face in the video and names the other – were caught almost immediately. They had no criminal record and were unknown to the police; one had an “irreproachable” academic record, says Sandrine Carroz, a coordinator with the municipality’s education services. The other was going through a “fragile period, where communication with his parents was complicated”. But there had been nothing to indicate he might erupt in this way. Sylvie Normand, the deputy mayor of Meyzieu, the area served by École Marcel Pagnol, says: “I think these were young people who dared each other to do something and who came up with a bad idea, which went through their heads without them thinking about the consequences.”
The online lynch mob assembled: “Give them another chance – they were just expressing their anger at having to retake year 3 for the fifth time” is one sarcastic comment under a news report posted on YouTube. Others hint at the societal and ethnic tensions inflaming French public life – heightened in Lyon, which is a centre of far-right activity: “Kick them out of the country, along with the parents who are taking our family allowances.” (Based on the name mentioned by one of the boys in the videos, and their slang, many commenters assumed they had immigrant origins; their identities as minors are of course protected by law.) Tiffany Joncour, the local RN candidate, was quickly on the scene to film a video declaring: “It’s time to stop these delinquents who act with impunity and spoil all our lives.”
The pair received four-month suspended sentences and were placed under special court supervision for 18 months. The municipality agreed with the two families to send their siblings to other schools. Over the road from École Marcel Pagnol, boulangerie worker Miriam is more circumspect than most: “It could have been my child – because you never know, especially with the influence of social networks these days. I hope it knocks some sense into them. And their families, too, because they have to take some responsibility.”
As the Marcel Pagnol perpetrators are minors, it’s impossible to ask them the crucial question: what led them to break down the front door on that day? But perhaps it’s possible to pursue a second one: what do these messy tremors from the teenage subconscious collectively say about French society?
‘They think it’s not worthy of respect – so they trash it.” Outside Louise-Michel primary school in Arles earlier this year in March, parent Etienne Becker suggests it was a fundamental disdain for national institutions that led four youths, aged between 11 and 13, to break and enter and do approximately €30,000 worth of damage there in July 2025. He’s dropping his six-year-old son off at a squat, tan complex with a barracks-like air. Louise‑Michel is on the edge of Griffeuille, a marginalised neighbourhood dominated by hal‑rendered blocks of public housing in which 57% live below the poverty line.
The values of the French state – “Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité” – are displayed on insignia outside almost all the country’s schools (as Becker points out, they are curiously absent at Louise-Michel). It’s in places like Griffeuille where it’s easiest to assume that school trashings may be a form of aggression, conscious or not, towards how these lofty ideals translate in practice. Éric Debarbieux, a veteran researcher who formerly directed the International Observatory of Violence in School and has advised the French government, corroborates this, suggesting that for the attackers, “it’s a way of saying: schools don’t keep their promises. The values displayed aren’t the same as the values in reality.”
That might explain why this form of mayhem occurs so consistently in France, where schools are adorned with the livery and rhetoric of the Fifth Republic. But it’s hard to exactly quantify it, as the national annual statistics on school violence don’t list incident numbers. Only a percentage breakdown for property damage (3% in primary schools and 4% in secondary schools/sixth-form colleges in 2024-25) among total incidents reported is given. Verbal and physical violence are far more common (45% and 34% of incidents reported in primary schools).
Just because school trashings are statistically less frequent doesn’t mean they aren’t significant. It’s precisely their intensely visible character – the unbridled violation of a public space – that gives them power. Debarbieux emphasises the particular character of these acts: “They’re a kind of game. There’s possibly a kind of group jubilation behind them: it’s these children’s manner of expressing themselves.” He believes such incidents have been occurring at least since the 1990s – when statistics on French school violence first began – and have steadily risen since.
As in Lyon, silence has gathered around the series of incidents that hit the east side of Arles last year. The municipality won’t comment, and one teacher I encounter says they have been forbidden by the education board from talking about them to the press. The parents outside Louise-Michel speculate about the motivations of the invaders, who were caught after tripping an alarm and in some cases were forced by their parents to participate in the clean-up. But no one here today knows their identity, or anything specific.
The same is true at Victoria Lyles nursery school in the neighbourhood of Trébon, 2km to the north. It was ransacked, along with a nearby primary school, by eight secondary school pupils from the area in February 2025, who were caught on security cameras and convicted of vandalising school property. Again, some had younger siblings at Victoria Lyles; they urinated in the classrooms where pupils studied.
Lazy brown mosquitoes swarm the parents picking up their offspring on this March lunchtime. A general air of incomprehension and resignation reigns regarding the break-in. “We were afraid for our children, as there isn’t any proper security here,” says one of a group of three mothers. Resources are strained in the commune; France’s largest by surface area, with lots of schools, but a low tax base. In the wake of the three 2025 trashings, the Arles municipality invested €650,000 in better security for the affected schools, including linking their alarms to a central surveillance centre.
In the cornershop down the road, I’m told no one in Trébon will break the general “omertà” regarding the eight offenders. Neighbourhoods like this and Griffeuille are hotspots for the driving factors behind school violence. Laurent Mucchielli, a specialist in the sociology of delinquency at the French National Centre for Scientific Research, points out three key indicators for troublemakers: academic failure; coming from “poor or stigmatised” neighbourhoods; and difficulties within the family. But he insists the first is paramount: “Until they’re 18 years old, school is the essential structure of collective social integration for young people, what you might call the society of children. So academic failure is the first form of exclusion from society.” It’s not hard to see why such children might react by channelling their anger against the site of their humiliation.
Mucchielli stresses that overall levels of school violence in France have remained stable since the 1990s – counter to the media and political narrative of feral youth. He also downplays the effect of social media, saying it doesn’t create new forms of behaviour. But it’s clear that it shapes some individual incidents; providing not just, as in École Marcel Pagnol, the means of dissemination, but also of incitement. Two sources tell me that the break-in at Louise-Michel was in response to online “challenges” teenagers set each on social networks; one of them, from Arles town hall, says the offenders came from outside Griffeuille to vandalise the school. But it’s not easy to track this social network peer pressure, often posted as ephemeral Snapchat or TikTok stories, with generic, algorithm-bait hashtags. Normand, the deputy mayor speculates that online content has a desensitising effect: “They see stuff like that, it’s virtual, but then they identify with it and they make the leap.”
Speaking on condition of anonymity, two teachers who have had to deal with such incidents agree on another explanation that pre-dates 21st-century social media: boredom. They believe that this is the primary motivating factor – especially with many trashings taking place during school holidays that stretch out for two months. “Given the long period without anyone in school buildings, it’s maybe easier to spontaneously decide to get up to some mischief,” says one. Parental neglect exacerbates this, says the other: “When children have nothing to do during the holidays, it’s too young to be left to their own devices the whole day.”
The first teacher offers yet another interpretation: over the last decade, she has seen a rise in a desire among her pupils for a sense of belonging. “It’s wanting to be part of a group, to share the same codes,” they say. Perversely ironic though it is to take it out on a community asset, perhaps this need for togetherness can take more destructive forms: the urge to go and smash up school property together, whatever the origins of the participants.
Debarbieux thinks the concept of the solidarity of vandals has merit. He remembers going to school in the 1960s in the northern city of Tourcoing and taking part in a phenomenon he calls le chahut: collective heckling of certain unforunate teachers. Almost nostalgically, he says this ritualised torment helped cement bonds between working-class pupils. And perhaps school trashings, in a 21st century dominated by identity politics, are a resurgence of this bonding through anarchy – only this time, out of classroom hours.
There is no official recognition of school trashings as a national problem, or any kind of problem, by the French ministry of education. When I send the ministry a list of the 16 incidents reported online in 2025, it replies via a spokesperson: “You refer to 0.3% of school buildings. It’s difficult to talk about a ‘phenomenon of trashings’.”
But statistics don’t tally the impact on the ground. The official emphasis on property, not people, is telling. There is no will at government level to analyse this wave at a deeper emotional level; to understand the juvenile offenders individually or as a group phenomenon. With local authorities reluctant to draw further attention to themselves after such incidents, and teachers generally bound by a duty of confidentiality as public servants, they are quickly swept under the carpet.
France’s network of Maisons des Jeunes et de la Culture and Maisons des Adolescents should in theory provide support services for troubled children and a sounding board for the psychological health of French youth overall. But, as with British youth clubs, these organisations, in part state-subsidised, are under increasing financial pressure, and many are closing. In the absence of any wider grasp of the problem, the response remains piecemeal. The ministry of education stresses each local municipality – the owners of school premises – must investigate, prosecute, reinforce security and find other solutions.
Shocking terrorist attacks on teachers, such as the beheading of Samuel Paty in Éragny in 2020 and the fatal stabbing of Dominique Bernard in Arras in 2023, have accelerated the trend in recent decades towards bolstering school security. Following Bernard’s murder, 1,000 “at risk” French schools were earmarked for beefed-up protection – such as alert buttons, CCTV, and alarms linked to video surveillance centres and security gates. But Debarbieux believes such measures reinforce the sense of “bunker-fied” Republican institutions defined in opposition to the communities they serve, which is counterproductive: “The more schools close in on themselves, the more you ‘protect’ them from the surrounding neighbourhood, the more they look like the enemy.”
The ministry of education says it takes all incidents of school trashing seriously, stresses its spokesperson. They point out how Laurent Nuñez, minister of the interior, and Édouard Geffray, the education minister, recently visited Champollion secondary school in Dijon following an arson attack in December last year. Reportedly a reprisal for anti-narcotraffic operations in the surrounding Grésilles neighbourhood, it was in the small minority – 5% – of cases where violence in French schools is committed by external perpetrators (the Paty and Bernard attacks being at the extreme end of this). The other 95%, including many school trashings, stems from actors within the system itself: teachers, pupils, other staff. So a response beyond perimeter security is required.
Seated on a bench in a small park down the hill from École Marc Bloch, on the north-western edge of the southern city of Montpellier, the president of the parents’ association, Manuella Delbecq, talks of her anger and exasperation in the face of attacks there: “We knew in effect it was kids from the neighbourhood who were breaking in, setting fire to, stealing from and trashing schools. So the message we wanted to get across was: this is your little brother’s, your cousin’s school.”
The most serious trashing at Marc Bloch occurred over the weekend of 5-6 August 2023. The intruders had an easy entry point, thanks to scaffolding that had been erected to upgrade the premises. They deactivated the alarm, then set about the usual mayhem: laying waste to seven classrooms, spraying them with paint from the cupboards and overturning an aquarium, in which luckily there were no fish.
A teacher at the school says the interlopers left a few calling cards: a half-eaten salad with a fork still in it; an opened but untouched beer bottle. The tags of “DZ” – the international abbreviation for Algeria – sprayed on the wall suggested their background. The police took fingerprints from the desecrated classrooms, but no arrests or convictions were made. A nightwatchman and a dog surveilled Marc Bloch for the rest of the summer, while the renovations continued; they stopped yet more intruders before the start of the school year in September. Most pupils, shielded by their parents, had no idea about the destruction.
Delbecq is accompanied by Naïma Hamada and Nadia Abzaoui, the parents’ association’s secretary and treasurer, respectively. Their neighbourhood of Les Hauts de Massane is the comparatively affluent tip of the larger, rundown La Mosson district on Montpellier’s west side. The trio, along with other parents, had already protested outside the school after an earlier trashing in 2020, in which intruders caused €30,000 worth of damage in a new annexe. No one has ever been held responsible for any of these incidents.
As much as demanding reinforced security at Marc Bloch itself, the group said they were signalling their outrage to the perpetrators themselves – that such disrespect of community property wouldn’t stand. In doing so, they wanted to show they were the kind of parents who took active interest in the quality of their children’s education. “We don’t drop them off and then they can do whatever they want,” says Abzaoui. “No – we’re involved in their lives.” Their aim was counteracting stereotypes of disenfranchised, disengaged families with immigrant backgrounds. “It’s that kind of stigmatisation and fingerpointing that means a lot of parents don’t get involved,” she says.
They hoped to shift the mood among the parents. “There’s a kind of shame,” says Delbecq. “They think they don’t have the right to be heard.” Before arriving in the southern city in 2002, she grew up in the 1980s in the underprivileged Parisian district of Vitry-sur-Seine. “There was a mutual respect between parents and schools then,” she says.
The association tried to organise a silent march in March 2021 after other schools on the west side of Montpellier were similarly targeted. But the parents from those schools, who had initially approached them, never showed up; only the trio and a handful of other mothers from Marc Bloch marched with their banners towards the hulking tower blocks in La Mosson. Hamada was crestfallen; people seemed unwilling to turn out for fear of reprisals from the drug gangs, who were either protecting the teenagers involved in the trashing, or didn’t want any spotlight on the neighbourhood that might interrupt their trade.
This inertia is mirrored within the walls of Marc Bloch itself, the trio believe – something else they wanted to shake up through protesting. Delbecq describes a pattern of self-imposed silence from the school after disruptive incidents like the trashings: “They don’t want to talk about them.” She adds: “It doesn’t say anything, in the hope that it will buy peace. But, in fact, it’s led to something else, which is that disruptive youth are able to take up more and more space.”
The stonewalling the group describes seems consistent with the culture of #pasdevague (don’t make waves), to quote the ironic hashtag under which French teachers have for years posted on social media about the lack of support from their hierarchy when faced with school violence, especially when caused by ethnic and cultural conflicts. In the case of École Marc Bloch, the parents’ association claims it was told to stop speaking to the media and frozen out. The school did not reply to inquiries for this article.
The association has ceased its activities now; a rift that seems to be typical of what Debarbieux describes as the “catastrophic” levels of parental input into the French education system. In Meyzieu, Normand, the deputy mayor, says rebuilding these links between schools, support workers and parents is her priority in the wake of the Marcel Pagnol arson. “You have to get down on the ground,” she says. “It’s those people who’ll help you improve things.”
Outside École Marcel Pagnol, the heatwave has broken, the school year is winding down, and all is back in good order. The fire damage has been erased; the gate monitors watch the perimeter for disruptions (they interrogate one annoying Guardian journalist). But once the stream of excited faces have passed inside, what happens there? Maybe not even those in uniform can tell us. Before they melt away into the suburbs, two mothers marvel at what really disturbed their offspring: “The only thing they were shocked about was the fact it was other children who did it.”
