Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:00:17 UTC
14:00:17 KST

Christian nationalism in Britain is being driven largely by people who rarely attend church and are more concerned with defending the country’s Christian heritage, according to research.
The report, by the thinktank Theos, identified five different groups within the UK in a survey that looked at their attitudes to Christianity and Britishness.
The group whose views most closely resembled Christian nationalism, termed “identity integrationists” by the researchers, accounted for 11% of respondents, making it the smallest of the five groups.
Although 81% of this group identified as Christian, just 13% attended church weekly, only slightly above the 11% average across the population surveyed. Less than a third (31%) prayed weekly, while 47% expressed an interest in the Bible.
The group was strongly hostile to immigration and Islam. Just 19% agreed that Christian values required welcoming and supporting asylum seekers, while 30% supported the equal treatment of religions in public life.
In contrast, another group in the survey with high levels of Christian affiliation, were considerably more religiously observant and less hostile to immigration and religious diversity. They comprised 13% of respondents.
Among these “belief integrationists”, 31% attended church weekly, 46% prayed weekly and 62% expressed an interest in the Bible.
Almost half (48%) agreed that Christian values required welcoming and supporting asylum seekers, while 63% supported the equal treatment of religions in public life.
Although they are the group containing the highest proportion of practising Christians, only 18% of belief integrationists think that defending Britain’s Christian culture and heritage is important for being Christian, compared with 90% of the Christian nationalist group.
At a time when crosses have been carried at Unite the Kingdom rallies and crowds have chanted “Christ is King” at protests, the research challenges the idea that the growing prominence of Christian nationalism in Britain reflects a revival of Christianity.
Instead, the findings suggest that Christianity is increasingly being invoked as a marker of British identity amid wider anxieties about immigration, Islam and cultural change.
The results are based on a survey of 1,765 adults conducted in April 2026, which identified five distinct groups according to their attitudes towards Christianity and British national identity.
More than half of Britons surveyed (55%) said they would be unhappy if their local church closed and became a mosque, including 37% who would be very unhappy.
More than a third (37%) agreed with the conspiracy theory that the white population of Europe was being deliberately replaced by migrants from Muslim countries, sometimes known as the ‘great replacement’ theory.
Nick Spencer, a senior fellow at Theos and one of the report’s authors, suggested that the difference between the two most highly affiliated Christian groups’ attitudes towards asylum seekers might partly reflect their religious practice and ethnic composition.
The more practising Christian group were the most ethnically diverse of the five groups, with 20% identifying as non-white, while identity integrationists were among the least diverse.
Spencer added that there was also “a difference between Christianity as an idea and Christianity as an embodied practice”.
“If it matters enough for you to haul yourself out of bed on a Sunday morning, to spend time with people who you don’t choose – you don’t choose who you’re sitting next to in the pew, you don’t choose who’s next to you in the communion rail – it becomes a bit more human and more humane.”
Arun Arora, Church of England bishop of Kirkstall in Leeds, said the distinction between cultural Christianity and practising faith was central to understanding the findings.
“What is it to be a disciple? It’s threefold: deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow me,” he said.
“And what I think’s interesting about the nationalists is that they want to take up the cross at marches, and display it, but there’s less of an interest in denying themselves and following Jesus.”
He argued that the lessons for church leaders weren’t just to encourage church attendance, but to be out in the community.
“If as the church we’re going to wait for people to come into the ark to be saved, to use Noah’s ark analogy, then we’re going to be waiting a while,” he said.
“Whereas the responsibility for us is to bring that full gospel message of discipleship, of what that requires, the costly nature of discipleship, to be able to expound and articulate that, and the passionate love of God for his people, and his world, and not just those who carry certain passports.”
The Rev Dr Helen Paynter, a theologian who has researched the far right’s use of Christianity, said the findings highlighted the responsibility of churches to welcome people across the political spectrum.
But, she added: “The church is and has been since its inception a multi-ethnic, multinational group, and may not rightly be equated with any nationality or ethnicity. In fact, the ‘average’ Christian in the world today is poor, female and black.”
For Paynter, one of most important findings is the starkly different attitudes evidenced by those who are practising Christians, compared with those who claim the label.
“The Christian faith is not just an identity that we can put on like a coat; it involves an encounter with transcendence which must be transformative of all our values.”

Retrofit schools and consider moving exams to beat extreme heat, says teaching union leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:00:17 UTC
14:00:17 KST

Schools should consider changing start and finish times, reordering holidays and moving exams from the summer months in an effort to adapt to the UK’s increasingly severe heatwaves, according to the leader of the country’s biggest education union.
Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the National Education Union (NEU), said this summer’s repeated bouts of extreme heat had a devastating impact on teachers and pupils, as classroom temperatures topped 40C and hundreds of thousands of young people were sent home.
Speaking to the Guardian, Kebede called on the government to roll out a mass retrofitting programme to ensure schools – which he said had been built “for a different climate” – were better equipped to deal with extreme heat ahead of next summer’s El Niño-charged temperatures.
And he said it was time for a national conversation about other measures that could help schools adapt to the reality of a rapidly warming climate.
“There needs to be a really serious discussion about how we make sure there is the continuity of education in this changed climate,” he said. “You might want to consider moving the school year around, or having a longer summer holiday – in hot countries they tend to have a longer summer holiday. You might consider an earlier start and earlier finish … and perhaps we don’t want exams to be happening in the hottest part of the year.”
Kebede said he had been inundated with messages from teachers during this summer’s heatwaves urging the union to help.
“The last time I felt that level of panic in the profession was during the Covid pandemic,” he said. “I was being routinely contacted by members in distress … they felt there was a real risk and danger to themselves and to their pupils.”
At least 760,000 schoolchildren in England and Wales missed lessons owing to school closures during this summer’s June heatwave – one in five in the UK in the space of a few months – with pupils missing more than 15m hours of lesson time.
School staff told the Guardian that learning was almost impossible as temperature records were broken, with pupil behaviour and attention deteriorating rapidly.
One primary school teacher said: “Everyone was lying or sitting on the floor with their water bottles, sweating, moaning and feeling tired, [complaining of] headaches and nausea. The adults barely coped and most of the children were calling for their mummies and daddies. There was no learning, just surviving the best we could.”
This summer’s severe heat was not confined to the UK: brutal temperatures and devastating wildfires hit countries across Europe. One of the key demands of the student protesters that have taken to the streets in France this week has been action to make classrooms bearable during extreme heat.
Kebede warned that in the UK the impact of these bouts of extreme weather was falling hardest on more disadvantaged communities. He said children were often being sent home to flats that were unsuited to extreme heat, and to parents and carers who were unable to work from home or take time off.
“It is having a really uneven impact and it’s particularly impacting children who live in deprived urban areas … you will have a two-tier system where schools in more affluent areas are able to cope with extreme heat.”
Kebede said many of the UK’s schools were housed in either old Victorian-era buildings or those built in the 1960s and 1970s, and neither style was equipped to cope with the extreme heat that is expected to become a feature of UK summers.
He said a major capital building programme could transform schools, making them “fit for the century we are living in” and also creating good unionised apprenticeships and jobs, revitalising local communities.
“We really need plans in place now because [what we experienced this summer] is going to be the norm,” Kebede said.

Capital punishment is surging in the US – but after Christa Pike’s botched execution, what is its future?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:00:16 UTC
14:00:16 KST

It took more than an hour to establish the two intravenous lines through which Christa Pike would be injected with a giant and normally lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital, and in that time she did everything she could to assist those who were attempting to kill her.
“Please try here,” she said over and over again to Tennessee’s execution team, pointing to specific parts of her body where she thought they might find a vein as they repeatedly stabbed her with needles. “Please try here, I think it will be OK. Please try up on my shoulder, higher.”
When the team finally achieved what they thought would be a working line, allowing her execution to proceed, Pike, 50, made a point of thanking them. “Miss Pike was kind, and she was cooperative,” her lawyer Randy Spivey, a witness in the death chamber, said.
The world knows what happened next. For reasons as yet not fully understood, the drug did not enter her bloodstream, probably spilling into her arm tissue.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder when she was 18 of her classmate Colleen Slemmer, remained alive. She is the only person ever to survive a full “lethal” injection execution.
On Tuesday she remarkably regained consciousness. She is now able to talk and walk around the room, her lawyers have said.
In comments to reporters, Spivey said that he was haunted by the harrowing failed execution. “What I saw is not something that should ever happen again. It was done in all of our names.”
The events of the past 10 days – starting with Pike amicably assisting her executioners and ending with her waking up shackled to a Nashville hospital bed, her arms grotesquely swollen, facing a long and uncertain road to recovery – has thrown America into a frenzy. If this is the outcome of a punishment carried out in “all our names”, then what are we doing about it?
“This is a very big moment,” said Laura Porter, executive director at the US Campaign to End the Death Penalty, an alliance of 60 abolitionist groups. “When you see something as horrific as this, the impact is enormous, as it throws attention on the death penalty’s flaws.”
Porter has been closely involved in America’s struggle with capital punishment for almost a quarter century, since she became a leader of New Yorkers Against the Death Penalty in 2003. At that time death row prisoners were still being killed at a rate of more than one a week.
There were 71 executions that year in the US (down from the 1999 pinnacle of 98). Since then, Porter has watched and agitated as the number has steadily declined for almost two decades, reaching a low of just 11 judicial killings in 2021.
“I believe that the death penalty will die by a thousand cuts,” she said. “Every time there’s a botched execution like Christa’s, or a wrongful conviction, or the execution of an intellectually disabled person, public understanding of the system’s flaws grows.”
How great a difference a few years can make. Six years ago, there was such confidence in the historic fading away of the practice that the authoritative Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) began its yearly report with the words: “Capital punishment continued to wither across the US in 2019”.
But as Mark Twain might have put it, reports of the death penalty’s own death turned out to be an exaggeration. Fast forward to last year, and DPI was recording that the 47 executions carried out in 2025 marked the highest incidence in 16 years.
No awards for guessing the key individual behind the resurgence. Less than a year after DPI’s “withering” pronouncement, Donald Trump embarked on one of the most concentrated bursts of US state killing of its own citizens in modern times.
Toward the end of his first presidency, the Trump administration executed 13 federal death row prisoners. They included Lisa Montgomery, a woman with such a shocking history of childhood sexual abuse it bears comparison to Pike’s own.
Since his return to the White House last year, Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions. On his first day back he issued an executive order on “restoring the death penalty” in which he said it was “an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes”.
The statement was a classic Trump fabrication. The US justice department itself has concluded that there is no proof that the punishment deters criminals. Many prisoners on death row cannot be described as the most heinous, not least the 4% who by conservative estimations are innocent.
At federal level, Trump has been hampered by Joe Biden, who before he left office commuted the death penalties of all but three prisoners on federal death row. Using his power as commander-in-chef, Trump still managed this week to order the military execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooter.
On Thursday the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, breathlessly announced that Hasan would face a firing squad of soldiers at Fort Hood on 3 December in the first public execution to be staged in the US since 1936. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”
The Pentagon’s plan to livestream Hasan’s execution prompted a second wave of desbelief that ricocheted around the globe , threatening to drown out even the consternation over Pike’s treatment. US politicians denounced the idea as “disgusting”, while the UN issued the US government with the same stern warning it has given Afghanistan and Iran that the move would be tantamount to torture.
When not presiding over an administration that seems determined to turn the clock back 100 years, Trump has also used his squawk box to exhort death penalty states, where most capital punishment activity occurs, to hit the gas. Many have obliged.
First among them has been Florida. The outgoing governor, Ron DeSantis, appears to have been so inspired by Trump’s 2020-21 killing spree that he greenlit a record 19 executions last year.
DeSantis will come close to matching that shattering number in 2026. Florida has already put to death 16 prisoners this year, with two more executions pending, though the governor cancelled a lethal injection procedure on Friday without giving an explanation.
Nationwide, the US is set to kill up to 38 people this year – the most recent just on Wednesday when Texas executed convicted murderer Jamaal Howard. That tally would be down from last year’s high, but still represent a larger display of state killing than in any year since 2013.
In cheerleading the revival of executions, Trump has been backed by a supporting cast of Christian nationalists. These Bible thumpers have injected their eye-for-an-eye brand of retributive justice into the wider Maga movement.
Brooklyn Walker, an assistant professor at the University of Tennessee Knoxville, has studied Christian nationalist views on justice. She has found them to be far more embracing of retribution, including the death sentence, than other US religious groups.
Christian nationalist leaders frequently invoke Old Testament notions of punitive justice “as part of the idea of creating a social order, and then requiring people to fit within it,” Walker said.
Doug Wilson, an Idaho pastor who wants to turn America into a theocracy and has close ties to Hegseth, has pushed for legal appeals to be streamlined. That way death row prisoners could be dispatched more quickly.
Joel Webbon, another leading Christian nationalist pastor from Texas, has argued for the death penalty to be expanded to include women who make false sexual assault accusations. The day after Pike’s failed execution he posted to his 120,000 followers on X that “you cannot be pro life without being pro death penalty”.
The energy blown into capital punishment from such far-right religious pundits is affecting the furious debate that has now erupted in Tennessee over what should happen to Pike. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for Tennessee governor, wants to plug back in the electric chair.
Blackburn’s call for the return of “Old Sparky” speaks volumes about the state of capital punishment. The horrifying scenes at Pike’s attempted execution were part of a wider unravelling of lethal injections, the protocol that has been dominant in the US for almost 50 years.
By DPI’s calculations, there have been 12 botched executions in the past five years alone. Five of the condemned prisoners involved, including Pike herself, survived the procedure meaning that they were rendered immobile while a team of masked strangers failed to kill them for up to several hours.
Amid such unconscionable suffering, the claim made on behalf of lethal injections that they are a medicalised and humane form of ending a life has come unstuck. Who would dare to classify what Pike endured as humane?
Proponents of the ultimate punishment have been forced to seek alternatives that might avoid some of the pitfalls of lethal injections. But the moment they have introduced such often archaic methods they have run into a whole new set of headaches.
Two of the prisoners who survived recent lethal injections, Alan Miller and Kenneth Smith, were executed by Alabama a year later under the experimental technique, nitrogen gas. The method is regarded by veterinarians as too cruel for the euthanisia of cats and dogs, and it has now been blocked for human use by a federal court.
Other states have tried the firing squad. But when South Carolina took this path last year with Mikal Mahdi, a convicted murderer, the marksmen missed the target of the prisoner’s heart, causing him a prolonged and likely agonising death.
Such an avalanche of mishaps, spanning botched executions, experimentation, and even dark insinuations of deliberate miss-targeting, is what Porter means by her “death by a thousand cuts”. It gives her and her army of abolitionists the material they need to sustain a long campaign.
As a seasoned abolitionist, Porter knows that she is facing tough adversaries in Trump and the Christian nationalists. But she draws sustenance from the 23 states that have scrapped the death penalty which, if you add the four states that have put the practice on hold, pushes them into the majority.
Then there is the growing number of young Americans who no longer support the punishment. In the most recent Gallup poll that asked the question, from 2024, only 42% of 18 to 34 year olds approved. (In last year’s poll the overall extent of support had fallen from a 1995 high of 80% to 52%).
She also takes heart from the burgeoning ranks of Republican state lawmakers willing to raise objections. And by the increasing unwillingness of juries to mete out new death sentences.
Most of all, she’s buoyed up by the powerful accord she has found from an unlikely source: families of capital murder victims. Amid their grief, some families have had the strength and conviction to join the fight to spare the lives of those who killed their loved ones.
“In every campaign I’ve been part of where we’ve ended the death penalty – in Connecticut, Maryland, Virginia, and many more – victims’ families have been among the lead voices,” Porter said.
To those voices we may perhaps, in time, be able to add one more. It would be the most unlikely voice of all – that of a woman whom the modern state, with all its paraphernalia, could not silence: Christa Pike.
Her lawyers tell us that she is angry and confused, her mind foggy. But she is also able to inquire after the well-being of others, including, poignantly, the family of her victim, Colleen Slemmer.
She is not out of the woods: on Saturday she was released from hospital and returned to the women’s prison in Nashville, where she will still receive medical care. But coming from a state of unconsciousness so profound that even her own legal team feared she might be brain-dead, her reemergence has been nothing short of astonishing.
It all leaves so many questions, her lawyer Spivey said ruefully on Wednesday. “We have to ask, ‘How much suffering is enough?’”
Spivey directed the question at Tennessee. He might just as well have been addressing America.

From silence to scandal: How Lithuania’s media portrayed LGBT people after independence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

In 1993, Lithuania decriminalised consensual same-sex relations, opening the way for LGBTQ people to speak more openly about their place in a newly independent society. But as the community became more visible, so did public debate – and, at times, hostility.
Three decades later, a researcher examining Lithuanian media archives from 1994 to 2004 says coverage of sexual minorities reveals a society struggling to move beyond Soviet-era attitudes while confronting new questions about human rights, European integration and social change.
Rasa Navickaitė, a researcher at Vilnius University’s Institute of International Relations and Political Science, has studied how LGBTQ people were portrayed in the media during the first decade after decriminalisation. She discussed her findings while examining LRT's archives for the LRT RADIO program Buvo nebėra.
From Soviet silence to public debate
During the Soviet era, LGBTQ people were largely absent from public discourse. When homosexuality was mentioned, it was often portrayed as a harmful Western influence. Same-sex relations were criminalised and could result in punishment.
“Homophobia was deeply rooted in institutions,” Navickaitė said. “The KGB and police used it as a tool of blackmail and humiliation. The medical system was partly involved, venereal disease clinics and the psychiatric system were used for persecution.”
As a result, she said, people could reach adulthood without ever encountering anything positive about homosexuality.
Lithuania was the last of the three Baltic states to decriminalise same-sex relations, doing so in July 1993. Two years later, the Lithuanian Gay League, or LGL, the country’s first organisation representing gay people, was established.
Media began reporting on homosexuality as a new phenomenon in an independent Lithuania.
Early coverage was generally cautious. Some reports grouped homosexual people together with religious sects and other groups that were portrayed as unfamiliar features of the newly open society.
“It is interesting that different things are placed next to each other – sects and homosexual people,” Navickaitė said. “They are treated as new phenomena in a free, independent Lithuania. Things can no longer simply be suppressed; they have to exist openly. And the question arises of how the majority of society will accept them.”
The subject attracted growing attention. Television programs and newspapers sometimes used provocative approaches, while images from pride events in Western Europe became common ways of illustrating stories about LGBTQ people.
A more hostile turn
According to Navickaitė, coverage became significantly more hostile around the turn of the millennium.
In 2000, the tabloid Vakaro žinios (Evening News) began publishing the names of people it claimed were connected to the LGBTQ community. Articles appeared under titles referring to a “queer mafia” and in a series called “They Are Called Gays”.
The reports claimed to expose homosexual people in public life, including politicians, government officials and media figures. Some of those named were not actually gay, Navickaitė said.
The publications prompted a strong reaction, and the Commission of Ethics in the Provision of Information went as far as describing Vakaro žinios as “violent”, according to Navickaitė.
She believes the timing may have been connected to Lithuania’s preparations to join the European Union.
EU membership required Lithuania to amend some laws and strengthen protections for human rights, while European institutions and organisations supported LGBTQ rights initiatives. That created an opening for opponents of LGBTQ rights to portray homosexuality as something being imposed on Lithuania from abroad, she said.
“The media began escalating the issue, suggesting that gays were sabotaging our accession to the EU,” Navickaitė said.
Coverage increasingly relied on old stereotypes while also creating new conspiracy theories.
One recurring narrative suggested that gay men held important positions in municipalities, government and the media and formed a powerful elite controlling public life.
“It creates the image of a malicious, small elite,” Navickaitė said. “We can compare it very well with antisemitic stereotypes. It is a conspiracy theory that creates the image of an all-powerful gay elite.”
She said homosexuality was also increasingly linked in public discourse with paedophilia, further reinforcing fears and stigma.
Navickaitė sees the campaign as part of a broader polarisation. While some people were moving toward more respectful discussion, she said, the Respublika publishing group, one of the biggest at the time, chose to turn the issue into a scandal and a way of attracting readers.
Building a community
Despite the hostility, LGBTQ people were establishing their own networks and institutions.
They created clubs and organisations and began publishing their own magazines. In 1993, Stasys Dimbelis, who worked at an AIDS centre, launched the magazine Naglis. Amsterdamas followed a year later.
Nightclubs catering to LGBTQ people opened in Vilnius, though they remained largely invisible in mainstream public life.
But distributing LGBTQ publications was not always easy. Some retailers were reluctant to stock them, while potential buyers sometimes avoided purchasing them to prevent unwanted attention.
Being openly gay in public remained unusual.
Navickaitė points to Dimbelis and several other figures, including Vladimir Simonko and Eduardas Platovas, the founders of the Lithuanian Gay League, as exceptional for their willingness to come out publicly and campaign for LGBTQ rights.
“You could count such people on the fingers of one hand,” she said.
One of the more striking examples came in 1997, when LRT TV’s flagship news program, Panorama, reported on a symbolic wedding ceremony involving gay men at Vilnius Cathedral.
Obviously, the ceremony was not legally recognised. Its organisers sharply criticised the authorities, while Catholic clergy accused the television program’s staff of provoking a controversy.
For Navickaitė, the episode illustrates both how far Lithuania had come and how much remained unresolved.
Thirty years later
Lithuania has changed substantially since the early 1990s. LGBTQ people have become more visible in public life, organisations representing the community have grown and discussions about LGBTQ rights have become a regular part of political and social debate.
But some of the questions raised in the 1990s remain unresolved.
Navickaitė points to a more recent symbolic marriage between two men as an example. Like the ceremony reported in 1997, it had no legal effect.
“We recently had another symbolic marriage between two men, Albinas and Vitalius,” she said. “It seems that we are still ready only for symbolic marriages. Civil partnership has still not been regulated.”
She said she discusses the 1997 episode during tours and is struck by how close LGBTQ rights appeared to be at the time.
“It is sad that in 1997 it seemed that LGBTQ rights were already so close,” Navickaitė said. “But 30 years later, that issue is still seen by society as a provocation.”

Rogue AI targeted US government websites – tech giant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:59:09 UTC
13:59:09 KST

Rogue AI targeted US government websites – tech giant
American AI giant Anthropic has published a report detailing previously undisclosed instances of “unintended” actions by its artificial intelligence model, which included attempts to provide falsified information to the US authorities for the first time.
Some of the cases investigated by the company “involved websites run by US government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels,” Anthropic stated in a press release published on Friday, adding that it had briefed the White House and all the relevant agencies on the incidents.
In one instance mentioned in the report, its Claude Haiku 4.5 model filled out a police tip form linked to an ongoing homicide investigation. “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area,” the AI model wrote, telling the police they can contact the sender “if this information is relevant” while leaving the name and contact fields empty.
According to Anthropic, the message was flagged as spam and never handed over to investigators. On Friday, Philadelphia police slammed the company for detecting the flaw too late. “The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable,” they said. According to Reuters, the bogus tip was submitted in mid-July.
Anthropic linked the incident to “ambiguous” instructions given to the model and “a misconfiguration within the environment” that prompted the model to fill out real forms instead of dummy ones prepared by the company.
Another case that was separately made public by the US Department of State on Friday involved Anthropic AI models filing a total of 20 visa applications on its website between May and August. According to the department, all of the applications were incomplete and were not processed. “At no time were any of the Department’s systems compromised or hacked by the Anthropic model,” it added.
Other incidents mentioned by Anthropic in its report involved the AI “exploiting a basic flaw in software to run commands on a server” or accessing “data that was gated by a token or a fee,” including on the government-run websites, by employing various workarounds. The company still described the newly revealed incidents as “significantly less severe from an alignment and security perspective” than the ones it had reported earlier.
The development adds to a pile of earlier incidents linked to rogue AI behavior reported by Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. The tech giants have investigated tens of thousands of instances of problematic behavior by their frontier models, Axios reported in late September, adding that the list of cases involved the AI bypassing safeguards, hijacking websites, and evading monitors in testing and real-world settings.

BERLIN, October 11. /TASS/. Representatives of five political parties and public groups from the German federal state of Brandenburg will visit Belarus from November 6 to 11 and Russia in April to restore inter-municipal and twin-city ties severed at Berlin’s initiative, Sven Hornauf, a Brandenburg Landtag member from the BSW party, who organizes the trip, said.
"We are going to Belarus from November 6 to 11, 2026, and to Russia - presumably in the first week of April. Initially, we wanted to combine these trips, but due to the scale of the countries and the organizational requirements, we decided to split them. Especially since we have four partner cities in Belarus, and ten in Russia," Hornauf told TASS.
According to him, the main goal of the trip is to send a signal.
"We want to restore the contacts and partnerships that were artificially severed at the initiative of the German government. Through these two trips, representatives of all the cities and districts in Brandenburg that have twinning ties will be able to resume these contacts simultaneously," he said.
"We strive to ensure that people from these two or three countries could again meet in person - without the obstacles created by ‘big politics’ (at least on the German side) and to interact at all levels, as is customary among friends and partners: in the spheres of art, culture, sports, the church, and so on," Hornauf continued. He said that representatives of the five different political parties, as well as a wide variety of social groups (orchestra musicians, theatre professionals, firefighters, clergy, athletes, municipal and state politicians), would take part in the November trip.
"At the same time, we want to send a signal in favor of further mutual understanding between our countries and peoples. We openly declare that we consider the severance of contacts, the embargo, and the hostility on the part of the [German] government to be mistaken steps. Attempts to drive a wedge between our countries and peoples are artificial and do not serve the interests of our citizens," Hornauf said.
The visit program, he noted, is currently under coordination. It is expected that the German delegation will meet with the leadership of municipalities, as well as with representatives of the departments overseeing issues related to culture, sports, and inter-church dialogue. On November 7 in Minsk, the German representatives intend to take part in the ceremonial events marking Belarus’s national holiday.

Coalition defends migration cuts on economic grounds, rejects One Nation-style bans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:37:34 UTC
13:37:34 KST

In Brief
- Coalition says cutting migration to 100,000 would lift productivity by prioritising higher-skilled workers.
- Taylor rejected One Nation-style country bans, saying migrants should be judged on conduct and character.
Opposition leader Angus Taylor has defended the Coalition's proposed migration overhaul as an economic reform designed to boost productivity, while rejecting the idea of banning migrants based on their country of origin.
The Coalition's plan would cut net overseas migration (NOM) to 100,000, about a third of current levels, while increasing the share of "high-value" migrants entering Australia.
They have called it the "biggest cut to immigration in Australian history".
However, Taylor's comments to ABC's Insiders on Sunday also appeared to mark a shift in tone from his last appearance on the show.
This time, he repeatedly framed the changes as an economic measure aimed at boosting productivity and competitiveness, rather than focusing on national security or cultural concerns.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Taylor highlights migration plan as economic reform
Taylor argued Australia's migration system should be focused on attracting workers with skills that increase productivity, rather than relying on population growth to drive economic activity.
"We are reducing the numbers and raising the standards," Taylor said.
"Because we are raising the standards, raising the incomes and tax paid of people coming into this country, that can be budget-neutral.
"It will raise productivity, it will raise competitiveness, it will raise the average income of the people coming into this city."
Taylor said the policy would increase the average skill level of migrants entering Australia while reducing overall numbers through changes to a range of visa programs, including student, graduate and bridging visas.
He repeatedly argued migration settings should be geared towards lifting productivity rather than simply increasing population growth.
"What's happening under Labor is they are driving economic growth through population growth alone," he said.
Bringing in more highly skilled migrants would put downward pressure on inflation because it would raise productivity, Taylor argued, saying "this is pretty simple economics".
"When you bring someone to Australia, you are bringing demand and supply. If that person is low-skilled, you are bringing more demand than supply. If they are high-skilled, you are bringing the opposite, actually bringing more supply.
"One of the reasons why we've had a collapse in productivity in this country ... is that our immigration program has not been working to drive up our productivity and it should be."
He also defended the Coalition's proposal to halve Australia's humanitarian intake to 10,000 places, saying "charity begins at home" and such measures were designed to "balance the budget".
Taylor distances Coalition from One Nation approach
While much of Taylor's defence of the policy focused on economics, he also sought to draw a distinction between the Coalition's approach and proposals advanced by One Nation.
The comments marked a different emphasis from Taylor's previous appearance on the same program in April, when he argued migrants from "bad countries" posed a higher risk to Australia.
Pressed at the time on which countries he considered "bad", Taylor pointed to Iran and referred to security concerns involving people arriving from Gaza.
Asked on Sunday why the Coalition had not gone as far as One Nation in proposing immigration restrictions based on nationality, Taylor rejected the comparison.
"I've always said we will discriminate not based on the country someone comes from or their race or their religion, but based on the person and whether that person is a suitable person to be a resident or citizen of this country," he said.
"That's what we should focus on, and we should judge people on their character and conduct, not the colour of their skin."
Taylor maintained that some countries could present higher risks for security agencies to assess.
"It is true that risks are higher where there is a bad regime — there is no question about that."
"That doesn't mean screen them all out. That means make sure you are assessing those risks appropriately."
One Nation has previously proposed measures targeting migration from specific countries, including pausing new migration from countries subject to a federal government 'do not travel' warning.
However, Taylor also linked the Coalition's migration policy to a broader focus on screening prospective visa holders.
"People who do not believe in our system of law, people who do not believe in our basic freedoms, they shouldn't be coming to this country," he said.
"If they've got here on a visa, they should be thrown out."
Later on Sunday, other Coalition figures reiterated those sentiments, following reports that the flydubai co-pilot accused of attempting to hijack a flight bound for Israel was allegedly radicalised while studying in Melbourne.
Opposition home affairs spokesperson Jonno Duniam said there was no place for "hate preachers who spread extremism, glorify terrorism or encourage violence".
"That is why the Coalition will tighten visa laws to keep those who preach hatred out of Australia and deport non-citizens who promote violent extremism," he said.
“At a federal level, we also need stronger visa screening, better intelligence sharing and properly resourced counter-terrorism agencies. That is why the Coalition has committed to establishing an Enhanced Screening Coordination Centre to bring together our intelligence, policing and border protection capabilities."
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Australia had its toughest-ever powers to prevent violent extremists entering the country.
"I've been using them to be able to scan and assess whether someone has a history of being a problem before we give them a visa, and we've been cancelling visas when people are here, and we've been stopping people from coming here in the first place," he told News24 on Sunday.
The economic debate over immigration levels
Taylor's argument rests on the idea that a smaller, more highly skilled migration intake would boost productivity while reducing pressure on housing and infrastructure.
However, the economic impacts of migration cuts remain heavily debated among economists, migration experts, business groups and policymakers.
Critics argue lower migration can reduce labour supply, tax and visa revenue, population growth, consumer spending and business activity, particularly in industries that rely heavily on migrant workers.
A 2021 Treasury paper estimated each skilled migrant provides a $198,000 benefit to the Australian economy because they generally arrive in the country after finishing their education.
The average Australian costs the budget $85,000 across their lifetime because they receive more money back in services than they pay in taxes.
Debate over migration's impact on housing has also intensified in recent years. While higher migration can increase demand for homes, some experts argue migrant workers are also needed to address labour shortages in the construction sector.
In September, Burke said migration cuts would inevitably come with economic trade-offs and warned no industry would be immune from their effects.
"No matter what you do, if you are lowering (immigration) numbers, there are challenges across the visa system and across the Australian economy," he told SBS News.
"I can't quarantine any sector of Australia. What I can do is make sure — as numbers are lowered, and they need to be lowered because of the challenges we have with housing supply — I want the rest of the economy to have the softest landing possible."
Labor plans to cut NOM down to 225,000 by 2028, focusing heavily on "visa hopping", international students, backpackers, and bridging visas.
One Nation plans to cap visas at 130,000 per year, which they say will ease pressure on housing, wages, and infrastructure.

The restrictions also extend to social media. Soldiers are prohibited from expressing political positions on any platform, including liking, commenting on, sharing or distributing posts by political parties or politicians. What is permitted? Soldiers may publicly follow the accounts of candidates or political parties solely to stay informed. Attendance at political gatherings or campaign events is also subject to strict conditions: soldiers may attend only as spectators, must wear civilian clothing and may not identify themselves as military personnel.
Reservists who are not on active duty are exempt from these restrictions on political expression and may voice political opinions online, provided they do not use military uniforms or IDF insignia.
How will I know when and where to vote?
Military polling stations will operate on Election Day from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. Each unit will appoint an election officer responsible for informing soldiers of their polling station's exact location and operating hours.
Fixed polling stations will be established at military bases and facilities, while mobile stations will travel between troops stationed at military outposts, protecting communities, participating in training exercises or carrying out operational missions. Military polling stations will also operate in hospitals so that hospitalized soldiers registered with the IDF's medical liaison system, known as Ram 2, can vote.
Soldiers may vote at any military base where they are present on Election Day, even if it is not their permanent base. They may also choose to vote at a civilian polling station, provided they cast only one ballot. Voting more than once is a criminal offense.
How does identification work at military polling stations? 
Each military polling station will have an election committee consisting of two soldiers who will undergo training before Election Day and will be responsible for verifying voters' identities using military identification or valid civilian documents.
Active-duty soldiers may identify themselves using a military ID card, national identity card, valid driver's license bearing their photograph or valid Israeli passport accompanied by proof of military service. There is no need to bring the voter notification received by mail.
For combat troops operating beyond enemy lines without identification documents, including those deployed in Lebanon, identity verification may be carried out using military dog tags, identification by another soldier or a photographed copy of an identity document, such as a national ID card, driver's license or military ID.
At hospital polling stations, soldiers must present a military identification card bearing their photograph, whether as an enlisted soldier, officer or noncommissioned officer. Alternatively, they may present a civilian photo ID, such as a national identity card, driver's license or valid Israeli passport, together with a voting authorization form issued by hospital staff.
How does voting work?
Military voting uses a double-envelope system. Behind a privacy screen, soldiers place their chosen party's ballot slip inside a blue envelope. That envelope is then placed inside a white envelope bearing the soldier's personal details.
How are ballot secrecy and election integrity protected? 
At the end of voting, military ballot boxes will be transferred, locked, to the Central Elections Committee at the Knesset in Jerusalem for counting. The sealed ballot boxes will be collected by designated personnel trained as regional election officers and remain under their supervision until formally handed over at the Knesset.
How are the votes counted?
During the counting process, the blue envelope containing the ballot is separated for counting, while the white envelope bearing the soldier's personal information is destroyed. The entire process of opening ballot boxes and counting votes is conducted by the Central Elections Committee without IDF involvement.
When does early voting begin in the IDF? 
Combat soldiers deployed in operational areas and beyond enemy lines, including Gaza, Syria and Lebanon, will be eligible to vote beginning at 10 p.m. on October 20. Mobile polling stations will reach troops in the field to collect their ballots. Soldiers scheduled to participate in operational missions on Election Day will also be given the opportunity to vote in advance.
Can soldiers run for office or join political parties?
Soldiers are permitted to register as members of political parties, provided they do not identify themselves as military personnel. Senior civilian employees of the IDF and career military personnel may run as party candidates only if they terminate their military service at least 100 days before the election. Conscripts must arrange a deferment of military service at least 100 days before Election Day, while reservists on active duty must end their service at least 30 days before the election.
Can soldiers work at polling stations? 
Soldiers may work at civilian polling stations on Election Day in politically neutral roles, including election committee secretary, usher or election integrity inspector, provided they obtain their commander's approval. They may not serve as election committee members, party observers or employees of political parties.
Is photography allowed? 
As at civilian polling stations, photography is strictly prohibited inside military polling stations.
Do soldiers get Election Day off? 
Unlike civilians, IDF personnel are not entitled to a day off for the election. Military operations and routine activities will continue as usual.

US opens antitrust probe into TV networks halting Trump coverage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:30:10 UTC
13:30:10 KST

US opens antitrust probe into TV networks for halting Trump coverage
Department of Justice says it’s investigating whether the White House press pool’s decision violated antitrust laws.
The United States Department of Justice has opened an investigation into television networks’ decision to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month.
A spokesperson said on Saturday that the department was investigating whether the networks violated federal antitrust laws by their boycott, which followed a White House decision to pull the credentials of reporters from three news organisations, including CNN.
The networks under investigation are ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News, said Emily Convington, the Justice Department spokesperson.
“Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act,” she said of the antitrust legislation.
“The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”
The investigation is the latest in a series of clashes between the Trump administration and major news organisations. Trump has repeatedly called the mainstream media “fake news” and frequently clashes with reporters during encounters with the press.
The action also puts legal and potentially financial pressure on the media to continue coverage of the president even when they disagree with how the White House handles them.
The networks did not immediately comment on the announcement.
The Justice Department’s move came after the television pool of five broadcasters last month ceased presidential coverage after the administration barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
The White House said on September 19 that covering the president was a “privilege – not a right”. The outlets sued the administration, alleging the exclusions violated the First Amendment and that the White House was retaliating over their coverage.
CNN is one of the five news organisations – along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – that make up the primary White House television pool.
They share the costs of covering the president, take turns organising coverage, and share the footage with outlets around the country.
All of the five television networks that cover the White House, including Fox News, suspended coverage in solidarity and refused to provide replacement coverage.
The White House reinstated the credentials on September 24 after US District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the ban was likely unconstitutional and ordered the administration to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” their access.
However, disputes over access to specific presidential events and pool assignments continued.
Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists’ Americas director, on Saturday criticised the administration’s decision to investigate.
“The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access,” Zamora said on X. “The public’s right to know depends on that access.”

One year after ceasefire, Gaza’s promised ‘day after’ has yet to arrive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:23:51 UTC
13:23:51 KST

One year after the ceasefire took effect in the Gaza Strip, all the Israeli captives have been returned, but much of what the agreement promised the Palestinians remains unrealized.
Israeli attacks have continued, the military withdrawal has stalled and partly reversed, governance arrangements remain incomplete, and large-scale reconstruction has yet to begin.
Most of Gaza’s roughly 2.1 million people remain displaced, many living in tents, damaged buildings, or amid rubble, as Palestinian authorities say the continuing attacks are an extension of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, launched on Oct. 8, 2023.
The ceasefire took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, after mediation by Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, and the US providing for a phased Israeli withdrawal, expanded aid, new governance arrangements, and reconstruction.
Israeli captives returned
On Oct. 13, 2025, Hamas released the remaining 20 living Israeli captives as Israel freed 1,968 Palestinian detainees, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross.
The transfer of remains continued until Jan. 26, 2026, when the Israeli army announced the recovery of the last body.
Israeli attacks continue
But the ceasefire did not bring an end to Israeli attacks in Gaza.
Over the past year, Israeli violations of the agreement have killed more than 1,470 Palestinians and wounded over 5,180, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Egypt, Qatar, and Türkiye said in August that continued Israeli attacks violated the agreement and were obstructing implementation of its second phase.
Israeli withdrawal reversed
Before the ceasefire was declared, the Israeli army controlled about 75% of Gaza.
The agreement initially brought a partial withdrawal to the so-called “yellow line,” leaving around 53% of the enclave under Israeli military deployment, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
But the pullback stalled and later reversed.
By late June, OCHA said Israeli forces had expanded westward beyond the yellow line, leaving 64.9% of Gaza under direct Israeli control or tighter restrictions.
By August, the UN said nearly two-thirds of the enclave was inaccessible to Palestinians or subject to severe restrictions.
Second phase remains stalled
A 15-point roadmap linked restrictions on the weapons of Hamas and other Palestinian factions to additional Israeli withdrawals, deployment of an international force, transfer of governance, and reconstruction.
Egypt, Qatar, and Türkiye said on Aug. 3 that Hamas and other Palestinian factions had accepted the roadmap, including its provision on weapons.
Later that month, eight countries, including Türkiye, Egypt, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia, said Israel had rejected the roadmap, obstructing implementation of the broader plan.
Governance transition incomplete
A technocratic National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, headed by Ali Shaath, was formed in January to oversee civilian affairs during the transitional period.
But the transfer of governing responsibilities remains incomplete, while a planned international stabilization force has yet to be deployed.
Reconstruction still out of reach
Despite provisions to increase humanitarian aid, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said in September that Kerem Shalom remained the only operational crossing for goods after the Zikim crossing was closed in May.
Israeli restrictions also continued on materials needed for shelter and construction.
The UN, European Union, and World Bank estimate Gaza will need $71.4 billion over 10 years for recovery and reconstruction, including $26.3 billion in the first 18 months.
Their assessment found that 1.9 million Palestinians had been displaced and 371,888 housing units damaged or destroyed.
OCHA said in September that Israeli restrictions were still blocking urgently needed shelter supplies, including thousands of tents and construction materials.
One year after the ceasefire, the issue of the captives is closed. For Gaza’s displaced population, however, the promised transition from war to recovery has yet to arrive.
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Israeli attacks on Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed, according to Palestinian figures.

Russell took the lead but lost control of his Mercedes in the final corner of the opening lap after running wide, according to BBC Sport.

Anthony Gordon opened the scoring two minutes in, cutting inside past two defenders before firing a shot that deflected off Mario Martin and into the net. It was Gordon's first goal for Barcelona.
The hosts dominated possession and created several chances with Dani Olmo, Gavi, and Eric Garcia. Getafe goalkeeper David Soria made several saves.

US Justice Department probes major TV networks for suspension of Trump pool coverage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:05:56 UTC
13:05:56 KST

Esra Tekin
11 October 2026•Update: 11 October 2026
The US Justice Department on Saturday launched an antitrust investigation into five major television networks after they temporarily refused to provide pool coverage of President Donald Trump, NBC News reported.
The probe targets NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN, and Fox News, which collectively make up the White House television press pool, and take turns covering the president’s public engagements and trips. They suspended pool participation last month after three major outlets – CNN, MS NOW, and website Politico – were all banned from the White House.
A Justice Department official confirmed that the five networks were issued “civil investigative demands” on Friday as part of the investigation.
“Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act,” said department spokeswoman Emily Covington.
“The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”
In the pool, the network assigned to pool duty shares its reporting materials, including video and audio recordings, with other news organizations.
When contacted for comment on the investigation, the White House did not provide a response.
ABC News said it had yet to receive a formal notice from the Justice Department but anticipated receiving one. NBC, CBS, and CNN declined to comment, while Fox News did not respond to a request for comment.
The investigation comes amid growing tensions between the Trump administration and the White House press corps.
In September, Trump accused journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico of spreading “FAKE NEWS” and barred their outlets from the White House grounds. The three later filed a legal challenge to the ban which is still playing out in court.
Following CNN’s removal from the pool rotation, the remaining television networks temporarily withdrew from their coverage assignments.

Unsung turtle conservation heroes in Malaysia’s Sabah unite to fight poachers
A group of volunteers is helping to stem the illegal trade of protected turtles by monitoring the movements of poachers
Roziah Jelali has a tip or two on catching a turtle poacher: carrying a pair of binoculars and having patience in spades are key to doing the job well.
The 36-year-old Malaysian volunteer ranger once spent three months in Sabah tracking a man whom she suspected of illegally capturing protected turtles. Once thriving off the azure seas of Omadal Island in the Malaysian state, many turtles had been hunted down, killed and sold for their meat, according to conservation experts.
Recounting the 2023 incident, Roziah said she patrolled the beach from dawn daily to keep an eye on the poacher. She would scribble detailed notes on her target’s movements at her stilted home, backed by tips from her network of part-time conservationists on nearby islands.
“Every day after my patrol, I would sit near my house with my binoculars and watch him. He was initially operating on Bum Bum Island, then he came to Omadal,” Roziah told This Week in Asia.

Admission scores for physiotherapy degree programmes at three Hong Kong tertiary institutions fell by as much as 10 per cent this year compared with 2025, amid gloomy career prospects in the sector, the latest data shows.

The denuclearisation of North Korea has become an “increasingly improbable” goal and the United States and its allies should move beyond it to devote their diplomatic efforts to talks on arms limitations and crisis communication, the director of the US-based North Korean analysis website 38 North said.
Recalling the 20 years since North Korea carried out its first nuclear test on October 9, 2006, Jenny Town said in a written interview that “a pivotal moment” in Pyongyang’s weapons development came in 2017 when the country’s first test-firing of an intercontinental ballistic missile took place.

‘I get really upset when I visit’: the harsh reality of life in a high-security hospital in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:00:16 UTC
13:00:16 KST

Rampton high-security hospital in Nottinghamshire was built in 1912. Everything about the bleak, remote facility for mentally ill people is forbidding, says Jan Neate. “I get really upset going there,” she says. “Even though I really want to see Jake, visiting is an ordeal.”
Jake, 45, is Neate’s son. He has been held at Rampton for eight years. In 2017, many years after being diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, he killed his partner, Suzanne Brown, and was deemed mentally unfit to stand trial.
When Neate visits him, her fingerprints and biometrics are taken before she is escorted in. Jake is searched when he is brought into the room and searched again when he leaves. Mother and son are permitted a hug, which is often distressing. “Both of us usually cry when we hug,” says Neate. “It reminds me of what our lives were like before and I think it reminds Jake of that, too.”
England has three high-security hospitals – Rampton, Ashworth in Merseyside and Broadmoor in Berkshire. According to the NHS trust that manages Rampton, secure hospitals are for people with severe mental health disorders who pose grave or immediate danger to themselves or to the public. They have accommodated some of the country’s most abhorred criminals, including Peter Sutcliffe, Ronnie Kray, Ian Brady, Ian Huntley and Beverley Allitt. Valdo Calocane, who was convicted of killing three people in 2023 and diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, has spent time in Rampton.
These high-security hospitals have been in the spotlight this year, after it was reported that Axel Rudakubana – who murdered three young girls at a dance class in Southport in 2024 – had been moved from Belmarsh, a category A high-security prison, to Broadmoor, which has security equivalent to a category B prison. Officials said the move was due to the deterioration of his mental health and the fact he could no longer be safely managed in prison. The plan is to return Rudakubana to Belmarsh after treatment.
Throughout its history, Broadmoor has had a reputation for being tough, even menacing, given the notoriety of various people housed within its walls. Nonetheless, some saw this move as the start of a “cushier” life for Rudakubana and an attempt by him to manipulate the system. Mark Fairhurst, the chair of the Prison Officers’ Association, said the move would afford him freedoms not available in a high-security prison.
Relatives of those incarcerated in high-security hospitals are usually unwilling to speak out because of the understandable stigma attached to the violent acts committed by those inside. But while Jake did something terrible, Neate is keen for people to understand the reality of this form of incarceration.
What happens inside high-security hospitals raises important questions about how we treat people who have committed extreme violence but who are also vulnerable themselves. These are difficult, emotive questions about mental health, retribution and rehabilitation.
Jake is sometimes placed in a form of segregation known as seclusion; Neate knows of at least two periods of seclusion so far this year. In both cases, she believes the seclusion lasted several days. She is given very little information about what happens to him during these periods, which she says is terrifying: “I dread the phone ringing one day and staff telling me that something terrible has happened to him.”
If Jake refuses his medication, his doctors have permission to administer it via injection.
He has been having seizures and injuring himself. “On one occasion, he fell and injured his shoulder when he was having a seizure,” says Neate. “On another occasion, also when he was thought to be having a seizure, he fell and injured his head.”
Jake was taken to an ordinary hospital after receiving these injuries, but Neate wasn’t given any information about where he was. Whenever she calls Rampton, to see how Jake is, she gets the briefest of replies – confirmation that he is eating, drinking and sleeping, but nothing else. “Anyone who thinks Rampton is an easy option for someone like Jake really doesn’t understand how things are,” she says.
Inspections of Rampton carried out by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) between July 2019 and June 2023 identified a number of failings, including a shortage of staff. Some therapy staff were used on wards to plug the gaps, leading to a reduction in patients’ therapeutic programmes. Concerns were also raised about overnight lock-ups in patients’ rooms being extended due to staff shortages, along with periods of “confinement” during the day. Poor medicine management was identified and there were repeated issues with the safeguarding of patients.
A focused review of Rampton by the CQC in March 2024 said staffing levels had improved and the use of confinement had decreased, but there remained a “culture of relying on therapy and education staff to cover nursing gaps”. While medicine management had also improved, staff did not always follow the correct procedure, “which could constitute an assault and trespass against the person”. The review added: “While we observed staff providing person-centred care, we remain concerned that people in long-term segregation were not always treated with dignity, compassion and respect.”
In a May 2025 CQC report, the hospital had its rating upgraded from “inadequate” to “requires improvement”. It was found that the trust still had work to do to address staff shortages and to support staff.
As a boy, Jake was happy and playful, says Neate: “We went on loads of outings like swimming, football and visits to museums. He was a really nice boy.” When he was 17, he started to get ill. “He became paranoid and was admitted to hospital for two weeks as a voluntary patient. The doctors said if he stopped smoking skunk, he would recover.”
He went on to study geography at the University of Birmingham, but left when he was headhunted by a bank in Canary Wharf, London. Then, at 20, he was diagnosed with schizophrenia. He had to leave his job, but he built up a window-cleaning round where he lived in Essex and he was popular with his customers. To treat his schizophrenia, he was put on the drug clozapine and he gave up recreational drugs, living successfully in the community. At that point, says Neate, Jake had an illness, but he also had a life.
In 2007, Jake and Suzanne met at a disco in Harlow. “He was 26 and she was 23,” says Neate. Suzanne, who was known as Sue, worked as a nursery nurse. “Sue had such a sweet, kind nature. Whenever she came to my house, she would always bring a homemade cake with her. She really looked after Jake, made sure he took his medication and went to all his appointments with him. She was a very giving person. I miss her.”
At this stage, “Jake had dreams and ambitions and he loved Sue to pieces”, says Neate. “His schizophrenia then was nothing like it is now. He was never violent. I don’t think he and Sue even argued with each other.” When they bought their first flat together, in Braintree, they had a new kitchen fitted and were full of plans for the future.
Jake had received excellent care and support from the NHS mental health trust in Harlow, but their move meant Jake’s care was transferred to a new trust. For 10 years, clozapine had kept him stable. But in 2017, after he started to experience physical side-effects – severe constipation, urine retention and an inability to eat or sleep – the drug was stopped suddenly.
Withdrawal from clozapine is supposed to be closely monitored, but Jake, Sue and Neate were unaware of this. “None of us had any idea what could happen as a result of him being taken off clozapine,” says Neate. “Sue and Jake really trusted their clinical team. I thought that the worst that might happen would be that Jake might have a row with Sue. I had no concept of the gravity and severity of it all. It’s a heavy-duty drug and taking him off it should have been treated as a medical emergency.”
Jake began to experience psychosis and repeatedly tried to seek help, but little was forthcoming. Jake wrote to his doctors, listing the symptoms he was experiencing after being taken off clozapine, but he didn’t receive a response. Neate says she made dozens of phone calls and sent numerous emails during this period, trying to get help for Jake, but this didn’t result in any interventions. She believes that, had there been effective responses to the pleas she, Sue and Jake were making, the horror that followed could have been avoided.
In texts to his mother in this period, Jake said he had been researching private hospitals. “I feel a bit angry that no one told me of the implications of going on to this drug,” he wrote. “I would like to be an inpatient to deal with all the issues.”
His condition worsened. On 15 December 2017, a mental health worker visited the couple’s flat and said telephone support would be put in place and a home visit organised for the following week. That evening, Neate received a call from Sue, “screaming and hysterical”. She said Jake was hurting her. Neate told her to get out of the flat and immediately called the police.
Three hours after that call, police officers arrived at the flat. By then, it was far too late. Jake had stabbed Suzanne 173 times.
Neate says she didn’t understand the severity of what was happening until the police called her and said: “‘We’ve taken the dead woman from the flat.’ All I could say was: ‘Oh my God, what do you mean?’ … I am always asking myself if I could have prevented this happening if I had been close by.”
Jake was initially charged with murder, but was found to be unfit to stand trial. He said he had been hearing voices coming out of the TV urging him to kill Sue and was having terrible thoughts about God, the devil and the battle between good and evil.
When a person is deemed mentally unfit to stand trial, a trial of the facts takes place. Rather than deciding on a defendant’s criminal guilt or innocence, this determines whether the defendant carried out the alleged acts. The trial found that Jake had killed Sue. The jury heard that Sue was devoted to Jake and that she had looked after him when he was unwell with “the patience of a saint”.
“I miss Sue so much,” says Neate. “I miss her lovely sunny nature … We used to go on outings together, to spas and to the cinema. I feel so lonely. I don’t have Jake as he was and I don’t have Sue. Jake was a perpetrator, but I believe he was also a victim of the system.”
A report on mental health services after Sue’s killing identified eight failings and made seven recommendations for change. It found that an up-to-date risk assessment was not carried out after the sudden cessation of clozapine and that there was neither appropriate professional monitoring nor guidance for Jake and his family. It also found that clinical information was not communicated consistently within and between teams.
An investigation for the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) found that the police response was delayed because it was initially miscategorised by the call handler. The IOPC did not identify any misconduct, but found that two members of staff in the control room “had not met expected standards”.
When Jake was sent to Rampton, it was supposed to be temporary. Neate was told that when he was more stable he could be moved to a medium-security unit with a less restrictive regime. Jake is held at Rampton on what is known as a section 37 order; the Home Office has to give permission for the release of those held under this type of indefinite hospital order.
In a letter to Neate on 28 July 2026, Jake’s doctor at Rampton wrote: “In recent years we have seen several episodes of decline in his condition, but overall he is making progress.” He also described Jake as having a serious mental health disorder that is “very resistant to treatment”.
A spokesperson for Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS foundation trust said: “While we cannot comment on the care of individual patients, we fully understand that families want the very best for their loved ones and we recognise how difficult it can be when progress feels slow. We always welcome families raising concerns with us and are committed to working with them openly.
“Decisions about moving a patient to a lower level of security are made carefully, taking account of their recovery and wellbeing alongside wider safety considerations. For many patients at Rampton these decisions also involve the Ministry of Justice and the receiving service, which can mean the process takes time.”
Neate firmly believes Jake is deteriorating at Rampton. “Jake says he is fighting a battle between good and evil and says he has to rescue Sue,” she says. “He isn’t the same person he used to be … I don’t think he’s always treated as a human being, as a person. Everything is so clinical there. They talk about his presentation, as if he’s a thing, rather than a human with a heart.
“I feel like I’m banging my head against a wall trying to help him. All I want for Jake is a life that’s reasonable, with some hope in it. People who are mentally ill are entitled to a bit of care. But I don’t believe Jake’s getting that. It’s not at all cushy or luxurious for him in Rampton, very far from it.”

Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:00:15 UTC
13:00:15 KST

Developing countries face a triple shock from the energy crisis, El Niño and surging borrowing costs and need urgent support from the international community, the UN’s development arm has warned.
Speaking before the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, the UNDP’s administrator, Alexander De Croo, called for “solidarity and global action”.
“Developing countries, their hands and legs are being pulled in different directions: it’s truly hard for them,” he said.
Before the meetings, the UNDP published a report, No Time to Recover, which lays out the risks of what it calls the “compounding crises” of energy, climate and debt.
Oil prices have been driven back above $100 a barrel in recent weeks since hostilities resumed in the Middle East.
The report says that since the Iran war broke out earlier this year, up to 130 million of the world’s poorest people have been shielded from the full impact of high prices by emergency government measures.
But it warns many of them are now at risk, as governments run out of the resources needed to keep cushioning their populations against soaring costs.
“What we see now is that countries are pivoting their policy and letting the price hikes flow through. They’re pivoting the policy because they have no choice, because their fiscal space is completely eaten up,” De Croo said.
“We are witnessing a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty.”
Meanwhile, the worst El Niño climate pattern in perhaps 1,000 years is expected to cause widespread crop failures and increase the risk of extreme weather events, while at the same time the global bond sell-off is driving up government borrowing costs.
De Croo said: “The cost today for bond financing for developing countries, it’s 9%. That is really, really high.”
He added that the situation was expected to deteriorate between now and the spring. “For each of the three things that we mentioned – fuel prices, El Niño and the bond markets – unfortunately for each of those at the moment, we don’t see any light at the end of the tunnel.”
His warning chimes with the findings of separate research published on Sunday by the campaign group Debt Justice, underlining the social impact of high debt servicing costs.
It shows that low-income countries classified by the IMF as either in, or at risk of, debt distress have cut their education budgets by an average of 8% since 2019, and wider public spending by 2%.
Heidi Chow, the executive director of Debt Justice, said: “High levels of debt are having a devastating impact on people’s access to healthcare and education.”
Debt Justice is calling for the outright cancellation of some of the most burdensome debts, and overhaul of the IMF-administered common framework for debt restructuring.
Chow said: “We urgently need debt cancellation – especially from the highest interest lenders like banks, hedge funds and oil traders.”
De Croo said the UNDP did not oppose efforts to secure debt relief for some of the hardest-hit countries – but argued it would take many months to negotiate, and instead called for more urgent action.
“We urge the international community – multilateral lenders, donors, and partners – to step up access to affordable finance so countries can sustain support for their most vulnerable households,” De Croo said.
He praised the IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva’s recent call for spending restraint in developed countries, in the hope of taming bond yields.
But he said: “We also need to have a coordinated policy for developing countries. And that coordinated policy for developing countries cannot just be, ‘you are at the end of the line and we’ll see what happens’.”
He declined to say what the specific response should be, but stressed that it should create “time and space” for developing countries to carry out much-needed changes.
During the Covid crisis, G20 nations implemented a temporary standstill on debt repayments for developing countries.
De Croo also pointed to liquidity measures available to central banks, such as the currency swap lines implemented by the US Federal Reserve during recent financial crises, to prevent markets seizing up. “What would help is a certain level of liquidity,” he said.
