Awarding the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay has drawn sharp criticism from both Israel and the US.
Pillay was given the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize “for her efforts to promote peace and international law,” according to the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
She previously served as a UN high commissioner for human rights and as a judge at the International Criminal Court, and later chaired a UN commission of inquiry concerning Israel and the Palestinian territories.
Nobel Committee's decision draws sharp criticism
The Norwegian Nobel Committee noted that this body, officially called the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including east Jerusalem, has drawn sharp criticism from Israel.
As part of this commission, Pillay’s report found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee said that she held states and national leaders accountable, brought hope to victims of violence and conflict, and demonstrated a firm moral compass throughout her long career.
“A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time,” the committee said.
Netanyahu responded to the decision by calling Pillay a “bigot” and the prize committee “misguided.”
“The Nobel Prize committee has lost its moral compass,” the Prime Minister’s Office wrote on X/Twitter. “It has awarded its highest honor to a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the only Jewish state.”
Pillay’s “proudest achievement was to legitimize a corrupt prosecutor who turned to her fabrications against Israel, hoping that by joining her bigoted lynch mob, [ICC prosecutor Karim Khan] would beat a rape charge,” the post went on to say.
“Khan, who his own ICC employees accused of raping and sexually molesting them, used Pillay’s lies to build a fake case against Israel,” the Prime Minister’s Office continued.
“Now, the misguided members of the Nobel committee are honoring the woman who propagated this demonization of the Jews and this travesty of justice,” it said.
Israel accuses Pillay of promoting hatred and lies
The Foreign Ministry also condemned the decision, accusing Pillay of promoting lies, hatred, and blood libels against Israel.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a front-runner,” the ministry said, describing her report findings as part of a politically motivated campaign to demonize the Jewish state.
Further, the Foreign Ministry rejected Pillay’s genocide allegations, calling them “the biggest lie of the 21st century,” adding, “[Nazi propagandist] Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
Trump responds:'I've never heard of that person'
US President Donald Trump slammed the Norwegian Nobel Committee on Friday in remarks of his own, saying that the prize should have gone to the US, and effectively, to him.
“Despite ... [America’s] unbelievable accomplishments, the Nobel Prize was given out today to a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of. I’ve never heard of that person,” Trump said during a campaign rally in Syracuse, New York.
“I know a lot of people. I’ve never heard of this particular person, but congratulations anyway,” he added.Trump then said that the UN had played no role in the conflicts he helped resolve.
“In all of the wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations. They were of no help to me,” Trump said. “The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t.”
Norway, where the Nobel Peace Prize committee is based, was also mentioned in the US president’s remarks on the subject.
“This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people who made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump said.
“The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really, enemies of civilization. And we will not forget Norway,” he said.
US imposes sanctions on ICC
Hours after the Nobel announcement, Trump’s administration imposed sanctions on the ICC on Friday, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies. ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan condemned the sanctions, saying they would not halt the tribunal’s work.
The Trump administration has long been hostile toward the court founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide. In the past, the Trump administration has imposed sanctions on ICC prosecutors and judges. Friday’s move would go far further, by potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.
“President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” US State Secretary Marco Rubio said in a statement, first published by Reuters.
“That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off its resources and crippling its ability to operate,” Rubio said.
The ICC deputy prosecutor told Reuters the sanctions “must be condemned.”
“The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing,” Khan said. “Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations, and our prosecutions.”
The sanctions are “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do,” the ICC said in a statement.
“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” it said.
“The designation is aimed at disrupting the court’s operations and at intimidating those who work for or cooperate with the court. The court, for its part, will not be deterred ... Yet the court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it,” the ICC continued.
Washington has denounced the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Netanyahu, and a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC has since closed.
Netanyahu also commended Trump and Rubio for taking the “critical decision” to impose the sanctions in a post on X on Friday.
“The ICC is not a court,” he said. “It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty. Thank you for your leadership.”

====================================================================================================

Israel’s security partnerships must be built on reciprocity, not convenience - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
21:32:14 UTC
06:32:14 KST

Security alliances are not tested at signing ceremonies. They are tested when the missiles arrive. Peaceful relations are also tested when one partner must publicly stand beside the other.
An all too convenient pattern has emerged in the Middle East. Countries seek Israeli intelligence, technology and security assistance, but when the time comes to vote in the international arena, they find it remarkably easy to raise their hands against Israel.
A widening divide has emerged between cooperation behind closed doors and conduct in public. Israel can no longer accept this disparity as inevitable.
Saudi Arabia is a prime example of this contradiction. The Houthis threaten its infrastructure, trade routes, and position as the guardian of Islam’s holy sites. Abdul Malik al-Houthi is not merely issuing a military threat. By portraying his followers as more loyal to Mecca and the Kaaba than the kingdom’s rulers, he is challenging the religious legitimacy of the Saudi royal family.
Ceremonial declarations of support are not enough to confront such a threat. Saudi Arabia needs intelligence, early warning systems, and a genuine defensive capability.
The defense agreement Saudi Arabia signed with Turkey and Pakistan in August was intended to provide that security. The commitment to treat an attack against one country as an attack against all sounds impressive, but signatures do not intercept missiles.
Reuters reported that the countries’ military commanders met in Riyadh in September to deepen intelligence cooperation and military coordination. The meeting itself does not constitute a failure, but neither does it prove that the alliance is already capable of providing the protection it promised.
When danger approaches, Israel suddenly becomes a practical address. Israel Hayom reported that contacts mediated by US Central Command were taking place over possible Israeli intelligence assistance against the Houthis and the protection of strategic sites in Saudi Arabia.
This is where the absurdity becomes apparent. Israeli capabilities are highly desirable, yet publicly acknowledging Israel’s value remains something that can be postponed. The intelligence is requested now, while the diplomatic gesture is promised, if at all, for a future that never seems to arrive.
Israel should therefore be cautious about recurring reports that normalization with Saudi Arabia is merely a matter of time. A need for intelligence does not constitute recognition of Israel, and a secret meeting is not an embassy.
Shared interests may be bringing the countries closer, but there is no justification for turning every security discussion into a diplomatic celebration. As long as Riyadh seeks to benefit from cooperation without publicly acknowledging it, the road between Mecca and Jerusalem remains far longer than we are being told.
The problem, however, is not limited to countries that have yet to establish relations with Israel. Jordan and Egypt raise an even sharper question: What is the meaning of a peace agreement when practical cooperation exists alongside repeated opposition to Israel in diplomatic forums?
Peace does not require agreement with every Israeli action. It does, however, justify an expectation of fairness, a distinction between Israel and its enemies, and a willingness to occasionally depart from the chorus of automatic condemnations.
A peace agreement cannot remain a document invoked only when it is useful. When Israel is regarded as a necessary partner in matters of security and stability, that reality should also be reflected in diplomatic language and international voting.
Israel cannot be expected to show endless consideration for the domestic sensitivities of its neighbors while those same countries treat Israeli sensitivities and Israeli citizens as though they deserve no consideration at all.
A vote against Israel is not necessarily a vote against its very existence, and every resolution must be evaluated on its merits. That is precisely why Israel should demand independent judgment rather than automatic opposition.
Where is the willingness to reject a one-sided resolution? Where is the demand to mention the hostages, Iran’s threats to destroy Israel, and the actions of terrorist organizations? Friendship is also measured by the willingness to say uncomfortable things in a hostile forum. A partnership that exists only when convenient is a very limited partnership.
The Flydubai flight incident illustrated this divide in a troubling way. Four Israelis acted courageously to subdue the attacker and assist the wounded captain, helping to save the aircraft and its passengers.
The Indian captain and the crew members who helped land the plane deserve full recognition. The Israelis also deserve explicit and public acknowledgment. This is not a competition over heroism. It is a basic demand that the identities of those who risked their lives to save others not be obscured.
The plane landed in Saudi Arabia, and the passengers eventually returned to Israel on an alternative flight. However, Saudi authorities refused to authorize an Israeli rescue flight.
These passengers had endured a terrible trauma and wanted to return home. Yet even at that moment, the diplomatic barrier remained in place. Saudi Arabia permitted the aircraft to land and assisted in managing the emergency, but why could it not also allow an Israeli rescue flight?
If even a limited humanitarian gesture is met with refusal, what readiness for normalization are we talking about?
Israel's relation with the United Arab Emirates
The United Arab Emirates took an important diplomatic step by establishing relations with Israel. It should therefore also be expected to publicly recognize the Israelis who participated in the rescue.
Emirati authorities rightly praised the bravery of the Indian pilot, but not a single word was said about the four Israeli heroes who helped save the aircraft and everyone aboard it.
The achievements of the Abraham Accords create higher expectations of the Emirates. Saying “thank you” does not create a strategic risk, and recognizing Israeli heroism does not require surrendering a diplomatic position. A country capable of cooperating with Israel should also be capable of giving Israelis the respect they deserve.
Israel must draw practical conclusions. It need not end assistance that also serves its own security interests. But that assistance should not be provided out of habit, subservience, or a vague hope that one day someone will express gratitude.
Every form of cooperation should be evaluated against what Israel receives in return: protection for its citizens, humanitarian gestures, fair treatment in international institutions, and diplomatic progress.
Not every piece of intelligence requires an immediate concession in return. But a continuing relationship requires a clear balance of responsibility and reciprocity.
Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and other countries have their own interests and domestic pressures. Israel has interests and pressures of its own. It is not obligated to use its capabilities to finance the diplomatic comfort of countries that seek its assistance in secret while distancing themselves from it in public.
National dignity is not a substitute for strategic judgment, but strategic judgment is not a justification for erasing national dignity.
The time has come to raise this demand in the discussions themselves, attach measurable objectives to it, and monitor whether they are fulfilled. Vague promises of a better future are not adequate compensation for assistance provided today. The true test of a partnership is the willingness to accept responsibility.
Israel is not a mistress these countries can hide while seeking to enjoy the benefits of its intelligence and other capabilities. Anyone who wants Israel’s help must also be prepared to treat it with fairness, respect and reciprocity.

On September 29, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled his plan to combat antisemitism. He noted that Jews are about 12% of the city’s population but the victims of roughly half of its reported hate crimes. He promised a city where Jews would be “not only safe, but celebrated” and pledged more money for hate-crime prevention.
On October 7, the third anniversary of the worst single-day massacre of Jews since the Holocaust, he posted a statement that undid every word of it.
That post, viewed more than 13 million times, runs about 210 words. Roughly 50 concern October 7. Some 140 indict Israel: An “ongoing genocide in Gaza,” “occupation and apartheid,” food aid “turned away,” and “our tax dollars” funding “war crimes.” Hamas is named once and never again. By the end, Israel is the only perpetrator.
This is now how antisemites posing as mourners mark the date. Mamdani wrote that Hamas “killed more than 1,100 Israelis,” dropping the foreign workers from Thailand, Nepal, and elsewhere among the roughly 1,200 dead. His statement has no women raped at the Nova music festival, no children shot in front of their parents, no families burned alive in their safe rooms, no terrorist hacking the head off a body while another filmed it on a GoPro. It never mentions Kfir Bibas, abducted at nine months old and murdered in Gaza along with his four-year-old brother, Ariel, and their mother, Shiri. Hamas’s conduct over the next two years also goes unmentioned.
That conduct answers the question he dodges: who kept this war going? Brett McGurk, president Joe Biden’s lead hostage negotiator and no Benjamin Netanyahu partisan, served an administration that paused arms shipments to Israel. His new book describes Hamas lying about how many hostages it held, refusing to release the young women promised under the November 2023 deal, and sitting for weeks on an American offer that met most of its demands while six hostages – among them Hersh Goldberg-Polin, Carmel Gat, and Eden Yerushalmi – were murdered in a tunnel under Rafah. McGurk says the war would never have ended without the hostages coming home. Hamas spent two years bargaining over the living and the dead.
Mamdani’s numbers fare no better. His “more than 21,000 children” comes from Hamas’s health ministry, which in March 2025 quietly dropped some 3,400 “fully identified” deaths from its lists, 1,080 of them children. His “more than 1,400 Palestinians” killed since the ceasefire includes at least 420 Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad terrorists and ignores the dozens of Gazans Hamas executed in the streets to reassert control. As for food aid “turned away,” a UNICEF-coordinated survey in July put acute malnutrition in Gaza at 0.2% to 0.8%, at or below prewar levels and far under the global child-wasting rate of nearly 7%. Gazans have described Hamas seizing aid in the war it started and reselling it to them at black-market prices.
Mamdani blames every destroyed building on Israel, too. Hamas dug some 600 kilometers of tunnels beneath Gaza’s homes, schools and hospitals and let no civilian shelter in them. Senior official Mousa Abu Marzouk said in October 2023 that the tunnels were for fighters and that protecting civilians was the UN’s and Israel’s job. When the IDF warned Gazans to leave combat zones, Hamas told them to stay. A mayor honoring the dead might have mentioned the terrorist army that used them as cover.
Mamadani right that the suffering did not begin on October 7, but the history undercuts his antisemitic fable. Arab mobs murdered Jews in Jerusalem in 1920, Jaffa in 1921, and Hebron in 1929, where in a single morning they slaughtered 67 Jews after the circle around Haj Amin al-Husseini, the Mufti of Jerusalem and the era’s dominant Palestinian Arab leader, spread the lie that Jews were plotting against al-Aqsa. There was no Jewish state then, and no “occupation” to blame.
Husseini’s leadership rejected a Palestinian Arab state in 1937, 1939, and 1947. He spent World War II in Berlin as Adolf Hitler’s honored guest, urging Arabs over Nazi radio to kill Jews wherever they found them. His successors were offered a Palestinian Arab state in 2000, 2001, and 2008 and refused each time. In 2005 Israel pulled every soldier and civilian out of Gaza; Hamas answered with terror, rockets, a violent takeover and, eventually, October 7. Hamas’s charter declares the land from the river to the sea an Islamic trust no one may surrender and quotes a hadith about Muslims killing Jews. Ninety-four years after Hebron, Hamas named its invasion and massacre “Al-Aqsa Flood.” From the mufti to Hamas, the throughline is a violent, fascist Islamist rejection of Jewish sovereignty anywhere in the land.
None of this is hidden. The mayor left it out on purpose.
The genocide-libel itself collapses against the record. Genocidal regimes do not warn civilians to evacuate, pause fighting to vaccinate children against polio, or truck food to the people they are supposedly exterminating. In every genocide on record, the killers controlled when the killing stopped. In Gaza, Hamas could have ended the war any day by freeing the hostages and surrendering. Spreading that libel as mayor of the largest Jewish city outside Israel is reckless at best.
Anti-Jewish hate crimes rise in New York

Nine days later, the mayor delivered that same language to an audience of millions.
Most Jewish New Yorkers have no use for grant programs from a mayor who marks one of the worst days in Jewish history by calling the Jewish state a “genocidal apartheid regime funded by their taxes.” They have seen where that rhetoric leads: to their campuses, their synagogues, their streets.
Mamdani’s plan was written to show he takes antisemitism seriously. His October 7 statement showed it was written to give him cover for the hatred he keeps feeding.

On October 7, Hamas’s goal was not the Nova festival - it was New York - opinion

I never thought I would ever write a book.
At The Jerusalem Post, I wrote more than 10,000 articles, but I don’t think any of them exceeded 4,000 words. How could I ever write 60,000? Some magazine articles I wrote covered six pages, but that’s far from 200 pages.
I had every reason to doubt that I would be able to concentrate and maintain focus for the time it would take.
But when Wicked Son Publishers in New York presented an opportunity and a unique professional and personal situation permitted it, I jumped at the chance.
After more than 20 books in English and Hebrew were written on what went wrong on the military and intelligence battlefronts, I became aware of the glaring need for a book presenting an Israeli insider’s perspective on what went wrong on the media battlefield for Israel and the international Jewish community. After all, every day since Oct. 7 has arguably gotten progressively easier on the military battlefield, while every day since the massacre has gotten progressively harder in the narrative war.
It could also be argued that while most of the lessons from the blunders on the military battlefield that led to Oct. 7 have long been learned and implemented, the media battlefield’s mistakes are still far from being internalized, and they have led in part to the antisemitism that is currently spiraling out of control in America and around the world.
My book reveals that unleashing that overwhelming and no longer shocking hatred of Jews was actually the goal of Hamas head Yahya Sinwar and the Hamas leadership, who were unaware of the Nova music festival taking place 5 km. (3.1 miles) east of the Israel-Gaza border fence.
They were, however, well aware that the Palestinian cause was gradually being forgotten, as the Abraham Accords were about to expand to Saudi Arabia and then to other countries and leave them behind. They wanted to bring the Palestinians to the forefront of the world’s agenda, and no one can deny that they have succeeded beyond their wildest dreams.
Hamas’s political bureau head Ismail Haniyeh said very openly in a speech to the International Union of Muslim Scholars in Doha, Qatar, on January 9, 2024, that Hamas initiated what it strategically called Operation Al-Aqsa Flood to return the Palestinians to the international agenda.
“The world, the international community, and global decision-making circles no longer raised the issue of Palestine,” Haniyeh complained as he justified the attack. “The world began to deal with it as an internal Zionist matter, to be handled in its own way. There were no international resolutions, no conferences, and not even talk of a two-state solution. Such talk was no longer circulating among decision-makers worldwide. The issue became completely marginalized.”
The element of surprise
SO HOW DID they succeed in drawing back the world’s attention? By using what Haniyeh called “verbal jihad” and taking advantage of several assets, which are each explained from behind the scenes in the book.
Their first asset was the element of surprise, which caught both the Israeli government and the American Jewish establishment completely off guard. And Israel was even less prepared for Oct. 7 on the media battlefield than it had been on the military battlefield.
The IDF may have mishandled Oct. 7 completely, and its functioning was briefly limited, but at least it continued to exist. The Israeli government employed no English spokesperson on Oct. 7, nor did it have a consul-general in New York, where most of the international media is based. There was no strategic plan ready to deal with a crisis and media circus of this magnitude.
Hamas, by contrast, did have a strategic plan for the narrative war – formulated by their notoriously brilliant veteran propaganda chief Abu Obeida – which Hamas documents have revealed was prepared well in advance, alongside their military plans. They also had an army of trained journalist loyalists who worked for top international media outlets during the war, due in part to Israel’s decision not to let independent media into Gaza since 2014.
These terrorists, whom the world accepted as journalists, became part of the blood libel machine, funded by the Qataris who maintained an open channel of communication between Hamas and their government mouthpiece Al Jazeera, which was deeply involved in all aspects of strategically broadcasting the war to the world.
This all overwhelmed the leadership of the American Jewish community, which had been concentrating on building bridges with progressive groups to deal with intersectionality but found itself abandoned by purported allies when it needed them most. Jewish college students were nowhere near ready to go on defense in a fight forced on them and certainly not to go on offense.
Just like Hamas had 16 years to prepare for this war while Israel had not one day, anti-Israel groups in the United States and other countries around the world had been preparing for Oct. 7 for decades, with unlimited funding at their disposal. They were an integral part of the strategic plan – and the blood libel machine – and unlike Hamas, Hezbollah, Syria, and Iran, their success has not been halted.
Continuing to spread hatred of Jews and of the State of Israel
They have continued to spread hatred of the Jewish people and the Jewish state, gaining positions of influence and scaring ordinary Jews who had no connection to what was going on in the Middle East, some 12,000 km. away. They exploit their numerical advantage and their head start on social media and AI platforms in what is nowhere near a fair fight.
Sinwar’s goal was to initiate a future multifront war that could succeed after Israel lost the world’s support, and ideally after Iran obtained a nuclear capability. That may appear more unrealistic now because of Israel’s military successes on seven fronts, but if international condemnation of Israel continues making the Jewish state even more isolated, it certainly cannot be ruled out.
That is why the book urges future governments of Israel to make the narrative war a top priority – as this column has repeatedly – which even Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu himself admits openly has not been the case since Oct. 7. It is also why the book offers readers more than 30 tools for fighting for Israel on social media and AI platforms.
Those tools were praised in the book’s endorsements by hasbara (public diplomacy) heroes Natan Sharansky, Michael Oren, Nachman Shai, and Gil Troy, as well as Noa Tishby, who put the book in context in the foreword she wrote.
Because the narrative war has been at the forefront of international headlines lately, Wicked Son advanced its publication by a month, and it went on Amazon on the eve of the massacre’s Jewish calendar anniversary, Simchat Torah. I symbolically – and chillingly – received my first copy from the Pomeranz bookstore in Jerusalem on Oct. 7.
So I really did write a book, and I hope it makes the positive impact it needs to, so there won’t be anything like Oct. 7 ever again – on either the military or media battlefields. ■
The writer is the author of the book The Blood Libel Machine: Exposing the Anti-Israel Hate Network and How to Fight Back, which can be ordered from Pomeranz Books in Israel and Amazon around the world.

Australia has no need to buy fuel from Russia, despite US President Donald Trump’s move to bring Russian diesel back to world markets. Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen says that imports from Russia will remain banned to ensure the country does not benefit from its invasion of Ukraine, Bloomberg reports.
Trump has agreed with Russia's President Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel onto global markets, a move Ukraine says funds a war that has killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days.
“We don’t need or want Russian fuel in Australia. We do not want Vladimir Putin to benefit from this war in the Middle East. What the United States does is a matter for them, but we won’t be changing our approach,” Bowen said.
The deal Australia is turning down
Trump announced on 9 October a series of cargoes beginning this month totaling about 13.5 million barrels of Russian diesel. The release upends years of sanctions, as the White House looks for ways to tame soaring fuel prices before the US midterm elections.
Bowen draws a clear line between that approach and Australia’s. What the US does is its own affair, he stresses, but Canberra will maintain its arrangements with trading partners to keep Russian fuel out of the market.
Enough fuel to hold the line
Australia can hold out without Russian supply, Bowen argues. The country has 43 days’ worth of petrol, two days more than a week earlier, and 31 days’ worth of diesel, one day less, he notes.
He adds that Australia stays in close contact with domestic refiners to keep them running at full capacity. The stance lets Canberra wait out high prices rather than buy fuel that would send money to Moscow.
Australia’s fuel costs have stayed high since the war between the US and Iran disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the route that normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil and gas.

In AI, India’s choice needn’t be between a US leash or Chinese hook

Dhruv Atreja is head of AI research at Fastino Labs in New York, where he has led post-training collaborations with leading US technology companies, working with open-weight models from American and Chinese developers. 
On June 12, two of the world’s most capable artificial intelligence models went dark. An American export directive barred foreigners from using Anthropic’s two flagship AI models, and because the company could not check every user’s nationality, it switched them off. Access returned on July 1 but the warning is clear: India’s AI future can be switched off from Washington.
In September, Beijing came calling. At the Brics summit in New Delhi, Chinese President Xi Jinping promised China would “be a pioneer in establishing a Brics AI open-source community”. It is a seductive offer. Chinese open models are capable, cheap and free to adapt; once downloaded, no one in Washington can take them away.
But this is a choice between a leash and a hook. American access can be yanked away overnight. Chinese models cannot be switched off once downloaded, but they arrive with Beijing’s sensitivities built in. Asked whether Arunachal Pradesh is an Indian state, DeepSeek’s chatbot declined to answer. No country of 1.4 billion people should run its banks, courts and public services on either.
Delhi’s response so far has been to chase size. Start-up Sarvam AI plans to build a trillion-parameter model; so does state-backed BharatGen. The government is reportedly exploring an anchor investment of up to 200 billion rupees (US$2.08 billion) in a new frontier AI fund, on top of the 103.7 billion rupees the “IndiaAI Mission” approved in 2024.

Tennessee death row inmate discharged from hospital after surviving botched execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
21:29:03 UTC
06:29:03 KST

Christa Pike discharged from hospital after botched execution
Death row inmate Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder in the US state of Tennessee, has been discharged from the hospital after surviving a botched execution. She was sent back to prison on Saturday, days after regaining the ability to walk and talk after receiving a double lethal injection, her lawyers said.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow Job Corps student in Knoxville. Her execution, which was scheduled for September 30, was expected to be the first execution of a woman in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
The inmate did not lose consciousness after two syringes of pentobarbital were administered and complained of pain in her arm instead. She eventually lost consciousness but could be heard breathing heavily and snoring and still had a heartbeat nearly 90 minutes into the execution, prompting an ambulance to take her to the hospital, media reports suggest.
The woman was initially unconscious and on a ventilator. According to The Guardian, she was declared brain dead on Monday before suddenly regaining consciousness on Thursday. One of her lawyers said at the time that she was “up and walking,” though she was “somewhat foggy.”
On Saturday, Pike was returned to the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she had spent 30 years. “She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” her lawyers said, adding that she “is continuing to receive medical care at the prison.”
The authorities provided no official explanation as to why Pike survived the execution. The New York Times reported earlier, citing medical experts, that Pike probably survived the procedure because the lethal drug leaked into tissue around the insertion sites instead of entering her bloodstream. The woman’s lawyers had warned that her medical history and small veins increased the risk that she would experience unnecessary pain.
The incident prompted the resignation of Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada. The state’s governor, Bill Lee, ordered an independent review of the botched execution and suspended the only other execution scheduled for this year. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis canceled a planned lethal injection execution in his state as well on Friday.
Pike, then aged 18, was convicted of first-degree murder after she, her boyfriend, and another accomplice lured Slemmer, a fellow student, to an isolated area near the University of Tennessee agricultural campus, where Pike brutally beat her and cut her throat.
Her case is the second botched execution in Tennessee this year. In May, the execution of death row inmate Tony Carruthers was halted after officials repeatedly failed to establish intravenous access to administer pentobarbital. The governor granted the man a one-year reprieve and he was returned to death row. The incident raised questions about the state’s lethal injection procedures months before Pike’s execution.

Indonesia’s Energy Investment Potential

The recent economic headlines in Indonesia have been pessimistic to say the least. There are serious concerns that President Prabowo Subianto’s signature social development initiatives – the free nutritious meals (Makanan Bergizi Gratis, “MBG) program and the Red-White Village Cooperatives (Kopdes Merah Putih) – are straining the national budget and will limit long-term growth. The president’s reluctance to abandon or significantly downsize these programs has helped inspire protests in June against an agenda which many fear is “bankrupting Indonesia.” Protestors and investors alike have additional complaints about Indonesia’s policy trajectory, including creeping militarization of the civil service, state control over key commodities sectors, and weaponization of the legal system against the government’s political opponents. Amidst the uncertainty, the rupiah and the Indonesian stock market have also experienced major slides, with the currency hitting an all-time low against the U.S. dollar on June 8 and the Jakarta Composite Index falling 36 percent from a record high in January.
Despite the serious economic headwinds, there are still opportunities for investors in the Indonesian economy, particularly in the energy sector. Indonesia ranks among global leaders in terms of energy potential and has recently improved its regulatory environment for international developers in upstream oil and gas as well as renewables. Major agreements are being signed and capital is being deployed by leading international energy companies. This momentum in domestic energy production and exploration is unfolding against the backdrop of renewed conflict in the Middle East, which has sharpened investor and policymaker focus on the risks of import dependence across the APAC region.
Recent studies have estimated that the country has technical renewable energy potential of 3,686 GW, with hundreds of suitable locations for solar, wind and hydropower facilities. To tap more of this potential, the Indonesian government has set a target energy mix of 35 percent from renewables, up from the current level of 18 percent, by 2035. However, Indonesia’s proven oil and gas reserves are also immense, totaling 2.33 billion barrels and 34.8 Tcf respectively. To utilize these reserves, Indonesia has opened 116 new oil and gas blocks to global investors.

Trump Says U.S. May Join Saudi Strikes on Houthis After Riyadh Airport Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
21:22:07 UTC
06:22:07 KST

President Donald Trump said Saturday that the United States “may” join Saudi Arabia’s strikes on the Iran-backed Houthi militia group, which is based in Yemen, after airport attacks killed at least 18 people in recent days. The latest attack led to near-complete shutdown of public air traffic into and out of the capital.
“We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn of the White House, prior to departing for a rally in Tennessee. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
His comments came shortly after a fresh attack on Saturday, in which a missile struck the complex housing Terminals 3 and 4 of King Khalid International Airport (KKIA), the second-busiest airport in Saudi Arabia. Twelve people were killed and over 300 were injured, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA). The Houthis, who claimed attacks on the airport earlier in the week, did not immediately claim the latest strike.
It was the latest in a series of attacks over the past week, which began just days after Yemen’s Saudi-backed government announced a major offensive against the Houthis on Oct. 4.
Two took place on Tuesday and Wednesday, although the information about each has been scarce. A strike on the more southerly Abha International Airport killed two women—one Algerian and one Moroccan—while an attack on KKIA left one Sudanese man dead, the country’s civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday.
The Houthis said they again targeted KKIA on Thursday; three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, died.
The victims of the past week’s strikes were primarily Saudi but also included individuals from Algeria, Bangladesh, Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, Pakistan, the Philippines, Sudan, and the United States.
Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen, said in a statement on Friday that the attacks “will not go unpunished.”
Airport strikes are a signature strategy from the Houthis; a similar move on Abha in 2019 was denounced as an apparent war crime by the Human Rights Watch.
Brigadier General Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesperson, on Thursday reiterated an earlier warning for international airlines and passengers to avoid airspace over Saudi Arabia, which had on Monday been declared an open military operations zone. He also warned employees to avoid Saudi oil facilities so as not to endanger their lives, since they are also considered primary targets. He also .
The GACA announced that Riyadh had suspended operations at its main airport on Saturday and was assessing the damage; FlightAware showed 400 cancellations into and out of KKIA as of 11 p.m local time.
The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh also issued a security alert, warning Americans to avoid KKIA and its surrounding areas as of Saturday.
“U.S. citizens should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions. We recommend checking your flight departure status directly with the airline and with the airport,” its website said.
Why has the Saudi-Houthi conflict escalated?
The latest airport attacks followed months of escalating threats to air travel and shipping.
In July, the Houthis accused the Saudis of bombing Sanaa International Airport. Yemen’s Saudi-backed government claimed responsibility, saying it had sought to prevent an Iranian plane from landing there.
In response, the Houthis said that they would impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis last month captured both the port city of Mokha and Perim Island in a bid to control the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. With shipping through the Strait of Hormuz already disrupted by the U.S. war with Iran, a threat to traffic through Bab el-Mandeb could deepen the global oil crisis.
In the weeks to follow, Saudi-backed forces have since claimed to retake both seized areas, but the claim has not been independently verified and control remains disputed.
In September, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called to urge Trump to act against the Houthis. The request came as the militia group gained ground over vital chokepoints in the Red Sea.
Although the two nations are allies, Washington explained last month that it did not have plans to get involved in the conflict. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment as the situation evolves.
Trump’s renewed consideration of strikes in Yemen comes as the war with Iran remains deeply unpopular at home: 69% of Americans said it had not been worth fighting in an AP-NORC poll from Oct. 1.
On Thursday, Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterms—a pledge that does not address possible strikes on the Houthis in Yemen.

Hundreds of doctors demand World Medical Association suspend Israel
Physicians accuse Israeli Medical Association of remaining silent as Palestinian healthcare is systematically destroyed.
Hundreds of doctors have gathered outside the World Medical Association (WMA) summit in the Netherlands, calling for the suspension of the Israeli Medical Association (IMA) from the grouping of physicians.
On Saturday, 81 healthcare workers removed their scrubs and hung them in a line facing the WMA assembly in Rotterdam, each bearing the name of a Palestinian healthcare worker currently held in illegal Israeli detention.
It was part of a protest against the continued membership of the Israeli association in the WMA, “despite them breaching almost every ethical principle in the WMA’s Code of Medical Ethics”, the IMA Out! coalition that organised the demonstration said in a statement.
“These scrubs should not be empty. Our colleagues belong with their patients, not in Israeli prisons. Today, we literally placed their names at the WMA’s doorstep,” said Mejrem Ahmetaj, a general practitioner and member of IMA Out!.
Since October 2023, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 1,700 Palestinian healthcare workers and destroyed nearly all the hospitals and healthcare facilities in the enclave.
The campaign accused the Israeli medical association of remaining silent as Palestinian healthcare has been systematically destroyed.
“The IMA is not a bystander. It defends these attacks and blocks international condemnation while Palestinian healthcare is being destroyed. That is not medical neutrality. That is complicity,” added Ahmetaj.
At a meeting of international doctors, medical leaders and human rights activists during the WMA summit on Thursday, the destruction of Palestinian healthcare and the responsibility of the international medical community were discussed, the campaign said.
“Our Palestinian colleagues are being killed and imprisoned, where they are starved and tortured. Their hospitals have been destroyed and patients driven out or murdered. The IMA has said and done nothing about these war crimes against health workers, patients and hospitals,” said a statement by Jonathan Fluxman on behalf of IMA OUT!.
“Thirty years of WMA dialogue with the IMA has done nothing but give the IMA a sense of impunity … It is time for national medical associations and the WMA to speak out and take action. Break your ties with the IMA and suspend the IMA from the WMA now,” he added.
The IMA OUT! campaign said it delivered a petition calling for the IMA’s suspension, signed by more than 6,500 health workers from around the world.
They also demanded accountability for the complicity of Israeli doctors in the starvation, torture and medical neglect of Palestinian prisoners.
Among those held by Israel is Dr Hussam Abu Safia, head of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, whose unlawful detention has prompted an international outcry.
He was briefly held at the notorious Sde Teiman detention camp and has been subject to torture and medical neglect. Doctors protesting in Rotterdam held up placards demanding his release.
Abu Safia’s son Elyas, addressing a meeting organised by the campaign, said, “My father and all Palestinian detainees must be treated in accordance with medical ethics, and doctors must abide by the Hippocratic oath they have taken. Care cannot be given based on whose life is deemed worthy.”

Indian Family Offices Eye Southeast Asia’s Startups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
21:11:00 UTC
06:11:00 KST

India’s family offices are becoming a significant force in the global economy. According to a report by The Economic Times and market intelligence firm 1Lattice, the country now hosts more than 300 family offices managing over $30 billion in assets. High-net-worth families with more than $30 million in assets are projected to nearly double, from 16,000 in 2025 to 26,000 by 2030, with intergenerational wealth transfer reaching $1.3-1.5 trillion over the next decade. A generational shift is underway as well, with over half of family offices now featuring millennials or Gen Z members in investment decisions.
The rise of younger generations has helped precipitate a change for Indian family office investment strategy: roughly 30% now favor startup allocations in healthtech, fintech, and AI, versus traditional investments such as real estate and gold. According to Tracxn data cited by CNA, family office-backed startup funding nearly doubled to $1.62 billion in 2024 from $876.7 million the year before. Analysts attribute this shift to family offices’ “patient capital” — funds without the eight-to-ten-year return pressure that constrains institutional VC — making them attractive to founders navigating longer development cycles. Cases like Sattva Group’s family office (which diversified from real estate into tech, backing firms like InCred) and Artha India Ventures (an early Oyo investor) illustrate the trend. Geopolitical volatility has reinforced the appeal of relationship-led capital, though PwC’s Falguni Shah notes governance and intrafamily alignment remain key challenges as these offices scale.
One notable growth trend among Indian family offices is the rise of impact investing, those made to achieve measurable social or environmental outcomes alongside financial returns, distinct from pure philanthropy and blended finance. Between 2021 and 2024, 923 unique HNW families made impact investments, with 86 investing through formal family office structures. Climate-tech has emerged as a leading sector, along with financial inclusion platforms and healthcare. While engagement is still early-stage and often exploratory, it signals a meaningful shift toward more value-based capital deployment among India’s wealthiest families.

Hurricane Simon strengthens to Category 4 off Mexico’s Pacific coast
Puerto Vallarta businesses board up windows as Hurricane Simon threatens Mexico’s west-central coast.
Hurricane Simon has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 storm off Mexico’s Pacific coast, packing winds of up to 241km/h (150mph) as it threatens to bring destructive winds, storm surges and life-threatening flooding to southwestern Mexico.
The US National Hurricane Center said that Simon was expected to approach or move just inland of Mexico’s west-central coast late on Saturday or early Sunday. The storm was about 115 miles (185km) south-southwest of Manzanillo, with further strengthening possible before landfall.
The hurricane could bring 10 to 20 inches (25 to 51cm) of rain to parts of southwestern Mexico through Sunday.
“This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain,” the agency warned, urging residents to complete preparations to protect lives and property.
Authorities issued a hurricane warning for parts of the Pacific coast south of the resort city of Puerto Vallarta, including the area around Manzanillo, the country’s largest Pacific port. A tropical storm watch was in effect farther south towards Lazaro Cardenas.
Jalisco suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas. Officials also urged hotels and other tourism businesses in Puerto Vallarta to ensure workers and visitors had access to shelters or safe locations.
Businesses in the popular tourist destination boarded up windows and placed sandbags at entrances as the storm approached.
The hurricane centre also warned of a dangerous storm surge and large and destructive waves near where Simon makes landfall.

Houthi strike on Riyadh airport kills 12, injures over 300 (VIDEOS)
A Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday killed 12 people, including an American citizen, and injured another 309, Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) confirmed on Sunday.
The Saudi aviation authority said the fatalities included four Saudi citizens and eight foreign nationals, including two Bangladeshis and one each from the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine, and Sudan. Some of the 309 injured remain in critical condition, GACA said, adding that the extent of the damage to the airport is still being assessed.
The attack comes almost a week after Yemen’s internationally recognized and Saudi-backed government launched a major offensive to retake territory from the Iran-backed Houthis, including areas near the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Saudi-led forces have supported the operation with airstrikes, while the Houthis have retaliated with missile and drone attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh’s international airport.

At least 316 flights to and from Riyadh airport were canceled on Saturday, according to data from flight-tracking service Flightradar24. The US Embassy and several other Western diplomatic missions urged citizens to avoid the airport and warned of major travel disruptions.
Asked whether US forces could join the Saudi strikes against the Houthis, US President Donald Trump told reporters: “We may. We’re going to look at it.”
Saudi Arabia has led a military campaign against the Houthis since 2015. The hostilities largely subsided following a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022 before flaring up again this July following a strike on Sanaa Airport by Saudi-backed Yemeni forces.
Fighting escalated further in September as the Houthis made their biggest territorial gains in years, capturing the strategic port of Mocha and expanding their control along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital international shipping route.
Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior official and spokesman for the Yemeni group, also known as Ansar Allah, confirmed responsibility for the strike in an exclusive interview with RT, saying they were intended to force Saudi Arabia to agree to a “comprehensive and permanent peace” and an end to the war and mutual blockade.
Al-Bukhaiti accused Riyadh of destroying Yemen’s civilian infrastructure over the past 12 years, including airports, seaports, schools, hospitals, markets, and even wedding and funeral halls. He said the Houthis are now responding in kind to Saudi attacks, but insisted that the strikes are intended to pressure Saudi leaders into accepting a lasting peace agreement rather than motivated by revenge.
“Our military operations deep inside the Saudi entity will continue and will not end except by destroying all Saudi infrastructure belonging to the government,” he warned, specifically naming military facilities, airports, ports, and other vital installations.

Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an ‘emergency brake’ that humans control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:59:28 UTC
05:59:28 KST

Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella on Saturday called for advanced artificial intelligence systems to be built with containment, independent controls and an "emergency brake" that lets authorized people pause or shut a model down mid-task.
"We need to surround non-deterministic models with strong, deterministic system design, human controls, and reliable operating procedures, and establish industry standards where existing ones are insufficient," Nadella wrote in a post on social media platform X.
"Treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system," he said.
Nadella's comments come amid warnings from top tech executives and researchers — including Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — about insufficient AI safety protocols and claims that the technology is moving too fast.
An AI researcher quit Anthropic last month and accused the company, and its chief rival, OpenAI, of "gambling with our lives." Later that day, an alignment lead at Anthropic focused on AI safety said there's a greater than 10% chance that the technology could "kill all humans" within the next decade.
Conversely, President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed AI extinction risks and has instead emphasized that the industry needs to stay ahead of China. Trump also recently introduced a new "AI Force," led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, to help facilitate the industry and root out bad actors.
Microsoft's Nadella wrote Saturday that AI systems should be designed around "principles of observability."
They include model diversity; a human-readable footprint of the model's actions; continuous system testing; independent controls and auditability; containment; and incident disclosure, Nadella wrote.
"The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most," he wrote. "It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least."

Despair after 200-year-old ‘grandmother’ tree toppled for Trump’s border wall: ‘It crushes your heart’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:57:32 UTC
05:57:32 KST

A 200-year-old cottonwood tree near the US-Mexico border, known as the “grandmother”, has been destroyed to make way for the construction of Donald Trump’s border wall, despite a months-long effort by protesters trying to save it.
In late July, land defenders began a tree-sit in the ghost town of Lochiel, Arizona, taking turns occupying a platform high in the tree’s canopy. The group remained there for more than 70 days.
Then, on Monday at dawn, more than 80 federal agents swarmed the protesters’ camp, which is located on private land, making arrests and preventing people from reaching the cottonwood. Some agents in a steel basket on an extendable crane lift forcibly removed the person in the tree platform, according to videos and photos shared on social media and descriptions of people there at the time. Others were shoved and tackled as they tried to rush toward the tree to prevent its destruction, according to witnesses.
Contractors with Fisher Sand & Gravel, a company building this section of wall, then used an excavator to push over the tree, which cracked and crashed to the earth. Land defenders shrieked, cried and yelled at the federal agents.
“Seeing that – it crushes your heart,” said Erick Meza, the Sierra Club’s Borderlands coordinator who has been working to save the trees for months, beginning with a series of letters to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).
“That tree brought a lot of people together,” he said. Now, he added, “there’s a community response of outrage. People are pissed off.”
The cottonwood’s toppling was filmed by a team from Turning Point USA, the far-right political group, who appeared to be embedded with border patrol and allowed free access to roam throughout the closed off public road.
One of the land defenders had scaled another ancient cottonwood tree situated right on the border with Mexico. On Thursday, CBP and Mexican police, who have been present for several days and visibly working with American authorities, removed the tree-sitter’s platform, food and water supplies, according to Alex Chabbott, a land defender who has been present at the camp on and off for over a month.
Late on Friday, the tree-sitter came down on their own volition after not being resupplied for several days.
The agents involved include border patrol officers, part of CBP, and a special forces tactical unit called Bortac, whose self-described purpose is to “respond to terrorist threats”.
The tree-sit began shortly after contractors knocked over and killed three other ancient cottonwood trees nearby on 27 July.
Two 30ft-tall walls are being built throughout this area, known as the San Rafael valley, a remote and once idyllic high elevation prairie where the movie Oklahoma was filmed. The valley, and the Patagonia and Huachuca mountains on either side of it, form one of the most important regional wildlife corridors between the US and Mexico, providing passage to animals including jaguars, ocelots, bears and even beavers and porcupines in recent years.
Already, government contractors have finished 88 miles (140km) of secondary wall, which is a second 30ft fence set at some distance from a primary wall of the same height. Another 444 miles of secondary wall are under construction, according to DHS, much of that in Arizona, using billions of dollars allocated by Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Protesters say that construction in the area is progressing rapidly, 24 hours a day. In recent days, Fisher Sand & Gravel has completed the secondary wall, which includes placing 30ft steel panels within a trench filled with rebar and cement, along a part of the private property where the camp is located, including up to the point where the tree stood.
These trees, which depend on a regular supply of water underground, are a hallmark of riparian forests, an endangered ecotype throughout Arizona and the south-west, said Russ McSpadden, an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. The ecological importance of these trees is one of the animating factors behind the land defenders.
Water use for wall construction has depleted wells throughout the south-west, threatening natural features such as Quitobaquito Springs. CBP does not say how much current construction uses, but in 2008 it estimated a smaller wall nearby could use up to 710,00 gallons per mile for construction; the current project likely uses more, as it is larger.
‘We are starting a movement’
Since Monday, dozens of land defenders have been arrested, many for entering the road between the private property and the border, which was ordered closed by federal authorities in late September due to wall construction. Protesters have been doing prayers in the road near the tree every morning.
Some of those arrested were physically hit and came back with bruises and black eyes, Chabbott claimed.
Several more people attempted to use nonviolent tactics to halt or delay construction, including one woman who locked herself to a cement truck on 7 August, according to videos shared on social media.
The protester was sprayed in the face with mace and wrestled by several agents, and her limbs forced into painful positions, according to witnesses and social media videos.
The truck was later driven away while the land defender was still attached, and cut from the vehicle later that evening, according to witnesses. She is now in custody, according to what authorities have told the land defenders’ lawyers.
Julia Butterfly Hill, who spent two years living in a redwood in California’s Humboldt county in the late 1990s, said she was horrified to see how roughly border patrol treated this woman on a livestreamed video, she said.
This land defender’s courage and commitment to nonviolent resistance in the face of brutality “brought tears to my eyes”, Butterfly Hill said. “She’s a hero of the highest order.”
CBP did not respond to a request for comment about this and other clashes, but has previously said that walls in areas like this will help combat unauthorized immigration. The sheriff of Santa Cruz county, David Hathaway, who did not respond to a request for comment for this story, has previously said a wall in this area is senseless since this remote valley has no history of significant illegal activity. Fisher Sand & Gravel did not respond to a request for comment.
In a press conference on 8 October, Adelita Grijalva, a congresswoman who represents the area, said she was “heartbroken” about the loss of the “grandmother” trees, and said she plans to try to introduce a bill that will revoke the DHS’s ability to waive any and all laws in building border infrastructure.
The tree-sit began shortly after contractors knocked over and killed two other ancient cottonwood trees nearby on 27 July.
In felling the tree, the contractors and federal agents “try to break us, but we are not broken”, said Kate Scott, one of the leaders of the tree-sit. “We are starting a movement, and we’re not going anywhere. We are rooted, like the grandmothers.”

Inside the conservative conference where Angus Taylor comes second to Pauline Hanson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:48:21 UTC
05:48:21 KST

analysis
Angus Taylor went where no Liberal leader has before, but Pauline Hanson already ruled the room
When Angus Taylor finished speaking to a room of conservative faithful in Brisbane this weekend, about 50 people stood to applaud him.
A few minutes later, hundreds rose to their feet to give Pauline Hanson a standing ovation simply because the One Nation leader had walked out onto the stage.
Such was the contrast in reception, that anyone might reasonably question why Taylor had bothered to attend this year's Australian Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) at all.
No sitting Liberal leader before him had attended CPAC, a gathering once viewed as too far to the right of the Coalition's mainstream.
But as the Liberals and Nationals have adopted more of the populist conservative policies championed at the conference, the distance between them has narrowed.
Taylor's address hit many of the same points as the speech delivered by Hanson, but it was clear the audience was giving all the credit to the latter.
The opposition leader also pulled his punches when it came to One Nation despite the party's surge in the polls correlating with the Coalition's decline.
Hanson showed no such qualms, delivering a sharp jab in Taylor's direction as she noted while voters did not want Anthony Albanese as prime minister, neither were they keen on a "smarmy management consultant".
When speaking to the media later in the afternoon Hanson denied her words were aimed at Taylor, but she may as well have winked as she said so.
Taylor may not have won hearts and minds, but his willingness to participate had a notable effect on the tenor of the proceedings.
United by a common enemy
The line to get into CPAC snaked outside the Brisbane venue on Saturday morning as hundreds of attendees arrived early, eager to get a good position for the headline speeches.
Inside, the lights cast an eerie red glow over the crowd, while posters featuring giants of conservative politics adorn the walls.
Under the stern gazes of Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan, the audience sat through an introductory video urging them to back "Angus", "Pauline", and "Matt" (Nationals leader Matt Canavan).
The organisers made no secret of their desire to emphasise what united the three parties rather than what divided them.
Taylor's presence made that possible, even if Hanson remained the undisputed favourite.
Throughout the day the audience oscillated between rapt attention and listlessness with heckles generally targeted not at the speakers, but the subjects of their shared ire.
Net zero, eSafety commissioner Julie Inman Grant (the "Karen of the internet" according to Hanson), Anthony Albanese, "woke" school curriculums and Welcome to Country were among the topics most likely to elicit a boo.
And nothing revived a fading crowd more than a dig at Energy and Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen, whose name came up so often he was probably owed an appearance fee.
CPAC chair Warren Mundine revealed Bowen's name alone gave him "chills" and recounted his visceral reaction when the pair once crossed paths in the street.
"My mate had to grab me to say, 'It doesn't go well on your CV if you murder a federal minister,'" Mundine quipped.
The fight for the right
But a shared opposition to Labor does not entirely resolve the Coalition's electoral woes.
The question hanging over the conference was whether the Liberals were witnessing the consolidation of a broader conservative movement or the gradual erosion of their own place at the centre of it.
One unsurprising absence from the CPAC line-up was Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie.
Rather than compete with One Nation on its own turf, Hastie has increasingly sought to make the conservative case to voters beyond the Coalition's traditional base.
Last week, he appeared on a live episode of the Brine & Biff, a podcast billed as a place for thoughtful political debate, albeit where one host is portrayed as a cartoon gherkin.
Hastie cracked out the sales pitch for the Coalition's plan to slash migration but also argued "chasing One Nation down the rabbit hole" was not going to win his side government.
His willingness to confront One Nation, rather than accommodate it, puts him at odds with the political future CPAC's organisers are trying to build.
The Australian event's founder Andrew Cooper closed day one by painting a vision for a future "Coalition of the willing" between the country's three conservative political parties.
In the meantime, he urged the Liberals, Nationals and One Nation to "share" preferences at the next election.
He warned "ego" and infighting over "minor differences" would only "hand power" back to Labor.
And thanked the audience for showing "respect" to every speaker and thus starving the "noisy rabble outside" — including the media — of the ability to spin a narrative about "division" in the conservative ranks.
But the media was not outside, we were in the building wearing bright red lanyards emblazoned with the tagline "fake news".
They're standard issue at every CPAC, where the ambition to become part of the political mainstream has apparently not extended to retiring jokes from its fringe days.

"According to all the data, there is no alternative government to the government of Netanyahu, (National Security Minister Itamar) Ben-Gvir and (Finance Minister Bezalel) Smotrich that can be formed without negotiating with the Joint List," he said.

Jabareen said: "We will be a safety net, but first and foremost a safety net for our people."
He said the bloc's demands would include combating crime through a clear plan with a timetable, budget and oversight mechanisms.
Other demands include ending home demolitions, approving master plans, providing land for young couples and recognizing unrecognized Arab villages in the Negev, he added.

The poll also showed that a majority of Israelis opposed Arab parties joining the next government in the 120-member Knesset, Israel's parliament.
Recent polls have shown neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition able to secure a governing majority independently ahead of the election scheduled for Oct. 26.

Matt Renshaw's 190 turns Durban Test, providing Aussie batting blueprint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:44:26 UTC
05:44:26 KST

Like many great plans, it was deceptively simple. Stillness. Balance. Patience. Concentration. No frills, no fast moves and no undue risks, just decisive action when needed.
Not for the first time at Test level, a burly Queenslander, a three-pound cleft of willow and a healthy dose of self-confidence was the difference between Australian success and failure.
That Matt Renshaw resurrected an Australian first innings which teetered near oblivion at 6-124 was the first point of order.
Of consequences further-reaching, the left-hander resurrected his entire Test career overnight in Durban, sweeping, clipping and crashing his way to 190 from 397 deliveries across 465 minutes of life-affirming Test batting.
Numerous records fell or threatened to. Renshaw's epic was the highest score by an Australian in Durban, the fourth highest overall by an Aussie against South Africa, and the best by a number-five of any nation at Kingsmead.
It was also a new Test personal best for Renshaw, usurping the 184 he made nine years ago as a boyish tyro against Pakistan in Sydney, back when the world was at his feet.
Renshaw is 30 now — a husband, a father of two children and an entirely different cricketer. He knows his own mind and understands his place in the scheme of things.
For a nation which has been crying out for big, important runs by someone not named Smith or Head, his Daddy hundred here was one for the ages.
Practically speaking, Renshaw helped Australia to a first-innings total of 390, which was at least 150 more than had seemed optimistic when he first took guard.
On a deeper level, it restored belief in the value of grinding out an innings of depth and character. It was the real deal — the proper Test match batting the Australian cricketing public has been craving.
No mistake should be made about the high degree of difficulty, either. When Renshaw began shepherding the tail a day earlier, Australia was at the mercy of a vigorous and versatile South African pace attack jagging the ball all over the place.
Waiting in the wings were the Proteas' twin spin options of Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer, with 1700+ first-class wickets between them.
Australia has struggled against left-arm spin in recent times. Last time they played a Test in Durban, Maharaj took nine wickets. And Australia's selection for this match — four left handers in the top six — was said to favour right-arm off-spinner Harmer even more.
So much for that, in the end. Renshaw swept, reverse-swept and paddled Maharaj into irrelevance and by the time Harmer finally removed the top-scorer for spin's first wicket of the game, the horse had well and truly bolted.
As it turned out, the sterner challenge was curbing the influence of the quicks, who'd posed constant difficulties for the rest of Australia's batters.
A microcosm came when Renshaw was on 130, yet still not able to relax. He was struck a scary blow to the grille of his helmet from an absolute snorter by Anrich Nortje, who bowled with genuine pace and accuracy in short, sharp spells.
Handling the wily and indefatigable Wiaan Mulder was no cinch either. Early on day two, the all-rounder scythed through Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc and threatened to blow the game open.
That he didn't was not exclusively a matter of Renshaw's dominance but of the rearguard partnerships which have so often saved Australia's bacon in recent times.
Renshaw shared stands of 86 across 32 overs with Pat Cummins and a monumental and possibly series-shaping 134 from 47 overs with Nathan Lyon.
Australia will not be looking too far ahead, but there was a blueprint here, not just of personnel but of general batting philosophy: know your game, make them bowl to you, stick around and wear them down.
Australia's total was the most obvious metric of success, but its innings duration of 137.2 overs will surely please Andrew McDonald and his analysts just as much.
In Australia's 35 Test innings in the two years before this match, they'd batted past the 100-over mark only six times, compared with 13 times in the 42 innings of the two-year period preceding.
That downward trend has, of course, coincided with a proliferation of the result pitches which characterise the World Test Championship era.
Concurrently, it is agreed by most involved in the Australian domestic scene, it has been difficult for Test batting candidates to put their best feet forward, or get in the habit of playing long innings, when the primary bloc of red-ball cricket occurs in spring, when Sheffield Shield pitches sometimes resemble Monty Don's perennial beds.
Without peering too far into the future or wishing disruption on a player who's just delivered something so special, one awkward talking point that will be aired soon enough is if and when Renshaw might move up to his normal position of opener.
The theory going into this game was that in batting down the order, he could blunt the influence of the spinners, which he assuredly did. But he would surely be just as assured against the new ball as he was here against the second new ball.
And yet, who'd be an opener these days? Late on day two, Ryan Rickelton provided a study in contrasts for the Proteas.
Having spent the better part of two days chasing leather in the field, and perhaps daydreaming that he was in Renshaw's shoes, he lasted only three deliveries before chasing Josh Hazlewood outside his off-stump and sending an edge to the cordon.
The more telling image of day two arrived an hour earlier, on the stroke of tea, when an exhausted Renshaw removed his helmet and trudged off for refreshments.
Appearing on the balcony of the player's area, Australian skipper Cummins peered down on the centurion with something like a look of love on his face.
Ray Illingworth once said a captain needs the patience of a saint, the diplomacy of an ambassador, the compassion of a social worker and the skin of a rhino. Colleagues who can bat for eight hours help, too.
