Cara Nachshon: The grandma with a red nose in her pocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
19:13:13 UTC
04:13:13 KST

Once a week, Cara Nachshon dresses in silly clothing and heads off to volunteer at Shaare Zedek Medical Center in Jerusalem.
Four years ago, this British-born grandmother from Modi’in completed a six-month Simchat Lev course in which teacher Jeff Gordon taught her how to use performance arts, humor, and playful interaction to relieve fears and aid in the healing process.
“I think I’ve always been a clown. It’s always been inside me. But I finally did the course that entitled me to put on a red nose,” she said. “At 58, it was the right time in my life to do it.”
Using the nom de plume Miss Cara (read “Mascara” in Hebrew) and wearing red, black, and white – symbolic of life, as these are the colors a newborn differentiates first – she works with adult patients in the wards, emergency room, physiotherapy department, and surgical waiting rooms at Shaare Zedek Medical Center.
She has also volunteered at a school for children on the autism spectrum; at Keren Or – The Jerusalem Center for Blind Children; at ADI Jerusalem, a rehabilitative care facility for children and young adults with severe disabilities; and at sheltered housing.
And occasionally she clowns on the fly.
“I always have a [red] nose with me because I never know when I’ll be needed. One time I clowned in a mall when I came across a little girl screaming because they’d pierced her ear and she didn’t want the other one done. And then there are grandchildren who fall and get hurt and need to be calmed down. They know that Booba will end up doing a bit of shtick.”
Her shtick is informed by listening and observing to assess the situation before choosing which direction to take. She brings a range of accessories to capture attention and engage people through color, touch, sound, or movement. Sometimes the accessories are imaginary and she uses pantomime.
One time she fashioned a violin from balloons for a patient who was an orchestral violinist, and the two of them made pretend music together. Another time, Cara telephoned an artistic friend, who was dying of cancer, and guided her by voice in “painting” a picture on an imaginary canvas.
A tragic Shabbat in 1986
The notion that it is possible “to give a little bit of a lift, even momentarily, in very difficult situations of trauma and stress” germinated in Cara’s mind on a tragic Shabbat back in 1986. That morning, she discovered her second-born child, 10-week-old Catriel, lifeless in his crib.
For the remainder of the agonizing hours until sundown, when their son’s body could be removed for burial, Cara and her husband, Tony, were kept company by some close friends.
“It takes a lot of guts to walk into a house under those circumstances. But they sat in our living room and made us laugh. I don’t know how I laughed; I don’t remember what they said. Somehow, they made us laugh. What happened there made me think, many years later, that it doesn’t matter what the situation is; you can always find joy in pain, light in darkness – though sometimes it’s quite challenging,” Cara said.
She and Tony went on to have four more children. Their oldest, Avital, today is the mother of four. Sons Avinoam and Ze’ev also have four kids each. Daughter Tchiya is the mother of two. The youngest Nachshon child, Aderet (“She’s the cherry on the cake”), was born 12 years after Ze’ev.
'We couldn’t wait one more minute'
GROWING UP in England, Cara and Tony belonged to the Zionist youth movement Bnei Akiva. They made aliyah in 1983, a year after getting married. “Israel was crying out, ‘Come, come, come!’ and we couldn’t wait one more minute.”
They started out at Kibbutz Alumim, moved to the Gilo neighborhood of Jerusalem a year later, and went on to spend 38 years in Givat Ze’ev, about five kilometers northwest of Jerusalem.
“Our children grew up there, and it was a wonderful life. One by one, they left to embark on their own lives.
“Four years ago, our children said to us, ‘It’s time for you to move, Mom and Dad,’ so we downsized and moved to Modi’in when our youngest finished school, in August 2023. And we’ve been very happy there. Sometimes your children do know best,” said Cara, who returns to Givat Ze’ev once a week for pottery classes.
She believes that making changes at certain stages of life keeps things from getting stale. “That goes for marriage, parenthood, your profession, and where you live, too.”
The Hamas-led massacres of October 7 occurred just two months after the big move to the smaller home. On October 8, some of Avital’s family and a friend’s family arrived on their doorstep from Ashkelon. Without enough beds for all nine visitors, Cara reached out to her new community for help.
“A beautiful family I had never met gave us their home while they were in America. Avital’s family stayed there for five months, and the children were welcomed in school and kindergarten,” Cara said.
Cara emphasized that her “wonderful husband and children are a source of inspiration for me, together with their families.” Her granddaughter Odeya came clowning with her once a month for a year at ADI Jerusalem as a pre-bat mitzvah project. She learned a lot from her Booba.
“One of the things Jeff Gordon taught us was to always look for the ‘shakuf,’” the person in the room who feels invisible. “When you look at somebody who’s shakuf, it doesn’t matter what they look like on the outside; what’s going on inside is what needs to be noticed. And with God’s help, always with God’s help, I tend to pick up on it,” Cara said.
For a week after Oct. 7, Cara couldn’t bear to do her usual hospital volunteering. “But then I realized I had to. It was a need for me and for the patients. Of course, I was with [wounded] soldiers, and with soldiers who came to visit those soldiers, because they also needed clowning.
“Medical clowning is very rewarding – it’s the best profession in the world. I get much more than I give.” ■
Cara Nachshon, 64
From South End, England,
to Kibbutz Alumim, 1983;
to Jerusalem, 1984;
to Givat Ze’ev, 1985;
to Modi’in, 2023

Who are we today, and who  would we like to be tomorrow? A reflection for the Jewish new year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
19:12:36 UTC
04:12:36 KST

With the High Holy Days barely behind us and a very important election on the horizon, today is the perfect time to take stock of where we stand, both individually and collectively, and where we would like to be in the coming year.
We pray that this election will bring us the calm we have always longed for, along with the much-needed unity within our small and precious country.
We recognize that we are still in the early stages of grieving for all that we have lost in the past several years. After all, how can we fully grieve when we are still caught up in our daily fight for survival?
That said, as we reflect on the incredible miracle after a horrific airplane disaster was averted, we must acknowledge just how much we have to be thankful for.
The day after this past Rosh Hashanah, the young community to which my children belong, along with various friends and family members, launched a crowdfunding project in memory of my precious three-and-a-half-year-old grandson who died after a courageous battle with cancer.
The family came together to write a Torah scroll for their community to carry Yishai’s memory forward.
Full of joy, mischief, light, and love, he had the kindest eyes, the biggest heart, and the purest smile. His story was about the child he was, the goodness he brought into the world, and the lasting mark he left on everyone who knew him. In his short life, he touched countless hearts and brightened the lives of those around him.
All of this, however, is really background. The real story is that in just under 36 hours – less than two days, all the money they had hoped to raise was reached through the generosity of more than 1,000 people, each of whom donated between NIS 10 and NIS 10,000. None of us could have imagined such caring and kindness, especially from so many who did not even know Yishai, his story, or his family.
The second silver lining in Yishai’s story is that he was the first person in Israel, having died at home, to donate any kind of organ or tissue. Up until now, all transplants have come from hospitalized patients or through Abu Kabir. Yishai donated both of his corneas: one to a soldier and the other to a young woman.
SO, THIS year, as I sat in synagogue asking for forgiveness, I began to contemplate not just my past actions and behavior, but how and what I could and should do differently.
Our behavior offers a message that we hand down to future generations
How we behave with our loved ones, our friends, and those we do not even know is a choice for each of us to make.
Our behavior, both subtly and overtly, offers a message that we hand down to future generations – to our children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren. It is a huge responsibility for each one of us and one not to be taken lightly.
Rather, it is a gift to be given the opportunity to rethink and recalculate our personal behavioral GPS in a way that will influence others.
In a world that, in many ways, feels damaged, you can decide how you want to take the generosity and caring of others, as well as the many stories of both hope and tremendous sadness, into the new year.
Having heard about the harshness of earthquakes, fire, horrific weather, plagues, and more over the holidays, how does it affect the seriousness of your prayers and actions?
Having personally said Yizkor for my two parents last year, and now doubling that to four this year, comes with deep sadness that we are forced to acknowledge that not every person’s allotted time is as we imagine.
Some will depart earlier, through tragedy and misfortune. Perhaps this is a reminder for all of us to make better decisions about what really matters, as we attempt to find meaning and focus on who we want to be and how we see ourselves executing a strategy to get there.
While many of the disasters spoken about are not within our control, respect between us and others, how we choose to spend our precious time and with whom, and other aspects of our lives as we move forward are very much within our control.
Individually and collectively, we are accountable for our mistakes.
Have we taken responsibility for our actions? Did we examine the consequences of our behavior? What could we have done differently, and were there other choices that we opted not to see?
Were we caring and compassionate, sensitive to the pain and suffering of others, even those who were not our close friends?
Did we stop long enough to think before we spoke? Were we helpful or hurtful?
Could we have listened more? Were we there for our family, friends, and others?
Perhaps we owe it to ourselves to do the accounting of each of these questions so future generations might benefit from our insight.
Watching clips from the recent attempted hijacking/terror attack on a Flydubai flight, I, like most others in this country, had such a profound sense of gratitude toward the Israeli passengers who knew just what to do given both the dangerous aviation situation and the medical emergency involved.
Hearing the passengers sing “Am Yisrael hai” was a real reminder of the pride we carry and just who we are.
We have heard countless stories about our hostages, too, and their life changes since they were released. We learned what was important to them, and we would do well to evaluate this in our own lives today.
So ask yourself what you can do to make things better. Are you proud of your behavior and that of your loved ones?
What are your short- and long-term goals? Have you discussed them with your children, and have you respectfully listened to their thoughts and ideas?
How have you used your time? Did you and other family members use your time wisely or waste your time mindlessly scrolling?
Is there something you would like to do differently, and if so, what would it be?
Perhaps today is the perfect time to have these discussions. We know just how short life is. Have you told others how much you love them? Have you told them what you need to have to feel calm? Have you been a good friend, neighbor, parent, child, spouse, and family member, and what can you do to be better?
Experiencing the firsthand generosity of others was a real eye-opener for me about appreciation and giving.
I recognize that only I can set my personal goals for my family, friends, work, my emotional and physical health, and more.
And if I fail, and we all will in some way, I can remind myself that even when it feels impossible, I can still take small steps, one at a time, at a pace that I can manage, as I work to make the most of my day.
What are your plans?■
The writer is a licensed clinical psychologist in private practice in Ra’anana and coauthor of The Jewish Journey through Loss: From Death to Healing (Koren Publishers). She has written about psychology in The Jerusalem Post since 2000, specializing in trauma, loss, grief, and bereavement. batyaludman@gmail.com; drbatyaludman.com

People of Israel party chairman Brig.-Gen. (res.) Ofer Winter said that his support for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was not unconditional in an interview with Channel 12’s Meet the Press on Saturday, emphasizing that Netanyahu must abide by his party’s demands if he wishes to retain that support.
“If not, then I’m telling you, Bibi can kiss my ass,” he said when asked how he would respond if Netanyahu did not do so. “I mean this seriously; I don’t work for a person.”
The demands listed by Winter include a decisive military outcome in Gaza, emigration from Gaza, the passing of a law requiring haredi (ultra-Orthodox) citizens to draft to the IDF, and a right-wing coalition that does not depend on United Torah Judaism’s Yitzhak Goldknopf for its 61st Knesset seat.
He told Channel 12 that he would refuse to sit in a government that does not work toward these goals, saying that his party will “not (be) part of it.”
Netanyahu responded to Winter's comments in a video later on Saturday, with the prime minister describing the People of Israel party chairman as "(former prime minister Naftali) Bennett 2."
"If it walks like Bennett, and it sounds like Bennett, it's Bennett," said Netanyahu.
Winter further described the government proposed by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot as “a danger to the State of Israel,” due to its inclusion of Democrats party head Yair Golan and “Arabs.”
“The time has come for true, responsible leadership that unites the true Right and brings it to fight for the people of Israel,” he said. “I disqualify Yair Golan.”
Winter says Hamas 'prepared' for war in built-up area
Winter described a previous conversation with Eisenkot in which he laid out his plan for emigration from Gaza.
“Hamas prepared this war for the built-up area, because it knew it couldn’t stop the State of Israel,” he explained.
“So it puts you in a fight in a built-up area with a population so that it can shout ‘Genocide,’ and the world will stop you. I said: ‘Separate the population, push them away, defeat them.’”
Asked if he ruled out the haredi parties, Winter said that he was “not against the ultra-Orthodox community.”
“I respect Torah scholars,” he said. “But the time has come. ... With Goldknopf, this won’t happen, and we won’t allow it.”
Winter says he will run People of Israel election campaign 'to the end'
Winter added that he plans to continue running his election campaign “to the end.”
“I am a fighter,” he stated. “I don’t stop a fight in the middle, and I will say more than that: I have never abandoned my fighters.”
Winter further described himself as a “public servant,” saying that he fights “for a path, not for a party.”
“We want change, and anyone who wants change – let them vote for the People of Israel,” he concluded.

Four dead as Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida panhandle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
19:08:54 UTC
04:08:54 KST

At least four people were reported dead on Saturday amid Isaias after it made landfall late on Friday on Florida’s panhandle as a category 2 hurricane, according to authorities.
The storm also took down trees, knocked out electricity for hundreds of thousands and flooded highways – but as Saturday evening approached, the region was reopening.
Despite warnings of storm surges ahead of the storm, several major routes along the coast were open by daybreak on Saturday and free of downed trees and power lines typically seen after major hurricanes.
Two of the deaths reported during Isaias occurred in Escambia county, Florida, and two others were reported in Alabama, as the storm moved inland, local officials said. Of those deaths, one each occurred in Escambia and Birmingham, Alabama, when trees fell on homes.
Another person whose death was linked to Isaias was found in a closed garage with a running generator in Escambia county. Four members of that person’s family have been transported to the hospital with carbon monoxide poisoning, the Escambia sheriff’s office said.
“Don’t run any generators inside your home, it can be very, very hazardous,” Florida governor Ron DeSantis said in a press conference.
In Alabama, governor Kay Ivey said Isaias – predicted to dissipate on Sunday – “cannot clear fast enough”.
Meanwhile, though it had weakened on Saturday to a post-tropical cyclone as it passed through central Alabama, Isaias still posed flooding and tornado threats as it moved inland, forecasters and officials warned.
Hurricane-force winds in the Florida panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city’s mayor said the airport “took some damage”. The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach.
A worker in a condominium parking lot swept piles of the building’s insulation while others put back beach chairs that had been tossed about.
“Remember, there can still be flooding from rising rivers,” Jared W Perdue, the secretary of Florida’s state transportation department, said at a news conference. “I’m just going to remind all of you – please, if there’s standing water or flowing water on top of a road, please do not drive through it.
“It does not have to be that deep, and it can wash away your car, it can wash away a human, it can become very dangerous very quickly.”
Nearly 550,000 customers were still without power across Florida, Alabama and Georgia on Saturday afternoon as those in the path of the storm began the cleanup process, according to PowerOutage.us. Though still high, the number of outages was down from more than 900,000 earlier on Saturday.
Storm surge and tropical storm warnings associated with Isaias by then had been discontinued, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned there would still likely be “considerable impacts” associated with Isaias across much of southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and south-western Georgia.
“Flash, urban and river flooding is possible across the region,” the NHC said in a Saturday-morning advisory, adding that there was a considerable potential for flash flooding and landslides across the southern Appalachians. “A risk for tornadoes will persist … through [Saturday] afternoon across parts of the eastern Florida panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas.”
Isaias through Sunday is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 4-8in across southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and Big Bend regions, and south-west Georgia. Localized totals up to 15in are possible, particularly within rain bands across the Florida panhandle and Big Bend.
Across much of the remainder of the south-east US, rainfall amounts of 2-5in are expected, and localized higher amounts up to 10in are possible, especially across the southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas.
The hurricane’s maximum sustained winds were 105mph (169km/h). That was intense enough to sound like “a train whistle”, Tim Mowry told the Associated Press after enduring the storm as his home in Pensacola, Florida.
Mowry described losing power on Friday afternoon but said could rely on a generator. He said his son tried to drive to his home after his place about 15 minutes away lost power but had to turn around because downed trees and power lines blocked the road.
All things considered, Mowry said he was “really fortunate” with respect to how he fared during Isaias.
Along Alabama’s Gulf coast, authorities in Mobile reported numerous downed trees and power lines.
Maranie Adams, who rode out the storm with her family and their chickens in Gulf Shores, Alabama, said the winds rocked their home, but it was nothing like Hurricane Sally, which left water under their elevated house.
“I feel very much more relieved today,” she said.
Donald Trump has allowed the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to provide resources to Georgia to help grapple with the ongoing storm, including possible tornadoes, the agency said on Saturday.
Several roads have already been blocked by fallen trees around Atlanta, local outlets have reported.
Trump previously approved emergency declarations for Florida and Alabama ahead of the landfall of Hurricane Isaias.
While the stronger El Niño seemed to limit the number of hurricanes in the Atlantic for the year so far, Isaias forming in October with maximum sustained winds of 105mph marked a stark contrast from historical trends.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) predicted a quiet year in terms of hurricanes at the beginning of a season that officially begins annually on 1 June. Noaa anticipated between three and six hurricanes, well below the average of seven. An August forecast from Noaa cut the expected number to between two and six.
Isais is one of the two latest-forming Atlantic hurricanes on record, tying a record set on 8 October 1905. Otherwise, the second-latest date for the first Atlantic hurricane was 11 September – in 2002 and 2013.
None of the eight previous named storms of the 2026 Atlantic season intensified above tropical storm status.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

US man shoots off-duty ICE agent who allegedly attacked him and daughter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
19:03:30 UTC
04:03:30 KST

A 72-year-old man shot an off-duty Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) official in California early on Friday morning after the “intoxicated and agitated” official assaulted him and his daughter on their property, local authorities allege.
The Fresno police department said that the ICE official was receiving medical care after being shot in the midsection. The official, identified as David Gonzalez, is facing felony charges for assaulting the father-daughter duo, Fresno police said.
It was not immediately clear for how long Gonzalez had been with ICE and what exactly he did for ICE. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, referred all questions about Gonzalez to Fresno police.
According to Fresno police, at about 3am, a woman found Gonzalez sleeping on her and her father’s front lawn. She told her 72-year-old father, who was inside, and then attempted to shoo Gonzalez off their property.
But when Gonzalez was awakened, “he appeared intoxicated and agitated” and physically assaulted the 72-year-old father, forcing him to the ground, police said. When the father’s daughter tried to intervene, Gonzalez physically attacked and took her to the ground as well, police said.
The father feared for his and his daughter’s physical safety and shot Gonzalez once, police said. Shortly thereafter, the daughter’s boyfriend, an off-duty police officer, arrived and placed handcuffs on Gonzalez.
“It is unknown at this time why Gonzalez was in the area at the time of the [shooting], but it has been confirmed he was off-duty and alone,” local authorities said.
Fresno police on Friday said the investigation into the shooting was continuing while Gonzalez was in custody and receiving medical treatment. He was booked with battery likely to cause great bodily injury, felony vandalism and battery.
The father and daughter were not booked with any crimes as they recovered from injuries of their own, police said.
The confrontation that led to Gonzalez’s shooting is one of the latest cases in which federal ICE officials have fallen under scrutiny for alleged criminal behavior. ICE has also been met with nationwide criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second term for the agency’s aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics.
Lawmakers have also criticized ICE’s hiring practices amid the agency’s rush to bring on more officials to carry out the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda. In August 2025, an ICE supervisor filed a whistleblower complaint to the DHS office of inspector general alleging that the agency was skirting basic vetting and violating federal rules during its hiring spree.
In July, an ICE officer shot and killed a Colombian immigrant in Biddeford, Maine. The ICE officer in question had reportedly been a recent hire by the agency despite an alleged history of violence and mental health problems.
Meanwhile, in April, a longtime ICE officer in Cincinnati was arrested after allegedly lying to DHS about domestic violence allegations against him. Local news reports say police had been called more than 20 times in the past to years to the home he shared with his girlfriend.
The Ohio Immigrant Alliance, a pro-immigrant group, released a report in August documenting more than 150 federal immigration officials accused of abuse and crimes. One of the latest entries in their report cited allegations that an ICE official reportedly broke into an ex-girlfriend’s apartment in south-east Louisiana.

Retracing the steps of Mark Dennis, 'brilliant' barrister with a dark side

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10

Retracing the steps of Mark Dennis, the 'brilliant' barrister with a dark side
Warning: This article contains references to child sexual abuse and suicide.
There is a small terrace house in Sydney's inner west that always gave builder Chad Loxsom an uneasy feeling.
"I've been in thousands and thousands of people's houses," he said, but this one "was a little bit strange".
The Leichhardt property belonged to Mark Dennis SC, a criminal defence barrister, who Loxsom said had a "weird demeanour" and was "just odd".
But what he saw inside is what gnawed at him for years.
"All over the walls of his house, he had dozens upon dozens upon dozens of pictures of him with little kids," he said.
In some photos, Loxsom said Dennis was hugging shirtless children.
Loxsom shared his suspicions with an electrician.
"His gut was this guy was doing something bad with kids as well," he said.
The electrician first noticed the "come back with a warrant" doormat, and then the large mirror fixed to the ceiling above Dennis's bed.
But, like Loxsom, what really alarmed him was the sheer volume of photographs in almost every room, even the kitchen.
"It was just disturbing. Like, these kids weren't happy," he said.
Eventually, Loxsom decided to make a report with the child protection hotline.
"I didn't do it straight away, which now I regret," he said.
In January, Dennis came onto the police's radar again when he was searched at Sydney Airport as he returned from a trip to Cambodia.
What was found on his devices led to his arrest, a raid of his house, and child abuse material charges from evidence prosecutors described as "disturbing".
Dennis was released on bail, and soon after, was found dead in his home.
Codenamed Operation Queenstown, Cambodian and Australian national police have been quietly probing Dennis's network and links to famous children's charity Sunrise Cambodia all year.
The ABC travelled to Cambodia in June to retrace Dennis's steps to reveal the inside story of how an accused predator accumulated power within a high-profile charity and gained access to vulnerable children.
In an investigation that combines a tranche of internal documents with dozens of interviews, the ABC can reveal allegations that Dennis sexually harassed a former Sunrise staff member and made teenage girls feel uncomfortable by excessive touching.
The claims raise important questions for all children's charities that must balance the need to fundraise with child safety, as multiple former Sunrise staff say they saw Dennis's bad behaviour but felt they could not report it.
"They saw this," one former staff member told the ABC through a translator. "But they could not do anything because he's a big sponsor."
A spokesperson for Sunrise said they were never aware of any complaints about Dennis and police had told them no current or former Sunrise child had been identified as one of his victims.
The charity defended its child protection policies, saying the children always came first.
'Married to the profession'
Dennis grew up in a large family on Sydney's northern beaches, and by 2001, was a criminal defence barrister with a room at the prestigious Forbes Chambers.
"You don't get to go to Forbes unless you are absolutely brilliant," says one solicitor who briefed Dennis.
"He was one of those people who was married to the profession."
His nickname was "Dark Menace" — a play on words that several acquaintances said reflected his personality and black sense of humour, exemplified by his "WASNTME" personalised number plate.
Across his career, Dennis was known to have mentored junior lawyers and published papers under provocative titles and on topics like defending accused paedophiles and cross-examining child witnesses.
"You need to watch the child witness carefully and assess matters such as intelligence, level of vocabulary and articulation, degree of self-confidence, general demeanour," he wrote in 2017.
One lawyer who knew Dennis for more than a decade said he was "not shocked" by the charges because he had a reputation for sexual harassment and aggression towards women.
"It's one of those situations where, and I know I'm not the only person who's thought about this, I think a lot of us in retrospect are like, 'This was actually f***ing obvious,'" he said.
Three lawyers told the ABC about an incident where Dennis was intoxicated at the 2012 Aboriginal Legal Service (ALS) Christmas party in Sydney, when he lunged at a woman with an open fist.
He was then banned from ALS Christmas parties.
Barrister Charles Waterstreet, who worked at Forbes alongside Dennis for more than a decade until facing his own sexual misconduct allegations, described his former colleague as "very ambitious" but "an oddball".
"He loved a drink, especially on Friday nights," he said. "He sort of became another personality."
In 2011, Dennis began hosting legal conferences to raise funds for his charity, Reasonable Cause, that pledged to help "disadvantaged young Cambodians to further their education".
Tickets cost $450, and the guest list included magistrates, silks and politicians, according to the 2024 invitation.
In interviews with more than 20 sitting Forbes barristers, some were quick to defend their late colleague — insinuating the evidence was thin, based on industry rumours, and one said they did not think his charity work should be "smeared".
"It did such good work. I don't think it was connected … to some sexual interest," they said.
However, despite some celebrating his work and attending his legal conferences, many could not name the charity the money went to.
From sponsor to chairman
The largest recipient of Dennis's fundraising was Sunrise Cambodia — a high-profile children's charity founded by Adelaide-born Geraldine Cox.
Cox has spent decades crisscrossing the globe, and according to her 2011 report, delivering speeches to company executives in the United Arab Emirates, government officials in Australia, private schools, and lawyers like Dennis.
"I flew to Sydney to address a group of lawyers at an event arranged by sponsor Mark Dennis, where over $14,000 was raised. Who said lawyers do not have hearts!" Cox wrote.
Her work has been celebrated internationally. She has won awards, been praised by Australian media and rubbed shoulders with Hollywood celebrities and Australian prime ministers.
Starting in 2008, Dennis personally sponsored a handful of children at Sunrise whom he visited in the orphanages each year. Over time, he backed the whole organisation — raising at least $340,000 in seven years through the legal conferences.
In 2010, he also began funding and attending Sunrise's annual beach holidays to Sihanoukville, a once-sleepy Cambodian coastal town now filled with scam compounds and casinos.
Itineraries for these trips obtained by the ABC show the children played football, shared meals, performed concerts and socialised with sponsors, including Dennis.
Photographs from these trips show Dennis on the beach, and hugging and playing with young children at the hotel. There is no suggestion the photographs are sexual.
A spokesperson for Sunrise said sponsors were not permitted to initiate contact with children.
"However, if a child comes running at a sponsor for a hug, the sponsor is not expected to push them away as this can be very emotionally damaging to a kid who may actually feel safe for the first time in his/her life," they said.
A former Sunrise employee told the ABC it was during one of these beach trips that Dennis was swimming when he went under the water and touched her leg in a sexual manner.
"I felt really afraid," she said. "I kicked Mark off. I was very terrified. He apologised later."
A Sunrise spokesperson said the charity did not know about this allegation and was "very sorry to hear this".
"Had they reported this, we could and would have dealt with it at the time," the spokesperson said.
The woman did not complain formally, but said staff were concerned about Dennis's behaviour and agreed they needed to be "careful" around him to "protect the kids".
The same former employee said she was also concerned about Dennis's behaviour towards an autistic teenage girl living in Sunrise, whom he regularly tried to come close to, and touched her breasts.
She said she saw Dennis entering the girls' and boys' bedrooms at Sunrise, but staff felt there was nothing they could do "because he's a big sponsor" and therefore did not report this.
Eng Sopheak, who lived at Sunrise from the age of five and then worked as Cox's personal driver, also said he witnessed Dennis regularly entering the girls' dormitories.
"I was personally worried," he said, because men were typically not allowed to enter the dormitories.
Sopheak said there needed to be greater separation between sponsors and children.
"My recommendation to sponsors is just that they donate the money, but they don't need to have a relationship with the child," he said.
"So I'd want it to stop."
A spokesperson for Sunrise said dormitories were private areas and as of last year, sponsors were no longer invited to Sihanoukville. They said they had plans to phase out individual child sponsorship but did not specify when.
However, Sunrise's website still allows sponsors to preference the age and gender of children whom they can visit for $50 per month.
'Big boss'
By 2018, Dennis was appointed chairman of the Australian Cambodian Foundation, the registered Australian charity managing donations for Sunrise at the time.
In this role, Dennis was involved in almost every aspect of Sunrise's operations — managing redundancies, approving wages, signing off on hiring policies and even becoming a 49 per cent shareholder of Sunrise's Sihanoukville property, which was valued at more than $US3 million in 2017.
"He was the big boss," said Yi Soksan, who held senior positions at Sunrise between 2011 and 2018.
Soksan said staff were told by Cox to "just trust" Dennis because he was a donor and lawyer, and recalls her saying: "He's my friend, he's one of the big donors and sponsors. He loves Sunrise."
"She advised us, 'He's also the lawyer, so he understands, you know, the rules, the laws. So, just trust him.'"
Cox said she had no recollection of discussing Dennis with staff. While she considered him a friend, she said she had no knowledge of his personal life and never witnessed any bad behaviour.
While chairman, Dennis wielded power over Cox. In an email sent in November 2019, Cox asked for his approval for Sunrise to cover personal expenses.
"Since I offered to reduce my salary … around the time you took over, Mark, I am finding it increasingly difficult to have any sort of normal life," she wrote.
He agreed.
While their relationship was financial and social, it was also fractious.
Emails show Dennis privately described Cox as an "unreliable historian" and "something of a compulsive spender" — descriptions Cox said she could not comment on.
Dennis was granted access to Sunrise's bank accounts in 2018, allowing him to use Sunrise's money to make purchases for children.
Sunrise said this was normal practice, and its current policy permitted donors to purchase gifts for individual children on special occasions like birthdays, capped at $20 per year.
Maggie Eno, who runs Cambodian child welfare charity M'Lop Tapang, was critical of everything from sponsors attending beach holidays to giving gifts to children.
"Individual purchasing … it's grooming," Eno says. "It's horrifying."
Eno, who did not want to comment on Sunrise specifically, said sponsors should never have access to children because criminals were "sophisticated" and "always" had the goal of getting "direct access to the children".
"Paedophiles or child sex offenders don't just groom the child, they groom the family of the child, and they groom the organisation taking care of the child," she said.
"The majority of people are good, kind people, but there is always a risk."
A spokesperson for Sunrise said work was underway to distance relationships between sponsors and children.
'Godfather'
Former Sunrise resident Sok San, now aged 28, was among the children Dennis bought gifts for and socialised with on the beach trips.
He first learned that Dennis was charged and had died when contacted by the ABC, and said he cried.
"He promised to buy me an iPad," San said in June, adding Dennis wanted him to download Facebook on the device.
San said his mother died when he was young, there was violence in his childhood, and he started living in Sunrise at around 10 years old.
He first met Dennis in the orphanage as a child and said Dennis bought him a small watch and gave "toys, books and cookies" to other children.
"He's a good person, and he also came to watch a traditional dance," San said.
He called Dennis "godfather" and said they kept in touch outside Sunrise when he became an adult. They met for ice cream in Siem Reap, and Dennis made promises, like paying for his university studies in America, he said.
Dennis also continued relationships with other children outside Sunrise after his chairmanship ended in 2020.
Facebook messages obtained by the ABC show Dennis maintained direct contact online with children he met through Sunrise.
"I am incredibly proud of you," Dennis wrote to one boy in September 2024.
"Thank you for your support all the years," the boy responded.
Behind Sunrise's gates, emails show staff had been concerned about these relationships for years.
One email shows an employee contacted Sunrise's former operations manager, Rob Madsen, in 2020 for help when he learned Dennis was sending money to a 17-year-old outside Sunrise.
"He has been still supported by Mak [sic] Dennis," the email said. "Many kids living outside [Sunrise] have been supported/sponsored by him secretly."
"Kids requested me to keep it secret as he doesn't want [Sunrise's] managers to know about his support. He buys motorbikes for all kids, school fees, etc."
Sunrise said it had no record of this. They said all children were trained on the dangers of maintaining contact with sponsors after leaving the orphanage, but Sunrise did not have the power or resources to monitor what graduates did.
Final visit
Dennis flew to Cambodia for one final trip in January this year, where he visited Cox's personal residence, a wooden villa on the grounds of Sunrise.
He was in Cambodia on a golfing trip, Cox said, and saw her as a "concerned friend" after hearing she was bedridden following a fall.
Little did she know, this would be Dennis's last visit to Sunrise.
Loading...
When he returned to Sydney, he was intercepted by Australian Border Force officers at the airport who searched his devices and allegedly discovered child abuse material.
Documents released to the ABC under Freedom of Information laws reveal Dennis was communicating this material between 2023 and 2025 to two people, including an account with an Australian number and username "Kanje".
Dennis denied possessing child abuse material in a police interview, but never entered a formal plea.
In a bail hearing the following day, prosecutors said they had discovered an image of a boy aged between six and 10 on his phone, and chat logs where he expressed a desire to rape a 16-year-old.
Commonwealth prosecutor Jon Kisch described the material on Dennis's phone as "disturbing" and "very serious offending", which, if proven, would attract a long jail sentence.
The judge allowed Dennis to be released under strict conditions. Less than three weeks later, he was found dead, leaving behind many unanswered questions.
"I want to know what happened," said one young woman Dennis met through Sunrise.
“I want to know [if] this is true or not. I want to know why. I want to know what happened to him.”

MOSCOW, October 10. /TASS/. The Russian government has partially lifted the country’s ban on diesel exports following agreements reached by the presidents of Russia and the United States, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump, the cabinet said in a statement.
"The government has decided to partially lift Russia’s ban on diesel exports. The decision is aimed at implementing the agreements reached by Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump. It takes effect on October 10, allowing 500,000 metric tons of diesel fuel to be supplied to the global market at this stage," the statement reads.
"Pursuant to the decision, Russian oil companies will immediately begin contracting diesel fuel supplies with foreign counterparties in coordination with the government," the cabinet added.

Putin and Trump held a phone call on October 9, particularly discussing petroleum product supplies. The Russian president said that Moscow had reiterated its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the United States and global markets. According to Novak, Russia will lift its ban on diesel exports ahead of schedule and is ready to supply 300,000 tons of diesel in October, increasing the volume to 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons in December. Monthly supplies could subsequently reach 3 million tons. The US administration, in turn, issued a general license authorizing Russian diesel supplies to the global market until April 7, 2027.

The first half ended with Fenerbahce holding a 1-0 advantage.

The final whistle confirmed a 3-0 away win for Fenerbahce, who claimed all three points with a strong finish to the match.

The moment I knew: We were babysitting my younger siblings and he wore a tutu to make them laugh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
19:00:08 UTC
04:00:08 KST

In 2017 I was 16, went to an all-girls Catholic school in Melbourne and had zero tolerance for teenage boys and their nonsense. Instead I spent a lot of gossip time lamenting Jake, who broke my tiny heart in primary school and then moved hours away.
A debutante ball was coming up. It was an expensive tradition that was fundamentally at odds with my values but I couldn’t say no to a pretty dress and dancing – I was a teenage girl, after all. Some friends asked cousins or co-workers from our part-time jobs to be partners. I got knocked back by everyone. When I complained to my mother, she let me know Jake had moved back to town, and did she want me to ask his mum if he would be willing?
Jake accepted and we spent weeks rehearsing. My mum would pick him up on the way to the dance hall and we would sit in the back seat, catching up on the last five years and laughing at our juvenile romance. It felt as though we just clicked again, and our giggly behaviour during dance rehearsals earned us more than one disapproving look from the teacher.
I was done for. I frantically asked my friends: did they think he might like me too? Should I ask him to my year 11 formal? Should I kiss him on deb night?
The ball was wonderful. While everyone else hit the dancefloor, Jake and I hit the couch in the foyer and stayed there all night talking. We missed dessert and I couldn’t find the courage to kiss him but he asked me to see a movie with him the next day.
On our first date – where we were dropped off at the local cinema with a curfew – I had my first kiss. I almost chipped my tooth.
The first months of our relationship were full of nonstop texting during the day and after-school visits with my bedroom door wide open.
I was surprised at how earnest he was; I felt as though I didn’t have to pretend to be a cooler version of myself. I wrote in my diary about how excited I was to finally have my “ill-fated teenage whirlwind romance”. I figured if I held on to the idea that we’d break up, then I wouldn’t get hurt.
About two months into our relationship, my mother tasked Jake and I with babysitting my younger siblings. We weren’t technically allowed to spend the evening in my room with the door closed but that didn’t stop us. After a few hours of laughing at YouTube videos, I went to have a shower and heard a crash down the hallway. My little sister had dropped a plate and it had shattered all over the tiles. I rushed out to help before she started crying. But when I got there, she and Jake were already cleaning up together and giggling. I snuck back to the bathroom with relief. Jake was good with my siblings and that was important to me.
Later that night I wandered into our lounge room to find Jake elbow-deep in our dress-up box and wearing a bright-orange tutu. My sister was beside him wearing a white wig. They ran around the room, Jake spinning like a ballerina to make her laugh. Neither of them noticed me. I stood and watched as I came to terms with the sudden feeling of certainty in my chest.
Lying in the dark that night, I told Jake I loved him. It flew out of my mouth before I could stop myself. I remember my heart playing jazz while I waited for his response. He whispered, “I love you too” and hearing him sound so sure made me cry.
Nine years on, my “ill-fated teenage whirlwind romance” has turned into a loving, long-term relationship.
Jake and I make each other laugh more than anything else. Life might throw a curveball but one of us is sure to make a joke about it. We often fall into comedic improv bits when we’re together, and I’m sure our neighbours think we are completely nuts when they hear us bicker like old people for the fun of it. But it’s safe. And it’s home.
Being with the same person since age 16 might seem crazy but I always say that kids are dumb, not stupid. I knew back then what I know now – that the right person will show up even if it seems too early. You just grow together. Jake may have broken my little heart once but I’m willing to have him hold it now for good.

Scientists may have found a shortcut to fusion energy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
18:57:27 UTC
03:57:27 KST

Scientists may have found a shortcut to fusion energy
Scientists have uncovered a potentially far more efficient path to fusion ignition that could bring the dream of practical fusion energy closer to reality.
- Date:
- October 10, 2026
- Source:
- Princeton University
- Summary:
- Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory may have found a dramatically more efficient route to fusion energy by reversing the traditional approach: heating plasma first, then increasing its density. Their calculations could help future reactors reach self-sustaining fusion with far less energy while avoiding hidden problems that make ignition harder.
- Share:
Scientists at the U.S.Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) have identified a potentially much more efficient way to achieve fusion ignition, a major milestone in the pursuit of practical fusion energy. Their calculations suggest that changing the order in which plasma is heated and compressed could dramatically reduce the energy needed to reach a self-sustaining fusion reaction.
For more than seven decades, fusion researchers have relied on a mathematical rule to determine whether plasma can remain sufficiently hot and dense, for a long enough period, to sustain fusion without additional external heating. Known as the Lawson criterion, this equation defines the conditions required for ignition. However, it does not explain the most efficient way to achieve them.
Now, PPPL physicists Luis Delgado-Aparicio, Masayuki Ono, and Jonathan Menard have developed a more comprehensive version of the criterion. By incorporating four additional factors that influence fusion performance, they have mapped a promising route to ignition that could require substantially less energy than alternative approaches.
Their findings were published in the journal Physical Review Letters.
The research focuses on plasma, often called the fourth state of matter. Plasma forms when a gas becomes so energetic that its particles carry electrical charges. In fusion reactors, this extremely hot material contains the atomic nuclei that researchers hope to combine, releasing energy through nuclear fusion.
The ultimate goal is to produce a burning plasma, in which fusion reactions generate enough heat to sustain the process without continued external heating. Reaching this state efficiently remains one of the most important challenges in fusion energy research.
Scientists Find a Shortcut to Fusion Ignition
Delgado-Aparicio compares the discovery to finding a more efficient route through a mountain range.
Imagine that the energy requirements for fusion ignition form a landscape dominated by a towering mountain. The destination lies on the other side, but there are several possible routes to reach it.
Many proposed fusion strategies effectively attempt to climb directly over the mountain. They begin by increasing the density of the plasma and then supplying the enormous amount of heat needed to reach ignition.
The new calculations suggest that a different sequence could be considerably more efficient. Instead of increasing density first, researchers could heat the plasma before making it denser. This alternative route avoids the highest energy requirements while still reaching the desired conditions.
"A lot of companies want to climb the mountain head-on and spend enormous energy to get there," Delgado-Aparicio said. "Go around the peak instead. You reach the same place in a much smarter way, and you use far less energy."
The Hidden Mountain Pass in Fusion Physics
The researchers identified a particularly important region of this mathematical landscape called the Cordey saddle.
In geographical terms, a saddle is a low passage between higher elevations. In fusion physics, the Cordey saddle represents a relatively accessible point along the boundary separating plasma that still needs outside heating from plasma capable of sustaining its own fusion reactions.
To evaluate different routes, the scientists used a measurement called Q, which compares the power produced by fusion reactions with the external heating power supplied to the plasma.
For example, a Q value of 5 means the fusion reactions produce five times as much power as the external heating system delivers.
In an idealized plasma containing only pure fusion fuel, the Cordey saddle occurs at approximately Q = 5. However, actual fusion systems are much more complicated. Contaminants within the plasma and extremely strong magnetic fields can shift the location of this passage, increasing the Q value needed to reach it.
Understanding how these conditions change is essential for determining whether a proposed fusion reactor can realistically achieve ignition.
A More Realistic Roadmap for Future Fusion Reactors
The findings could influence the design of two major types of magnetic fusion devices: tokamaks and stellarators.
Both approaches use powerful magnetic fields to confine plasma while it is heated to the extraordinary temperatures needed for fusion. Tokamaks, which have a characteristic doughnut shape, are among the leading technologies being investigated for future fusion power plants.
Research institutions and private companies are pursuing several different ways to generate electricity from fusion and eventually deliver that power to the electrical grid. Identifying an efficient route to ignition could help engineers design more practical systems while avoiding costly mistakes.
For PPPL, this work is part of a broader effort to address the scientific and technological challenges that must be overcome before commercial fusion power becomes possible, including the development of future fusion pilot plants.
One of the study's major advances is that it evaluates several important physical processes together rather than examining them separately, as much previous research has done.
The researchers incorporated four additional factors that can influence whether a plasma reaches and maintains ignition:
- Helium ash buildup: Fusion reactions produce helium as a byproduct. As this spent fuel accumulates, it can dilute the remaining fusion fuel and reduce performance.
- Plasma contamination: Light and heavy impurities can enter the plasma from materials lining the inside of the reactor, interfering with fusion conditions.
- Synchrotron radiation: Electrons traveling through magnetic fields emit radiation, carrying energy away from the plasma.
- Heat loss: Energy continuously escapes from the plasma, and these losses can become greater as its temperature rises.
Accounting for these effects produces a more realistic picture of the conditions future reactors must achieve.
"When you leave these effects out, you say the design will work fine," Ono said. "When you put them in, the picture changes, and it becomes quite important."
According to Ono, the goal is to establish a more reliable, widely applicable model that scientists can use to evaluate fusion reactor designs before construction begins.
Treating the Lawson criterion as a single unchanging threshold overlooks physical processes that can substantially alter the requirements for ignition. Including those effects early in the design process could prevent expensive problems later.
"Fusion experiments cost a great deal of money, and you do not want to make mistakes you could have caught beforehand," he said.
Tiny Amounts of Tungsten Could Make Fusion Much Harder
One particularly striking finding concerns tungsten, an extremely heat-resistant metal selected for the interior walls of more than a dozen next-generation fusion machines.
Tungsten is attractive because fusion reactors must withstand conditions involving plasma temperatures greater than those found at the center of the sun. However, the material also presents a significant challenge if even tiny quantities enter the plasma.
The team's calculations show that tungsten contamination at a concentration of just one part in 10,000 can approximately double the pressure required to achieve fusion ignition.
That is a substantial increase caused by an exceptionally small amount of material.
The calculations were initially developed in two dimensions. When the researchers extended their analysis to three dimensions, they found that the pressure needed for ignition could exceed the limits at which the plasma remains stable.
This suggests that seemingly minor contamination could have major consequences for the feasibility of certain fusion reactor designs.
How Energy Losses Could Help Stabilize Fusion
Surprisingly, some of the processes that make ignition more difficult may also help fusion reactors operate more safely and consistently.
Scientists have long investigated the possibility of thermal "runaway" instability. This occurs when heat from fusion reactions increases the reaction rate, producing still more heat and potentially creating a self-reinforcing cycle.
The researchers found that energy losses within the plasma can naturally counteract this effect.
Although those losses increase the difficulty of reaching ignition, they also provide a balancing influence that could allow a burning plasma to maintain a stable operating state without constant adjustments.
This balance could be valuable for future reactor designs.
(Unlike a fission power plant, a fusion system holds only seconds of fuel at a time, so losing control means the plasma cools and the burn stops rather than anything worse.)
Liquid Lithium and Advanced Fuel Could Improve Fusion Efficiency
The study also identifies technologies that might help overcome some of the obstacles revealed by the calculations.
One possibility involves coating the inside of fusion reactors with liquid lithium, a technique PPPL researchers have investigated for years.
These coatings could help prevent tungsten from entering the plasma while reducing heat losses, making it easier to maintain the extreme conditions necessary for fusion.
Another promising approach uses spin-polarized fuel. This involves preparing the atomic nuclei so that their spins are aligned before fusion occurs, which can increase the fusion reaction rate.
Together, these strategies could improve the performance of future reactors and make the path to ignition more achievable.
What Comes Next for the New Fusion Strategy?
Despite the promising findings, the proposed heat-first approach has not yet been demonstrated experimentally.
The research is theoretical and relies on mathematical calculations rather than direct measurements. Existing fusion experiments have not reached the temperatures associated with the Cordey saddle, preventing scientists from testing the predicted route under those conditions.
The PPPL team plans to investigate the approach further through digital experiments, using computer-based simulations to explore whether heating plasma before increasing its density can deliver the expected advantages.
If future studies confirm the calculations, the findings could provide an important foundation for designing more efficient fusion systems and help researchers make better decisions about reactor construction.
"While more study is needed, we are excited by these results, and they suggest a clear path forward for future research in this area," said Menard.
The work was supported by the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences, under contract DE-AC02-09CH11466. Additional support came through a 2015 Fusion Energy Sciences Early Career Award, a 2018 Diagnostic Innovation and Development award, and the 2021 and 2025 Long-Pulse Tokamak Research Programs.

Loneliness may steal nearly 6 years of good health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
18:57:02 UTC
03:57:02 KST

Loneliness may steal nearly 6 years of good health
Loneliness and social isolation may cost people years of healthy life, with an especially striking toll on mental health.
- Date:
- October 10, 2026
- Source:
- Tulane University
- Summary:
- A large study suggests loneliness and social isolation can cost people years of healthy life, especially when it comes to mental health. Men experiencing both lost about 5.8 years free from depression and anxiety, while women lost roughly 3.7 years.
- Share:
Loneliness and social isolation are widespread in the United States. According to a 2023 report, about half of U.S. adults experience loneliness, while nearly as many are socially isolated. Despite health consequences that can rival other major risk factors, both problems remain relatively overlooked as urgent public health concerns.
Until recently, however, researchers had little idea how many years of good health might actually be lost to loneliness and social isolation.
Loneliness Linked to Fewer Healthy Years
Researchers at Tulane University's Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public and Tropical Medicine have now attempted to put a number on that toll. Their first-of-its-kind observational study, published in Nature Communications, found that loneliness and social isolation were associated with the loss of nearly six years of life free from mental disorders such as depression and anxiety. The effects on physical health were smaller, but still significant.
"Overall, the study found that social isolation and loneliness can have a significant impact on disease-free life expectancy," said lead author Lu Qi, HCA Regents Distinguished Chair and professor in Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public and Tropical Medicine at Tulane. "This includes both physical and mental disease."
Although loneliness and social isolation are often treated as the same thing in everyday conversation, researchers distinguish between them. Social isolation refers to an objective lack of social connections. Loneliness, by contrast, describes a person's subjective dissatisfaction with the quality of their relationships, regardless of how many social interactions they actually have.
"The findings weren't surprising to me," Qi said. "Previous studies found that social isolation and loneliness are related to mortality, especially premature mortality, and this study provides additional evidence."
Tracking More Than 277,000 Adults
The researchers analyzed data from 277,489 adults between the ages of 40 and 69. At the beginning of the study, none had seven major chronic conditions: diabetes, heart disease, lung disease, dementia, cancer, depression and anxiety.
Using age 50 as a reference point, the team calculated how loneliness and social isolation were associated with the number of years participants could expect to live without these diseases.
Compared with people who experienced neither loneliness nor social isolation, women experiencing both had 2.4 fewer years free from physical disease. Men experiencing both had 1.7 fewer years.
The difference was even larger for mental health. Women experiencing both loneliness and social isolation lived about 3.7 fewer years without mental disorders, while men lived approximately 5.8 fewer years free from those conditions.
"This comes down to the gender differences between men and women," Qi said. "Our research found men are more susceptible to being affected by loneliness. We also know that women tend to live longer than men. There are gender advantages with certain diseases."
Healthy Habits Help With Isolation, but Not Loneliness
The researchers also examined whether lifestyle could alter these associations. Healthier habits, including better diet, regular exercise, sufficient sleep, and not smoking, measurably reduced the loss of disease-free years associated with social isolation.
Loneliness produced a different pattern. A healthier lifestyle did not significantly reduce the additional health risks linked to feeling lonely. That distinction suggests loneliness and social isolation may require different approaches when it comes to protecting health.
The research team plans to study additional population groups in the future and use clinical trials to investigate whether loneliness and social isolation directly cause the health effects observed in the study.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Tulane University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Xuan Wang, Hao Ma, Yoriko Heianza, Zhaoxia Liang, Oscar H. Franco, Lu Qi. Associations of loneliness, social isolation and healthy lifestyle with life expectancy free of major physical disease and mental disorder. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-74498-8

MIT astronomers catch a star in a feast that could last billions of years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
18:56:25 UTC
03:56:25 KST

MIT astronomers catch a star in a feast that could last billions of years
Scientists discovered a star slowly eating its brown dwarf companion in a cosmic feast that could last billions of years.
- Date:
- October 10, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- Astronomers have discovered a bizarre star system about 300 light-years from Earth where a small star is slowly devouring a nearby brown dwarf, an object too massive to be a planet but too small to be a true star. Unlike stars that rapidly swallow their companions, this one is gradually stealing material in a process that could continue for billions of years.
- Share:
Astronomers have discovered an unusual star system about 300 light-years from Earth where a small star is gradually consuming a nearby brown dwarf. Instead of swallowing its companion in one dramatic event, the star is steadily pulling material from it, creating a cosmic feeding process that could continue for billions of years.
Most planets, including Earth, travel around their stars in relatively stable orbits. But these peaceful arrangements can sometimes end violently. If a planet ventures too close to its host star, the star's gravity can drag it inward and eventually engulf it.
Scientists have observed many planetary systems with stable orbits, along with a small number of stars caught rapidly swallowing their planetary companions. Now, researchers have identified something that falls between those two extremes.
In a study published October 5 in Nature Astronomy, an international team led by scientists at MIT describes a star that is slowly feeding on a brown dwarf, an object more massive than a typical planet but not massive enough to sustain the hydrogen fusion that powers ordinary stars.
The system, designated ZTF J0440+2325, lies within our Milky Way galaxy approximately 300 light-years away. It is the first observed example of a low-mass star steadily drawing material from another low-mass object.
Even more remarkably, the transfer of material appears to be happening so slowly that the star could continue feeding on its companion for hundreds of thousands of years, potentially even billions.
"When we think of stars interacting with planets or brown dwarfs, the picture is always that the star eventually swallows the other thing," says Kevin Burdge, assistant professor of physics at MIT. "This is what will happen to the Earth when the sun becomes a red giant. But here, we've found an alternative: Instead of swallowing the thing up, the star can gradually eat it, for billions of years."
The MIT research team also includes Aaron Householder, Kaitlyn Shin, Saul Rappaport, Joheen Chakraborty, and Emma Chickles. Additional collaborators contributed from Caltech, the University of Hawaii, the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias and Universidad de La Laguna in Spain, and the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics.
A Mysterious Signal That Puzzled Astronomers for Years
The first clue to this unusual stellar relationship came from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF), an astronomical survey that searches for objects whose brightness changes over time.
Operating with a telescope at Palomar Observatory in California, ZTF repeatedly photographs large sections of the night sky. Its sensitive camera can detect sudden or unusual changes in light that may indicate powerful cosmic events, including exploding stars called supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and collisions between neutron stars.
Several years ago, while examining observations collected by ZTF, Burdge noticed a particularly strange pattern.
Astronomers study changes in an object's brightness using a graph called a light curve. For some supernovae, these graphs form a rounded, bell-like shape as the exploding star grows brighter and then gradually fades.
The signal Burdge encountered looked completely different. Instead of a smooth rise and fall, the brightness repeatedly traced something resembling a triangle.
"I remember first looking at this and thinking, stars don't make triangular waveforms like this," he recalls.
At the time, Burdge and his colleagues were investigating another unusual signal that turned out to originate from a system known as a "black widow binary."
These systems contain a neutron star, the extraordinarily dense remnant of a massive star, that spins rapidly while stripping material from a much smaller companion. They are named after black widow spiders because of the way the neutron star gradually destroys its partner.
Burdge initially considered whether the repeating triangular signal might come from another black widow system. However, the observations did not match what astronomers normally expect.
In a typical black widow binary, the strong contrast between the masses of the two objects produces a distinctive motion. The smaller companion moves rapidly around the much heavier neutron star, creating detectable changes in the light reaching Earth.
But the mysterious triangular signal showed no evidence of the same pronounced motion.
"We weren't seeing that whipping back and forth here," Burdge says. "It didn't make any sense. We couldn't explain what this was."
That discrepancy led the researchers to consider another possibility. Perhaps the system did not contain one extremely massive object paired with a much lighter companion. Instead, both objects might have relatively small masses, allowing them to orbit each other with much less dramatic motion.
"If you have less mass in the system overall, things can gently orbit each other without whipping back and forth," Burdge says. "That was the idea. But we never had any proof. And this weird triangle just sat for years."
A Brown Dwarf That Orbits Its Star Every 87 Minutes
Eventually, Burdge and Aaron Householder, a graduate student in MIT's Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, returned to the unexplained signal.
Using the original ZTF observations, they identified its source as an object roughly 300 light-years away in the Milky Way. They then directed several telescopes toward the system, ZTF J0440+2325, to investigate its properties in greater detail.
A key measurement involved determining how much the system's objects move in response to their mutual gravitational attraction. Although the researchers detected some wobbling, it was far smaller than the motion typically associated with black widow binaries.
"That was the real clincher for this system," Householder says. "When we measured that wobble, we found we were not seeing a black widow. This was a low-mass star that's orbited by a brown dwarf. The wobble was too small in amplitude to be anything else."
The observations revealed two unusually compact objects orbiting at an extremely close distance.
The central star has approximately 85 times the mass of Jupiter, while the brown dwarf weighs about 25 Jupiter masses. For comparison, the Sun is more than 1,000 times as massive as Jupiter.
The brown dwarf completes a full revolution around its host star in just 87 minutes. Its entire orbit is so small that it would fit within the diameter of the Sun.
That extraordinarily close arrangement suggested that gravity might be doing more than simply keeping the objects in orbit. The researchers suspected that the star could be actively pulling matter away from the brown dwarf.
Scientists Discover a New Form of Stellar Cannibalism
When one astronomical object draws gas or other material from another, astronomers call the process accretion.
Accretion is especially familiar in systems involving black holes and neutron stars. Although these objects can be extremely massive, their physical dimensions are relatively small. Material falling toward a black hole, for example, often forms a swirling disk around it before moving inward.
But ZTF J0440+2325 appears to work differently.
Rather than a black hole or neutron star collecting matter, an ordinary low-mass star is receiving material from a nearby brown dwarf. Because the star has a much larger physical surface than a compact object such as a black hole, the incoming material can strike it directly.
"The difference here is, the thing absorbing matter is not a tiny black hole but a star, which is relatively big in size," Burdge explains. "So matter just pummels directly onto the surface, at very high speeds, like an asteroid hitting the Moon."
To investigate whether this was actually happening, the researchers created computer simulations of the system.
They modeled particles originating from the brown dwarf and calculated how those particles would move under the gravitational influence of both objects. The simulations incorporated the measured properties of the star and its companion, along with the physical equations governing orbital motion.
The results supported the team's suspicion. Material leaving the brown dwarf followed trajectories that carried it directly into the star.
"When we track those test particles, we see they indeed fall right onto the surface of the star," Householder says. "This is the first time we've caught a low-mass star actively accreting from another low-mass object."
A Cosmic Feast That Could Continue for Billions of Years
The team also estimated how quickly the brown dwarf is losing material.
According to their calculations, the star is consuming approximately one hundred-thousandth of Earth's mass every year.
That amount may sound insignificant, but it represents an enormous quantity of material. The researchers compare it to approximately 40 million dump trucks' worth of matter, or about 1.3 trillion one-pound burritos every second.
Despite those staggering figures, the brown dwarf is so massive that this material loss represents only a tiny portion of its total mass.
In astronomical terms, the feeding process is remarkably gradual.
Based on the properties of the system and the estimated rate of mass transfer, researchers believe the star could continue drawing matter from its companion for billions of years.
Instead of a sudden, catastrophic collision that destroys the smaller object, the star appears to be sustaining a relatively steady flow of material from its neighbor.
That realization also helped explain the strange triangular light pattern that first attracted Burdge's attention.
As matter streams from the brown dwarf toward the star, it strikes the stellar surface at high speeds, generating an intensely heated region.
This bright hotspot acts like a persistent fireball on the star.
As the brown dwarf moves through its 87-minute orbit, the hotspot repeatedly rotates into and out of the observer's view. Those changes in visibility produce the distinctive pattern of brightening and dimming that the astronomers had struggled to understand.
"It's like you've got this continuous fireball onto one of the objects, and as one orbits the other, that hotspot comes in and out of view, and the peak of the triangle signal is when you're looking right at the fireball," Burdge explains.
A Strange Star System Opens a New Window Into Planetary Evolution
With the triangular signal finally explained, the researchers are now interested in identifying other stellar systems that behave in similar ways.
Until now, observations of close interactions between stars and their planetary companions have largely emphasized either stable orbits or relatively rapid engulfment events.
ZTF J0440+2325 demonstrates that another possibility exists. Under the right conditions, a small star can steadily extract matter from a nearby brown dwarf without immediately destroying it.
Finding additional examples could help astronomers determine how common this process is, how long it can persist, and what ultimately happens to objects trapped in such extraordinarily close relationships.
The discovery may also provide new insights into the evolution of planets and brown dwarfs that orbit near their host stars.
"It's inspiring a lot of new searches on our part," Householder says. "I think we're going to learn a lot about a different kind of way that planets and brown dwarfs interact with their host stars."
This research received partial support from the National Science Foundation.
Story Source:

Kulkarni, Pablo Rodríguez-Gil, Andrew Vanderburg, Samuel Whitebook. Stable mass transfer from a substellar object onto an M dwarf. Nature Astronomy, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-02992-6

AI generated
GENEVA – The World Health Organisation said on Oct 10 that it still does not know what caused the pneumonia that killed a Russian laboratory worker at an anti-plague research centre in Siberia this month, and that no case of plague had been registered.
The WHO said the Russian state regulator reported that tests of the laboratory worker and those who came in contact with her were negative for the high-threat pathogens tested, that her contacts still showed no symptoms, and that no further linked cases of severe pneumonia had been identified.
“Based on the information provided... WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event. A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker,” it said in a statement.
The lab worker fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on Oct 2, prompting the authorities to quarantine about 200 people and causing public health fears.
Global health officials have been extra alert to fatal pneumonia cases of undetermined cause since the Covid-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading fatal respiratory illness in China.
The cause of individual pneumonia cases often cannot be determined.
Russian authorities have said the lab worker was appropriately vaccinated and that they found no micro-organisms linked to her work in her body.
On Oct 8, Russia said it had completed health checks on all the worker’s contacts.
It says it provided full information to the WHO according to established procedures. REUTERS

Pentagon raises US troop death toll in Iran war to 21
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
