Ukrinform presents ‘Commanders of Victory’ book at Donbas Media Forum 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:28:00 UTC
02:28:00 KST

Ukrinform presents ‘Commanders of Victory’ book at Donbas Media Forum 2026
Ukrinform Director General Serhii Cherevatyi stressed the importance of telling the public about the efforts of Ukrainian service members to defend the country and shape its modern history in order to counter negative information trends.
“We began this project as a series of interviews. The first was with Pavlo Palisa, who at the time commanded the renowned 93rd Kholodnyi Yar Brigade and with whom I had the honor of serving in the Khortytsia Operational-Strategic Group of Forces. As we worked on all the materials, we realized that publishing the interviews on our website would not be enough. We needed a larger project to preserve the experience of Ukrainian commanders, document the contemporary history of the war and bring it to the public. That is how the idea for the book we are presenting today came about,” he said.
According to the agency’s head, Commanders of Victory is not merely a collection of interviews with leaders from various branches of Ukraine’s Defense Forces, including Kyrylo Budanov, Oleksandr Pivnenko and Oleh Ivashchenko, but also a historical document. He also noted that the project is available online.
Andrii Yusov, a representative of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine, emphasized the importance of high-quality publications that can serve as gifts and research resources and be made available in libraries and government institutions.
“This is not just a book. It is an entire communications project, both multimedia and physical. Most importantly, it is about people. Ukraine has heroes. Ukrainian heroes are outstanding. We need to talk about them. This matters to service members who continue serving under difficult conditions, to veterans, to growing children and to Ukrainian citizens as a whole. And it matters for securing support for Ukraine around the world,” he said.
Yusov added that the world must be continually reminded of Russian aggression.
The book was created by the Ukrinform team, which independently handled every stage of production, from preparing and editing journalistic materials to design, layout and prepress work.
A distinctive feature of the publication is its clasp, which incorporates a cartridge case and a bullet at the end. These elements were specially created for the project by Olha Konoval, wife of Hero of Ukraine Serhii Konoval and Head of the Serhii Konoval Foundation.
She explained that the cartridge cases came from the Serebrianskyi Forest, allowing readers to literally touch an object connected to the war.
“Every cartridge case you hold in your hands has already done its job. It has been spent. I put this element together in a very interesting way. The cartridge case is from an M4A1, while the bullet is from a Kalashnikov rifle. In other words, we combined things that do not go together; this is not a live round,” she said.
The presentation also featured a panel discussion with people profiled in the book: Pavlo Kurylenko, Deputy Head of the Current Operations Directorate at the Headquarters of the Joint Forces Command; Oleksandr “Pryvyd” (“Ghost”), a sniper platoon commander with the Separate Presidential Brigade named after Hetman Bohdan Khmelnytskyi; and Dmytro Finashyn, an adviser to Ukraine’s Minister of Internal Affairs on veterans’ policy and a Hero of Ukraine.
1 / 14
The discussion focused, in particular, on the role of the media in documenting the war and preserving the voices of those directly leading Ukraine’s Defense Forces toward victory.
As reported, Ukrinform previously presented Commanders of Victory to cadets at the Kyiv Institute of the National Guard of Ukraine.

The Kyiv City State Administration has urged residents of the capital to stock up on water and food, insulate their premises, and charge power banks and portable charging stations.
Source: Kyiv City State Administration (KCSA)
Quote: "Power engineers are working round the clock to restore electricity to all consumers, while utility services are working to return water supplies to normal.
Advertisement:
However, the intensity of the attacks is increasing. Therefore, the city authorities, as in previous years, are urging Kyivites to take care of the most essential individual supplies."
Details: The KCSA has released the following recommendations for Kyiv residents:
- Stock up on drinking water and water for household use. Each adult needs 3 litres of drinking water and 10-12 litres of water for hygiene and cooking per day. Ideally, you should have enough supplies to last at least three days. In Kyiv, 155 pump rooms are equipped to operate on generators during power cuts.
- Charge power banks and portable charging stations.
- Insulate your premises – seal window joints and check the external insulation of windows, and place Alufom or other heat-insulating material between the wall and the radiator.
- Stock up on torches, battery-powered lamps, candles, matches, batteries, etc.
- Stock up on long shelf-life food and food that does not require electricity to prepare.
- Ensure safe movement on the streets in the dark. Wear reflective clothing or reflective strips on your sleeve, bag or backpack.
- Follow official information from the city authorities.

Russian Attack on Ukrainian City Kills 20, a Day After Trump Eases Diesel Sanctions on Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:26:05 UTC
02:26:05 KST

Twenty people, including three children, were killed in a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Saturday, a day after United States President Donald Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel in a major setback for Kyiv.
"Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, in some of his sharpest criticism yet of the White House.
Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment with strikes intensifying in the past few months.
A 6-year-old girl was among those killed when one strike reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled it from the wreckage.
"Her birthday would have been at the end of the month," he said through tears.
Eighteen others were wounded in the attack on the industrial city, with a pre-war population of over 700,000 and whose outskirts lie less than 30 km (20 miles) from the front line.
Russia Escalating Attacks on Ukrainian Cities
It was the third mass-casualty attack on Ukraine this week.
Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, including at least 30 killed by a bomb in the eastern garrison city of Kramatorsk and 22 others by a missile in the town of Pryluky, 80 miles east of Kyiv.
A senior official in Zaporizhzhia, Mykhailo Semikin, said Russia had hit several locations simultaneously in the early hours of Saturday.
Rescuers clambered through crumbled masonry to pull other residents of the building out alive. One man, whose leg was trapped in the rubble, screamed in pain as he was being freed.
"If (the Russians) have money, they’ll be able to carry on fighting us," said Nataliia Malysheva, a 49-year-old local resident whose parents died in hospital after being pulled from the rubble.
"How many lives have been lost here, how many homes have been destroyed? How many innocent people have died in the meantime?"
Moscow Needs "Different Signals"
"Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed," Zelensky said.
A missile attack on Saturday afternoon also hit a restaurant, wounding seven people in Kyiv.
Russian drones flew over Kyiv throughout the day, part of a vast new wave of bombardment of the capital, the heaviest since the early days of the war.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Saturday its drones had struck a data-processing centre in Kyiv and a cargo ship carrying military supplies to the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
Trump Lifts Diesel Sanctions
Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports comes as his administration seeks to curb fuel prices, which have risen sharply during the U.S. conflict with Iran.
Kyiv had instead urged Washington to increase pressure on Moscow in an effort to force it into serious negotiations to end the four-and-a-half-year war.
Trump, meanwhile, has criticised Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he claims have driven up global prices. Kyiv has said it wants a total halt on all energy strikes by both sides as Moscow pummels Ukraine's power grid.
On Saturday, parts of Kyiv and the surrounding region were left without power, bringing the city's metro trains to a complete halt for the second time this week.
The latest strikes came after Ukrainian and European officials held talks with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday aimed at developing a common proposal for ending the war, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
Trump announced the diesel deal while the negotiations were underway, a move Zelensky said had caught Kyiv by surprise.
The Ukrainian delegation was headed home on Saturday, presidential aide Dmytro Lytvyn was cited by the Interfax Ukraine news agency as saying.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said after a call with Trump that an immediate resumption of peace talks was unlikely, citing Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow.
U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may visit Moscow within the next two weeks, Russian state news agency TASS reported on Saturday, citing a source.
Four civilians were killed and five others were wounded as a result of Ukrainian attacks on the Russian-controlled Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine, the Russian-installed governor said on Saturday.
Reuters could not independently verify the report and there was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

Finland to send F-16 ammunition to Ukraine within days
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:21:26 EEST
02:21:26 KST

Finland will supply ammunition for Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets within the coming days, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Saturday, 10 October, following a telephone conversation with Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
The delivery forms part of Finland's 35th military assistance package to Ukraine, valued at approximately €1 million, as Russia intensifies missile and drone attacks across the country.
Zelenskyy disclosed the planned shipment in a Facebook post following his discussion with Stubb. He said the ammunition would help Ukrainian forces intercept Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, which Moscow has deployed in attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
The Ukrainian president did not specify the type or quantity of ammunition Finland would provide.
Stubb also confirmed the conversation in a post on X, stating that air defence was a central component of Finland's latest military assistance package.
The Finnish Ministry of Defence announced the package on Friday, 9 October, after the government accelerated its response to an urgent request from Kyiv.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said Helsinki had brought forward its decision because of Ukraine's immediate defence requirements.
"We will not close our eyes to Ukrainians’ hour of need. Instead, we will stand with Ukraine and continue our materiel assistance deliveries," Häkkänen said in the ministry's statement.
The Finnish president formally approved the shipment on 9 October following a government proposal.
According to the Defence Ministry, the package consists of a single category of military equipment drawn from Finnish Defence Forces stocks.
The announcement brings the total value of Finland's military equipment assistance to Ukraine to approximately €3.6 billion since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Helsinki has also begun preparing another, more extensive assistance package, although officials have not announced its value or expected delivery date.
Ukraine has relied on Western-supplied F-16 aircraft to strengthen its air defences and counter Russian aerial attacks.
Denmark and the Netherlands supplied approximately 40 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine during 2024 and 2025. Ukrainian authorities have not disclosed how many remain operational.
During Saturday's conversation, Zelenskyy and Stubb also discussed the recent agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin concerning Russian diesel supplies to American and international markets.
Russian strikes across south-eastern Ukraine early on Saturday killed 15 people, including three children. Zelenskyy accused Moscow of responding to the US decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports by launching five glide bombs at residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia.
Zelenskyy described the agreement as a new challenge and said Ukraine and Finland were coordinating further diplomatic discussions and responses.
Earlier in the week, Russian attacks reportedly killed nearly 80 civilians across Ukraine over two days.

US military has lost 81 aircraft in Iran war according to Congressional report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:21:01 UTC
02:21:01 KST

Eighty-one aircraft in the US military have been destroyed or damaged during the war with Iran, a congressional Research Service report released this week said.
Among the aircraft lost are some of the most advanced weapons in the US arsenal, including the F-35A fighter jet and the E-3 Sentry, which has four jet engines and a radar dome on its fuselage used to track targets and manage airspace during engagements.
MQ-9 Reaper drones accounted for more than half of the losses found in the report. Reaper drones are used in the Iran war for gathering intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance.
The total cost of the aircraft lost since February is between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion, according to the report, which cited figures from the congressional Budget Office.
US Central Command estimated that the ongoing war with Iran has cost the US roughly $44 billion total in September. However, that number does not include damage to infrastructure at US bases in the Middle East, according to reporting from the Washington Post.
CNN reported that some of the aircraft may have returned to service after being damaged, including eight F-15 Strike Eagle fighter jets after they were damaged during an Iranian strike on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on the night of September 8.
The report examined statements and figures from the Department of Defense; its inspector general; CENTCOM; and external media reports reviewed by the CRS.
Senators accuse Pentagon of withholding information
Bipartisan criticism of the Pentagon has mounted over defense officials' unwillingness to be transparent with Congress about the cost of the Iran war and the Trump administration’s National Defense Strategy.
Following a meeting with Defense Undersecretary Elbridge Colby and the Senate Armed Services Committee, Senator Jacky Rose of Nevada said Colby “was not forthcoming” and “did not really address our concerns or issues.”
In a separate instance this week, US Senator Chris Murphy said on Tuesday that the US Defense Department denied him access to a key military base in Qatar during a visit to the Middle East. He described it as part of a US government effort to conceal the impact of the Iran war.
"This trip confirmed for me that there is an active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort underway to hide the costs of this war and the implications of this war from Congress and the American people," Murphy told a group of journalists in Riyadh, the second stop on his trip.
Analysts cited by CNN said actions in the Middle East, including the Iran war and conflicts with Iran’s proxies, have taken a toll on the MQ-9 Reaper drones. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told Congress that the MQ-9 was the “most valuable player” in the war with Iran
The US military is believed to have roughly 135 MQ-9 drones in its arsenal, the Air Force Times reported in May, 2026.
The military lost 45 of the drones in the Middle East this year alone, in what the Atlantic Council describes as losses at an “alarming rate.”
The US military has not experienced loss of aircraft at such a rate since Operation Desert Storm in 1991.

Israel’s election is a choice between sanity and political survival - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:20:21 UTC
02:20:21 KST

For more than a decade, every Israeli election has been sold to the public as a referendum on one man, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. We are told that the choice is simple: Yes Bibi or no Bibi.
On October 27, Israelis have an opportunity to reject the premise of this doctrine.
After three long years of war and bloodshed, the question on the ballot in the election, arguably the most significant in the country’s history, is far simpler, yet far more demanding and decisive for the future of the State of Israel: what kind of country do we want for ourselves, and for our children? A sane nation among the nations, or an unsustainable pariah state?
It is, above all, a referendum about whether it will be led by those who cherish accountability, including for the failures of October 7, and those who would rather bury it to shield themselves and avoid giving answers.
Surely, none of the current political options is flawless, and the real dividing line is not between ultimate good and ultimate evil. Instead, it runs between those who believe in the state and its institutions and those who view them as an obstacle.
It is between those who can – and must – make the burden of building this country, defending it, and making it prosperous and more just for all be shared, and those who glorify sectarianism and identity politics to safeguard personal and partisan political survival.
Israels toxic sectarian political culture
On the one hand, the opposition – stretching from nationalists and liberals to social democrats, socialists and Islamists – is fractured, and full of contradictions. Most of its leaders insist on presenting themselves as the ultimate alternative while promising more of the same toxic sectarian political culture.
Nowhere is this clearer than in their rhetoric toward Arab and haredi (ultra-Orthodox) political representation. Their pledge to form a “Zionist government” – a term that whitewashes the normalizing of excluding 35% of Israelis, Arab and haredi citizens alike – has proved again and again to be not only undemocratic, but counterproductive.
Polls show the opposition falling short of the 61 seats needed to govern, precisely because of their decision to rule out a fifth of the country’s population, and a fifth of Israel’s Jewish population, thus not only failing to embody the alternative they claim to present, but also adopting Netanyahu’s terms, and handing him the deadlock he needs to survive.
On the other side stand those who cast their leader as the ultimate savior of the Jewish people, the Churchill of his time, the one and only leader capable of “finishing the job” and safeguarding Israel’s security – while gaslighting Israelis and ignoring the fact that he had two decades in power to do exactly that.
Certainly, some of the military achievements of the last three years under Netanyahu are real. Hezbollah has been hit hard, Hamas has been significantly weakened, and Iran’s Islamic regime’s network of proxies has been badly damaged.
But a country is not a battlefield scoreboard, and it cannot be sustained through life on the sword. After all, the same years delivered the worst failure in our nation’s history: the deadliest mass murder of Jews since the Holocaust, and the largest massacre in the history of the Jewish state – on this outgoing government’s watch, not to mention the alleged Qatari infiltration into the Prime Minister’s Office.
Three years later, no one at the top has taken responsibility, and a state commission of inquiry is still being resisted.
Meanwhile, the government continues to relentlessly smear the country’s democratic institutions and security establishment; the prime minister’s criminal trial drags on, an international wave of sanctions is isolating Israel, and the arrest warrant against him has burst his attempt to cast himself as the only one capable of safeguarding Israel’s deepest strategic depth – its international standing.
The same honesty is owed to the opposition.
Surely, Arab parties are mostly outdated, sectarian closed clubs that have failed to offer their constituents real change, and they share their part in the responsibility for the decline in Arab voting turnout.
But that doesn’t mean Arab citizens should be sidelined and excluded from governance. After all, it was the historic participation of an independent Arab party in a governing coalition that ousted Netanyahu for the first time in 12 years.
The “Government of Change” was messy and short-lived, but it revealed a largely unseen side of Israel and proved something many had insisted was impossible: that Arab citizens can and, in fact, must be partners in governing the state, not just subjects of it. Abandoning that precedent now, out of fear of Netanyahu’s attacks, means choosing his rules over our future.
The same logic applies to the haredi public. The problem is not haredi Israelis; it is the political alliance Netanyahu has solidified with corrupt, misogynist ultra-Orthodox politicians to safeguard the continuity of his rule, and the stability of his coalition.
With exemptions for some and endless reserve duty for others, with sectarian allocations of public money to settlements and illegal outposts while draining the country’s Galilee, Golan and Negev regions, his coalition managed to survive a full four-year term – the first Israeli government in decades to do so.
A sane government does not demonize an entire sector of society. It brings it in – into the army or national service, the workforce and shared responsibility – on equal terms. A sane country is one in which institutions outlive any one leader, the national burden is carried by all, and accountability is cherished.
An insane country, on the other hand, is one that mistakes isolation for strength, and confuses the survival of its leader with the survival of the state. It is a country governed by those who wage war against the very same institutions that have shielded the country throughout many of its existential crises.
Indeed, no option on the ballot is optimal, and this election is not about whether you love or hate Bibi. Instead, it’s about whether we still know the difference between a leader and a state, and whether we want more of the same reality, or an alternative that revolves around equality for all, and positions collective and national interests of the nation and its future on top of their priorities.
On October 27, we must choose sanity over insanity.
The writer is an independent queer Arab Israeli writer, speaker, and political and geopolitical commentator. A former LGBTQ activist and reporter, during the Bennett-Lapid government, Eden was a co-creator of the Knesset’s first-ever Arab LGBTQ forum promoting the rights LGBTQ Arabs, and secured government funding that facilitated the launch of Beit Almeem, one of Israel’s first Arabic speaking LGBTQ centers.

US lethal injection survivor Christa Pike returns to prison
Unknown

US lethal injection survivor Christa Pike returns to prison
- Christa Pike, 50, survived a botched execution in Tennessee after two doses of pentobarbital failed. She has been discharged from hospital and returned to Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center.
- Her lawyers said she is still receiving medical care and asked Governor Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison. Lee has paused executions pending an independent investigation.
- The case has reignited debate over capital punishment in the US, after anger over a planned live-streamed firing squad execution and Pope Leo's statement that the death penalty is 'inadmissible'.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The convicted murderer who survived a botched execution attempt in the US state of Tennessee last week has been discharged from hospital and returned to prison, her lawyers said Oct 10.
Christa Pike, 50, was administered two lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital on Sept 30 that failed to kill her.
She was transported to hospital in critical condition but later regained consciousness, with her lawyers saying this week that she was walking around but in a “foggy” mental state.
“Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she has been housed for more than 30 years,” her lawyers said in a statement Saturday.
Pike was sentenced to death in Tennessee for murdering a classmate, a crime committed when she was a teenager.
“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” the statement went on.
Pike “is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery,” the lawyers said.
The attempted execution came after days of last-minute legal wrangling that ultimately reached the Supreme Court.
Pike’s legal team had previously objected to the execution IV protocol, saying it would have caused needless suffering due to her small veins and a blood condition.
Since the botched execution, her lawyers have repeatedly called on Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison.
Lee has suspended executions in Tennessee pending an independent investigation.
Pike’s stunning survival renewed focus on the ethical debate surrounding capital punishment in the United States.
That debate has intensified following the Pentagon’s announcement this week that it intends to live-stream an execution by firing squad later this year.
The move has prompted outrage from a broad array of public figures in the United States, including many Republicans supportive of the death penalty.
Pope Leo, the first American pontiff, posted on Oct 10 on X that “the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person.”
“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” he said.
The death penalty has been abolished in 23 of the 50 US states, while three others – California, Oregon and Pennsylvania – have moratoriums in place.
The federal government instituted a moratorium under president Joe Biden, but President Donald Trump’s administration lifted it when he returned to office in 2025. AFP

Trump’s Russian diesel deal, which drew fury in Ukraine, is unlikely to lower prices, experts say

US President Donald Trump said on 9 October that he had agreed with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to bring Russian diesel to world markets to lower energy prices. However, energy analysts say the deal, which drew fury in Ukraine, is unlikely to lower diesel prices meaningfully, CNN reports.
Trump wrote on social media that Putin would “immediately supply” more than 300,000 tons of diesel, with another 500,000 tons in November. Together, those volumes would cover about a day and a half of US demand, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
Meanwhile, former head of the Center for Countering Disinformation Andrii Kovalenko says that US diesel consumption alone is about 16 million tons per month, and global consumption is roughly 120 million tons.
The US experts read the move as politics more than a market shift. Trump spoke in tons rather than barrels because the figure looks bigger to an ordinary observer, said Dan Pickering, founder of Pickering Energy Partners, calling it “more politics than a game changer.”
Doubts Russia can even deliver
Former US officials question whether Putin holds the diesel Trump described, as Ukrainian strikes strain Russia’s refineries. A former senior State Department official says it hardly matters whether the fuel arrives, because Putin “has already achieved the result he wants,” with Trump believing he has a pre-election card that could move markets.
Even if the fuel flows, it would be a temporary measure. Gregory Brew of Eurasia Group says that he suspects Putin expects Ukraine to halt its strikes on Russian refineries in return, and that he cannot imagine Zelenskyy agreeing.
A win for Putin without conditions
For Putin, the gain is plain, Kovalenko says: he pushes for sanctions relief and for no new US sanctions, all without any demand to end the war in Ukraine.
"Trump’s bet was more on the news itself, driving prices down somewhat, because, in reality, figures like these shouldn’t bring prices down," Kovalеnkо believes.
He adds that Trump will "make a big fuss about diesel ahead of the elections, nothing more," and that the average American is unlikely to feel any lasting effect.”
Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that allowing Russia to sell petroleum products abroad without securing a lasting de-escalation agreement would help finance Moscow's war against Ukraine.
He criticized the decision, calling it "a birthday gift for Putin," per Axios.
The next day after the announcement, Russia launched six bombs on Zaporizhzhia, killing 17 people.

Tehran Theater to host Francis Veber’s comedy “The Dinner of Fools”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:15:07 UTC
02:15:07 KST

Tehran Theater to host Francis Veber’s comedy “The Dinner of Fools”
TEHRAN – Tehran's Sahne-ye Abi (Blue Stage) Theater will host the comedy play “The Dinner of Fools” by Francis Veber from October 15 to 24.
Kourosh Heydari has directed the 70-minute play. The cast includes Ahura Ghanbari, Mahbod Mirzadeh, Mohsen Oliasani, Raheleh Heydari, Sajad Abedi, Shabnam Shahrasbi, and Mahvash Rahmani.
The comedy was written in 1991. The play invites the audience to see the strange ways of Pier Broshan, a Parisian publisher, and his friends. They are collectors. They collect idiots. Every Wednesday, the company of young aristocrats organizes a dinner, to which the members have to bring one idiot. A person whose idiot turns out to be the most believable wins the game.
With the help of an idiot scout, Brochant manages to find a gem, François Pignon, a Finance Ministry employee whose passion is building replicas of landmarks with matchsticks. After Brochant starts to suffer from lower back pain, his wife, Christine, leaves him shortly before Pignon arrives at his apartment. Brochant initially wants Pignon to leave, but instead becomes reliant on him because of his back problem and his need to resolve his relationship problems. He solicits Pignon's assistance in making a series of telephone calls to locate his wife, but Pignon gaffes each time, including revealing the existence of Brochant's mistress, Marlene Sasseur, to his wife, Christine.
Brochant is also able to make amends with an old friend, Juste LeBlanc, from whom he stole Christine. Arriving at the apartment, LeBlanc switches between assisting Brochant and laughing uncontrollably at his discomfiture. Brochant believes Christine has gone to Pascal Meneaux, a notorious philanderer. Brochant does not know how to locate Meneaux, so Pignon tries to help by bringing in a friend, Lucien Cheval, a civil servant who has Meneaux's details on his files. Cheval arrives, but turns out to be a tax inspector, to the further distress of the wealthy Brochant, who has been evading tax, and is forced to quickly hide most of his valuables. In the act of calling the womanizer Meneaux, the tax auditor makes an unpleasant discovery about his own wife and leaves, threatening to audit Meneaux and possibly Brochant as well.
Pignon eventually discovers the truth behind the dinner that Brochant wanted to take him to. His feeling is hurt, but, well-intentioned as ever, he tries to make up for all his mistakes by calling Brochant's wife, who had been involved in a car accident after leaving the apartment for the second time (the first time being when Pignon had sent her away thinking she was really Brochant's mistress). For once, he makes no mistakes in this conversation, speaking emotionally and sincerely about his own marital breakup (in response to which he took up his hobby), and making up almost perfect excuses on the spot.
However, after encouraging Christine to return home, Pignon makes a final gaffe: he picks up the telephone when she calls to talk to Brochant despite having previously told her he was in a phone booth, thus arousing her suspicions that he has simply been repeating lines fed to him by Brochant (as he indeed had been in previous conversations).
Francis Veber, 89, is a French film director, screenwriter, producer, and playwright. He has written and directed both French and American films. Nine French-language films with which he has been involved, as either writer or director or both, have been remade as English-language Hollywood films.
Some of his screenplays started as theater plays. “The Dinner of Fools” was turned into a movie by Veber in 1998 titled “The Dinner Game”. In 2010, a Hollywood remake of the film was made under the title “Dinner for Schmucks,” starring Steve Carell and Paul Rudd.

Halal tourism shifts focus to destination readiness, traveler trust as industry leaders meet in London

Halal tourism shifts focus to destination readiness, traveler trust as industry leaders meet in London
Industry executives highlight global connectivity, education, digital innovation and collaboration as key to turning growing demand for Muslim-friendly travel into economic value
Aysu Bicer
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
Halal tourism shifts focus to destination readiness, traveler trust as industry leaders meet in London
LONDON
The global halal tourism industry is shifting its focus from demonstrating market potential to improving destination readiness and traveler experiences, industry leaders said Saturday at a forum in London.
Speaking at a session titled The Halal Traveler Economy: From Demand Signals to Destination Value, representatives from aviation and tourism organizations emphasized the importance of connectivity, education, technology and industry partnerships.
Melih Sukru Ecertas, an independent board member at Turkish Airlines, said halal tourism was undergoing a transformation as travelers increasingly sought experiences combining religious requirements with cultural discovery, comfort and personalized services.
"We believe that halal travel economy is experiencing now a profound paradigm shift," Ecertas said.
He highlighted Turkish Airlines' network of more than 360 destinations across over 155 countries and Istanbul's role as a strategic hub connecting markets across Asia, Europe and the Americas.
Ecertas stressed that airlines could contribute to destination development beyond transporting passengers, adding that cooperation across the tourism industry was essential to creating lasting economic value.
"No single entity can own entire customer journey," he said.
"Airlines bring travel to the gateway, but sustainable destination value requires open innovation across the ecosystem."
He also emphasized that halal-friendly services and premium travel standards could complement each other.
Industry education, trust key to destination readiness
Hafsa Gaher, CEO of Halal Travel Network, said the sector had moved beyond proving its market potential and was increasingly focused on helping destinations serve Muslim travelers effectively.
She identified education and training as priorities for hotels, tour operators and destinations seeking to understand travelers' needs and build trust.
Gaher said travel professionals needed accurate, accessible booking information, including reliable rates, appropriate images and clear product descriptions.
She also urged tourism businesses to understand their target audiences before investing in promotional campaigns.
Gaher said destinations should identify suitable travel agents and industry partners to reach their intended customers.
Trust, technology shape future of Muslim-friendly tourism
Fazal Bahardeen, CEO of CrescentRating and HalalTrip, said research, destination benchmarking and traveler trust were central to the industry's development.
He said CrescentRating, established in 2008, initially focused on raising awareness of Muslim travelers' needs.
The sector has since advanced toward improving service quality, adopting digital technology and offering more immersive experiences, he added.
Bahardeen highlighted CrescentRating's partnership with Mastercard in 2015 to launch the Global Muslim Travel Index, which assesses destinations based on accessibility, communication, environment and services.
The index's 11th edition was launched this year, he said.
"What makes a traveler go from intention to booking is the trust," Bahardeen said.
He stressed the importance of reliable halal food options and comprehensive Muslim-friendly tourism services in converting travel interest into bookings.
The London Halal Forum opened Saturday, bringing together entrepreneurs, investors, policymakers and industry leaders.
Organized by Halal360, a joint initiative of the Islamic Chamber of Commerce and Development and the Halal Products Development Company, the event has Anadolu as its global communications partner.
Under the theme "Halal Tayyib for Humanity," the forum explores opportunities in investment, tourism, technology, supply chains, branding and international trade.

“Shootinga” takes top honors at 38th Isfahan children’s film festival
TEHRAN- The film “Shootinga” emerged as one of the leading winners at the 38th edition of the International Film Festival for Children and Youth in Isfahan, receiving awards for best children’s film, best director and technical achievements at the closing ceremony on Thursday.

The film also earned Golden Butterfly awards for visual effects, presented to Amir Valikhani and Reza Mahmoudian, and cinematography, awarded to Davoud Rahmani. The special Minab Award in the children’s category was presented to Seyyed Javad Hashemi for directing “Someone Will Come for Me,” while the award in the teenage category went to “Verkana,” with Meysam Sajjadi recognized for direction and Seyyed Mohammad-Ali Davoudi for production.

The International Film Festival for Children and Youth is one of Iran’s longstanding cinematic events dedicated to young audiences. Held in the central Iranian city of Isfahan, the festival provides a platform for filmmakers working in children’s and youth cinema, recognizing achievements in filmmaking, acting, animation and technical production. It also seeks to encourage the development of films that address the experiences, imagination and concerns of younger generations.

Pedro Sánchez kicked off his 29 November campaign in the so-called "lucky city" of Dos Hermanas in Seville before some 5,000 people.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez kicked off his election campaign for the 29 November election in Dos Hermanas, Seville, where more than 5,000 people gathered to hear him speak.
The choice of that town is no coincidence, as it is the largest city in Andalusia where the Socialists remain in power following the most recent regional elections.
It was there in 2017 that Sánchez began his bid to secure the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party's (PSOE) general secretariat. His campaigns in 2019 and 2023 also began in what Alejandro Moyano, deputy secretary for Organisation of the PSOE in Andalusia, describes as the party's "lucky city".
The Socialists have a long way to go to win back voters after losing the last series of elections: the 2022 Andalusian poll, the 2023 local and general elections, the 2024 European vote and the Andalusian elections earlier this year.
Sánchez paid tribute to Maricarmen Abascal, who has become a symbol of Spain's housing protests, saying that "the social cause bears the name of an 87-year-old woman". He also repeated one of her phrases: "What I have suffered, I don’t want anyone else to go through".
The prime minister described his political opponents as a bloc that has spent eight years spreading "messages of fear". By referring to the fable of 'The Boy Who Cried Wolf', Sánchez drew his own conclusion: "They are the wolf."
He summed up the dilemma facing the People's Party (PP) as "susto o muerte" ("fright or death"): if they are in opposition they hurl insults, and if they govern they make cuts.
Opposition leader and People's Party president Alberto Núñez Feijóo also launched his pre-election campaign in Madrid on Saturday. In his speech, he pledged to give his all for those in attendance and for the millions of Spaniards seeking change.
The People's Party presdient launched a sharp attack on Sánchez, arguing that he (Feijóo) does not come "from the saunas or the sewers" but from a background in management: from presenting and balancing budgets, maintaining public services and stepping up in good times and in bad.
After Sánchez called an early general election for 29 November, 2,769,645 voters holding a Spanish passport and residing abroad have been called to vote. This represents an increase of more than 19%, or 444,335 more voters than in the 2023 election, underscoring the impact of the so-called "Grandchildren's Law."
Since 2023, Spain's overall electoral register has grown by 1.26 million people, while 1.6 million young people have reached voting age and become eligible to cast their vote for the first time.

Martyr Leader’s “Cell No. 14” published in Armenian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10

Martyr Leader’s “Cell No. 14” published in Armenian
TEHRAN – The Armenian translation of the book “Cell No. 14,” which is the autobiographical memoir of the martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei was unveiled at the Faculty of Oriental Studies of Yerevan State University in Armenia on Friday.
Translated by Maryam Zazian, an Iranologist and translator, the book recounts Ayatollah Khamenei's memoirs from his years of struggle and imprisonment before the victory of the 1979 Islamic Revolution in Iran, ISNA reported.
Speaking at the unveiling ceremony, Iran’s Minister of Sports and Youth, Ahmad Donyamali, said that the book is an account of a journey that begins in a simple home and reaches the days when the history of Iran enters a new phase.
He noted that the significance of the book lies in its account of the distance between Ayatollah Khamenei’s youth and the figure who later played a decisive role in Iran’s political developments, and the years marked by “patience, solitude, choices, and paying the price.”
“The book takes readers back to a period when Ayatollah Khamenei’s future political standing had not yet taken shape; a time when study, literature, teaching, engagement with the people, and gradual involvement in social and political issues constituted a significant part of his life,” he added.
Donyamali also described “resistance to foreign domination” as one of the prominent themes in Martyr Leader’s political thought, saying that confronting global arrogance and supporting resistance movements had occupied a central place in his international policy.
In another part of his remarks, the minister said that within this framework of thought, acceptance of social, religious, and political differences within the country finds meaning alongside preserving independence and confronting attempts by foreign powers to impose their will.
In conclusion, Donyamali stressed the importance of expanding cultural relations between Iran and Armenia, expressing hope that the publication of the Armenian translation of this book would pave the way for greater mutual understanding between the two nations and the development of cooperation between universities and young people in the two countries.
In the book, the author skillfully transports readers to a tangible and realized space through simple yet comprehensive literature. The book's narrative is devoid of imposing or imaginative elements, resulting in a striking sense of concreteness and realization.
It is a remarkable saga of a young cleric blessed with an indomitable spirit who fights a dictatorial regime with his sermons and speeches as well as with his organizational abilities. He never loses hope despite being sent to prison and exile, and finally emerges victorious against all odds.
The book serves as a source of inspiration to all activists around the globe who are trying to bring about social and political change.
It also contains unpublished photos of the Leader, his father, and his children, in addition to a photo collection of paintings related to the topics in the book.
The book was first published in Arabic under the title "Indeed, with Patience Comes Victory" and was published in Persian as "The Heart's Blood That Turned to Ruby" in 2019.
Since then, the book has been translated into several languages, including Spanish, Portuguese, Russian, Urdu, Bengali, and Chinese.
Ayatollah Khamenei was martyred during US-Israeli airstrikes that targeted his office in central Tehran on February 28.

Three shards of glass under his eye and espionage charges: how a UP employee was kept handcuffed in an Austrian hospital
On 8 October, Mykhailo Tkach, head of investigative journalism at Ukrainska Pravda, and his colleague Yaroslav Bondarenko were detained in Vienna while on an assignment to track down fugitive former prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko.
Yaroslav, who was injured during the detention, recounts how the arrest unfolded.
...In broad daylight (at 15:00), as we were driving from one place to another in a rental car, we were brutally taken down by Austrian special forces at a traffic light.
They smashed both windows, and within seconds we were on the ground. Mykhailo Tkach "got lucky" – on his side there was a verge with a flowerbed and grass, whereas I was shoved face-first into the tarmac, and they pressed down on me with their whole body weight right into the shattered glass. My left arm was in the grip of a police officer, while my right was trapped under my body... they started yanking it out. It was cut to ribbons. Gashes and lacerations on my right arm.
They twisted my left arm so hard that I cried out loud from the sudden sharp pain. It felt like they were about to break my arm.
Then they clamped handcuffs on my left wrist so tight that after only 15-20 minutes I was begging them: "Please relax this! Please! It's no good! Please relax!" I don't speak German. Sorry :))
From the moment of that takedown, with the smashed windows, Mykhailo and I were separated with absolutely no way to communicate!
Looking to the side was FORBIDDEN – it was instantly "face the wall!"
Blood was pouring down my face, soaking my clothes, trousers, and my new trainers (I could see they were ruined). I looked at my arm – it was bleeding. A police medic came over with hydrogen peroxide to take a look at me and give first aid. That's when I noticed Mykhailo being bundled away somewhere in the distance. I heard him say more than once: 'We are Ukrainian journalists!'
They confiscated all our belongings. A van showed up. They put us in and drove off in an unknown direction. It turned out later to be a detention centre.
The whole time, NO EXPLANATION whatsoever, not even "YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO..." – absolutely nothing, just complete confusion and uncertainty about "what just happened and what comes next". And then: processing at the detention centre.
An examination by the prison medics. That's when I saw the state I was in. I had to spend some time washing the dried blood off my face with an antiseptic, and that's when I noticed a "bump" under my eye. I took a closer look. "There's glass in there," I told the medics. "I think I need medical attention," I continued.
21:30. Taken out of the temporary holding cell, handcuffed behind my back. Into the van. The journey to hospital.
It felt sickening. I was taken from the prison to the hospital to have the glass removed from my face, all while handcuffed behind my back... two police officers walking me through the corridors of a civilian hospital, through crowds of people, like some kind of criminal mastermind.
Frightened children's eyes staring at you :(( and that was just awful. And that was probably the hardest part of this whole ordeal.
Because no matter how hard you try to talk to the police and explain, "I'm not a criminal! I'm not a threat! I'm an investigative journalist from Ukraine! Just look me up online! You'll find everything about me, about us and our work. It's all there – you'll see for yourself and understand"... none of it makes any difference!
And even after the X-ray, when it's time to lie down on the operating table, the doctor looks flustered and says, "Handcuffs behind your back? That's not good!" So I tell the police officers again: "I'm not a threat! I'm not a criminal. I'm a photographer, a cameraman. Believe me. At least take the handcuffs off for the operation." But it's no use.
Facial surgery, right under my eye – with my hands cuffed behind my back.
They got the glass out and stitched me up. I asked to see the fragments. Three pieces of glass. My right arm, cut from the elbow upwards, was treated and bandaged with the kind of adhesive plasters used to close cuts.
Then, still handcuffed, it was back to cell "303", which had strange things scrawled on the walls about Jesus, Allah and "Thieves rule". But the most interesting words were right in front of me, above the cell door: "95 REGION".
Interesting. That reminds me of something.
It echoes something I've seen in Ukraine.
The police questioned me at length. The accusations against me are extremely serious:
- Espionage.
- Working for a foreign intelligence service.
- Conspiring to harm the Austrian state.
I tried to explain the nature of our work and what we'd achieved (right there on the table, among the things they'd seized, was an international award for freedom of speech and for best investigative journalist which we'd just received in Norway). And yet I still had to prove that we weren't criminals.
The Austrian lawyer and the interpreter, Maryna (sorry, I didn't ask her surname), are both true professionals.
And my personal thanks to Consul Yurii for visiting me in the pre-trial detention centre and taking the time to speak with me. When you're in "complete isolation from the outside world", when you have no explanation of "WHAT ON EARTH IS GOING ON?!", that means a great deal. Thank you.
After the interrogation, my lawyer applied for my immediate release from the cell, arguing that I posed no threat. Three police officers, including the chief, clearly understood the situation by then and, after making several calls to the prosecutor, managed to secure my release. Friday evening.
If it hadn't been for that, I'd have spent Saturday and Sunday in cell "303", staring at the door marked "95 region" and doing push-ups – just like in the movies :))
Right, back to work…
	Yaroslav Bondarenko

Yemen hits Riyadh airport again as Saudi flights collapse
TEHRAN — Riyadh’s airport was hit again on Saturday, two days after Yemeni missiles killed three Saudis there. Regional officials told the Associated Press that air traffic stopped and the airport was evacuated.
A hospital source told Euronews that dozens were injured, at least five in intensive care. Riyadh confirmed the strike by evening but Sanaa had yet to claim it. Three Western embassies warned citizens away, and Kuwait Airways scrapped its Riyadh flights.
Thursday set the pattern. Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority admitted two attacks on King Khalid International Airport, one on facilities and one on a Saudia aircraft, that killed Captain Hamoud Ali Alkalthami and two other Saudis. CNN verified images of smoke over Terminal 4.
Brigadier General Yahya Saree said Yemeni forces also fired on Najran airport and a Saudi air base. Earlier strikes on Abha and Riyadh airports had already killed three and wounded 36, by Riyadh’s own count.
The commercial damage came fast. Cirium counted 169 of 378 scheduled Riyadh departures cancelled or not operating by late Thursday afternoon, nearly 45 percent.
Lufthansa grounded its Riyadh service through October 16. Turkish Airlines dropped all four departures. Air India, IndiGo and Philippine Airlines followed, and European regulators extended their warnings to Riyadh, Tabuk, Medina and Yanbu.
Saree told airlines, for the last time, that Saudi airspace outside the holy cities is a theater of operations.
Sanaa describes all this as reciprocity. Saudi jets bombed Sanaa International Airport on July 13, after Riyadh threatened Yemen over a flight to Tehran. Human Rights Watch found three munitions on the only working runway, the first coalition strikes since the 2022 truce.
Sanaa declared a blockade of Saudi ports a week later. On Saturday Al Masirah reported four more raids on it. Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, called it an “airport-for-airport equation.”
Riyadh’s answer is “Dawn of Yemen,” the offensive its Yemeni clients launched last Sunday with a stated aim of retaking every area Ansarallah holds, Sanaa included. Its government claims 2,750 strikes in a day and 1,400 fighters “neutralized,” and the coalition says it hit 136 targets.
The same camp claimed Mocha on Tuesday, and Ansarallah answered with video of its fighters inside the city. Saree says Saudi F-15s and Typhoons flew 129 raids in 48 hours in mid-September.
The International Organization for Migration counts more than 200,000 people displaced since September, and UN envoy Hans Grundberg now speaks of full-scale war.
The geography explains Riyadh’s panic. With ongoing developments in the Strait of Hormuz due to the war on Iran, Saudi crude leaves through the East-West pipeline to Yanbu and then past Bab al-Mandab.
Drones hit that pipeline on September 10 and, according to Kpler, flows stopped for at least 11 days. Riyadh blamed launches from Iraq. Ansarallah seized Mayyun Island, also called Perim, in the strait last month.
On Thursday, ten years after the Saudi bombing of Sanaa’s Great Hall killed more than 140 mourners and wounded hundreds, Ansarallah leader Sayyed Abdul-Malik al-Houthi called the war a strategic failure for Riyadh.
He said Yemeni forces can strike enemy assets across the Red Sea and Arabian Sea from anywhere in the country, and accused Riyadh of serving American and Zionist ambitions while posing as guardian of the holy sites.
The kingdom is buying muscle elsewhere. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey activated the so-called Mecca pact on October 5. Pakistan reportedly keeps about 8,000 troops in the kingdom, with JF-17 jets and HQ-9 air defenses, and Reuters reported four planeloads of Pakistani weapons landing in Aden.
Islamabad says its forces will not cross the border. Sanaa’s acting foreign minister, Abdulwahid Abu Ras, has urged Islamabad and Ankara to stay out.
Washington hedges as of now. President Trump reportedly refused the crown prince’s September request for strikes after Ansarallah promised to spare American shipping, though Secretary of State Marco Rubio now vows to honor the U.S. defense commitment.

Trump seethes that no one knows her; Navi Pillay has rattled US and Israel anyway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:12:44 UTC
02:12:44 KST

Trump seethes that no one knows her; Navi Pillay has rattled US and Israel anyway
TEHRAN — Within hours of Navi Pillay being named the Nobel Peace Prize laureate, the American president had shared a post calling her a hater of America and Israel, and his secretary of state had sanctioned an entire international court. Israel summoned Joseph Goebbels.
Nobody had to explain what the 85-year-old South African jurist did to earn this. The reactions did it for her.
The Nobel deserves no reverence here. Oslo handed its peace medal to Henry Kissinger in 1973 while American bombers pounded Indochina, to Barack Obama in 2009 before drone strikes became his signature, and to Aung San Suu Kyi, who later stood before the ICJ to defend Myanmar’s generals against a genocide charge.
The prize launders power so reliably that a laureate who prosecutes it is the anomaly. Pillay needed no committee to vouch for her.
From Clairwood to Rwanda
Pillay was born in 1941 in Clairwood, a working-class Indian neighborhood of Durban, South Africa. Her father drove a bus. Neighbors raised the money for her law degree at the University of Natal. She clerked for ANC lawyer N.T. Naicker, whose house arrests pushed her into court early.
White firms refused to hire her, so in 1967 she opened her own practice, the first non-white woman in Natal to do so, in a profession that barred her from judges’ chambers and white-only law libraries.
In 1973 she won Robben Island prisoners, Nelson Mandela among them, access to lawyers and law books. When police detained her husband, she won an order forbidding his torture and sent sworn affidavits to anti-apartheid groups at the UN, which pushed the world toward a Convention Against Torture.
Then came Rwanda. She was the only woman on the tribunal’s bench for its first four years, later its president, and co-authored the 1998 Akayesu judgment, the first to hold that rape can be an act of genocide and that propaganda alone can amount to incitement.
The ICC followed, then the UN human rights office from 2008 to 2014. She now sits as an ad hoc ICJ judge in the same Myanmar genocide case.
The verdict on Gaza
In 2021 she took over the UN commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory. Its September 2025 report found Israel had committed four of the five acts listed in the Genocide Convention, with intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza, and that President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former war minister Yoav Gallant had incited it.
It asked whether genocidal intent was the only reasonable inference from the pattern of conduct, the standard the ICJ applies, and found that it was.
Israel’s stated aims of “self-defense, defeating Hamas and recovering hostages” explained little of what it documented, she told Middle East Eye, because most of those acts had no military objective she could see. Gaza’s Health Ministry now counts more than 74,000 dead.
Pillay made a point Western governments dislike hearing. Nobody has to wait for The Hague. The Genocide Convention binds every state to prevent the crime, she argued, and those still shipping weapons and jet fuel to Israel risk complicity.
She also warned that Trump’s Gaza plan, which sidelines Palestinians and leaves Israel in security control, ignores the ICJ’s ruling that the occupation must end.
Trump rants, Israel smears, Washington sanctions
Trump did not congratulate her. Hours after the announcement he reposted a message saying the committee had “shamed itself beyond repair” and calling Pillay “an unabashed hater of America and Israel.”
Late Friday, after a rally in Syracuse, he posted her photograph and wrote that she got the prize “over the Great United States of America, whose Representative, ME, settled eight Wars.” No one had ever heard of her, he added, except that she “hates Israel.” It was an “indelible stain” on Norway.
In a follow-up he insisted, “I settled 8 WARS, am close to ending or settling 2 more.” His tally counts the June 2025 war on Iran, which U.S. bombers joined in illegal strikes on civilian sites. In July he told reporters 15 million people had been beheaded in the Congo war, roughly four times the usual death estimate.
He has also launched an illegal campaign of aggression against Iran, beginning on February 28. The war has killed civilians in repeated attacks, including at least 155 people, mostly children, in the Minab school massacre; at least 21 in U.S. strikes on Lamerd; and five more near a wedding in Kuhestak, where 67 were wounded.
He also invaded Venezuela earlier this year. Last year’s laureate, the Venezuelan María Corina Machado, handed Trump her medal, a gesture the Nobel Institute says does not change the official award.
Washington’s real answer to Pillay winning the prize came the same day. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sanctions on the International Criminal Court itself, the next step in a campaign to dismantle it “brick by brick.”
The U.S. had already sanctioned its president in August. The goal is no secret. Officials want the arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant dropped. The ICC condemned the move and welcomed her prize.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry called the prize “the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice” and said Goebbels was “applauding from hell.” Netanyahu, himself wanted by the court, issued his own rebuke.
Support came quickly elsewhere. UN chief António Guterres, rights chief Volker Turk, ICC President Tomoko Akane and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa all hailed her. Hamas’s Bassem Naim called the prize a message that “humanity still resists the forces of evil targeting international justice.” Amnesty’s Agnès Callamard, beside her in Nuremberg, noted she is a former ICC judge while Washington tries to destroy the court.
Pillay learned the news at the Nuremberg Forum and told applauding supporters that if they kept clapping, she “may share this prize with Trump.” Then she turned serious, warning of a world where “power rather than law determines whose suffering matters.”
Washington and Tel Aviv have spent two years trying to bury her report. The prize has handed it a bigger stage, whatever the committee’s record.

Three elections on the horizon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:12:11 UTC
02:12:11 KST

Three elections on the horizon
TEHRAN – Three elections loom: Israeli Knesset elections, the U.S. midterms, and Palestinian legislative elections.
Each will unfold amid ongoing wars, domestic crises, shifting public opinion, and mounting international pressure. But not every election can reshape the political landscape in a region burdened by wars, divisions, and international shifts.
As for the Israeli regime, the contest appears to be between Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot. In the United States, the focus is increasingly on President Trump’s ability to pursue his agenda without greater constraints from Congress. In Palestine, the question is whether the Zionist regime will allow Palestinians a democratic choice and strong international representation.
The Israeli elections scheduled for October 27 are taking place, for the first time, after three years of genocidal war in Gaza. Those three years have been marked by major security, political, social, and economic crises within the Zionist regime. All of these issues pose challenges for Netanyahu, making it difficult for him to secure another government.
However, the opposition camp may also face a major challenge in successfully forming a stable government. The equation within the regime’s political landscape remains uncertain for either side, despite opinion polls favoring Eisenkot. Leading a political camp in terms of votes does not, by itself, give it the ability to determine the outcome. What matters is the ability to form a bloc of 61 seats in the Knesset.
Netanyahu could lose the election without losing his grip on power if he succeeds in forming a new coalition. Likewise, his political opponents could emerge on top without possessing the keys to forming a cohesive and strong alternative government.
The failures of Netanyahu’s coalition are also substantial: the cost of the illegal wars he has waged against Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran; the internal divisions over judicial issues and military conscription; and the damage to the regime’s image internationally.
One important aspect remains at the forefront: if Netanyahu leaves the political scene, that does not mean the regime will abandon a right-wing fascist ideology. The region is facing an extremely quasi-Nazi Israeli right giving way, perhaps, to a camp that is only marginally less extreme. Netanyahu may be replaced as prime minister, while the political and security structures that produced the same policies remain in place, with Eisenkot, another criminal, taking center stage.
In the United States, the real electoral battle will be over the limits of presidential power. The congressional midterm elections are approaching on November 3 and will determine all seats in the House of Representatives and one-third of the seats in the Senate. If the Democratic Party regains control of either chamber, or both, Trump will face a Congress with greater capacity to exert influence and oversight in two important areas: federal spending and legislation.
Here, an important issue arises: If the Democratic Party succeeds, how will it deal with the Zionist regime amid the shift taking place within the party’s supporters? Observers argue that reducing the matter to the assumption that a Republican defeat would automatically mean a decline in U.S. support for the regime would be a superficial reading.
U.S. foreign policy is not made by Congress alone. The president and lobby groups retain broad political powers and tools for managing America’s relations with the regime.
Yet what could realistically change? Analysts believe a change in the composition of Congress may raise the political cost of certain U.S. policies relating to the regime. This would come on the backdrop of public opinion shifting amid the U.S.-backed genocide in Gaza.
Such a shift has already begun, particularly among younger people, university students, and other segments of American voters. At that point, the elections would not represent a sudden turning point, but rather one stage in a longer process that could redefine the boundaries of the U.S.-Israeli relationship.
In the Palestinian case, the ballot box is the most important and sensitive of the three. Legislative elections, originally scheduled for November 28, 2026, have now been postponed until September 11, 2027, when presidential elections are also set to take place. The delay extends an electoral freeze that has left Palestinians without legislative elections since 2006 and presidential elections since 2005. The two votes would mark a significant moment in Palestinian political life, offering a long-overdue opportunity to renew the leadership's mandate amid deep divisions and mounting public frustration.
Palestinian elections face a fundamental question that goes beyond who will win and who will lose, particularly amid reports of political challenges and alliances now taking shape. The more important question is: Can Palestinians conduct an electoral process in a political geography that is enduring a genocidal war, settler terrorism, and Zionist occupation?
The success of any Palestinian election should not be measured by opening polling stations and announcing the results. It begins with ensuring that elections are held free of Zionist terror and occupation. The reason cited for the reported delay is “that the anticipated political, security and economic conditions, on which the scheduling of the legislative elections for 28 November, 2027 was based, have not materialized.” This is hardly surprising.
Some analysts argue that there is an opportunity for Palestinians that goes beyond simply electing a new legislative council. It is an opportunity to rebuild a new political compact based on reforming the institutions of the Palestine Liberation Organization, redefining the role of the Palestinian Authority, uniting Palestinians at home and abroad, and developing a clear national strategy for confronting the occupying regime.
To do that, Palestinians need genuine global recognition and representation. As of last week, that was supposed to be the case. Now the Zionist regime is trampling on this too.
This is where the three elections intersect. Netanyahu may lose without the regime’s policy changing its treatment of the Palestinians. The Republican Party may lose control of one of the chambers of Congress without U.S. military support for the regime coming to an end. And the Palestinian people may proceed without a new political map emerging.
The U.S. and Israeli elections will produce little for Palestinians and the wider region. Recent history demonstrates that sustainable peace cannot be achieved by a change of policymakers in Washington or Tel Aviv.

US sanctions the entire ICC to shield American and Israeli war criminals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:11:12 UTC
02:11:12 KST

US sanctions the entire ICC to shield American and Israeli war criminals
TEHRAN — The United States placed the International Criminal Court under sanctions on Friday, October 9, dropping any pretense that its quarrel was limited to individual judges and prosecutors.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the measure in a video statement that left little room for interpretation. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” he said.
Rubio called the tribunal a “rogue court” and promised to “ban transactions” with it, “cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.”
He said Trump “will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” then told allies who sit on the court while relying on American troops for their defense to “rein in the court.”
A blacklist with a clock attached
The Treasury Department added the court to its list of Specially Designated Nationals. All property the ICC holds in the United States is blocked, and no one under American jurisdiction may supply it with funds, goods, or services.
The court has about 900 staff. Banks, insurers, and software vendors that keep serving it now risk penalties, and since banks tend to over-comply with sanctions, the real damage could exceed the legal text, up to exclusion from dollar transactions.
Washington attached a 180-day general license covering maintenance of operations, with narrower carve-outs for cloud and software services, the pension plan and detainees.
The State Department says the window exists so member states can show “meaningful progress” on “fundamental U.S. concerns,” and that it can be adjusted if they fail. Critics see an ultimatum with a calendar.
The court prepared for this, swapping Microsoft for Germany’s openDesk, dropping insurer Axa and paying staff months ahead. More than 90 percent of its processes had relied on U.S. technology. Mark Kersten of the University of the Fraser Valley warned that “the worst-case scenario has come about.”
Diplomats at the court’s annual assembly said in December that the administration had pressed it to drop its investigations in Palestine and Afghanistan, and to amend the Rome Statute so nationals of non-members, meaning Americans and Israelis, could never be prosecuted. The assembly refused, though it did not name Washington.
Condemnation and political messages
Hours earlier, the Nobel Peace Prize went to Navi Pillay, a South African jurist and former ICC judge who oversaw the 2025 UN report concluding that Israel’s actions in Gaza constituted genocide.
The committee said judges and institutions of international law are “under political attack.” Law professor William Schabas called the prize “a kind of polite endorsement” of that report. “There’s often a political message lurking behind the award of the Nobel Peace Prize, and I think this year is no exception,” he said.
The ICC called the sanctions “an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order” and warned that “the Court cannot stand alone.” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply alarmed,” and rights chief Volker Turk called the measures “unacceptable.”
Human Rights Watch’s Philippe Bolopion said the aim is to “destroy” the court and “shield U.S. and Israeli officials from facing charges.” Amnesty International said this “existential attack must fail.”
Israel cheered. “Thank you for your leadership,” Netanyahu wrote, calling the ICC “a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide.” The charge comes from a man the court wants arrested.
Britain, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Canada and Japan said they “regret and strongly disagree.” Belgium’s Maxime Prevot said “Europe must act” and urged activating the EU Blocking Statute, which would bar European firms from complying with the sanctions.
Palestinian rights groups say similar calls have gone unanswered since April, calling that “complicity through inaction.”
The warrants behind it
The trigger came in November 2024, when judges issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former War Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, chiefly the use of starvation as a method of warfare.
Neither Israel nor the United States belongs to the court. The ICC has long held that crimes committed on the territory of a member state, Palestine included, fall within its reach whatever the suspect’s passport says.
Washington’s second grievance is Afghanistan, where an inquiry could touch CIA torture at secret sites in Romania, Lithuania and Poland. The court has deprioritized that strand since 2021 and has never sought to prosecute an American.
That has not slowed the campaign. Executive Order 14203, signed February 6, 2025, opened the way. Sanctions fell on 13 ICC officials, among them half of the 18 judges and former prosecutor Karim Khan, then on UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese in July 2025 and on the Palestinian groups Al-Haq, Al Mezan and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights in September.
Last month Trump told the UN General Assembly the court was an “evil group of people” and demanded that members withdraw.
A 2002 law, nicknamed the “Hague Invasion Act,” authorizes the president to use “all means necessary and appropriate” to free certain Americans and allied personnel detained by the court. The threat of force has thus been enshrined in U.S. law against a tribunal that has never prosecuted a U.S. citizen.

Christa Pike has been discharged from the hospital after surviving Tennessee’s botched 30 September attempt to execute her by lethal injection and is back in prison, her lawyers said on Saturday.
Pike, 50, returned to the Deborah K Johnson rehabilitation center, where she has been imprisoned for the last three decades, her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in a statement.
“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” Pike’s lawyers added. “She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery.”
Saturday’s update about Pike came 10 days after the death row prisoner was given two doses of pentobarbital, a lethal injection drug, in what proved to be a failed execution attempt. She was hospitalized after surviving the botched execution and was declared brain dead on Monday.
But in a shocking turnaround, on Thursday her lawyer said that she was “up and walking” – though she remained “somewhat foggy” and wasn’t able to use her arms very much.
Pike said that her arms were burning during the failed execution and asked if it was supposed to feel that way. Witnesses present in the chamber said that “nothing was normal” while officials have maintained that they followed every step of Tennessee’s approved execution protocol.
There has been no official explanation about why Pike survived the execution. Medical experts speculate that perhaps some or much of the drug missed her vein and went into surrounding tissue, that one of her veins blew, that the drug was faulty, or a combination of such factors.
Her lawyers months earlier had flagged that Pike’s veins were problematic.
Pike was convicted in 1995 for the torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, then 18 and her classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. According to court filings, Pike, who was also 19 at the time, was worried Slemmer was trying to take her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, then 17.
Shipp and Pike were convicted of taking Slemmer into a wooded part of the University of Tennessee campus and murdering her. She was given the death penalty, and Shipp was sentenced to life in prison because he was younger than 18.
After Slemmer’s murder, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders, her attorneys said.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”
Pike’s survival of the botched execution has shocked many in the US and overseas and galvanized critics of the death penalty.
Tennessee’s top prison official has announced his resignation.
Meanwhile, the state’s governor, Bill Lee, has paused executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. And Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, on Friday canceled a planned lethal injection execution in the state.
But they continue elsewhere.
For instance, the Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that it planned to livestream the execution by firing squad in December of former army psychiatrist Nidal Hassan, who killed 13 people at Texas’s Fort Hood, prompting condemnation from the United Nations.
Donald Trump on Saturday said Hassan “was vicious – he was violent” and that he would “make a decision” about the plans to livestream his execution.
“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show,” the president remarked. “Because you know by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”

UK Greens' deputy leader Mothin Ali warns of rising racism in UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:10:26 UTC
