Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:42:00 UTC
01:42:00 KST

Britain’s Northern Ireland secretary on Friday banned a contentious Protestant parade through a mostly Irish nationalist and Catholic district after a nearly two-week standoff.
The Parades Commission, Northern Ireland’s independent body regulating contentious processions, had authorized 35 Orangemen to march silently along the mostly Irish nationalist enclave of Garvaghy Road in Portadown, without bands or supporters from 8am on Sept. 27.
However, thousands blocked the procession, halting the first parade, which had been allowed along the route in almost three decades.
Photo: AFP
The Orangemen have since remained at nearby Drumcree Church, demanding to complete the march, while residents maintained their protest.
“I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions,” the minister, Chris Bryant, said in a statement.
In the interest of public safety, Bryant said circumstances under which the procession was given the go ahead had now “changed considerably.”
“As a result, the procession cannot go ahead as it was determined,” he said, adding that “no one wants a return to the past.”
The procession last went along Garvaghy Road in Portadown, 40km southwest of Belfast, in 1997.
It was barred the following year, soon after a peace accord largely ended three decades of conflict over British rule in Northern Ireland.
Police Service of Northern Ireland Chief Constable Jon Boutcher welcomed the decision.
Boutcher said he wrote to Bryant on Friday asking him to review an earlier decision by the province’s Parades Commission.
Boutcher said he outlined his assessment “that all available, lawful and proportionate options to facilitate completion of the procession had been exhausted.”
Any operation to allow the march to go ahead would have carried an “unacceptable” risk of serious injury and disorder, and would have had “catastrophic long-term consequences,” he said.

Several injured after attack on Saudi Arabia's Riyadh Airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:42:00 UTC

Saudi Arabia: 12 killed, hundreds injured in Riyadh strike
Published October 10, 2026last updated October 11, 2026
At least 12 people were killed and hundreds were injured in an attack on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday.
"King Khalid International Airport was targeted by an attack, amid continued attacks targeting civilian aviation facilities in the kingdom," the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in an initial statement.
Hours later, the authority announced that 12 people had been killed, including four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese national.
At least 309 others were injured in the attack, the aviation authority said, adding that "all injured individuals are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals."
Operations at the airport had been suspended until further notice.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen also announced that "a projectile" had also landed near King Fahd International Airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
Coalition vows to respond
On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government accused the Houthis of carrying out the deadly attack on Riyadh's international airport. The coalition vowed to respond "decisively."
In a statement, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki described the attack as a "war crime" and vowed the coalition "will respond decisively to this terrorist attack."
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump called the attack on Riyadh's international airport "not acceptable."
He also told reporters that he will speak with Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
When asked if the US might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the United States strongly condemns recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, confirming that an American citizen was killed in the strikes.
"These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now," Rubio wrote on X.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" by the Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport.
"Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law," Guterres said. "These attacks must cease immediately."
What do we know about the Riyadh attack?
A Saudi official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the Associated Press that many people were wounded after a missile hit a passenger terminal.
The AFP news news agency also reported that a number of people were injured, citing a local medical source who also spoke on the condition of anonymity.
"ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," the source told AFP. "We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh."
Several Western embassies in Riyadh, including those of Germany, the United States, Canada and Spain, urged citizens to avoid the airport.
The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks" at the airport. Spain's embassy referred to a "new attack" by the Houthi rebels in Yemen while Canada's embassy warned of "ongoing military activity."
What did the Houthis say?
The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen did not immediately claim responsibility for the attack.
However, after the attack, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree retweeted his own post from a day earlier in which he said that only pre-approved humanitarian flights would be allowed to land at Riyadh airport.
In the retweet on Saturday night, Saree wrote: "A reminder."
When asked about the attack, US President Donald Trump said the US would soon decide whether to join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We move very quickly."
Strikes hit Riyadh airport earlier this week
Fighting has intensified between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen.
The Iran-backed Houthis have been launching strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia, including several this week on the airport in Riyadh that killed four people, injured several others, and damaged planes.
Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways canceled multiple flights between their respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Kuwait Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday.
Last month, Houthi rebels made advances on important strategic locations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces seeking to take back those gains.
The Houthis have responded by launching attacks into Saudi Arabia, which represents a significant escalation in their multi-year conflict with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government after a peace deal unraveled in July.
The Saudi-backed government in Yemen last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, especially those around the Bab al-Mandab strait.

Brazil lowers fuel prices ahead of runoff election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:59 UTC
01:41:59 KST

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s government on Friday announced new fuel tax cuts and extended subsidies aimed at lowering fuel prices, just over two weeks before a closely contested presidential runoff.
Fuel prices are a particularly sensitive issue for voters, who on Oct. 25 are to decide whether to elect Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, a son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, or grant Lula a fourth term.
Flavio Bolsonaro received about 2 million more votes than Lula in the first round on Sunday last week.
Photo: AFP
A new decree eliminates federal taxes on the import and sale of gasoline for 30 days, with the possibility of an extension. The measure was effective from Friday, the same day previous measures that lowered taxes expired. It extends a tax exemption and increases a subsidy for ethanol.
The government also said it would provide an additional subsidy to importers of diesel, who will receive 1.40 reais (US$0.28) per liter for 30 days.
That amount is in addition to the 2.12 reais per liter subsidy already in effect.
“The aim is to ensure that imports remain economically viable at a critical time for fuel supply,” the government’s secretariat for social communication said, adding that the measures were in line with the strategy adopted by the government since the start of the Iran war.
The fiscal impact of the measures would be offset by the revenues from the federal government’s oil assets, it added.
Crude oil prices shot up shortly after Israel and the US began their war with Iran in late February, largely because the fighting halted most shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway where roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil supply passed before the conflict.
“The international situation has deteriorated since the measures announced in September,” the Brazilian government said, adding that international diesel and gasoline refining margins had risen to more than double their pre-war levels.

A birthday of Taiwanese’s choosing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:59 UTC
01:41:59 KST

Yesterday, flags fluttered and fireworks lit up the sky to celebrate the 115th Double Ten National Day of the Republic of China (ROC) — but when will Taiwanese be able to celebrate a national day of their own choosing?
On Oct. 10, 1911, the Wuchang Uprising set the Xinhai Revolution in motion, leading to the fall of the Qing Dynasty and the founding of the ROC on Jan. 1 the following year.
When the first shots rang out in Wuchang (武昌), Taiwan was still under Japanese colonial rule. After Japan’s defeat in 1945, the ROC government came to Taiwan to govern. Taiwanese had hoped for postwar stability, but instead faced political corruption, social unrest and the 228 Incident in 1947, the violent suppression of an anti-government uprising.
After losing the Chinese Civil War in 1949, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) government retreated to Taiwan, bringing with it the authoritarian politics of China’s civil war.
Taiwan remained under martial law for 38 long years, from May 20, 1949, to July 15, 1987. During this period, known as the White Terror era, countless people were arrested, imprisoned or even killed because of their speech, beliefs and political views. How can this history possibly be glossed over with the phrase “years of hardship?”
Taiwan’s democracy was not a favor bestowed upon it by its rulers, but something Taiwanese fought for at a great cost.
Martial law was lifted in 1987, and Taiwan held its first direct presidential election in 1996. Taiwanese could finally elect their own head of state and bring about peaceful transfers of power through the ballot box. This democratic Taiwan has long since outgrown the political character of the ROC as it was established in China.
Even so, Taiwan continues to face pressure from China when participating in international events under the name ROC, with restrictions imposed even on the name it can use. Why can the democratic achievements of Taiwanese not be proudly presented to the world under the name Taiwan?
Double Ten National Day fireworks light up the sky every year, yet they cannot illuminate Taiwan’s own national birthday. How many more years must Taiwanese celebrate a Chinese revolution from more than a century ago before they can, on a national day of their own choosing, raise their heads high and proudly proclaim to the world, “We are Taiwan.”?
Steve Ho is a retired engineer.

Health minister defends drug harm reduction programs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:57 UTC
01:41:57 KST

Drug harm reduction programs do not encourage drug use or ask social workers to give out drugs, Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said yesterday amid accusations that Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋) had advocated giving out illicit drugs and needles at community centers.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀), a spokeswoman for Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) re-election campaign, on Friday said that “community centers are where people dance and exercise,” but they will be turned into places where social workers give out drugs and create addicts.
Earlier, Chiang’s campaign accused Shen, the Democratic Progressive Party’s Taipei mayoral candidate, of advocating the distribution of drugs and clean needles at community centers.
Photo: Lo Pi, Taipei Times
Shen later said that his comments merely mentioned a program that has already been implemented elsewhere in Taiwan.
The Taipei-based National Union of Professional Social Worker Associations, Taiwan on Friday called on Lee to publicly apologize for her comments.
“Social workers are not drug providers,” the association said in a statement. “Please stop misleading the public about professional social work.”
Lee’s remarks falsely linked the professional role of social workers and drug harm reduction policies, which can easily lead to public misunderstanding and distrust of frontline social workers, it said.
“The social work profession has long been dedicated to substance addiction prevention and treatment, psychosocial support, family relationship restoration, community resource linkage and social reintegration services,” it said, adding that describing social work as providing drugs and creating addicts is inconsistent with the professional duties of personnel in the work.
In international public health, harm reduction programs minimize health and social risks associated with drug use, including disease transmission, overdoses, family dysfunction and social exclusion, the association said.
“Drug harm reduction does not mean encouraging drug use, nor does it mean providing drugs indiscriminately,” it said, adding that public figures should avoid spreading false information that undermines the social work profession and the people they serve.
“I must emphasize again that harm reduction programs do not encourage drug use and programs do not ask social workers to give out drugs,” Shih said yesterday. “I must solemnly state: Do not let unnecessary [political] mud-slinging distort or disrupt the programs.”
Harm reduction programs include syringe provision, methadone maintenance treatment, infection screening and social reintegration, work that relies on the collaboration of many professionals, he said.
The programs have yielded significant results, he added.
People should stop interfering with the work of frontline professional workers, Shih said.
Lee yesterday said that she agrees with the association that effective anti-drug policies should be grounded in scientific evidence, cross-disciplinary collaboration and a comprehensive social support system.
She said she firmly opposes a model in which community centers provide drugs and clean needles to drug users.
Social workers are not drug providers, she said, adding that their professional roles and responsibilities should not be undermined, and community safety should not be jeopardized.
Addiction prevention and harm reduction should follow the practice of providing methadone substitution therapy through medical institutions, where people must take the medication on-site under direct medical supervision and are not allowed to leave with it, Lee said.
The roles and responsibilities of medical professionals, social workers, drug abuse prevention centers and other specialists should also be clearly defined, she said, adding that cross-disciplinary collaboration and a clear division of responsibilities are essential to minimize the harm drugs cause to people and society.

Official outlines plans for Stinger missiles from US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:56 UTC

Taiwan is to receive 500 Stinger missiles and 178 launchers from the US by the end of the year, the first batch under a planned two-stage acquisition totaling 2,621 missiles and 763 launchers, a defense official said yesterday on condition of anonymity.
The portable missiles would play a vital role in the nation’s air defense capabilities, the source said.
The army plans to deploy 2,235 missiles and 657 launchers to defend Taiwan proper and outlying islands, they said, citing military documents.
Photo courtesy of the Military News Agency
The navy is allotted 295 missiles and 85 launchers to arm the Marine Corps and some surface vessels that lack air defense firepower, they said.
An additional 91 missiles and 21 launchers would be issued to the military police assigned to the defense of Taipei and the surrounding region, the source added.
The US has separately delivered a batch of Stinger missiles as part of a defense aid package, the source said, adding that those weapons have been spotted in the hands of military police over the past two years.
Military police have test fired Stinger systems, and used them at drills involving Taipei MRT stations and Wanban Bridge (萬板大橋).
In August, marines fielded a four-ship formation of M109 assault boats armed with Stinger air defense systems and Javelin guided anti-tank missiles in an asymmetric warfare coastal defense drill.
The Stinger missile is battle-tested with a proven record of performance in the Soviet-Afghan War and Russia’s ongoing war with Ukraine.
The Stinger is a fire-and-forget weapon that primarily targets aircraft. Weighing 15.7kg, the system can be carried by a lone infantry soldier to engage aerial targets up to 8,000m away, assuming ideal conditions. Practical range is more typically limited to 4,800m.
The most modern iteration of the Stinger missiles uses a dual-spectrum infrared and ultraviolet seeker module to defeat flares deployed by aircraft as a countermeasure against heat-seeking missiles.

Is Russia’s place on the UN Security Council legal?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:54 UTC
01:41:54 KST

“We the peoples of the United Nations determined to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war,” so begins the UN Charter. Yet Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is well into its fourth year, confirming just how far the UN has strayed from its foundational promise.
The problem is not simply that the UN has failed to stop a major war. It is that the state waging the war exercises a veto within the very body that the Charter entrusts with preserving international peace and security. Last month, the Security Council met once again to discuss Ukraine, and once again, the world saw how Russia has turned the Soviet Union’s permanent seat, which it usurped in 1991, into a license for impunity. If ever the Council tries to respond to Russian aggression, the Kremlin blocks it from doing so.
This perverse arrangement is usually described as an unfortunate, but unavoidable flaw of the system — but is it? The UN has never examined how the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (RSFSR) or its successor, the Russian Federation, acquired membership in the organization and on the Security Council in the first place. Yet surely this matter warrants closer scrutiny. On the basis of which documents, exactly, did Russia inherit the Soviet Union’s veto-wielding position?
Illustration: Constance Chou
The answer is remarkably thin. Article 23 of the Charter still lists the “Union of Soviet Socialist Republics” as a permanent member of the Security Council. The Soviet Union was a founding member of the UN in 1945, as were Ukraine and Belarus. The same cannot be said for the RSFSR or the Russian Federation.
To be sure, on Dec. 8, 1991, Belarus, Russia and Ukraine declared that the Soviet Union was ceasing to exist “as a subject of international law and a geopolitical reality;” and on Dec. 21, in Alma-Ata (now Almaty), the members of the new Commonwealth of Independent States, including Ukraine, expressed support for Soviet Russia’s continuation of the USSR’s UN membership, including its permanent seat on the Security Council.
However, then no legal steps were taken to secure this status ever. Instead, on Dec. 24, former RSFSR president Boris Yeltsin sent the UN secretary-general a letter stating that the Soviet Union’s membership was being “continued” by the Russian Federation. It is hard to assign legal weight to this letter, because no state called the Russian Federation existed when Yeltsin sent it.
Moreover, the UN Charter explains clearly what membership requires: a formal application, Security Council consideration, an assessment of compliance with Article 2, a recommendation to the General Assembly, deliberation and a vote in the Assembly, parliamentary ratification of the Charter and a deposit of the instrument of ratification with the designated authority. There is no evidence that Russia completed this process, or even attempted to begin it.
Russia’s usurpation of the Soviet seat has no comparable precedent in UN history. When the former Yugoslavia tried the same dubious maneuver in 1992, the Security Council (Resolution 777) unequivocally rejected its claim to be a continuing state. Yet in December 2022, when Ukraine’s parliament and foreign ministry formally stated that Russia’s UN membership had never been properly established, the response was silence — a tacit admission that no one could offer a credible legal rebuttal.
The proper response is obvious. Russia should be stripped of the right to represent the Soviet Union, on the grounds that it came to its permanent membership on the Security Council illegitimately. Now that its usurpation of the Soviet Union’s rights has enabled it to wage a war of aggression, putting the political and legal question of its membership on the agenda is crucial for upholding the UN’s core mission and securing punishment for the crimes against humanity that have been committed as part of an attack on a UN member state.
The UN has at least two precedents to draw on here. The first is China. In 1971, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758, recognizing the representatives of the People’s Republic of China as “the only legitimate representatives of China” and removing Chiang Kai-shek’s (蔣介石) representatives. The vote was 76 to 35, with 17 abstentions. The PRC also assumed the permanent seat on the Security Council, although Article 23 was not amended (it still refers to the “Republic of China”).
The cases are not identical. In China’s case, two governments claimed to represent a state that continued to exist, but this distinction only strengthens the case for revisiting Russia’s status. If deciding who represented an existing state required a vote, why was the question of who would inherit the seat of a vanished state settled by a letter?
The second precedent is Yugoslavia. Here, a state had broken apart, its largest remnant declared itself the continuing state, and the UN Security Council plainly said no. This answer was given to Belgrade, but never to Moscow — not for legal reasons, but for political ones. There were no arguments to support it, and the issue was simply never brought up for discussion. Yugoslavia had neither nuclear weapons nor designs on a permanent seat.
Against this backdrop, a third instrument has acquired renewed significance since 2022: Resolution 377 (V), known as “Uniting for Peace.” Adopted in 1950, it addresses situations in which a disagreement among permanent members prevents the Security Council from fulfilling its responsibilities. On Feb. 27, 2022, the Council invoked this provision to adopt Resolution 2623 by 11 votes to one, with three abstentions, calling an emergency special session of the General Assembly. Since the decision was procedural, Russia could not veto it.
However, this instrument has its limits. It bypasses Russia’s veto without questioning its right to occupy the seat from which it is cast. The General Assembly can identify Russia as an aggressor, reaffirm Ukraine’s territorial integrity, condemn annexation, and recommend mechanisms for accountability, but those decisions are recommendations. Russia retains the power to paralyze the body whose decisions are binding, even though the legality of its presence in that body has never been established.
The debate over Russia’s status must therefore be separated from the seemingly hopeless debate over Security Council reform. There is no need to abolish the veto to challenge Russia’s use of it. There is no need to rewrite the Charter to ask whether Russia is entitled to powers the Charter assigns to the Soviet Union. There is not even a need for a separate resolution. The General Assembly already has a Credentials Committee, the mechanism through which the South African delegation’s credentials were rejected in 1974.
What would happen to the Security Council if the seat is left empty? Nothing. When the Soviet Union boycotted the Council from January to August 1950, the Council adopted its resolutions on Korea. An empty seat is not a veto.
Some might argue that even raising the question is dangerous. Whatever Russia has done, they would say, a nuclear power must remain inside the UN, and a channel of communication must stay open. However, reviewing Russia’s status would neither end diplomacy nor invalidate every Security Council decision adopted with Russia’s participation. The question is whether diplomacy should continue to rest on a legal fiction.
The General Assembly should do what it failed to do in 1991: formally examine the legality of the Russian Federation’s representation of the former Soviet Union. The answer need not be predetermined, but the question must finally be raised.
Member states can examine Yeltsin’s letter, the Alma-Ata papers, the practice of state succession, the Charter, the precedents of China and Yugoslavia, and three decades of subsequent practice. Russia can present its case, others can present theirs and the General Assembly can vote. That is how a rules-based international order should work. A nameplate does not confer the right to a seat at the table. The rules do.
Denys Shtilierman, co-owner and chief designer of Fire Point, is co-founder of #unrussiaUN, the initiative group for expelling Russia from the UN.

Ministry releases video on Taiwan’s path to democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:54 UTC
01:41:54 KST

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs released a video titled “The Album of a Nation” to mark Double Ten National Day, highlighting Taiwan’s democratic development and resilience in the face of adversity.
It is available in 13 languages, including Chinese, English, Spanish, Japanese, Thai and Vietnamese.
As this year marks the 30th anniversary of Taiwan’s first direct presidential election, the video used artificial intelligence (AI) to help showcase Taiwan’s journey toward freedom, diversity and democracy, combining historical footage and interviews, the ministry said.
Photo: Screen grab from the video
The five-and-a-half-minute video opens with the narrator saying: “This is our family album. Its pages tell the story of Taiwan’s journey to the present day.”
Veteran Chang Yung-cheng (張永正) guides viewers through key moments in Taiwan’s history, the ministry said.
The video recounts Taiwan’s withdrawal from the UN in the 1970s and the diplomatic setbacks that followed, which left the nation increasingly isolated internationally, it said.
Then, it traces Taiwan’s democratic transformation through events such as the Wild Lily Student Movement after martial law was lifted and the 1996 Taiwan Strait missile crisis ahead of the nation’s first direct presidential election, the ministry added.
The film weaves together Taiwan’s national development with Chang’s personal experiences, illustrating how the nation persevered through hardship, never gave up on hope, and emerged with a stronger sense of determination and resilience, it said.
The video highlights Taiwan’s growing international presence, featuring interactions between President William Lai (賴清德) and leaders of diplomatic allies, as well as Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim’s (蕭美琴) speech at an Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China forum, the ministry said.
It also includes pivotal moments, such as Taiwan becoming the first nation in Asia to legalize same-sex marriage in 2019, the nation’s contributions during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, and its role as a key hub in global AI and semiconductor supply chains, it added.
The film ends by revisiting major milestones in Taiwan’s history through an intergenerational lens, including Taiwanese athlete Yang Chuan-kwang (楊傳廣) winning the nation’s first Olympic medal in 1960, the lifting of martial law in 1987 and the 921 earthquake in 1999, it said.
Taiwanese have moved forward despite crises and challenges, and the memories of hardship and achievement have not only strengthened national identity, but also shaped the unique spirit of “Team Taiwan,” the ministry said.

Dialogue welcome, but do not distort history: Lai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:53 UTC
01:41:53 KST

Taiwan welcomes efforts by the US and China to reduce the risk of war through dialogue, but they must respect the historical record of World War II and the Taiwanese people’s right to exist, President William Lai (賴清德) said yesterday in his Double Ten National Day address.
Faced with sustained “gray zone” pressure from China, Taiwan has increased defense spending and worked to bolster society’s overall ability to defend itself by combining government and civilian capabilities, Lai said.
Such efforts are not a provocation, but ensure dialogue can take place on the basis of “dignity and parity,” he said.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
“We welcome the US and China managing their competition through dialogue and reducing the risk of conflict and war,” he said. “But we must also point out that maintaining regional security, peace and stability requires a correct understanding of how history has unfolded.”
“There must be no tolerance for distorting the history of World War II. There must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist,” Lai said. “We are open to exchanges, but will not accept subordination.”
Taiwan is “going farther, step by step, with our diplomacy,” he said, citing his visit in May to Eswatini, Taiwan’s sole African ally, despite Chinese attempts to block the trip. China had pressured three African states to deny his chartered flight access to their airspace, causing a delay to his initial visit.
He also cited as an example Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim’s (蕭美琴) June visit to Palau, another ally of Taiwan, and her speech last month at the European Conference of Ventotene for Freedom and Democracy in Italy.
Taiwan has worked with international partners on healthcare, agriculture, energy, technology, education and sustainable development to meet their needs, and has improved lives through those efforts, Lai said.
“‘Taiwan Can Help’ is not just a slogan. It is a commitment — our willingness to share our capabilities and shoulder responsibility,” he added.

Missouri hosts world tree climbing championship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:50 UTC
01:41:50 KST

Nearly 100 arborists clad in helmets and rope harnesses scaled pine, sweetgum and oak trees in a park in St. Louis, Missouri, during the International Tree Climbing Championship.
This year is the competition’s 50th anniversary, where contestants from 22 countries are showcasing their climbing finesse over three days, beginning on Friday.
During the belayed speed climb, fellow competitors cheered as climbers raced to the treetop under a sunny, blue sky. Spectators in camping chairs craned their necks to watch the arborists weave through branches to find a dummy during the aerial rescue event.
Photo: AP
EJ Turner’s favorite event was the work climb, where competitors scramble through the 25m to 35m trees and ring bells at the end of branches to simulate cuts an arborist would make on the job. Turner, a third-generation climber and winner of five Midwest chapter competitions, said participants are graded on speed, route planning and poise.
“It’s a lot more climbing involved, and a lot more movement throughout the tree, jumping and swinging,” Turner said. “It’s kind of like being a kid.”
Along with the belayed speed climb, aerial rescue and work climb, climbers participate in ascent and throwline events during the first round. Those with the highest scores advance to the Masters’ Challenge.
The championship showcases what arborists do in their day-to-day jobs, said Caitlyn Pollihan, CEO of the nonprofit International Society of Arboriculture, which organizes the event. Many of the 52 men and 39 women in this year’s contest have competed against one another before.
“There’s this just fascinating camaraderie that you wouldn’t necessarily expect at a competition,” Pollihan said.
The first International Tree Climbing Championship was hosted in St. Louis in 1976. Pollihan said they chose to host the competition in the same city as a nod to the first contest. Organizers plan to make speeches and hand out keepsakes for the 50th anniversary.
“We have some fun nods to the fact that this is a big milestone,” Pollihan said.

Taiwan in Time: Surviving the White Terror, remembering the condemned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:50 UTC
01:41:50 KST

Oct. 12 to Oct. 18
After 11 years in prison on Green Island, Yen Shih-hung (顏世鴻) was finally due for release when a camp guard asked him for NT$20,000 to help pay his bride price.
Yen refused. The next day, officials deemed that he had “failed to improve his thinking” and ordered him to undergo further political reeducation on Siaoliouciou (小琉球), where prisoners were also subjected to forced labor. He spent another 19 months there before regaining his freedom in January 1964.
Photo courtesy of Taiwan Cultural Memory Bank
Yen’s punishment stemmed from his joining the Taiwan Provincial Student Affairs Committee (台灣省學生工作委員會), a Chinese Communist Party (CCP) organization, in January 1950. Before he participated in any activities, the government launched a crackdown on Taiwan’s communist underground. Of the more than 30 people implicated in Yen’s case, 11 were executed that November — including Yeh Sheng-chi (葉盛吉), who had recruited Yen.
Between his arrest in June 1950 and his release, Yen spent time in the major military detention centers in the Taipei area during the White Terror: the north and south stations of the Secrets Bureau, and the Military Law Bureau’s facilities on Qingdao E Road and in Ankeng, Sindian District (新店). The Jingmei Military Detention Center, now the Jingmei White Terror Memorial Park, did not open until 1968.
In 2012, the physician and author published his memoir, No. 3, Qingdao East Road: My Hundred-Year Memories and Taiwan’s Outrageous Era (青島東路三號:我的百年之憶及台灣的荒謬年代), recounting his life and reflecting on his experiences.
Photo: CNA
ANTI-JAPANESE FAMILY
Yen was born on Oct. 13, 1927 in Kaohsiung to a family with a history of resisting Japanese rule. His grandfather fought in the Republic of Formosa resistance before it fell in 1895, and several of his maternal uncles were involved in anti-Japanese activities while living in China. His fifth uncle, Chang Hsi-chun (張錫鈞), was a noted intelligence agent during the Second Sino-Japanese War.
His father trained as an ophthalmologist and moved the family to Quanzhou, Fujian Province, around 1930 to practice there. Involved in Taiwanese anti-colonial resistance in China, he strictly forbade speaking Japanese at home, Yen recalls.
Photo courtesy of National Central Library
The family returned to Taiwan in 1937 for reasons that are unclear. His father was detained for 11 days soon after, and again for two months in 1938. The family fell on hard times as his father could not practice openly in Taiwan and suffered from poor health after going on hunger strike during his imprisonment.
Yen was accepted into Taihoku Imperial University’s medical school in March 1945. But amid concerns that US troops would invade Taiwan, the students were sent to Tamsui to build fortifications and learn how to fight. He contracted malaria while visiting his family in Tainan and spent the rest of the war in isolation.
COMMUNIST UNDERGROUND
Photo courtesy of Wikimedia Commons
Yen was moved to tears of joy when Japan announced its surrender. He returned home to find his family living in a metal-roofed shack, all of them recovering from malaria. His father was more interested in politics than practicing medicine, Yen recalled, and the family was so poor that, after resuming medical school in Taipei, he survived by selling his blood until he earned a scholarship in 1949.
By this time, Yen had become disillusioned with KMT rule and was reading voraciously, including leftist literature. He met Yeh in 1947, and the two worked together in the student self-government association and lived in the same dorm.
Yeh had joined the Chinese Communist Party’s Taiwan Working Committee in 1948 and was allegedly in charge of its student branch at National Taiwan University (NTU). He revealed his role to Yen in 1949, and on Jan. 23, 1950, Yen officially joined. Just six days later, Working Committee leader Tsai Hsiao-chien (蔡孝乾) was arrested, and Yen’s first order was to lay low and refrain from all activities.
Photo courtesy of Center for GIS, RCHSS, Academia Sinica
Tsai escaped and was re-arrested in April, after which he “repented” and provided authorities with information about Taiwan’s communist network. Mass arrests began in May, including several NTU medical department heads and physicians. Yeh was caught on May 29.
Yen spent the next few weeks on edge, lingering on campus as he waited for final exams. Many of his friends had already been detained. On June 21, police showed up at his door.
IMPRISONMENT AND RELEASE
Yen was first detained by the Criminal Police Corps and sent to the south station of the Military Law Bureau, which was so crowded that prisoners had to take turns sleeping. He was then moved to the north station, where he was questioned and confessed to joining the committee.
He arrived at 3, Qingdao E Road (青島東路三號) on Sept. 2, where he underwent a military trial without a lawyer. He recalled prisoners being interrogated for days, many of whom received death sentences or lengthy prison terms. In the morning, guards would call people’s names, and those inmates would be taken to Machangding (馬場町) in today’s Wanhua District (萬華) to be executed.
Yen wrote his farewell letter, but he was spared capital punishment and received 12 years. He said that he clearly remembered the morning of Nov. 29, when Yeh and 10 other prisoners in his case were called out.
On May 13, 1951, the prisoners were handcuffed together and marched in rows from Qingdao E Road to the now-defunct Huashan Railway Station, where they boarded a train to Keelung before taking a boat to Green Island.
Unable to return to NTU after his release, Yen continued his studies at Taipei Medical University and began practicing at a charitable hospital in Tainan that treated poor and chronically ill patients.
On Oct. 23, 1971, he visited Machangding alone during a business trip to Taipei. It was chilly and drizzling, just like the morning when Yeh and the others were executed. He stood there for 20 minutes. The next day was Frost Descent, one of the 24 solar terms, which would become the title of the first version of his memoir, published in 1988.
“I believe no one has the right to decide whether another person lives or dies, so I wrote this long, childish piece for your deaths,” he wrote.

There was a time when Chinese master Yuan Shimao thought martial arts were all about punching and kicking. As a young practitioner, he focused on speed and strength. “I trained that way for many years without becoming still enough to search within myself,” said Yuan, who founded a kung fu academy in central China in 2004. “But as you gradually settle into stillness, you begin to understand what the scriptures mean by spirit,” he added. “You can begin to rediscover yourself.” That process is known as “entering the Dao” in martial arts. It is a guiding principle at Yuan’s academy in the sacred
There was a time, a few decades ago, when the men who owned the world’s biggest pornography businesses were happy to be famous. They paraded a lifestyle they hoped looked glamorous, appearing in public dressed in silk pajamas or with a woman in swimwear on each arm. Porn moguls like Hustler’s Larry Flynt or Playboy’s Hugh Hefner were household names. “Say what you want about these old perverts, who once set the tone of our sexual culture, but at least you knew who they were and what they were selling,” Patricia Nilsson writes in her new book, Guilty Pleasure: The Pornification
In 1904 the Japanese introduced caning to Taiwan. As a punishment, caning was applied by the Japanese to Taiwanese and Chinese subjects, never to the Japanese themselves (it had been outlawed in Japan in 1882). An imperial and colonial act, caning thus functioned to define and display social class boundaries. So it is with the new legislation permitting caning proposed by Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) legislators last week. According to the KMT proposal, individuals committing major fraud, aggravated sexual assault, driving under the influence of drugs and child abuse may be subject to caning. These are high-profile offenses that generate great
As skyscrapers claw at the sky across the nation’s major cities, urban renewal efforts continue. Planners face a daunting environment. Nearly 60 percent of the housing stock is over 30 years of age, with Penghu, Yunlin and Chiayi counties exhibiting the highest average building ages, all over 40 years. In Taipei, 673,000 residences — over 70 percent of all homes — are over 30 years old, with an average age of 39.1 years. Taiwan’s shining office towers conceal a world of aging homes badly in need of replacement. Rising housing prices are killing more than just the future of Taiwan’s young.

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday urged Taiwan to become a “city upon a hill” amid authoritarian expansion and global upheaval, adding that Taiwan cherishes peace, but will not give up its freedom.
“In this era marked by war, authoritarian expansion and a rapidly shifting global order, what kind of nation should Taiwan strive to be? My answer is this: We must become a ‘city upon a hill,’ built with courage and confidence,” Lai said in a Double Ten National Day speech titled “Taiwan’s Future: A City upon a Hill, the Salt and Light of the World” at a ceremony in front of the Presidential Office Building in Taipei.
“This is not to sing our own praises, but rather to declare our aspirations for the nation’s future,” he said. “It is also a responsibility Taiwan stands ready to shoulder.”
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
“City upon a hill” and “salt and light” are elements from Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount.
“This city upon a hill is built atop a chain of guardian mountains that is the splendid outcome of democratic governance which grants us a solid basis for peace of mind,” Lai said, adding that it must stand on a firm foundation and that “the well-being of our people is the very foundation of Taiwan.”
Lai pledged that his administration would pursue pragmatic governance by raising wages, cutting taxes, expanding welfare and easing financial burdens, so everyone can enjoy greater economic security and a better quality of life.
Photo: CNA
Facing China’s far larger military, which is adding advanced new weapons such as stealth fighter jets, aircraft carriers and a huge array of missiles, Taiwan is ramping up defense spending and modernizing its armed forces, he said.
The government’s increased investment in defense aimed to deter war, not provoke it, he added.
“And we are strengthening our self-defense not to abandon dialogue, but to ensure that dialogue can take place on the basis of parity and dignity,” he told the crowd at the event, during which he watched military displays and dance performances.
Peace cannot rely solely on “wishes,” Lai said. “Taiwan cherishes peace, but we will not give up our freedom. We are open to exchanges, but will not accept subordination.”
“There must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist,” he said.
Lai urged democracies in the Indo-Pacific region to join forces to retain the “status quo” of peace and stability in the region.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
China has exerted pressure in an attempt to change the “status quo” across the Taiwan Strait, Lai said. The nation’s “resolve” is not just about its own survival in the face of “authoritarian expansion,” it is also about whether the international community still believes that force cannot override rules.
The US welcomes Lai’s commitment to maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait, a senior White House official said, adding, in reference to China, that “a routine speech is no justification for aggressive or coercive actions.”
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office later yesterday criticized Lai’s speech, saying that it “disregards facts, distorts the truth, misleads the public and reveals ulterior motives.”
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
In his speech, Lai “stubbornly clung to ‘Taiwan independence’ separatist thinking” and exaggerated the “threat from the mainland,” the office said.
“There is only one China in the world and Taiwan is part of China — this is the true status quo in the Taiwan Strait,” it said, adding that Taiwan’s future “can and must be decided jointly by all the Chinese people, including our compatriots in Taiwan.”

Two elderly farmers who went on an agricultural technology exchange program in Japan 60 years ago were reunited yesterday after one of them made a chance appearance on television earlier this month.
Taichung men Chao Shih-tung (趙世通), aged 95, and Su Cheng-feng (蘇成峰), aged 89, were among the 10 elite tangerine farmers the then-Council of Agriculture selected to participate in the one-year program in Japan’s Ehime Prefecture.
Chao and Su, Taichung compatriots who respectively hailed from Dongshi (東勢) and Waipu (外埔), became inseparable friends during their stay in Japan, visiting Kagoshima in Kyushu during their free time.
Photo courtesy of Chao
Chao used the knowledge he aquired at the Chen Tung Tangerine Orchard to develop his own citrus-growing techniques, eventually becoming one of the nation’s foremost experts in citrus farming.
Su stayed in Waipu and continued to grow tangerines before transitioning to rice agriculture, which was more suited to the locality’s hydrographical conditions.
The two men drifted apart following their return, as they branched into different agricultural fields and began families.
Photo: Chang Husan-che, Taipei Times
On Oct. 7, Su’s daughter saw a human-interest story about Chao, in which the renowned tangerine farmer lamented losing touch with his best friend during their time in Japan.
Recognizing the shared history, she contacted Chen Tung Tangerine Orchard, which reconnected the old friends.
Su and Chao had a tearful reunion yesterday at the latter’s orchid, with their extended family in tow.
The duo shared their photographs from their time in Japan and promised to meet again.

All Blacks hammer Wallabies 50-19
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:48 UTC
01:41:48 KST

New Zealand lifted some of the gloom that gathered after their series loss in South Africa by beating Australia 50-19 in the first of two rugby Tests on Saturday to retain the Bledisloe Cup for the 24th year.
The character of an All Blacks team on a three-match losing streak was tested when Wallabies fullback Tom Wright scored the first try of the match at Eden Park, where the Wallabies have not won since 1986 and New Zealand is unbeaten against all comers in 54 matches.
However, an area that had been a weakness against South Africa became a strength as the All Blacks won contested kicks to set up tries for Peter Lakai and Tupou Vaa’i and to regain the lead. And selections which had been contentious, including Lakai’s in the No. 7 jersey and Damian McKenzie’s at flyhalf proved astute.
Photo: AFP
McKenzie’s line breaks contributed to the All Blacks’ first-half tries and he kicked a penalty which made New Zealand’s lead 17-7 after 33 minutes.
SORELY TESTED
The All Blacks’ backbone was measured again when Wallabies captain Harry Wilson put flyhalf Ben Donaldson into a gap and stayed in support to score a try that cut New Zealand’s lead to three points at halftime.
The Wallabies started the second half strongly and Beauden Barrett — another contentious selection at fullback — was forced to make two vital saves as the last line of defense.
However, the momentum turned and New Zealand scored twice in five minutes, through scrumhalf Cam Roigard and captain Codie Taylor, to create an important 17-point buffer at 31-14.
The All Blacks’ domination in the air continued along with a physical advantage in the collision and at the breakdown which had been missing in South Africa. They showed patience and composure with the ball in hand and built phases in a way that was lacking against the Springboks.
Jordie Barrett provided the spearhead of the All Blacks’ defense with some superb spot tackles.
ROIGARD’S RALLY
Roigard scored after a prolonged lineout drive in which several New Zealand backs participated. He sent the Wallabies defense the wrong way close to the line with a neat head fake. Taylor scored off Roigard’s pass after a concerted All Blacks buildup.
Roigard and Lakai featured in a try to winger Leroy Carter in the 66th minute that brought the All Blacks’ lead to 38-14. Asafo Aumua, Kyle Preston and Josh Moorby combined for a short-side raid that led to the All Blacks’ fifth try which increased the margin.
Fittingly, McKenzie had the last say. After the Wallabies had scored through Josh Nasser, McKenzie scored and converted the last try to bring up 50 points.
“Winning here is everything,” Taylor said. “This is home for us as All Blacks.”
“To come here, play in front of our people, to see ex-All Blacks...you want to do it for those people who went before you and continue the legacy,” he added.
EARLY CONFIDENCE
The Wallabies came into the match confident after their win over South Africa at home. They started both halves strongly and managed to pick holes in the All Blacks pressing defense, first through Max Jorgensen who made Wright’s try, then through Donaldson.
However, they could not match the All Blacks in the air or at the breakdown and there were periods of indiscipline which cost them field position. Set pieces were even, although the Wallabies stole a couple of All Blacks’ lineouts.
Wilson was superb again for Australia, Jorgensen was a hovering danger and Donaldson opportunistic at times. However, the Wallabies eventually were overwhelmed by an All Blacks team which had been depleted by injuries and down on their luck.
The second Test is in Sydney next weekend. New Zealand had to win only one of the Tests to retain the Bledisloe Cup which it has held since 2003.

Unknown Publisher

16:41:47 UTC

Tree preservation advocates yesterday rallied in front of the Presidential Office Building calling for safeguarding of the forest at Kaohsiung’s Ciaotou Sugar Refinery (橋頭糖廠).
The more than 100,000 trees around the refinery could be cut down for real-estate development, after the Kaohsiung New Town third-phase development project was approved by the Ministry of the Interior’s Urban Planning Commission in July, the protesters said.
“We call on the government not to ‘develop urban forests with the left hand and destroy existing forests with the right hand,’” said Chuang Chieh-jen (莊傑任), chairman of the Forest City Association, Taiwan.
Photo: CNA
The project would convert the more than 150 hectares of woodland into residential land, while the surrounding 400 hectares of building land remains idle, he said.
Given that Kaohsiung’s birthrate continued to decline over the past decade, the projected demand for such massive amounts of residential buildings is also questionable, Chuang said.
He called on Lai to help redefine the refinery’s woodland as a national-level urban forest demonstration zone in line with his urban forest development initiative.
Among the protesters was 83-year-old Chiang Huang Nu (蔣黃女).
Chiang Huang registered as a Kaohsiung city councilor candidate for next month’s local elections despite her advanced age, as she sought to help attract public support for preserving the woods around the refinery.
She said she became a temporary worker at the refinery when she was 13 and worked there for many years.
Her work involved various tasks such as planting sugarcane, hoeing the weeds, and weighing or shaving sugarcane, she said.
Chiang Huang used to walk for two hours every day to travel from her home at the Wulilin (五里林) community in Ciaotou District to the refinery, she said.
“I now take a walk for more than an hour in the woods every day,” she said, adding that cutting down the trees would deprive her of the delight that the woods offer.
Chiang Yao-chian (蔣耀賢), her eldest son, who convinced her to run for election, has long been dedicated to preserving the refinery’s historical and cultural heritage.
“We are not against development... We are asking for the road to be moved southward,” he said, referring to the project’s planned 60m-wide road that would cut through the woods.
Procedural injustice existed in the National Land Management Agency’s passage of the NT$36.5 billion (US$1.15 billion) project, which threatens more than 100,000 trees, he said.

Judge convicts Mexicans over killings of surfers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:46 UTC
01:41:46 KST

A local judge on Friday found three Mexicans guilty of the murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in April 2024 in the Mexican state of Baja California.
The trial for the triple homicide that shocked Mexico and drew international attention concluded on Friday after Judge Raul Hernandez in the coastal city of Ensenada ruled that Jesus Gerardo Garcia, alias “El Kekas,” Irineo Francisco “N” and Angel Jesus “N” were responsible for the murders of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson, and American Carter Redd Rhoad.
The defendants, who had been in custody for more than two years, were also found guilty of armed robbery and armed carjacking.
Photo: Reuters
“Today’s guilty verdict is a significant moment in our long and painful journey to seek justice for our beautiful sons, Callum and Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad, whose lives were so cruelly taken from them in 2024,” said father Martin Robinson.
The three traveled to Baja California in April 2024 to surf, but shortly after arriving in the town of Punta San Jose, about 80km from Ensenada, they were reported missing.
Their bodies were found on May 3 in a well.
Garcia, identified as the perpetrator of the murders, was arrested in May 2024 in connection to the case, along with his ex-partner Ary Gisell Silva Raya, Irineo Francisco “N” and Angel Jesus “N.”
During the month-long trial, chilling details of the brutal crime were revealed. Silva Raya testified last month during a hearing that Garcia confessed to her that he arrived with a 9mm pistol at the tent where the foreigners were staying.
Upon seeing him, they began throwing their belongings to prevent him from attacking them and one of them begged for his life, which the assailant ignored, she said.
The state prosecutors’ office reported that Silva Raya arrived in Punta San Jose on April 27, 2024, where she met the three foreigners and “instigated one of her companions to rob them,” which was carried out the following day.
The woman, who was found in possession of one of the victims’ cellphones, was sentenced in November 2025 to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to “aggravated robbery with violence” and “vehicle theft with violence” in an expedited proceeding.
However, Garcia and his two accomplices went to trial.
The judge is scheduled to announce the final sentence on Friday.
The Baja California State Attorney General’s Office requested for each defendant the “exemplary sentence” of 210 years in prison.
“No outcome can ever undo this tragedy, but we hope today marks an important step towards justice and allows us to continue honoring their lives and the extraordinary young men they were,” Martin Robinson said. “They will never be forgotten.”

AI directions leading to increasing calls for wilderness rescues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:41 UTC
01:41:41 KST

The route up the Widowmaker Arete, a 518m cliff in British Columbia, is deceptively described as “mostly easy slab climbing,” interspersed with “short steep sections that can include finger cracks, blocky face climbing.” It requires careful planning and the right equipment.
When 16-year-old Bryce Vincent Gowryluk found himself facing its sheer headwall last week, he had neither. He had asked the artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude for directions.
Gowryluk had to be rescued after those directions proved wildly incorrect, in the latest incident to raise questions about the reliance on digital maps for wilderness navigation.
Photo: Bloomberg
On a Saturday morning, Gowryluk took a gondola up to the top of Grouse Mountain and, while ascending, asked Claude to plan a route to nearby Crown Mountain and back. After navigating scree and more than 600m of elevation gain, the summit promises panoramic views of Greater Vancouver, the Fraser valley and the Capilano watershed.
The trek takes eight hours and hiking guides warn it is not for beginners.
As Gowryluk, an indoor climber, navigated down the Crown Pass and up through Crater Slabs and into a boulder-strewn valley, the directions from Claude took him away from the planned course.
He found himself at the final headwall of the Widowmaker Arete — a climb that requires ropes, cams and a clear plan for ascent. As he climbed, Gowryluk soon realized the terrain was far too steep and that he was stuck at the base of a cliff. He phoned his mother, then called emergency services for help.
Police notified North Shore Rescue, which launched a helicopter, but Gowryluk was too close to the rock face for the rotors, so two members of the rescue team were hoisted down to lift him up. He was flown to the rescue base near the Cleveland Dam.
In their debrief the rescue crew said Gowryluk was “far off” his intended route. While the incident could be the first time a hiker got lost because of AI, it is the latest in a string of mishaps in the mountainous region of south-western British Columbia, where hikers increasingly rely on imprecise directions.
In July, three people were rescued after they planned a route on the Howe Sound Crest Trail using Google Maps, which gave them wildly inaccurate time estimates, suggesting a route that often takes as long as 14 hours could be done in just more than five.
Search manager Paul Markey said that mountaineers should not rely on the directions of AI, and that proper preparation was key.
“In this particular case, the boy had a headlamp. He had good clothing. He had a good pair of boots, spare battery and spare food. He was pretty well equipped for hiking and scrambling. But he was certainly not prepared or equipped for rock climbing,” Markey said.
“Claude in this particular situation, has never been in the area that this 16-year-old boy found himself in. Claude can only go so far with regard to describing what the area may be like,” Markey said. “There’s definitely a trend towards using electronic applications as opposed to map and compass skills. But there is really no substitute for good map and compass training and education.”
He said that in some cases, apps give too much information.
“We have found that some of the apps have identified trails in areas where, really, our preference as a rescue team would be that those trails or routes are not actually identified,” he said, adding that people see routes they think are good trails only to get into trouble.
“The main thing is: do not blindly rely on AI as a route planning tool,” Markey said. “It can never substitute for good education, good training, a good experience, good decision making in the field.”

Taiwan’s modest Asian Games tally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:40 UTC
01:41:40 KST

Led by Taekwondo athlete Wang Chieh-ling (王婕菱) as the flag bearer at the closing ceremony for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games in Japan, the Taiwanese team — which competed as “Chinese Taipei” (TPE) — entered the stadium after Syria and before Tajikistan. The teams were filed in in alphabetical order, with Taiwan going in at “T” instead of “C.”
The Taiwanese team gleaned a modest five golds, 17 silvers and 33 bronzes, the first time since the 2006 Doha Asian Games that its number of gold medals failed to reach double digits. It also set a new low since winning only seven golds at the 1994 Hiroshima Asian Games.
The performance served as a warning sign to Taiwan’s sports development. However, the two biggest surprises were the gold medals in high jump and swimming. Although Taiwan took home 14 fewer gold medals than the last time, falling from sixth place to 15th in the medal tally, track-and-field athlete Fu Zhao-xuan (傅兆玄) claimed victory in the men’s high jump — Taiwan’s first gold in men’s track and field since the 1966 Bangkok Asian Games, while swimmer Eddie Wang (王冠閎) claimed victory in the men’s 200m butterfly event — the nation’s first gold in men’s swimming.
Logistics support for Taiwanese athletes was also highly praised. The Asian Games ran into one problem after another, such as accommodation, transportation and schedules. Even the supply of food was a mess. However, Taiwanese athletes remained unaffected, with many praising the logistics center set up by the Ministry of Sports.
After winning gold in women’s 60kg boxing, Lin Yu-ting (林郁婷) expressed her gratitude to the logistics team.
Former World No. 1 golfer Yani Tseng (曾雅妮) after winning a women’s team bronze said that compared with her previous solo efforts in professional tournaments, the logistics team’s support allowed everyone to focus on the competition without any worries.
The talent gap between generations is testing Minister of Sports and two-time Olympic gold medalist Lee Yang (李洋). While the logistics support received recognition from Taiwanese athletes, the unsatisfactory performance was undeniable. Many veteran stars on the team are 30 or older, such as Tseng, 37; Lin, 31; tennis player Hsieh Su-wei (謝淑薇), 40; weightlifter Kuo Hsing-chun (郭婞淳), 33; and gymnast Lee Chih-kai (李智凱), 30.
The “golden generation” that secured medals in the past two Asian and Olympic Games have been the backbone of Taiwan’s sports for more than a decade. However, as they enter the later stages of their glorious careers, the talent gap they leave behind is perhaps the biggest concern for Taiwan’s competitive sports.
How to deepen grassroots development, cultivate more talented athletes and enhance their competitive strength internationally are the greatest challenges for Lee and his ministry.
Nien Miao-yun is a journalist.

Opposition urges Lai to ‘fix’ constitutional crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:40 UTC
01:41:40 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) caucuses yesterday urged President William Lai (賴清德) to communicate with opposition parties to resolve the constitutional crisis.
Lai in his Double Ten National Day speech yesterday said that the gates of this “city upon the hill” must be wide open to the world, but he has built high walls between himself and Taiwanese who have different opinions, KMT caucus deputy secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said.
The Executive Yuan’s refusal to countersign bills passed by the Legislative Yuan has caused a constitutional controversy, yet Lai has not initiated effective dialogue, she said.
Photo: Screen grab from the video
The magnanimity of a president lies in their willingness to open doors to those with differing opinions, Hsu said, adding that democracy does not mean that the winner of an election can monopolize the state, nor demanding that opposition parties obey the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP).
Lai in his speech boasted that Taiwan’s economic growth rate is expected to exceed 11 percent this year, yet he turns a blind eye to the nation’s worsening K-shaped economy, she said.
While artificial intelligence and semiconductor industries report growing profits, traditional sectors bear the brunt of tariffs, exchange rate fluctuations and rising costs, Hsu said.
Even as the stock market hits record highs, many working-class families remain overwhelmed by soaring prices and overinflated housing costs, she added.
The KMT caucus calls on Lai to promptly invite all political parties for substantive dialogue and consultation, focusing on addressing constitutional disputes, livelihood legislation and budgetary issues, while establishing a mechanism for continuous dialogue, she said.
Taiwanese want to live and work in peace, not political illusions; cross-party reconciliation, not high walls of confrontation, she added.
KMT Chairperson Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) said economic growth should benefit older manufacturing industries, services, agriculture and fisheries, and not be concentrated in the high-tech sector.
Meanwhile, TPP Chairman Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) called on Lai to promulgate laws passed by the legislature.
The Legislative Yuan has not yet begun committee review of the central government’s budget for next year and a supplementary budget for this year, Huang said, accusing Lai of creating a misleading impression that lawmakers were deliberately delaying their passage.
Lai had called on lawmakers to swiftly review and pass the budgets.
Lai in his speech said that “political parties may compete, and opinions can differ, but the Taiwan we are so firmly rooted in should not be divided as a result,” but the president and his DPP government have “torn Taiwan apart” by launching a recall against opposition lawmakers and refusing to countersign laws passed by the legislature, TPP caucus whip Jacky Chen (陳清龍) said.
Chen urged Lai to set aside partisan differences, listen with an open mind, and respect the legislature as well as democracy’s system of oversight and checks and balances.

Vintage collector reunites family with 60-year-old album
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:40 UTC
01:41:40 KST

A Kaohsiung vintage item collector has reunited a family with a 60-year-old photo album, helping the family reconnect with a piece of their history.
Lee Huang (李煌), the former operator of a cafe famed for its extensive vinyl record collection in Kaohsiung’s Hunei District (湖內), bought a family photo album from a vendor at a market in Tainan’s Shanhua District (善化) late last year, he said on Tuesday.
The album consisted of 120 black-and-white photographs that recorded the daily life of a family, Lee said.
Photo: Su Fu-nan, Taipei Times
Clues in the photos led him to identify the family patriarch as Ko Chih-sun (葛?蓀), a former patent section at the National Bureau of Standards, the predecessor of the Bureau of Standards, Metrology and Inspection and Intellectual Property Office, he said.
Lee published samples of the photos and shared his discoveries on social media, and thought that would be the end of it, he said.
To his surprise, Ko’s granddaughter Ko Huan-chun (葛奐君) contacted him in August, saying the album had belonged to her family before going missing 30 years ago, he said.
She asked to buy the album from him, as most of the people in it have since passed away and she hoped to have the photobook as a keepsake, Lee said.
Lee on Tuesday gave the album to the family free of charge, later commenting on his business Old Record Cafe’s (老唱片主題咖啡館) social media page that he had never been prouder as a vintage collector in his life.
A visibly tearful Ko Huan-chun, who traveled with her mother, Wang Yu-chih (王玉治), to meet Lee, said she was grateful he had helped save the family’s history.
Wang said her father, who was the youngest among his siblings, passed away at an early age.
Finding the album would help the family preserve its legacy, she said.
Wang said her father-in-law moved with his family from China and worked for the National Bureau of Standards for the rest of his life to raise his six children.
No one in the family could explain when or how the album went missing, or its story before being found in Tainan, he added.

Surging gold drives up centenarian gifting costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:38 UTC
01:41:38 KST

Taiwan’s aging population and soaring global gold prices are making the Double Ninth Festival’s tradition of gifting golden charms to centenarians more expensive, officials said.
The Ministry of Health and Welfare’s Social and Family Affairs Administration Director Chou Tao-chun (周道君) on Friday said that there are 6,489 Taiwanese aged 100 years or older this year, up from 5,749 last year.
He made the remarks ahead of this year’s festival on Oct. 18.
Photo courtesy of the ministry’s Social and Family Affairs Administration
The figure includes 2,490 Taiwanese who became or are becoming centenarians this year, qualifying them for the ministry’s customary gift of golden lock-shaped charms, weighing about 5.6g apiece, he said.
With rising gold prices, the ministry spent NT$97,221,346 (US$3 million) on the charms, up from NT$76,990,000 last year, he said.
Officials had feared the expenses would exceed NT$100 million before gold prices fell from a high of NT$5,066 per gram, he added.
Giving charms to older people is a gesture in traditional culture of respect and expression of care for the elderly, whose welfare is being looked after by the agency, Chou said.
Officials organize activities in community centers to encourage older people who are active to eat together and engage in activities while those with declining faculties are placed under long-term care, he said.
The agency is working to include older people who are living alone in its care network to ensure their safety and wellbeing, he said.
On the same day, the ministry staged a Double Ninth celebration at Taipei Main Station that attracted a large crowd, including young and old.
The event featured games including tops and pinball machines, nostalgically styled general stores, a high-tech health screening station, an oral health clinic, financial management advisers and an information desk for elderly commuting needs.
Deputy Minister of Health and Welfare Lu Chien-te (呂建德) said that more than 4.8 million Taiwanese were 65 years old or older as of last count, or 20.7 percent of the total population.
The government is confronting the challenge of Taiwan’s aging demographics with the healthy Taiwan, Long Term Care 3.0 and elderly care initiatives, with the latter targeting senior citizens living alone, he said.
Taiwan’s NT$115.3 billion long-term care budget this year represents a significant increase more than the NT$92.7 billion last year, with an additional NT$6.25 billion to fund care for older Taiwanese who live alone over the next two years, he said.
The nation has more than 5,200 community-based care centers for senior citizens, which are operated by volunteers and older people in the area, he said.

French sailor readies for a world-first solo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:33 UTC
01:41:33 KST

Alexia Barrier looks impossibly small at the helm of IDEC Sport-CIC, a 32m trimaran capable of tearing across the ocean at more than 40 knots (74kph). Soon, she is going to be entirely alone.
On Nov. 1, the 46-year-old French sailor is going to climb aboard the giant vessel in Saint-Malo and attempt something no woman has done before: race solo in the giant Ultim class in the Route du Rhum.
“It’s the biggest machine participating in offshore sailing around the world,” Barrier said in an interview. “Only eight of this kind are on the planet. So I’m happy, proud and privileged to be skipper of this machine.”
Photo: Reuters
On a bright October morning in Brest, Barrier appears tiny on the deck of the huge red trimaran, 23m wide with a mast towering 34m above the water.
She hoisted the mainsail to the sound of the Black Eyed Peas’ “Meet Me Halfway,” rehearsing maneuvers she soon has to perform entirely alone. Even in the light breeze, the boat quickly accelerated toward 23 knots.
“The sails are huge. It’s really powerful. A sail is more than 100 kilos. I’m 55 kilos,” she said. “It goes so fast and if you make a mistake, it can be terrible because you can hurt the boat and hurt yourself. I’m super happy, but I’m more focused than ever.”
The boat has reached speeds of about 46 knots. Barrier laughs about the prospect of matching that herself.
“The record is about 46 knots, but you have to be a bit crazy to be at the helm at that speed,” she said jokingly.
FIRST ALL-FEMALE CREW
Nine months ago, Barrier was leading the first all-female crew to set a reference time for the Jules Verne Trophy, sailing non-stop around the world. Now, she trades that camaraderie for the peculiar solitude of single-handed ocean racing.
“When I came back from the Jules Verne Trophy, for me it was obvious,” she said of taking on the Route du Rhum alone. “It feels like it was in another life when I’m sailing solo. I miss my crewmates. Sometimes I catch myself looking around, searching for one of them at her usual station and she’s not there.”
Music is one companion. Barrier is still working on the playlist that would carry her through about a week alone at sea.
There is little time for distraction aboard a machine where the combination of enormous power, speed and physical demand means a small error can quickly become a serious one.
Barrier knows that this voyage is about more than a finishing position.
One of only 13 women to have completed the Vendee Globe, and now the skipper who led the all-female Jules Verne attempt, she has become used to being the first woman through doors that have traditionally been difficult to open.
“It’s part of my career. I’ve been racing for 20 years now, and it’s my life. For me, it’s a new step,” she said. “In a way, it’s cool to be the first. I can open a path for other women or little girls that are still wondering: ‘Shall I try, shall I do it.’”
ELITE OF SAILING
Breaking into Ultim racing required Barrier to find not only the experience but the money and team needed to operate at what she calls “the elite of sailing.”
Even now she can scarcely believe where that journey has taken her. Standing on the dock in Brest, Barrier recalled thinking of the challenge ahead: “I dreamed too big.”
With the Route du Rhum approaching, the dream has become very real.
Barrier, naturally, is already dreaming a little bigger.
“In my dreams, if the magic happens, reaching the podium would be amazing,” she said. “It’s also important to allow yourself to dream big.”
Nobody knows that better than Barrier.

ANALYTICAL ENGLISH 解析英語(常春藤)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:41:31 UTC
01:41:31 KST

Continued from yesterday（延續自昨日）
https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/lang
The kiwi is about the size of a chicken and is full of surprises. Kiwi pairs are famously loyal and often mate for life. They share the same burrow and raise their chicks together. Even more astonishing is the size of the kiwi’s egg. A single egg can weigh about 20 percent of the mother’s body weight. To put that in perspective, it would be like a human giving birth to a four-year-old child.
Photo: AdobeStock 照片：AdobeStock
After the mother lays the egg, the father takes responsibility for most of the incubation. Because of this devoted, stay-at-home fatherhood, New Zealanders use the term “Kiwi husband” to describe a man who is family-oriented.
The kiwi’s importance to New Zealand extends further. During World War I, New Zealand soldiers were nicknamed “Kiwis” because the bird appeared on their uniforms. The nickname later came to refer to all New Zealanders. The nation’s military honors this flightless creature even today. The Royal New Zealand Air Force features a kiwi in its official roundel, which might seem funny given that the bird itself cannot fly.
Unfortunately, habitat loss and introduced predators have caused kiwi populations to fall sharply over the decades. The kiwi is now a protected species, and dedicated conservation programs across New Zealand are working hard to increase its numbers. For a bird that cannot fly, it has come too far to disappear.
Photo: Ivy English 照片：常春藤解析英語
奇異鳥的大小跟雞差不多，還充滿了驚喜。奇異鳥夫妻以忠誠聞名，常常是終身保持同一配偶。牠們住在同一個巢穴中，共同養育雛鳥。奇異鳥蛋的大小更為驚人。一顆蛋的重量可以達母鳥體重約20%。客觀來看，就像是人類要生下四歲孩童。
鳥媽媽下蛋後，鳥爸爸會承擔起大部分的孵育責任。因為這樣全心投入、家庭主夫的角色，紐西蘭人使用Kiwi husband（編按：Kiwi用以指人的時候，K必須大寫）這個詞來形容愛家好男人。
奇異鳥對紐西蘭的重要性不止於此。一戰時，紐西蘭士兵因為制服上有奇異鳥而被暱稱為Kiwis。這個綽號後來演變為指稱所有紐西蘭人。至今，該國的軍隊仍向這隻不會飛的生物表達敬意。紐西蘭皇家空軍的官方圓標上有一隻奇異鳥，考慮到這種鳥本身並不會飛，這點可能滿有趣的。
遺憾的是，棲地喪失與外來掠食者的引入導致奇異鳥的數量在過去幾十年急遽下降。奇異鳥現在是受保護的物種，全紐西蘭專門針對奇異鳥的保育計畫正在努力增加其數量。對不會飛的鳥兒來說，牠們一路走來歷經漫長歲月，實在不該就此消失。
What Did You Learn?
1. What led New Zealanders to use the term “Kiwi husband”?
(A) The kiwi’s lifelong loyalty to its mate.
(B) The male kiwi’s role in caring for the egg.
(C) The female kiwi’s ability to lay an unusually large egg.
(D) The kiwi’s appearance on New Zealand’s military uniforms.
2. Why does the author conclude the passage by saying “For a bird that cannot fly, it has come too far to disappear”?
(A) To show that the kiwi is an important symbol worth protecting.
(B) To emphasize that the kiwi’s difficulties should be valued more.
(C) To argue that the kiwi can protect itself without conservation efforts.
(D) To suggest moving the kiwi to safer environments outside New Zealand.
答案： 1. B 2. A
Words in Use
1. loyal a. 忠誠的，忠心的
A loyal friend will stand by you when everyone else has left.
當其他人都已離去，忠誠的朋友會陪在你身邊。
2. astonishing a. 驚人的
Kent’s quick progress in learning English is astonishing.
肯特學英文迅速進步，很驚人。
3. perspective n. 觀點
put sth. in/into perspective 客觀來看某事物，把某事物放在正確的比較基準下看
Peggy was upset about the comment, but to put it in perspective, it was just one opinion.
佩姬因為那個評論而難過，但客觀來看，那只是其中一個看法而已。
4. devoted a. 全心全意的
The devoted volunteers spent a lot of time helping people in need.
這些盡心盡力的志工花了許多時間援助需要幫助的人。
5. extend vi. 延伸，延續
The fashion celebrity’s influence extends across the whole industry.
那位時尚名人的影響力遍及整個產業。
Practical Phrases
1. mate for life （動物）終身保持同一配偶
Penguins often mate for life and return to the same partner each breeding season.
企鵝常終身保持同一配偶，每個繁殖季都會回到同一個伴侶身邊。
2. give birth to. . . 生下……（孩子）
Elephants usually give birth to one calf at a time.
大象通常一次只生一隻小象。
3. take responsibility for. . . 承擔起……責任，為……負責
The company took responsibility for the incident and issued an apology.
該公司對那起事件負責，並發表道歉聲明。
4. refer to. .. 意指∕指的是……
On this map, the tent icons refer to designated camping areas.
在這張地圖上，帳篷的圖示意指指定的露營區。
5. given that + S + V 考慮到∕有鑑於……
Leo did an excellent job on the presentation, given that he only had two hours to prepare.
考慮到里歐只有兩小時能準備，他的簡報做得真棒。
