Israeli medics face ICC complaint over torture of Palestinian detainees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:22:53 UTC
01:22:53 KST

The Hind Rajab Foundation has filed a complaint with the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Israeli medical officials over torture and mistreatment of Palestinian detainees at the Sde Teiman military detention facility.
Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth reported on Saturday that the Brussels-based rights group submitted the complaint to the ICC prosecutor under Article 15 of the Rome Statute.
The complaint targets the Israeli Medical Association, Health Ministry officials and medical personnel over their involvement in abuses at the facility in southern Israel.
The foundation said the practices amounted to war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Allegations of systematic mistreatment
Since October 2023, the Sde Teiman military base in Israel’s southern Negev desert has been used to hold thousands of Palestinians from Gaza, most of them civilians, including men, women, children, older people, journalists and health and humanitarian workers.
The foundation said that detainees were classified as "unlawful combatants," a designation it described as a means of denying them basic legal protections and holding them without charge or trial.
The complaint said Israel's Health Ministry established a medical facility at Sde Teiman shortly after October 7, 2023.
According to the foundation, medical personnel were required to sign documents placing them under military police authority rather than the army's Medical Corps.
The complaint seeks investigations into officials from Israel's health and defence ministries, medical personnel, hospital administrators and the Israeli Medical Association.
Those named include former health ministers Moshe Arbel and Uriel Buso, association chairman Zion Hagay, director general Leah Wapner and ethics board chairman Yosef Walfisch.
Detainees restrained during medical treatment
The foundation said a Health Ministry directive issued on December 19, 2023, required medical personnel to treat detainees while they were handcuffed and blindfolded.
According to the complaint, the directive also permitted forced medical treatment without adequate safeguards.
Medical staff were allegedly instructed not to disclose their names and to sign medical records using only their professional titles.
The foundation argued that these practices obscured individual responsibility and hindered documentation of injuries.
Amputations, surgeries without adequate pain relief
The foundation cited accounts from Israeli medical workers and former Palestinian detainees describing abuses at Sde Teiman.
According to the complaint, a doctor wrote to Israeli authorities in April 2024 that two detainees had undergone leg amputations within one week because of injuries caused by shackling.
The doctor reportedly described shackling as routine at the facility.
The foundation also cited medical workers who told the Associated Press they had witnessed surgeries performed without adequate pain relief.
One account described an elderly detainee screaming and shaking during leg surgery.
Other workers reported detainees being blindfolded, forced to wear diapers and restrained by all four limbs to hospital beds.
The foundation said at least 29 detainees had died at Sde Teiman by November 2025 because of physical violence, medical neglect or both.
Medical association accused of complicity
The complaint accused the Israeli Medical Association of helping legitimise torture and mistreatment at the facility.
The foundation said the association responded to allegations of medical complicity with general reminders about professional ethics rather than sufficient investigative action.
It also said findings from an internal Health Ministry ethical assessment following a visit to Sde Teiman were not publicly released.
"Instead of investigating the allegations, leaders of the association publicly defended the medical care provided at Sde Teiman," the foundation said.
Established in February 2024 and based in Brussels, the Hind Rajab Foundation has pursued legal cases in several countries against Israeli officials and military personnel over violations in Gaza.
Since October 2023, Israel's genoc’de in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures.

- The plan has sparked strong opposition, while Donald Trump has not decided and J.D. Vance said he would not watch the broadcast.
AI generated
ROME - Pope Leo renewed his condemnation of the death penalty on Oct 10, saying it violates the sanctity of human life and deprives people of the chance of redemption, days after the Pentagon said it planned to live-stream an execution.
The US military will live-stream the upcoming firing squad execution of a gunman who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Oct 8, in what would be an unprecedented broadcast of a US execution.
“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” Leo, the first pope from the United States, said in a social media post, without mentioning the Pentagon plan.
“The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” he added in the message posted on the World Day Against the Death Penalty.
Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, is set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945.
The livestream plan, championed by Hegseth, has drawn opposition from lawmakers, including from President Donald Trump’s Republicans, religious leaders and international observers.
Trump himself has said he has not yet decided whether to allow the live feed, while Vice-President J.D. Vance, who is a Catholic, expressed scepticism over whether the Pentagon would proceed with livestreaming the scheduled Dec 3 execution.
Vance also said he would not watch the livestream if it went ahead.
The execution plan comes amid heightened debate in the US over the death penalty following a botched lethal injection of a Tennessee woman last week. REUTERS

The Hind Rajab Foundation filed a complaint with the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Israeli medical officials over torture and mistreatment of Palestinian detainees, Israeli media reported Saturday.
The complaint targets the Israeli Medical Association, Health Ministry officials and medical personnel over abuses at the Sde Teiman military detention facility in southern Israel.
According to the Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, the Brussels-based rights group submitted the complaint to the ICC prosecutor under Article 15 of the Rome Statute.
The foundation said that Israeli medical personnel and officials were involved in practices amounting to war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Allegations of systematic mistreatment
Since October 2023, the Sde Teiman military base in Israel’s southern Negev desert has been used to hold thousands of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, most of them civilians, including men, women, children, older people, journalists and health and humanitarian workers.
The foundation said that detainees were classified as "unlawful combatants," a designation it described as a means of denying them basic legal protections and holding them without charge or trial.
The complaint said Israel's Health Ministry established a medical facility at Sde Teiman shortly after Oct. 7, 2023.
According to the foundation, medical personnel were required to sign documents placing them under military police authority rather than the army's Medical Corps.
The complaint seeks investigations into officials from Israel's health and defense ministries, medical personnel, hospital administrators and the Israeli Medical Association.
Those named include former health ministers Moshe Arbel and Uriel Buso, association chairman Zion Hagay, director general Leah Wapner and ethics board chairman Yosef Walfisch.
Detainees restrained during medical treatment
The foundation said a Health Ministry directive issued on Dec. 19, 2023, required medical personnel to treat detainees while they were handcuffed and blindfolded.
According to the complaint, the directive also permitted forced medical treatment without adequate safeguards.
Medical staff were allegedly instructed not to disclose their names and to sign medical records using only their professional titles.
The foundation argued that these practices obscured individual responsibility and hindered documentation of injuries.
Amputations, surgeries without adequate pain relief
The foundation cited accounts from Israeli medical workers and former Palestinian detainees describing abuses at Sde Teiman.
According to the complaint, a doctor wrote to Israeli authorities in April 2024 that two detainees had undergone leg amputations within one week because of injuries caused by shackling.
The doctor reportedly described shackling as routine at the facility.
The foundation also cited medical workers who told the Associated Press they had witnessed surgeries performed without adequate pain relief.
One account described an elderly detainee screaming and shaking during leg surgery.
Other workers reported detainees being blindfolded, forced to wear diapers and restrained by all four limbs to hospital beds.
The foundation said at least 29 detainees had died at Sde Teiman by November 2025 because of physical violence, medical neglect or both.
Medical association accused of complicity
The complaint accused the Israeli Medical Association of helping legitimize torture and mistreatment at the facility.
The foundation said the association responded to allegations of medical complicity with general reminders about professional ethics rather than sufficient investigative action.
It also said findings from an internal Health Ministry ethical assessment following a visit to Sde Teiman were not publicly released.
"Instead of investigating the allegations, leaders of the association publicly defended the medical care provided at Sde Teiman," the foundation said.
Established in February 2024 and based in Brussels, the Hind Rajab Foundation has pursued legal cases in several countries against Israeli officials and military personnel over alleged violations in Gaza.
Since October 2023, Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures.

Without explicitly referring to the scheduled execution of the Fort Hood killer, the Pope reiterates the Church’s opposition to the death penalty. In the US, Vice-President Vance says he will not watch the execution by firing squad, which is due to be live-streamed in December
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement of the execution by firing squad of Fort Hood gunman Nidal Malik Hasan continues to fuel controversy. Former US Army Major Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people and wounding another 32, is expected to be put to death in a live-streamed execution, most likely on 3 December.
Pope Leo XIV has also intervened in the debate, without commenting directly on the case. Marking the World Day Against the Death Penalty on 10 October, he declared on Saturday that capital punishment is “inadmissible”.
In a post on X, the US-born Pope cited the revised Catholic teaching on capital punishment introduced by Pope Francis, according to which the death penalty attacks the inherent dignity of a human being.
“The common good can be safeguarded and the demands of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” reads the post published on Leo’s account, @Pontifex. “Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens and at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.” The post ends with the hashtag #nopenadimorte.
The Pope did not refer to either the planned execution or the botched lethal injection in Tennessee that recently reignited the debate over the death penalty in the United States. However, his post came just hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, had explicitly stated that the planned public execution in the United States was “unacceptable” and that it was “unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle”.
In 2018, Pope Francis amended official Catholic teaching to declare the death penalty “inadmissible” in all circumstances.
Previously, the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the official compendium of Church teaching, stated that it did not rule out recourse to capital punishment “if this were the only possible way to defend effectively human lives against an unjust aggressor”.
The head of the US bishops’ conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed “shock” and “great sorrow” at the Pentagon’s plans. “In no way can Hasan’s actions be condoned, but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,” he said in a statement on Friday. “The public execution even of those who have done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and represent a stain on the conscience of its people,” he added.
Vance will not watch the execution if it is broadcast
Although he has not opposed Hasan’s execution, US Vice-President JD Vance has said he will not watch the live broadcast and has even questioned whether the Pentagon’s plan for a public execution will actually go ahead.
According to Vance, the planned method of execution is distracting attention from the seriousness of Hasan’s crimes. “This is a man who carried out, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil since 11 September,” the US vice-president said, adding: “The people he was supposed to care for, the Army soldiers he was meant to treat for mental illness and other problems, he struck at their moment of maximum vulnerability and mowed these people down right where they lived.”
“Whatever controversy there is over the method of execution, I hope people do not forget that this is a man who brutally murdered many innocent people,” he continued.
President Trump is a staunch supporter of the death penalty. In the first nine months of 2026, 30 executions have been carried out in the United States. The Pentagon said on Monday that the president had approved the execution of Major Hasan.

Missile strikes Riyadh airport terminal, leaving multiple people wounded
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:05:32 UTC
01:05:32 KST

Riyadh’s international airport in Saudi Arabia was struck Saturday night by a missile launched by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, two days after another deadly attack on King Khalid International Airport. The attack marked the deadliest strike in a Gulf Arab country since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February, and came as President Donald Trump said Washington could join Saudi military strikes against the Houthis, although no decision had been made.
A regional official familiar with the details told The Associated Press that the missile struck an area housing passenger Terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights, and that there were “many casualties.”
Saudi aviation authorities later said at least 12 people were killed and 309 wounded in the attack.
According to the statement, those killed included an American citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian, a Palestinian, a Sudanese national, two Bangladeshis and four Saudis.
Reports said the airport was evacuated and numerous ambulances were dispatched to the scene. Saudi authorities deployed heavy security at the complex and warned against circulating any footage of the Houthi attacks. So far, no footage from the airport has been released.
The New York Times cited two Western officials and one Arab official, all speaking anonymously because they were not authorized to discuss the attack publicly. Earlier, a medical source at a Riyadh hospital told AFP that at least two people had been killed, identifying one as an Egyptian crew member working for a Saudi airline and the other as a Palestinian carrying Egyptian travel documents.
Saudi authorities initially confirmed injuries without providing a casualty toll. The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said it was still assessing the damage at the airport and announced the temporary suspension of operations. Incoming flights were diverted, departures were delayed or canceled and passengers were evacuated as emergency crews responded.
The missile struck the complex housing the airport's domestic terminals, triggering panic among passengers and staff. Witnesses described hearing an explosion and seeing injured people near boarding gates. Foreign embassies urged their citizens to avoid the airport and surrounding areas.
Senior Houthi official Mohammed al-Bukhaiti claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack, saying it was retaliation for Saudi strikes in Yemen, including attacks he said had targeted civilian infrastructure. He argued that the protections afforded to civilian facilities should apply equally in Yemen and elsewhere, citing airports, seaports, hospitals, markets and venues for weddings and funerals.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said later Saturday in a statement that a projectile had fallen near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam. The airport, in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Region, has become an important alternative to Riyadh airport following the spate of attacks on the capital.
The attack in Riyadh came just two days after another deadly Houthi assault on the airport. Saudi authorities said three Saudi citizens, including an airline pilot, were killed in Thursday's strikes, which also damaged an aircraft belonging to the national carrier Saudia.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure in recent weeks, seeking to disrupt air traffic and increase pressure on Riyadh. The group has warned international airlines against flying through Saudi airspace, declaring much of it a military operational zone.
The repeated attacks also threaten Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's efforts to transform Riyadh into a major international business and travel hub, with high-profile international events scheduled in the Saudi capital in the coming weeks.
Trump weighs joining Saudi strikes
Asked Saturday whether the United States would join Saudi Arabia's military campaign against the Houthis, Trump said the administration was considering the possibility.
"We may. We're going to look at it," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "We move very quickly."
Trump said Washington had only recently learned of the latest attack and would decide how to respond. His comments raised the possibility of more direct American involvement in a conflict that has intensified across Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
Saudi warplanes have been conducting airstrikes against Houthi targets in Yemen in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which has launched a major counteroffensive aimed at retaking territory captured by the rebels.
The Houthis say Yemen has been subjected to hundreds of Saudi airstrikes in recent weeks, including attacks that they claim have killed children and other civilians. The Saudi bombing campaign and the Houthis' attacks on civilian aviation facilities have intensified the conflict on both sides of the border.
The renewed fighting has centered on the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and serves as a vital maritime passage for international commerce and energy shipments.
The Houthis seized significant stretches of Yemen's western coastline during a rapid offensive last month, threatening maritime traffic through the strait. Saudi-backed government forces subsequently launched an operation known as Yemen Dawn, seeking to reverse those gains.
Government forces have claimed progress in recapturing territory around the strait, while the Houthis have disputed some of those claims and said they repelled attacks. Heavy fighting has also continued in areas around Taiz, with both sides reporting casualties.
Pakistan and Turkey drawn into Saudi defense efforts
The escalation has also placed renewed attention on Saudi Arabia's defense cooperation with Pakistan and Turkey, which signed a trilateral agreement in Mecca in August.
The three countries agreed to implement collective defense arrangements and deploy military capabilities to Saudi Arabia in response to the growing threat.
Pakistan, however, has emphasized that its role is defensive. Islamabad has said its forces will not cross into Yemen to carry out offensive operations against the Houthis, although they may assist in protecting Saudi territory and sovereignty.
Turkey has also framed its involvement within the trilateral defense arrangement, while Saudi Arabia continues its military campaign in support of the Yemeni government.

Ronaldo informed the federation that he was leaving, but it remained unclear whether the decision would be deemed justified under the regulations.
“I have already apologised, but I know that actions must have consequences. Anyone in the world of football, just like me, knows that, regardless of one’s status, the rules are the same for everyone,” Ronaldo wrote in the letter in question.
The federation said on Saturday that the case is before the disciplinary inquiry committee (CD) and that the information gathered will remain confidential until it reaches a conclusion.

Family background may explain much of the mental health gap tied to sexual orientation, twin studies suggest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
16:00:45 UTC
01:00:45 KST

New research indicates that a large portion of the mental health differences between non-heterosexual and heterosexual individuals might be rooted in shared family background rather than social stigma alone. When non-heterosexual people were compared with their own heterosexual siblings and twins, the mental health gap shrank by about half, and by roughly two-thirds among identical twins. The findings were published in Psychological Medicine.
On average, people who identify as gay, lesbian, or bisexual report higher rates of anxiety, depression, and other mental health difficulties compared to heterosexual people. The most common explanation for this gap is Sexual Minority Stress Theory, which proposes that the excess social stress faced by sexual minorities, such as discrimination, bullying, and systemic stigma, is the primary driver of their worse mental health outcomes.
Supporting evidence includes studies linking experiences such as victimization to distress. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 indicated that higher levels of same-sex attraction were linked to psychological distress, a relationship that was partly explained by experiences of victimization.
Other factors, however, might also play a role in these disparities. Mental health problems and human temperaments, such as a tendency to experience negative emotions, are strongly influenced by genetics. These factors emerge early in life, often before sexual orientation becomes apparent. The research, led by Péter Przemyslaw Ujma of Semmelweis University, sought to test whether the association between sexual orientation and mental health might actually reflect these shared familial causes.
Genetically informed studies, which compare non-heterosexual people with their own heterosexual brothers and sisters, have produced conflicting results on whether these disparities stem from minority stress or from shared family genetics and upbringing. For instance, an early 1999 study comparing identical male twin pairs found that gay men still reported higher rates of suicidal thoughts than their heterosexual twin brothers, suggesting family background alone did not explain the disparity.
On the other hand, a 2011 twin study found evidence that shared genetic and environmental background factors partly accounted for the higher rates of depression seen in non-heterosexual people. These conflicting outcomes directly prompted the current authors to synthesize the full body of evidence into one comprehensive analysis.
Ujma and his colleagues conducted a systematic multilevel meta-analysis, a statistical technique that combines the results of multiple independent studies to identify overall trends. The authors searched academic databases for English-language studies in which twins or non-twin siblings reported on both their sexual orientation and their mental health, identifying 17 that met their criteria. They set aside one very large Swedish sibling study from the main analysis because it measured sexual orientation through same-sex marriage and reported its results in a different statistical format.
The researchers extracted data from these studies to calculate effect sizes, representing the difference in mental health between heterosexual and non-heterosexual participants, and organized them into three types of comparisons. First, they looked at the mental health gap in the general, unmatched population, meaning all heterosexual people compared to all non-heterosexual people without considering family ties. Second, they compared heterosexual and non-heterosexual individuals across all available pairs of family members, which included a mix of non-twin siblings, fraternal twins, and identical twins. Finally, they isolated comparisons strictly between identical twin pairs where one twin was heterosexual and the other was not.
The results showed a noticeable drop in the mental health disparity as genetic and family relatedness increased. In the unmatched general population, non-heterosexual participants showed worse mental health by about 0.41 standard deviations, a gap typically considered small to moderate. When the researchers controlled for any family relationship, comparing participants to their siblings or twins, the mental health disparity was reduced by 47.5 percent.
Identical twins share nearly 100 percent of their genes and generally experience the same early upbringing, making them the most rigorous test for family-level traits. When comparing a non-heterosexual individual specifically to their identical heterosexual twin, the mental health disparity dropped by 65.7 percent.
Although this reduction was larger than the one for family members in general, the difference between the two estimates was not statistically significant, likely because only a handful of studies reported identical twin comparisons. The authors interpret these results as evidence that roughly two-thirds of the population gap reflects familial factors, such as shared genes and upbringing, rather than minority stress.
Including the large Swedish sibling study, which the authors analyzed separately, shrank the estimated reductions to 27.8 percent for family members overall and 53.7 percent for identical twins.
The identical twin analysis also showed that the gap did not disappear entirely. Non-heterosexual identical twins still exhibited higher rates of mental health symptoms than their heterosexual twins, meaning roughly one-third of the disparity stems from factors the twins do not share. The authors describe sexual minority stress as one candidate explanation for this remaining gap, alongside other possibilities, such as differences in the life paths of non-heterosexual and heterosexual people. More broadly, they argue that much of the disparity has been wrongly attributed to minority stress and that their results partly falsify the theory.
“The key takeaway is that shared familial factors may account for a substantial portion of mental health disparities associated with sexual orientation,” Yiwen Wang, an assistant professor of sociology at the University of Central Florida who was not involved in the research, told PsyPost. “However, accounting for familial background reduces these disparities but does not eliminate them. The study provides an important complement to the minority stress literature by highlighting familial sources of mental health disparities that have received comparatively less attention. I would view these findings as complicating, rather than overturning, minority stress theory.”
“One thing I would caution against is interpreting these findings as evidence that minority stress does not matter,” Wang added. “Accounting for familial factors reduces the disparities, but it does not tell us exactly what mechanisms are responsible for that reduction. Importantly, a meaningful mental health disparity remains even among identical twins.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding these findings. The authors detected borderline publication bias in the population estimates, meaning the starting mental health gap might be slightly inflated. The studies included in the meta-analysis varied widely in how they defined sexual orientation and which demographic groups they included. The mental health measures and results also differed considerably from study to study, which prevented the researchers from drawing specific conclusions about individual disorders like anxiety or depression in isolated populations.
“The genetically informed design is a notable strength, and the overall pattern is compelling,” Wang noted. “I would be more cautious about the magnitude of the estimates and their causal interpretation, given substantial heterogeneity across studies and the relatively limited evidence from identical twin comparisons.”
Another limitation is that the analyses could not cleanly separate genetic causes from shared environmental causes. The authors suggest the larger reduction among identical twins points toward genetic factors, though the difference between the identical-twin and broader family estimates was not statistically significant.
In addition, because identical twins who differ in sexual orientation are relatively rare, the sample sizes for the strict identical twin comparisons were small, meaning the statistical estimates for that specific group have a wider margin of error. The authors recommend that future studies use highly standardized clinical measures of mental health and prioritize gathering data on both regular siblings and identical twins to build a more precise picture of these dynamics.
“I would like to see studies combine genetically informed designs with direct, longitudinal measures of discrimination, stigma, and other minority stressors,” Wang said. “That could help us better understand how family background and social experiences work together to shape mental health, rather than treating them as competing explanations.”
The study, “How much is sexual minority stress confounded with familial causes? A systematic multilevel meta-analysis,” was authored by Péter Przemyslaw Ujma, John D. Haltigan, and J. Michael Bailey.

Space Power - The Invisible Force Behind Modern Operations
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:00:00 BST
01:00:00 KST

From navigating a journey with a smartphone to enabling military operations across the globe, space has become an essential part of modern life. Yet for many, it remains largely unseen. That was one of the key messages emerging from this year's UK Space Power Conference, where military leaders, government officials, industry partners, academics and international allies gathered to discuss the future of the space domain and the capabilities needed to protect it.
Hosted by UK Space Command, the conference highlighted a growing reality: space is no longer a niche area of interest or a future aspiration. It is a critical operational domain underpinning national security, military effectiveness and economic prosperity.
Wing Commander Neal Henley, Chief of Staff of the Joint Force Space Component, the operational arm of UK Space Command, believes understanding that dependency is now more important than ever.
"There is now a growing recognition of our dependency upon space. It's no longer optional. We better understand our vulnerabilities and therefore what needs protecting and assuring to ensure we have access to the services we need for the warfighter, but also for wider society."
What is Space Power?
Much like air power, space power is about the capabilities, people, services and effects that enable military operations.
From secure satellite communications and missile warning systems to intelligence gathering, navigation and weather forecasting, space-based capabilities support almost every aspect of modern defence activity.
"Space power is the range of activities we conduct to deliver the missions and roles that the integrated force depends upon," explained Wing Commander Henley.
The UK's military also relies on space for secure command and control, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, and increasingly for the operation of autonomous and uncrewed systems.
Without those capabilities, military effectiveness would be significantly degraded.
Operating in a Contested Domain
A recurring theme throughout the conference was the increasingly contested nature of space.
As reliance on space-based services grows, so too does the need to protect them. Adversaries can target space capabilities in a variety of ways, from cyber attacks and electronic interference to attacks against supporting ground infrastructure.
The challenge is not limited to systems on Earth.
"There are a number of potential adversary satellites on orbit and one of our key tasks is to detect them, track them and characterise them," said Wing Commander Henley.
Understanding activity in the space domain is therefore fundamental to maintaining operational advantage and ensuring continued access to critical services.
A New Squadron for a New Challenge
One of the most significant announcements made during the conference was the establishment of No. III Space Effects Squadron.
The new unit will become the RAF's first dedicated squadron focused on supporting the control of space mission.
For UK Space Command, control of space is not about conflict in orbit. Rather, it is about ensuring freedom of action within the domain and protecting the capabilities upon which both Defence and society depend.
"Control of space is about gaining and maintaining the freedom of action and access to the space domain so that we can deliver the products, services and effects that the integrated force relies upon."
That mission begins with understanding the environment.
"We need to be able to detect, characterise and attribute activity in space and, if necessary, respond in an appropriate manner."
From Strategy to Capability
The conference also showcased a number of major programmes that are transforming the UK's military space capability.
Among them is the Skynet 6 programme, which will provide the next generation of sovereign military satellite communications. Building on a heritage stretching back to the launch of the first Skynet satellite in 1969, the programme will ensure resilient communications for UK and allied forces well into the future.
Other initiatives include Project ISTARI, delivering space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities, as well as the Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability, designed to monitor objects in orbit as far away as the geostationary belt, approximately 36,000km above Earth.
Meanwhile, the development of the Noctis sensor network and Borealis mission system will strengthen the UK's ability to track, monitor and understand activity across the space domain.
Space Is a Team Sport
While sovereign capability remains important, another key message from the conference was that no nation can operate effectively in space alone.
"Space is very much a team sport," said Wing Commander Henley.
Working alongside allies through initiatives such as Operation Olympic Defender and the Combined Space Operations initiative allows nations to share information, improve collective understanding and coordinate responses to challenges in space.
Partnerships also extend beyond Defence. Collaboration with industry, academia and government departments is helping create a more integrated national approach under the banner of "One Space", ensuring investment is coordinated, capability development is aligned and resources are used effectively.
Why Space Matters to Everyone
Perhaps the most powerful takeaway from the conference was that space is not simply a military concern.
Most people interact with space-enabled services every day without realising it. Navigation systems, internet services, financial networks, weather forecasting, power distribution and transport infrastructure all depend, in some way, on space-based capabilities.
"Space is a hidden enabler of day-to-day activity," said Wing Commander Henley.
"It's much like electricity. You turn on the light switch and expect it to work. Space is the same. It's there in the background supporting modern life."
As the UK continues to develop its space capabilities, the challenge now is turning strategy into action. For RAF personnel and Defence more broadly, the message is clear: space is no longer a supporting function operating in the background. It is an operational domain in its own right, integral to the success of modern military operations and increasingly vital to the security and prosperity of the nation.
Or, as the conference reinforced, space is no longer science fiction. It is part of everyday life, and protecting it has become a strategic necessity.

Verstappen takes maiden Singapore GP pole as Hamilton misses out
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
23:58:40 CST
00:58:40 KST

by F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
SINGAPORE, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Max Verstappen continued his dominance Saturday at the Singapore Grand Prix by claiming his first pole position at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, edging Ferrari's Charles Leclerc after earlier winning the weekend's Sprint race.
The Red Bull driver set a fastest lap of 1 minute, 31.373 seconds, beating Leclerc by just 0.054 seconds, with Lewis Hamilton third in the other Ferrari.
Verstappen's pole completed a remarkable turnaround at a circuit that had previously eluded him. Before Saturday, Singapore was the only venue on the current Formula 1 calendar where the four-time world champion had never won, but he broke that drought with victory in the Sprint after having also topped Friday's Sprint qualifying session.
"Very happy to be on pole because this is the one I wanted," said Verstappen.
"The car has been pretty strong all weekend. There are always things that can be better but it was enough for pole.
"We have been on a positive trend, so for us it's very special to take pole here."
Qualifying took place on a dry track after a torrential downpour before the Sprint had delayed the start of that race.
Hamilton had appeared the man to beat in the opening two segments, topping both Q1 and Q2 as he pursued his first Grand Prix pole position since the 2023 Hungarian Grand Prix, when he was driving for Mercedes.
The seven-time world champion set a time of 1:31.529 in Q2, 0.110 seconds quicker than Verstappen, raising hopes of Ferrari's first pole position of the 2026 season.
However, Verstappen found more pace when it mattered, setting the benchmark on his first run in Q3 with a lap of 1:31.373, putting him 0.123 seconds ahead of Hamilton.
Neither driver improved on their second runs, with Hamilton suffering a slide in the final sector that cost him around two-tenths of a second.
Leclerc, meanwhile, produced a late improvement to split the pair and secure a front-row start alongside Verstappen.
Championship leader Kimi Antonelli qualified fourth in his Mercedes, ahead of McLaren's Lando Norris and George Russell in the second Mercedes.
However, Russell is set to start Sunday's race from the back of the grid after exceeding his permitted allocation of power unit components following an engine failure at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
McLaren's Oscar Piastri qualified seventh, followed by Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Racing Bulls teammates Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad.
Earlier, the opening segment was disrupted by mechanical problems for Racing Bulls driver Isack Hadjar, who twice reported losing power and gears before failing to set a competitive lap time.
"The engine is off," Hadjar told his team as he slowed on track, briefly triggering yellow flags.
Although he managed to get moving again, the problem returned, leaving him unable to set a time and consigning him to last place.
In Q2, Nico Hulkenberg, Oliver Bearman, Ocon, Carlos Sainz, Gabriel Bortoleto and Franco Colapinto were eliminated, with the latter suffering a sizeable slide on his final attempt that prevented him from improving.
In addition to Hadjar, Fernando Alonso, Alex Albon, Lance Stroll, Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas were also eliminated in Q1.
Alonso is also set to start from the back after an engine change, while Esteban Ocon narrowly avoided the barriers after locking up and complaining of a lack of brakes. Stroll suffered a similar moment.
Verstappen will now seek to complete a clean sweep of the Singapore weekend in Sunday's Grand Prix, having already claimed sprint pole, sprint victory and Grand Prix pole at a circuit where he had previously never reached the top step of the podium. ■

ZAGREB, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- A freight train carrying grain derailed near the Meja railway station in western Croatia on Saturday morning, causing heavy material damage but no casualties, according to the national broadcaster Croatian Radiotelevision (HRT).
The accident occurred at approximately 9:25 a.m. local time (0725 GMT) as the train, operated by the carrier Transagent, was traveling toward the Adriatic port city of Rijeka, according to HZ Infrastruktura (Croatian Railways Infrastructure). 11 wagons plunged into a ravine, while the locomotive and two wagons remained at the station.
Prior to the derailment, the train driver notified the dispatcher that the brakes had failed, and he was unable to stop the train, HZ Infrastruktura said.
The Meja railway station, located about 15 kilometers east of Rijeka, has sustained significant damage, and the affected railway line has been closed to all traffic. An investigation into the exact cause of the accident is underway. ■

The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early on Sunday, with some in a critical condition. A Saudi-led coalition blamed Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen.
A missile struck a King Khalid international airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorised to speak to the media.
A Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.
The US president, Donald Trump, said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, called the attacks “reprehensible” and said “they must stop now”.
One witness at the Riyadh airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded.
“I was on gate 403,” at the domestic terminal, the witness told the Agence France-Presse news agency. “I saw [gate] 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”
The relative of one injured person said they had been wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass and taken to hospital.
A projectile also fell near the King Fahd international airport in Dammam, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis. The Dammam airport has become an important alternative to Riyadh amid the recent spate of attacks.
There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sana’a international airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
Schools in Riyadh will move to remote learning for a week, according to the education ministry, following the deadly attack.
Saturday’s incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis on the kingdom. The airport has already been attacked twice this week, leaving four people dead and others wounded, and badly damaging an aircraft.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.
The attack came as forces allied to the UN-recognised government in Yemen claim to have mounted a successful offensive to retake the Bab al-Mandab strait from Houthi rebels, but accounts vary as to whether the push has been repelled.
A Houthi spokesperson said forces from the Saudi-backed government based in Aden “were targeted with a large number of ballistic missiles, artillery support and heavy weapons, resulting in the destruction of more than 22 armoured vehicles and the killing and wounding of dozens, including a number of commanders.
“More than 30 ambulances arrived in Aden to transport the dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations.”
By contrast, the Saudi ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed al-Jaber, said: “Blessed Friday and victory for every Yemeni and Arab. Bab al-Mandab has been cleared of the remnants of the Houthi terrorist militia.”
The exposed 5 sq mile (13 sq km) Perim Island straddles the strait, acting as a lookout point for all traffic from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden and towards the Indian Ocean. Aidarous al-Zubaidi, the president of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), one of the main political forces in the south of Yemen, claimed the island and coastal area had been recaptured from Houthi hands.
An official military spokesperson for the UN-recognised government forces qualified the claim, saying only half the area had been recaptured so far. Waddah al-Dabish said newly established Houthi defensive lines had been broken on the land next to the strait, leading to the death of thousands of Houthi fighters.
It is thought that as many as 500 Houthi fighters are stationed on the island, and Saudi Arabia is desperate to be able to report that the strait has been reclaimed to show that the land counteroffensive it launched at the beginning of the week is advancing.
The report came as the United Nations’ special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, admitted to the UN security council in New York that Yemen – one of the poorest countries in the world – had lapsed back into full-scale war and said the first victims would be women and children.
The Houthis seized control of the strait two weeks ago and said no Saudi-linked commercial traffic would be permitted to go through the narrow waterway. The Houthis are waging a war to remove Saudi influence from Yemen, and have been mounting missile attacks on Riyadh in support of this objective.
There have been previous premature reports of military breakthroughs by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government since it launched its counteroffensive at the start of the week, but the recapture of the land by the strait and Perim Island (also known as Mayyun Island) is a military prize western governments desperately need.

Rights group files ICC complaint against Israeli medical officials over torture of Palestinian detainees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:52:52 UTC
00:52:52 KST

The Hind Rajab Foundation filed a complaint with the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Israeli medical officials over torture and mistreatment of Palestinian detainees, Israeli media reported Saturday, Anadolu reports.
The complaint targets the Israeli Medical Association, Health Ministry officials and medical personnel over abuses at the Sde Teiman military detention facility in southern Israel.
According to the Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, the Brussels-based rights group submitted the complaint to the ICC prosecutor under Article 15 of the Rome Statute.
The foundation said that Israeli medical personnel and officials were involved in practices amounting to war crimes and crimes against humanity.
– Allegations of systematic mistreatment
Since October 2023, the Sde Teiman military base in Israel’s southern Negev desert has been used to hold thousands of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, most of them civilians, including men, women, children, older people, journalists and health and humanitarian workers.
The foundation said that detainees were classified as “unlawful combatants,” a designation it described as a means of denying them basic legal protections and holding them without charge or trial.
The complaint said Israel’s Health Ministry established a medical facility at Sde Teiman shortly after Oct. 7, 2023.
According to the foundation, medical personnel were required to sign documents placing them under military police authority rather than the army’s Medical Corps.
The complaint seeks investigations into officials from Israel’s health and defense ministries, medical personnel, hospital administrators and the Israeli Medical Association.
Those named include former health ministers Moshe Arbel and Uriel Buso, association chairman Zion Hagay, director general Leah Wapner and ethics board chairman Yosef Walfisch.
– Detainees restrained during medical treatment
The foundation said a Health Ministry directive issued on Dec. 19, 2023, required medical personnel to treat detainees while they were handcuffed and blindfolded.
According to the complaint, the directive also permitted forced medical treatment without adequate safeguards.
Medical staff were allegedly instructed not to disclose their names and to sign medical records using only their professional titles.
The foundation argued that these practices obscured individual responsibility and hindered documentation of injuries.
– Amputations, surgeries without adequate pain relief
The foundation cited accounts from Israeli medical workers and former Palestinian detainees describing abuses at Sde Teiman.
According to the complaint, a doctor wrote to Israeli authorities in April 2024 that two detainees had undergone leg amputations within one week because of injuries caused by shackling.
The doctor reportedly described shackling as routine at the facility.
The foundation also cited medical workers who told the Associated Press they had witnessed surgeries performed without adequate pain relief.
One account described an elderly detainee screaming and shaking during leg surgery.
Other workers reported detainees being blindfolded, forced to wear diapers and restrained by all four limbs to hospital beds.
The foundation said at least 29 detainees had died at Sde Teiman by November 2025 because of physical violence, medical neglect or both.
– Medical association accused of complicity
The complaint accused the Israeli Medical Association of helping legitimize torture and mistreatment at the facility.
The foundation said the association responded to allegations of medical complicity with general reminders about professional ethics rather than sufficient investigative action.
It also said findings from an internal Health Ministry ethical assessment following a visit to Sde Teiman were not publicly released.
“Instead of investigating the allegations, leaders of the association publicly defended the medical care provided at Sde Teiman,” the foundation said.
Established in February 2024 and based in Brussels, the Hind Rajab Foundation has pursued legal cases in several countries against Israeli officials and military personnel over alleged violations in Gaza.
Since October 2023, Israel’s war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures.

Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel, which various bodies – including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based – have said is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
A ceasefire was declared a year ago but Israeli airstrikes have continued in Gaza. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people. Settlers have also ramped up their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025.
Husam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador to the UK, shared a video from the march on social media. “Three years on, Israel’s atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank continue, and so does the solidarity of the British people. Louder, bigger and not going anywhere. Thank you all,” he said. By Saturday afternoon, organisers said 250,000 people were at the march.
The Met have imposed conditions on the event – which is organised by the Palestine Coalition, which has organised more than 30 mass demonstrations since October 2023, with a counter-protest by Stop The Hate – to “minimise the risk of serious disruption to communities”.
The Met posted on X saying: “The front of the procession has now entered Whitehall where a rally will take place.
“Several arrests have been made so far including a woman and a man with placards declaring support for proscribed organisation Palestine Action.
“We have also arrested a number of protesters on suspicion of criminal damage after they climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial on Victoria Embankment.”
The national march is the first held since the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements and declared the UK government would take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety. He also told the Commons that settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.
At Labour party conference last month, Miliband appeared to reference the marches, which at their peak regularly numbered hundreds and thousands of people, telling the audience in Liverpool: “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.”
Deputy assistant commissioner Carl Galvin said: “We know Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.”
Galvin, who is leading the policing operation this weekend, said the force’s presence on Saturday will be “significant”.
“We will also be using powers under the Public Order Act requiring anyone in the protest area wearing face coverings to deliberately conceal their identity to remove them,” Galvin continued.
The Met have imposed conditions on the march and require the group to travel via Westminster Bridge, York Road, Waterloo Bridge and The Strand on to Whitehall, with a rally concluding by 6.30pm. The force has said that any speeches and music must conclude by 5.30pm.
A counter-protest by Stop The Hate is also taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside New Scotland Yard, some with flags.
The force has also imposed conditions on the demonstration “to minimise the risk of serious disruption”. The demonstrators must remain within a designated area outside the Met’s headquarters, with the assembly concluding at 2.30pm.
Last Saturday, on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, when Hamas militants broke across the Israeli border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals, killing at least 1,209 people, a small pro-Palestine student demonstration in central London was held.
The Met publicly appealed to those behind the demonstration to “exercise [their] right to protest on a different date” and admitted that finding the organisers had been “frankly difficult”. In the end, it went ahead and about 100 people attended. Five people were arrested for breaching conditions imposed on the march.
The Palestine Coalition organising the march includes Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Stop the War, CND, the Muslim Association of Britain, Friends of Al Aqsa and the Palestinian Forum in Britain.

India detains thousands of youth protesters as anger grows against Modi and election chief
Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters on Saturday.
India's youth "Cockroach" movement had sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Police moved to break up the demonstration before it could begin, intercepting demonstrators on their way to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of India's capital, chasing off some and detaining many others. Some were dragged away before being bundled into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centers. Several "Cockroach" movement leaders, opposition lawmakers and student activists were detained before arriving, effectively crippling the protest ahead of its start.
The crackdown extended beyond the protest venue, with police stopping buses, cars and other vehicles at checkpoints on routes into the capital and searching for demonstrators. Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Restrictions on mobile internet and access to parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters.
Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late. Sambit Patra, a spokesperson for Modi's party, dismissed the demonstrators as "anarchic elements." "Their flop show has been completely demolished," Patra said.
A large-scale crackdown
The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities' determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi. The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the "Cockroach" movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi's education minister to resign in July.
Leaders of the "Cockroach" movement, Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. A video shared by the "Cockroach Janta Party" on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men.
"The pre-planned interception by Delhi Police aims to cripple the leadership of today's peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site," the movement said in a statement.
Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas, with police briefly detaining some of them.
Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained.
"We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn't we fight for our rights?" said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. "Why is Modi afraid of India's young people?"
The police response marked an extraordinary show of force in a capital where Modi's government has repeatedly sought to contain public dissent in the past. Under Modi, authorities have often used arrests and restrictions on public gatherings to contain demonstrations, raising questions about the space for protests in the world's largest democracy.
Opposition leaders accuse government of curbing dissent
The latest crackdown renewed criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent.
"Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out," opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press. Brittas was later detained by police.
The protests center on India's Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters. Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far.
The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.
For the "Cockroach" movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.
The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years.
For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi's home state, will test the party's standing.

Cornell’s Jane Doe targeted in 'swatting' incident at parents' home, lives in fear, lawyer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:51:47 UTC
00:51:47 KST

Cornell’s Jane Doe, the woman who alleged that she was drugged and raped by seven Cornell University students, was targeted in a police "swatting" incident at her parents' home on Tuesday, her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, told CNN on Thursday.
According to Giuffra, police entered the home after receiving a false report that “someone was killing people in the house,” drawing their weapons on Doe's family and her boyfriend.
Swatting is the deliberate, malicious act of falsely reporting a crime or emergency to trigger an aggressive law enforcement response, often involving a SWAT team. This response targets the victim's home or workplace, subjecting them to harassment and intimidation.
The false report, which was given to police at 7:00 p.m. on Tuesday, was that a man had shot and killed his mother before turning the gun on his sister, according to a police report CNN obtained. The officer who received the report then rushed to the home and stopped a vehicle carrying Doe's boyfriend and brother as it pulled out of the driveway.
Doe's father then came to the front door, identified himself to the officer, and asked what was happening. He told the officer that his family was “being threatened by numerous unknown people,” amid the Cornell case.
Giuffra: 'Somebody could have ended up dead,' luckily brother 'put his hands up'
Giuffra emphasized the good fortune that Doe's brother "put his hands up" when the officer stopped his vehicle, saying her boyfriend was "thrown on the ground."
“If you had a trigger-happy cop, or somebody had done the wrong thing, somebody could have ended up dead,” he said.
Giuffra noted that Doe, whom he described as "a little paranoid," spent Wednesday taping paper to the windows of the home “so people can’t see into her house to take a shot at her.”
"I don’t think she’s in a good spot now; she’s scared,” said Giuffra. "Before, it was just a lunatic fringe, which you can be dismissive of. Now it’s somebody taking real steps to harm you, and that’s pretty frightening."
Both the police and FBI are investigating the swatting incident, Giuffra said.
“I don’t get shook up very easily, but this shook me up," he said. "I didn’t want to have a body on my hands."
He added that Doe's father is "concerned" for her. "He can’t believe this has happened out of something where she’s just trying to stand up for herself and be heard, but the parents are really strong people, and they’re going to protect their daughter."
The lawyer noted that Doe "doesn’t seem to function well" when she is away from her family.
Cornell's Jane Doe receives threatening phone call while police still at home
In a further incident, while the police were still at her parents' home, Doe received a phone call that "wouldn’t stop ringing," causing her to "begin panicking," CNN reported, citing Giuffra and police reports.
“These people have done so much research,” Giuffra said, noting that his wife also claimed to have received a threatening phone call that same day.
In a call recording Giuffra shared with CNN, a man is heard identifying himself as "the person who called your client."
“I’m telling you guys simply, I think you should advise your client to withdraw the case," the man said. "Otherwise, blood will be shed."
New York A-G recusal sought by Cornell case defendant
Following the swatting and phone threat incidents, Cornell case defendant Winston Lee's attorneys filed a motion to recuse New York Attorney-General Letitia James from grand jury proceedings, NBC News reported on Friday.
Jane Doe accused Lee of unconsensual oral sex and snorting ketamine off of her body.
The attorneys, identified by NBC as Teny Geragos, Marc Agnifilo, and Jacob Kaplan, argued that the court has the ability to intervene in the grand jury process to ensure fairness.
A spokesperson for James' office told NBC that “in this and every investigation, the Office of the Attorney-General is committed to conducting a comprehensive review of nothing but the facts, the evidence, and the law.”
Before her appointment as special prosecutor in the Cornell case, James called the allegations "horrific and unacceptable," according to NBC.
"To her (Doe) and all other survivors: You’re not alone," she wrote. "We stand with you.”
Zvika Klein contributed to this report.

Hurricane Isaias: Four dead and thousands without power in US Southeast

Hurricane Isaias, the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, has killed at least four people and left hundreds of thousands of customers without power across the southeastern United States.
The storm made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday evening as a Category 2 hurricane before weakening as it moved inland through Alabama overnight.
Two people died in Alabama, and two died in Florida. Local authorities said one death in Florida was caused by trees falling during the storm.
Isaias hit land with sustained winds of 169km/h (105mph), bringing powerful gusts and heavy rain to the Florida Panhandle. By Saturday morning, the storm had weakened to a post-tropical cyclone with wind speeds of about 55km/h (35mph).
More than 900,000 electricity customers in Florida, Alabama and Georgia were without power early Saturday morning. That number has since gone down to less than 700,000, according to PowerOutage.us.
Fallen trees and downed power lines caused widespread disruption, while flooding forced road closures in parts of southern Alabama, including Houston County. Alabama Governor Kay Ivey said on Saturday morning that her team was concerned about “strong winds, heavy rain and possible spinoff tornadoes”.
Local officials in Pensacola, Florida reported strong winds that damaged an airport and tore the roof off a hotel. Trees and power lines also came down across the city, leaving some residents without electricity and roads blocked.
Despite the storm’s weakening, officials warned that dangerous conditions could persist. Heavy rainfall threatened flash flooding across parts of the Southeast.
“The flooding story is not over,” DeSantis said on Saturday, warning that saturated ground and continued rainfall could cause dangerous flooding a day or two after the storm passed. He said state search and rescue resources would remain available in case rapidly rising waters required emergency rescues.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also warned residents to be alert for contractors seeking to exploit storm victims as homeowners begin repairing damaged properties.
The US Energy Department announced on Saturday that it will release up to four million barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve as an emergency exchange meant to address the disruption of supply caused by Hurricane Isaias.
“With this emergency exchange, the Energy Department is acting swiftly to help maintain refinery operations, limit disruptions to fuel supplies, and ensure American families and businesses continue to have access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy,” Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said in a statement.

Trump ends decades-old restrictions on direct US-Lebanon flights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:44:48 UTC
00:44:48 KST

Breadcrumb
Trump lifts decades-old restrictions on direct flights between US and Lebanon
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun on Saturday welcomed a decision by his US counterpart, Donald Trump, to lift decades-old restrictions on air travel with Lebanon, paving the way for direct flights between the two countries to resume.
Direct flights have been suspended since 1985, when Washington halted air links following the hijacking of TWA Flight 847 and the killing of an American serviceman during the Lebanese civil war.
Restrictions imposed under presidential decrees issued in 1985, 1992, 1998 and 2007 "are no longer necessary to ensure the security of aircraft operating flights to or from Lebanon and to protect them from unlawful seizure", according to a presidential memorandum signed by Trump at the end of September.
Under Presidential Order 2026-25, Trump revoked the four orders and directed the US secretary of transportation to implement the decision immediately and cancel any conflicting regulations or directives.
The resumption of direct flights was discussed during Aoun’s visit to the White House in July, when Trump announced that flights would resume, months before signing the latest presidential orders.
The decision reflects "confidence in the measures taken by the Lebanese state to ensure civil aviation safety, protect air traffic to and from Beirut, and enhance the security of flights connecting Lebanon with countries around the world", the Lebanese Presidency said in a statement on X.
Aoun also reaffirmed Lebanon’s commitment to international aviation safety standards, saying the country continued to prioritise passenger safety and the security of Beirut’s Rafic Hariri International Airport.
The Lebanese Embassy in Washington also welcomed the decision, describing it as a sign of confidence in the security measures taken by Lebanese authorities.
However, the decision does not mean direct flights will resume immediately. Any restart of services would still require US technical and security assessments, including reviews of airport infrastructure, passenger screening procedures, aviation safety systems and cooperation between Lebanese and American authorities.
Reports have suggested that Beirut–New York could be among the first routes to resume. Lebanon’s national carrier, Middle East Airlines, said in July that it had aircraft capable of operating the route.
A resumption of direct flights would benefit Lebanon’s large diaspora in North America, who are often forced to making connecting flights via Europe. Non-stop services could cut journey times, support tourism and investment, and strengthen commercial ties as Lebanon seeks to revive its crisis-hit economy.
Lebanon is also seeking to expand its aviation infrastructure. Beirut is currently the country’s only civilian airport, while plans are under way to reopen Rene Mouawad Airport in the north for international civilian flights, with its first departure scheduled for mid-November. At least two new airlines are also expected to launch next year.
