In November, TMC captured Madarihat, which the BJP had held since 2016. Even in June 2025, less than a year before its Assembly rout, Trinamool retained Kaliganj by more than 50,000 votes.
Suvendu's promise
There have been exceptions to the incumbent's advantage. In 2023, Congress, supported by the Left, defeated the ruling TMC in Sagardighi by nearly 23,000 votes. However, the MLA concerned, Bayron Biswas, soon joined TMC.
Why BJP's victories still matter
In Nandigram, BJP's Hasi Rani Rath defeated Congress candidate Milan Pradhan, who had Mamata's support, by 1,22,753 votes. In Rejinagar, BJP's Shankharavh Sarkar defeated Aam Janata Unnayan Party candidate Golam Nabi Azad, son of party founder Humayun Kabir, by more than 75,000 votes.In both constituencies, BJP polled more votes than all its opponents combined. Rejinagar witnessed notable outreach from the CM, with Suvendu even saying that Muslims did not need to chant "Jai Shri Ram". He also urged them to turn over a new leaf and extend a hand of friendship to the new government.Following the result, Adhikari attributed BJP's success partly to support from beneficiaries of the Annapurna welfare scheme, under which eligible women receive ₹3,000 per month. Whether the BJP can really secure a share of the Muslim vote in elections with bigger stakes remains to be seen. But if it does, Suvendu's dream of a clean sweep in the Lok Sabha election may well look more realistic.
Allegations of electoral excesses
The Opposition, though, has refused to grant legitimacy to the Assembly bypolls, citing alleged malpractices by the ruling machinery. Bengal Congress president Subhankar Sarkar demanded fresh elections in both constituencies, alleging booth capturing, intimidation, bogus voting and the forcible removal of polling agents. AJUP, which had won the seat previously, alleged that its candidate received zero votes in 33 booths and just one vote in another 19 booths. Mamata's TMC faction made similar allegations of rigging, while the rival Trinamool faction and the Left also complained about polling agents being prevented from functioning.In Nandigram, Congress candidate Milan Pradhan alleged that party agents had been driven out of booths and voters prevented from voting. His earlier arrest in connection with an old case related to the Nandigram land movement had already prompted allegations of political harassment.
BJP supporters in Rejinagar
BJP rejected the rigging allegations, maintaining that polling was peaceful. The Election Commission described voting as largely peaceful despite receiving complaints. One widely circulated claim that BJP had received more votes than the number of registered voters at a Rejinagar booth was subsequently rebutted by election officials, who said the original electorate figure was incorrect.Such allegations are not new to Bengal's electoral politics, one of the reasons why the opposition have frequently asked for central forces to conduct polls. The 2018 panchayat elections witnessed widespread reports of violence and intimidation. More than a third of the seats were won uncontested, overwhelmingly by Trinamool, amid allegations that opposition candidates had been prevented from filing nominations. A year later, the BJP increased its Lok Sabha tally in Bengal from two seats in 2014 to 18 in 2019.Political observers have linked that breakthrough partly to resentment over the conduct of the panchayat polls. Very recently, Abhishek Banerjee’s Diamond Harbour model of winning by record margin of votes had also come under scrutiny. For BJP though, barely a few months into power, the chances of pushback to any alleged excesses remain relatively modest.
What's next for the Opposition?
The INDIA bloc has upped the ante in the capital, demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar over alleged vote manipulation during the SIR process. Leaders such as Rahul Gandhi, Mamata Banerjee and even those from the Left have been sharing the stage. With a common goal, the confluence is organic. But the state-level dynamics are very different, something that has affected the INDIA alliance for a long time.An INDIA alliance is unlikely to become a reality in Bengal, with Left and TMC cadres rarely seeing eye to eye. An alliance between Mamata's TMC and Congress remains an open question, with state leaders of the grand old party lukewarm about giving space to a leader who did not allow them much room to grow while in power.Mamata came to power in 2011 in alliance with Congress, but the two soon parted ways. Since then, the parties have hardly worked together politically, until this by-election. There have been several overtures from Congress in the past, but these were rebuffed by the then West Bengal CM, who wanted to maximise her political capital. Now that the script has flipped, Congress may not give in so easily.Former state Congress president Pradip Bhattacharya disclosed in September that the state leadership had advised against a proposed bypoll arrangement under which Congress would contest Nandigram and Mamata's Trinamool would fight Rejinagar. Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury's recent invitation to Mamata to return to Congress with her remaining MLAs and MPs came with a condition about leaving behind her political baggage, widely interpreted as a reference to Abhishek Banerjee.Even the Nandigram understanding was not a formal seat-sharing arrangement. Mamata supported Milan Pradhan after her faction's candidate withdrew. In Rejinagar, both parties contested separately. Many Congress leaders believe that it is time to rebuild the party in the state when opposition space is up for grabs. The BJP is still getting to grips with governance, and teething troubles in several areas, including the rollout of government schemes, have made headlines.The organisational crisis within Trinamool adds another dimension. Following the Assembly defeat, the party split into rival factions, prompting the Election Commission to temporarily freeze its original name and symbol. The Mamata-led faction and the Ritabrata Banerjee-led Democratic Trinamool Congress contested under different identities in the bypolls. Neither performed well. In Rejinagar, Mamata's faction received 3,847 votes, while Democratic Trinamool polled 2,044.
Mamata Banerjee's political journey before becoming CM
The Left, meanwhile, continues to face the challenge of translating political visibility into electoral support. Younger leaders such as Satarup Ghosh, Dipshita Dhar and Srijan Bhattacharya have attracted attention, particularly on social media, but the party's electoral recovery remains limited.There were, however, modest improvements in the latest bypolls. In Nandigram, the CPI's Santi Gopal Giri increased his tally from 2,997 votes in May to 5,779. Congress also improved its vote count in both constituencies, although the Nandigram comparison is complicated by Mamata's support for its candidate.
Municipal elections: The next big battle
The immediate electoral focus now shifts to the Kolkata and Howrah municipal polls, where voting is tentatively expected in late November. The stakes extend far beyond the two Assembly bypolls.In the 2021 Kolkata Municipal Corporation election, Trinamool won 134 of 144 wards, securing more than 72% of the votes. BJP won just three wards and Congress two. Interestingly, the Left Front, with nearly 12% of the vote, finished ahead of BJP in vote share despite winning fewer seatstThe forthcoming election will also be fought on a substantially altered map. Kolkata's wards have increased from 144 to 209, and Howrah's from 50 to 68. For both factions of TMC, this election will be the first major test of who enjoys greater public support. For Mamata Banerjee, south Kolkata remains her pocket borough, and following the humiliating defeat in Bhabanipur, she would be desperate to turn around her fortunes. For Firhad Hakim and others, it will be an opportunity to prove that they can win on their own without Didi's support.Congress and the Left have long been marginal forces in both Kolkata and Howrah, barring a few pockets. The Left appears inclined to contest independently in several areas, although the CPM has encouraged local discussions with Congress. Some Congress district leaders, meanwhile, have argued that the party should contest all 209 Kolkata wards on its own.The decisions are yet to be finalised, leaving Congress with a difficult choice between rebuilding independently, cooperating with the Left and exploring an understanding with Mamata.
Road to 2029
Nationally, Rahul Gandhi's success in rallying different INDIA bloc parties in the campaign demanding the resignation of the CEC has done his popularity no harm. The bonhomie between Sonia Gandhi and Mamata Banerjee at the recent press conference was there for everyone to see. They have maintained cordial personal relations despite the ebbs and flows in their political exchanges. But the political calculations in Bengal remain very different. Rahul's pointed attacks on Trinamool over corruption during the Assembly campaign had reinforced the Congress's adversarial position in the state. For local Congress workers, a sudden statewide alliance with Mamata would require a significant political adjustment. Didi however, remains in the frontlines in the protest against Election Commission and was detained on Saturday even as Rahul Gandhi skipped the protest and went to Chennai.
Former Bengal CM Mamata Banerjee detained during protest in New Delhi
At the same time, Mamata faces one of the most difficult phases of her political career, while the BJP confronts increasingly coordinated opposition protests at the national level. Hence the political equations could well change. After the municipal elections in Kolkata and Howrah, polls in more than 100 other civic bodies are expected next year, followed by panchayat polls in 2028 and the Lok Sabha election in 2029. Those who have power in the grassroots are likely to have a headstart in the Lok Sabha election.Suvendu has already set his sights on winning all 42 Lok Sabha seats in Bengal. Such a result would have significant implications for the BJP's national parliamentary tally. For Congress, the calculation is therefore not confined to the revival of its Bengal organisation. Its leadership must also consider the wider political ramifications of allowing the BJP a free-run in the state.
For the Opposition, national unity over electoral issues is one thing. Building an effective political arrangement in Bengal is quite another. The coming municipal elections will provide the first major opportunity to see whether those differences can be bridged.

60 countries participate in historic Global Day of Action for Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:41:23 UTC

The Global Day of Action for Palestine called for today, 10th October, has received massive support worldwide. Convened by the Global Alliance for Palestine with the support of the Anti-Apartheid Movement (AAM) and SANED, this historic international mobilisation unites over 200 organisations through 325 mapped events across 60 countries and six continents. From London to capitals and cities worldwide, people of conscience are rising together to declare that the genocide and suffering of the Palestinian people will never be swept aside, and Israel’s illegal occupation will never be normalised.
A press statement from the organisers said the scale of today’s mobilisation demonstrates that solidarity with Palestine has blossomed into a thriving, borderless movement, with communities everywhere finding their voice:
- Europe (176 actions across 24 countries): Anchored by massive turnouts, including 64 actions in Italy and 38 in Spain, alongside major demonstrations at Rome’s Colosseum, Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate, and Brussels’ Israeli Embassy.
- Oceania (45 actions): Kicking off from the earliest hours in Australia and New Zealand, featuring the powerful Hīkoi for Palestine marching from the New Zealand Parliament to Civic Square in
- Latin America & the Caribbean (36 actions across 8 countries): Highlighted by major marches in Santiago, Chile (organised by FECh, Coordinadora Feminista 8M, and CIP), alongside active mobilisations spanning Mexico City, Colombia, Peru, and Uruguay.
- Africa (32 actions across 10 countries): Centred around a Global Mass March in Cape Town, moving from Muir Street Masjid in historic District Six to the Western Cape Provincial Parliament.
- North America & Asia: Featuring a demonstration outside the Israeli Consulate in Los Angeles organised by CODEPINK, a gathering outside the Israeli Embassy in Bangkok, and extensive nationwide mobilisations across Malaysia — including a mass rally and memorandum handover at the US Embassy in Kuala Lumpur, strategic forums, and community advocacy training by MyCARE and PACE.
Diversity of Action
Beyond the traditional marches and demonstrations, this international mobilisation breathes through a remarkable mosaic of cultural, educational, and creative community defiance, proving that resistance takes many forms across the globe. Communities are channeling their solidarity with Palestine into powerful artistic and educational expressions: in Alessandria and Cape Town, solemn memorial processions carry staggering 25-metre and 20-metre shrouds bearing the names of Palestinian children killed by Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
This creative resistance spans continents through events such as ‘Birdwatching for Palestine’ hosted by Colectivo Cardenales and ComPalestina Yucatán in Mexico, the staging of the powerful theatre performance ‘Mashahidi wa Gaza (The Martyrs of Gaza)’ by Friends of Palestine Tanzania in Dar es Salaam, a funeral-themed public commemoration and reading of names at Place Kléber in Strasbourg, a two-day Palestine Solidarity Festival at the Lycabettus Theatre in Athens, and a children’s kite-flying event organised alongside the international conference ‘Ecocide: The Silent War Crime’ in Tehran.
Pushing for tangible accountability
Brought together by established anti-war coalitions, trade unions, student federations, and grassroots networks, participants worldwide stand shoulder-to-shoulder under uncompromising and fierce demands directed squarely at ending Israeli state impunity:
Governments can no longer hide behind empty statements of concern or complicit silence. Tangible measures must be enforced immediately to hold Israel accountable, impose military embargoes, halt arms supplies, and prosecute those responsible for war crimes and state atrocities.
Today’s mobilisation is not a passing wave, but a defining turning point in a sustained international struggle. Palestine is not alone, and this global movement will not falter until Israeli impunity is shattered and true justice, freedom, and liberation for the Palestinian people are achieved.

- The attack follows earlier Houthi strikes on Oct 8, as Saudi Arabia and the Houthis keep fighting and the conflict spreads across the region.

RIYADH – Yemen’s Houthis attacked Riyadh’s international airport with a missile on Oct 10, according to a diplomatic source, with dozens reported wounded and a witness describing panic at the terminal.
Saudi authorities did not confirm any new attack or evacuation, but one witness reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded.
“I was on gate 403” at the domestic terminal, the witness said. “I saw 401 hit. I saw (people) injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”
A source at a local hospital said five people were in intensive care after being wounded at the airport, saying “dozens of people were injured” in all.
The relative of one injured person said they were wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass, and were taken to hospital.
Three witnesses confirmed people being evacuated from the airport.
“Houthis are attacking civilian targets. Riyadh airport is a civilian target,” the diplomatic source said, adding that the airport was hit by “a missile around 3pm” (8pm, Singapore time).
The airport was hit by deadly attacks claimed by Yemen’s Houthis on Oct 8, though the Iran-backed group did not announce any fresh strikes on the facility on Oct 10.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of strikes hitting civilian targets are relatively rare, with officials issuing few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
The scale and frequency of the recent strikes targeting Riyadh are unprecedented in the eight months of war that has spread across the Middle East.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that supports Yemen’s government militarily, and has found itself drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbour’s civil war.
Both Riyadh and the Houthis have signalled a willingness to keep fighting rather than pursue diplomacy.
‘Contact your airline’
Earlier on Oct 10, Riyadh airport urged passengers to check their flight status before coming, echoing an advisory sent on Oct 8, when attacks killed three people, including a pilot for Saudia, the national airline.
“Please contact your airline directly and confirm your flight status before heading to the airport,” read a statement posted on the airport’s official X account.
The Houthi-claimed attacks on Oct 8 also badly damaged a grounded Saudia plane.
Meanwhile, in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas they captured in September around the Bab el-Mandeb strait, military sources said.
The Yemeni government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the group seized Yemen’s entire western coastline in a lightning offensive.
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab el-Mandeb area – a key chokepoint for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping – but they claimed to have repelled the assault.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult. AFP

Woman, 3 children killed in shelling by RSF-allied forces in Sudan's South Kordofan: Medical group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:39:47 UTC
00:39:47 KST

Adel Abdelrheem and Mohammad Sio
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
A woman and her three children were killed in artillery shelling in Sudan's South Kordofan state, the Sudan Doctors Network said Saturday, blaming forces allied with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
The nongovernmental medical group said the attack targeted residential areas in Kadugli, the state capital, and was carried out by the Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), led by Abdelaziz al-Hilu.
In a statement, the network condemned the shelling "in the strongest terms," saying it caused civilian casualties, including children.
It described the attack as "a new violation of international humanitarian law, which prohibits targeting residential areas and civilians."
The network said an entire family – a mother and her three children – had been killed, highlighting "the human cost of attacks on residential neighborhoods in the city."
"Targeting civilians with indiscriminate shelling is a condemnable crime and a clear violation of international conventions," the group said.
It added that such attacks compounded the suffering of residents already facing severe humanitarian and security conditions.
The network held the SPLM-N responsible and called for an immediate end to attacks on civilians and respect for international humanitarian law.
It also urged the UN and human rights and humanitarian organizations to document and condemn violations, hold perpetrators accountable and ensure civilian protection in conflict areas.
There was no immediate comment from the SPLM-N on the network's accusations.
SPLM-N alliance with RSF
The SPLM-N faction led by al-Hilu has fought the Sudanese government since 2011, seeking autonomy for the South Kordofan and Blue Nile regions.
On Feb. 22, 2025, the SPLM-N, RSF and several Sudanese political groups and armed movements signed a political charter in Nairobi, Kenya, to establish a parallel government to the authorities in Sudan.
Sudan's three Kordofan states — North, West and South — have witnessed fighting between the army and RSF since Oct. 25, 2025.
Sudan has been engulfed in war between the army and the RSF since April 2023, leaving tens of thousands dead and displacing around 13 million people, according to UN and international estimates.

Mexico eyes ‘sustainable’ fracking to cut US imports, sparking local backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:36:31 UTC
00:36:31 KST

In mid-August, a week after Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum announced plans to evaluate unconventional gas extraction, a group of protesters gathered outside the Government Palace in the northern state of Nuevo Leon to demonstrate against hydraulic fracturing, commonly known as fracking.
“Here in the Northeast, we do not want this to happen,” says environmental activist Alejandra Guillen.
Guillen belongs to “Noreste sin Fracking,” a collective network formed in northern Mexico after a presidential panel of experts recommended evaluating potential fracking sites across Nuevo Leon, Coahuila, and Tamaulipas. The proposed expansion into the northern Burgos and Sabina basins is part of a government initiative to boost domestic gas production and reduce dependence on US energy imports. Mexico imports 75% of the natural gas it consumes.
“As part of energy sovereignty, to avoid depending more and more on foreign supply, we have publicly opened up the possibility of using unconventional gas in certain areas of the country, where social justice and a minimal environmental impact are guaranteed,” President Sheinbaum said at her morning press conference on August 6.
Activists and residents, however, question claims of minimal environmental impact, arguing that the extraction method threatens water supplies and causes irreversible environmental harm. Furthermore, experts note that the steep financial costs of fracking not only cast doubt on its long-term viability but also raise questions about national sovereignty, as the operations would rely heavily on major foreign corporations, primarily from the US.
Fracking relies on blasting a high-pressure liquid mixture deep underground to crack open dense layers of rock and extract trapped oil and natural gas. Luca Ferrari, a researcher at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), explains that the technique uses toxic chemicals that threaten to pollute air, surface water, and underground aquifers.
“It is not a technological miracle,” Ferrari says. “It is an act of desperation because oil is running out.”
The committee convened in April and recommended a strict ban on hydraulic fracturing in the Tampico-Misantla basin, located along the coastal plain of the Gulf of Mexico, to protect biodiversity and dense regional populations following widespread local opposition.
The panel left the door open for the northern Sabinas-Burro-Picachos and Burgos basins, but made further exploration conditional on confirming by exploratory wells of the presence of deep saltwater, a measure designed to safeguard freshwater reserves required for human consumption. On October 6, Alicia Barcena, Mexico’s environment secretary, clarified that President Sheinbaum has not authorized fracking pilot tests, only tests to verify the availability of deep, saline water.
Carrying banners with slogans such as “Protect our water. Prohibit fracking” and “We are not a sacrifice zone,” demonstrators challenged the concept of sustainable fracking and questioned the decision to only prohibit the practice in areas deemed rich in biodiversity and dense in population.
“Many people live here too, and there are many highly valuable ecosystems,” Guillen added. "Just because they aren't as popular doesn't mean they lack value.”
On the morning of September 24, more than 60 chairs lined the community center in Bustamante, a town located within the Sabinas Basin, two hours from Monterrey. The meeting was organized by Nuevo Leon’s environment minister and Pronatura, an environmental non-governmental organization, to inform residents about a proposal to declare a portion of Bustamante a protected natural area.
Adults filled half the room, while schoolchildren occupied the rest in an effort to engage younger generations; however, the turnout remained low for a town of more than 3,600 people. Although the proposal was not openly presented as a strategy to oppose fracking in the region, some attendees and the town’s mayor viewed it as a way to shield the municipality.
Mario Resendez, the mayor, acknowledged that oil reserves are in decline and that turning to shale gas is being proposed as the alternative. However, he said that doing this in Bustamante, a town that relies heavily on tourism and agriculture, would have a major impact. Although the federal government has not mentioned which specific areas of the basin it will focus on, Resendez said that, judging by the map, Bustamante is included.
“If Bustamante is part of those plans, it will kill us,” he added. “Huge amounts of water are used, and on top of that, chemicals are added; our town would disappear.”
Antonio Hernandez, a biologist with Pronatura, warned that fracking operations threaten local water supplies in an already arid region. He noted that hydraulic fracturing is linked to induced seismicity, which could further affect water availability for both domestic use and agriculture.
Bustamante is no stranger to fracking plans. In 2018, the local government declared Sierra Gomas, identified as an area for unconventional hydrocarbon exploration and extraction, a protected natural reserve. Amalia Martinez, a resident of Bustamante, was part of the group of citizens who protested those initial plans. She noted that she believed former president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador’s pledge to avoid fracking would continue under Sheinbaum’s administration.
The current government faces mounting pressure as a widening gap between soaring domestic demand and stagnant domestic output drives up natural gas imports. The National Center for Natural Gas Control (Cenagas) stated that the country has enough gas reserves to last up to three days if US imports are cut off.
The Ministry of Energy’s latest development plan outlines an aggressive target: ramping up domestic dry natural gas production to nearly 5 billion cubic feet per day. Currently, Mexico consumes roughly 9 billion cubic feet of natural gas daily, while the heavily indebted state oil giant Pemex supplies just 2.3 billion cubic feet of that total.
Ferrari says that although Mexico is in a critical position, fracking produces less than conventional wells -- 10 to 100 times less, according to him -- and is highly expensive. “Consequently, 10 to 100 times more wells must be drilled,” he added.
Physicians for Social Responsibility, a US nongovernmental organization, said in a 2023 report that fracking cannot be practiced in a manner that does not threaten human health and the climate.
Ignacio Villarreal, who moved to Bustamante from Monclova, Coahuila, five years ago, says he and his wife, Sylvia Valdes, have witnessed the impact of exploratory gas activities firsthand. In Castanos, a town neighboring Monclova, exploratory drilling to determine shale viability fueled local tensions as the arid region grappled with rapidly declining aquifers. “We often visited family and friends there, and the water supply was already fragile,” he said.
Lourdes Gonzalez, a local nurse, echoed Villarreal’s concerns, emphasizing that greater public awareness and community mobilization are critical to bolstering opposition and safeguarding local water supplies. However, Hernandez, the biologist, noted that the region’s low population density and high levels of violence made it difficult to organize a mobilization with significant political weight.
While Sheinbaum has stated that communities will be consulted before any plans move forward, attendees expressed hope that the concerns raised at the meeting would resonate throughout the town and drive broader participation. González said that building community awareness is vital, noting: “Fracking poses a significant threat to our water supply and the life of our town. Something must be done.”

The Italian Consulate in Izmir, Turkey’s third-largest city on the western coast bordering the Aegean Sea, celebrated the anniversary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi, the patron saint of Italy, with a concert at St. John’s Cathedral. Archbishop Martin Kmetec attended the event, while the concert was performed by the Italian group Micrologus, which, with its program “The Jesters of God,” brought medieval music to life by performing the Canticle of the Creatures before an audience from the Levantine community.
The Canticle, composed by Francis in 1224, is considered one of the earliest texts in Italian vernacular literature.

Fatigue, 'carelessness' causing casualties among Israeli forces

Breadcrumb
Fatigue, 'carelessness' causing deaths, injuries among Israeli forces in Gaza and Lebanon
A series of recent incidents resulting in deaths or injuries among Israeli soldiers, particularly those deployed in Lebanon and Gaza, have raised alarm in Israel.
Authorities in Israel are concerned that the prolonged deployment of soldiers and their routines may be eroding attentiveness and adherence to safety procedures.
These concerns have been heightened by the deaths of three Israeli soldiers over a two-week period in what have been described as incidents involving safety and security procedures. The incidents occurred in northern Gaza and in the Litani River area of Lebanon.
The latest incident resulted in the death of an officer and the injury of three soldiers when a military Humvee overturned in the Litani area on Thursday.
On Friday, Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth reported warnings from officials within Israel’s security establishment that prolonged deployment along “defensive lines” exposes troops to threats from “hostile parties” and weakens their level of vigilance.
The series of serious incidents in the military has raised deep concern among senior military commanders about complacency and declining operational readiness among troops deployed in the field.
The Hebrew-language report also noted that the Israeli army has been operating on all fronts for a considerable period in what it calls a state of “offensive defence". The widespread deployment of troops along border lines without effective manoeuvring creates an exhausting routine which, the newspaper said, contributes to serious safety incidents.
Meanwhile, the military leadership recognises the complexity of the situation under the current “routine” along the “defensive lines", in the absence of offensive initiative. This situation could result in troops being injured or killed in a wide range of scenarios, from road accidents and training incidents to the erosion of security measures along the “yellow lines” in Gaza and Lebanon, turning these positions into stationary targets for attacks.
Added to this are security incidents inside Syrian territory, where occupying Israeli forces continue their attacks on the population and the surrounding areas.
Faced with threats from Hamas, Hezbollah, and other parties, as well as internal risks stemming from declining vigilance, some within the military establishment are suggesting stricter measures.
According to operational plans, the Israeli military is expected to gradually reduce the size of its forces in the “security buffer zones” and shift towards controlling these areas with smaller units while establishing effective security protocols.

The national carrier said flight KU775 from Kuwait to Riyadh and return flight KU776 were canceled on Oct. 10.
"Kuwait Airways announces the cancellation of flight KU775 (Kuwait to Riyadh) and flight KU776 (Riyadh to Kuwait) today, Saturday, 10 October 2026, due to the closure of the airport resulting from the security situation," an airline statement said.
The carrier urged passengers to monitor their flight status, saying updates would be sent through notifications and text messages to contact numbers registered with bookings.
Saudi authorities had not issued an official announcement confirming the airport's closure as of Saturday.
However, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh urged passengers to contact their airlines directly and verify their flight status before heading to the airport amid reports of disruptions to air traffic and passenger evacuations.
“We would like to inform passengers of the need to communicate directly with air carriers and verify the status of their flight before heading to the airport,” the airport said in a passenger advisory.
The airport thanked passengers for their understanding and cooperation but did not provide further details on the nature or cause of the disruptions.
This came amid heightened aviation concerns following a series of Houthi attacks targeting Saudi airports and other facilities.
Saudi authorities said Friday that three citizens were killed and others injured in two attacks Thursday targeting facilities at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and a Saudi Arabian Airlines aircraft.
Operational activities later resumed, and air traffic returned to normal, according to the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation.
The Houthis have claimed responsibility for several missile and drone attacks on King Khalid International Airport and other Saudi airports in recent days.

On the night of October 10, Ukrainian drones struck a railway bridge in the Vygonitsky district of Russia’s Bryansk region. The strike damaged the railroad tracks.
This was announced by the governor of the Bryansk region, Yegor Kovalchuk.
Due to the damage, rail service on the Bryansk–Unecha–Gomel route has been disrupted.
Trains on certain sections have been replaced by buses, and the Moscow–Novozybkov train will run to the Bryansk-Orlovsky station.

Meanwhile, commuter trains will run to Vygonichi Station, from where passengers will be transported by bus.

It is known that the Ukrainian Defense Forces are using drones to strike the aggressor country’s railway infrastructure. In particular, on September 28, in several districts of the Bryansk and Kaluga regions of Russia, drone attacks damaged the tracks and caused dozens of railcars to derail.
On the Dyatkovo–Lyudinovo section between the Bryansk and Kaluga regions, part of a railway bridge collapsed after being struck by a drone. Due to the structural damage, 10 freight train cars derailed.
Another incident occurred in the Unetsky district of the Bryansk region, where a drone attack also caused a railway accident. As a result of damage to the tracks, 18 empty flatcars derailed.
In addition, railway infrastructure in the Navlinsky district of the Bryansk region was struck. There, damage to the railroad tracks was recorded as a result of the attack.
On the night of September 29, unknown individuals damaged the railroad tracks while a train was traveling from Smolensk to Bryansk on the Trosna–Rzhanitsa section. It can be ruled out that members of the resistance movement in Russia may have been involved in the damage to the tracks.

Pope says death penalty "inadmissible" amid U.S. plans to livestream execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:28:45 UTC
00:28:45 KST

Pope Leo calls death penalty "inadmissible" as U.S. plans to livestream Fort Hood execution
Pope Leo XIV declared that capital punishment is "inadmissible" as the United States plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.
The American pope, in a post on X marking the World Day Against the Death Penalty, quoted the revised Catholic teaching on capital punishment ushered in by his predecessor, Pope Francis. The Catholic teaching states that capital punishment attacks the inherent dignity of a human being.
"The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment," read the post under Leo's official handle, @Pontifex. "Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption."
The U.S. Defense Department announced Thursday that the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base, will be livestreamed. Hasan, scheduled to be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others. It would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961.
The decision to livestream the execution has drawn fierce criticism.
Leo's post didn't refer specifically to the planned execution in the U.S. or the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee late last month which has revived debate over the death penalty in the United States. However, it is common for the pope's official social media accounts to post messages marking such commemorations like the World Day Against the Death Penalty.
However, Leo's post came just hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said explicitly that the planned U.S. public execution was "unacceptable."
Speaking specifically about the United States, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said the planned livestreamed execution was "truly incomprehensible" and "unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle."
"The Church's position is one of total opposition to the death penalty; it is incompatible with human dignity and serves as no deterrent… ," Parolin said in comments carried by Vatican News. "It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this system today — I don't know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle; even if the person is guilty, of course, there are other methods."
The head of the U.S. bishops conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed "shock" and "great sorrow" at the Pentagon's plans.
"In no way can Hasan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he said in a statement Friday. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."
On Friday, President Trump said he approves of Hasan's execution by firing squad.
"He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad," Mr. Trump told reporters before flying to Syracuse, New York, for a political event. "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."
Mr. Trump did not appear to answer when asked whether it was appropriate to livestream the event or whether he was going to watch the execution.
Vice President JD Vance, who is a Catholic convert, appeared to cast doubt on Friday about the livestream, telling reporters he wouldn't watch it and, "I don't know that that's actually going to happen."

With or without Hamas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:19:41 UTC
00:19:41 KST

With or without Hamas
Hamas’s fate will not profoundly shape Gaza’s future.
As we begin the fourth year of a war that has brought the near-total destruction of Gaza, calls for Hamas to surrender administrative authority and evacuate the Strip are intensifying. For Gaza to have any viable future, it is argued, the group’s political and military wings must be dismantled.
While Hamas’s fate is a critical question, charting a meaningful path towards recovery is impossible without addressing the realities that gave rise to it in the first place.
What is happening today in Gaza is directly related to the origins of the Palestinian-Israeli question, which has little to do with any particular armed group.
Hamas did not exist in 1948, when hundreds of Palestinian villages, including Naj and Huj, were depopulated and destroyed during the Nakba – the Palestinian catastrophe that accompanied the creation of the State of Israel – to make way for the establishment of Sderot, Or HaNer and numerous other Israeli cities and villages built upon their ruins.
The group had not yet been established in 1967, when the Arab-Israeli War took place and Israel initiated its military occupation of the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, while simultaneously seizing and unilaterally annexing East Jerusalem—actions that actively set the stage for the broader Israeli settlement project.
In the following decades, the occupation profoundly affected Palestinian society. That, combined with growing religious influence—as the number of local mosques tripled from 200 to 600 between 1967 and 1987 — and a vacuum left behind by a fading secular nationalist leadership, prepared the ground for the rise of faith-based nationalist factions. The outbreak of the First Intifada in 1987 was a political turning point that directly triggered the creation of Hamas.
The group was established by a group of Palestinian men, including three prominent figures. Ibrahim al-Yazouri, was born in Bait Daras, near today’s Ashdod, and was just eight years old when soldiers of the Haganah killed members of his family and expelled the survivors to Khan Younis, south of Gaza City.
Another founder, Abdulaziz al-Rantisi, was born in Yibna—a village near Jaffa whose ruins now sit beneath the Israeli city of Yavne. He was only a year old when Israeli forces expelled his family to Khan Younis.
Lastly, Ahmed Yassin, was born in al-Jura, a village near Ashkelon that was razed to the ground by the Israeli military. He was 12 years old, when he and his family had to flee their home and settle in al-Shati refugee camp on the Gaza coast.
Highlighting this history should not be misunderstood as an attempt to downplay Hamas’s responsibilities. However, the group’s actions cannot be separated from the historical context and the role the State of Israel has played throughout this process.
Unlike the self-proclaimed ISIL (ISIS) and other groups that have emerged in recent years—which lack deep roots in local societies and rely on obsolete ideologies—Palestinian factions are deeply intertwined with local society and national identity.
While Hamas’s trajectory is marked by several disastrous decisions—most notably its fatal decision to launch the assault on Israel on October 7, 2023—the group remains, above all, a symptom of a century of suffering, oppression and a relentless struggle for self-determination.
Any proposed solution – with or without Hamas – to the war in Gaza that fails to address these underlying realities is bound to fail. It must be emphasised here that the widespread tendency in the West to frame the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination as a “reward for Hamas” is deeply flawed. It stems from a systemic prejudice that must not be normalised.
The right was enshrined in international law and supported by an overwhelming majority of nations long before Hamas’s attack.
It is also a mistake to equate Hamas’s actions with the will of the Palestinian people. Today, nearly 50 percent of the population of the Gaza Strip is under the age of 18; when Hamas won the elections in 2006, more than half of Gaza’s current residents had not even been born.
Furthermore, in an Arab Barometer survey conducted in the West Bank and Gaza between late September and early October 2023, only 29 percent of Gaza respondents said they trusted the Hamas-led government. The majority blamed poverty on internal factors; 31 percent directly pointed to the Hamas authorities as being responsible for the situation.
Crucially, a majority (54 percent) supported a two-state solution to the conflict; 73 percent favoured a peaceful resolution. Just 20 percent favoured military action.
The presence of Hamas in Gaza cannot justify the Strip’s wholesale destruction and the crimes committed against civilians that have resulted in Israeli officials facing accusations of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Hamas was not present at al-Nasr Hospital in November 2023, when the Israeli army left newborns to die in incubators after forcing their caregivers to evacuate and prevented their return. Hamas was not in the car with Hind Rajab, the young Palestinian girl, when Israeli forces fired 335 bullets into it in January 2024.
Ironically and unsurprisingly, Hamas has long been viewed as useful by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to maintain the argument that there are no moderate Palestinian partners with whom to negotiate.
This strategy aligns closely with the 2017 Subjugation Plan—officially titled “Israel’s Decisive Plan”—a political and ideological framework presented by Israeli far-right politician Bezalel Smotrich in 2017, which explicitly advocated for disregarding Palestinian national aspirations.
This refusal to address the structural roots has frozen the contemporary diplomatic landscape. The Israeli unwillingness to engage in dialogue with Palestinian interlocutors contrasts sharply with the pragmatic realism historically articulated by Israeli General Moshe Dayan, who famously observed that peacemaking requires negotiating with enemies rather than friends.
Today’s diplomatic landscape is defined by a deep imbalance in expectations. For many years, Palestinian factions have faced strict, non-negotiable prerequisites to attain international political legitimacy—such as the explicit recognition of Israel, the renunciation of violence and adherence to past accords.
Conversely, no reciprocal demands have been placed on Israeli authorities, who face no requirement to recognise a sovereign Palestinian state, honour previous treaties, or renounce violence.
In fact, Israel’s own political evolution is intertwined with factions that utilised political violence. Paramilitary organisations such as the Irgun, led by Menachem Begin, and the Lehi, led by Yitzhak Shamir, conducted operations that targeted civilians, yet both leaders eventually transitioned into mainstream politics and became prime ministers.
This power imbalance directly manifests as a diplomatic asymmetry also in recent ceasefire negotiations, which remain deadlocked by Israel’s demand for the complete disarmament of Hamas. By establishing the eradication of the group’s military capabilities as a precondition for a permanent truce, Israel’s leadership sets a political threshold that effectively forecloses a negotiated settlement.
This allows the Israeli government to perpetuate a status quo that yields significant strategic, territorial and political dividends.
Ultimately, doing away with Hamas will not do away with the Palestinian demand for freedom, nor will it satisfy Israel’s and Palestine’s legitimate right to security. The conflict did not begin with the rise of a militant faction and it will never end until all involved parties finally realise that, as Peruvian Indigenous jurist Dionisio Inca Yupanqui warned two centuries ago, “a nation that oppresses another ultimately forges its own chains”.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Yogi criticised the previous SP government over its handling of Ayodhya. He alleged that the temple town received only three to four hours of electricity and was littered with heaps of garbage during the party’s tenure.
NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Saturday accepted Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav’s challenge to contest the upcoming assembly elections from Ayodhya. Addressing a public meeting in Balrampur, Adityanath invited Yadav to contest against him from the temple town, saying the two leaders should face each other directly.“Akhilesh ji, Ayodhya is our sacred abode. I visit Ayodhya repeatedly to ensure that there is no lapse in its development, and the identity of Uttar Pradesh is not tarnished in any way. It is a centre of our faith and devotion. We go there not to contest elections, but for its development,” Adityanath said.
“I invite you to file your nomination from Ayodhya, and I will too, and try my luck there once. Let it be decided! The fight should be face-to-face,” he added.The challenge comes two days after Yadav dared the chief minister to contest from Ayodhya. The SP chief had claimed that the BJP was conducting surveys after his party announced its candidate but had failed to find a suitable nominee for the seat.Adityanath currently represents the Gorakhpur Urban assembly constituency. The Uttar Pradesh assembly elections are expected to be held early next year.
Yogi targets SP over Ayodhya’s development
Adityanath also criticised the previous SP government over its handling of Ayodhya.
He alleged that the temple town received only three to four hours of electricity and was littered with heaps of garbage during the party’s tenure.He further claimed that the SP government had imposed restrictions on Ramlila performances and erected barricades in the city.“The same Ayodhya is today writing a new chapter of development while giving shape to a new concept of Ram Rajya,” he said.The political exchange comes after the SP won the Faizabad Lok Sabha seat, which covers Ayodhya, in the 2024 general elections. SP candidate Awadhesh Prasad defeated the BJP’s Lallu Singh.
Yogi accuses SP of dynastic politics

That is why I say the real meaning of 'PDA' is 'Pradesh Dubao Alliance' (sink-the-state alliance),” he said.The chief minister was referring to Yadav’s political slogan, PDA, which stands for pichhde, Dalit and alpsankhyak, or backward classes, Dalits and minorities.Adityanath also accused the SP of dynastic politics. He alleged that the party had failed to give adequate representation to Dalits and backward communities in its Rajya Sabha nominations.He claimed that one of the two seats won by the SP had gone to party leader Ram Gopal Yadav, Akhilesh Yadav’s uncle, while the other had been given to a wealthy businessman. The SP also nominated industrialist and sports administrator Dhanraj Parimal Nathwani to the Rajya Sabha.
CM highlights jobs and development
Adityanath also accused successive governments led by the Bahujan Samaj Party and the SP of failing to complete a bridge at Mathura Ghat in Balrampur. He claimed that work progressed only after the BJP came to power.The chief minister said his government had provided government jobs to 9.5 lakh young people over the past nine-and-a-half years. He also pledged that Balrampur would not be left behind in development.
Adityanath said his government had established a system to provide assistance and compensation to families affected by disasters within 24 hours. He added that steps were being taken to ensure prompt compensation in cases of human-wildlife conflict.

Ninety consecutive seasons of top-rated concerts is an impressive record, and the Israel Philharmonic Orchestra (IPO) will celebrate it this season.

Star-studded guest roster
Joining the orchestra for these concerts will be notable artists such as violinist Nikolaj Szeps-Znaider, performing Sibelius Violin Concerto; cellist Mischa Maisky, performing Shlomo by Ernest Bloch; soprano Chen Reiss, singing in the last movement of Mahler’s Symphony No. 4; pianist Kirill Gerstein, playing the Piano Concerto by British composer Thomas Adès; and clarinetist Ron Selka, performing with the orchestra Pastorale Variations by Paul Ben-Haim.
In addition, Shani and the IPO will perform a new IPO-commissioned work, Concerto for Orchestra, by Yosef Bardanashvili.
Throughout the season, the IPO has scheduled programs that will combine beloved symphonic repertoire with contemporary works.
The audience comes first with the IPO, and since the orchestra’s start in 1936 by violinist Bronisaw Huberman, who arranged for 75 musicians from Europe to come to Israel and form the base for what was called the Palestine Symphony, the orchestra and management have been cognizant of the tastes, desires, and needs of its public.
In the pre-state and early years of Israel, the IPO would perform in Jerusalem, traveling in armored vehicles to protect the orchestra members from ambush. Why, may one ask? The orchestra decided the residents of Jerusalem needed music to maintain their morale, and the orchestra answered their need.
In 2023, the opening IPO concert was televised and played to an empty auditorium with only the photos and names of the 125 people who were taken hostage by Hamas arranged on the seats. Why? Because the orchestra believed that was what was needed.
This year, the IPO is presenting 13 different series of concerts, including one series in Jerusalem, two in Haifa, and the rest in Tel Aviv. Each is different; on different days; and at different times.
There are concerts with presenters, moderators, or lecturers; those that are just glorious music; and those that start later and/or start earlier. In essence, there are many possibilities to enjoy.
Throughout its history, the IPO has attracted the very best artists and conductors. Maestro Arturo Toscanini conducted the opening concert in 1936, and this celebratory season, Shani, will be on the podium for several performances throughout the year.
The 90th anniversary festival lineup
Yair Mashiach, secretary general of the IPO, points out one of the most significant aspects of this season is the return of artists and conductors whose relationships with the orchestra have developed over many years.
“We are very pleased to welcome back Kirill Petrenko, music director of the Berlin Philharmonic,” Mashiach said. “Later in the season, we will host Sir Andras Schiff, Semyon Bychkov, Gil Shaham, Yefim Bronfman, Alisa Weilerstein, Reiss and Ivan Fischer.”
“Maestro Zubin Mehta, music director emeritus of the IPO, will be with us in May 2027, showcasing Mahler Symphony No. 1.
“Prior to that, in January 2027, Mehta will be with us for the 90th IPO Anniversary Festival, one of the highlights of the year.
“We will be delighted to have with us renowned pianist Martha Argerich, violinist Maxim Vengerov, conductor Gianandrea Noseda, violinist Pinchas Zuckerman, cellist Amanda Forsyth and, of course, Lahav Shani.
“Zubin Mehta will conduct a Mozart program with Lahav as pianist; Martha Argerich and Maxim Vengerov will perform a Beethoven recital; and another festival program we are looking forward to will bring together Argerich, Shani, and the Israel Jazz Orchestra.”
Honored friend of the orchestra, Vasily Petrenko, will perform two programs in November. The first features Rachmaninov’s Symphonic Dances and the first IPO performance of The Music Makers by Edward Elgar with mezzo-soprano soloist Kathryn Rudge and the Gary Bertini Israel Choir.
The next series will present the IPO premiere of piano soloist Anna Shelest and two works which are first-time IPO performances: The Distant Princess by Alexander Tcherepnin and Symphony No.3 (The Divine Poem) by Alexander Scriabin.
In December, concerts will be led by Kirill Petrenko and will feature the Schnittke Viola Concerto with soloist Amihai Gross, Fountains of Rome by Respighi, and La Mer by Claude Debussy.
Noted Israeli conductor Omer Meir Welber will conduct IPO in late December and on Jan. 1, 2027, in a series of concerts which include Haydn Symphony No. 49, a first IPO performance of Out of the Depths I have cried out onto Thee, O Lord by Aharon Harlap with noted soprano Hila Baggio, and Dvorak Symphony No. 8.
IPO concert audience attendance is full. One thing the gives IPO management great satisfaction is the significant presence of younger members filling the seats.
Mashiach noted, “The increase we are seeing this year continues a trend of several years. Last season, we reached a record number of young people attending our concerts. At the same time, our series, “Concert Baktana”, a format we developed for younger audiences, has become a major success. There is a younger audience here that wants to hear classical music, and we intend to continue deepening that connection.
Shani will bring the IPO’s 90thseason to a close in July with cellist Alisa Weilerstein performing Simfonia Concertante by Sergei Prokofiev and violinist Clara-Jumi Kang performing Prokofiev’s violin Concerto No. 1.
For further information, visit IPO.co.il

The seventh Jerusalem International Women’s Film Festival is to take place October 12-16 at the Jerusalem Cinematheque and other venues around the city, presenting dozens of Israeli and international films that spotlight cinema from a female point of view.
Founded and directed by Lihi Sabag and Shira Meishar, the festival operates under the Women in the Picture association and was established through the Jerusalem Filmmakers Guild. It is held with the cooperation and support of the Jerusalem Municipality, the Jerusalem Foundation, the Culture and Sport Ministry, and the Jerusalem Cinematheque.
The opening film will be Wild Things, the debut feature by Kalil Kovesh, starring Odelia Rand and Alma Zack. Rand plays a young woman who returns to her kibbutz after being released from detention, with her driver’s license revoked.
Fired from her job in the cowshed, she reluctantly becomes a classroom aide, working with a withdrawn third-grader in foster care. Their friendship offers both a chance to grow, even as she struggles with her parents and estrangement from friends.
One of the highlights will be a tribute to Hanna Azoulay-Hasfari, an actress/writer/director who has made films such as Orange People about several generations of Moroccan women. She will receive the festival’s achievement award for her work as an actress, playwright, screenwriter, director, and activist, particularly her exploration of Mizrahi women’s lives.
Jerusalem Women's Film Festival honors Hanna Azoulay-Hasfari with tribute screenings
The tribute includes Sh’Chur, the autobiographical film she wrote and starred in, directed by Shmuel Hasfari, and Orange People, about three generations of Moroccan women who believe in magic, which she wrote, directed, produced, and starred in.
Episodes from her documentary series about working women will also be shown. Her new short, Brit Olam, stars Yael Abecassis, Irit Sheleg, Shai Lee Atary, and Yuval Segal, and examines the repercussions of a secret kept for 30 years.
One unusual aspect of this festival is that its activities continue throughout the year. A year-round project brings films, meetings with directors, and workshops in writing, acting, and video therapy to shelters for women who have experienced violence.
This year’s program also highlights people with disabilities and mental health difficulties, with screenings at the Jerusalem Cinematheque and Jerusalem’s Kfar Shaul Mental Health Center.
Four Israeli competitions cover features and documentaries, independent shorts, student films, and films by high school students.
Israeli feature films compete at Jerusalem Women's Film Festival
The feature competition, supported by the Beracha Foundation, includes Dina Zvi-Riklis’s Blue Marks, adapted from Emilie Moatti’s novel about a young woman from Netanya whose life changes in Paris, and Shiran Shaharabani’s Spikes, about three childhood friends on a hitchhiking trip.
Other entries include Reut Akerman’s Home!, about an adopted girl contacted by her dying biological mother; Nurit Jacobs-Yinon’s Alice.
Last Conversations, documenting feminist pioneer Alice Shalvi’s final year; Emmanuelle Mayer’s The Woman in White, uncovering a woman’s overlooked role in the history of peace with Egypt; and Shir Huri Abu’s Sarah’s Life, following a young woman who leaves the ultra-Orthodox world.
The independent shorts address subjects ranging from fertility treatments and audition-room boundaries to sexuality, family secrets, and urban life in Israel.
The international selection includes Uta Briesewitz’s American Sweatshop, starring Lili Reinhart as a social media content moderator drawn into an obsessive investigation, and Petra Volpe’s Frank & Louis, featuring Kingsley Ben-Adir and Laurence Fishburne in a story about prisoners and redemption.
Mélisa Godet’s A Place for Her stars Karin Viard in a drama about women helping survivors of violence, while the animated Tangles features the voices of Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Bryan Cranston, and Seth Rogen.
The Ktzarot pitching event, held with the Gesher Multicultural Film Fund, will award a NIS 250,000 production grant.

A stand-up evening will feature Mai Sayag, Hagit Weiner, and Rotem Weissberg. Selected movies will stream for free at jwff.co.il, where the full program is available and tickets are sold.

Three injured in third school attack in Poland in less than a week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10

Three injured in third school attack in Poland in less than a week
The attack comes after police announced the detention of 76 people across Poland in connection with previous incidents.
Three people have been injured in a stabbing attack at a further education college in Warsaw, in the third attack on a school in Poland in less than a week.
The series of incidents has stoked concerns in Poland about copycat violence among young people, and ushered police to check tens of thousands of schools and detain dozens of people across the country earlier on Saturday.
In the latest attack, a 21-year-old woman used a “dangerous object” on Saturday at about 12:30pm local time (10:30 GMT) to attack a 17-year-old woman, said Jakub Filipiak, a spokesman for Warsaw police.
The suspect also ended up hurting two other people, aged 17 and 24 respectively, he said.
“One person was injured and transported to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. Two other bystanders also sustained injuries but did not require hospitalisation,” Filipiak added.
The police did not identify the educational institution, but said it was open on a Saturday because it is a higher education establishment. The attacker did not know any of the victims, the police said.
National Wyborcza newspaper identified the institution as TEB Edukacja, a school that gives post-secondary education. The suspect studied at this school, according to national media reports.
Seventy-six detained
The attack came after police on Saturday said they detained 76 people across Poland and checked nearly 50,000 schools nationwide as part of efforts to prevent further violence following two school attacks earlier in the week.
On Friday, schools across Poland stepped up security, with some suspending classes, many parents keeping children at home and police patrols deployed to educational institutions after two attacks at schools earlier in the week left one person dead and several others wounded, including children.
On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in the Mazovian province in central Poland attacked fellow students, teachers and passersby with a sharp object, injuring nine people before fleeing and being arrested nearby.
The following day, a 15-year-old killed a school custodian and wounded two others in a knife attack at his former school in the same province.
The assaults, both carried out by Polish nationals, shocked a country where school violence by minors is a new phenomenon.
By Thursday night, rumours that the attacks were coordinated and that there would be more on the culmination day dubbed “bloody Friday” were being shared in parents’ online groups and by mainstream media.
Fifty-nine schools pre-emptively suspended classes on Friday across Poland, the majority in the Mazovian district, where the capital Warsaw is located. School directors sent messages announcing stepped-up security measures including extra school staff placed at entrances and voluntary backpack checks.
“There will be no compromise here. The safety of the youth is the most important thing,” Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said.
The government earlier said that it had so far found no evidence that an internet challenge promoting school attacks was ongoing. There is also no official confirmation that any of the attacks are linked.

Russia quietly grows fleet that funds its war: one shell firm in Marshall Islands buys two gas tankers from Chinese and Greek owners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:11:18 UTC
00:11:18 KST

Ukraine has published data on 20 vessels that carry Russian oil and liquefied natural gas or refuel the sanctioned fleet, parts of the logistics network the Kremlin uses to fund its war, Ukraine's Defense Intelligence reports. All 20 are under British or Ukrainian sanctions, and only one faces US restrictions.
Russia’s shadow fleet runs on roughly 500 aging ships of uncertain ownership that dodge sanctions and keep oil money flowing. That seaborne oil trade is worth more than 80 billion euros a year.
The headline vessel is the Russian ship Portovyy, an LNG carrier and floating gas store owned by the sanctioned Gazprom since 2021, according to the agency. On 15 August 2026, it left the Gulf of Finland with Russian LNG for the first time since November 2021, sailing the Northern Sea Route to the Chinese port of Beihai to unload.
Portovyy is now at the Zhoushan Huafeng Shipyard in China, which has been set as the site for its maintenance, intelligence says, an example of the foreign yards Kyiv wants closed to the sanctioned fleet.
Russia buys up gas carriers through shells
Two more gas carriers show how Moscow expanded the fleet in spring 2026 through front companies, intelligence said. The Avacha, once owned by China’s Jovo Energy, was bought by the little-known Tudor Maritime of the Marshall Islands, took the Russian flag in June, and now ships gas from the Arctic LNG 2 project to Beihai.
The Chaivo, formerly owned by Greece’s Maran Gas Maritime, was also bought by Tudor Maritime and moved under the Russian flag in July. Now it carries cargo to Beihai from a floating gas storage facility off Kamchatka, intelligence says.
A call to close the loopholes
Intelligence urged partners to act together: tighten control over sales of commercially owned ships, block servicing of the sanctioned fleet at foreign yards, and cut off the energy revenue that Russia turns into weapons against civilians.
Russia is building ice-class ships at home and, at the same time, widening its shadow fleet through offshore networks. The UK Foreign Office made the same point on 1 October, saying Moscow is assembling a new shadow fleet to keep its gas revenues flowing.

Shipping an oil tanker now costs more than launching a SpaceX rocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:10:57 UTC
00:10:57 KST

Global oil shipping costs have skyrocketed amid the volatile security situation in the Gulf, with shipping a tanker from the United States to China costing more than a space rocket launch, Bloomberg reported on Friday.
Brokers at SSY, a large shipbroking house, note that even after adjusting for inflation, current shipping rates are the highest since the first supertankers began operating in the 1960s, surpassing the peaks of the 1980s "Tanker War" between Iran and Iraq in the Gulf.
According to Bloomberg, the drastic spike in expenses is due to a global shortage of tankers, Iranian pressure on the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi attacks in the Gulf and a global shortage of oilers.
Gibson, a shipbroking firm, said that shipping oil from the United States to China costs about $80 million, compared with $74 million for a standard launch of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. At the beginning of the year, this amount was enough to purchase full ownership of a tanker.
The root of the crisis lies in a logistical bottleneck: "There's really not quite enough shipping to go around," said Vitol Group CEO Russell Hardy, one of the world's biggest oil traders. "We've had pretty parabolic pricing."
The uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz led to tankers looking for business elsewhere. Now, with the Gulf's recovery, their return to the scene takes weeks.
Additionally, the halt of Iranian oil exports to China is forcing Beijing to purchase oil from alternative sources through the regular commercial market, which increases demand for tankers.
Also, damage from Iranian attacks has idled vessels for repairs, while other ships are circumnavigating Africa to evade Houthi attacks, adding thousands of miles to their routes.
Middle Eastern oil producers are being forced to offload and transfer oil between vessels outside the Strait of Hormuz, a process that adds a week to each journey and pushes the global tanker fleet to its limits. Shipping through the strait has recovered to only about 80 percent of prewar levels, further straining capacity.
This week, a U.S. shipping deal was struck at a rate equivalent to $41 per barrel of oil, compared with an average of just $4.50 per barrel on the same route last year. The rate amounts to about 45 percent of the price of a barrel of West Texas Intermediate crude, which traded at around $91.
For tanker owners, a relatively exclusive group of Greek shipping families, Norwegian tycoons and a South Korean shipping magnate, the surge in rates translates into enormous profits. The largest publicly traded companies in the sector have a combined market value of more than $70 billion.
The industry is adapting to the squeeze on capacity. Cargoes from West Africa and South America that would normally be shipped on supertankers are being split between two smaller vessels, freeing up the larger tankers for oil shipments.
This shift has spread the shortage of available vessels to other markets, pushing average daily earnings for these ships to more than $680,000, five times the level at the beginning of October.
Oil producers including Iraq, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait have also begun buying their own tankers to hedge against supply risks, driving secondhand tanker prices to a record $240 million per vessel.
The crisis is also taking a toll on the refining sector. Although European refiners initially benefited from higher prices amid a diesel shortage, data from RBC Capital Markets shows that refining margins fell by more than half in October as shipping costs surged.
Analysts warn that if freight rates continue to rise, refineries may be forced to cut output, potentially disrupting or even halting global trade flows.

News Analysis: China's trade strength rooted in competitiveness, not currency depreciation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
23:09:45 CST
00:09:45 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- China has reaffirmed its stance on its foreign exchange policy amid increased discussions over the yuan's valuation, as solid facts and figures support the view that the country's export strength is rooted in its industrial competitiveness rather than currency valuation.
China has neither the need nor the intention to gain trade advantages through currency devaluation, the People's Bank of China (PBOC) said in a policy statement released on Thursday, stressing that the country has never resorted to competitive devaluation.
The statement came as some countries pointed to currency valuation as a cause of trade imbalances, thereby oversimplifying the dynamics between exchange rates and trade.
The conventional view that currency appreciation weakens export competitiveness largely reflects a short-term and static perspective. Over a longer horizon, competitiveness is shaped by much more than exchange rates, analysts have said.
This is particularly evident in China's case. The international competitiveness of Chinese products has at times continued to strengthen even as the RMB appreciated. From 2020 to 2021, the RMB appreciated by about 9 percent against the U.S. dollar, while China's share of global exports increased by 1.7 percentage points in this period, according to the PBOC.
In 2022, by contrast, the RMB depreciated by more than 8 percent against the dollar, while China's share of global exports fell by 0.7 percentage points, PBOC said.
These figures showed that China's imports and exports are relatively insensitive to exchange-rate movements, while neither its goods trade surplus nor its current-account surplus has a simple linear relationship with the RMB exchange rate, said Guan Tao, chief economist at Huafu Securities Co., Ltd.
Attributing China's export strength primarily to currency depreciation or other purported factors including "overcapacity" reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of the sophistication and competitiveness of the country's industrial sector.
At its core, China's trade growth is underpinned by its vast domestic market, comprehensive industrial and supply chains, well-developed infrastructure, abundant and highly skilled workforce, and steadily improving research and innovation capabilities, the central bank noted.
Dong Ximiao, chief economist at China Merchants Union Consumer Finance, said that historically, the world's major trade surplus countries have generally been those with strong industrial competitiveness.
For deficit economies, their deeper challenges lie in structural factors such as low savings rates, high consumption and insufficient industrial competitiveness, issues that cannot be resolved simply by focusing on the exchange rates of their trading partners.
"Declining trade competitiveness in some countries reflects their own structural difficulties," said Hao Yubiao, director of the National Center for Economic Security Studies at Capital University of Economics and Business. "Pointing the finger at other countries' currency exchange rates amounts to avoiding the need for domestic adjustment and does little to solve the underlying problems."
At a time when currencies in neighboring countries have been depreciating, China has refrained from pursuing beggar-thy-neighbor policies or competitive devaluation. This year, both the onshore and offshore RMB have strengthened past the 6.7 mark against the U.S. dollar.
China had never resorted to competitive currency devaluation to boost exports to offset intensive external shocks in the past, the central bank said.
Over the past two decades, the RMB has experienced multiple cycles of appreciation and depreciation, reflecting increasingly pronounced two-way movements and greater exchange-rate flexibility.
The PBOC said that looking ahead, both appreciation and depreciation factors remain in play and that the future direction of the RMB exchange rates remains uncertain. Such two-way fluctuations are consistent with China's efforts to make the exchange rate more flexible and market-oriented.
As a responsible major economy, China has also been committed to addressing such trade imbalances via international cooperation.
At a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors last month, PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng said structural reforms are needed across economies to address global trade imbalances. He called on deficit economies to reduce fiscal deficits and raise domestic savings rates, while surplus economies should appropriately promote growth in consumption and investment.
Countries should formulate medium- and long-term policy plans, make clear commitments and follow through on those commitments, Pan said. ■

Feature: At Frankfurt Book Fair, Chinese publishers offer gateway to get to know China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
23:09:10 CST
00:09:10 KST

FRANKFURT, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- At the Frankfurt Book Fair, books are more than products on display. For many international readers and publishing professionals, they offer a window into China, its history, culture, society and changing ways of life.
This year, about 170 Chinese publishing institutions are taking part in the five-day fair, with up to 55 events ranging from discussions and rights negotiations to signing ceremonies and new book launches. Through books, translations and face-to-face exchanges, Chinese publishers are seeking to bring more stories about China to global audiences while deepening ties with their international counterparts.
The presence of Chinese publishers at the world's largest book fair is driven by the growing interest in learning more about China and its culture.
Speaking for readers in his country, Mohamad El Khatib, CEO of Digital Future, a Lebanese publishing house, told Xinhua that China is becoming more famous in many countries, especially in Arab countries.
Chinese stories resonate with readers in Arab countries because they "share a lot of values", Khatib noted.
"That makes us look a lot into values and talk about Chinese culture-its values, how it respects families, how it respects life, parents and all of these things."
Christina Werum-Wang, German director of the Frankfurt Confucius Institute, believes that book is one of the best ways for people to understand China if they do not have a Chinese friend.
She made the remarks at an event named "Curated Classics: Chinese Masterpieces" organized by China International Book Trading Corporation (CIBTC).
This event brings together several distinguished Chinese publishing houses, each presenting its latest flagship title. From literary fiction to scholarly works, the selected books represent some of the best of contemporary Chinese publishing, offering international rights professionals a curated window into China's vibrant literary landscape.
Literature is the true mergence of language and culture, the expression and reflection of culture by means of language, Werum-Wang explained and added that European readers have gained yet another gateway to discover excellent Chinese books through the "Literary Selection" initiative.
The exhibits at the shared booth of the Chinese publishers at the Frankfurt Book Fair go far beyond books.
At a corner of the booth, lines of panda plush toys are displayed on racks, attracting swarms of curious visitors among whom Alexander B. Voegele looked pleased to receive one panda plush toy as a gift.
As a Berlin resident, Voegele is no stranger to the panda mania as pandas in the Zoo Berlin are among the most popular animals.
For Voegele, the panda is a "very likable animal" that doesn't need to speak. "It wins people's hearts." Voegele is giving the panda plush toy to his niece's daughter. "She's getting it so she can start developing a feeling for China."
Beyond physical cultural symbols like pandas, digital publishing products showcased by gaming enterprises such as HoYoverse have also drawn substantial crowds to the China booth.
A HoYoverse insider noted that video games serve as a novel cultural entry point. Players are often drawn to traditional cultural motifs within gameplay, which subsequently inspires them to read books, appreciate traditional performances, and explore authentic cultural roots offline. Creating this seamless trajectory from virtual gameplay to multidimensional cultural experiences is precisely what the company hopes to achieve. ■
