DAR ES SALAAM, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Tanzania's food self-sufficiency level has increased from 130 percent in the 2024/2025 agricultural season to 133 percent in the 2026/2027 season, reflecting continued improvement in domestic food production, an official said on Saturday.
Tanga Regional Commissioner Batilda Buriani announced the figures while briefing journalists ahead of national World Food Day celebrations scheduled for Oct. 16 in the northern coastal region of Tanga.
Buriani said that despite improved food availability, Tanzania continued to face nutritional challenges, including malnutrition and stunting among young children, prompting the government to pursue targeted interventions to improve dietary outcomes.
She said the celebrations would provide a platform for the government and stakeholders in agriculture, livestock and fisheries to showcase technologies and innovations aimed at increasing production and promoting healthier diets.
Theophord Ndunguru, acting assistant director for crop monitoring and food security at the Ministry of Agriculture, said the government was promoting biofortification through agricultural research institutions.
He explained that biofortification involves developing crop varieties with enhanced nutritional value to increase the supply of essential nutrients through food consumption.
Ndunguru added that the government was also encouraging industrial food fortification, which involves adding essential vitamins and minerals to processed foods, including maize flour, to combat malnutrition.
The two approaches are intended to improve nutritional outcomes and public health nationwide, he said. ■

TAIYUAN, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- China's top diplomat Wang Yi held the 28th China-France Strategic Dialogue with French President's Diplomatic Adviser Emmanuel Bonne in Datong, north China's Shanxi Province, on Saturday.
Wang, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and director of the Office of the Central Commission for Foreign Affairs, had lengthy and in-depth discussions with Bonne on deepening China-France strategic cooperation, and the two reached broad consensus. They also spoke positively of the progress made through the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism.
Wang said the China-France Strategic Dialogue has served head-of-state diplomacy and consolidated political mutual trust. China and France should strengthen communication and coordination, jointly promote the implementation of the four global initiatives proposed by President Xi Jinping, and work together to build a more just and equitable global governance system, Wang noted. He added China hopes that France will honor its commitment to the one-China policy and safeguard the political foundation of China-France relations.
Bonne said France is ready to work with China to continuously build a comprehensive strategic partnership characterized by mutual respect, friendship and mutual trust, solidity and vitality. France adheres to the one-China policy, he added.
France looks forward to closer high-level exchanges, stronger people-to-people and cultural exchanges, and deeper mutually beneficial cooperation with China in various fields to better benefit the two peoples, Bonne said. France will continue to provide a predictable business environment for Chinese enterprises, he noted.
Bonne spoke positively of China's global initiatives and said France is willing to strengthen multilateral coordination with China.
Wang said China and the EU are fully capable of properly handling economic and trade differences via dialogue and bringing bilateral relations back to a track of stable and sound development. He expressed hope that France will continue to play a constructive role in promoting mutually beneficial China-EU cooperation.
Bonne said the EU does not want a trade war with China, nor does it seek to "decouple" from China, and is willing to be a trustworthy and reliable partner of the country. ■

Zheng Qinwen hits a return during the women's singles semifinal between Zheng Qinwen of China and Elise Mertens of Belgium at 2026 China Open tennis tournament in Beijing, China, Oct. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Chenlin)
BEIJING, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- China's Zheng Qinwen defeated Belgium's Elise Mertens 7-5, 6-2 here on Saturday to reach the China Open women's singles final for the first time, while home veteran Zhang Shuai and the Czech Republic's Katerina Siniakova advanced to the women's doubles final.
Zheng, a wild card, broke 13th seed Mertens in the second game, but the Belgian broke back in the seventh to level at 4-4. After a tight finish to the opening set, Zheng prevailed 7-5 before taking control of the second to seal the victory.
The result marked Zheng's best performance at the event and made her the first home player in tournament history to reach the singles final.
"The best version of me will come in the future," reflected Zheng right after the match. "I spare no effort here (China Open). I will give it all out and present a good match tomorrow."
Zheng will face this year's French Open champion Mirra Andreeva in Sunday's final after the fourth seed cruised past the Czech Republic's Nikola Bartunkova 6-2, 6-2 in the other semifinal.
"I'm very happy and excited to be in the final," said Andreeva. "Obviously she (Zheng) is aggressive, she likes to hit a lot of balls, she tries to play fast. I will try to play my best in the final."
In the women's doubles, top seeds Zhang and Siniakova defeated Indonesia's Aldila Sutjiadi and New Zealand's Erin Routliffe 6-4, 6-2 to reach the final.
The women's singles and doubles finals are scheduled for Sunday. ■

Xinjiang scientific expedition finds "most resilient desert plant"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
23:08:54 CST
00:08:54 KST

URUMQI, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- A type of moss discovered in a desert in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region can survive conditions that would kill most plants, including severe dehydration, intense radiation, extreme cold and Mars-like space environments.
This finding is among the major advances of the Third Xinjiang Scientific Expedition, which were released on Saturday in Urumqi, the regional capital city. Scientists describe the moss, Syntrichia caninervis, as "the most resilient desert plant found to date."
The latest evidence of its remarkable resilience was uncovered in space. In March this year, the dried moss was carried aboard China's test cargo spacecraft Qingzhou for an orbital life-restart experiment. Facing microgravity and cosmic radiation, a controlled watering system gave the plants only a tiny amount of liquid water. Yet, the dried moss revived, changing from gray-black to yellow-green.
"This is the first case in which a complete plant has been brought into low Earth orbit and successfully revived," said Li Xiaoshuang, a researcher at the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography under the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
Continued in-orbit observation found the moss regenerating and thriving, indicating that it is an ideal material for deep-space life science research, Li added.
In 2024, Li, as the first author, published the moss study in an academic journal, The Innovation, saying it is a promising pioneer plant for "colonizing extraterrestrial environments."
Before the space test, scientists had already determined its genetic potential on Earth.
Researchers of the Xinjiang scientific expedition discovered the plant in the Gurbantunggut Desert. After lab analysis, researchers found that the plant could tolerate the dehydration of more than 98 percent of its cells, survive rapid freezing at minus 196 degrees Celsius, and overcome strong gamma radiation.
To understand how it endures such extremes, researchers obtained high-quality chromosome-level genetic information and found a large number of stress-related genes, unraveling the molecular code underlying this species' tolerance to extreme conditions.
It can provide genetic material for improving crops and restoring desertified land, Li said.
The Third Xinjiang Scientific Expedition was launched in 2021 by the Ministry of Science and Technology. The previous two were conducted in the 1950s and 1980s, respectively.
Over the past five years, the expedition team carried out studies on Xinjiang's ecology, land and agriculture, biodiversity and biological resources, mineral, energy and water resources. ■

Exclusive: 'It felt like a trap,' how Ukraine was blindsided by Trump's Putin pivot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:01:00 UTC
00:01:00 KST

Exclusive: 'It felt like a trap.' How Ukraine was blindsided by Trump's Putin pivot
U.S. President Donald Trump and Russia's President Vladimir Putin arrive for a press conference at Joint Base Elmendorf- Richardson, Aug. 15, 2025, in Anchorage, Alaska. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)
When U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner told Ukraine's delegation on Oct. 9 that President Donald Trump was preparing to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, the Ukrainians struggled to believe what they were hearing.
The delegation had traveled to the United States to discuss a possible energy ceasefire with Russia. Instead, Kyiv's negotiators found themselves blindsided by a decision they feared would hand Moscow fresh revenue to finance its war against Ukraine while undermining Kyiv's leverage in negotiations.
"It was not just our delegation there, but a European one as well," one senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent. "It's just that everyone was sitting there like fools."
Washington was asking Ukraine to restrain its attacks on Russian energy while giving Moscow an economic reprieve — all as Trump faced consequences from the war against Iran.
"And yet he's the one who got everyone dragged into a war in Iran — a war with no way out — and is selling us out… Just to get a temporary, deceptive reprieve a few weeks before the election," the official said.
The Kyiv Independent spoke with several Ukrainian officials involved in or close to the negotiations. All of them were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
For Ukraine, the key question was why Kyiv should surrender a major means of pressuring Moscow if Russia faced no obligation to stop attacking Ukraine's energy system.
A deal Kyiv never saw coming
President Volodymyr Zelensky had sent a Ukrainian delegation to the United States for talks scheduled for Oct. 9-10. The agenda included a possible energy ceasefire with Moscow and a separate arrangement to halt attacks in the Black Sea.
Instead, the talks were derailed after Trump announced that Russia would supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Kyiv had not been informed of the decision in advance. Although Zelensky publicly acknowledged that Washington was considering a deal with Moscow, Ukrainian officials said they had not known the details before the announcement that evening.
For the delegation, the revelation raised questions about whether Washington had already negotiated terms with Moscow while Ukrainian and European officials were still trying to establish the parameters of an energy truce.
"It felt like a trap," the senior Ukrainian official said.
"To be honest, everyone was shocked as f*ck."
The timing of the U.S. decision only deepened the suspicion.
Following Trump's direction, the U.S. Treasury Department announced that its Office of Foreign Assets Control was "immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
One Ukrainian official pointed to April 7, the date on which the waiver was set to expire, as evidence that Washington had planned the measure around a specific timetable.
"They lifted the sanctions until April 7... So they were preparing this for Oct. 7. It's a birthday present for Putin. They're counting the six months," the official said.
Trump's demand to stop Ukraine's strikes
The dispute had been building for weeks.
Trump had previously pressed Zelensky to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities, arguing that Kyiv should stop disrupting Russia's fuel production.
"Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump told Zelensky on Sept. 13.
Kyiv rejected the premise that Ukraine should halt its strikes unilaterally. Ukrainian officials said Zelensky had repeatedly made clear that any energy ceasefire would have to apply to both sides, with Russia also stopping its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
That distinction is central to Kyiv. Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, terminals, and other energy facilities aim to disrupt a major source of funding for Moscow's war effort. Russia, meanwhile, has systematically targeted Ukrainian power plants and substations, seeking to deprive civilians of electricity and heating.
A ceasefire that stopped only Ukrainian attacks would therefore leave Russia's campaign against Ukraine's energy system intact while protecting infrastructure that helps sustain the Russian war machine.
Yet, Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that U.S. negotiators presented the issue differently during the talks, framing Zelensky as responsible for the impasse because he had refused to halt attacks on Russian refineries.
The Ukrainians were also told that Washington would cut off intelligence sharing that has helped Kyiv identify and strike targets inside Russia, one person present at the talks told the Kyiv Independent.
U.S. intelligence has played an important role in Ukrainian attacks, and restricting access to it would weaken Kyiv's ability to conduct strikes deep inside Russian territory.
One senior Ukrainian official involved in the talks responded with bitter humor.
"I hope the Americans don't give them Patriot (air defense systems) to protect their oil refineries," the official said.
The remark, however, captured a broader fear in Kyiv.
Washington already ended up helping Moscow shield the infrastructure that finances its war while pressuring Ukraine to surrender a means of striking back.
Another senior Ukrainian official said Ukraine had not agreed to stop attacking Russian refineries and would not commit to doing so without reciprocal Russian action.
For Kyiv, the principle remained unchanged. An energy truce could work only if both countries accepted the same restrictions.
"It was just f**king stupid to bury the idea of an energy truce with that move," one official said, suggesting that Washington was trying to strip Ukraine of its greatest source of leverage in the negotiations.
The war continues on both sides
Events on the ground showed how little the announcement had changed.
Just hours after Trump's announcement, Ukrainian drones struck an oil loading terminal in Russia's Rostov-on-Don. The terminal handles petroleum products for export and supplies fuel to Russia's military.
Russia, meanwhile, launched a drone attack followed by a missile strike on Kyiv on Oct. 10, also targeting Ukrainian energy facilities.
Neither side had agreed to stop striking energy infrastructure, and the U.S. announcement had done little to bridge the gap between their positions.
Zelensky addressed the decision in a voice message to reporters late on Oct. 9, warning that allowing Russia to export diesel would just give Moscow additional revenue to sustain its war.
"This only fuels Putin and enables him to wage more war," Zelensky said. "And at the moment when we are talking about peace, the U.S. is allowing Russia to export diesel."
He also questioned the purpose of sending a Ukrainian delegation to negotiations under those circumstances.
"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. This is certainly not honest, and it is certainly not how partners should act," Zelensky said, calling the decision "a weak decision by our strong partners."
Ukraine was being asked to make concessions on the battlefield even as Moscow continued to attack its cities and energy infrastructure.
For one senior Ukrainian official, the explanation for Washington's move was straightforward: Trump was trying to deflect blame for the consequences of his own foreign policy.
"Clearly, Trump doesn't want to admit that it was his war against Iran that caused so many problems for Americans," the official said.

Blast reported at Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:01:00 UTC
00:01:00 KST

Saudi Arabia: 12 killed, hundreds injured in Riyadh strike
Published October 10, 2026last updated October 11, 2026
At least 12 people were killed and hundreds were injured in an attack on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday.
"King Khalid International Airport was targeted by an attack, amid continued attacks targeting civilian aviation facilities in the kingdom," the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in an initial statement.
Hours later, the authority announced that 12 people had been killed, including four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese national.
At least 309 others were injured in the attack, the aviation authority said, adding that "all injured individuals are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals."
Operations at the airport had been suspended until further notice.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen also announced that "a projectile" had also landed near King Fahd International Airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
Coalition vows to respond
On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government accused the Houthis of carrying out the deadly attack on Riyadh's international airport. The coalition vowed to respond "decisively."
In a statement, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki described the attack as a "war crime" and vowed the coalition "will respond decisively to this terrorist attack."
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump called the attack on Riyadh's international airport "not acceptable."
He also told reporters that he will speak with Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
When asked if the US might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the United States strongly condemns recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, confirming that an American citizen was killed in the strikes.
"These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now," Rubio wrote on X.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" by the Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport.
"Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law," Guterres said. "These attacks must cease immediately."
What do we know about the Riyadh attack?
A Saudi official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the Associated Press that many people were wounded after a missile hit a passenger terminal.
The AFP news news agency also reported that a number of people were injured, citing a local medical source who also spoke on the condition of anonymity.
"ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," the source told AFP. "We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh."
Several Western embassies in Riyadh, including those of Germany, the United States, Canada and Spain, urged citizens to avoid the airport.
The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks" at the airport. Spain's embassy referred to a "new attack" by the Houthi rebels in Yemen while Canada's embassy warned of "ongoing military activity."
What did the Houthis say?
The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen did not immediately claim responsibility for the attack.
However, after the attack, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree retweeted his own post from a day earlier in which he said that only pre-approved humanitarian flights would be allowed to land at Riyadh airport.
In the retweet on Saturday night, Saree wrote: "A reminder."
When asked about the attack, US President Donald Trump said the US would soon decide whether to join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We move very quickly."
Strikes hit Riyadh airport earlier this week
Fighting has intensified between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen.
The Iran-backed Houthis have been launching strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia, including several this week on the airport in Riyadh that killed four people, injured several others, and damaged planes.
Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways canceled multiple flights between their respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Kuwait Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday.
Last month, Houthi rebels made advances on important strategic locations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces seeking to take back those gains.
The Houthis have responded by launching attacks into Saudi Arabia, which represents a significant escalation in their multi-year conflict with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government after a peace deal unraveled in July.
The Saudi-backed government in Yemen last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, especially those around the Bab al-Mandab strait.

Camden council was warned about paedophile nursery worker years before arrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:00:01 UTC
00:00:01 KST

A paedophile nursery worker was cleared by an investigation overseen by a local authority three years before he was arrested.
In February, Vincent Chan was jailed after pleading guilty to 56 offences, including assault by penetration on three-year-old girls in his care at a Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road in north-west London. After his conviction, prosecutors described him as a “prolific sexual predator”.
The Guardian can now reveal that Chan was the subject of an earlier safeguarding investigation, carried out by Bright Horizons, with the oversight of Camden council. It followed what were described as “significant concerns” raised with the nursery in 2021 about Chan’s conduct and behaviour by the parent of a young girl, including concerns about what her daughter was saying to her about Chan.
Bright Horizons referred the matter to Camden council, which advised the nursery to investigate. Chan was put on duties that involved no contact with children while the investigation by Bright Horizons took place. After it was completed, Chan was cleared to return to his role caring for young children in the nursery.
A year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself sexually abusing three-year-old girls at the Bright Horizons nursery.
Chan was first arrested in June 2024, initially on suspicion of child cruelty, after nursery staff discovered videos Chan had filmed of distressed children in his care.
After Chan’s devices were searched by police as part of this investigation, they discovered that he was a prolific sexual offender, with tens of thousands of child abuse images on his computer. He had also committed sexual offences in his previous job as a teaching assistant at St Mary’s Church of England primary school in Dollis Park, north London, including upskirting female pupils. In February this year, Chan was sentenced to 18 years in prison.
The revelation that Camden council and Bright Horizons were aware of concerns about Chan three years before his arrest, and that there had been an investigation into his behaviour, will raise questions about whether there were earlier opportunities to stop him. It will also raise wider questions about whether existing safeguards for nurseries are adequate.
In early 2024, prior to Chan’s arrest, other parents say that they raised concerns with Bright Horizons about Chan’s conduct at work. They say they warned Bright Horizons that their children were telling them that Chan shouted at them, was “angry” and a “bad man”. These parents say these concerns were dismissed. After Chan’s first arrest, the Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road closed in June 2025.
Nurseries have a responsibility to refer to local authority designated officers (LADOs) when there are concerns that a nursery worker has been accused of harming or posing a risk of harm to children, may be guilty of criminal conduct, or has exhibited behaviour that makes them unsuitable to work with children.
Local authorities have the ultimate responsibility for managing allegations raised that relate to adults who work with children.
LADOs can recommend that a matter be referred to the police if they believe it meets a criminal threshold. It is understood that the Metropolitan police did not receive a referral in 2021 regarding Chan, and were only notified of the concerns subsequently.
After Chan’s sexual offending came to light, Camden council carried out a rapid review of the decision to clear him to return to work after the Bright Horizons investigation. The review concluded in November 2025, and Camden council subsequently commissioned a local child safeguarding practice review, led by an independent reviewer, to examine how Chan was able to abuse children at the Finchley Road nursery, in addition to offences committed in his previous role.
The review, which has been pushed back repeatedly, is expected to be published in early 2027 according to Camden council. It is expected to be critical of the safeguarding culture within Bright Horizons. But Camden council has said publicly that it cannot investigate Bright Horizons under health and safety laws because it is conflicted due to its participation in the safeguarding review. Local authorities have the power to prosecute businesses that do not comply with health and safety legislation.
In a letter to the parent of a child at the nursery, seen by the Guardian, Camden council said that the purpose of the safeguarding review was “not conducted to hold individuals, organisations, or agencies to account”. The review is not expected to satisfy the parents of Chan’s victims because it is unlikely to apportion blame to executives at Bright Horizons.
There has been no explanation of why the review was pushed back from summer 2026, when the independent reviewer was initially expected to submit her report. The council has also rejected a freedom of information request from the Guardian relating to Chan’s employment at the nursery, citing a desire to “manage” the release of information.
It is understood that, in addition to the 2021 referral involving Chan, Camden council received other unrelated safeguarding referrals from Bright Horizons between 2017 and 2024, the time Chan worked at the nursery.
A spokesperson for Camden council said: “Children deserve the best care in a safe environment and the ongoing independent local child safeguarding review into this case presents a pivotal opportunity to prevent abuse like this from happening again. Our participation in the review is thorough, and we have disclosed all relevant documents and information.
“We are ready to receive the review’s recommendations once it is published and take action. We are determined to make a real and tangible impact on safeguarding arrangements for the future.”
A spokesperson for Bright Horizons said: “Our thoughts remain with the victims of Chan’s shocking crimes and their families. As the Camden local authority’s child safeguarding practice review is ongoing, we will not be able to comment without the express written authorisation of that committee as we do not wish to prejudice that process. We will respond as soon as we are able, once we have received the committee’s response.”

A replica of Donald Trump’s Oval Office goes for the gold in Washington DC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Sitting behind a replica Resolute Desk, nine-year-old Sydney Wright posed for the camera like a future US president. “I love it,” she smiled. And what about the dazzling gold appliqués, gold leaf and gold trim surrounding her? “It’s cool.”
Sydney was among a steady stream of visitors on Thursday to The People’s House: A White House Experience, an interactive museum – with an orientation film narrated by The West Wing star Martin Sheen – at 1700 Pennsylvania Avenue, just 150 yards from the real thing.
Run by the White House Historical Association, the tourist attraction has just unveiled an elaborate overhaul of its full-scale Oval Office to match Donald Trump’s second-term aesthetic, described by the New York Times as a “gilded rococo nightmare”.
Gone is the understated, plain decor of Joe Biden and his predecessors. In its place is a spectacle of two dozen portraits in heavy carved frames, swirling wall onlays, gleaming brass vases and decorative knickknacks crowding nearly every available surface.
Barack Obama had pictures of two former presidents on the wall; Biden put up a total of seven paintings. Trump has stacked the walls with historical figures including George Washington, Andrew Jackson and Benjamin Franklin. Ronald Reagan appears twice, while there is only one woman on display: former first lady Jackie Kennedy.
A bust of former president Theodore Roosevelt by James Earle Fraser glowers from a bookshelf, flanked by bound volumes of the 26th president’s works. Other books on display include Hawthorne’s Works and Writings of Washington. There are two mirrors and a copy of the Declaration of Independence.
But for all the detail, the people’s house cannot recreate the experience of former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, who reportedly entered the Oval Office one day to find Trump in DIY mode, using superglue in an effort to stick gold ornaments to the fireplace.
Still, for many tourists arriving in the nation’s capital, this is as close as they will get to the heart of presidential power, especially with the White House currently undergoing extensive demolition and construction work.
Sydney’s father, Drew Wright, a 36-year-old firefighter from Athens, Georgia, said he viewed the room’s additions as “paying homage to the people who laid the pathway that we have to raise our children in this great nation”.
Asked about the goldening, Wright, who voted for Trump twice, replied: “There’s always going to be critics. There’s always going to be haters. Just because they’re the loudest ones in the room doesn’t mean they’re right. I don’t know what it looked like before but I think it’s a pretty classic look.”
Cheri Lujan Hamilton, 54, the chief clerk of the New Mexico state senate, also likes what Trump has done with the place. “I’m kind of in awe,” she said. “I was disappointed we couldn’t get into the White House for a tour so this is the next best thing.”
Taking in all the gold, Hamilton remarked: “It’s grand. I like everything that’s grand. I do think all the gold around the doors is maybe a little too much. But I like it on the top.”
Pedro Robles, 50, a police officer from Nashville, Tennessee, called the replica “pretty cool” and disputed the notion that the gilding crosses into bad taste. “I don’t think so,” he said. “I don’t think it looks tacky.”
Such opinions would be music to the ears of Trump who, when asked by Time magazine what he would miss most about the White House after he leaves, answered: “This beautiful room that nobody should be allowed to rip down. The Oval Office.”
A team of specialised designers visited Trump’s actual office while he was away to ensure authenticity. They used 3D scanning in Indianapolis and crafted hand-carved gold frames in California, while teams in Canada and Virginia worked on replicas of vases and other tabletop pieces.
The replica transition took one week with more than 25 crew members onsite. They used laser levels and temporary adhesive to fix items to the walls, checking their work for accuracy against renderings of the actual office before nailing many adornments to the walls.
Matthew Costello, chief education officer at the White House Historical Association, said in an email: “As we have seen throughout White House history, each president transitions the Oval Office according to his own tastes. It is our hope that through the evolutions of our Oval Office replica, people will be inspired to learn more about and even see themselves in White House history.”
There is, however, one key difference between the real Oval Office and its imitator. While the actual workspace relies on gilded gold leaf, the museum opted for a specialised gold paint solution to protect against chipping or other wear and tear from visitors.
The transformation provides a microcosm of an aggressive campaign by Trump to remake Washington DC in his own image.
Beyond the Oval Office makeover, Trump knocked down the East Wing to build a $400m ballroom, paved over the Rose Garden’s traditional grass lawn to build a white stone patio reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, added a row of presidential portraits that replace Biden with an autopen and constructed a granite helipad on the south lawn.
He also initiated a troubled overhaul of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, proposed a towering 250ft triumphal arch near Arlington national cemetery and threatened to tear down the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts if it does not bear his name.
Washington purists and architecture critics have recoiled at Trump’s ostentatious tastes. But Carl Wilkerson, 73, a retired marine wearing a US Marine Corps T-shirt, offered an impassioned defense of presidential swagger, saying: “We need to have a little bling-bling, man. This is the United States of America. This is the greatest country on the planet, so we need to show it off.”
Drawing on his time overseas, Wilkerson, from Hereford, Arizona, argued that US presidential architecture had fallen behind the competition, saying: “You go over there in the east. He’s walked in their palaces and it’s like, boom. It pops. Their palaces outdid the White House 10 to one. We need to step up our game a little bit. We are the greatest country on the planet. So you need to act like it – and look like it.”

Sixteen more Ukrainians brought back from Russian occupation: 1986 Chornobyl disaster first responder among them – photos
Sixteen more Ukrainians have managed to leave the Russian occupation for Ukrainian-controlled territory. Among them is a woman whose health issues prevented her from making the journey alone and a 1986 Chornobyl disaster first responder Known as "liquidators", the first responders were civil and military personnel called in to deal with the immediate and long-term aftermath of the nuclear disaster, at great personal risk whose wife passed away before they could reunite with their daughter.
Source: Dmytro Lubinets, Ukrainian Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights, recounting the Ukrainians' stories of fleeing Russian occupation
Details: The evacuation took place through the Novi Yarylovychi border crossing point with Belarus in Chernihiv Oblast. Among those evacuated is a woman who had spent a long time living alone under occupation despite her health problems and limited mobility.
She couldn't make the journey back on her own, so special transport, a medical escort and a safe route were arranged for her. Everything had to be organised discreetly to avoid attracting Russian attention and putting her in even greater danger.
A man who had served as a first responder during the Chornobyl nuclear disaster and was living in Luhansk Oblast with his seriously ill wife also managed to reunite with his family. His wife had suffered a massive stroke in April and needed constant care. Her husband had health problems of his own and could no longer look after her properly.
An urgent evacuation to Kyiv, where their daughter was waiting for them, was arranged for the married couple. But the woman died before they could leave, and her husband had to make the journey out of the occupied territory alone.
Lubinets said: "The return of 16 Ukrainians from the temporarily occupied territories represents 16 different stories, circumstances and journeys to safety. For some, the journey home was a chance to finally receive medical care; for others, it was a chance to reunite with their loved ones.
Every such return requires an individual approach, careful preparation and coordination among many people."
He added that Ukrainians returning from the temporarily occupied territories face numerous challenges as they try to rebuild their lives in safety. They are provided with medical treatment, help restoring their documents and finding temporary accommodation, assistance with travel arrangements, psychological support and help reuniting with their loved ones.
Background: Previously, three young people were brought back from Russian occupation. Two of them had ended up under Russian control when they were still children, and their parents later moved them to Russia.

Former Biden administration official Phil Gordon on Saturday rejected attempts by supporters of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to portray Brett McGurk’s new book and interviews as vindication of Netanyahu’s conduct of the war in Gaza.
“Netanyahu supporters seem to be taking advantage of Brett McGurk’s book and interviews to claim vindication for Netanyahu’s conduct of the war in Gaza,” Gordon wrote in a post on X/Twitter.
“But while Brett’s front-row account is valuable, that doesn’t mean it is definitive or its perspectives widely shared – including among former members of the Biden administration.”
“I would say most of my former colleagues think that president (Joe) Biden should have put more pressure on Israel to conduct the war differently and end it sooner,” Gordon wrote, adding that “few think that the biggest mistake Biden made was to show daylight with Israel.”
Gordon argued that even McGurk’s own account showed that securing the release of the hostages was not Netanyahu’s top priority, and that US pressure on Israel could produce results when it was actually applied.
As an example, he pointed to Biden’s phone call with Netanyahu after the World Central Kitchen strike, saying US pressure after that incident “worked.”
Biden aide says Netanyahu went against Israeli security chiefs, delayed Gaza deal
Gordon said, however, that McGurk’s account omitted another significant episode: a July 4, 2024 phone call in which Biden pressed Netanyahu to conclude a hostage deal after Hamas had, according to Gordon, accepted the basic framework.
“Hamas had finally accepted the basic framework, dropping its demand that Israel commit to a permanent ceasefire before any hostages were released,” Gordon wrote.
Rather than agreeing, Gordon alleged, Netanyahu introduced a series of additional conditions “against the advice of his own security chiefs,” making a deal impossible for another six months.
Gordon said that during that period, nearly 9,000 additional Palestinians were killed and more Israeli hostages died, including the six hostages executed by Hamas in August.
Among the Israeli changes cited by Gordon was a demand that Israel retain forces “along Gaza’s entire border with Egypt,” which the IDF had seized only after the original proposal had already been made.
He also cited “a new enforcement mechanism to screen Gazans who were returning home to the north,” which he said would have required Israeli troops to remain in central Gaza.
Gordon emphasized that both of those conditions were ultimately dropped from the agreement reached in January 2025.
Ex-Biden aide: No version of Gaza war ‘vindicates’ Netanyahu
Gordon went on to sharply criticize Netanyahu’s broader handling of the war, arguing that nothing in McGurk’s “book or elsewhere changes the reality that October 7 happened on Netanyahu’s watch.”
He accused Netanyahu of prioritizing “total victory” and “the maintenance of his coalition” over either a hostage deal or an end to the war.
Gordon also wrote that Netanyahu’s conduct of the war and his management of its humanitarian consequences were “catastrophic,” arguing that they had left Israel “more isolated and insecure” and had “deeply damaged, perhaps irreparably, Israel’s relationship with the United States.”
The former Biden official said Washington should have done more “to change Israel’s conduct rather than enable it.”
“There was never an easy way forward in Gaza,” Gordon concluded, “but no version of the story vindicates Netanyahu.”

Police detained more than 2,000 protesters and the founder of the "Cockroach" youth movement in Delhi on Saturday as security forces locked down parts of the capital to thwart a rally demanding the resignation of India's election chief.
Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the city, mobile internet services were suspended in the central business district, and dozens of metro stations and markets were shut as authorities moved to stop a demonstration organized by the Cockroach movement.
The protest was aimed at Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, but security forces sealed off the area before the demonstration began.
A home ministry official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters more than 2,000 people were detained in Delhi. Local media said about 400 protesters were held in Mumbai, India's financial hub.
Police did not immediately comment on the detentions.
Small protests broke out elsewhere in Delhi, including at a popular crafts market and the memorial to freedom movement leader Mahatma Gandhi, with demonstrators demanding Kumar's resignation.
"Long live the revolution," some young protesters chanted as police chased them and dragged scores of others into buses to be taken away, even as more arrived, a Reuters witness said.
"This is violating the rights of the people and the country will not tolerate this anymore," Yogendra Solanki told Reuters as police escorted him away.
Cockroach Janta Party leaders taken into custody
Police detained Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and senior leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka when their flight from Mumbai landed in Delhi, the group said in a statement.
Television footage showed Dipke challenging officers who approached him on board the aircraft.
"I have come to be arrested, arrest me ... I am not afraid of you guys," he said.
"No, this is not an arrest," one officer replied. "Please cooperate."
The movement condemned what it called the "authoritarian detention" of its leaders, demanded their release and vowed to continue protesting.
"We will continue our protest tomorrow, day after day... until Gyanesh Kumar resigns. We will be on the streets," CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde told reporters.
CJP also said authorities refused to provide updates on the leaders' whereabouts or health, even after news arrived of the death of Dipke's grandmother. Police said Dipke was informed of her death and was offered help to return home for the funeral.
Some opposition lawmakers and former chief ministers Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal, Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi, and Pinarayi Vijayan of Kerala were also detained, TV channels showed.
Representatives of two digital news outlets said police briefly detained four of their reporters while they were covering the demonstrations. A Reuters journalist was also detained briefly before being released.
Across the capital of about 20 million people, security forces set up checkpoints on major roads and entry points, boarded buses searching for protesters and inspected vehicles. Barricades and concrete blocks disrupted traffic while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear-gas launchers guarded key routes.
New challenge to Modi
The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi, stemming from allegations that election authorities improperly revised voter rolls ahead of recent state polls.
Protests intensified after the Indian Express reported last week that two election commissioners had questioned Kumar's voter-list revisions that removed roughly 130 million names from voter lists.
Kumar has not commented, but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied allegations of wrongdoing.
The BJP says its electoral success reflects Modi's popularity and India's economic growth, and accuses opposition parties of spreading misinformation.
The near-daily protests come just months after demonstrations over exam paper leaks forced his education minister to quit.
The unrest also comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027.
Rahul Gandhi, leader of the main opposition Congress party, said Modi's opponents would not back down.
A senior BJP member, Ravi Shankar Prasad, said the party was not opposed to demonstrations but the street protests had been "weaponized" by rivals due to election defeats.
Deletions affected state polls, opposition alleges
Opposition parties say the deletions affected the outcome of recent state elections won by the BJP and have cast a shadow over voting in the world's largest democracy.
Election Commission data show about 130 million voter entries were removed during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated, 30 million who could not be traced, and 28 million who had died.
The commission says the removals relate to entries identified during the draft revision process and that any eligible voter incorrectly deleted can re-enroll.

Saturday's attack occurred without warning, with no alert issued by Saudi Arabia's threat warning system. This week's two previous attacks on King Khalid International Airport left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.
This week's deadly strikes exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom's self-defense capabilities as it wages an air campaign against the Houthis to support a ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group.
Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have claimed hundreds of strikes on targets in Houthi-held territory. The Houthis have said these killed civilians, including women and children.
Reuters could not independently verify those claims.
All flights were diverted from Riyadh on Saturday, and operations at the airport that serves a city of roughly 8 million people were temporarily suspended, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
The head of the Houthi media office said in a post on X/Twitter after the attack that the group had "shut down Riyadh international airport." The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group on Monday.
US President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House, was asked whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks, saying they "demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life."
Eyewitnesses saw wounded on ground in airport
One eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing towards the facility. A video verified by Reuters showed ambulances at the airport.
An injured traveler told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed.
The US embassy in Riyadh said it was "aware of attacks" and "strongly recommends all US citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas."
Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of the Yemeni capital Sanaa. The Houthis had stormed Sanaa the previous year, pushing out government forces.
The war was fought to a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine. Saudi Arabia struck a 2022 deal with the Houthis, freezing the conflict.
That ceasefire unraveled over the summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive this week to try to retake that territory, which has so far made slow gains, even as the Houthis put the country's third-largest city, Taiz, under siege.
Etihad Airways, Qatar Airways, Kuwait Airways cancel Riyadh flights amid Houthi attacks
Flight-tracking site flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or canceled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point.
Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences.
Organizers of those conferences said on Saturday they would go ahead as planned, and they sought to reassure attendees of their security.

The winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, judge and former UN rights chief Navi Pillay, has called sanctions announced by the US on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of, unacceptable".
"There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague," Pillay said via video link from Nuremberg during an event at the Nobel Peace Centre in Oslo on Saturday.
Pillay also lamented that "there are hundreds of staff who feel they are under threat".
"Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable," the 85-year-old South African lawyer said.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee on Friday announced that Pillay, who once sat on the ICC, was this year's recipient of the prestigious Nobel Peace Prize.
Both the United States and Israel condemned her being awarded the honour.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would ban transactions with what he described as a "rogue court", escalating a long-running campaign by US administration against the Hague-based tribunal.
The court rejected the US sanctions as an attack on international law and warned in a statement that "history will judge this moment".
In addition to serving on the ICC, Pillay was the UN human rights high commissioner from 2008 to 2014, and she headed the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry (COI), which found last year that genocide was occurring in Gaza.

Three shards of glass under his eye and espionage charges: how a UP employee was kept handcuffed in an Austrian hospital
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
17:51:00 EEST
23:51:00 KST

Three shards of glass under his eye and espionage charges: how a UP employee was kept handcuffed in an Austrian hospital
On 8 October, Mykhailo Tkach, head of investigative journalism at Ukrainska Pravda, and his colleague Yaroslav Bondarenko were detained in Vienna while on an assignment to track down fugitive former prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko.
Yaroslav, who was injured during the detention, recounts how the arrest unfolded.
...In broad daylight (at 15:00), as we were driving from one place to another in a rental car, we were brutally taken down by Austrian special forces at a traffic light.
They smashed both windows, and within seconds we were on the ground. Mykhailo Tkach "got lucky" – on his side there was a verge with a flowerbed and grass, whereas I was shoved face-first into the tarmac, and they pressed down on me with their whole body weight right into the shattered glass. My left arm was in the grip of a police officer, while my right was trapped under my body... they started yanking it out. It was cut to ribbons. Gashes and lacerations on my right arm.
They twisted my left arm so hard that I cried out loud from the sudden sharp pain. It felt like they were about to break my arm.
Then they clamped handcuffs on my left wrist so tight that after only 15-20 minutes I was begging them: "Please relax this! Please! It's no good! Please relax!" I don't speak German. Sorry :))
From the moment of that takedown, with the smashed windows, Mykhailo and I were separated with absolutely no way to communicate!
Looking to the side was FORBIDDEN – it was instantly "face the wall!"
Blood was pouring down my face, soaking my clothes, trousers, and my new trainers (I could see they were ruined). I looked at my arm – it was bleeding. A police medic came over with hydrogen peroxide to take a look at me and give first aid. That's when I noticed Mykhailo being bundled away somewhere in the distance. I heard him say more than once: 'We are Ukrainian journalists!'
They confiscated all our belongings. A van showed up. They put us in and drove off in an unknown direction. It turned out later to be a detention centre.
The whole time, NO EXPLANATION whatsoever, not even "YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO..." – absolutely nothing, just complete confusion and uncertainty about "what just happened and what comes next". And then: processing at the detention centre.
An examination by the prison medics. That's when I saw the state I was in. I had to spend some time washing the dried blood off my face with an antiseptic, and that's when I noticed a "bump" under my eye. I took a closer look. "There's glass in there," I told the medics. "I think I need medical attention," I continued.
21:30. Taken out of the temporary holding cell, handcuffed behind my back. Into the van. The journey to hospital.
It felt sickening. I was taken from the prison to the hospital to have the glass removed from my face, all while handcuffed behind my back... two police officers walking me through the corridors of a civilian hospital, through crowds of people, like some kind of criminal mastermind.
Frightened children's eyes staring at you :(( and that was just awful. And that was probably the hardest part of this whole ordeal.
Because no matter how hard you try to talk to the police and explain, "I'm not a criminal! I'm not a threat! I'm an investigative journalist from Ukraine! Just look me up online! You'll find everything about me, about us and our work. It's all there – you'll see for yourself and understand"... none of it makes any difference!
And even after the X-ray, when it's time to lie down on the operating table, the doctor looks flustered and says, "Handcuffs behind your back? That's not good!" So I tell the police officers again: "I'm not a threat! I'm not a criminal. I'm a photographer, a cameraman. Believe me. At least take the handcuffs off for the operation." But it's no use.
Facial surgery, right under my eye – with my hands cuffed behind my back.
They got the glass out and stitched me up. I asked to see the fragments. Three pieces of glass. My right arm, cut from the elbow upwards, was treated and bandaged with the kind of adhesive plasters used to close cuts.
Then, still handcuffed, it was back to cell "303", which had strange things scrawled on the walls about Jesus, Allah and "Thieves rule". But the most interesting words were right in front of me, above the cell door: "95 REGION".
Interesting. That reminds me of something.
It echoes something I've seen in Ukraine.
The police questioned me at length. The accusations against me are extremely serious:
- Espionage.
- Working for a foreign intelligence service.
- Conspiring to harm the Austrian state.
I tried to explain the nature of our work and what we'd achieved (right there on the table, among the things they'd seized, was an international award for freedom of speech and for best investigative journalist which we'd just received in Norway). And yet I still had to prove that we weren't criminals.
The Austrian lawyer and the interpreter, Maryna (sorry, I didn't ask her surname), are both true professionals.
And my personal thanks to Consul Yurii for visiting me in the pre-trial detention centre and taking the time to speak with me. When you're in "complete isolation from the outside world", when you have no explanation of "WHAT ON EARTH IS GOING ON?!", that means a great deal. Thank you.
After the interrogation, my lawyer applied for my immediate release from the cell, arguing that I posed no threat. Three police officers, including the chief, clearly understood the situation by then and, after making several calls to the prosecutor, managed to secure my release. Friday evening.
If it hadn't been for that, I'd have spent Saturday and Sunday in cell "303", staring at the door marked "95 region" and doing push-ups – just like in the movies :))
Right, back to work…
	Yaroslav Bondarenko

Editing: Artem Yakymyshyn

Netanyahu promised answers after Oct. 7. Three years later, Israel is still waiting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
14:50:05 UTC
23:50:05 KST

Three years after the October 7 Hamas massacre, Israel has yet to establish a commission of inquiry into the intelligence, military and political failures that allowed the attack to unfold, despite repeated promises by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that those responsible, including himself, would be required to provide answers.
The issue returned to the spotlight this week when retired Maj. Gen. Avi Gil, Netanyahu's former military secretary, gave his first media interview since the massacre. Gil said he would have preferred to provide his account before an official state commission of inquiry rather than in a televised interview.
Netanyahu remains the only senior political or security figure who held a leading position on October 7, 2023, who has not endorsed the establishment of a state commission of inquiry. Former IDF chief Herzi Halevi, former Military Intelligence chief Aharon Haliva, former Shin Bet director Ronen Bar and former defense minister Yoav Gallant have all expressed support for such an investigation.
In the early months of the war, establishing a state commission appeared to command broad political support, including among some Likud lawmakers and ministers. Over time, however, alternative proposals emerged, including a government-appointed panel and a commission whose members would be chosen through an agreement between coalition and opposition representatives.
None of those proposals has resulted in an inquiry.
October 2023: everyone will have to answer
On October 25, 2023, less than three weeks after the massacre, Netanyahu publicly addressed the question of responsibility for the first time.
"The failure will be investigated thoroughly. Everyone will have to provide answers, including me," he declared, calling October 7 a dark day in Israel's history.
But Netanyahu also attached a condition to his promise: the investigation would take place after the war.
That position became a recurring feature of his statements over the following three years. While repeatedly acknowledging the need for an investigation, he delayed its establishment and left open the question of what form it would take.
In January 2024, asked specifically about establishing a state commission of inquiry, Netanyahu said investigations should take place "at the end of the war, certainly not in the middle of it."
He argued that military commanders should not have to spend time consulting lawyers while directing combat operations. He also made clear that the government would determine the appropriate investigative mechanism when the time came.
Under Israeli law, a state commission of inquiry is established by a government decision, but its members are appointed by the president of the Supreme Court. That distinction would become central to the political dispute.
From postponement to a battle over appointments
Throughout 2024, coalition lawmakers began promoting alternatives to a traditional state commission of inquiry, including a government-appointed body or one established with agreement between the coalition and opposition.
Opposition leaders rejected those arrangements, insisting on an independent state commission under the existing law.
President Isaac Herzog also proposed a compromise involving Chief Justice Yitzhak Amit and his deputy, conservative Justice Noam Sohlberg, in forming a state commission. Netanyahu rejected the proposal.
By March 2025, Netanyahu was publicly setting out additional conditions for an investigation.
"It is important and essential to thoroughly investigate everything that happened to us on October 7 and what preceded it," he told the Knesset, calling for an "objective, balanced and independent" commission.
He also warned against establishing a commission "whose conclusions are already known in advance," reflecting his objections to the existing appointment process.
The disagreement was no longer simply about when an investigation would begin. It increasingly concerned who would select the investigators and whether the resulting commission would command sufficient public trust.
In the summer of 2025, after the government informed the Supreme Court that it did not intend to establish a state commission at that stage, Netanyahu again addressed the issue during a closed meeting of the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee.
"I am still trying to understand what happened," he said. "How could they enter here wearing flip-flops and carrying Kalashnikovs? Such a small force. How could this happen? I demand answers. I need answers."
Netanyahu acknowledged that he could have established a government commission earlier but argued that such a body would lack public confidence.
"I could have established a government commission of inquiry yesterday, but it would have no public trust," he said.
He then outlined his preferred alternative: a commission composed of 50% coalition representatives and 50% opposition representatives.
Netanyahu has repeatedly described that model as a commission representing the people. His opponents argue that a politically appointed panel could not provide the independence required to investigate the government's own conduct before and during the massacre.
November 2025: a promise to testify first
In November 2025, Netanyahu again defended his approach during a Knesset debate.
"The question is not only what is investigated. The decisive question is who investigates the truth," he said, arguing that substantial parts of the public would not accept a commission established through the existing mechanism.
He pointed to the bipartisan commission that investigated the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the United States as a possible model.
Netanyahu also pledged to cooperate with the eventual investigation.
"I will be the first to appear and answer every question," he declared.
Legislative efforts followed. In December 2025, lawmakers advanced a proposal for a special inquiry mechanism. In February 2026, Netanyahu reiterated that the State Comptroller's examination of the failures could not replace a dedicated commission and again called for a politically balanced national inquiry.
In July 2026, legislation proposing a state-national commission of inquiry passed its first reading in the Knesset. The bill received 59 votes in favor, with the opposition boycotting the vote.
However, the legislation was not completed before the Knesset was dissolved, leaving the proposed commission without the legal framework required for its establishment.
Three years after the massacre, neither a conventional state commission nor Netanyahu's preferred alternative has begun investigating the events.
The inquiry becomes an election issue
With Israel's October 27 election approaching, the dispute over the October 7 investigation has become a significant political issue.
Opposition leaders, including Gadi Eisenkot, have pledged that establishing a state commission of inquiry under the existing law would be among their first decisions if they form the next government.
Such a move would have precedents in recent Israeli history.
In June 2021, during its first meeting, the government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid approved the establishment of a state commission of inquiry into the Mount Meron disaster, which killed 45 people. The decision came just 52 days after the tragedy, which occurred under Netanyahu's previous government.
In January 2022, the same government approved a state commission of inquiry into the submarine and naval vessels affair, following a proposal by then-defense minister Benny Gantz.
For now, the October 7 investigation remains unresolved. Netanyahu has never withdrawn his promise that the failures would be investigated and that he would answer questions, but his government has not established a commission to carry out that investigation.
As Israel prepares to vote, the central dispute remains the same: not whether October 7 should be investigated, but who will be entrusted with finding the answers.

Andy Burnham reiterated his “complete solidarity” in a call with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders agreed to meet in person in the coming days to continue talks.

“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she said on Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist.
Major European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationships with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine.
The German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions”, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering”.
Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish prime minister, expressed “regret” at the US agreement, saying energy revenues were “a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression”.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia “must feel its losses” and has promised to respond. In the Russian-occupied Luhansk region, Ukrainian attacks in the past 24 hours had killed four civilians and wounded five, the region’s Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said on Saturday.
Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same.
Russia’s fuel production has become a key point of contention between Zelenskyy and Trump, who has attempted to stop Ukraine from bombing Russian refineries, which he says exacerbates a global diesel shortage. The Ukrainian leader has rejected such requests unless Russia stops attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

Germany warns EU that €159B budget cuts are not enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
14:43:21 UTC
23:43:21 KST

Friedrich Merz is pictured during a meeting with the British Prime Minister (not in picture) on October 8, 2026 at the Chancellery in Berlin. | Tobias Schwarz/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Germany and its allies rebuffed Ireland’s plan to downsize the bloc’s next seven-year budget, arguing that the proposed cuts are not enough.
On Saturday, the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the talks, proposed cutting around 8% from the bloc’s total budget from 2028 to 2034 in a bid to assuage a German-led camp demanding reductions of several hundred billions euros.
But Dublin’s hopes of facilitating a deal were immediately dashed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, one the key players in the negotiations as his country contributes to approximately one-quarter of the bloc’s common budget.
Advertisement
“We are still a long way from an agreement. The amount of the new proposal is not a basis for an agreement. The EU budget must be affordable for those who bear the brunt of the financing,” Merz wrote in a statement on Saturday.
Germany leads a group of six “frugal” countries — Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands, Finland and Austria — which contribute 40% of the Union’s common budget.
Most frugal countries criticized Ireland’s proposed €159 billion in cuts in current prices from the Commission’s nearly €2 trillion proposal, saying they were insufficient.
Sweden’s Europe minister Jessica Rosencrantz described the negotiating document, or negobox, on X as a “wildly unaffordable increase,” as the overall amount would still be higher than the current budget.
Austrian Europe Minister Claudia Bauer echoed that criticism, saying that the new budget remained "miles away from an Austrian yes.”
Tensions will come to a head during a summit of EU leaders next Thursday and Friday, where they will discuss the negobox.
Advertisement
EU governments are racing to reach a budget deal among themselves by the end of the year — before elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027 threaten to derail negotiations.
But Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen warned on Saturday that “at this rate, there will be no deal by the end of the year.”
Ireland’s Minister of State for European Affairs Thomas Byrne, who leads the negotiations, dismissed criticism and described the proposal as a balanced compromise.
“The negotiating box acts to bridge the many differences between the Member states,” Byrne told reporters on Saturday.
Divided Union
The EU is split between frugal countries pushing for cuts across the board and a rival camp of southern and eastern states, the Friends of Cohesion, opposing reductions to farmers’ subsidies and regional payouts known as cohesion policy.
Advertisement
These areas account for almost half of the total budget and are politically sensitive because of pressure from farmers' lobbies and regions.
In a concession to the 17 Friends of Cohesion, Ireland left the agriculture and regional budgets untouched and focused cuts on other priorities such as competitiveness, defense and development aid.
“There was a strong support for heading one [agriculture and cohesion] from almost all of the member states, including some of the countries who would be considered to be net contributors” to the budget, Byrne told reporters.
Reactions to the negobox from the Friends of Cohesion were more conciliatory than those of their frugal peers.
“It’s an excellent starting point to have recovered the money for the CAP [Common Agricultural Policy], but we’re still not satisfied,” said Italy’s Agriculture Minister Francesco Lollobrigida.
Poland's Europe minister Ignacy Niemczycki welcomed the fact that his country "continues to receive the largest allocation," but noted that the "change in the overall size of the budget does not match the EU’s ambitions."
The frugals were also are disappointed that the cuts disproportionately target innovative policies such as defense and competitiveness, which they favor.
“They’re cutting the future to protect the past,” said one EU diplomat from the frugal camp.

Major Saudi conferences to proceed despite deadly airport attack
The organisers of two major Saudi energy and investment conferences said their events will go ahead this month and reassured visitors on security, after missile attacks on Riyadh's airport left four people dead and an airliner heavily damaged this week.
The attacks led to widespread flight disruptions, with people taking land routes or circuitous alternative flights. The UK, France and Germany have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh.
Riyadh is sticking to plans to convene global events and trying to draw in investment even amid escalating war with the Iran-backed Houthis in neighbouring Yemen that has seen the kingdom attacked dozens of times over the past weeks.
Organisers of the World Petroleum Congress, set to host top global oil executives and policymakers from Sunday to Thursday, said it would proceed as planned with foreign leaders and ministers in attendance, an email sent to delegates said.
"Your comfort is our priority," it said, noting that alternative routes to Riyadh, including via a four-hour drive from Dammam on the kingdom's eastern coast, were available.
Italian Energy Minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin on Friday said he would not fly to Riyadh for the International Energy Forum Ministerial Meeting, an event on WPC's sidelines, but would participate via video link.
The Future Investment Initiative, launched by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman as the kingdom's flagship investment conference a decade ago, would also proceed as planned from 26-29 October, organisers said.
"Safety and well-being remain our highest priority," a statement attributed to FII CEO Maha Al Saud said.
"Comprehensive security measures will be in place at Riyadh's airports, our conference venues and official hotels, with coordinated arrangements for participants' transportation," it said.
Chief executives of some of the world's biggest financial institutions such as JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon and Citi's Jane Fraser were on the list of expected attendees. Citi and JPMorgan did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group earlier this month.
Germany's Lufthansa has suspended Riyadh flights through 16 October while Gulf carriers Etihad Airways and Flydubai have cancelled flights to and from the Saudi capital scheduled for 10 October.
Saudi Arabia has responded to Houthi attacks with a wave of strikes on missile launcher sites, vowing to protect the kingdom, and says it has intercepted many ballistic missiles fired by the group.

Mexican judge sentences three men for murders of Australian, US surfers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
14:37:26 UTC
23:37:26 KST

Mexican judge sentences three men for murders of Australian, US surfers
The trial in Baja California revealed chilling details of the triple homicide of the surfers.
A Mexican judge found three men guilty of the murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in April 2024 in the Mexican state of Baja California.
The trial for the triple homicide that shocked Mexico and drew international attention concluded Friday after Judge Raul Hernandez in the coastal city of Ensenada ruled that Jesus Gerardo Garcia, alias “El Kekas”, Irineo Francisco “N,” and Angel Jesus “N” were responsible for the murders of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and American Carter Redd Rhoad, 30.
The defendants, who had been in custody for more than two years, were also found guilty of armed robbery and armed carjacking.
“Today’s guilty verdict is a significant moment in our long and painful journey to seek justice for our beautiful sons, Callum and Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad, whose lives were so cruelly taken from them in 2024,” said father Martin Robinson.
The three travelled to Baja California in April 2024 to surf and camped near the coastal city of Ensenada, but shortly after arriving in the town of Punta San Jose, about 80 kilometres (50 miles) from Ensenada, they were reported missing. Their bodies were found on May 3 in a well, all with gunshot wounds to their heads.
Garcia, identified as the perpetrator of the murders, was arrested in May 2024 in connection to the case, along with his ex-partner Ary Gisell Silva Raya, Francisco, and Jesus.
During the monthlong trial, chilling details of the brutal crime were revealed. Silva Raya testified last month during a hearing that Garcia confessed to her that he arrived at the tent where the foreigners were staying with a 9mm pistol.
Upon seeing him, they began throwing their belongings to prevent him from attacking them, and one of them begged for his life, which the assailant ignored, she said.
She said Garcia had bragged about “how beautifully” the victims cried and about items he robbed from them.
The state prosecutor’s office reported that Silva Raya arrived in Punta San Jose on April 27, 2024, where she met the three foreigners and “instigated one of her companions to rob them”, which they did the following day.
The woman, who was found in possession of one of the victims’ cellphones, was sentenced in November 2025 to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to “aggravated robbery with violence” and “vehicle theft with violence” in an expedited proceeding. However, Garcia and his two accomplices decided to go to trial.
Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists.
The judge will announce the final sentence on October 16. The Baja California State Attorney General’s Office requested for each defendant the “exemplary sentence” of 210 years in prison.
“No outcome can ever undo this tragedy, but we hope today marks an important step towards justice and allows us to continue honoring their lives and the extraordinary young men they were,” said Martin Robinson. “They will never be forgotten.”
