The electoral threshold is distorting Israel's democracy - time to rethink it - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Israel should take another look at its electoral threshold.
The logic behind raising it to 3.25% in 2014 was hardly absurd. Israel once had a threshold of just 1%, meaning tiny factions could enter the Knesset and exercise influence wildly disproportionate to their support.
In a 120-seat parliament where 61 seats make a government, a faction representing a sliver of the electorate could become indispensable to a coalition and extract an extraordinary price for its support. In 2014, the Knesset raised the threshold from 2% to 3.25%, with proponents arguing that consolidation would reduce fragmentation and improve governability.
Politics also played a role. Critics argued that the change was aimed partly at making it harder for small Arab parties to enter the Knesset.
The result was almost comically counterproductive: the Arab parties united and performed better than ever, with four parties joining forces in response to the higher threshold and creating the Joint List, which won 13 seats in 2015 and became the Knesset’s third-largest faction.
The threshold had produced precisely the consolidation its supporters advertised, although perhaps among the last parties some of those supporters wished to strengthen.
Then came 2022, and the other side of the experiment became impossible to ignore.
Former prime minister Yair Lapid pleaded with Labor leader Merav Michaeli to run together with Meretz. Both parties were perilously close to the threshold, and Lapid understood the arithmetic. Michaeli refused.
She believed the two parties would perform better separately, while Meretz leader Zehava Galon favored an agreement. Michaeli rejected incentives offered by Lapid to facilitate a joint run, and the decision became one of the great electoral miscalculations in recent Israeli history.
Meretz received 150,696 votes, or 3.16%, and fell just 4,124 votes short of entering the Knesset. Balad, running separately from the other Arab parties, received another 138,093 votes, about 2.9%.
Together, the two parties collected 288,789 votes, more than 6% of all valid ballots and the raw-vote equivalent of more than seven Knesset seats.
The consequences were enormous. Netanyahu’s four-party bloc emerged with 64 seats against 56 for everyone else, an apparently decisive victory.
Yet the underlying vote was remarkably close. The Likud-Religious Zionist Party-Shas-United Torah Judaism bloc (plus another party that failed by a wide margin to cross the threshold) received 2,360,757 votes, while the eight parties against him received 2,330,464, including the votes for Meretz and Balad that yielded no representation.
The precise counterfactual depends on which parties had combined and how surplus-vote agreements played out, but the central fact is extraordinary: an electorate divided almost evenly – indeed with a tiny majority opposing Netanyahu’s coalition – produced a 64-56 Knesset in his favor.
Exactly what would have happened under a different threshold is impossible to know, because changing it affects more than Meretz. One post-election analysis found that if Meretz alone had crossed 3.25%, Netanyahu’s bloc probably would still have won 61 or 62 seats.
Pollster Dudi Chassid calculated that a Labor-Meretz merger combined with a reunited Joint List including Balad could instead have reduced it to 60, while Israel Democracy Institute modeling found another plausible combination that produced only 59 for Netanyahu, meaning Lapid would have stayed in power.
Instead, Netanyahu took office with an eight-seat majority. Within days, Justice Minister Yariv Levin unveiled the judicial overhaul, beginning an effort to shift power dramatically toward the elected government.
Israel plunged into months of demonstrations and an extraordinary constitutional confrontation over the power of a parliamentary majority and the institutional restraints upon it. To critics like me, Netanyahu was trying to “Putinize” Israel.
A few thousand votes therefore helped separate radically different political outcomes. That degree of distortion deserves scrutiny in any democracy, and especially in Israel, where elections routinely produce closely divided blocs and the consequences of a handful of seats can be profound.
The irony is that the threshold has delivered only a limited version of its promised benefit. Individual legislators can still destabilize governments when they are sufficiently determined to defy their parties.
The 2020 election illustrated the problem. Benny Gantz had a potential route to a 62-member majority involving his own bloc, with outside support from the Arab Joint List.
That route collapsed when individual lawmakers, including Orly Levy-Abekasis (who ran with the Labor Party and Meretz) and Blue and White members Yoaz Hendel and Zvi Hauser, refused to support a government dependent on the Joint List.
The larger parties produced by Israel’s electoral system therefore failed to prevent a tiny number of legislators from exercising exactly the kind of leverage that the threshold was supposed to diminish.
The Bennett-Lapid government demonstrated the point even more dramatically. In April 2022, coalition whip Idit Silman left the coalition, immediately reducing Bennett’s 61-member coalition to 60 seats and depriving it of its majority. Amichai Chikli, another Yamina MK – currently Diaspora affairs and combatting antisemitism minister – had already rebelled against the coalition shortly after it was established.
Then came Meretz MK Ghaida Rinawie Zoabi. In May, she announced that she was leaving the coalition, temporarily reducing the government to just 59 seats.
Three days later, after intense political pressure, she reversed herself and returned. One legislator had briefly placed the government on the brink of collapse.
This is precisely the phenomenon the threshold was supposed to ameliorate. Basically, it cannot be fully eliminated: in the United States, one senator’s vote can scuttle appointments and legislation and – in extraordinary circumstances – remove a president.
There is still a case for some threshold. It discourages vanity parties, encourages alliances and makes it harder for every ambitious politician with a personal following to establish a one-person parliamentary faction.
Yet the benefit has proved much smaller than advertised, while the potential cost is enormous. Hundreds of thousands of citizens can cast perfectly valid votes in a national election and receive zero parliamentary representation.
Meanwhile, individual MKs retain ample ability to threaten governments, defect from coalitions and transform the parliamentary arithmetic.
Israel therefore has reason to reconsider the entire design rather than treating 3.25% as some scientifically determined democratic sweet spot.
Raising threshold for entering Knesset
One option would be to lower the threshold dramatically, accepting greater fragmentation in exchange for greater proportionality and ensuring that almost every significant body of voters receives representation.
Another would be to move decisively in the opposite direction, perhaps toward 5%, creating such a formidable barrier that political camps would have overwhelming incentives to consolidate before Election Day rather than gamble with their voters’ representation.
This would presumably have prevented Michaeli’s catastrophic miscalculation.
Under such circumstances, fewer voters would risk small parties, reducing their support further. The cost there would be a smaller diversity of views on the party level.
Either approach has drawbacks. At least each follows a coherent principle.
The current threshold occupies an uncomfortable middle ground, and it is not working.
The writer is a former Cairo-based Middle East editor and London-based Europe/Africa editor of the Associated Press. He served as chairman of the Foreign Press Association in Jerusalem and authored two books about Israel.

New York Times report on AIPAC hides a central truth about Israel’s unpopularity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

At first glance, that recent New York Times article on AIPAC, the wealthy pro-Israel lobbying organization, may have looked promising. It ran on the front page of the Sunday print edition, the week’s most prominent location. It jumped inside, where it covered nearly an entire page. It was 53 paragraphs long. The byline indicated that 4 Times reporters had worked on the article.
But, astonishingly, not a single one of those 53 paragraphs explained that AIPAC’s efforts to influence American elections have changed dramatically in recent years. These days, the organization often actually hides its pro-Israel views, even though promoting Israel is the only reason it exists in the first place. Instead, it dumps money into political campaigns and frequently raises issues that have absolutely no connection to Israel and Palestine.
Let’s take, for example, the Democratic primary earlier this year for the House seat in New Jersey’s 13th Congressional district. AIPAC decided to target Tom Malinowski, a former congressman who had the temerity to mildly suggest that military aid to Israel should be “conditioned” on its human rights record. This site’s estimable Michael Arria succinctly explained how AIPAC acted:
“Of course, AIPAC can’t actually run ads telling Democratic voters to reject Malinowski for being sufficiently pro-Israel as the [Democratic] base has completely soured on the country, and lobbying groups supporting that relationship.
“So, the AIPAC-funded [television] ads attack Malinowski for allegedly supporting Trump’s immigration policies. The allegation stems from a 2019 vote, in which that year Congress passed a funding bill that included money for law enforcement at the southern border. Most Democrats, including Malinowski, backed the package.”
(In that race, AIPAC’s strategy backfired. It dumped $2 million into TV ads attacking Malinowski — which apparently damaged him enough so that Analilia Mejia, who is even more progressive on Israel/Palestine, won the Democratic primary, and is presently in Congress.)
AIPAC’s new stealth strategy was by no means a secret. Both Politico and MS Now covered the New Jersey race, and revealed the Israel lobby’s behind the scenes maneuvering.
AIPAC deployed the same stealth strategy in August, when it helped defeat progressive former Rep. Cori Bush’s effort to win back her seat in Missouri’s Democratic primary. The pro-Israel lobby had already helped her opponent, Wesley Bell, two years before. This time around, AIPAC’s ads sidestepped Israel again, and instead emphasized Bush’s alleged missed votes in Congress and her supposed criticism of the Biden administration.
So: how did 4 NYTimes reporters, who were handed 53 paragraphs of space, miss this vital Stealth AIPAC angle? How did the echelon of editors who reviewed the report also fail to do anything? The only plausible explanations are institutional bias and conscious whitewashing and self-censorship.
There’s another side to the AIPAC story that the long Times article also “missed.” Once upon a time, AIPAC held gigantic annual conferences in Washington, D.C, at which politicians from both parties came to genuflect. Up to 18,000 people attended. Sometimes even foreign leaders flew in to display their pro-Israel bona fides.
But then, starting in 2021, AIPAC canceled the annual confabs. Since then, nothing. Surely, any survey of AIPAC today should have included this telling fact. But — in 53 paragraphs — 4 New York Times reporters reported nothing.

In return, he accepted money and property worth 60.5 million yuan, the verdict noted.
The court said Zhou received a lenient sentence because he truthfully confessed to his crimes and disclosed additional bribery facts previously unknown to investigators, while some of the bribery offenses were attempted rather than being completed. He had also pleaded guilty, expressed remorse, and actively returned what he received in bribes, with most of the illegal money and property already recovered, the ruling said.
The court stated that these circumstances warranted leniency in sentencing.
The case was heard publicly on July 9.
China's top anti-graft agency announced the decision to expel Zhou from the Communist Party of China and dismiss him from public office in January 2026. ■

Chen Qun, UNESCO assistant director-general for education, speaks at the award ceremony of the 2026 UNESCO Prize for Girls' and Women's Education in Paris, France, on Oct. 9, 2026. PARIS, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- The projects from Morocco and Peru became the laureates of the 2026 UNESCO Prize for Girls' and Women's Education in Paris on Friday.
One of the 2026 laureates, Project Soar, was recognized for its Project Soar in a Bag initiative, which helps underserved adolescent girls in Morocco and beyond stay in school and shape their futures. Since 2017, the initiative has reached more than 8,000 adolescent girls across five countries.
CARE Peru was recognized for its "Girls with Opportunities" project, which helps rural and Indigenous adolescent girls complete secondary education and build pathways to further study and decent work. Since 2016, the initiative has benefited more than 37,000 rural girls aged 14 to 19.
Speaking at the award ceremony, UNESCO Director-General Khaled El-Enany said the winning projects were helping advance gender equality through concrete actions and demonstrating that when girls are given opportunities, support and confidence to shape their own futures, they become powerful agents of change for their families, their communities and their societies. He also thanked China for its continued support for the prize and UNESCO's efforts to promote education.
The ceremony was held ahead of the International Day of the Girl Child, observed on Oct. 11. Chen Qun, UNESCO assistant director-general for education, said that 133 million girls worldwide remained out of school, while women accounted for nearly two-thirds of all adults unable to read.
He stressed the need to use evidence to understand where inequalities persist and why, and to turn successful approaches into lasting change. Advancing gender equality in and through education is central to UNESCO's mandate, he added.
Ren Youqun, China's vice minister of education, said at an event following the ceremony that education is far more than access to knowledge: it opens doors, creates opportunities and empowers every person to realize their full potential. When girls and women are empowered through education, families flourish, communities grow stronger and entire societies prosper, he added.
On the same day, UNESCO organized a roundtable discussion on the gender-focused component of its 2026 Global Education Monitoring Report.
Since China established the prize in cooperation with UNESCO in 2015, the award has continued to exert a positive impact and received extensive attention and high recognition from the international community. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Justice on Saturday announced the launch of a public database of foreign-related legal resources for Chinese enterprises and citizens, including Chinese translations of foreign laws and representative cases involving foreign-related matters.
The database, "LexCom," began operating fully on Saturday, following a pilot that started in July, the ministry said.
It currently contains more than 1,500 entries of legal resources covering 187 countries, and over 1,800 Chinese laws, regulations and rules concerning foreign matters, Zheng Wei, a ministry official responsible for foreign-related legal affairs, told a media conference in Beijing.
"Our research shows that enterprises and citizens have a strong demand for high-quality foreign-related legal resources and easy access to laws and regulations concerning foreign-related matters, foreign laws, and representative cases involving enterprises expanding overseas," Zheng said.
According to Zheng, users can also submit inquiries on foreign-related matters through the database website, which provides either AI-generated answers based on searches of its resources or responses from a team of legal professionals working with the platform.
The launch of LexCom is part of China's endeavor to promote foreign-related legal services for its enterprises and citizens, and to protect its national interests in general, according to Vice Minister of Justice Wu Yanjun.
Wu noted at the news conference that China has also been encouraging its law firms to broaden their overseas service networks and support the development of international commercial arbitration centers.
"China is gradually emerging as a new destination for international commercial arbitration," he said, adding that Beijing, Shenzhen and Shanghai are now among the world's most preferred arbitration seats.
According to a new set of regulations issued by China's State Council, which took effect on July 1 this year, professional providers of consulting and evaluation services, legal services, accounting and auditing, credit rating, mediation and arbitration, and intellectual property services are encouraged to improve their international service capabilities and provide high-quality professional services.
Investors are also encouraged to resolve disputes related to overseas investment through negotiation, mediation, arbitration, litigation and other means to safeguard their lawful rights and interests, as stated in the regulations. ■

Explainer: How is Panama faring after a powerful earthquake, aftershocks?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
21:26:18 CST
22:26:18 KST

PANAMA CITY, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- A powerful earthquake and a series of strong aftershocks rattled Panama on Friday, causing damage to buildings and roads and prompting evacuations across the country.
As of 8 p.m. local time Friday (0100 GMT Saturday), Panama's National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC) said in its second bulletin that 27 people had been injured.
THE QUAKE
According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), the initial earthquake was centered on the Azuero Peninsula in south-central Panama, about 40 km from Tonosi, a town in Los Santos province, and 60 km from Santiago, the capital of Veraguas province and a regional transport and commercial hub. The epicenter lies in a largely rural area with a sparse population.
The USGS initially reported the earthquake at magnitude 8, then revised it to 7.6 and later to 7.7. Multiple aftershocks continued to rattle Panama, with seismologists at the University of Panama recording more than 45.
Despite the strength of the successive quakes, Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino said authorities had not documented anyone killed by Friday evening, though he cautioned that could change in the coming hours or days.
Mulino said the entire government had been mobilized for the response, and that he had ordered agencies to promptly report the earthquake's effects and deploy personnel, resources and aid to affected communities.
"The disaster we are facing is severe," Mulino told reporters when visiting Penonome in Cocle province to assess the damage, adding that some roads had been destroyed and urging residents to remain calm and follow instructions from SINAPROC.
IMPACTS
Health Minister Fernando Boyd said Cocle, Los Santos and Herrera were among the hardest-hit provinces.
Buildings partially collapsed in Penonome and cracks appeared in roads, while in Los Santos province, the Church of San Atanasio, a colonial-style Catholic church declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938, had collapsed, according to local reports.
The USGS estimated economic losses could amount to 1-10 percent of Panama's GDP, and electricity provider Naturgy reported power outages in six provinces.
Tocumen International Airport in Panama City, one of the region's busiest airports, temporarily suspended operations after the first quake but reopened Friday afternoon. Meanwhile, the Panama Canal Authority said canal operations remained normal, adding that it had activated emergency procedures and begun inspecting facilities.
SEISMIC RISKS
Earthquakes are common in Panama, particularly near its border with Costa Rica and along its Pacific coast, due to the interaction of several tectonic plates, including the Cocos, Nazca and Caribbean plates.
Panama also lies along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a zone of frequent earthquakes and volcanic activity surrounding the Pacific Basin.
Carlos Valdes, head of the Seismology Department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, said Panama's relatively low death toll compared with other Latin American countries may be attributable to its strict building codes, particularly those governing high-rise construction in the capital.
The earthquake came just three days before Panama was scheduled to hold a national evacuation drill for dealing with a major earthquake. ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: One seed, a shared harvest: China-Pakistan agricultural cooperation bears fruit
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
21:26:17 CST
22:26:17 KST

WUHAN, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- In the summer of 2003, Zhu Xiaobo, an agricultural technician from central China's Wuhan city, landed in Pakistan with two suitcases of hybrid rice seeds and an electronic dictionary that cannot produce sound.
She spoke little English, nor the regional language, Urdu, and of the 38 seed companies she had emailed before her departure, only a family business run by Tahar Salimi in northeastern Pakistan's Lahore did not brush her off.
After three days of fruitless door-knocking visits, Zhu climbed into the car of Salimi, a man she barely knew, and took a six-hour drive to his farm. "We could not understand each other at that time," she recalled.
Unable to explain what hybrid rice was, Zhu sketched out the growing process: sowing, transplanting, fertilizing and harvesting. Salimi's brother, a farmer-turned-businessman, scrutinized the drawings and nodded. But by then, the sowing season had all but ended.
"I kept telling him, 'You must plant them. If you plant them, there is still hope,'" said Zhu, now general manager of Wuhan Qingfa Hesheng Agricultural Development Co., Ltd. Moved by her courage, Salimi decided to try the hybrid rice.
Even after Zhu's return, she emailed Salimi frequently, reminding him when to apply fertilizer and pesticide, and how to look after the paddy.
The gamble paid off. Yields came in 40 percent to 50 percent higher than those of many local varieties, and experts from Pakistan's rice research center described the panicles as "a huge surprise."
The partnership later registered Pakistan's first commercialized hybrid rice variety, QY0413, drawing in a host of Chinese seed companies.
According to Zhu, Chinese seeds now account for over 90 percent of Pakistan's hybrid rice seed market, and Pakistan has risen to become the fourth-largest rice exporter in the world. Hundreds of thousands of farmers also saw their incomes grow.
Since 2010, the firm has sent staff members to Pakistan, training farmers in everything from seed soaking to pest control. Among them is Su Zhongxiang, formerly deputy director of an agricultural research institute in Hubei, China's major rice-producing province.
"Selling seeds is not enough," Su said. "We should also provide after-sales services, going directly into farmers' fields and solving problems."
In 2007, Zhu's team turned its attention to rapeseed, aiming to cut Pakistan's reliance on imported edible oil. Pakistan imports most of its cooking oil, largely palm oil from Southeast Asia.
Developing suitable rapeseed varieties proved far harder than breeding rice. Pakistan has a warmer climate, which causes crops to mature very fast. "The plants look great, but you get empty seed pods after harvest," Zhu said.
After repeated failures in more than a decade, the company successfully registered a new variety of rapeseed in 2019.
For Zhu, agricultural cooperation requires more than simply applying Chinese planting methods overseas. "Technology, services, and management must all be localized," she said.
As the two countries mark the 75th anniversary of diplomatic relations, younger generations are injecting fresh blood into the relay of China-Pakistan agricultural cooperation.
Zhang Ao, a 23-year-old molecular biology master's graduate, spent more than two months visiting farms in Pakistan's Lahore, Gujranwala, and Multan shortly after joining Qingfa Hesheng. He studied how Chinese crop varieties performed under local soil and climatic conditions.
The experience taught him what international agricultural cooperation means. "People there were very friendly to Chinese," Zhang said. "You are not only representing yourself, but also your country."
During his stay, Zhang met local people his age, who were eager to talk about artificial intelligence, Chinese electric vehicles, and technological development. "They talked with me about DeepSeek and BYD," Zhang said. "And they see 'made in China' as a label for affordable, good-quality goods."
For Zhu, exchanges such as these are what make agricultural cooperation meaningful. Gesturing toward a company slogan on the wall, Zhu said, "One seed can change the world. I have no doubt about it." ■

Xinhua Commentary: Dialogue, not harsh rhetoric, drives progress in China-EU trade ties
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
21:26:07 CST
22:26:07 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- China and the European Union (EU) made pragmatic progress in resolving trade differences at high-level talks in Beijing, reflecting the willingness and wisdom of both sides to promote the stable development of bilateral economic and trade relations through dialogue and consultation.
Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic wrapped up the two-day second trade and investment consultation meeting on Friday, securing 16 consensus points covering trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization (WTO) reform.
Despite some harsh voices from the European side calling for more protectionist measures, the two sides pledged to explore WTO-compliant tariff cuts for certain goods and reached an understanding on hybrid vehicle trade, a looming trade concern from the European side.
The developments underscore the value of equal, pragmatic dialogue in stabilizing the world's two major economic powers' trade ties, which carry far-reaching global implications. A stable and healthy China-EU economic and trade relationship not only benefits businesses and people in both China and the EU and serves the common interests of both sides, but also injects certainty and positive energy into global economic growth and the stability of industrial and supply chains.
As key trade partners, China and the EU bear shared responsibilities for upholding free trade and multilateralism. Rooted in complementarity and mutual benefit, China-EU economic and trade relations can achieve a dynamic balance through development. The popularity of China-made air-conditioners in Europe this summer illustrated the complementary and mutually beneficial nature of China-EU trade.
The EU has regarded its trade deficit with China as a major concern. However, China has never deliberately sought a trade surplus with trading partners. China's export growth stems both from its economies of scale and enhanced innovation capacity, and from the demand arising from green transition and industrial development in various countries.
Trade surpluses are actually a result of the global division of labor, and supply and demand patterns. In recent years, the growth of China's exports to Europe has been mainly driven by photovoltaic devices, new energy vehicles, lithium-ion batteries and chemical products, which reflects how the green transition has fueled the demand for such products.
Furthermore, intermediate goods account for around half of China's exports to Europe, helping European companies reduce the costs of finished products and sharpen their competitiveness.
Industrial headwinds facing parts of the EU economy stem from structural problems within the 27-member bloc, not from China. However, China can serve as a partner in solving them.
Notably, Chinese companies are investing in production and innovation in European countries. Official statistics show that China's direct investment in the EU more than doubled in 2025, reaching 12.17 billion U.S. dollars.
Chinese corporate investment has boosted local industrial upgrading and job creation across Europe. After its factory in Germany started production at the end of 2022, Chinese battery giant CATL began trial battery cells production at its Hungary plant in September this year. Chinese carmaker Chery has also partnered with Spanish brand Ebro to revive production at a former Nissan plant in Barcelona.
Prior to the consultations in Beijing, France and Germany proposed strengthening the bloc's trade instruments. But interdependence is not a risk, and convergent interests are not a threat.
"Building walls and barriers" cannot boost competitiveness. On the contrary, tariffs may weaken the incentive for protected industries to innovate while increasing costs for businesses, eroding their competitiveness.
A more balanced China-EU trade relationship should be achieved by expanding trade and investment for both sides, rather than blocking the flow of goods. To reduce the trade imbalance requires efforts from both sides, not from China alone. Sustained dialogue and strategic patience are also vital for this lasting progress.
The China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism provides an institutionalized platform. The two successive meetings since June have demonstrated that sustained dialogue can bear fruit. Both sides have agreed to hold the third meeting next March and maintain close communication in the meantime, including through a ministerial video conference next January.
Against a backdrop of global economic uncertainty and complex international geopolitics, closer communication, enhanced mutual trust and expanded cooperation between China and the EU have grown more critical than ever. Both sides should ensure the implementation of the relevant outcomes and consensus, and work together with a strategic and long-term vision to strive for stable and more balanced economic and trade relations. ■

====================================================================================================

New large docodont fossil sheds light on Jurassic mammaliaform diversity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
21:26:05 CST
22:26:05 KST

This picture shows a restored image of Megacauda sungei. (Shenyang Normal University/Handout via Xinhua)
SHENYANG, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- An international team led by Chinese scientists has discovered a new docodont mammaliaform species, the largest known of its kind, in Jurassic strata dating back about 160 million years, enriching scientific understanding of Jurassic mammaliaform diversity.
The new species has been named Megacauda sungei. Its fossil specimen, discovered in Ningcheng, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, measures roughly 52 centimeters in length and is estimated to have weighed around 2 kilograms, making it the largest known docodont mammaliaform. Its skull is clearly preserved, its trunk is robust, and its most striking feature is an unusually long, coiled tail.
The specimen also retains well-preserved pelvic bones, hind limbs and tail vertebrae, suggesting it was adapted for swimming. Based on its distinctive teeth, researchers believe it could have hunted small animals living in the same environment, with a lifestyle possibly similar to that of the modern platypus.
The study also sheds light on the animal's throat structure. The bones in its throat are similar to those of modern mammals, suggesting that behaviors such as swallowing, lapping and suckling may have already existed in the early ancestors of mammals, long before modern mammal groups appeared.
"Mammaliaforms from the Mesozoic are often imagined as tiny creatures under dinosaur feet, but Megacauda sungei clearly raises the size limit of this group," said Li Yikun, an associate professor at Shenyang Normal University in northeast China.
The study was published online in the journal Nature on Oct. 7. ■

High silver prices threaten Lucknow’s famed bridal nagra craft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:25:35 UTC
22:25:35 KST

In Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh and a city known for its Nawabi heritage and artisanship, 55-year-old Azhar Hussain sits at the bench where he has spent years making decorative footwear. His tools are still there, but the customers are not. Amid soaring silver prices over the past year, demand for his work has plummeted.
The small workshop sits beside Chowk Bazaar, one of Old Lucknow’s oldest and busiest markets, a famed hub for wedding shopping full of silver jewellery and handcrafts.
For three decades, Hussain has been one of the bazaar’s busiest craftsmen, making a distinctive form of silver slip-on shoes, known locally as nagras.
He starts by cutting a thin silver sheet into the outline of a nagra, then sketches floral and leaf motifs onto the metal. Hussain then rests the sheet on heated lac, a soft natural resin that cushions the metal while he uses a hammer and engraving tool to tap intricate designs into place.
Hussain then bends the silver around a foot-shaped furma, or mould, before fitting it over a base of cardboard, rubber and velvet, soldering the pieces together and polishing the pair. Craftsmen have used this process to make silver nagras since the 1600s.
Originally, the decorative shoes were made for daily use by the Nawabi, Muslim rulers of the former kingdom of Awadh.
“Silver nagras used to be the most important part of a nawab’s attire,” said 68-year-old Nawab Masud Abdullah, an eighth-generation descendant of Nawab Muhammad Ali Shah, the ninth Nawab of Awadh, who ruled from 1837 until he died in 1842.
“They were not just footwear; they represented our culture and heritage,” he added.
Once reserved exclusively for Nawabs, silver nagras have become a cherished wedding tradition over the last century, embraced by Lucknow’s middle and upper classes alike.
“Our forefathers wore silver nagras every day. Later, they became reserved for celebrations and eventually only for special occasions,” Abdullah explained. “The good thing was that the tradition spread beyond the Nawabs. People, particularly brides across Lucknow, embrace it as their own and now a bride is considered incomplete without a nagra.”
Hussain and his family of craftsmen have seen this transformation firsthand.
“In the past, only Nawabs could afford these shoes because they symbolised wealth, power and status,” he said. “But over the last seven or eight decades, they became popular among middle-class and wealthy families too, especially for weddings and special occasions.”
There are two types of silver nagras — open-toed chappals and closed-toed jutis, and customers can choose different patterns, ornamentation and designs.
Lucrative trade vanishes
Hussain’s family has been making nagras since the early 1900s and the trade has provided a comfortable living. Before each wedding season, he has typically made about 10 pairs a month, he says, with each priced between $105 and $230 (10,000 and 22,000 rupees).
“We lived with dignity,” he said quietly. “We earned enough to feed our family, educate our children and save a little every month. We never imagined that one day we would struggle even to run our household.”
Over the past year, however, the orders have vanished with the rise in silver prices. The metal was already costing a bit more before the U.S.-Iran war launched in February, owing to tight supplies and growing investor demand. But the conflict added another jolt, as uncertainty in global markets drove investors towards silver and put the metal — and the nagras — out of reach for many Lucknow shoppers.
War-driven price rises
Prices for precious metals actually began rising with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine back in early 2022, but economists say prices surged significantly with the US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
In 2023, silver prices in India largely fluctuated between $725 (70,000 rupees) and $830 (80,000 rupees) per kilogramme, rising to around $985 (98,000 rupees) in 2024. But this year, amid the conflict with Iran, silver prices briefly soared as high as $4,670 (450,000 rupees) per kg before easing after the ceasefire. Even now, after some decline, prices are hovering around $2,600 (250,000 rupees) per kg, more than three times their levels just a few years ago.
Dr. Salahuddin Ayyub, an economist and international trade expert with India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, said geopolitical conflicts have triggered unprecedented volatility in global commodity markets.
“When stock markets become volatile, investors move their money into safer assets, such as gold and silver,” Ayyub explained. “This sudden surge in demand pushes the prices of precious metals sharply upwards.”
The consequences have been particularly severe in India, he said, because gold and silver remain deeply intertwined with weddings, other cultural traditions and family savings. As prices continue to rise, many households are increasingly opting for lower-cost alternatives, such as artificial jewellery.
He warned that while consumers may find substitutes, those whose livelihoods depend on the precious metals industry, including artisans, silversmiths, jewellery shopkeepers and traditional craftsmen, have far fewer options.
“The impact extends well beyond consumers,” Ayyub said. “Entire communities whose incomes depend on these metals are now facing shrinking demand and growing economic uncertainty.”
The surge in silver prices has had another consequence that is often overlooked by the government and policymakers. According to Ayyub, when a country witnesses a sharp rise in demand for imported precious metals, governments often intervene to curb imports and protect their foreign exchange reserves.
“India depends heavily on imported silver. A sudden spike in imports puts pressure on the country’s foreign exchange reserves, so the government tries to discourage excessive imports through tariffs and other restrictions,” Ayyub said.
These import duties are eventually passed on to consumers. “As tariffs increase, the landed cost of silver rises. That is one of the reasons why silver prices in India are currently trading above global prices,” he said.
Globally, silver currently costs $2,100 (201,000 rupees) per kg, but in India, it’s more than 20 percent higher because of heavy government import taxes and strict licensing that chokes off supply. India depends on imports to meet more than 80% of its domestic silver demand and its purchases account for over 20 percent of the global trade in refined silver.
India more than doubled its effective import taxes on gold and silver in May. That saw silver imports plunge by 87 percent to just $75.6 million that month, down from $566.2 million the previous year, the country’s lowest level in over three years.
High silver prices are now forcing Lucknow’s brides to make tough, sometimes devastating, decisions.
Bridal choices
For 28-year-old Lucknow resident Uzma Siddique, who is set to marry in December, owning and wearing a pair of silver nagras on her big day has always topped her wedding wishlist.
“My mother wore silver nagras at her wedding in 1992. So did my grandmother and so did my great-grandmother,” Siddique said. “I always imagined myself wearing them and taking my wedding photographs in them and posting them on Instagram. It was never just footwear; it was an emotion and a family tradition.”
But when she visited the market with plans to order a pair, the prices stunned her.
“A pair that cost around $156 to $208 (15,000 to 20,000 rupees) just a few years ago is now selling for nearly $673 (65,000 rupees),” she said.
Determined to have a pair, she decided to give up on other wedding luxuries instead.
“I had to cut back on many other wedding expenses. I bought a lighter lehenga (long skirt), reduced the number of suits I planned to purchase, and trimmed my budget in several places, just so I could afford these nagras.”
Despite the financial strain, she says giving up the footwear tradition was never an option.
“They have become incredibly expensive, but our emotions are attached to them. That’s why I still bought them,” she said.
But many of her friends have had to go without.
“Some had dreamed of wearing silver nagras on their wedding day, but they had to let go of that dream because they simply couldn’t afford them. They are deeply hurt by it,” she said.
Not far from Siddique’s home lives her friend, 25-year-old Safiya Khan, who is also getting married in December. Unlike Siddique, Safiya has not been able to buy silver nagras for her wedding.
From a lower middle-class family, she says soaring prices put upholding that tradition out of reach.
“My entire wedding shopping budget is around $1,250 (120,000 rupees). I simply cannot spend more than half of it on a pair of shoes,” Khan said, noting that she was sad to end the family tradition.
“I think this tradition will end with my generation,” she said. “My mother had a pair of silver nagras, but she had to sell them last year because of financial difficulties. We always believed we would buy another pair for my wedding. Had we known silver prices would rise so dramatically, we would never have sold them.”
She has been shocked by how a distant war has so negatively affected this beloved local tradition.
“I know the recent conflicts have pushed silver prices higher, but I never imagined that a war thousands of km away could take away a tradition so close to my heart,” she said. “I had always dreamed of taking my wedding photographs in silver nagras. Now that dream will never come true.”
Silver memories
Naseem Jahan, a Lucknow resident in her late seventies, still treasures the pair of silver chappals her mother gave her for her wedding in 1972.
“I remember my mother paid around $2.50 (250 rupees) for this pair,” Jahan recalled. “We had to wait nearly seven months after placing the order before it was finally ready. Those were beautiful days.”
More than five decades later, the silver slippers remain one of her most cherished possessions. She has them polished every three years and proudly wears them to weddings and other important family gatherings, as do many of the older women in Lucknow.
“Every time I wear them, people come to admire them and praise their beauty. That makes me so happy,” she said with a smile.
But Jahan fears the tradition may not continue into the next generation.
“Today, very few people can afford such footwear,” she said.
When she recently visited the market to buy a similar pair for her granddaughter, the soaring price of silver made it unaffordable.
Still, she wants her granddaughter to have traditional bridal footwear, so she has made a tough decision.
“I have decided to gift her my own pair,” she said. “Let these slippers adorn her feet now. I want them to continue their journey.”
As the only precious keepsake she has preserved from her wedding, Jahan knows how connected brides feel to the shoes.
“I have developed an emotional bond with them. They remind me of my mother, my wedding day and the Lucknow I grew up in. I only wish silver prices would come down again so that more people could experience this tradition.”
Jahan’s decision to part with her silver nagras will keep a pair in her family, but it will not bring new work to the craftsmen who once made the footwear for Lucknow’s brides. In Chowk Bazaar, dwindling demand has left many artisans facing the prospect of a trade that may not survive long enough to serve the next generation.
A dying breed
Jabbar Hussain, 48, a fourth-generation craftsman and shopkeeper who makes nagras and sells them in his shop, sits in his empty store in Lucknow’s Chowk Bazaar, struggling to understand what has happened to a business that once flourished.
Between June and September, Hussain’s shop would normally be crowded with customers placing orders for nagras. But over the past three months, Hussain says, he has not sold a single pair. He blames the unprecedented rise in silver prices for making the handmade footwear a luxury few can now afford.
“A pair that once sold for around $125 (12,000 rupees) now costs between $622 and $778 (60,000 and 75,000 rupees) because silver has become so expensive,” he said. “People still walk into the shop, admire the craftsmanship and ask about the price. But the moment they hear it, they quietly leave. Every customer who walks away feels like another piece of our family's future disappearing.”
Hussain, like others before him, now fears he will be forced to close his shop.
“There were nearly 30 of us not long ago,” he said. “Most have already abandoned the profession because silver has become too expensive and orders have dried up. Those who are still here are also thinking of leaving.”
He is now thinking of taking a loan to open a cafe, which he hopes will provide a steady income. “I need to find another way to earn,” he said.
Hussain had hoped to teach the craft to his sons so they could carry forward the family’s legacy, but now he is advising them to pursue other professions. He no longer sees a future in the silver nagras trade and blames the war in the Middle East.
“We have nothing to do with this war, yet we are paying the price,” he said, frustrated at how a conflict so far away has threatened his livelihood. “I don’t know what our future looks like anymore. Sometimes I think about what will happen to this craft and I cry. This wasn’t just our profession; it was our identity, our heritage and everything we were known for.”
Little relief in sight
Still, Hussain clings to the hope that silver prices will decline and orders will return. Economists and market analysts are less optimistic.
Ayyub said silver prices are expected to remain above $2,085 per (200,000 rupees) kg for the foreseeable future because once precious metal prices rise sharply, they rarely fall significantly enough to return to their previous levels. Historically, the same has been the case with gold.
“Even if prices decline, they are unlikely to return to their earlier levels,” Ayyub said.
Not far from Hussain’s workshop, 40-year-old former silver nagras maker Kuldeep Gautam now spends his days behind the counter of a jewellery shop.
Known for his intricate workmanship, Gautam once earned between $415 and $518 (40,000 and 50,000 rupees) a month making the ornate footwear. But he has not received a single order since January, he says. As orders disappeared and his savings dwindled, Gautam was forced to abandon the craft and take up a job as a salesman.
“I left the craft because I had no other choice,” he said. “Whenever I pass my old workshop, I don’t even look at it. It hurts too much.”
Beyond the loss of income, Kuldeep says he mourns the loss of the identity his craft had given him.
“People knew me for my work and appreciated my craftsmanship. It gave me dignity. Today, I earn only $155 (15,000 rupees) a month, and I struggle to pay my children’s school fees. I never imagined my life would come to this.”
“I still yearn to make nagras, but there are no buyers anymore. The war has destroyed our lives.”
Back in his shop, Azhar Hussain also faces the prospect of abandoning a craft that has carried his family for more than a century. His plan, he says, is to secure a bank loan to buy an electric rickshaw so he can start earning again.
“At least an e-rickshaw will earn me $5 to $7 (500 to 700 rupees) a day,” he said. “I don’t want to leave this craft, but I have no choice.”

Merz's CDU huddles to find way out of electoral free fall
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) will kick off a two-day leadership meeting on Sunday to plot a path out of the electoral crisis the party finds itself in after three dismal state elections.
The 25-member leadership meeting was called after the CDU — until now one of Germany's two largest popular parties — failed to even clear the 5% hurdle to enter Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's state legislature. The stinging loss, which Merz himself described as "a disaster," represented the first time in the party's history that it was booted from a statehouse.
The CDU has been struggling to hold off the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party and has been thrust into an identity crisis due to the rate at which it is losing voters to the party.
In one of the summer's other elections — in Saxony-Anhalt — the CDU dropped nearly 20 percentage points, getting clobbered by the AfD, which racked up over 40% of the vote.
This weekend's meeting is designed to address voter dissatisfaction with the CDU-led governing coalition with the Social Democrats (SPD), as well as looking at possible long-term solutions to the party's electoral death spiral.
Faced with this new electoral reality, leaders will reportedly look at the potential policy consequences of the party's losses, reconsidering whether to push on with much-needed reforms to the healthcare and retirement systems, for instance.
Party leaders will also grapple with the fundamental question of how to deal with the AfD in the long run, namely, whether to maintain the party's "firewall" policy rejecting any cooperation or to work with the anti-immigrant rightwing populists in hopes of remaining relevant.
Speaking with Germany's Welt am Sonntag newspaper ahead of the pow-wow, Hesse State Premier Boris Rhein said leadership, "has to deal with all of the issues that are important to everyday citizens: Cost of living, security, immigration and jobs."

Germany rejects proposed EU budget, calls for greater cuts
Germany swiftly rejected a proposed new budget for the European Union that was put forward on Saturday.
Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency, put forward a budget of €1.826 trillion ($2.046 trillion) for the next seven years — a reduction of around €159 billion compared to the European Commission's original proposal of nearly €1.985 trillion.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the budget cuts should go further.
"The size of the new proposal is no basis for an agreement," Merz said.
"The EU budget must be affordable for those who bear the main burden of financing," he added.
Germany is the largest net contributor to the EU budget. It and other net contributors including the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Austria and Finland all want the next budget to be slashed by hundreds of billions of euros.
But the second-largest net contributor to the EU budget, France, has instead argued that the 27-member bloc needs a more generous budget in order to overcome new challenges.
'Ragebait' named Germany's 2026 Youth Word of the Year
The Langenscheidt publishing house on Saturday named "ragebait" as Germany's 2026 Youth Word of the Year during the Frankfurt Book Fair.
Ragebait is social media content designed to draw people in by making them angry with provocative claims, lies, or outrageous opinions, thereby driving up clicks and interactions.
Langenscheidt, Germany's best-selling dictionary publisher, organized an online poll with 1 million young people taking part in this year's competition.
Ragebait took 36.5% of the vote, with runners-up including the terms "peak," meaning the best of the best, and "crashout," meaning when someone loses their cool.
Germany 'committed' to further Russia sanctions
Germany on Saturday said it would continue pursuing sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine, coming a day after US President Donald Trump announced a temporary US sanctions reprieve on Russian diesel.
"The federal government has taken note of the US decision relating to Russian diesel deliveries," government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said in a statement.
"The federal government remains committed to the decisions on sanctions against Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions," the statement added.
Germany's "support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing ... Diplomatic efforts for a peaceful solution continue," he added.
After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has been subject to round after round of sanctions packages led by the US and EU.
Russian crude and other oil products have been subject to EU sanctions since 2023, and Germany has not imported any oil or oil products from Russia since then.
A spokesperson for Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche said Saturday that "Germany stands fully behind the sanctions packages."
"Our supply is diversified in this area; we are independent of Russian oil," the spokesperson said.
Germany remains Ukraine's largest financial backer in Europe. During a visit to Kyiv last weekend, Chancellor Friedrich Merz reiterated Germany's unwavering support for Ukraine.
In what amounts to a major reversal in US policy, Trump on Friday said he would temporarily lift US sanctions to allow Russia to "immediately" supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US and global markets.
The move comes as diesel prices reach record levels after the war in Iran launched by the US and Israel sent diesel prices skyrocketing around the world. In the US, the high prices are putting political pressure on Trump's Republicans ahead of the midterm elections in November.
However, despite Trump's claims on social media, it remains unclear how much Russian fuel will reach global markets amid domestic fuel shortages as Ukraine continues to target refineries.
Ex-Chancellor Schröder criticized for Putin birthday visit
The appearance of Germany's Russia-friendly former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder at President Vladimir Putin's birthday party earlier this week has drawn criticism in Germany.
Franziska Brantner, the co-leader of Germany's Green party, called on Schröder's Social Democrats (SPD) to revisit revoking Schröder's party membership.
"Russia is now even attacking us in Germany with hybrid attacks. Schröder hasn't learned anything from this. A new approach needs to be put on the table," she told the Tagesspiegel newspaper.
"Schröder is celebrating Putin's birthday with him, while civilians in Ukraine are once again dying as a result of Russian attacks. This is politically unacceptable," said Brantner.
Anything less than expulsion from the party would be "a disastrous signal, not only to Ukraine but also to the people and their safety in our country," Brantner added.
The SPD's Hubertus Heil, who served as Germany's labor minister from 2018 to 2025, also criticized Schröder.
"The warm embrace between Schröder and Putin in Moscow deeply outrages and disturbs me," Heil told the Tagesspiegel.
Celebrating with a "dictator" whose "murderous imperialism causes horrific suffering every day" is "unjustifiable under any circumstances," he said.
Putin celebrated his 74th birthday in Moscow on Wednesday. The Kremlin said Putin learned that Schröder was on a business trip in the Russian capital via Russian media reports.
"The president invited his old friend to his home," the Kremlin said, with the Russian government releasing pictures of Schröder and Putin smiling and clasping hands,
Schröder's business and personal ties to Russia have drawn controversy since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Schröder's tax-payer financed Berlin office was closed in 2022 over his involvement in the Russian energy sector, but he fended off calls at the time by fellow party members to be expelled from the SPD.

Hundreds protests at FedEx Oakland over Israel arms shipments

Hundreds protests at FedEx in California over arms shipments to Israel
Three years after the outbreak of Israel’s war on Gaza, hundreds of demonstrators gathered in front of a FedEx building in Oakland, California to protest the shipping company’s arms deliveries to Israel.
FedEx, one of the world’s largest package shipping companies, currently sends weapons parts to Israel for its F-35 fighter jets, which has led to demonstrations against their role in Israel’s assault on Gaza. The shipments have been tracked from Oakland International Airport to their final destination of Nevatim Air Base in Israel.
On a warm Friday morning, demonstrators – represented by members of the Palestinian diaspora, labour unions, students, faith leaders and environmentalists – gathered in front of the FedEx entrance, holding signs reading: “No jets for genocide”, “Stop arming Israel” and “Arms embargo now”.
Speakers of different backgrounds took turns talking about their opposition to FedEx’s shipments of weapons parts to Israel, as well as other grievances with the corporation. Mohamed Shehk, an organiser with Arab Resource and Organising Centre (AROC) Action, spoke before a large crowd of demonstrators,
“We know that this did not start three years ago,” he said. “This genocidal apartheid state of Israel has been attempting to erase us, has been engaged in an ethnic cleansing campaign for 70 years.”
He said, “We’re here demanding that FedEx, this war profiteer, put an immediate end to military cargo being shipped to the apartheid state of Israel.”
He also criticised FedEx’s role in union crackdowns and alleged voter disenfranchisement in their home state of Tennessee.
“It’s also worth noting that FedEx isn’t just engaged in complicity in genocide. They are notoriously anti-union and anti-worker,” he said.
“Everyone remembers earlier this year when the Supreme Court shamefully gutted the Voting Rights Act of 1964. The state of Tennessee was the first state to exploit this ruling. Far-right politicians took the only majority Black district and split it up to weaken the Black vote and silence the Black voice,” he said.
“This why it is important for us to unite across all of these issues in this powerful coalition,” he said. “Solidarity with Palestine means solidarity with workers, solidarity with Black communities, and all communities that are oppressed by the capitalist and colonial class.”
Mick Glenn, a local resident, told The New Arab: “I wanted to make whatever difference I could by being there.”
He added, “The speeches were heartbreaking and motivating. I keep going to these demonstrations, but I hope they don’t have to go on much longer.”
A report by the Palestinian Youth Movement published in August 2025 noted that the Oakland airport is second only to Dallas-Fort Worth for the shipment of weapons parts to Israel.
The 15-page report, based on human rights investigations and on data exports, has found that since January, at least 280 military cargo shipments via FedEx have departed from Oakland International Airport, with Nevatim Airbase in Israel as the final destination. These shipments, supplied by Lockheed Martin, have included F-35 fighter jet components for carrying and releasing munitions and guided weapons.
More specifically, the report found that the shipments were consistently frequent (with only one week of a lull in transfers in six months); the materials delivered are wide-ranging, from lethal systems to small bolts; Nevatim is identified as the final destination for the materials; the shipments are coming from the Defence Logistics Agency in San Joaquín; and F-35s are confirmed to be used by Israel in Gaza.

Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets poll for Sept 2027

Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets presidential poll for September 2027
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday cancelled legislative elections scheduled for November due to worsening conditions within the occupied Palestinian territories and set a date of 11 September 2027 for both presidential and legislative elections, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.
Abbas' decree cited "obstacles posed by Israeli measures" to holding elections in November and the need to establish suitable political, security and on-the-ground conditions for "free, fair and inclusive elections". It called on Palestinians in the occupied territories of East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza to participate in the polls.
There had been serious doubts that the Palestinian Authority vote would go ahead in late November. The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-06, after which Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas' rival, the Islamist group Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists.
The decree said Israeli military attacks, settlement expansion, settler violence and movement restrictions in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, along with Israel's continued withholding of Palestinian tax revenues, created challenges to preparing for and holding elections on the previous date.
In Gaza, the decree pointed to "exceptional security and humanitarian conditions", the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces, the lack of progress in reconstruction and the failure to implement arrangements for deploying international stabilisation forces and police.
Israeli restrictions on access for election commission staff and international observers to Gaza and East Jerusalem also complicated preparations, the decree said.
The decision to postpone followed a resolution by the Palestine Liberation Organisation's executive committee and consultations with Palestinian factions and political forces. It also aimed to allow time for a comprehensive Palestinian national dialogue to strengthen unity and address challenges facing the electoral process.

Tehran tourism needs coordinated policies, not more infrastructure: council member

Tehran tourism needs coordinated policies, not more infrastructure: council member
TEHRAN – Tehran’s main tourism challenge is not a shortage of infrastructure but fragmented policymaking and limited public awareness of the capital’s existing attractions, a city council member said.
Seyyed Ahmad Alavi, head of the Tehran City Council’s Tourism and Cultural Heritage Committee, said better coordination among municipal bodies and stronger promotion of the city’s historical, recreational and tourism facilities were essential to expanding domestic tourism.
Alavi said responsibility for tourism and leisure facilities had been divided among several municipal organizations, resulting in separate decision-making processes and a lack of integrated planning.
He said the council had pursued the establishment of a municipal tourism company to address the problem, a proposal that was eventually approved after years of discussion.
Under the previous arrangement, different organizations oversaw various aspects of tourism and recreation, including amusement parks, cultural facilities and urban beautification projects. A unified structure could help coordinate their activities and make better use of existing assets, Alavi said.
He also highlighted a significant increase in the budget allocated to tourism tours and sightseeing buses, adding that further funding could be considered if the proposed tourism company presented viable plans that could be incorporated into the municipal budget.
Reviving neglected recreational facilities has been another priority, he said. The Basij amusement park, which had remained closed for about six years despite previous investment, was among the facilities targeted for reopening. The amusement park at the Abbasabad cultural and recreational complex had also been completed during the current council’s term, while plans were being developed for six additional amusement parks.
Alavi said the city was also expanding sightseeing bus services and establishing dedicated routes connecting historical landmarks and sites associated with Tehran’s cultural identity.
These services could help residents discover attractions they might otherwise overlook, he added.
He acknowledged that reorganizing the sector was complicated by competing interests among municipal bodies. Nevertheless, he said the council aimed to improve coordination, public access and promotion of existing attractions rather than focusing solely on building new infrastructure.
The broader objective, he said, is to enable more residents to benefit from Tehran’s historical, cultural and recreational resources.
