The land and sky of miracles: Flydubai hijacking reminded Israel of God's protection - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:59:23 UTC
20:59:23 KST

‘No, no, they can’t take that away from me…’ – George Gershwin
One of the many miracles recorded in the Torah is the falling of the manna in the desert, supplying the Israelites with nourishment for their 40-year journey from Egypt to Israel. A miracle-within-a-miracle, the Midrash says, was that the mana fell in direct correlation with the righteousness of the people.
For those who were truly righteous, it landed right at the opening of their tent, enabling them to reach down and collect the food, as one might today pick up the morning paper. Those who were not quite as righteous would have to walk out into their front yard, while others, even less righteous, would have to go deep into the field to collect their portion.
Thus, Heaven was revealing, in a miraculous fashion, just who were tzadikim in God’s eyes, and who were less so.
So, too, the dramatic events of flydubai’s flight 1073 – what I like to call “the miracle at 30,000 feet” – have brought to the surface a host of eye-opening revelations. One of them is the startling vulnerability of our much-vaunted security apparatus, with the Mossad and other departments not only failing to mark the Omani pilot as a potential terrorist, but admitting that several, if not dozens of unchecked pilots from hostile countries have flown planes into Israel over the years.
Numerous other governmental figures are also showing blood red on their faces after this near-mega disaster. Chief among them is Miri Regev, our transportation minister, who previously failed to provide alternate means of travel during the COVID pandemic, as well as in the current ongoing war, and sat idly by as our country’s faithful airlines mercilessly gouged the public. And her cohorts in the coalition, rather than using the near-disaster to check their own flaws and failures, merely spin the events to unabashedly seduce votes in the coming election.
The attempted hijacking and aborted suicidal crash of flight 1073 is a further indictment of the so-called “free press” and the obscene mania that possesses its editors. International outlets strove mightily to disguise and dispute the obvious anti-Israel, antisemitic nature of the attack. Their inane headlines exposed their biases as much as their unprofessionalism. “Fight in flight breaks out between two pilots”... “Near catastrophe averted due to on-board crew rescue”... Far be it from them to admit that a deranged hatred of Israel – fueled by their own selective condemnation of the Jewish state – now energizes the crazies of every society from Libya to London to attack Jews at will.
So radicalized are they that they just can’t bring themselves to acknowledge the ingenuity, gumption, and downright heroism of the average Israeli, as well as God’s perpetual guarding of the Jewish people. They are determined to take that away from us.
The brighter side of our story
WHICH BRINGS us to another side – a brighter side – of this story. It is the story of a nation that has merited the blessings of miracles that, if not outright suspensions of nature, are as close as you can get to glimpsing God.
Throughout our 2,000 years in exile, such miracles were virtually nonexistent. Yes, we did survive, and that alone can certainly qualify as miraculous. But it happened in a silent, below-the-surface fashion; it did not grab us, it did not cause us to jump up in amazement and force us to shake our heads in absolute wonderment. That kind of nes galui, revealed miracle, was reserved for Israel and Israel alone.
We saw it in 1967, when we humbled our boastful enemies in less than a week. We saw it in 1973, when we rose from a near-catastrophic defeat to overwhelm our adversaries in a military miracle that is still being studied in West Point and numerous other academies. We saw it in 1976, in the raid on Entebbe; we saw it in May of 1991, when a covert Israeli operation airlifted 14,325 Ethiopian Jews to freedom in Israel in just 36 hours.
And now we have seen it again, in just 12 minutes, over the skies of Saudi Arabia.
The full story has yet to be told, but the confluence of miracles is staggering: How did Captain Smit Machchhar manage to open the cockpit door – twice – while being brutally stabbed by terrorist Hamam al-Hammami? How did plumber Yaniv Hayoun and several other passengers have the courage to confront al-Hammami and subdue him? How did Hayoun know to grab the flight yoke and pull back on the controls to help level out the plane? How did another skilled pilot happen to be on the plane and so take over the controls? How were there not other accomplices on board – such as there were on the 9/11 flights – who would have aided the terrorist?
The very thought of that plane crashing into Ben Gurion Airport, setting it aflame and perhaps killing more than a thousand people, is mind-blowing in both its horror and the catastrophe that was prevented. I maintain that the flow of such deliverances from doom can only happen here, in the Holy Land.
The epic saga of our journey from Egypt to Israel is not only replete with miracles; it is marked annually by holidays that focus on those miracles. Pessah retells the story of our liberation, from the 10 Plagues to the splitting of the sea; Sukkot relates our ability to survive the harsh desert in flimsy, mobile shacks; Shavuot tells of the thunderous moments at the foot of Mt. Sinai when God gave us the Torah.
Marking our own modern 'checkpoints'
We would do well to mark our own modern “checkpoints,” our series of miracles that have graced and continue to grace us as we return to our land after centuries of dispersals, determined to rewrite history and re-establish ourselves as a sovereign nation.
The day our family arrived in Israel, over 34 years ago, my good friend Rabbi Kenny Cohen wisely told me: “You’ll endure some tough times here, to be sure, and encounter difficult, daunting challenges. You’ll get frustrated, maybe even fed up with some of the meshigas (‘craziness’) that goes on here. But then something extraordinary, some miraculous, “they can’t make this up” event will happen, and you will understand that this country is like no other, that it is a special privilege to live here, where we are watched over by God.”
The miracle at 30,000 feet was such an event; God is indeed watching, and no one can take that away from us.■
The writer is director of the Jewish Outreach Center of Ra’anana. 
rabbistewart@gmail.com

‘Rigged when you lose?’ 124 former bureaucrats defend EC &amp; SIR, challenge vote-rigging claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:58:21 UTC
20:58:21 KST

Former civil servants, including ex-Foreign Secretary Kanwal Sibal, former Ambassadors, and retired IAS officers, issued a joint open letter defending India's electoral integrity.
NEW DELHI: A group of 124 former IAS, IFS and allied services officers has issued an open letter to citizens defending the Election Commission (EC) and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, arguing that allegations of vote rigging must be backed by credible evidence.Citing safeguards in the electoral process, past election results and data from Bihar’s 2025 Assembly polls, the signatories have challenged claims questioning the credibility of the EC and the need for SIR.
The officers said India's electoral system had evolved significantly from an era marked by booth capturing, ballot-box stuffing and electoral violence. They cited multiple safeguards in the present system, including polling agents, electronic voting machine (EVM) sealing, strong-room security and voter-verified paper audit trail (VVPAT) verification.Referring to the 2025 Bihar Assembly elections, the signatories said the polls recorded no re-polling and the highest voter turnout since 1951."A system cannot be honest when you win and rigged when you lose," the letter said, pointing out that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which leads the government at the Centre, had lost several state elections under the same EC and also lost its parliamentary majority in 2024.
The signatories include former foreign secretary Kanwal Sibal and former IAS officers R D Kapur, Samirendra Chatterjee, Gopal Krishna, Vivek Bhardwaj and Navneet Sehgal.
Defending the EC's independence, the officers highlighted its multi-member structure and institutional safeguards. They also drew a distinction between questioning the electoral process and substantiating allegations against it."Questioning is every citizen's right. Proving is the accuser's duty," the letter said.
On SIR, the officers argued that the exercise was necessary to maintain accurate electoral rolls. Citing figures from Bihar, they referred to around 22 lakh deceased voters and seven lakh duplicate entries identified during the revision, alongside the addition of approximately 21.5 lakh new voters.
"An uncleaned roll does not protect the voter. It protects the fraudster," the letter said.The officers also pointed to safeguards available during SIR, including notices, hearings, appeals and the participation of political parties' booth-level agents. They said the Supreme Court had scrutinised the exercise, prescribed additional safeguards and upheld the EC's authority to undertake it.Concluding their argument, the signatories urged critics to examine allegations against the electoral system consistently, irrespective of election outcomes."If the system you call rigged is the same one that handed you your victories, ask yourself whether it is the system you doubt, or only the result," the letter said.

With over three years of experience, she focuses on national and global developments, conflict, diplomacy and their impact on India. Her work combines breaking news with in-depth analysis, offering readers context and clarity on the stories shaping the world.

Andrus Alber says that the digital euro will make payments more resilient to a crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:54:35 UTC
20:54:35 KST

The payment system is a critical piece of infrastructure in the same way that energy supplies and communications services are. The introduction of the digital euro will add a payment solution for the whole of the euro area alongside the non-European and regional European payment service providers, and it will make everyday digital settlements easier, increase resilience in the event of a crisis, and create a space for financial innovation.
“Having only one or two service providers dominate all card payments is far from ideal in terms of risk”, said Deputy Governor of Eesti Pank Andrus Alber at a conference on the digital euro held in Vilnius by the Baltic central banks that discussed payment habits in the Baltics and the role of the digital euro. “The digital euro would certainly be able to mitigate that risk”.
The risks are real. Estonia has experienced cyber attacks, GPS jamming, damage to underwater infrastructure, drones entering Estonian airspace, and extreme weather conditions in recent years. “People need to make purchases when any of these situations arises, and the payment system is clearly a critical piece of infrastructure that needs to be strengthened so it can withstand any crisis”, said Mr Alber.
The problem is that the European payment system is highly concentrated, and the large majority of card payment services are currently provided by a limited number of companies based outside the European Union. Estonia is one of the 13 countries that does not have its own local service provider. This did not seem to be a problem until geopolitical tensions made it apparent that excessive dependence on external providers could create a vulnerability to external pressure or coercion, or could lead to critically important services being interrupted. “Dependencies that are not immediately visible must also be considered”, Mr Alber pointed out. “Customers may have multiple accounts with different banks to spread their risks for example, but those banks might all use the same cloud services or electricity supplier. Alternatives and back-up solutions are needed and must be put in place”.
The digital euro that is being developed by the European Central Bank and the central banks of the Eurosystem is primarily an evolution of cash that reflects changes in the payment habits of Europeans and the increasingly common use of digital payments. An important additional benefit is that the digital euro can be used for electronic payments even if there is a power outage or if communications are interrupted. This strengthens the resilience of the payment system of the euro area.
Mr Alber said that this could only happen if the digital euro is widely used in the future and if people are aware of all the options it offers. “The challenge is not the technology, it is people and their habits”, he said. He gave the example of the crisis readiness exercise that Eesti Pank and the commercial banks ran in the spring in which systems still operated during a communications outage, but people were unable to pay because they did not have their physical card or any cash on them.
Asked whether the digital euro might crowd private-sector initiatives out of the market, Mr Alber drew a parallel with the recent football World Cup finals, where the number of teams competing had been enlarged. He said that the future of the digital euro could be seen in the similar way, as the overall value of payments is increasing year by year and the digital euro could create opportunities for new businesses that do not exist today, such as micro-payments or conditional payments.
A final decision about introducing the digital euro has not yet been taken, and will only come after the legislative framework for it has been agreed on. Negotiations between the European Parliament, the member states and the European Commission are expected to be concluded by the end of this year. If they are, the digital euro could enter into circulation in 2029–2030.
The conference on the digital euro was being held by the Baltic central banks for the second time. The first conference was held last September in Tallinn.

Ukrainian drone destroys Pantsir on Russian ‘Flakturm’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:50:21 UTC
20:50:21 KST

- The SBU’s Alpha unit released footage of a drone destroying a Russian Pantsir air defense system mounted on a “Flakturm”-style air defense tower.
- The SBU did not disclose the location, date or drone type used in the strike.
A Ukrainian drone has destroyed a Russian Pantsir air defense system on top of a “Flakturm,” one of the purpose-built anti-aircraft towers Russia has been putting up to stop Ukrainian drones, according to new footage released by the Security Service of Ukraine’s Alpha special operations unit.
The video shows the strike on the elevated platform, which Russia built to raise the air defense system above trees and terrain. The Security Service of Ukraine, known as the SBU, did not say where or when the strike took place, what type of drone was used, or whether the tower itself was destroyed along with the Pantsir.
The towers are widely nicknamed Flakturms after the Flaktürme, the massive concrete anti-aircraft towers Nazi Germany built to defend Berlin, Hamburg and Vienna from Allied bombers during World War II. Russia’s use of them became public in September 2023, when state television channel Russia-24 broadcast footage of Pantsir systems mounted on metal towers around Moscow.
Russia places air defense systems on these raised platforms to give their radars a clearer view of low-flying drones and to extend the distance at which they can spot targets. Ground-based radars have trouble seeing small drones that fly close to the ground or behind obstacles, and lifting the system several meters higher helps the radar look over them. The tradeoff is that a tower cannot move. Once its position is known, Ukrainian drone units can plan precision strikes against a target that will still be there when the drone arrives.
The Pantsir is a truck-mounted short-range air defense system that combines a radar, surface-to-air missiles and twin 30 mm cannons. It is one of the main systems Russia uses to shoot down drones and cruise missiles, and Ukrainian forces have made it a priority target. SBU head Vasyl Malyuk said in late 2025 that Ukraine had destroyed 48% of Russia’s Pantsir systems since the start of that year, adding that Russia builds about 30 a year, fewer than Ukraine was destroying.
The strike adds to a series of Ukrainian attacks on Russian air defenses this month. Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces hit another Pantsir-S1 near Kudepsta in Russia’s Krasnodar region on Oct. 8 and into Oct. 9, and Ukrainian FP-2 strike drones destroyed a Pantsir-S2 earlier in October, according to footage published online.

Feature: China's "Golden Week" sparks travel boom in Central Asia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
19:46:38 CST

BUKHARA, Uzbekistan, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- As the setting sun cast a golden glow over the ancient streets of Bukhara, the historic city bustled with tourists, while local vendors called out to passersby.
Holding a hand-painted ceramic bowl, Yan Hong, a tourist from northeast China's Harbin, marveled at the intricate floral patterns adorning the craft at a roadside stall, accompanied by her parents.
"Uzbekistan has so many historic cities along the Silk Road: Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva," she said. "I'd read about them in books. I had to see them for myself."
Walking through the ancient city, she said the experience surpassed her expectations, with history and modernity blending seamlessly and different civilizations engaging in a quiet dialogue.
Yan is among a rapidly growing number of Chinese travelers choosing Uzbekistan as a holiday destination.
A mutual visa-exemption agreement, which officially took effect on June 1, 2025, has given fresh impetus to cross-border tourism.
According to official reports from Uzbekistan's Tourism Committee, the number of Chinese tourists visiting the country increased by 3.5 times following the launch of the reciprocal visa-free policy.
"By now, the entire city of Bukhara knows that China enjoys a seven-day 'Golden Week' holiday in October," said Khamrayev, a local vendor specializing in miniature paintings and traditional handicrafts.
Recalling the holiday period last year, Khamrayev said Chinese tourists had flocked to his courtyard shop, making it his busiest sales period of the year.
A similar tourism boom is unfolding in neighboring Kazakhstan, which also benefits from a mutual visa-free arrangement with China.
At Shymbulak resort near Almaty, with the towering Tianshan Mountains in the background, Qi Yue and his wife from Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, waited in line for a cable car.
"We decided on a whim," Qi said. "Visa-free travel was a big factor." He added that many Chinese tourists now travel to Kazakhstan from Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region after exploring the region.
Some travelers are taking advantage of improved cross-border access to embark on longer and multi-country journeys across Central Asia.
Zhang Dongni, a solo backpacker traveling overland across the region, made her way from Almaty to Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan. She was heading to Osh, the country's second-largest city, before continuing to Khujand in Tajikistan.
"People here are remarkably warm and hospitable," Zhang said. While traveling from Bishkek to Osh, she was unable to board a bus because of her oversized luggage, so she arranged to share a taxi with local residents.
"We chatted using translation apps the whole way. When we arrived, they insisted on covering my fare as their guest," Zhang said. In return, she gave them traditional Chinese knots as tokens of appreciation.
In Tashkent, Uzbekistan's capital, Chinese tourists Zhou Yushan and Tang Suyu stopped to take photos outside the Holy Assumption Cathedral.
"We took three days off to bridge the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays," Zhou said. "That gave us enough time to explore Xinjiang alongside several destinations across Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan on a single trip."
As China and Central Asian countries continue to facilitate cross-border travel, growing tourism flows are increasingly becoming a two-way exchange, with more visitors from Central Asia also traveling to China.
According to data from the Guangzhou Baiyun exit-entry frontier inspection station, more than 90,000 passengers from the five Central Asian countries had passed through Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport by June 2 this year, up 286.6 percent year on year. Arrivals from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan rose by 258.4 percent, 351.9 percent and 660.6 percent, respectively.
Linked by mountains and rivers and bound by longstanding cultural ties, China and Central Asian countries are seeing closer people-to-people exchanges as cross-border travel becomes more convenient, opening new avenues for mutual understanding and lasting friendship. ■

Xinhua Commentary: China-EU trade ties need dialogue, not protectionism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
19:46:35 CST
20:46:35 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- The second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism has offered fresh momentum for stabilizing bilateral economic and trade ties, with both sides agreeing that it marks a new starting point for deepening China-EU cooperation.
By holding pragmatic and productive discussions and reaching a list of consensus outcomes, the two sides have demonstrated their willingness to deepen cooperation and work toward a stable and more balanced economic and trade relationship.
The outcome matters at a time when calls for protectionist measures are gaining ground in parts of Europe amid growing concerns over the EU's trade deficit in goods with China. Yet the way forward is not to erect more barriers, but to make better use of dialogue, expand mutually beneficial cooperation and properly address differences within the framework of WTO rules.
As the Chinese side has emphasized, China is not the source of the EU's problems, but a partner in solving them. The two sides should meet each other halfway and explore new opportunities for cooperation.
The EU's own trade figures show why the bilateral balance should not be viewed in isolation. According to EU official data, in the first quarter of 2026, the EU recorded a 12.7-billion-euro (or 14.58-billion-U.S. dollar) surplus in goods trade with non-EU countries. The trade deficit with China is only one part of Europe's broader global trade picture.
Meanwhile, China's services trade deficit with the EU reached 48.3 billion dollars in 2025, making the bloc China's largest source of such a deficit, according to China's official data.
These figures underscore a simple point: bilateral trade balances alone cannot fully reflect the breadth and mutual benefits of China-EU economic ties. Trade in goods is only one part of a broader relationship that also encompasses services, investment and deeply integrated supply chains.
As to the trade deficit in goods, the fact is that a considerable share of China-EU trade is generated by European companies operating in China. While products manufactured by these firms are recorded as Chinese exports, much of the profit, technology dividends and shareholder value ultimately accrues to European businesses. Restricting trade based on headline deficit figures risks overlooking these interdependencies and the benefits they bring.
Europe's competitiveness challenges extend well beyond trade with China. High energy costs, fragmented markets, regulatory burdens and gaps in innovation and investment have all weighed on the bloc's growth prospects.
More importantly, Europe's competitiveness challenge is also rooted primarily in the structural issues within the bloc. For example, the European Central Bank has estimated that internal EU barriers are equivalent to tariffs of around 44 percent on goods and 110 percent on services. These long-standing structural constraints cannot be resolved through tariffs or other restrictive measures targeting Chinese products.
Specific issues should be addressed through evidence-based consultations and established multilateral rules. Dialogue offers a way to clarify concerns, identify workable solutions and prevent individual disputes from spilling over into the broader economic relationship.
The latest Beijing meeting demonstrates the value of this approach. The significance of the meeting lies not in the assumption that all differences have been resolved, but in the willingness to address them through sustained engagement. The priority now is to implement the outcomes, maintain communication and translate areas of agreement into tangible benefits for businesses on both sides.
As two key trading partners, China and the EU have strong reasons to keep their economic ties stable and make them more balanced. Their cooperation matters not only to businesses and consumers on both sides, but also to global supply chains and the wider trading system at a time of heightened uncertainty.
Ultimately, a stable and more balanced China-EU economic relationship will be built not by narrowing the space for trade, but by expanding the opportunities it creates. Dialogue, openness and mutually beneficial cooperation offer a more sustainable path forward than protectionism. ■

Feature: Kenyan scientists develop climate-resilient crops to boost food security
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
19:46:32 CST
20:46:32 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Inside a laboratory at the University of Eldoret, about 300 km northwest of Nairobi, the Kenyan capital, tiny plantlets thrive in dozens of glass containers.
Each vessel holds about 10 delicate, centimeter-tall shoots, their fragile stems belying a remarkable resilience.
These plants form part of a broader national push to equip Kenyan farmers with climate-smart crops capable of withstanding shifting weather patterns.
Miriam Kinyua, a professor of plant breeding and biotechnology at the university, said the work uses tissue culture technology to produce clean, improved and more resilient planting materials.
"Many farmers are grappling with erratic weather, drought and rising crop diseases because of climate change. As scientists, we must ensure that we deliver planting materials that can overcome all these," she told Xinhua in a recent interview.
For Kinyua, the task is urgent. Climate change has fundamentally altered growing conditions, threatening both food security and livelihoods.
The surrounding region, one of Kenya's main breadbaskets, saw poor rainfall during the March-to-May rainy season, which caused widespread failure of maize, the country's staple crop.
Kenya is among the Horn of Africa nations bracing for El Nino rains from October to January 2027, which the World Meteorological Organization warns will trigger widespread flooding and destroy crops still in the fields.
"It is for such reasons that we have turned to tissue culture technology to develop potato, banana, coffee as well as pyrethrum seedlings which mature faster and are resistant to diseases and harsh climate," she said.
The process begins with a small piece of tissue taken from a mother plant, which is then sterilized and placed in a nutrient-rich growing medium containing ingredients such as sucrose and agar.
After about two weeks, the tissue develops into plantlets ready for multiplication.
"Once the roots grow, we either do a second cycle of culturing or multiplication or plant the seedlings for acclimatization," explained Kinyua.
After they are produced in the lab, the fragile plantlets are gradually exposed to conditions outside the carefully controlled laboratory environment. The process takes about three weeks before the seedlings are ready for planting.
The biotechnologist noted that the good thing with the technology is its speed, cleanliness and ability to mass-produce.
A single mother plant produces between 12 and 18 potato plantlets, allowing researchers to multiply desirable planting materials much faster than conventional methods.
Another key benefit of the technology is that farmers receive disease-free plantlets, noted Betty Gakii, a biotechnology researcher at the University of Eldoret.
She explained that the lab produces two potato varieties, Amani and Fanaka, that are highly favored by farmers for their disease resistance and superior yields.
With proper application of fertilizer and farm management of the crop, Gakii said both varieties, which mature in three months, produce between 25 and 60 tubers per plant.
This is higher as compared to traditionally produced varieties that take up to five months to mature, making them susceptible to the effects of climate change.
For Kenya, producing climate-resilient potato varieties is crucial as the crop is the country's second staple after maize.
Potatoes are farmed across roughly 225,976 hectares in Kenya, yielding about 2.15 million tonnes annually, according to the Agriculture and Food Authority.
Jackson Kimutai, a Kenyan farmer who has embraced tissue culture planting materials, said he has enjoyed steady harvests despite escalating weather challenges.
"I plant potatoes mainly alongside other crops. From potatoes, because the tissue culture variety I plant matures faster, I was able to get a good harvest despite the rains disappearing early," he said. ■

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese envoy on Friday called for efforts to de-escalate the situation in Ukraine.
"The urgent priority is to de-escalate the situation, prevent the conflict from spilling over beyond the battlefield, and avoid an escalation of hostilities," said Sun Lei, China's deputy permanent representative to the United Nations (UN).
The parties to the conflict should strictly abide by international humanitarian law, refrain from attacking civilians and civilian infrastructure, and avoid causing harm to third-country civilians and civilian assets, so as to create conditions for a political settlement of the crisis and preserve the prospects for an early realization of peace, he told an emergency meeting of the Security Council on Ukraine.
Recently, the situation has continued to escalate, he said. The two parties to the conflict have continued to carry out large-scale attacks against each other, causing heavy casualties and extensive damage to facilities. Various new types of drones and unmanned surface vessels continue to emerge, with growing lethality and destructive capacity, pushing the situation in an increasingly dangerous direction, said Sun.
"The spillover effects of the crisis are becoming increasingly severe and continue to impact global energy and food security. The Ukraine crisis must not be allowed to continue escalating and spiral out of control. The parties concerned and the international community should work together to seek a political solution," he said.
Sun noted that recently, the parties concerned have engaged in some interactions and contacts while significant differences in their positions remain. China hopes the parties concerned will maintain engagement, demonstrate political will, continue to build consensus, and work together toward a comprehensive, lasting, and binding peace agreement, he said.
Sun said the peaceful and amicable coexistence of Russia and Ukraine is the only realistic choice and is also the common expectation of the international community. China hopes the parties to the conflict will proceed from the fundamental and long-term interests of their respective peoples, respect each other's legitimate security concerns, address the root causes of the crisis on the basis of full, complete, and comprehensive adherence to the principles of the UN Charter, promote a balanced, effective, and sustainable regional security architecture, and truly achieve universal and common security, said Sun.
On the Ukraine issue, China has consistently maintained that the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all countries should be respected, the purposes and principles of the UN Charter should be fully observed, the legitimate security concerns of all countries should be taken seriously, and all efforts conducive to the peaceful settlement of the crisis should be supported, Sun said.
China will continue to work with the international community to make unremitting efforts to usher in the dawn of peace at an early date and achieve a political settlement of the crisis as soon as possible, he added. ■

The munitions transfer follows Helsinki’s approval on Friday of its 35th defense materiel assistance package for Kyiv. Valued at approximately €1 million ($1.13 million), the emergency package was expedited following an urgent appeal by Ukrainian defense authorities and drew a single, undisclosed defense asset directly from Finnish military stockpiles.
Rising threat of high-speed turbojet loitering munitions
The provision of aircraft munitions arrives as Ukrainian military commanders warn that Moscow is rapidly transitioning its long-range drone arsenal toward turbine-propelled models that outpace conventional low-altitude interception networks.
Russian forces have accelerated the deployment of jet-powered Shahed variants since July, presenting significant tactical hurdles for mobile air defense fire teams reliant on heavy machine guns and propeller-driven counter-drone aircraft. While baseline piston-engine Shahed-136 drones cruise at speeds between 180 and 200 km/h, current Russian turbojet drones fly at roughly 600 km/h (370 mph).
Ukrainian Air Force commanders anticipate that adversary technology will continue to advance. During an address to a parliamentary investigative commission, Deputy Air Force Commander Colonel Yurii Cherevashenko warned that Russian designers could eventually increase the dash velocity of jet-powered strike drones to between 800 and 900 km/h (500 to 560 mph).
“We have not seen such speeds yet, but we forecast them,” Cherevashenko said.
Cherevashenko noted that jet-powered drones currently constitute roughly 40 percent of unmanned strike waves deployed against Ukraine, with their share reaching up to 60 percent along specific operational axes.
Military planners project that high-speed turbine models could eventually comprise up to 80 percent of all Russian strike drone salvos, drastically compressing warning times and forcing Ukrainian defenders to rely more heavily on combat aviation.

Japan launches seventh Taigei-class submarine Shogei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:44:01 UTC
20:44:01 KST

- Mitsubishi Heavy Industries launched Shogei, the seventh Taigei-class submarine for Japan, at its Kobe shipyard on Oct. 8.
- The 3,000-ton lithium-ion battery submarine will be delivered to Japan’s Ministry of Defense during fiscal 2027 after outfitting.
Mitsubishi Heavy Industries launched Japan’s newest attack submarine, Shogei, at its Kobe shipyard on Oct. 8, the seventh boat of the Taigei class built for the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force.
The 3,000-ton diesel-electric submarine was named and floated out in a ceremony at the yard in Kobe’s Hyogo Ward. MHI will now complete outfitting of the hull, propulsion, electrical and weapons systems before handing the boat over to Japan’s Ministry of Defense during fiscal 2027, which runs through March 2028. The company did not disclose a construction cost or which base the submarine will be assigned to.
The Taigei class replaces the Soryu class as the backbone of Japan’s submarine force. Its main feature is lithium-ion batteries, which store more energy than the lead-acid batteries used in most conventional submarines and let the boats stay submerged longer and move faster underwater before they need to run their diesel engines to recharge. Japan first fitted lithium-ion batteries in the last two Soryu-class boats, Oryu and Toryu, and the Taigei class was designed around them from the start, dropping the separate Stirling air-independent propulsion system carried by most earlier Soryus. The boats are about 84 meters (276 feet) long, and the newer ones use more powerful Kawasaki diesel engines.
Shogei is the first Taigei-class boat launched by MHI since the fifth boat, Chogei, in October 2024. Mitsubishi and Kawasaki Heavy Industries, both in Kobe, alternate construction of the class. The lead boat, Taigei, was commissioned in March 2022, and a new boat has entered service every March since then. Taigei itself has since been reassigned as a test submarine. The sixth boat, Sogei, was launched by Kawasaki in October 2025 and is scheduled to be commissioned in March 2027.
Japan launches its submarines while still incomplete. A launch ceremony is when the boat receives its name and leaves the building berth, followed by more than a year of outfitting and sea trials before delivery.
MHI said it will keep working on reducing crew size, improving cybersecurity and cutting life-cycle costs, and that it is focused on developing a new submarine outside the current design approach. The company did not give details.
Japan’s defense plans call for a fleet of 22 submarines. With Shogei’s delivery planned for the 2027 fiscal year, the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force will have seven Taigei-class boats built or under construction.

Debate grows over Airbnb’s impact on Swiss housing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:43:12 UTC
20:43:12 KST

Debate grows over Airbnb’s impact on Swiss housing
The growth of booking platforms such as Airbnb is putting increasing pressure on housing markets in Swiss cities and tourist hotspots.
While tenants’ groups and hoteliers are calling for tighter rules, homeowners warn against disproportionate restrictions on property rights.
More
How the government is regulating Airbnb in Switzerland
Holiday lets listed on platforms such as Airbnb are popular with travellers and can be highly profitable for property owners. But when homes are used year-round for a steady flow of short-term guests, they are no longer available to local residents and workers. That is why several Swiss cities are tightening the rules.
Conflict over the 90-day limit
Since 2025, Lucerne has imposed a cap on short-term rentals. Homes developed for short-term letting since 2010 that have displaced or reduced the local housing stock can generally be rented out for no more than 90 nights a year. Property owners must also register them.
+ Housing shortages – what works and what doesn’t
Zurich and Interlaken have since introduced similar restrictions. Mario Stübi, president of the Lucerne Tenants’ Association, says the crackdown is long overdue, arguing that the trend is becoming more widespread at the expense of local residents.
He argues that ordinary homes should not be taken out of the housing market. Speaking during the discussion, he summed up his position with a simple principle: “Ownership comes with responsibilities.” Those who choose not to rent out their properties in the conventional way, he says, must be prepared to follow the rules set by the community.
More
Ticino rules on short-term holiday rentals attract federal ire
Damian Hunkeler, a member of the Lucerne cantonal parliament for the Radical-Liberal Party and president of the Lucerne Homeowners’ Association, takes a different view. “As a liberal, I am fundamentally opposed to laws, regulations and restrictions,” he says.
He argues that the 90-day limit is arbitrary. In Lucerne, there were around 330 Airbnb listings when the rule was introduced in 2025, compared with more than 48,000 homes in the city, less than 1% of the total housing stock. “A share that small does not warrant another layer of regulation that could ultimately lead to high enforcement costs for taxpayers,” he says. In Zurich, the city has already approved five new posts for a three-year period to police the rules.
Hoteliers and local residents under pressure
Concerns are also growing in Switzerland’s mountain regions. In Valais, the canton with the highest number of registered short-term rentals, hoteliers are sounding the alarm. Olivier Andermatt, president of the Valais Hoteliers’ Association, is calling for a level playing field between hotels and other forms of tourist accommodation.
More
Locals driven out by luxury homes in Swiss mountains
He argues that commercial short-term lets should meet the same requirements on fire safety, hygiene, employment law, tourist taxes and VAT as the hotel industry. He also says there is an acute shortage of affordable housing for both hotel staff and local residents. As a result, he is calling for a strict registration system run by local authorities.
Comments from listeners to Swiss public broadcaster SRF highlight the dilemma. One landlord says he lost CHF35,000 ($42,185) because of unpaid rent and damage to his property before turning to Airbnb. Another private host says the income helps fund their retirement. Meanwhile, critics warn about commercial investors turning entire apartment blocks into lucrative short-term rental units.
Several contributors to the discussion favour local solutions. They argue that popular tourist destinations need stricter rules than areas where demand for short-term rentals is lower.
Where next?
Despite their differences, both sides agree on one thing: reliable data is essential. The Swiss House of Representatives has backed a proposal to collect nationwide data on short-term rentals. The measure must still be approved by the Senate. Its supporters say the data will help identify where action is actually needed.

Calcutta high court says peaceful protest not an offence just because authorities dislike it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:43:06 UTC
20:43:06 KST

Under Section 141 of IPC, a gathering of 5 or more is unlawful only if its common object falls within specific categories defined by law. 'Thus, a demonstration does not become an offence merely because it was unwelcome to those in authority,' the court held.
NEW DELHI: The Calcutta high court has ruled that peaceful protests cannot be treated as criminal offences simply because they are unwelcome to those in authority. The court stressed that the right to dissent and assemble peacefully is an integral part of democracy.The HC made these observations while quashing criminal proceedings against six School Service Commission (SSC) job aspirants who protested against alleged recruitment irregularities in August 2021.
The ruling also comes amid a crackdown on protests in Delhi. Police have imposed security restrictions ahead of a planned mobilisation against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Opposition parties and left organisations have criticised the curbs. They have argued that such restrictions undermine the fundamental right to assemble and protest.Justice Anuj Singh said the police complaint failed to establish the essential ingredients of the offences charged against the protesters. These included unlawful assembly, wrongful restraint and acts likely to spread infection during the Covid-19 pandemic.“It is an unavoidable inference that the Petitioners are being punished for the protest, making it a vexatious and frivolous proceeding,” the court said.
Peaceful assembly not inherently illegal
The high ourt said merely gathering and raising slogans did not amount to an unlawful assembly. Under Section 141 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), a gathering of five or more people is unlawful only if its common object falls within specific categories defined by law.“Thus, mere protest and raising slogans cannot be said to be an unlawful common object under Section 141,” the court said.The judge cited an earlier Calcutta high court ruling in Association for Protection of Democratic Rights v State of West Bengal. It held that a large gathering of demonstrators was not inherently illegal or unconstitutional.“Article 19(1)(b) of the Constitution of India confers upon all citizens of India the right to assemble peaceably. Therefore, any large assembly of demonstrators would not per se be either illegal or unconstitutional,” the court quoted from the earlier judgment.The court also referred to the Supreme Court's decision in Javed Ahmad Hajam v State of Maharashtra. It said the right to dissent, criticise the government and protest peacefully within the law was integral to democracy.“Thus, a demonstration does not become an offence merely because it was unwelcome to those in authority,” the court held.
Police allegations failed to establish offences
The case arose from a protest on August 5, 2021. SSC job aspirants had gathered near Mayukh Bhawan in Salt Lake and were proceeding towards Bikash Bhawan. They were raising slogans against alleged recruitment irregularities.According to the police complaint, the gathering violated Covid-19 protocols and a prohibitory order under Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC). The complaint also alleged that the protesters refused to disperse, obstructed public movement and prevented officials from performing their duties.Thirteen people, including the six petitioners, were arrested.The petitioners argued that they were exercising their fundamental rights to freedom of speech and expression, and peaceful assembly. These rights are guaranteed under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Constitution. They also said the criminal proceedings could harm their future employment prospects.The court found that the FIR did not establish the common object behind the gathering. It also failed to show how the protesters had committed the alleged offences.On the charge of disobeying a public servant's order under Section 188 IPC, the court noted that the Section 144 CrPC order had not been placed on record. The complaint also failed to explain how the protest obstructed public movement or stopped officials from performing their duties.The charge of wrongful restraint under Section 341 IPC also lacked specific details. The FIR did not identify anyone who had been prevented from moving in a direction they were legally entitled to take.The court also rejected the allegations under Sections 269 and 270 IPC. These provisions deal with negligent or deliberate acts likely to spread infection. The FIR did not identify any specific act by the petitioners that could have spread Covid-19. Nor did it allege that they were infected or had reason to believe they were carrying the disease.The court said a general allegation of violating Covid-19 protocols was not enough to invoke Section 51 of the Disaster Management Act, 2005. The complaint did not specify which protocol had been breached. It also failed to explain how the petitioners had obstructed an official acting under the Act.
The HC relied on the Supreme Court's ruling in State of Haryana v Bhajan Lal. The ruling lays down that criminal proceedings can be quashed if the allegations, even when accepted in full, do not disclose an offence. The same applies when proceedings are manifestly attended by mala fides.The court concluded that the FIR did not establish a prima facie case against the six petitioners. It quashed the FIR registered at Bidhannagar North police station and all consequential proceedings.These included G.R. Case No. 901 of 2021, pending before the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bidhannagar.

UN warns Russian winter strikes imperil Ukraine humanitarian situation
Ukraine

14:42:22 EEST
20:42:22 KST

Intensifying Russian strikes against Ukraine threaten to trigger a humanitarian crisis ahead of winter, as attacks on cities and critical infrastructure could leave millions of people without electricity, heating, and water, Khaled Khiari, Assistant Secretary-General in the Departments of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and Peace Operations, said during a meeting of the UN Security Council, noting that Russian attacks had reached "a new horrifying level."
According to the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), over 100 civilians were killed and at least 429 injured in Russian strikes in Ukraine this week alone.
Khiari said that strikes on bridges, educational institutions, and energy infrastructure were disrupting electricity and water supplies, while prolonged air raid alerts were increasing psychological pressure on civilians. He called for an immediate halt to attacks on energy facilities and populated areas.
"All attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, wherever they occur, are a violation of international humanitarian law and must end immediately," the UN representative said.
During the meeting, Gemma Connell, Director of the Crisis Response Division in the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, speaking on behalf of Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher, announced a $358 million winter response plan. It provides for assistance to 2 million of the most vulnerable people through the provision of heating, shelter, and food.
"No amount of preparedness can substitute for protecting the infrastructure civilians depend on in the first place," Connell said, calling for civilian protection, unhindered humanitarian access, safe evacuations and the protection of humanitarian personnel.
Ukraine's Permanent Representative to the UN, Andriy Melnyk, said at the meeting that Russian attacks on civilians had reached an unprecedented level of brutality. According to him, UN monitors had confirmed that 2,222 civilians had been killed and more than 13,000 injured in Ukraine in 2026. He also referred to strikes on the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine and on bridges that provide civilians with access to hospitals, food, and safe places.
Head of the European Union Delegation to the UN Stavros Lambrinidis warned that attacks on Black Sea ports threatened global food security. According to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), wheat prices rose by 6.3% in September.
Khiari also drew attention to incidents involving drones entering areas near Moldova and attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea. Separately, he reported that, according to available information, approximately 2,000 civilians, including 35 children, remained trapped in occupied Oleshky without food or medical supplies. An urgent localized ceasefire is needed to evacuate them.

‘Makan’s Mission’: environmental storytelling project wrapped up honoring martyred students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:42:05 UTC
20:42:05 KST

‘Makan’s Mission’: environmental storytelling project wrapped up honoring martyred students
TEHRAN – The Department of Environment (DOE) has held the closing ceremony of an environmental storytelling project, titled ‘Makan’s Mission’, to honor students martyred in the US-Israeli war against the country.
Launched in May in cooperation with the Ministry of Education, the initiative was named after Makan Nasiri, one of the 168 schoolchildren killed in a deadly US strike on Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School on February 28, the first day of the imposed war.
The project portrayed Makan as a young environmental advocate whose mission was left unfinished following his martyrdom, encouraging other students to carry on his path and continue his efforts to protect the environment.
The project is actually a subcategory of an earlier project that aims to train eco-friendly students, or environmental helpers. Both projects aim to enhance the students’ environmental literacy.
Addressing the ceremony, Hadi Kiadaliri, the deputy head of the DOE for education and public participation affairs, highlighted the profound importance of environmental education at an early age, saying that environmental education for children is an investment in the country’s future, IRNA reported.
The cultivation of good environmental habits has to commence at a very young age; in addition to fostering awareness and knowledge among children, it is essential to strengthen their emotional affinity with nature, he added.
Referring to environmental challenges in the country, Kaidaliri said a significant part of our country is located within an arid and semi-arid climate, with low vegetation. Nevertheless, Iran boasts valuable biodiversity, including species unique to the country, and ecosystems that date back to millions of years ago. Therefore, protecting Iran’s environment is of particular importance.
Highlighting the role of children in bringing about lasting changes in society, Kiadaliri noted that one reason for the persistence of environmentally damaging behaviors is that many are bound by habits. Therefore, good habits have to be developed from childhood.
To teach children appropriate habits, giving mere advice is insufficient; instead, establish environments in which proper behavior is reinforced by positive outcomes and improper conduct leads to negative consequences. This way, children learn to make sound decisions and take on greater responsibility for their choices in the future.
Education is not merely about acquiring knowledge. Many may possess extensive environmental knowledge, but it does not necessarily result in appropriate environmental behavior. Children have to recognize their role in tackling environmental issues.
The official went on to say that investing in environmental education and the upbringing of children is not an expenditure, but an investment in the future.
The more we invest in educating the younger generation today, the less we will have to spend on improving environmental damage and correcting improper conduct in the future.
Accordingly, cooperation among the DOE, the Ministry of Education, and the Institute for Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults (IIDCYA) is a critical necessity for the development of a broad educational movement and engaging students in environmental conservation.
Addressing the unveiling ceremony of the environmental storytelling project in May, Kiadaliri said the project to train eco-friendly students kicked off in the Iranian year 1375 (1996). Back then, it was limited to a few provinces. However, the project faced some challenges that highlighted the need for its revision.
In January 2023, the DOE and the Ministry of Education unveiled the logo and the poster of the national plan for the project.
Highlighting the role of education in developing values such as responsibility, the official said teaching environmental issues to children will contribute to instilling eco-friendly behaviors in them, which will later turn into sustainable habits. Investing in children will enhance lifelong social outcomes.
If adults are responsible for current changes, children will play the same role in the future. The training needs to be constant and accessible, he added.
For his part, Education Minister Alireza Kazemi noted that the integration of environmental teachings into textbooks, from preschool to high school, is on the agenda to help promote the culture of preserving the environment.
The educational courses will not be limited to students; they have the capacity to train parents and teachers, as well.
Apart from textbooks that involve formal training, the Ministry of Education focuses on informal training that would promote students’ social participation in practice.
The official also announced the ministry’s readiness to expand training by establishing a vocational training center to provide practical skills in the environment sector, and even utilize available capacities to organize educational courses.
Education is the key to bringing about any change in the economy, culture, and social life; therefore, providing skills and training and proper behaviors will play a key role in improving the current situation, Kazemi highlighted.
The official went on to say that students who are environmental helpers have to be introduced and lauded; they should be allowed to have a more influential role, and feel more responsible for participating in environmental conservation programs.
In February, DOE and the Education Ministry discussed the possibility of developing a national education curriculum to promote environmental responsibility and awareness among children.
Referring to the inefficiency of short-term and incoherent teaching, Mohammad Medadi, an official with the DOE, said that achieving sustainable development and boosting the country’s resilience are not possible without institutionalizing an environmentally friendly attitude and lifestyle in society. So, educational approaches need to be reviewed, he added.
Environmental protection education should be taught from preschool to high school. In addition to scientific training, it should focus on ethical aspects based on cultural, religious, and social teachings.
The initiative also aims to train and empower parents and teachers, the official further noted.

Japan protests to top U.S. admiral over Okinawa killing

- Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi strongly protested to U.S. Indo-Pacific Command chief Adm. Samuel Paparo over a Marine’s arrest in an Okinawa killing.
- Koizumi demanded full cooperation with the investigation, tighter discipline and steps to prevent further incidents involving U.S. personnel.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi lodged a strong protest with Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, on Oct. 9 over the arrest of a U.S. Marine on suspicion of robbing and killing a woman on Okinawa.
The two met at Japan’s Ministry of Defense in Tokyo during Paparo’s visit, the ministry said. Koizumi demanded full U.S. cooperation with the police investigation, stricter discipline among American personnel and thorough measures to prevent further incidents and accidents. He also asked the U.S. side to respond appropriately to the victim’s family. Koizumi and Paparo also discussed security cooperation and agreed to keep working closely to strengthen the alliance, according to the ministry. Neither side released any statement from Paparo about the case.
Okinawa Prefectural Police arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, early on Oct. 4 on suspicion of killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi at a hotel in Naha, Okinawa’s capital, early the previous morning and taking her wallet and backpack. Police said security camera footage showed a man entering the hotel with Yagi and leaving alone with her belongings. Officers later spotted Ballard walking in an entertainment district in Okinawa City and arrested him. Police said Yagi died of asphyxiation, and Ballard has denied the allegations, according to Japanese police. Ballard is a combat engineer with Marine Wing Support Squadron 172 at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described the killing as extremely brutal and heinous, and Japan’s government lodged a protest with Washington shortly after the arrest. Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja summoned U.S. and Japanese officials over the case.
The U.S. military on Okinawa responded with some of its broadest restrictions in years. Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force and the senior U.S. officer on the island, ordered a 48-hour operational pause starting Oct. 7, with no off-base liberty and a complete ban on alcohol on or off base, while commanders held training on standards and discipline. From Oct. 9, all U.S. personnel on Okinawa are under a 30-day curfew requiring them to be in their quarters or off-base homes from midnight to 5 a.m. U.S. Forces Japan is also reviewing its liberty policies and will make recommendations to a joint coordinating committee.
The case has sparked protests on Okinawa and outside the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo. Okinawa hosts most of the roughly 60,000 U.S. troops in Japan, and crimes involving American personnel have long strained relations between residents, the prefectural government and Tokyo. Prefectural police said arrests involving U.S. service members and their families exceeded 100 last year.

Yemen govt say advancing against Houthis around Bab al-Mandeb
Yemen's military is advancing against the Houthis in areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait but has not yet secured control of the waterway, after the government launched an operation to recapture lost territory, according to military sources speaking to AFP.
The Saudi-backed government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the pro-Iran group seized Yemen's entire western coastline in a lightning offensive.
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandeb area, but they claimed to have repelled the assault.
Sources from the military of Yemen's internationally recognised government also said Mayun Island in the heart of the strait remained in Houthi hands as fighting continued.
Clashes in western Yemen, specifically around the strait, had killed at least 63 people in the past 24 hours, military sources from both sides told AFP on Saturday.
Thirty-five members of government forces had been killed, while 28 Houthis had died, the sources said.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.
On Friday, a Yemeni military source within the government confirmed to AFP that their forces had launched a "major operation" in the strait region, supported by air power from Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government.
Military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Telegram that the Houthis had succeeded in "driving back the Saudi-aligned troop concentrations that attempted to advance from the direction of Lahj towards Bab al-Mandeb".
After four years of relative calm, Yemen's civil war reignited in July before the Houthi gains on Yemen's western coastline.
Saudi Arabia leads an international military coalition helping the Yemeni government fight the Houthis.
Early on Saturday, the coalition said it had destroyed more than 130 Houthi targets in a "large-scale operation".
The Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel reported on Saturday that Saudi strikes had targeted the Bab al-Mandeb area.
In addition to battling Yemeni government forces on the ground, the Houthis have also been firing on targets inside Saudi Arabia, attacking transport hubs, oil facilities and other civilian targets with drones and missiles.
Riyadh said Friday that attacks on the Saudi capital's international airport had killed three people the previous day.
Saudi Arabia has been retaliating with strikes on key Houthi targets inside Yemen. Houthi media on Friday reported two people had died in attacks on the airport in the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa.
Ordinary civilians have been paying the price for the renewed fighting in one of the world's poorest countries, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.

Iran to raise US attacks’ environmental toll on Kharg Island at international forums
TEHRAN – A comprehensive report is being prepared on the environmental damage caused by US attacks on Kharg Island, southern Bushehr Province, with the aim of pursuing the matter through legal and international channels, including the United Nations.
Abdolrahman Moradzadeh, director general of Bushehr Province’s Department of Environment, said protecting the island’s natural habitats and wildlife species was part of the responsibility to safeguard the country’s national assets.
He added that documenting the damage could play an effective role in pursuing the issue through legal and international mechanisms.
At least 25 deer have been confirmed dead on Kharg Island following attacks during US-Israeli aggression against Iran, with environmental officials warning the actual toll is likely significantly higher.
The deaths represent one of the most visible impacts of the war on Iran’s wildlife, highlighting the often-overlooked environmental consequences of armed conflicts beyond human casualties.
“The latest reports indicate that at least 25 deer have died on Kharg Island,” Press TV quoted Masoumeh Safaei, deputy director of Iran’s Office for Wildlife Protection and Management, as saying.
“This figure only covers areas outside military zones, and the real number of casualties is higher than what has been recorded so far,” Safaei added.
Environmental experts warn that the effects of warfare on wildlife extend far beyond direct fatalities.
Explosions, habitat destruction, and prolonged exposure to intense noise can leave lasting physical and psychological scars on animal populations.
According to Safaei, severe stress caused by nearby blasts also affected animals held in captivity.
Shina Ansari, the head of the Department of Environment (DOE), has highlighted that remaining silent in the face of environmental destruction caused by warmongers is the same as accepting a threat that will, sooner or later, impact everyone.
“The environment is the first silent victim of war and the last to recover from its consequences. Nature does not recognize the end of armed conflict. Environmental destruction may continue to undermine human health, food security, water resources, and biodiversity for decades after the guns fall silent,” the official noted.
She made the remarks while addressing the ninth session of the Committee on Environment and Development (CED9) held from July 1-3 in Bangkok, Thailand.
Elaborating on transboundary environmental challenges such as climate change, air and marine pollution, biodiversity loss, land degradation, dust and sand storms, and waste management challenges, Ansari underlined that environmental destruction resulting from war and military aggression is the most severe and inhumane damage to the environment, as the impacts of these brutal attacks trigger a profound threat to the entire planet.
“When war targets the environment, the victim is not merely one nation—it is the shared heritage of humanity. Therefore, protecting the environment must become a common global responsibility; the aggressors must be held accountable for their crimes and provide full compensation for the environmental damage they have caused. Effective implementation of this principle not only serves justice for the affected State but also plays an essential role in preventing the recurrence of such devastation.”
Referring to some of the gravest war crimes and environmental catastrophes caused by the warmongering of major powers in the region in the past decades, she said that over the past year, the US-Israel coalition has imposed two illegal wars against Iran.

Three in five AI models fail terrorism safety tests, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:38:44 UTC
20:38:44 KST

Three in five artificial intelligence (AI) models have failed terrorism safety tests, with models stripped of safeguards consistently providing potentially dangerous information, according to research reported by CBC News on Friday.
The study, conducted by the UK-based nonprofit Tech Against Terrorism, evaluated more than 130 AI models using hundreds of requests resembling those a terrorist planning an attack might submit.
Researchers found that models modified through a process known as "abliteration," which removes safety safeguards, failed every test.
Meta's Llama 3.1 8B model scored 97 out of 100 on the organisation's safety benchmark before modification, compared with approximately three afterward.
Researchers said the modified model provided detailed responses to requests involving attacks, terrorist financing and radicalisation, while its original version refused such requests.
"Understandably, there's concern about loss of control, existential risk of AI," said Adam Hadley, founder and executive director of Tech Against Terrorism.
"The thing is actually, this has already happened because a lot of these open models have already been broken — it's just no one's noticed yet."
The organisation found more than 29,000 repositories advertising uncensored or unprotected AI models on Hugging Face as of late last month.
Hugging Face said it regularly moderates content violating its policies but warned that some recommendations in the report could undermine open research.
Meta said its models undergo safety evaluations and that its policies prohibit harmful or illegal uses.
The report found no evidence of terrorist or extremist groups using the tested models, apart from one extremist chatbot identified by researchers.
Tech Against Terrorism recommended independent safety benchmarks, stronger protections against safeguard removal and restrictions on distributing modified models.
"This idea that we can't have safety and progress, I think, is false," Hadley said.

Iran’s presence in world’s top 2% of scientists nearly doubles  
 
The number of Iranian researchers included in the world’s top 2% of scientists has nearly doubled, rising from 1,154 in 2020 to 2,678 in 2026, according to Scopus data provided by Elsevier.
An analysis of the rankings shows a steady upward trend in the number of Iranian researchers recognized among the world’s top 2% of scientists over the past several years.
The number rose to 1,701 in 2021 and 1,941 in 2022, before increasing to 2,137 in 2023 and 2,514 in 2024. The figure reached 2,678 in 2026, ISNA reported.
The majority of Iranian researchers are from 30 universities and scientific centers; the University of Tehran, with 123 researchers, is placed first. Followed by Tehran University of Medical Sciences (112), Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences (75), and Iran University of Science and Technology (74).
Tabriz University of Medical Sciences with 66 researchers, Iran University of Medical Sciences with 64 researchers, University of Tabriz with 61 researchers, and Tarbiat Modares University with 56 researchers are placed fifth to eighth.
Also, the number of highly cited Iranian researchers in the career-long index has experienced threefold growth, rising from 433 in 2020 to 1,380 in 2026.
Some 794 out of 1,380 researchers, amounting to 57.5 percent, are from 30 universities and scientific centers. University of Tehran (with 91 researchers), Sharif University of Technology (53), Amirkabir University of Technology and Tehran University of Medical Sciences (each with 48 researchers), and Iran University of Science and Technology (45), University of Tabriz and Tarbiat Modares University (each with 40 researchers) rank first to fifth.
Stanford University’s list of “World’s Top 2%” scientists is based on a 2 percent or above percentile rank, or the top 100,000 by c-score (with and without self-citations). This prestigious list identifies the world’s leading researchers, representing approximately 2 percent of all scientists worldwide.
It encompasses standardized data on citations, h-index, and a wide range of bibliometric indicators. Researchers are classified into 22 scientific fields and 174 sub-fields, drawing from Scopus data provided by Elsevier through ICSR Lab.
The esteemed ranking, derived from Scopus database data, highlights researchers whose work has had a significant impact across various scientific disciplines.
The ranking is based on a composite indicator (c-score) calculated from six citation metrics: Total citations (NC), H-index (H), Hm-index (H-index adjusted for the number of authors), Citations to single-author papers (NCS), Citations to single or first-author papers (NCSF), Citations to single, first, or last-author papers (NCSFL).

Japan signs deal for Ukrainian SkyFall interceptor drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:36:17 UTC
20:36:17 KST

- Japan’s Ministry of Defense has signed a contract to buy interceptor drones from Ukrainian manufacturer SkyFall, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said.
- Koizumi did not disclose the model, quantity, value or delivery date, saying only that Japan is working to get them delivered quickly.
Japan’s Ministry of Defense has signed a contract to buy interceptor drones from Ukrainian manufacturer SkyFall, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said, making Japan one of the first countries outside Europe to order Ukrainian drones built to shoot down Russian attack drones.
Koizumi announced the deal at a press briefing but did not say which SkyFall model Japan ordered, how many drones it is buying, what the contract is worth or when deliveries will begin.
“The Japanese Ministry of Defense has already signed a contract to purchase interceptor drones from the Ukrainian company SkyFall. We are currently working to ensure their delivery as soon as possible,” said Koizumi.
Koizumi also pointed to the speed of Ukraine’s development cycle, noting that drones with updated features reach Ukrainian units every two to three weeks based on battlefield feedback.
SkyFall builds the P1-SUN family of interceptors, small, fast drones that Ukrainian crews fly into Russian Shahed-type attack drones to destroy them. The company says Ukrainian forces shot down more than 3,500 Shaheds with P1-SUN interceptors over six months. Its newest version, the P1-SUN JetKiller, was unveiled in July at the Farnborough International Airshow to counter Russia’s faster jet-powered drones. SkyFall says the JetKiller reaches 370 km/h (230 mph), flies up to 30 km (18 miles), operates as high as 9,000 meters (29,500 feet) and carries a 500-gram (1.1-pound) warhead. Variants are offered with day or night cameras and with an AI module for automatic target detection and lock-on.
In late September, SkyFall released footage it said showed a JetKiller destroying a Russian Geran-5 jet-powered drone. The company has said it is aiming for a production rate of 50,000 interceptors a month and signed an agreement with Airbus Defence and Space in June to link the P1-SUN family to Airbus’s air command-and-control system for European air defense.
Japan has been moving quickly to field interceptor drones of its own. Its Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency launched a rapid acquisition program in June aimed at countering long-range one-way attack drones such as the Shahed, and received proposals from 38 companies. After the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force tested four candidate models between July 15 and Aug. 6, the agency signed a mass-production contract on Aug. 25 with Japanese firm Terra Drone for its Terra B1 interceptor.

This beer-making waste may offer a new stream for cleaner water
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:35:34 UTC
20:35:34 KST

Scientists still haven’t cracked how to turn water into wine—but they might have figured out how to turn beer into clean water. From the literal ashes of breweries’ by-products, researchers made a charcoal-like substance that clings to bacteria, and they are using it to test a new way of filtering water.
In a recent study, scientists heated up a common waste product from beer making called spent malt rootlets, which are little sprouts that grow from barley during the malting process, to produce biochar, a porous material created from burned organic matter. They found that when they mixed this substance with sand and sent water through it, the biochar was able to remove around five times as much Escherichia coli bacteria as a filtration system that used only sand.
Sending water through sand filtered bacteria like a colander: by physically stopping microbes from moving through. But when the team used a sand mix that was 10 percent biochar, the biochar actively glommed on to slow microbes’ passage.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Groundwater is constantly moving through soil. There it can become contaminated with agricultural waste or fecal matter—potentially infecting any humans who drink it. Adding biochar to certain soils could offer a public health solution and “a sustainable approach for water remediation and the protection of groundwater,” says Ioannis Manariotis, senior author on the study and an environmental engineer at the University of Patras in Greece.
Manariotis and his team have also tested whether waste from olive oil and coffee production can have similar water-purifying effects. Now that the researchers have found the beer by-product can filter out bacteria in laboratory conditions, he says, they plan to test its efficacy under more unpredictable real-life conditions. The results were published in the journal Biochar.
Using brewery waste for water filtration in this way is a “proof of concept,” says Alcina Johnson Sudagar, an independent chemistry researcher who studies other beer-making by-products and was not involved in the study. But the repurposing of by-products from this industry for other applications is already common, she says. Leftover brewery grain is frequently used to make animal feed, and other research suggests beer-making by-products can be used for everything from sunscreen to electricity. The brewing process can have up to 11 steps, and each step produces organic waste materials with different chemical makeups—potentially ideal for different uses.
Sudagar says she hopes Manariotis and his team continue to study biochar. Her most pressing question is whether the material can be used more than once for filtration. If it can trap bacteria only once, it quickly becomes waste again, negating its value as a consistent filtration system or sustainable brewery by-product.
As the global beer industry grows, these new and innovative ways of using the by-products are crucial to sustainability, Sudagar adds. “It’s important to continue because the waste produced will keep increasing, and you would need different applications,” she says. “You cannot just send it to one place and say that we are done with it.”

Iran proposes BRICS intl. network of photonics labs
TEHRAN – Iran has proposed the establishment of an international network of photonics laboratories among BRICS member states to strengthen scientific cooperation and facilitate access to advanced research infrastructure.
The proposed network would enable researchers across member countries to access laboratory equipment and specialized services, while making better use of existing capacities in fabrication, characterization, testing, and calibration, as well as other specialized infrastructure essential to photonics research.
Vahid Jan-Nesari, an official with the Headquarters for Science, Technology, and Knowledge-Based Economy, presented the proposal during the sixth meeting of the Photonics Working Group, held online from October 3 to 6 in Bengaluru, India.
He also highlighted the need for the promotion of interactions among researchers and scientific centers of BRICS member states, the expansion of collaborations through the exchange of professors, researchers, and students, the transformation of scientific cooperation into joint technological and industrial projects, and the development of targeted collaborative efforts.
Holding periodic meetings, establishing specific plans, and concentrating on a limited number of actionable and measurable objectives to be achieved by the next meeting were among Iran’s other proposals put forward at the meeting.
The 6th BRICS Working Group Meeting on Photonics convened BRICS delegates to advance photonics in communication, computing, and sensing.
The key outcomes focused on joint research, shared research infrastructure, human resource development, and stronger industry-academia partnerships across member nations.
