Turkish hunter drone destroys target by direct hit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:28:22 UTC
20:28:22 KST

- ASELSAN’s GÖKALP E1 interceptor drone destroyed a target drone by direct impact during a demonstration in Ankara, guided by AURA radar and DRONEDEF software.
- GÖKALP is part of Türkiye’s Steel Dome counter-drone layer, but no order, production schedule or price has been announced.
Turkish defense electronics maker ASELSAN has shown its GÖKALP interceptor drone destroying a target drone in mid-air by flying straight into it, in a live demonstration at the company’s Oğulbey Technology Base in Ankara.
In the test, ASELSAN’s AURA radar picked up the incoming target drone and passed tracking data in real time to a GÖKALP E1 interceptor through the company’s DRONEDEF command-and-control software. The interceptor then flew to the target and destroyed it by direct impact, an approach known as hit-to-kill. ASELSAN did not say when the demonstration took place, what kind of drone served as the target, or how far away and how high the intercept happened.
GÖKALP is a vehicle-mounted system that finds threats with radar and electro-optical sensors and launches interceptor drones that hunt down hostile drones on their own. ASELSAN pitches it as a mobile and cheaper option for dealing with drones, since an interceptor drone costs far less than a surface-to-air missile. Media in Türkiye, citing the company, reported an effective range of more than 1,000 meters (3,280 feet) against the smallest class of drones and more than 7,000 meters (4.3 miles) against larger ones.
The company unveiled GÖKALP in May at the SAHA 2026 defense exhibition in Istanbul, describing it as an AI-powered, high-speed interceptor built to destroy FPV attack drones and one-way attack drones. ASELSAN said then that the system is intended to protect tanks and armored personnel carriers from small drones in high-intensity combat. It also introduced MİĞFER, a separate hard-kill system mounted on a 4×4 armored vehicle to defend against FPV drones.
GÖKALP is part of DRONEDEF, ASELSAN’s counter-drone layer within Steel Dome, Türkiye’s integrated air defense network. DRONEDEF combines jammers, guns, lasers and high-power microwave weapons, including the İHTAR anti-drone system, the GÖKBERK laser weapon, the KORKUT 100/25 SB anti-drone gun and the EJDERHA high-power electromagnetic system. Türkiye approved the Steel Dome project in August 2024, with ASELSAN as its lead contractor. The company signed a $1.9 billion Steel Dome contract with Türkiye’s defense procurement agency in September 2025 and a further €780 million (about $905 million) deal this year, with deliveries planned from 2028 to 2032.
Interceptor drones have become a common answer to cheap attack drones, most visibly in Ukraine, where forces use them in large numbers against Russian Shahed-type drones. Several Western companies are developing similar systems for NATO armies.

Iran retains missile, drone production capabilities despite months of US-Israeli strikes - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:23:09 UTC
20:23:09 KST

Iran has retained the ability to manufacture ballistic missiles and drones despite eight months of US and Israeli airstrikes, allowing Tehran to replenish its weapons stockpiles as US President Donald Trump debates delaying further military action until after the November midterm elections, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing Western officials familiar with intelligence assessments.
The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Iran had preserved parts of its weapons manufacturing infrastructure despite extensive strikes targeting its military-industrial capabilities.
One Western official assessed that Tehran still possesses significant stocks of ballistic missiles and certain anti-ship weapons, with the capacity to manufacture additional munitions relatively quickly.
The official also claimed that Russia has been supplying Iran with missiles, consistent with a separate intelligence assessment from June. Russia's Defense Ministry did not respond to Bloomberg's request for comment.
The findings contrast with repeated assertions by Trump administration officials that the US-Israeli military campaign has effectively dismantled Iran's ability to threaten American military installations and regional allies.
Trump previously described Iran's military as "totally destroyed," while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on September 30 that US operations had destroyed Iran's "military industrial capacity" and "their entire defense base."
White House disputes assessment of Iran's military capabilities
White House spokesperson Anna Kelly rejected the Western officials' assessment, defending the effectiveness of American operations against Iran's nuclear and conventional military infrastructure.
“First, President Trump obliterated Iran’s nuclear facilities during Operation Midnight Hammer,” Kelly said in a statement.
“Then, Operation Epic Fury successfully destroyed the conventional shield that Iran sought to create over a nuclear program, including their ballistic missiles, production facilities, and navy.”
The extent of damage to Iran's missile industry has remained disputed. A September report, citing US and Middle Eastern officials, indicated that Tehran had resumed limited ballistic missile production using existing components, including at underground facilities, although manufacturing remained below prewar levels.
Trump announced on Thursday that the US would refrain from attacking Iran before the November midterm elections, after previously considering renewed military strikes amid escalating attacks on commercial shipping.
The pause could provide Tehran with additional time to restore production and replenish its arsenals, according to the Western assessments.
Iran has intensified attacks on vessels operating near the Strait of Hormuz, with at least 10 ships struck over the preceding week, according to the UK Navy.
The attacks have increased concerns about maritime security and potential disruption to global energy supplies, particularly as the US continues its naval blockade of Iranian oil exports.
In September, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that it could deploy different weapons and strike new targets if Washington launched another offensive, signaling its intention to maintain military pressure despite the damage sustained during the war.
Iran's remaining missile arsenal raises questions
The US-Israeli air campaign likely inflicted significant long-term damage on Iran's prewar missile production infrastructure, according to an assessment by Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst and visiting research fellow at King's College London.
However, the precise size of Iran's remaining arsenal remains uncertain.
Israeli estimates placed Tehran's ballistic missile stockpile at approximately 2,500 before the war, while Western intelligence assessments in June suggested Iran still possessed roughly three-quarters of its prewar munitions.
Earlier Israeli military assessments indicated that extensive strikes on Iranian military-industrial facilities could require years of reconstruction, although the ability to restore launchers and other components remained a concern.
The discrepancy between assessments of Iran's remaining stockpiles and its manufacturing capacity highlights the difficulty of determining how much military capability Tehran can regenerate without further external assistance.
A separate August assessment described how Iran had used periods of reduced fighting to repair launchers, restore access to underground facilities and accelerate efforts to rebuild missile and drone production. Analysts cautioned that such activity did not necessarily mean Tehran had recovered its full prewar capabilities.
For Washington and Israel, Iran's continued access to ballistic missiles and anti-ship weapons raises concerns about its ability to retaliate against renewed military action.
With the Islamic Republic facing mounting economic pressure from the US naval blockade, Western officials assessed that Tehran could increasingly rely on asymmetric operations, including attacks on maritime traffic, to impose costs on its militarily superior adversaries.

While casting his ballot at a polling station on Sept. 20, the party leader had written four Yabloko campaign slogans across the papers: “For Peace,” “For Freedom,” “For a Life Without Fear,” and “For a Ceasefire Agreement.”
Rybakov and his legal defense sought the dismissal of all administrative charges, maintaining that spoiling an election ballot constitutes a legally recognized form of political expression under Russian law.

Systemic crackdown on Yabloko

US Envoys Pressure Kyiv on Refinery Strikes
Three prominent Yabloko figures have received prison sentences over the past four months, including party activist Yelena Perepelitsa on Thursday. Ahead of the Sept. 18-20 legislative vote, electoral authorities systematically excluded Yabloko from contesting the party-list ballot for the lower house.
In single-mandate constituencies where individual members were permitted to launch campaigns, candidates faced arbitrary police detentions, disqualifications, and administrative interference.

The suppression of anti-war dissent widened following the election, in which the ruling United Russia party secured a record majority in the 450-seat State Duma.
On Sunday, Oct. 4, Russian police detained approximately 60 demonstrators during an authorized Communist Party (KPRF) demonstration in Moscow after attendees began chanting slogans criticizing censorship, demanding the release of political prisoners, and shouting “Down with the Tsar.”
Independent monitoring group OVD-Info reported that roughly 30 Yabloko members and 26 KPRF representatives were among those detained in the capital.
International non-recognition
The prosecution of opposition figures follows widespread international condemnation of the electoral process, which Russian authorities also conducted across occupied territories of southern and eastern Ukraine.
The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) adopted a formal resolution refusing to recognize the legitimacy of the newly formed State Duma, determining that the Sept. 18-20 vote was neither free nor fair.
Lawmakers representing 46 member states affirmed that forced participation in Russian-organized elections within occupied Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, and Crimea violates international law and cannot confer sovereignty to the Russian Federation.
The resolution called on European governments to enforce diplomatic isolation against the legislature, broaden personal sanctions against Russia’s Central Election Commission, and restrict Schengen visa privileges for Russian officials.
Ukrainian authorities and international human rights monitors documented that early voting in occupied Ukrainian settlements was conducted under the direct supervision of armed Russian servicemen and mobile election squads without independent observers from the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), prompting Kyiv to enact statutory sanctions against 44 individuals involved in administering the vote.

What has Trump’s Board of Peace achieved in a year since Gaza ‘ceasefire’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:19:24 UTC
20:19:24 KST

What has Trump’s Board of Peace achieved in a year since Gaza ‘ceasefire’?
Analysts say board has ‘failed’ in its attempts to secure lasting peace in Gaza.
It has been one year since United States President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace (BoP) brokered a “ceasefire” aimed at eventually ending Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.
However, rather than receiving relief and a chance to rebuild, Palestinians in the enclave continue to face attacks and be uprooted as Israeli forces have expanded control within the territory.
Trump first proposed the BoP in September 2025, saying it would stabilise Gaza and ensure lasting peace.
In November, a United Nations Security Council resolution recognised the board as a “transitional administration” in Gaza.
But what has the board achieved? Here’s what we know:
What were the BoP’s goals?
The BoP’s mission was laid out in Trump’s 20-point Gaza peace plan, as was the “ceasefire” between Israel and Hamas. The ceasefire began on October 10, 2025.
The plan envisioned steps for each side to take that could eventually create a “credible pathway” to Palestinian statehood.
It required Israeli forces to withdraw to about 50 percent of the Gaza Strip and cease aerial and artillery bombardments. It also required Israel to release 250 Palestinian prisoners and another 1,700 people jailed from Gaza since October 7, 2023, the day that Hamas led attacks into southern Israel and Israel began the war. The plan proposed reopening border crossings to allow much-needed aid into Gaza.
The peace plan required Hamas to release all Israeli captives. It also proposed a later phase in which the group would disarm and its members would be granted amnesty or a safe exit from Gaza.
The peace plan established the BoP as a transitional governing body until the Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the occupied West Bank, could take over.
An International Stabilization Force (ISF), led by the US, was supposed to take over security in Gaza from withdrawing Israeli forces, the plan stated. It also proposed the reconstruction and redevelopment of Gaza, whose people, it said, “have suffered enough”.
What has the BoP done in the past year?
In February, the BoP’s members, who each joined in exchange for a $1bn annual fee, met in Washington, DC, for its first summit, at which member states pledged $7bn in funding although aid agencies said reconstructing Gaza would cost closer to $70bn.
On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month, the BoP also unveiled a 66-project recovery plan worth $2.4bn.
What has BoP achieved?
The BoP’s achievements are tied to the success of the Gaza peace plan.
Under that, Hamas has released all 168 living captives and Israel has freed Palestinian prisoners.
Hamas has also announced the dissolution of its government in the Gaza Strip although Israel has dismissed that as a “stunt”.
Other goals under the peace plan have been only partially met.
Governance has been hampered. While a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), meant to act as the governing authority in Gaza, was founded, Israel has not granted it entry into the Strip. The NCAG reports directly to the board and is led by Chief Commissioner Ali Shaath and other Palestinian technocrats. It operates from Cairo. Israel has not stated why the committee is not permitted to enter Gaza.
Aid remains restricted. About 227 aid trucks enter the Strip daily when 600 trucks were supposed to, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) hunger monitor.
Israel has classified thousands of basic items, such as tents and essential equipment like ventilators, as “dual use” items, which means they have military and civilian applications, and has restricted their flow into the Strip. About 1.4 million Palestinians – or most of Gaza’s more than 2 million people – will suffer hunger until at least December, the IPC has noted. That is 200,000 more than those who faced hunger in May, suggesting a significantly deteriorating situation.
What has not been achieved?
Observers argued that the BoP has entirely failed to secure the “ceasefire” as Israeli attacks have continued almost daily on the Strip.
Since October 10, 2025, more than 1,400 Palestinians, mostly women and children, have been killed. In the three years since the war began, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, and thousands more are missing and presumed dead under the rubble.
Israel says its continuing attacks target Hamas members, but the group vehemently denies the claims.
Israel also now occupies about 60 percent of the Strip, more than the 50 percent agreed in Trump’s peace plan. The “Yellow Line”, which demarcates the area of Gaza under Israeli occupation, has been pushed farther into the Strip, causing further displacement and squeezing Gaza’s population into an ever-shrinking area. Palestinians unknowingly crossing the “Yellow Line” have been shot dead.
In December, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said the army “will never fully leave” the Strip.
Mohamad Elmasry at the Doha Institute of Graduate Studies told Al Jazeera that Israel is simply continuing a broader policy of “ethnic cleansing” in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. “They are making life miserable,” he said, adding: “This is all by design.”
Consequently, the BoP has also failed to ensure Hamas disarms so phase two of the peace plan could begin.
Although Hamas has agreed to hand its weapons over to the NCAG, it rejects the “disarmament” clause because Israel has not ceased its attacks or withdrawn from the Strip as agreed. At the same time, Israel has said it will not move forward with the plan if Hamas does not disarm, leaving the two sides in a standoff.
Meanwhile, no stabilisation force has been deployed. Six countries – Indonesia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, Albania, Kosovo and Uganda – have so far committed personnel to form a security force of 20,000 soldiers and 12,000 police headed by the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM).
There has been no meaningful reconstruction in Gaza. Palestinians continue to live in tent camps infested with rodents and insects with little to shield them from intense heat, or rain.
Will BoP take over from UNRWA?
The Trump administration and BoP have echoed Israel’s rejection of the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, or UNRWA, which has long provided lifesaving humanitarian aid, education, development programmes and social services in Gaza and employs about 11,000 Palestinians.
The BoP said last month that it will not work with UNRWA, essentially sidelining the agency.
A BoP official told The Associated Press news agency that UNRWA could continue working in Gaza if its programmes were deemed relevant but the agency’s “days are over”.
UNRWA said the move was “not logical”.
In June, the UN General Assembly voted overwhelmingly to extend UNRWA’s mandate until 2029. The BoP itself is mandated to oversee the peace process until December 2027 when its progress will be reviewed for possible renewal by the UN.
Analysts and rights groups have raised concerns that the BoP could take over all aspects of Gaza’s rebuilding. Countries too, including France and other European nations, have called out any attempts to replace the UN in the Strip.
But Elmasry said no country is willing to take action. “There are a lot of international actors that do not want to cross the US,” he said. That essentially leaves the fate of more than 2 million Palestinians to Trump, he added.
Ultimately, the BoP has “failed”, said Simon Mabon, a professor at Lancaster University.
“The failure to implement its own plan to end the Gaza conflict demonstrates its impotence and the inability to ensure that Israel and, to a lesser extent, Hamas, remain bound by their own commitments [and] has allowed the genocide to continue,” he concluded.

Downing Street's chief mouser Larry underwent surgery and returned to the government residence
Kyiv • UNN
The 19-year-old cat Larry underwent surgery to remove a cyst and returned to the government residence. He is gradually recovering and is once again wandering around the\r\nbuilding.
Larry the cat, who holds the position of chief mouser at Downing Street, has undergone surgery and has already returned to the British government residence. The 19-year-old Downing Street resident, who has served there since 2011, is gradually recovering. The Telegraph reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, after having a cyst removed, the 19-year-old cat is recovering and "feeling much better", despite a large scar and shaved fur.
In February, the tabby cat with white patches celebrated 15 years as chief mouser at the government office at 10 Downing Street.
He arrived from the Battersea Dogs & Cats Home in 2011 and became one of the few permanent residents of Downing Street. He now lives under the same roof as his seventh prime minister.
A Downing Street representative said that Larry is "feeling well" and "is already roaming the building again".
He is feeling much better but is gradually returning to his usual routine. We are grateful to the veterinarians for their exceptional care
Andy Burnham, who reportedly decided not to take his dog to the prime minister's residence out of concern that Axel and Larry "would not get along", is reportedly considering getting a cat for "10 Downing Street North" — the office he opened in Manchester shortly after taking office.
During Sir Keir Starmer's premiership, Larry shared Downing Street with Jojo, a cat rescued from a shelter, and a Siberian kitten named Prince.
Larry has already served more Downing Street residents than any of his predecessors. However, to become the longest-serving mouser, he will have to spend another two years battling mice in Westminster.
Since arriving at Downing Street in 2011, Larry has already lived with his seventh prime minister.
This record also belongs to Peter III, who held the position from 1947 to 1964, but served under only five prime ministers — Clement Attlee, Winston Churchill, Anthony Eden, Harold Macmillan and Alec Douglas-Home.
The first cat named Peter was the second cat to hold the official position of mouser, replacing a cat named Treasury Bill. He served in the position for 17 years.
Between the two cats was Peter II, who got the job when he was only two months old. However, six months later he was hit by a car on Whitehall and was put down shortly afterwards.

Lebanon bets on AI while struggling to keep the lights on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:15:48 UTC
20:15:48 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon wants to train 1 million people on AI skills. But there's a catch
The United Arab Emirates and Lebanon have launched an initiative to train one million Lebanese in artificial intelligence (AI), raising questions about how the country can turn the ambitious target into practical skills, jobs and economic growth amid a prolonged economic crisis.
The One Million Lebanese AI Experts initiative was announced on 25 September during a meeting between UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed and Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
It is among the first deals to emerge after a UAE delegation of 70 business leaders and government officials that visited Beirut in August and signed a series of bilateral agreements and memorandums of understanding aimed at strengthening economic cooperation.
Launched under the UAE’s Government Experience Exchange Programme in cooperation with the Lebanese government, the initiative will provide training in generative AI and prompt engineering, aiming to equip one million people with practical skills to use AI tools in their daily lives.
The initiative comes as Lebanon seeks to expand its role in the sector. President Joseph Aoun recently visited an AI exhibition in Beirut and urged parliament to expedite legislation establishing a dedicated Ministry of Artificial Intelligence. He also rejected suggestions that Lebanon was ill-equipped to keep pace with technological advances, saying more than 27 percent of the population used AI, according to local media reports.
Kamal Chehadeh, minister of the displaced and minister of state for technology and artificial intelligence, has been tasked with advancing the government’s digital transformation agenda. A dedicated ministry would formalise the role, but its establishment depends on the relevant legislation.
The broader challenge is whether training at such scale can translate into demonstrable skills, better employment prospects and wider economic benefits – and whether Lebanon’s ageing infrastructure can support the country’s AI ambitions.
Measuring success beyond the numbers
Sheila Jagannathan, vice president for strategic relationships at Saylor University, a non-profit online university, said the target was ambitious but realistic if the initiative focused on practical skills rather than attempting to produce one million AI engineers.
Success should be measured not only by enrolment and course completion, but also by whether participants can apply what they learn in their work, studies and businesses, she said.
"AI literacy is not simply knowing how to ask AI a question. It is knowing how to use the answer, verify it, challenge it – and when not to use AI," Jagannathan told The New Arab.
She said training should reflect the needs of different professions, from teachers using AI to develop lessons, to entrepreneurs researching markets and public officials analysing information or improving services. Employers and government agencies should help shape the programme, while learners should have opportunities to apply their skills through practical projects.
She also cautioned against treating AI training as a one-off exercise, arguing that participants would need ways to continue learning as the technology evolves.
Lebanon’s potential and what is missing
Lebanon’s universities and educated workforce provide a foundation for AI development, but turning those strengths into economic gains will require investment and a supportive environment for business and innovation.
Chronic electricity shortages have disrupted businesses, public services and everyday life for many people in Lebanon, adding to the challenges of expanding access to the digital tools needed for AI training and adoption.
Dr Zaher Dawy, provost and professor of engineering at the American University of Beirut, said Lebanon needed stronger infrastructure, appropriate regulatory incentives and partnerships between academia, industry and government.
"The way forward in Lebanon must include both adoption and innovation," Dawy told The New Arab, arguing that individuals and institutions should be equipped to use AI responsibly while the country develops an entrepreneurial ecosystem capable of creating AI-driven products and businesses.
Generative AI and prompt engineering could provide a starting point, but Jagannathan said building lasting AI capabilities would also require critical thinking, data literacy, verification and responsible use. Training would need to be tailored to different groups and professions, from public servants to software developers.
Can AI help Lebanon retain its talent?
Whether the initiative creates opportunities inside Lebanon will be central to its longer-term impact, particularly if better-trained workers struggle to find suitable jobs at home.
Dawy said sustained investment in data, computing and AI capacity could eventually help Lebanon export technology, products and services rather than its talent.
Achieving that would require more than training, however. Businesses would need to be able to employ skilled workers, access computing infrastructure, and attract investment, while entrepreneurs would need conditions that encourage them to establish and grow companies locally.
The one-million target therefore presents both an opportunity and a test for Lebanese-UAE cooperation. The number of people trained will measure the initiative’s reach; its wider success will depend on whether participants can apply their skills and whether Lebanon can provide opportunities for them to put those skills to work.

Prime minister slams US-Russia diesel pact: Deals with dictators 'road to hell'
Prime Minister Kristen Michal has sharply criticized the US decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying agreements with dictators lead to hell.
Trump said Friday that Russia had agreed to bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the world market immediately, with more to follow, under a temporary US licence.
Ahead of next month's midterm elections, US President Donald Trump has struck a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply millions of tonnes of diesel to the world market, a move Trump said was essential to bring down fuel prices.
The US issued a temporary license for Russian diesel supplies to the world market, valid until April 7 next year.
"This is a major miscalculation, because deals with dictators are the road to hell. Innocent people are being killed for gas and fuel money. And what is very likely is that the hoped-for fuel will not come," the prime minister noted on social media.
"Such an agreement runs counter to the Western world's long-standing efforts to limit the flow of money from energy carriers to [Vladimir] Putin. The US has until now persuaded its allies to abandon Russian fuel — we have too," Michal said.

"If it is true that this was accompanied by a Washington threat to Kyiv to stop sharing intelligence if the attacks continue, then this gives Moscow only one unambiguous signal — kill and destroy Ukraine, the US will not stand in the way," he added.
Mihkelson said Trump's efforts to end the war through negotiations have produced not the slightest result.
"The fighting is bloodier than at any previous moment in the entire full-scale invasion," he said. "If you give an aggressor oxygen, the war will not stop."
He stressed that Europe's allies have only one path — to ensure Russia's strategic attack goals fail and the Kremlin's imperial wars end in defeat.
"This clear strategic goal should also be in the US interest, because Russia's long-standing desire, together with China and Iran, to weaken the United States' leadership role is reaching a decisive phase," Mihkelson continued.
Ahead of next month's midterm elections, U.S. President Donald Trump has struck a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply millions of tonnes of diesel to the world market, reversing years of Western pressure on the Kremlin. Trump said the move was essential to bring down fuel prices, which have soared since Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and warned of a diesel export ban on any EU states that do not release reserves to counter the spike. The G7 agreed earlier this week to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from reserves.

"I would hope this will lead European allies to realize even more clearly the need to support Ukraine and try to close the loopholes in their own sanctions, so that even if this fuel reaches America, it won't find its way into Europe through the back door. I think this could mobilize Europeans to provide even more support for Ukraine because that's the only option," he said.
Terras added that Trump's actions are unpredictable and may not benefit him.
"The deal struck with Putin is a win-win for Putin. He came out ahead both economically and politically. He demonstrated to the world that Putin is needed to save the global economy. That's actually absurd," Terras said.
Kallas: US-Russia diesel agreement helping to fund Kremlin's war of aggression
An agreement between the United States and Russia to lift sanctions on Russian diesel fuel provides Moscow with "more revenue to wage the war," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Saturday. Kallas added that Russian attacks have caused the death of more than 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days and that Moscow has "intensified its hybrid attacks against Europe, both against EU member states and NATO allies."

====================================================================================================

US midterms: Women candidates could make history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:11:00 UTC
20:11:00 KST

US midterms: Women candidates could make history
October 10, 2026
Around 51% of the population of the United States is female, but that is not reflected in the make-up of the US Congress, where only 28.4% of the members are women. Nevertheless, with 152 women in total sitting in the House of Representatives and Senate, the number is higher than it has ever been in the history of the United States. The number of female governors of the 50 US states is also currently higher than ever before: Some 14 of them — 28% — are women.
There are a number of reasons why there are still comparatively few female representatives in the US Congress. "Some of them are structural: There are rules and processes in place in our political system that make it harder for any newcomers to break in," says Kelly Dittmar, director of research at the Center for American Women and Politics (CAWP) at Rutgers University. "Historically, women were newcomers."
Seats in the Senate only come up for election every six years. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms, but there is no limit to the number of times they can stand for reelection, so in theory they can stay in office for decades.
Also, as Dittmar points out, election campaigns in the US are very expensive. Women have historically been less able to access networks of rich donors — who, like many party leaders, are still most likely to be men. Leading male politicians are also more likely to recruit men to stand as new candidates. Finally, cultural biases also play a role: "Stereotypes and expectations about what women can and should do."
The elections on November 3 will decide whether more or fewer women will sit in the US Congress over the next two years. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election in the midterms. And in 36 states, the citizens will also decide who will move in to the governor's villa.
House of Representatives: Female Democrats outnumber female Republicans three to one
125 of the 435 representatives in the House are women. As in the Senate, and also with the gubernatorial posts, they are not evenly distributed between the two parties: There are more women among the Democrats than among the Republicans. At present, there are 95 women sitting as representatives for the Democrats, and 30 for the Republicans.
"There is a far less robust support infrastructure for women within the Republican Party," says Dittmar. She comments that organizations that specifically recruit, train, and fund women candidates are almost all either on the Democrat side, or non-partisan. Besides, she adds, "A lot of the [Republican] party leaders don't see an electoral incentive or pressure" to recruit more women. Diversity is more important to Democrat voters, who place greater value on seeing women among their elected representatives.
The Republicans currently have a majority in the House of Representatives, which means that they also get to appoint the Speaker or majority leader. At the moment, the position is held by Mike Johnson. Only one woman has held this powerful post to date: Nancy Pelosi, who was the Democrats' Speaker from 2007 to 2011, and again from 2019 to 2023.
US Senate: Even higher bar for women
Women currently constitute 27% of the US Senate – 16 Democrats and 11 Republicans. Each of the 50 states is represented by two senators. The term of office is longer in this chamber of the US Congress, and the majority of the officials here represent many more voters than the representatives in the lower house.
According to Dittmar, it's even harder for women to win a seat in the Senate. "With the Senate, it's an opportunity and timing issue," she says. Each seat comes up for election every six years. There are 100 in total, and every two years only a third of them are available. Little opportunity, then, for women who have not previously sat in the Senate to advance. A state-wide senatorial election campaign is also more expensive than the equivalent campaign for a seat in the House of Representatives — and studies indicate that female candidates are generally less wealthy than their male counterparts.
For one senatorial candidate, the November midterms could prove historic. If the Democrat Peggy Flanagan wins in Minnesota, she will be the first Native American woman to sit in the US Senate. Flanagan is Ojibwe, otherwise known as Chippewa, an indigenous people from the Great Lakes region spanning the US and Canada.
Flanagan currently holds the post of lieutenant governor of Minnesota. Polls suggest that her chances are good. She has a slight lead over her rival, the Republican Michele Tafoya, previously a sports reporter and advisor to conservative politicians.
First black woman state governor?
Ten of the current 14 female governors are Democrats, while four are Republicans. Six of the 14 are standing again, including Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the governor of Arkansas, who was President Trump's press secretary during his first term in office.
For the first time in US history, it is possible that a Black woman may be elected state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Tim Walz — Kamala Harris's vice-presidential candidate in the 2024 election — is not standing for reelection. The main rivals for his seat are the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the (Black) Republican Lisa DeMuth. Meanwhile, the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is running for governor of the state of Georgia.
Kelly Dittmar doesn't think DeMuth will win in Minnesota — the state is regarded as solidly Democrat. And Klobuchar is well known among the people there; she has represented Minnesota in the US Senate since 2007.
But in Georgia, according to Dittmar, it's a different story: "That race is considered a toss-up, 50-50." Dittmar believes that Bottoms "absolutely has a chance to be the first Black woman governor." Former President Barack Obama is her most prominent supporter, while President Trump has declared his support for the Republican candidate, Rick Jackson.

Iran to send 29 athletes to 2026 Youth Olympics

Iran to send 29 athletes to 2026 Youth Olympics
TEHRAN - Iran will compete with a 29-athlete delegation across 14 sports at the fourth edition of the Youth Olympic Games, set to take place in Dakar, Senegal, from Oct. 31 to Nov. 13, following a four-year postponement.
The final composition of Iran’s team has grown from the initial quota after additional places were secured in judo and fencing. However, Senegal’s hosting of the Games and a reduced sports program compared with the previous edition are expected to make the medal race more challenging for the Iranian delegation.
The 13-day event will mark the first time the Youth Olympic Games are held on the African continent, with athletes competing across 25 sports for medals.
Iran will be represented in two team events: girls’ futsal, featuring 10 athletes, and boys’ beach volleyball, with two competitors. In individual sports, the country will field four athletes in beach wrestling; two each in taekwondo and badminton; and one athlete apiece in swimming, wushu taolu, triathlon, table tennis, boxing, road cycling, athletics, judo and épée fencing.
Iran has competed in all three previous editions of the Youth Olympic Games and won medals at each one. At the inaugural Games in Singapore in 2010, Iran claimed two gold, two silver and one bronze medal. Four years later in China, the team secured three golds and three bronzes.
Iran recorded its best-ever result at the 2018 Games in Buenos Aires, Argentina, winning seven gold, three silver and four bronze medals.
Repeating that performance in Dakar, however, will be a difficult task. The number of sports and athletes has been reduced for this edition, limiting medal opportunities. One notable absence is weightlifting, traditionally a major source of medals for Iranian sport. According to the current program, the sport will not feature in Dakar, with Senegal lacking a national weightlifting federation.
Despite the challenges, Iran’s performance at the Asian Youth Games in Bahrain has raised hopes for the country’s emerging athletes. Dakar will also provide a valuable opportunity to assess the potential of different sports and give young competitors important international experience as they progress toward senior-level competition.
With 23 medals won across the three previous editions, Iran will arrive in Dakar aiming to maintain its record of reaching the podium. Although the narrower range of medal opportunities makes another record-breaking campaign less likely, the performances of the participating athletes could offer important indications of the next generation’s prospects in international sport.

US sanctions on ICC face broad opposition worldwide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
11:08:09 UTC
20:08:09 KST

- Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose arrest ICC has sought since November 2024, backs US sanctions
The US decision Friday to impose sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) drew widespread opposition Friday, including from Washington's closest allies, exposing a diplomatic divide over international justice amid the court's pursuit of Israeli leaders accused of war crimes in Gaza.
Six European countries, Canada and Japan jointly rejected the sanctions, while the EU and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres separately condemned Washington's decision.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions on Friday, warning that Washington would continue its campaign to dismantle the court unless it ended what he described as threats against Americans.
“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Rubio said, urging US allies that are members of the court to intervene.
The escalation came amid longstanding US opposition to the court's jurisdiction over American nationals and its November 2024 arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes in Gaza.
Neither the US nor Israel is a member of the ICC, which has 125 states parties.
 
- US allies reject sanctions
In a joint statement challenging Washington's decision, the foreign ministers of Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands and the UK, alongside their Canadian and Japanese counterparts, expressed their strong disagreement with the sanctions.
"We, the undersigned States Parties to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC), reaffirm our continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC," they said.
The eight countries warned that the sanctions could significantly affect the court's operations, staff and their families, pledging to work together to uphold international accountability.
Switzerland separately voiced opposition to the measures aimed at “undermining the independence of the Court and its ability to fulfill its mandate.”
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten also vowed to defend the Hague-based court.
"I think now the message to the United States is crystal clear: We will do whatever we need to defend the ICC," he said.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot strongly condemned the sanctions and called for the activation of the EU Blocking Statute to protect the court and those supporting its work.
"The Court's independence cannot depend on whom it investigates," Prevot said.
 
- EU considers measures to protect court
The European Commission described Washington’s announcement as "deeply regrettable" and reaffirmed the bloc's commitment to protecting the ICC's independence and operations.
"The EU stands ready to take any necessary measures to enable the Court to carry out its work both in investigating and prosecuting war crimes and crimes against humanity, and to protect the interests of EU operators within the Single Market," it said.
The bloc pledged to work with all 125 ICC member states to safeguard the institution and said the six-month period before the sanctions take effect provided an opportunity for dialogue with Washington.
Likewise, European Council President Antonio Costa said the EU would adopt "adequate measures" to protect the court, its members and staff.
 
- UN warns of blow to international justice
For the United Nations, Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the sanctions, warning that they threatened efforts to hold perpetrators of serious international crimes accountable.
"Today's decision marks a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar," he said in a statement issued through his spokesperson.
Guterres also expressed deep alarm over the potential impact on the court's ability to carry out its mandate and urged countries to uphold their obligations under international law.
 
- ICC vows to continue work despite sanctions
The ICC strongly rejected the US measures against itself, describing them as an assault on the rule of law and an attempt to obstruct justice.
The court said the sanctions sought to disrupt its operations and intimidate those working for or cooperating with the institution.
"The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes," ICC President Tomoko Akane said.
Akane, who was personally sanctioned by Washington in August, is among several ICC judges and prosecutors targeted by the US before the latest measures against the court itself.
The court urged its 125 member states to take concrete steps to safeguard its operations, stressing that the dispute went beyond the future of a single institution.
"This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law," it said.
 
- Israel sole public supporter of US sanctions
Israel, meanwhile, was the only country to publicly welcome the US sanctions among governments that had issued reactions as of Friday.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu praised President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Rubio for the decision.
“The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty,” Netanyahu wrote on X.

I Made Terrible Games With Google’s AI Playground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Neon Don is really pissed at his ex-wife’s lawyer. He’ll tell you any chance he gets while he shotguns lines of pixelated bad guys. He’s also not real—his likeness has only existed for a few minutes in a top-down cyberpunk-style shooter game, generated in the Google Labs service, Playground.
“Keep shooting!” Neon Don says as he mows enemies down. “Brenda took everything else away!”
Playground, which Google launched this week, is part of Google Labs, the company’s landing page for its various AI experiments that haven’t made it into an app or official service quite yet. (Google has done this before with things like music production). It works similarly to Horizon Create, the game generation service Meta announced in September.
Playground is essentially vibe coding for video games, letting people describe in plain language what kind of game they want to make in a chatbot-like interface. Playground then builds a working in-browser version of a game. You can add further instructions to tweak the design from there. If you have assets you want to use as a reference, you can upload photos, videos, or models. Otherwise, the visuals and designs are all AI-generated.
The process of making a game is very straightforward, conversational, and responsive. That means it is perfect for dummies like me with little to no video game development chops or even decent coding skills. By simply throwing out some ideas, I built three playable, stable, and not even remotely good games in one day.
Pork Drop
My first work was Pork Drop, a result generated from the prompt: “Tetris but with cute pigs instead of blocks.” I typed that in, hit build. The AI chugged, then spit out a farm-themed version of Tetris with little pig faces drawn on every block.
I had to iterate a bit to realize my vision, telling the AI not just to stick pig faces on the blocks, but to have the blocks shaped like distorted pigs. “Each block is a pig,” I wrote, “contorted into the shape of the Tetris blocks. Make ’em look a little squished, but still cute!” This resulted in a clean, playable version of Tetris, though the occasional block looked like a T-posed pig with its legs spread eagle. The AI suggested the title Piggy Stacker, but I thought mine was better. (I’m right.)
Dinner Darling
The next game idea came courtesy of my colleague Jay Dayrit, who, when asked what kind of game I should make, immediately requested, “Gay dinner party.” I typed that in.
With no follow-up requests, the result was a 2D flash-style game called Dinner Darling. The art looks like everyone is a Bitmoji. You’re placed in the shoes of a very stressed-out-looking host, Julian, who is tasked with hosting a fancy dinner party with fussy guests who can’t seem to sit in their chairs at the table. As timers count down, you have to prepare various artisanal bruschettas and espresso martinis for your increasingly angry guests.
After it generates, I give the game a shot and fail miserably, unable to figure out the controls in time to bring my guests a timely pastry or cocktail. (Sasha, one of the guests, required numerous espresso cocktails in a row.) “PARTY CATASTROPHE,” the game over screen read.
There is no mention of anybody’s sexuality in the game at all, but when I lost, Dayrit called from across the office, “See? You're bad at the game because you're straight!” Well played, Playground.
My colleague Reece Rogers was less impressed when he looked at the game. “This is very unrealistic because there’s not a vegan or dairy-free option,” he said.
Neon Don
The game that took the most work is the one that has since been played the most by random people on Playground (anyone can sign in with their Google account and play these user-generated games). I’m up to seven unique players as of publication, which apparently means this game is my masterpiece.
I asked the AI to make a “cyberpunk-style rhythm game” where you play as a “very divorced” grizzled ex-cop who battles waves of rogue agents and corrupt politicians. It started as a Beat Saber-type title, but I asked the AI to make it more like the top-down shooter Hotline Miami. The result was Neon Don (title mine), a top-down, arcade-like shooter with pulsing synth wave background music.
Neon Don is also the game I tried to push the content bounds on, to see what Playground would let me get away with.
I described the enemies, and Playground AI added its own details on top, including “bulky, wide builds with prominent beer bellies straining against their tight tactical shirts and cargo pants” and “custom tough-guy swagger animations.” OK Playground, go off.
The game had several small issues at first. I countered them and added features a little bit at a time. I dictated systems for level scaling, boss generation, and better enemy variety. I flagged mobility issues, like the player getting stuck, and it fixed them. (And occasionally introduced other problems.) I asked it to develop a text-based snark system that made the main character respond to combat with witty in-character quips like, “Keep shooting! Brenda took everything else away!” or “I’ve taken worse hits from my ex-wife’s lawyer!”
I imagine that a real game developer would know what to actually say to sharpen features and make the game more fun or playable. Some of the top games people have created on the platform are much better than mine, since I tended to lean on more vibe-based iterative changes like, “Make Don taller” or “more divorced.”
Game Plan
After a certain point, Google throttles your usage of its Playground service. Every new game and iteration therein uses up more of your allowance. (Note for all my new loyal fans: Updates on my titles will be coming on October 14 when my usage allowance refreshes.)
That means my games still have many issues. I wanted to add a “Backflip” button to Neon Don, but the AI called it “Doge flip,” which I think sucks but cannot change until my usage credits recharge. I want to change the difficulty and add more weapon options. I want to do a lot of things, but I ain’t paying for more usage credits.
Playground does make me interested in the actual art of making video games. It’s fun, somewhat intuitive, and there are tangible results you can play with in real time. People are probably going to make some interesting stuff with it. But the limitations keep it from being truly useful.
Also, when you scroll through the Playground games, an unmistakable sameness permeates everything. Different game genres wind up with almost identical menus and music. You start to see the same types of combat options and style choices.
Playground is fun for a bit. But soon it becomes pretty clear it’s AI slop all the way down. Tell that to your ex-wife’s lawyer.

Psychologists map the emotional borders between social anxiety and narcissism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:00:20 UTC
20:00:20 KST

Social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism share deep roots in feelings of inadequacy, yet they relate to different dimensions of human shame. A study of 400 adults revealed that social anxiety is uniquely tied to internal feelings of defectiveness, while vulnerable narcissism involves a wider array of emotional vulnerabilities, including a fear of outside judgment and a heightened expectation of rejection. The research was published in Personality and Individual Differences.
Social anxiety involves distress in situations that carry a potential for public scrutiny and negative evaluation. Some psychologists view this anxiety as an evolutionary mechanism designed to keep people affiliated with a group. By heightening a person’s sensitivity to status loss, social anxiety prompts self-protective behaviors in threatening interpersonal situations. When these feelings become severe, they can manifest as an impairing clinical disorder, but social anxiety also exists on a spectrum of everyday interpersonal concerns.
Elevated social anxiety often overlaps with certain personality traits, particularly those related to narcissistic vulnerability. Narcissism is generally understood as existing on a continuum, ranging from normal self-regard to pathological configurations. Psychologists divide clinical narcissism into two broad expressions: grandiosity and vulnerability. Grandiose narcissism features overt entitlement and arrogance, whereas vulnerable narcissism involves hypersensitivity to evaluation, fragile self-worth, and defensive behaviors designed to protect the ego.
Both social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism feature a heightened sensitivity to interpersonal threats. One primary mechanism connecting these traits is rejection sensitivity. This concept describes a disposition to anxiously expect, readily perceive, and intensely react to social rejection. This sensitivity is thought to develop from early experiences of criticism or exclusion, which bias individuals to interpret ambiguous social cues as signs of impending rejection.
This pattern aligns with a psychological framework known as the Interpersonal Acceptance-Rejection Theory. The theory posits that perceived acceptance or rejection in close relationships, particularly early in life, is linked to later psychological adjustment. Rejection experiences involving caregivers or peers have been linked to a greater tendency to perceive rejection and heightened anxiety in response to potential rejection. When this rejection-related distress is directed inward, it can trigger intense feelings of shame.
Shame acts as a powerful social emotion tied to feelings of inferiority. Psychologists categorize shame into two distinct types: internal and external. Internal shame involves viewing oneself as fundamentally flawed or inadequate, leading to harsh self-criticism. External shame centers on the perception that other people view one negatively, which often prompts defensive strategies like avoiding social contact or constantly trying to repair one’s public image.
Psychologist Giulia Rosa Policardo at eCampus University in Novedrate, Italy, alongside colleagues from Sapienza University of Rome and the Institute of Behavioural and Cognitive Psychology and Psychotherapy, designed a study to map these overlapping traits. Previous research had documented associations between rejection sensitivity, shame, and these two psychological profiles. It remained unknown how internal and external shame might differ in their unique associations with social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism when evaluated together.
To investigate these emotional profiles, the research team recruited 400 adult volunteers from the general population. The participants were predominantly Italian women, with an average age of 33 years. Because the researchers conceptualized both social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism as traits that vary across the general public, they opted to study a community sample rather than a specific clinical population.
The participants completed a series of online questionnaires designed to measure their psychological traits. To assess vulnerable narcissism, respondents rated their agreement with statements about feeling poorly about themselves when ignored by others. To measure social anxiety, participants rated their fear and avoidance of various social situations, such as making a phone call in public.
The researchers also assessed interpersonal rejection sensitivity by asking participants to imagine hypothetical scenarios, such as asking a family member for a financial loan. Respondents then rated their anxiety regarding the outcome and the likelihood of being rejected. Finally, the survey measured internal shame by asking respondents how often they felt something was fundamentally wrong with them, while external shame was measured by asking how frequently participants believed other people despised them.
In their initial analysis, the researchers looked at simple correlations between all the variables. They observed that interpersonal rejection sensitivity, internal shame, and external shame were all positively associated with both social anxiety symptoms and vulnerable narcissistic traits. At a surface level, individuals who scored high in either psychological profile tended to experience a broad range of shame and a persistent fear of rejection.
The researchers then ran multiple regression models, a statistical technique that isolates the unique contribution of each variable while holding the others constant. In the model predicting vulnerable narcissistic traits, they accounted for the participants’ age, sex, rejection sensitivity, and both types of shame. They found that vulnerable narcissism was associated with being younger, expecting more rejection, and experiencing high levels of both internal and external shame.
A distinctly different pattern emerged in the regression model predicting social anxiety symptoms. When all the variables were analyzed simultaneously, internal shame emerged as the sole independent predictor of social anxiety. Age, sex, interpersonal rejection sensitivity, and external shame were not statistically significant in this model.
These results suggest that while social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism share overlapping features, their emotional cores differ. Social anxiety appears specifically tied to an internalized view of the self as inadequate or defective. Even though socially anxious individuals fear public scrutiny, their distress is most strongly anchored to their own self-directed criticism rather than just the belief that others are judging them.
In contrast, vulnerable narcissism involves a much wider interpersonal and affective profile. The persistence of rejection sensitivity and both forms of shame in the model suggests that vulnerable narcissism involves a broad pattern of interpersonal vulnerability, which may be expressed through defensive strategies that protect a fragile self-image. People with these traits struggle with fragile self-worth internally, but they also remain highly preoccupied with how they are perceived externally and are constantly on guard for potential rejection.
The study relied on a cross-sectional design, meaning the data was collected at a single point in time. Because of this, the results establish associations but cannot confirm a sequence of events. It remains unknown whether heightened shame and rejection sensitivity cause the development of social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism over time, or if the relationship works in reverse.
The composition of the sample also limits how broadly the results can be applied. Women made up more than 80 percent of the participants in this particular cohort. The observed emotional patterns might be particularly characteristic of female respondents, and caution is required when extending these findings to men or populations with a different gender balance.
The researchers exclusively used self-report measures, which can sometimes inflate associations between variables. Participants might lack insight into their own psychological traits or misrepresent their feelings due to a desire to appear socially acceptable. This type of bias is particularly common when assessing narcissistic traits, as individuals may hesitate to admit feelings of entitlement or hostility.
The survey did not collect information regarding participants’ psychiatric history or previous psychological trauma. Shame and self-conscious emotions have been linked to trauma-related symptoms and broader psychological vulnerability. Some of the observed associations might reflect unmeasured trauma or previous mental health difficulties within the sample.
Future studies could benefit from longitudinal and experience-sampling designs that track how these processes unfold over time. Recruiting more gender-balanced samples and directly examining potential sex and gender differences would help clarify these psychological profiles. Additionally, accounting for participants’ trauma histories, psychiatric history, and previous psychological treatment could provide a more complete picture of how interpersonal vulnerabilities develop.
The study, “Internal and external shame and rejection sensitivity as correlates of vulnerable narcissism and social anxiety,” was authored by Giulia Rosa Policardo, Cristian Di Gesto, Nicola Marsigli, Francesco Lauretta, Duccio Baroni, and Gioele Salvatori.

Xinhua Headlines: Long March legacy inspires innovation breakthroughs in city of historic turning point
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
19:12:01 CST
20:12:01 KST

*The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March. The spirit of what American journalist Edgar Snow described as "an odyssey unequaled in modern times" continues to inspire China as it pursues its Second Centenary Goal.
*The Long March in Guizhou was about breaking through encirclement and relying on one's own strength. Today, we are far removed from the smoke of war, but in science and technology, we are also making breakthroughs.
*China's 15th Five-Year Plan, released in the first half of this year, sets out comprehensive arrangements for accelerating high-level self-reliance and strength in science and technology and fostering new quality productive forces.
ZUNYI, Guizhou, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Lei Guangren has crossed the weathered stone arch bridge countless times in Zunyi, a city in southwest China's Guizhou Province. Known as Yinghong Bridge, or "Welcoming the Red Army Bridge," it bears quiet witness to the Chinese Red Army's epic Long March more than nine decades ago.
Such Long March-associated place names pepper every corner of the mountainous city, earning Zunyi its resonant title: the "city of historic turning point."
"The Zunyi Meeting, held here during the Long March, marked a life-or-death turning point in the history of the Communist Party of China (CPC)," said Lei, 78, former curator of the Zunyi Meeting memorial museum. "From then on, the Party found the right direction and leadership, stayed the course toward its goals, defeated the enemies and embarked on a path of independence and self-reliance."
The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March. Lei believes the spirit of what American journalist Edgar Snow described as "an odyssey unequaled in modern times" continues to inspire China as it pursues its Second Centenary Goal.
In October 1934, the CPC was forced to retreat from the Central Soviet Area in east China's Jiangxi Province and move northwest after enduring a series of encirclement campaigns by rival forces of the Kuomintang party (KMT). The CPC-led Red Army fought its way across the Xiangjiang River in Guangxi and broke through the KMT troops' blockade, but suffered tens of thousands of casualties in the battle.
In downtown Zunyi stands a two-story gray-and-white building where Lei had worked for a decade. In January 1935, at a critical historical crossroads, the Zunyi Meeting was held in this building, establishing Mao Zedong's leading position in the CPC Central Committee and the Red Army in practice. The spirit of the Zunyi Meeting -- characterized by firm conviction, commitment to truth, independence and self-reliance, and unity -- continues to resonate today.
In his book "The Long March: The Untold Story," American journalist and author Harrison Salisbury wrote that China's course "had been set for at least half a century to come."
The Red Army subsequently won its first major victory since the start of the Long March at Loushan Pass in northern Zunyi and later broke out of enemy encirclement through its four crossings of the Chishui River.
"My mother told me that she was working when Red Army soldiers passed by our home. They borrowed a douqiang to shelter from the rain," Lei recalled.
A douqiang is a bamboo-woven tool traditionally used in southern China for drying grain. By the time the rain stopped, the soldiers had already reached the neighboring village. Before leaving, however, they asked local residents to make sure the tool was returned to Lei's mother.
Salisbury's book also mentions Kong Xianquan, a Red Army soldier who led troops in an assault during the Battle of Loushan Pass. Hit by six bullets in the hip, Kong was left behind in Guizhou to recover from his wounds. After the founding of the People's Republic of China, he helped establish the Zunyi Meeting memorial museum and became its first curator.
Today, his granddaughter Kong Xia has spent more than three decades sharing stories of China's revolutionary history.
"In Zunyi, stories of the Red Army are passed down like family heirlooms, reminding each new generation not to forget where we came from or where we are going," she said.
For 56-year-old Kong, Zunyi is a city where tradition and modernity coexist. Xiaolongshan, where some Red Army martyrs were buried, was renamed Hongjunshan, or Red Army Mountain. Year after year, visitors come to pay tribute here beside a bronze statue of a Red Army soldier draped in red silk by local residents.
Beyond these landmarks, a 10-minute walk from the site of the Zunyi Meeting stands the theater for "The Great Turning Point," a large-scale immersive production about the Long March, where history is retold through live performance.
Chen Jinghong, a visitor from southwest China's Chongqing Municipality, brought her 10-year-old daughter to see the show. "It is like planting a seed in a child's heart, allowing her to experience the culture of the Long March and gradually understand and appreciate it as she grows up," Chen said.
But Zunyi is far more than a museum of revolution. It has undergone dramatic transformation. When the Red Army passed through, its population stood at just over 30,000. By 2025, the permanent population of its central urban area exceeded 1.6 million, with an urbanization rate of 61 percent.
And it is not just Zunyi that has developed. Guizhou, a mountainous province with no natural plains, has emerged as a "museum of bridges." Nearly half of the world's tallest bridges stand here.
"The Long March in Guizhou was about breaking through encirclement and relying on one's own strength," Kong said. "Today, we are far removed from the smoke of war, but in science and technology, we are also making breakthroughs."
One striking example is the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge in Guizhou. Holding world records both as the highest and the longest-span steel truss girder suspension bridge located in mountainous terrain, it has been dubbed by Chinese internet users a bridge that is "world No. 1, both horizontally and vertically."
Its main cables and upper structural components were produced by Guizhou Wire Rope Co., Ltd. The core steel wires were both developed and manufactured in Guizhou, forming a critical lifeline for the project.
"Wire-rope production used to be dominated in many areas by European and American companies. After the efforts of several generations, our products are now widely used in major equipment across land, sea and air, helping overcome technological bottlenecks," said Yang Zhengyan, director of a product research and development office at Guizhou Wire Rope.
At Laoyashan, where fierce fighting involving the Red Army once took place, bullet marks can still be seen on the rocks. At the foot of the mountain lies the old factory compound of Guizhou Wire Rope.
It was there that Yang and his team conducted countless tests to develop a mooring cable for offshore engineering.
Such cables had previously been expensive and required long procurement cycles, posing constraints on the development of China's offshore oil and gas resources.
"There is no room for failure with a product like this, so for many tests that would normally have been conducted only once, we ran them over and over again. We also pioneered some testing methods," Yang said.
In August 2023, the first permanent mooring cable for a floating production, storage and offloading unit, or FPSO, developed by Guizhou Wire Rope, was successfully deployed in the mooring system of the "Nanhai Fenjin" FPSO. It marked China's first application of a domestically produced permanent mooring cable for an FPSO, ending the country's long-standing reliance on foreign products in this field.
The group is now capable of mass-producing the cable. It can be used not only for deep-sea oil production platforms, but also for offshore wind power platforms. The system can reduce the sea area occupied by conventional mooring systems to about one-tenth, while also reducing their environmental footprint.
"The spirit of the Long March tells me to find the right direction, not to act blindly, and not to fear hardship or failure," said Yang, a 46-year-old Guizhou native.
For another Zunyi native, 52-year-old Lin Guojun, chairman of Shenzhen Busbar Sci-Tech Development Co., Ltd., the city has also played an important role in his company's growth.
Busbar holds more than 580 patents and international certifications, with its products used in new energy vehicles, wind power, solar power, smart grids and other new energy industries.
"We began developing our new energy business in 2008. It was an attempt to overtake on a curve," Lin recalled. "Back then, we had neither a market nor the technology, and the world did not believe China could develop a new energy industry."
In 2012, when the company encountered difficulties and struggled to fulfill orders, Lin turned his attention to Zunyi.
"Some of our equipment would shut down when temperatures became too high. Zunyi has a favorable natural environment, supporting industries, access to many major surrounding cities, and supportive policies," said Liu Yong, production and operations manager of Zunyi Busbar Sci-Tech Development Co., Ltd.
A new factory was completed in just seven months. Inside the plant, many production processes are semi-automated, with more than 40 robots and robotic arms operating in an orderly fashion to ensure greater consistency in product quality.
The Zunyi facility now focuses on developing and manufacturing high-voltage system components for new energy vehicles, including charging connectors, charging piles, high-voltage relays and high-voltage wiring harnesses. Its products are supplied directly to domestic and overseas automakers.
Lin, who grew up listening to stories about the Red Army, said he sees parallels between the Long March and his own industry.
"From a time when China's new energy sector was little known globally to today, when Chinese new energy vehicles have won worldwide recognition, our work in this industry has itself been a breakthrough," he said. "It takes perseverance and conviction to see something like this through."
China's 15th Five-Year Plan, released in the first half of this year, sets out comprehensive arrangements for accelerating high-level self-reliance and strength in science and technology and fostering new quality productive forces. Among its seven major economic and social development goals for 2026-2030 is substantially boosting the country's capacity for independent innovation.
Zunyi's government work report this year also called for developing new quality productive forces in light of local conditions and accelerating the building of a modern industrial system.
The national vision also plays out in ordinary people's lives. Kong is thinking of replacing her family's gasoline car with a new energy vehicle. A frequent traveler across China, she recently took a high-speed train to Yan'an. The trip, which once took the Red Army nine months, now takes less than nine hours.
Her 27-year-old son Jiang Xiao carries the legacy forward as part of a youth lecture group, sharing stories of the Long March.
"Every generation has different experiences and its own interpretation of the Long March spirit," Kong said. "Yet the spirit never fades with time, and these stories deserve to be passed on." ■

High-frequency data points to China's improving economic momentum in Q3
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
19:11:28 CST
20:11:28 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- China's economy continued to improve in the third quarter of this year, with new growth drivers gaining momentum, official high-frequency data on consumption, trade and investment showed Sunday.
Consumer activity continued to recover, with offline consumption payments up 2.6 percent year on year in the third quarter, accelerating by 0.7 percentage points from the second quarter, according to data released by the State Information Center under the National Development and Reform Commission.
In September, offline consumption payments increased 3.1 percent from a year earlier, up 0.5 percentage points from August, marking three consecutive months of growth.
The data also showed that the weight carried by cargo ships departing from and arriving at major Chinese ports rose 43.1 percent and 0.3 percent year on year, respectively, in the third quarter.
On investment, the issuance of new special-purpose bonds rose 50.2 percent year on year in September, 43.6 percentage points faster than the August level, the data showed.
The value of contracts awarded for projects related to new infrastructure, including computing power, data and networks, increased 34.2 percent year on year in the third quarter and 50.4 percent year on year last month.
Capital investment in frontier sectors such as artificial intelligence and humanoid robots surged 184.1 percent year on year in the third quarter and 198.7 percent year on year in September, the data showed.
"Investment in frontier fields such as artificial intelligence has remained strong, supporting current growth while building momentum for the development of new quality productive forces," said Wei Ying, deputy director of the center's big data development department.
China has targeted 2026 growth at 4.5 to 5 percent and will strive for even better results in practice. In the first half of the year, the country's gross domestic product grew 4.7 percent year on year.
In another sign of a firming economy, China's manufacturing activity returned to expansionary territory in September, while non-manufacturing activity rebounded markedly. The purchasing managers' index for China's manufacturing sector stood at 50.1 last month, while the business activity index for the non-manufacturing sector reached 50.2. ■

====================================================================================================

Pope Leo XIV to have surgery in 'coming days' to remove nodule in lung
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:02:20 UTC
20:02:20 KST

"It was detected at a very early stage and is well localised," the pontiff said during an address in St. Peter's Square.
Pope Leo XIV announced on Sunday that he was scheduled to have surgery in the "coming days" to remove a nodule in his lung.
Speaking during his weekly address in St. Peter's Square, the 71-year-old pontiff said the nodule had been discovered during "recent checkups" and that doctors believed it would be best to intervene.
"It was detected at a very early stage and is well localised," he said.
"I have decided to undergo surgery to have it removed," he continued, adding that the procedure was "already scheduled for the coming days."
The operation will reportedly take place at Rome's Gemelli University Hospital.
The Vatican press office told reporters that the procedure is set to take place early in the week and that the expected recovery time is roughly one week.
Chicago-born Leo became pope in 2025 following the death of his predecessor, Francis.
According to the American Lung Association, a lung nodule is a "small mass of dense tissue on the lung" that can be spotted on chest X-rays or CT scans.
It says that while most lung nodules are benign, some can be cancerous.
"If the nodule looks cancerous (malignant) or your health history suggests a higher risk for cancer, physicians will order tests to learn more about your nodule(s)," the association says on its website. "These tests often include a combination of imaging scans, nodule and lymph node biopsies, and sometimes blood tests."
